NAMES.name: absorbed_power_of_beam_tracing_beam
NAMES.short: Net coherent-wave power absorbed by the plasma from one beam-tracing beam over its computed trajectory. It is the final path-integrated, species-summed deposited power, equal to the beam power entering the path minus the residual wave power at the end.
NAMES.long:
Absorbed power of a beam-tracing beam is the net coherent-wave power transferred from one traced beam to the plasma over its computed propagation path. It is the final path-integrated total for that single beam, summed over all absorbing species, and is distinct from scenario-level [absorbed power](name:absorbed_power) obtained by summing over beams or launchers.

For a ray arc length $s$ increasing along the direction of wave propagation, the endpoint absorbed power is

$$
P_{\mathrm{abs}} = P_0 - P_{\mathrm{end}} = P_0\left[1 - \exp\left(-2\int_{s_0}^{s_{\mathrm{end}}} \kappa_i^{\mathrm{tot}}(s)\,ds\right)\right]
$$

where $P_0$ is the [launched power] or entering beam power in W, $P_{\mathrm{end}}$ is the residual [power of the beam-tracing beam](name:power_of_beam_tracing_beam) at the end of the path in W, $s_0$ and $s_{\mathrm{end}}$ are the start and end arc-length positions in m, and $\kappa_i^{\mathrm{tot}}$ is the species-summed spatial amplitude-damping coefficient along the ray in m^-1. The factor of 2 appears because wave power is proportional to squared wave-field amplitude; positive damping therefore makes the remaining beam power decrease along increasing $s$.

In practice this quantity is computed by integrating local absorption along the beam-tracing trajectory using the plasma dielectric response and the wave dispersion relation. Species-resolved channels such as [electron absorbed power](name:electron_absorbed_power_of_beam_tracing_beam), [ion absorbed power], and [ion-state absorbed power](name:ion_state_absorbed_power_of_beam_tracing_beam) may be evaluated separately and summed to recover the total for the beam.

Typical values are bounded by 0 W and the power assigned to the traced beam. They can be near 0 W for weak damping or missed resonance, and can approach the assigned launched or entering power for strongly absorbed paths; in weighted beam-tracing calculations this can span roughly 10^0-10^6 W per traced beam depending on launcher power and beam subdivision.

NAMES.name: beam_major_radius_of_beam_tracing_beam
NAMES.short: Major radius R, in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, at which the central ray of a beam-tracing beam is tangent to a toroidal circle. It is a geometric launch parameter, not a statement about absorption, deposition, or current drive.
NAMES.long:
Beam major radius is the value of major radius $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame at which the central ray of a beam-tracing beam is tangent to a toroidal circle. Here $R$ is distance from the toroidal symmetry axis, $Z$ is vertical height, and a toroidal circle is a curve of constant $R$ and $Z$ with tangent direction $\hat{\phi}$.

The geometrical tangency condition for a true spatial tangency can be written for a central ray parameterized by arclength $s$ as:

$$
R_\mathrm{tan}=R(s_\mathrm{tan}), \qquad \left.\frac{dR}{ds}\right|_{s_\mathrm{tan}}=0, \qquad \left.\frac{dZ}{ds}\right|_{s_\mathrm{tan}}=0
$$

where $R_\mathrm{tan}$ is the beam major radius and $s_\mathrm{tan}$ is the arclength at the tangency point. At this point the remaining tangent component is toroidal, so the ray direction is parallel or antiparallel to $\hat{\phi}$; if only the horizontal projected tangency of an inclined ray is specified, $R_\mathrm{tan}$ is the major radius of that projection in the $(R, \phi)$ plane of the same right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

The value is computed from the specified launch geometry or from the central ray trajectory by locating the tangency point. For a straight central ray this is equivalent to finding the closest approach of its horizontal projection to the toroidal symmetry axis; for a curved ray it is found along the traced trajectory. It complements the radial and toroidal wave-vector components of a beam-tracing beam, which describe the local propagation direction rather than this tangency radius.

Typical values are comparable to device and plasma major radii: about 0.2-1.5 m in compact devices, 1-4 m in medium-size tokamaks, and 4-8 m in large tokamaks or large external launch geometries. More radial launch geometry gives a smaller tangency radius, while more tangential launch geometry gives a value closer to the launch or plasma major radius.

NAMES.name: beam_major_radius_of_neutral_beam_injector
NAMES.short: Tangency radius of the nominal central beamline of a neutral beam injector. It is the major radius of the toroidal circle coaxial with the machine symmetry axis that is tangent to the beamline in horizontal projection.
NAMES.long:
The beam major radius of a neutral beam injector is the tangency radius $R_\mathrm{tan}$ of the nominal central neutral beamline. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, it is the radius of the toroidal circle centered on the machine symmetry axis that is tangent to the horizontal projection of that beamline. This quantity is an unsigned geometric distance, so it does not by itself encode whether the injector is co-directed or counter-directed relative to increasing $\phi$.

Equivalently, in the right-handed Cartesian basis $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ with $\hat{z}=\hat{Z}$ vertical and the $z$ axis coincident with the machine symmetry axis, let $(x_0,y_0)$ be any point on the horizontal projection of the central beamline and let $\mathbf{u}_\perp=(u_x,u_y)$ be its projected direction. The tangency radius is the perpendicular distance from the symmetry axis to that projected line:

$$
R_\mathrm{tan} = \frac{|x_0 u_y - y_0 u_x|}{\sqrt{u_x^2+u_y^2}}
$$

where $x_0$ and $y_0$ are measured in meters, and $u_x$ and $u_y$ are dimensionless direction cosines; the same expression also applies to arbitrary scaled direction components because the scale cancels. If a signed tangency parameter is formed for orbit or momentum calculations, the sign of $x_0u_y-y_0u_x$ is positive for motion in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise when viewed from $+\hat{Z}$) and negative for the opposite direction.

The nominal value is determined from the injector mechanical survey, port geometry, and alignment of the central beam axis. Perturbed or time-dependent steering geometry is described separately by [perturbed beam major radius of neutral beam injector](name:perturbed_beam_major_radius_of_neutral_beam_injector), while beam-tracing models may use the corresponding [beam major radius of beam tracing beam](name:beam_major_radius_of_beam_tracing_beam). The associated vertical placement of the injection geometry is characterized by the [vertical coordinate of neutral beam injector](name:vertical_coordinate_of_neutral_beam_injector).

Typical tokamak values range from about 0-8 m. Nearly radial injectors can have $R_\mathrm{tan}$ close to 0 m, compact and medium-size devices often use 0.2-3 m, and large or strongly tangential injectors can use 3-8 m, with $R_\mathrm{tan}$ commonly comparable to the plasma major radius for the most tangential geometries.

NAMES.name: current_due_to_neutral_beam_injection
NAMES.short: Non-inductive toroidal plasma current produced by neutral beam injection through directed momentum transfer from fast beam ions to the background plasma during Coulomb-collision thermalization.
NAMES.long:
Current due to neutral beam injection is the neutral-beam contribution to the total non-inductive plasma current, current_due_to_non_inductive_current_drive. Injected neutrals are ionized in the plasma, become energetic fast ions, and transfer directed momentum to electrons and ions as they slow down, producing a net driven current.

At a global level, the driven current can be represented as the integral of a local NBI current-drive source density over the confined plasma volume:

$$
I_{\mathrm{NBI}} = \int_{V_p} S_{I,\mathrm{NBI}}(\mathbf{x})\, dV
$$

where $I_{\mathrm{NBI}}$ is the total NBI-driven current, $S_{I,\mathrm{NBI}}$ is the local driven-current source density in $\mathrm{A\,m^{-3}}$, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $V_p$ is the plasma volume, and $dV$ is a volume element in $\mathrm{m^3}$.

In practice this quantity is computed from neutral-beam deposition, ionization, fast-ion orbit and slowing-down physics, pitch-angle scattering, collisional momentum exchange, and the plasma equilibrium. It depends strongly on the injected and absorbed neutral-beam power, power_due_to_neutral_beam_injection and absorbed_power_of_neutral_beam_injector, as well as beam energy, tangency geometry, fast-ion confinement, electron temperature, density, and trapped-particle fraction.

Typical values range from $1\times10^4$-$1\times10^6$ A in present-day tokamaks, with lower values for weak or poorly aligned beams and values near or above $1\times10^6$ A in large, high-power, high-temperature plasmas.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the toroidal projection of the driven parallel plasma current flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame with basis $(\hat{R},\hat{\phi},\hat{Z})$, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height.

NAMES.name: electron_power_at_inside_flux_surface
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Cumulative net power transferred to electrons within the plasma volume enclosed by a specified magnetic flux surface. It sums power delivered to fast suprathermal electrons and to the bulk thermal electron population.
NAMES.long:
Electron power at inside flux surface is the cumulative net rate of energy transfer to all electron populations within the plasma volume enclosed by a specified magnetic flux surface. It is an enclosed-volume quantity: each surface includes all electron power deposition inside it, and the sum of fast and thermal electron components gives the total electron-channel contribution.

The quantity is defined by integrating the flux-surface-averaged net electron power deposition density over enclosed volume, using the flux coordinate $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$, the dimensionless normalized toroidal flux radius:

$$
P_e(\rho_s) = \int_0^{\rho_s} \left\langle q_e \right\rangle_{\rho} \frac{dV}{d\rho} \, d\rho
$$

where $P_e$ is the enclosed electron power in W, $\rho_s$ labels the bounding flux surface, $\left\langle q_e \right\rangle_{\rho}$ is the flux-surface-averaged net electron power deposition density in W m$^{-3}$, and $dV/d\rho$ is the differential enclosed volume in m$^3$ per unit $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$. The derivative $dP_e/d\rho = \left\langle q_e \right\rangle_{\rho} dV/d\rho$ is a power per unit normalized flux radius, not a volumetric density by itself.

In practice, local electron energy-transfer rates are mapped to magnetic flux surfaces from wave absorption, fast-particle slowing down, collisional exchange, or power-balance calculations, then flux-surface averaged and integrated outward from the magnetic axis. The decomposition corresponds to [fast_electron_power_at_inside_flux_surface](name:fast_electron_power_at_inside_flux_surface) for suprathermal electrons plus [thermal_electron_power_at_inside_flux_surface](name:thermal_electron_power_at_inside_flux_surface) for the bulk thermal electron population; at the outer closed surface it can be compared with [total_electron_power](name:total_electron_power) when the same source set and plasma volume are used.

Typical enclosed electron powers are 10^4-10^6 W in small or low-power experiments, 10^5-10^7 W for individual electron-heating systems in medium-size tokamaks, and 10^7-10^8 W in high-power or reactor-scale scenarios. For purely deposited auxiliary power, the value generally rises from about 0 W near the magnetic axis to the electron-channel total at the outer closed surface; decreases with increasing $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$ or negative values indicate net electron cooling or transfer of energy from electrons to another channel.
NAMES.sign: Positive when net power is transferred to the electron population.

NAMES.name: fast_electron_power_at_inside_flux_surface
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Cumulative wave power absorbed by non-thermal fast electrons inside a specified magnetic flux surface, equal to the enclosed-volume integral of the local fast-electron power-deposition density.
NAMES.long:
Fast-electron power inside a flux surface is the cumulative rate at which coherent-wave energy is absorbed by non-thermal electrons in the plasma volume enclosed by a closed magnetic surface. It represents the fast-electron part of the auxiliary wave-power deposition, distinct from deposition on thermal electrons or ions. The surface label should be an explicitly named flux coordinate, for example $(\psi,\theta,\phi)$ or $(\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}},\theta,\phi)$, where $\theta$ is a poloidal angle and $\phi$ is the toroidal angle of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame with $R$ major radius and $Z$ vertical height.

For a selected flux surface labeled by $\chi_s$, the enclosed fast-electron power is the volume integral

$$
P_{\mathrm{fast}\,e}^{\mathrm{inside}}(\chi_s)=\int_{\Omega_s} p_{\mathrm{fast}\,e}(\mathbf{x})\,dV
$$

where $\chi$ is the chosen flux-surface label, $\Omega_s$ is the plasma volume enclosed between the magnetic axis and the surface $\chi=\chi_s$, $p_{\mathrm{fast}\,e}$ is the local [fast_electron_power_density](name:fast_electron_power_density) in W m$^{-3}$, $dV$ is a volume element in m$^3$, and the result is in W.

In practice this quantity is obtained by integrating a local fast-electron wave-power deposition density over reconstructed magnetic-flux-surface volumes. Together with [thermal_electron_power_at_inside_flux_surface](name:thermal_electron_power_at_inside_flux_surface), it describes how absorbed wave power is partitioned within the electron population; at the outermost closed flux surface it corresponds to the global [fast_electron_power](name:fast_electron_power) for the same absorption definition. The analogous non-thermal ion quantity is [fast_ion_state_power_at_inside_flux_surface](name:fast_ion_state_power_at_inside_flux_surface), and all such channels contribute to the overall auxiliary-heating power balance represented by quantities such as [total_electron_power](name:total_electron_power).

Representative magnitudes range from near 0 W on surfaces enclosing little or no fast-electron absorption to the order of the coupled auxiliary-wave power. Depending on device size and heating scenario, enclosed fast-electron powers can span roughly 10^3-10^7 W, with megawatt-scale values possible when wave absorption is dominated by non-thermal electrons.

NAMES.name: fast_ion_power_at_inside_flux_surface
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Cumulative wave power absorbed by the fast (non-thermal) ion population within the plasma volume enclosed by a specified magnetic flux surface.
NAMES.long:
Fast-ion power at inside flux surface quantifies the running volume integral of RF wave power deposited into the suprathermal (non-thermal) ion population, profiling the radial distribution of enclosed fast-ion wave absorption. It forms the fast-ion component of [ion_power_at_inside_flux_surface](name:ion_power_at_inside_flux_surface), which includes both this quantity and the complementary thermal-ion contribution captured by [thermal_ion_power_at_inside_flux_surface](name:thermal_ion_power_at_inside_flux_surface).

The enclosed fast-ion power is defined as:

$$
P_\mathrm{fast}(\psi) = \int_{V(\psi)} Q_\mathrm{fast}(\mathbf{r})\, dV
$$

where $Q_\mathrm{fast}$ is the volumetric fast-ion wave power deposition density and $V(\psi)$ is the plasma volume enclosed within the flux surface at poloidal flux coordinate $\psi$.

This quantity arises primarily in scenarios such as ion cyclotron resonance heating, where waves resonantly accelerate minority ions to suprathermal energies and sustain a non-Maxwellian tail population. The profile of $P_\mathrm{fast}(\psi)$ accumulates with increasing enclosed volume, saturating at the total fast-ion absorbed power at the last closed flux surface. For the charge-state-resolved counterpart, see [fast_ion_state_power_at_inside_flux_surface](name:fast_ion_state_power_at_inside_flux_surface); the local deposition density from which this integral is constructed is given by [fast_ion_power_density](name:fast_ion_power_density).

NAMES.name: fast_ion_state_power_at_inside_flux_surface
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Cumulative wave power absorbed by fast (non-thermal) ions of a specified charge state within the plasma volume enclosed by a selected magnetic flux surface.
NAMES.long:
Fast ion state power at an inside flux surface quantifies the net wave energy per unit time deposited in the suprathermal (fast) population of a single specified ion charge state, accumulated over all plasma volume enclosed by a chosen flux surface. It is the fast-ion component of the total ion-state absorbed power [ion_state_power_at_inside_flux_surface](name:ion_state_power_at_inside_flux_surface); its thermal-ion counterpart is [thermal_ion_state_power_at_inside_flux_surface](name:thermal_ion_state_power_at_inside_flux_surface).

The cumulative power is the volume integral of the local fast-ion absorption density $p_{\text{fast},s}$ over the plasma volume enclosed by the flux surface labeled $\rho$:

$$
P_{\text{fast},s}(\rho) = \int_{V(\rho)} p_{\text{fast},s}(\mathbf{r}) \, dV
$$

where $V(\rho)$ is the volume enclosed by the flux surface and $p_{\text{fast},s}$ is the local fast-ion absorbed power density for charge state $s$, the volumetric counterpart [fast_ion_state_power_density](name:fast_ion_state_power_density).

This quantity is computed by RF wave-kinetic or full-wave codes that resolve the resonant energy exchange between the wave field and the non-Maxwellian fast-ion distribution on a per-charge-state basis, as occurs in ICRH minority heating and mode-conversion schemes. Aggregating over all charge states and ion species yields [fast_ion_power_at_inside_flux_surface](name:fast_ion_power_at_inside_flux_surface). The toroidal-mode-resolved complement [per_toroidal_mode_fast_ion_state_power](name:per_toroidal_mode_fast_ion_state_power) decomposes the same cumulative power by toroidal harmonic when the wave field is represented as a Fourier series in toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: forward_power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna
NAMES.short: Incident RF power carried by the wave propagating toward a lower hybrid antenna at its input reference plane. It is a per-antenna quantity, not a sum over multiple antennas.
NAMES.long:
Forward power of a lower hybrid antenna is the nonnegative RF power carried by the incident traveling wave at the antenna input reference plane. It represents power propagating from the generator and transmission-line side toward the antenna structure; "forward" specifies this propagation direction rather than a signed power convention. The quantity applies to one antenna, so totals over several antennas are separate quantities.

The launched RF power is the part of the forward power that remains after subtracting the oppositely propagating reflected power:

$$
P_\mathrm{launched} = P_\mathrm{forward} - P_\mathrm{reflected}
$$

where $P_\mathrm{forward}$ is the forward power, $P_\mathrm{reflected}$ is the reflected power, and $P_\mathrm{launched}$ is the launched power for the same antenna and the same reference plane. If a complex voltage-wave reflection coefficient $\Gamma$ is used, $\Gamma$ is dimensionless and $|\Gamma|^2$ gives the reflected-to-forward power ratio under the corresponding calibration convention.

In practice, forward power is inferred from calibrated RF measurements that separate waves traveling toward and away from the antenna, commonly using directional RF measurements or equivalent network measurements near the antenna input. Corrections may account for transmission-line attenuation, calibration factors, and the chosen reference plane. Forward power can exceed launched power when antenna-plasma mismatch or loading changes produce reflected power.

Typical per-antenna values in lower-hybrid heating or current-drive operation are about $10^5$-$5 \times 10^6$ W, while commissioning, conditioning, or low-power phases can use $10^3$-$10^5$ W.

NAMES.name: frequency_of_electron_cyclotron_heating_antenna
NAMES.short: Operating microwave frequency of an electron cyclotron heating antenna. It is a non-negative scalar that selects the cyclotron harmonic and constrains where resonance can occur in the magnetic field.
NAMES.long:
The frequency of an electron cyclotron heating antenna is the electromagnetic wave frequency produced by the antenna for electron cyclotron heating or current drive. It is a non-negative scalar; physically active heating uses $f>0$. The frequency helps select the electron cyclotron harmonic, while the actual absorption location and deposition width also depend on magnetic-field geometry, launch angle, wave polarization, density, temperature, and relativistic and Doppler effects.

In the simple cold, non-relativistic, Doppler-free resonance estimate, the antenna frequency matches an integer harmonic of the local electron cyclotron frequency:

$$
f \simeq n\,\frac{e B}{2\pi m_e}
$$

where $f$ is the antenna frequency in Hz, $n$ is the positive integer harmonic number, $e$ is the elementary charge in C, $B$ is the local magnetic flux density magnitude in T, and $m_e$ is the electron rest mass in kg. More complete resonance calculations include the parallel Doppler shift, relativistic mass correction, finite-temperature effects, and wave propagation constraints.

The frequency is normally set by the microwave source and transmission system and is verified by radio-frequency or millimeter-wave instrumentation. In scenario design it is compared with equilibrium magnetic-field values to identify accessible resonance surfaces, but it should not be interpreted by itself as fixing a unique radial power-deposition location.

Typical electron cyclotron heating frequencies are in the millimeter-wave range, about $3 \times 10^{10}$-$2 \times 10^{11}$ Hz for many magnetic-confinement applications, with the appropriate value set by the magnetic-field strength and chosen harmonic. Related antenna-frequency quantities include [ion cyclotron heating antenna frequency](name:frequency_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna) and [lower-hybrid antenna frequency](name:frequency_of_lower_hybrid_antenna).

NAMES.name: height_of_antenna_strap
NAMES.short: Full vertical height of the rectangular cross-section of an ICRH antenna strap conductor element, measured along the poloidal direction.
NAMES.long:
The height of an antenna strap is the full vertical (poloidal) extent of the rectangular cross-section of the current-carrying strap conductor in an ion cyclotron resonance heating (ICRH) antenna system. In ICRH antennas, the strap is the active radiating element that launches electromagnetic waves near the ion cyclotron frequency; its cross-sectional geometry governs current distribution, RF resistance, and coupling efficiency to the plasma.

For a rectangular strap cross-section, the three characteristic dimensions are height (this quantity), [width](name:width_of_antenna_strap) measured along the toroidal direction, and [thickness](name:thickness_of_antenna_strap) perpendicular to the strap plane. Height is measured along the vertical direction $Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle, and $Z$ is the vertical coordinate. For strap conductors with annular cross-sections, the analogous radial dimensions are the [outer radius](name:outer_radius_of_antenna_strap) and [inner radius](name:inner_radius_of_antenna_strap) of the conductor.

Typical ICRH strap heights range from a few centimeters to approximately 50 cm depending on antenna design and machine geometry.
NAMES.sign: Positive when measured in the direction of increasing $Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: inner_radius_of_antenna_strap
NAMES.short: Inner radius of the annular cross-section of an ICRH antenna strap, measured from the strap conductor axis to the inner cylindrical boundary of the conductor.
NAMES.long:
Inner radius of an antenna strap is the radial distance from the local strap conductor axis to the inner cylindrical surface of an annular strap cross-section. It applies to hollow or tubular ICRH strap conductors; straps with solid rectangular or otherwise non-annular cross-sections do not have this quantity. In a strap-local right-handed cylindrical $(r_s, \varphi_s, z_s)$ frame, $z_s$ follows the strap centerline or long current-carrying direction and $r_s$ is measured perpendicular to that axis.

The inner radius is the distance from the strap axis to the inner wall of the annulus:

$$
r_\mathrm{inner} = \left|\mathbf{x}_\perp - \mathbf{x}_\mathrm{axis}\right|
$$

where $\mathbf{x}_\perp$ is a point on the inner cylindrical boundary in a cross-section normal to the strap axis, $\mathbf{x}_\mathrm{axis}$ is the corresponding point on the strap centerline, and both positions are expressed in meters.

This quantity is obtained from antenna mechanical design, CAD geometry, or direct metrology of the conductor cross-section. Together with [outer_radius_of_antenna_strap](name:outer_radius_of_antenna_strap), it determines the annular conducting area, $A = \pi(r_\mathrm{outer}^2-r_\mathrm{inner}^2)$, and the wall thickness, $r_\mathrm{outer}-r_\mathrm{inner}$, which are important for cooling-channel design, RF current distribution, and impedance modeling at ion-cyclotron frequencies.

Typical ICRH tubular copper strap inner radii are about 0.005-0.03 m, depending on RF power, cooling requirements, and mechanical constraints. Larger high-power antenna conductors may use somewhat larger inner radii to reduce hydraulic resistance and thermal loading.

NAMES.name: ion_state_absorbed_power_of_beam_tracing_beam
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Wave power absorbed by ions of a specified species and charge state along a coherent-wave beam-tracing beam path. It is the charge-state-resolved contribution to the total ion power absorbed from that beam.
NAMES.long:
Ion-state absorbed power of a beam-tracing beam is the net power transferred from a coherent wave beam to ions of one specified species and ionization (charge) state along the traced beam path. It is the charge-state-resolved share of the ion power absorbed from that beam, and summing it over all charge states of a species recovers the species-level ion absorption.

The absorbed power is the integral of the local absorption rate per unit path length over the beam representation:

$$
P_{i,z} = \int_{\mathcal{C}} \frac{dP_{i,z}}{d\ell} \, d\ell
$$

where $\mathcal{C}$ is the traced beam path, $\ell$ is distance along that path in meters, and $dP_{i,z}/d\ell$ is the local net power transferred to ion species $i$ in charge state $z$ per unit path length, expressed in W/m. The integral runs along the beam path used to represent the propagating field, not over the full plasma volume; the corresponding volumetric deposition rates per unit plasma volume are tracked separately.

The quantity is evaluated by beam-tracing models, which extend geometrical optics to include finite beam-width effects by following a Gaussian wave packet through an inhomogeneous plasma. The local transfer follows from the wave field, plasma equilibrium, species composition, charge-state populations, and ion distribution functions, and may arise from any modeled wave-particle damping mechanism rather than only ion-cyclotron resonance. The species and charge state are fixed by the associated ion-state identifier.

Typical per-beam ion-state absorbed power spans a broad range, from near zero on weakly damped paths or for trace charge states up to of order the total coupled beam power for strongly resonant states; the value is bounded above by the available beam power in a passively absorbing plasma.
NAMES.sign: Positive when net wave energy is transferred from the beam to the specified ion charge state.

NAMES.name: launched_power_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher
NAMES.short: Net electron cyclotron radio-frequency power crossing from a single launcher into the vacuum vessel, defined as forward minus reflected power at the launcher aperture or reference plane. Evaluated after transmission-line and launcher losses and before any plasma absorption, reflection, or shine-through.
NAMES.long:
Launched power of an electron cyclotron launcher is the net radio-frequency wave power delivered by one electron cyclotron launcher across its launch aperture into the vacuum vessel. It is a boundary power for electron-cyclotron heating and current-drive calculations, defined as the forward power minus the power reflected back at the launcher aperture or reference plane, and before any plasma absorption, reflection from cutoff or resonance regions, wall interaction, or shine-through.

For a launcher represented by one or more launched wave beams, the launcher launched power is the sum of the launched powers of those beams:

$$
P_{\mathrm{EC,launched}}^{\mathrm{launcher}} = \sum_b P_{\mathrm{launched},b}
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{launched},b}$ is the launched power of beam $b$ in watts, taken after transmission losses and before plasma interaction. Equivalently, in terms of the directional power components at the reference plane, $P_{\mathrm{EC,launched}}^{\mathrm{launcher}} = P_{\mathrm{forward}} - P_{\mathrm{reflected}}$, with all terms in watts.

This power is typically derived from gyrotron or source output power corrected for transmission-line, window, switch, and launcher losses, or inferred from calibrated radio-frequency power monitors near the launcher. It is commonly used as the input power for ray-tracing or beam-tracing models; subsequent absorbed, reflected, or shine-through power is accounted for separately.

Typical values for a single electron cyclotron launcher are of order $1 \times 10^5$ to $2 \times 10^6$ W in present tokamak systems, with multi-beam or high-power launchers reaching several $10^6$ W.
NAMES.sign: Positive when electron cyclotron wave power flows from the launcher into the vacuum vessel.

NAMES.name: launched_power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna
NAMES.short: Net RF power entering the vacuum vessel from a single lower-hybrid antenna, equal to forward power minus reflected power at the antenna aperture.
NAMES.long:
The launched power of a lower-hybrid antenna is the net radio-frequency power injected into the vacuum vessel from one lower-hybrid antenna assembly per unit time. It quantifies the RF energy flux actually available to couple to plasma waves, distinguishing it from the gross input to the antenna system and from the fraction ultimately absorbed by the plasma.

The net launched power is defined as:

$$
P_\mathrm{launched} = P_\mathrm{forward} - P_\mathrm{reflected}
$$

where $P_\mathrm{forward}$ is the [forward power](name:forward_power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna) at the antenna aperture and $P_\mathrm{reflected}$ is the [reflected power](name:reflected_power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna) returning toward the transmission line. The coupling efficiency is $\eta = P_\mathrm{launched}/P_\mathrm{forward}$, which depends on the match between the antenna wave spectrum and the plasma density at the waveguide mouth.

This quantity is measured by directional couplers on the transmission line feeding each antenna and serves as the primary input to ray-tracing and full-wave calculations for lower hybrid current drive power deposition. Launched powers in current experiments range from tens of kilowatts to several megawatts per antenna.

The gross RF input to the antenna system before accounting for reflections is given by [power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna](name:power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna). The system-level aggregate over all launcher units is captured by [total_launched_power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna](name:total_launched_power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna), while the fraction deposited in the plasma is tracked by [total_absorbed_power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna](name:total_absorbed_power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna).

NAMES.name: length_of_antenna_strap
NAMES.short: Base length of the oblique trapezoidal cross-section used to represent an ICRH antenna strap conductor. It is a reference edge dimension of the conductor section, not the slant height of an inclined side.
NAMES.long:
Length of antenna strap is the reference base dimension of an oblique trapezoidal cross-section used to describe an ion-cyclotron-range-of-frequencies antenna strap conductor. It identifies the straight base edge of the section and should not be interpreted as the sloping side length, slant height, or inclined-face chord.

For an oblique strap section, this length is only one geometric parameter. The full non-rectangular outline also depends on the [width](name:width_of_antenna_strap), [thickness](name:thickness_of_antenna_strap), and inclination angles such as $\alpha$ in [alpha_angle_of_antenna_strap](name:alpha_angle_of_antenna_strap) and $\beta$ in angle_of_antenna_strap. No universal $1/\cos\alpha$ or similar conversion is implied unless the angle reference directions and the selected base edge are specified by the geometric construction.

In practice the value is taken from antenna engineering drawings, CAD geometry, or metrology of the strap conductor as the distance between the endpoints of the chosen base edge of the physical cross-section. It is used with the other strap dimensions and angles in electromagnetic, thermal, and structural models of ICRH antenna conductors.

Typical values are device- and design-dependent, but base lengths for conducting ICRH strap cross-sections commonly lie in the range 0.02-0.5 m, with larger values for high-power antenna straps and smaller values for compact test structures.

NAMES.name: outer_radius_of_antenna_strap
NAMES.short: Outer radial boundary of the annular cross-section of an ICRH antenna strap conductor, defining the larger of the two radii that bound the conductor annulus.
NAMES.long:
The outer radius of an ICRH antenna strap is the radial distance from the central axis of the strap conductor to the outer cylindrical surface of the annular cross-section. It marks the external boundary of the conductor material and, together with the [inner radius](name:inner_radius_of_antenna_strap), fully specifies the radial extent of the annular conductor.

For an annular cross-section, the radial conductor wall thickness follows $\Delta r = r_\mathrm{out} - r_\mathrm{in}$, where $r_\mathrm{out}$ is the outer radius and $r_\mathrm{in}$ is the inner radius. The nominal centerline radius reported by [radius_of_antenna_strap](name:radius_of_antenna_strap) is the mean $(r_\mathrm{out} + r_\mathrm{in})/2$.

This geometric parameter enters electromagnetic wave-coupling calculations and RF impedance modeling for ion cyclotron resonance heating systems. Together with the [width](name:width_of_antenna_strap), [height](name:height_of_antenna_strap), and [thickness](name:thickness_of_antenna_strap) of the conductor, it provides the complete geometric description needed for antenna strap simulations.
NAMES.sign: Positive when measured radially outward from the strap conductor axis.

NAMES.name: per_toroidal_mode_fast_ion_power
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Cumulative coherent-wave power absorbed by suprathermal ions inside a flux surface, resolved by toroidal mode number.
NAMES.long:
Per-toroidal-mode fast-ion power is the net rate of energy transfer from a coherent wave to the suprathermal ion population for one toroidal Fourier mode, accumulated over the volume enclosed by a chosen flux surface. Summing over toroidal mode numbers gives the total fast-ion wave power inside that surface, while charge-state-resolved and thermal-species analogs separate the same physical transfer by ion charge state or receiving population.

The cumulative mode-resolved power is defined by integrating the local net power-transfer density for that mode over the enclosed volume:

$$
P_{\mathrm{fast},n_\phi}(\psi) = \int_{V(\psi)} q_{\mathrm{fast},n_\phi}(\mathbf{x})\,dV
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{fast},n_\phi}$ is the cumulative power in W, $q_{\mathrm{fast},n_\phi}$ is the local net power-transfer density in W m$^{-3}$, $V(\psi)$ is the volume inside the flux surface labeled by $\psi$, and $dV$ is the volume element in m$^3$. The label $\psi$ may be a magnetic-flux coordinate in Wb or a normalized flux coordinate with unit 1, and $n_\phi$ is a dimensionless integer toroidal mode number defined with respect to the toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height.

In practice this quantity is computed by decomposing the coherent wave field into toroidal Fourier components and evaluating the wave-particle energy exchange with the modeled fast-ion distribution. The radial cumulative value is obtained by integrating the mode-resolved deposition density inside successive flux surfaces; direct experimental inference usually combines wave coupling information, equilibrium geometry, and fast-ion distribution modeling rather than a single diagnostic measurement. Closely related quantities include [per_toroidal_mode_fast_ion_state_power](name:per_toroidal_mode_fast_ion_state_power), [per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_power](name:per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_power), [per_toroidal_mode_thermal_electron_power](name:per_toroidal_mode_thermal_electron_power), and [per_toroidal_mode_fast_electron_power](name:per_toroidal_mode_fast_electron_power).

Representative values range from near 0 W for weakly coupled or nonresonant modes to a substantial fraction of the absorbed coherent-wave power for resonant modes. In megawatt-class radio-frequency heating, dominant individual toroidal modes are commonly of order 10^3-10^6 W, with the sum over modes bounded by the net wave power transferred to plasma particles.
NAMES.sign: Positive when net energy is transferred from the coherent wave field to the suprathermal ion population.

NAMES.name: perturbed_beam_major_radius_of_neutral_beam_injector
NAMES.short: Dynamic variation of the tangency major radius of a neutral beam injector during beam tilting, equal to the signed change in the major radius at which the beam centerline is tangent to a toroidal circle.
NAMES.long:
The perturbed beam major radius $\delta R_\mathrm{tan}$ is the time-varying deviation of the tangency radius from its nominal value during dynamic steering of a neutral beam injector beamlet group. The tangency radius is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame as the major radius $R$ at which the beam centerline is tangent to a toroidal circle centered on the machine symmetry axis; this quantity records its signed departure from the static injection geometry given by [beam_major_radius_of_neutral_beam_injector](name:beam_major_radius_of_neutral_beam_injector).

The instantaneous tangency radius during tilting is decomposed as:

$$
R_\mathrm{tan}(t) = R_\mathrm{tan}^0 + \delta R_\mathrm{tan}(t)
$$

where $R_\mathrm{tan}^0$ is the nominal (unperturbed) tangency radius and $\delta R_\mathrm{tan}(t)$ is this perturbed component.

Dynamic NBI tilting is employed in beam emission spectroscopy applications, where the beam is periodically steered to sweep the measurement volume radially across the plasma cross-section. The radial extent of this steering is quantified by the perturbed tangency radius, complementing perturbed_angle_of_neutral_beam_injector, which captures the simultaneous change in vertical inclination angle of the beam.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $\delta R_\mathrm{tan}$ shifts the beam's tangent point outward to a larger major radius $R$ relative to the nominal injection geometry.

NAMES.name: poloidal_angle_of_electron_cyclotron_beam
NAMES.short: Poloidal steering angle of an electron cyclotron beam in the R-Z plane of the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, defined by atan2(-k_Z, -k_R) from the mean wave-vector components. It describes the vertical tilt of the beam relative to inward radial propagation.
NAMES.long:
The poloidal angle of an electron cyclotron beam is the signed steering angle of the beam mean wave vector projected onto the poloidal $R$-$Z$ plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height. It describes the vertical tilt of the EC ray or beam relative to an inward radial direction and is used together with launch position and toroidal steering to specify the beam propagation direction.

Using $\operatorname{atan2}(y,x)$ for the quadrant-preserving angle from the positive $x$ axis toward the positive $y$ axis, the poloidal angle is defined by:

$$
\theta_\mathrm{pol} = \operatorname{atan2}(-k_Z, -k_R)
$$

where $k_R$ and $k_Z$ are the radial and vertical components of the beam mean wave vector in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, typically expressed in rad m$^{-1}$. With this definition, $\theta_\mathrm{pol}$ is measured from the inward radial direction $-\hat{R}$ toward the downward vertical direction $-\hat{Z}$.

In practice this angle is obtained from launcher mirror geometry, steering calibration, or ray and beam tracing that reconstructs the mean wave vector at launch or near resonance. It is interpreted together with quantities such as the [toroidal angle of the electron cyclotron beam](name:toroidal_angle_of_electron_cyclotron_beam), [vertical coordinate of the electron cyclotron launcher mirror](name:vertical_coordinate_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror), [toroidal angle of the launching position](name:toroidal_angle_of_launching_position), and [launched power of the electron cyclotron antenna]; the poloidal angle influences the resonance interception and power-deposition location, but those also depend on the magnetic equilibrium, wave frequency, polarization, and plasma profiles.

For near-radial injection the value is close to 0 rad; larger absolute values indicate stronger poloidal tilt. The principal-value output of $\operatorname{atan2}$ lies in the interval $-\pi$ to $\pi$ rad, while the operational steering interval is set by the launcher design and is usually narrower.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the beam direction in the poloidal plane is rotated from the inward radial direction $-\hat{R}$ toward the downward direction $-\hat{Z}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: power_due_to_electron_cyclotron_heating
NAMES.short: Net RF wave energy absorbed per unit time by plasma electrons via electron cyclotron resonance from a single ECRH launcher. It is the coupled heating power, distinct from the RF power launched toward or into the vessel.
NAMES.long:
Power due to electron cyclotron heating is the net rate at which RF wave energy from a single electron-cyclotron launcher is absorbed by plasma electrons through cyclotron-resonant interaction. It represents coupled electron heating power, not the launcher output power or the power merely entering the vacuum vessel.

For a launcher-resolved absorbed power density, the total absorbed power is

$$
P_\mathrm{EC} = \int_{V_\mathrm{p}} p_{\mathrm{EC},e}(\mathbf{x}) \, dV
$$

where $P_\mathrm{EC}$ is the absorbed electron-cyclotron heating power in W, $p_{\mathrm{EC},e}$ is the volumetric RF power density deposited in electrons in W m^-3, $\mathbf{x}$ denotes position, $dV$ is a volume element in m^3, and $V_\mathrm{p}$ is the plasma volume over which the launcher-specific deposition is evaluated.

In practice this quantity is inferred from calibrated launcher power, transmission-line losses, stray-radiation or unabsorbed-power estimates, ray or beam-tracing calculations, and power-balance constraints. It is therefore usually lower than or equal to the corresponding [launched_power_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher](name:launched_power_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher), with the difference accounting for propagation, coupling, reflection, shine-through, and other losses not deposited in the plasma electrons.

Typical absorbed powers for one launcher range from about 0.1-2 MW in many present-day experiments, while large multi-megawatt systems can deliver several MW per launcher depending on frequency, injection geometry, plasma density, magnetic field, and optical depth.
NAMES.sign: Positive when net RF wave energy is transferred from the electron-cyclotron wave field to plasma electrons.

NAMES.name: power_due_to_ion_cyclotron_heating
NAMES.short: Net ion cyclotron resonance heating power absorbed by the plasma from one ICRH launcher. It is the RF wave energy deposition rate in the plasma and is distinct from power launched by the antenna or lost in the RF system.
NAMES.long:
Power due to ion cyclotron heating is the net rate at which radio-frequency wave energy from one ion cyclotron resonance heating launcher is absorbed by the plasma. It includes energy deposited into the plasma bulk through ion-cyclotron, harmonic, electron, and mode-conversion channels, and excludes reflected power and losses in transmission lines, antenna structures, or surrounding material. As a scalar absorbed power, it is not affected by magnetic-field or plasma-current sign conventions.

The launcher-resolved absorbed power is the time rate of absorbed RF energy, equivalently the volume integral of the local RF absorption rate:

$$
P_{\mathrm{ICRH},a} = \frac{dE_{\mathrm{abs},a}}{dt} = \int_{V_p} p_{\mathrm{abs},a}(\mathbf{x}) \, dV
$$

where $a$ labels the launcher, $E_{\mathrm{abs},a}$ is the RF energy absorbed in the plasma from that launcher, $p_{\mathrm{abs},a}$ is the local absorbed power density, and $V_p$ is the plasma volume.

In practice this quantity is obtained from calibrated RF forward and reflected power measurements corrected for transmission and antenna losses, from wave-coupling and absorption calculations, or from plasma power-balance analysis. It differs from the launched antenna power because only the net energy absorbed by the plasma is counted. Summing this quantity over all ICRH launchers gives [total_power_due_to_ion_cyclotron_heating](name:total_power_due_to_ion_cyclotron_heating); spatially resolved absorption rates integrate to this launcher-resolved scalar value, and time-resolved values follow changes in RF drive, antenna loading, and plasma conditions.

Typical values are $10^5$-$10^7$ W per launcher in present-day tokamak discharges, with high-power systems reaching several $10^7$ W. Values near 0 W occur when the launcher is off, poorly coupled, or when most injected RF power is reflected or lost before absorption.

NAMES.name: power_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna
NAMES.short: Net RF power launched from a single ion cyclotron resonance heating (ICRH) antenna into the vacuum vessel, equal to forward power minus reflected power at the antenna reference plane.
NAMES.long:
The power of an ion cyclotron heating antenna is the net RF power delivered across the antenna aperture into the vacuum vessel, representing the difference between the forward (incident) and reflected traveling-wave powers at a defined reference plane on the transmission line. It quantifies how effectively the antenna couples RF energy from the generator circuit into the plasma-facing side of the antenna structure.

The net launched power is related to its directional components by:

$$
P_\mathrm{launched} = P_\mathrm{forward} - P_\mathrm{reflected}
$$

where $P_\mathrm{forward}$ is the [forward power](name:forward_power_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna) carried by the incident traveling wave and $P_\mathrm{reflected}$ is the [reflected power](name:reflected_power_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna) carried by the backward wave, both evaluated at the same reference plane on the feed line.

This quantity is measured using directional couplers installed on the coaxial or waveguide transmission lines feeding each ICRH antenna port. Coupling efficiency depends on plasma edge density, antenna-to-separatrix distance, and operating frequency relative to the local ion cyclotron resonance layer.

Individual ICRH antennas on medium-to-large tokamaks typically launch 1–5 MW; the system-level sum over all antennas is [total_power_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna](name:total_power_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna). The analogous per-injector quantity for neutral beam heating is [power_of_neutral_beam_injector](name:power_of_neutral_beam_injector), and the corresponding ECRH quantity is [launched_power_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher](name:launched_power_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher).

NAMES.name: forward_power_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna
NAMES.short: The incident RF power traveling from the generator toward the ion cyclotron heating antenna along the transmission line, before any reflection occurs at the antenna-plasma interface.
NAMES.long:
Forward power is the incident traveling-wave RF power propagating from the RF generator toward the ion cyclotron heating antenna along the coaxial transmission line. It represents the total power available at the antenna reference plane before coupling to the plasma, and is the primary input quantity used to compute coupling efficiency together with the returning wave power.

The net power launched into the vacuum vessel is determined by subtracting the reflected wave power:

$$
P_\mathrm{net} = P_\mathrm{fwd} - P_\mathrm{ref}
$$

where $P_\mathrm{fwd}$ is this forward power, $P_\mathrm{ref}$ is the [reflected power of the antenna](name:reflected_power_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna), and $P_\mathrm{net}$ corresponds to the [net launched power](name:power_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna). The antenna coupling efficiency is $\eta = (P_\mathrm{fwd} - P_\mathrm{ref}) / P_\mathrm{fwd} = 1 - |\Gamma|^2$, where $\Gamma$ is the voltage reflection coefficient at the antenna aperture.

Forward power is measured using calibrated directional couplers installed on the coaxial transmission line between the RF generator and the antenna strap feed, providing real-time monitoring for power control and antenna protection against excessive reflected power.

Typical forward power levels per ICRH antenna range from 1 to above 10 MW on large tokamaks, with coupling efficiencies between 70% and 95% depending on plasma edge density, strap phasing, and plasma-antenna gap.

NAMES.name: radial_centroid_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror
NAMES.short: Major radius coordinate of the geometric center of an electron cyclotron launcher mirror, measured from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The radial centroid of an electron cyclotron launcher mirror is the perpendicular distance $R$ of the mirror's geometric center from the machine toroidal symmetry axis, defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame where $R$ is the major radius in meters. Together with [vertical_coordinate_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror](name:vertical_coordinate_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror), it fully locates the mirror center in the meridional plane, establishing the geometric reference point from which EC beam injection angles and trajectories are computed.

The centroid position in the machine frame combines with the mirror rotation [angle_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror](name:angle_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror) and any mechanical [offset_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror](name:offset_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror) to define the complete launch geometry used in ray-tracing and beam-tracing models for electron cyclotron heating and current drive. The local boundary contour of the mirror surface is described separately in the mirror-fixed planar frame via [x1_coordinate_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror](name:x1_coordinate_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror) and [x2_coordinate_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror](name:x2_coordinate_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the mirror centroid lies at a finite major radius from the toroidal symmetry axis ($R > 0$), which holds for all physical in-vessel launcher positions.

NAMES.name: radial_normalized_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam
NAMES.short: Radial direction cosine of the electromagnetic wave vector along a beam-tracing ray, equal to the radial component $k_R$ divided by the total wave-vector magnitude $|\mathbf{k}|$.
NAMES.long:
The radial normalized wave vector is the direction cosine of the local wave vector projected onto the major-radius direction $\hat{R}$ of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, evaluated at each point along the beam or ray path in beam-tracing calculations. It encodes what fraction of the instantaneous wave propagation direction is oriented radially — outward from or inward toward the machine symmetry axis.

The quantity is defined as:

$$
k_{R,\text{norm}} = \frac{k_R}{|\mathbf{k}|}
$$

where $k_R$ is the [radial wave-vector component](name:radial_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam) and $|\mathbf{k}|$ is the total wave-vector magnitude. Together with the [toroidal normalized wave vector](name:toroidal_normalized_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam) and the [vertical normalized wave vector](name:vertical_normalized_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam), this component forms a unit direction vector satisfying $k_{R,\text{norm}}^2 + k_{\phi,\text{norm}}^2 + k_{Z,\text{norm}}^2 = 1$.

In beam-tracing or ray-tracing simulations for RF heating, the normalized wave-vector components track the instantaneous wave propagation direction as the ray refracts through an inhomogeneous magnetized plasma. Values are dimensionless and bounded to the interval $[-1, 1]$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $k_R$ points in the direction of increasing major radius $R$, away from the machine symmetry axis.

NAMES.name: reflected_power_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna
NAMES.short: Reflected power of an ion cyclotron heating antenna is the non-negative RF power carried by the backward-traveling wave from the antenna toward the feed line at a specified reference plane. It quantifies antenna matching and coupling shortfall, but equals forward power minus plasma-coupled power only when losses and reference-plane effects are excluded.
NAMES.long:
Reflected power of an ion cyclotron heating antenna is the RF power in the wave traveling back from the antenna load toward the transmission line source. It is reported as a non-negative power-flow magnitude at a specified antenna or feed-line reference plane, not as a signed net power.

At the same reference plane, the reflected power is related to the forward and net powers by the local power balance:

$$
P_{\mathrm{refl}} = P_{\mathrm{fwd}} - P_{\mathrm{net}}
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{refl}}$, $P_{\mathrm{fwd}}$, and $P_{\mathrm{net}}$ are powers in W; $P_{\mathrm{fwd}}$ is the incident power traveling toward the antenna, and $P_{\mathrm{net}}$ is the net RF power crossing the reference plane toward the antenna-plasma load. Only when losses between the reference plane and the plasma are negligible does $P_{\mathrm{net}}$ approximate the power coupled to the plasma.

In practice, reflected power is obtained from calibrated directional couplers or from a voltage-current traveling-wave decomposition in the antenna feed system. The reference plane should be specified because standing waves, impedance transformations, and transmission-line or antenna losses can change the apparent reflected power measured at different locations.

Typical reflected powers range from near 0 W in well-matched conditions to 10^3-10^6 W in high-power ion-cyclotron operation. Well-matched systems commonly aim for reflected fractions $P_{\mathrm{refl}}/P_{\mathrm{fwd}}$ below about 0.05-0.2, while poor coupling or rapid load changes can produce much larger fractions approaching unity.

NAMES.name: reflected_power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna
NAMES.short: RF power returning from a lower hybrid antenna back toward the transmission line, representing the portion of forward power not coupled into the plasma.
NAMES.long:
Reflected power from a lower hybrid antenna is the component of incident RF power that fails to couple into the plasma and propagates back toward the transmission line source. Poor coupling arises from unfavorable edge plasma density gradients, suboptimal launcher–plasma distance, or antenna phasing conditions that mismatch the slow-wave accessibility window of the lower hybrid wave.

The power reflection coefficient $|\Gamma|^2$ relates reflected power $P_\text{ref}$ to forward power $P_\text{fwd}$:

$$
|\Gamma|^2 = \frac{P_\text{ref}}{P_\text{fwd}}
$$

where $P_\text{fwd}$ is the total power delivered to the antenna from the transmission line. The [launched power](name:launched_power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna) into the vacuum vessel is the difference $P_\text{fwd} - P_\text{ref}$, and the [total absorbed power](name:total_absorbed_power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna) accounts for remaining waveguide and plasma losses. The gross RF input to the antenna system is captured by the parent quantity `power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna`.

Reflected power is monitored in real time using directional couplers embedded in the transmission line feeding the lower hybrid launcher. In well-coupled regimes, $P_\text{ref}/P_\text{fwd}$ is typically below 5–10%; transients such as L–H mode transitions or edge density fluctuations can briefly increase the reflected fraction to 30–50%, triggering protection interlocks. The analogous quantity for ion cyclotron systems is [reflected power of an IC antenna](name:reflected_power_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna).

NAMES.name: thermal_electron_power_at_inside_flux_surface
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Cumulative wave power absorbed by the bulk thermal electron population within the plasma volume enclosed by a specified magnetic flux surface.
NAMES.long:
Thermal electron power at an inside flux surface quantifies the total rate at which coherent wave energy is absorbed by the bulk (Maxwellian) thermal electron population within the plasma volume bounded by a given flux surface. It represents the radially cumulative wave deposition profile for the thermal electron channel, complementing the fast-electron contribution [fast_electron_power_at_inside_flux_surface](name:fast_electron_power_at_inside_flux_surface) to form the total [electron_power_at_inside_flux_surface](name:electron_power_at_inside_flux_surface).

The quantity is obtained by integrating the flux-surface-averaged [thermal_electron_power_density](name:thermal_electron_power_density) $p_{\mathrm{th,e}}$ over the enclosed plasma volume:

$$
P_{\mathrm{th,e}}(\rho) = \int_0^\rho p_{\mathrm{th,e}}(\rho') \frac{dV}{d\rho'} \, d\rho'
$$

where $\rho$ labels the flux surface and $dV/d\rho'$ is the differential volume element per unit radial coordinate.

This profile is computed by RF wave propagation and absorption solvers; the value at the outermost closed flux surface gives the total wave power absorbed by thermal electrons. The analogous quantity for thermal ions is [thermal_ion_power_at_inside_flux_surface](name:thermal_ion_power_at_inside_flux_surface), and the charge-state-resolved thermal ion analog is [thermal_ion_state_power_at_inside_flux_surface](name:thermal_ion_state_power_at_inside_flux_surface).

NAMES.name: thermal_ion_power_at_inside_flux_surface
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Cumulative wave power absorbed by the thermal ion population within the plasma volume enclosed by a specified magnetic flux surface.
NAMES.long:
Thermal ion power at an inside flux surface is the cumulative rate at which wave energy is deposited in the bulk ion population inside the volume enclosed by that magnetic flux surface. It represents thermal-ion heating integrated from the magnetic axis to the chosen surface and excludes direct deposition to electrons and fast ions.

The cumulative power for a flux surface labeled by the dimensionless radial coordinate $\rho$ in a flux coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$ is defined from the local thermal-ion wave-power density:

$$
P_{\mathrm{th\,ion}}(\rho) = \int_{V(\rho)} p_{\mathrm{th\,ion}} \, dV'
$$

where $V(\rho)$ is the plasma volume enclosed by the flux surface, $p_{\mathrm{th\,ion}}$ is the local net wave-power density for thermal ions in W m^-3, $dV'$ is a volume element in m^3, and $P_{\mathrm{th\,ion}}$ is the cumulative power.

In practice this quantity is computed by integrating wave-power deposition densities from wave propagation and wave-particle absorption modeling over the reconstructed plasma volume. Experimental constraints include injected wave power, coupling losses, ion temperature evolution, species composition, and other heating and transport terms needed to separate thermal-ion absorption from electron or fast-ion channels.

Typical values are near 0 W at the magnetic axis and increase toward the total thermal-ion absorbed wave power at the plasma boundary. Medium-size tokamak discharges commonly have 10^4-10^6 W, while high-power wave-heating scenarios in large devices can reach 10^6-2 x 10^7 W within the outer flux surfaces.
NAMES.sign: Positive when wave energy is transferred to the thermal ion population.

NAMES.name: thermal_ion_state_power_at_inside_flux_surface
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Cumulative radio-frequency wave power absorbed by a specified thermal ion charge state inside the plasma volume enclosed by a selected magnetic flux surface. It is the volume integral of the charge-state-resolved absorbed power density.
NAMES.long:
Thermal ion state power at an inside flux surface is the cumulative radio-frequency wave power transferred to one specified thermal ion species and charge state within the volume bounded by that magnetic flux surface. It is the charge-state-resolved contribution to cumulative thermal-ion RF absorption.

The cumulative absorbed power for charge state $z$ of ion species $s$ inside the flux surface labeled by $\rho$ is defined by the volume integral of the local absorbed power density:

$$
P_{\mathrm{th},s,z}(\rho) = \int_{V(\rho)} p_{\mathrm{th},s,z}(\mathbf{x})\, dV
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{th},s,z}$ is in W, $p_{\mathrm{th},s,z}$ is the local RF power density transferred to that thermal ion charge state in W m$^{-3}$, $dV$ is the differential volume element in m$^3$, and $V(\rho)$ is the plasma volume enclosed by the magnetic flux surface labeled by the dimensionless normalized flux-surface coordinate $\rho$.

In practice this quantity is computed from wave propagation and wave-particle interaction models by integrating the charge-state-resolved absorption over nested equilibrium volumes. Summing over all relevant charge states and all thermal ion species gives the total cumulative RF power absorbed by thermal ions inside the same flux surface; summing over charge states for only one species gives the species-resolved contribution.

Typical values for an individual thermal ion charge state range from near 0 W for weakly absorbing states to 10^5-10^7 W when the state is a dominant RF absorber. The value depends on coupled RF power, resonance location, ion composition, charge-state population, temperature, density, and the chosen flux surface.
NAMES.sign: Positive when net RF energy is transferred from the wave field to the specified thermal ion charge state.

NAMES.name: toroidal_angle_of_electron_cyclotron_beam
NAMES.short: Toroidal steering angle of an electron cyclotron beam, defined by the arc sine of the toroidal wave-vector component divided by the total wave-vector magnitude. It specifies the signed toroidal part of propagation in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal angle of an electron cyclotron beam is the signed steering angle associated with the toroidal component of the beam's local mean wave vector. It measures how much of the propagation direction is along $\hat{\phi}$ rather than within the plane spanned by $R$ and $Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

The angle is defined from the projection of the wave vector onto the toroidal basis direction:

$$
\alpha_\phi = \sin^{-1}\!\left(\frac{k_\phi}{|\mathbf{k}|}\right)
$$

where $\alpha_\phi$ is the toroidal beam angle, $k_\phi$ is the component of the mean wave vector along $\hat{\phi}$, and $|\mathbf{k}|$ is the total wave-vector magnitude. Both $k_\phi$ and $|\mathbf{k}|$ have units of rad m$^{-1}$, equivalently m$^{-1}$ when radians are treated as dimensionless, so the ratio is dimensionless and $\alpha_\phi$ is in rad.

In practice, this angle is determined from EC launcher geometry, calibrated steering-mirror orientation, or ray and beam-tracing calculations by decomposing the mean wave vector in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. Together with [poloidal_angle_of_electron_cyclotron_beam](name:poloidal_angle_of_electron_cyclotron_beam), launch position, frequency, and magnetic geometry, it contributes to the parallel refractive index through the local projection $N_\parallel = c\,\mathbf{k}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{b}}/\omega$, where $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$ is the unit vector along the magnetic field, $\omega$ is the wave angular frequency, and $c$ is the speed of light. The toroidal angle controls the $k_\phi$ part of that projection but does not by itself determine $N_\parallel$ because the magnetic-field pitch and the poloidal propagation component also enter; it is complementary to EC beam power, which specifies wave energy flow rather than propagation direction.

Typical values are launcher dependent. The principal-value definition gives a mathematical interval from $-\pi/2$ to $+\pi/2$ rad; EC heating launch is often near zero toroidal angle, while current-drive-oriented launch commonly uses nonzero angles of order a few tenths of a rad. Hardware steering limits and access constraints determine the available range for a given device.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the toroidal component of the beam wave vector points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: total_absorbed_power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna
NAMES.short: Net RF power deposited into the plasma by the lower hybrid antenna system, aggregated over all individual antennas.
NAMES.long:
The total absorbed power of the lower hybrid antenna system quantifies the net RF energy deposition rate from the LHCD launcher array into the confined plasma, summed over all individual antennas. It is the primary power accounting metric for lower hybrid current drive and supplemental electron heating, governing the wave energy available for driving non-inductive plasma current.

The absorbed power is defined as the volume integral of the local LH wave power deposition density over the plasma volume:

$$
P_\text{abs} = \int_V q_\text{LH}(\mathbf{r}) \, dV
$$

where $q_\text{LH}(\mathbf{r})$ is the volumetric LH wave absorption density at position $\mathbf{r}$ within the plasma volume $V$.

This quantity is distinct from the [total launched power](name:total_launched_power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna), which represents power entering the vacuum vessel and can exceed the absorbed power by any residual absorption in the edge region or scrape-off layer that does not reach the confined plasma. In practice, the absorbed power is estimated from directional-coupler measurements of the [forward power](name:forward_power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna) and [reflected power](name:reflected_power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna) on the high-power RF transmission lines, corrected for resistive dissipation in the launcher structure and waveguide network.

In current LHCD systems on medium-to-large tokamaks, total absorbed power levels range from 1-10 MW.

NAMES.name: total_power_due_to_electron_cyclotron_heating
NAMES.short: Total radiofrequency power absorbed in the plasma by electron cyclotron heating, summed over all electron cyclotron wave sources. It represents deposited heating power, not launched, transmitted, or reflected power, and is zero or positive.
NAMES.long:
Total power due to electron cyclotron heating is the aggregate rate at which electron cyclotron waves transfer electromagnetic energy to the plasma through resonant interaction with electrons at the cyclotron frequency or its harmonics. It is an absorbed heating power: it counts only the power that is actually deposited in the plasma, excluding power that remains in transmission paths, is reflected, or shines through without absorption.

The total absorbed electron cyclotron heating power is the sum of the absorbed powers from the individual electron cyclotron wave sources:

$$
P_\mathrm{EC} = \sum_{i=1}^{N_\mathrm{EC}} P_{\mathrm{EC},i}
$$

where $N_\mathrm{EC}$ is the number of contributing electron cyclotron wave sources, $P_{\mathrm{EC},i}$ (in W) is the heating power absorbed in the plasma from source $i$, and $P_\mathrm{EC}$ (in W) is the total deposited power. The per-source contribution is reported by [power_due_to_electron_cyclotron_heating](name:power_due_to_electron_cyclotron_heating).

In practice this quantity is obtained from power-balance and wave-deposition analysis that combines the launched radiofrequency power with absorption estimates from ray-tracing or beam-tracing calculations, accounting for single-pass absorption efficiency and shine-through losses. It enters the electron energy balance as a heating source term and is therefore closely related to [total_electron_power](name:total_electron_power).

Representative integrated values range from a few hundred kilowatts to several megawatts in present-day auxiliary-heated experiments, and reach tens of megawatts in high-power systems, with the exact value depending on source power, coupling efficiency, plasma density and temperature, magnetic field, and the absorption location. The value is zero when no electron cyclotron heating is applied.

NAMES.name: total_power_due_to_ion_cyclotron_heating
NAMES.short: Total net radio-frequency power absorbed by the plasma through ion cyclotron resonance heating, summed over all ion-cyclotron launchers or antenna systems. It excludes power that is launched but reflected or lost before coupling to the plasma.
NAMES.long:
Total power due to ion cyclotron heating is the aggregate rate at which radio-frequency electromagnetic energy in the ion-cyclotron frequency range is deposited in the plasma. It includes resonant and mode-converted wave absorption from all active ion-cyclotron launchers or antenna systems, and excludes reflected power and non-plasma losses.

The total absorbed ion-cyclotron heating power is the sum of the absorbed powers from the individual contributing systems:

$$
P_{\mathrm{IC,tot}} = \sum_{k=1}^{N_{\mathrm{IC}}} P_{\mathrm{IC},k}
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{IC}}$ is the number of contributing ion-cyclotron launchers or antenna systems, $k$ indexes those systems, and $P_{\mathrm{IC},k}$ is the net power absorbed by the plasma from system $k$ in watts.

In practice, this quantity is inferred from an RF power balance using measurements of forward, reflected, and coupled power together with estimates of transmission-line, matching-network, antenna, and other non-plasma losses when available. It may also be constrained by wave-heating analysis, modulation experiments, or global plasma energy-balance checks; it is not the generator output power or the purely launched RF power.

Typical values are $1\times10^5-1\times10^7$ W in medium-sized tokamak experiments and can reach $2\times10^7-4\times10^7$ W in large high-power ion-cyclotron heating scenarios. The value is zero when no ion-cyclotron RF power is coupled to and absorbed by the plasma.

NAMES.name: total_power_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna
NAMES.short: System-level net radio-frequency power launched into the vacuum vessel by all ion-cyclotron heating antennas. It is the sum over antennas of forward power minus reflected power, so it represents launched rather than absorbed heating power.
NAMES.long:
Total power of the ion-cyclotron heating antenna system is the system-level net RF power launched through the antenna array into the vacuum vessel. It is the aggregate of the per-antenna launched powers, distinguishing launched power from the power ultimately absorbed by the plasma, such as [total_power_due_to_ion_cyclotron_heating](name:total_power_due_to_ion_cyclotron_heating).

The total launched power is defined by summing the net contribution from each antenna:

$$
P_{\mathrm{ICRH,tot}} = \sum_{a=1}^{N_{\mathrm{ant}}} \left(P_{\mathrm{fwd},a} - P_{\mathrm{refl},a}\right)
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{ant}}$ is the number of ion-cyclotron heating antennas, $P_{\mathrm{fwd},a}$ is the forward RF power for antenna $a$, and $P_{\mathrm{refl},a}$ is the corresponding reflected RF power, with all powers expressed in W. The per-antenna net term corresponds to [power_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna](name:power_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna), while the reflected component is represented by [reflected_power_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna](name:reflected_power_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna).

In practice, the forward and reflected RF powers are inferred from calibrated measurements in the antenna feeding system and combined over the active antennas. The value is used as a launched-power input for heating efficiency and power-balance analysis; it should not be interpreted as the absorbed ion-cyclotron heating power, because coupling losses, reflection, edge interactions, and wave absorption determine the fraction deposited in the plasma.

Typical total launched ICRH powers range from about $10^5$-$10^7$ W, depending on antenna configuration, coupling conditions, and device size. High-power tokamak systems commonly operate in the MW range.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the net RF power flow is from the antenna system into the vacuum vessel.

NAMES.name: total_power_of_neutral_beam_injector
NAMES.short: Aggregate neutral beam injection power carried by all active injector units into the vacuum vessel, evaluated before plasma absorption, shinethrough, charge-exchange, wall, or other downstream losses are applied.
NAMES.long:
Total neutral-beam-injector power is the aggregate rate at which kinetic energy is carried by neutral atoms from all active injector units into the vacuum vessel. It is a launched source power for the neutral beam injection system, distinct from absorbed_power_of_neutral_beam_injector and from net plasma-heating quantities such as power_due_to_neutral_beam_injection.

The total is defined by summing the launched power of each active injector unit:

$$
P_{\mathrm{NBI,total}} = \sum_{k \in \mathcal{A}} P_{\mathrm{NBI},k}
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{NBI},k}$ is the [power_of_neutral_beam_injector](name:power_of_neutral_beam_injector) for injector unit $k$, and $\mathcal{A}$ is the set of active injector units. The accounting direction is into the vacuum vessel: each term is the kinetic-energy flux delivered across the vessel interface toward the plasma region, and later shinethrough, ionization, charge-exchange, wall, or plasma-absorption losses are not subtracted from this total.

In practice, this quantity is evaluated from injector operating measurements such as acceleration voltage, extracted beam current, neutralization efficiency, species and energy fractions, beamline transmission, and pulse timing, with calorimetry or dedicated beam diagnostics used for calibration. For multi-energy neutral beams, each injector contribution includes the weighted kinetic-energy flux of all neutral species components launched by that injector.

Representative values range from $10^5$-$10^6$ W for small or commissioning injectors to $10^6$-$5 \times 10^7$ W for multi-injector tokamak heating systems; the value is zero when no neutral beam injector is active. It is the neutral-beam analog of aggregate launched-power quantities for other auxiliary heating systems, such as [total_power_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna](name:total_power_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna) and total_power_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher.

NAMES.name: vertical_angle_of_neutral_beam_injector
NAMES.short: Vertical inclination angle of the central beamlet of a neutral beam injector, measured from the horizontal plane to the beamlet axis.
NAMES.long:
The vertical angle of a neutral beam injector characterizes the elevation of the central beamlet axis with respect to the horizontal plane, encoding the upward or downward tilt component of the beam's injection direction. Together with the toroidal pointing geometry described by [angle_of_neutral_beam_injector](name:angle_of_neutral_beam_injector) and the tangency major radius [beam_major_radius_of_neutral_beam_injector](name:beam_major_radius_of_neutral_beam_injector), this angle fully specifies the 3D trajectory of the central beam axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

The angle $\alpha_v$ is the elevation of the central beamlet unit direction vector $\hat{b}$ above the horizontal plane:

$$
\alpha_v = \arcsin\!\left(\hat{b} \cdot \hat{Z}\right)
$$

where $\hat{Z}$ is the vertical unit vector and $\hat{b}$ is the unit vector along the central beamlet axis, with $\alpha_v = 0$ for a perfectly horizontal beam and $|\alpha_v| < \pi/2$ for any physical configuration.

This geometric parameter is fixed by the physical design and alignment of the injector unit and its duct orientation, established from engineering design specifications and optical survey measurements. The vertical_width_of_neutral_beam_injector describes the vertical spatial extent of the full beamlet group at the injector aperture, complementing this directional quantity.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the central beamlet is directed upward, in the $+Z$ direction above the horizontal plane.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna
NAMES.short: Vertical coordinate of the reference point used to locate an ion cyclotron heating antenna. It is the Z component in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, where R is major radius and Z is vertical height.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate of an ion cyclotron heating antenna is the $Z$ component of the antenna reference point in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The reference point is a defined geometric point for the antenna placement; it is not necessarily a physical endpoint or aperture center unless the antenna geometry defines it that way.

Together with the [major-radius coordinate] and toroidal angle of the same reference point, this quantity specifies the antenna reference-point position in the cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The same coordinate concept is used for other actuator placement reference points, including lower-hybrid antennas, neutral-beam injectors, and electron-cyclotron launcher mirrors.

In practice, the value is obtained from mechanical design geometry, installation alignment, or survey data for the antenna reference point, expressed in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. Any uncertainty is usually dominated by the definition of the reference point and by mechanical alignment tolerances rather than by plasma conditions.
