Typical values are device- and origin-dependent. For antennas mounted near a machine midplane the coordinate is often close to 0 m, while upper or lower port locations have positive or negative offsets with magnitudes from fractions of a meter to several meters depending on device size.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the antenna reference point is displaced in the $+Z$ direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_lower_hybrid_antenna
NAMES.short: Vertical Z-coordinate of the reference point of a lower hybrid antenna in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, where R is major radius, φ is toroidal angle, and Z is vertical height.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate of a lower hybrid antenna is the $Z$ value of the antenna reference point in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It specifies the vertical placement of the launcher reference datum, typically relative to the $Z=0$ midplane of the device geometry.

The coordinate is the $Z$ component assigned to the antenna reference point:

$$
Z_\mathrm{ant} = Z_\mathrm{ref}
$$

where $Z_\mathrm{ref}$ is the vertical coordinate of the nominated reference point and $Z_\mathrm{ant}$ is the corresponding lower-hybrid-antenna coordinate.

The reference point is usually a mechanical or geometric datum of the launcher, such as a mounting datum, aperture center, or defined antenna center. It is determined from engineering geometry or installation survey data and, together with the complementary major-radius and toroidal-angle coordinates, fixes the antenna position in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. Row-specific vertical positions are represented separately by [vertical_coordinate_of_lower_hybrid_antenna_row](name:vertical_coordinate_of_lower_hybrid_antenna_row).

Typical values are device- and installation-dependent. Midplane launchers often have $Z_\mathrm{ant}$ close to 0 m, while vertically displaced launchers can have offsets of order 0.1-1 m; larger offsets are possible in large devices or for antennas deliberately mounted away from the midplane.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the reference point lies in the direction of increasing vertical coordinate $Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_lower_hybrid_antenna_row
NAMES.short: Vertical Z coordinate, in meters, of the geometric reference point of a lower hybrid antenna row in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It locates the row's height relative to the machine equatorial plane and is not the row height or row spacing.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate $Z_\mathrm{row}$ is the height of the specified geometric reference point of a lower hybrid antenna row in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The datum is the row reference point used to locate the row geometry; this coordinate does not describe the physical vertical extent of the row.

For a row reference point with cylindrical coordinates $(R_\mathrm{row}, \phi_\mathrm{row}, Z_\mathrm{row})$, its position may be written as:

$$
\mathbf{x}_\mathrm{row} = R_\mathrm{row}\,\hat{R}(\phi_\mathrm{row}) + Z_\mathrm{row}\,\hat{Z}
$$

where $\hat{R}$ and $\hat{Z}$ are basis vectors of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $R_\mathrm{row}$ is the major-radius coordinate, $\phi_\mathrm{row}$ is the toroidal angle coordinate, and $Z_\mathrm{row}$ is the vertical coordinate in meters.

This coordinate is normally obtained from the antenna mechanical geometry, alignment survey, or design model using the same row reference point as the companion major-radius and toroidal-angle coordinates. Together these three coordinates specify the location of the row reference point in space.

There is no device-independent typical range for this coordinate. Rows mounted near the equatorial plane have $Z_\mathrm{row}$ close to $0$ m, while rows placed above or below the midplane take positive or negative values set by the launcher port location and row spacing.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the row reference point lies in the $+\hat{Z}$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame from the $Z=0$ equatorial plane.

NAMES.name: x1_coordinate_of_aperture
NAMES.short: First local transverse coordinate of a neutral-beam injector collimating-aperture outline vertex, measured from the aperture origin in the local aperture-plane Cartesian (X1, X2) frame.
NAMES.long:
The $X_1$ coordinate of an aperture is the signed distance of an outline vertex along the first axis of the local aperture-plane Cartesian $(X_1, X_2)$ frame with in-plane basis $(\hat{X}_1, \hat{X}_2)$. The frame origin is the aperture reference point, normally the nominal beam-axis intersection with the aperture plane or the mechanical center used for alignment; $X_1=0$ is the line through that origin parallel to the $X_2$ axis. It is not a coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame; it describes transverse position within the injector aperture plane.

Together with [x2_coordinate_of_aperture](name:x2_coordinate_of_aperture), ordered vertices define the closed planar aperture boundary: consecutive vertices lie on adjacent boundary segments, and the final vertex is connected back to the first. The coordinate is determined by projecting each vertex position in the aperture plane onto the $+\hat{X}_1$ axis after the local origin and axis orientation have been established from component geometry and alignment.

Typical neutral-beam collimating apertures have transverse half-widths of 0.01-0.3 m, so individual $X_1$ vertex coordinates commonly span from about -0.3 m to 0.3 m. Small beamlet or mask openings may be at the 0.001-0.02 m scale, while large shaped collimators can approach 0.5 m in full width.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the vertex displacement from the aperture origin is along the $+X_1$ direction of the local aperture-plane Cartesian $(X_1, X_2)$ frame.

NAMES.name: x1_coordinate_of_neutral_beam_injector
NAMES.short: Position along X1 of a neutral beam injector source-outline vertex in the beam-local Cartesian (X1, X2) frame, referenced to the aperture center.
NAMES.long:
The $X_1$ coordinate of a neutral beam injector source-outline vertex is the signed displacement of that vertex along the first transverse axis of the beam-local Cartesian $(X_1, X_2)$ frame. This frame has basis axes $(\hat{X}_1, \hat{X}_2)$ in the source extraction plane, transverse to the nominal beam propagation direction. The origin is the source-aperture center, i.e. the intersection of the nominal beam centerline with the extraction plane.

Together with the [X2 coordinate](name:x2_coordinate_of_neutral_beam_injector), this quantity defines a vertex of the closed outline of the beam extraction surface. The outline geometry is usually obtained from the source-aperture design or as-built metrology; vertices are normally ordered consistently around the aperture, clockwise or counterclockwise as viewed along the nominal beam direction. A rectangular source outline uses four vertices, while chamfered, rounded, or segmented extraction surfaces may use more.

The local source outline complements global injector-position quantities such as the [vertical coordinate of a neutral beam injector](name:vertical_coordinate_of_neutral_beam_injector), which are expressed in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle increasing counterclockwise when viewed from $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height.

Representative absolute values of $X_1$ for neutral beam source outlines are typically 0.05-0.5 m, depending on source size and whether $X_1$ is aligned with the wider or narrower aperture dimension; large high-power source modules can be larger.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the source-outline vertex is displaced from the local origin in the $+\hat{X}_1$ direction of the beam-local Cartesian $(X_1, X_2)$ frame.

NAMES.name: x2_coordinate_of_aperture
NAMES.short: Second local coordinate of a neutral beam injector collimating-aperture outline vertex in the transverse (X1, X2) aperture plane. With the paired first coordinate, it gives the signed in-plane position of a beam-limiting boundary point relative to the aperture origin.
NAMES.long:
The X2 coordinate is the signed scalar component of an aperture-outline vertex along the second axis of the local aperture-plane Cartesian frame $(X_1, X_2)$ with basis $(\hat{X}_1, \hat{X}_2)$. The local origin is the point represented by $x_1=x_2=0$, and all aperture vertices use the same origin and in-plane basis. Paired with [x1_coordinate_of_aperture](name:x1_coordinate_of_aperture), it identifies a point on the boundary of the neutral beam collimating opening.

Given an aperture-plane origin $\mathbf{r}_0$ and unit basis vectors $\hat{X}_1$ and $\hat{X}_2$, the local reconstruction of a vertex position is

$$
\mathbf{r}_v = \mathbf{r}_0 + x_1\hat{X}_1 + x_2\hat{X}_2
$$

where $\mathbf{r}_v$ is the vertex position in the aperture plane, $x_1$ is the paired first local coordinate, and $x_2$ is this second local coordinate.

Aperture-outline coordinates are specified from the mechanical definition of the collimating aperture or from a measured outline of the hardware. They are used when the beam-limiting opening is represented by explicit boundary vertices rather than by a reduced geometric parameter such as width_of_aperture for a rectangular description or [neutral_beam_radius_of_aperture](name:neutral_beam_radius_of_aperture) for a circular description.

Values are expressed in meters and may be negative, zero, or positive depending on the vertex location and the chosen local origin. The applicable range is aperture-specific; for an opening centered on the local origin, X2 coordinates span roughly from $-a_2$ to $+a_2$, where $a_2$ is the half-extent of the aperture along $\hat{X}_2$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the vertex is displaced from the local aperture-plane origin in the $+\hat{X}_2$ direction.

NAMES.name: fast_electron_power
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Total wave power absorbed by the fast (suprathermal) electron population from a coherent wave, globally integrated over the plasma volume.
NAMES.long:
Fast electron power is the volume integral of the local wave energy absorption rate by the non-thermal (suprathermal) electron population, representing the globally integrated fraction of coherent wave energy transferred to electrons whose velocities substantially exceed the bulk thermal velocity.

The defining relation is:

$$
P_\mathrm{fast,e} = \int_V p_\mathrm{fast,e}(\mathbf{r})\, dV
$$

where $p_\mathrm{fast,e}$ is the [fast electron power density](name:fast_electron_power_density) — the local volumetric wave-energy absorption rate on the suprathermal electron population and $V$ is the total plasma volume.

This quantity is computed from wave-kinetic or quasilinear solvers that partition the electron velocity distribution into thermal and suprathermal components; in electron cyclotron resonance heating scenarios, the fast electron channel captures absorption at harmonic resonances and energy transfer during suprathermal tail formation. The thermally absorbed complement is [thermal_electron_power](name:thermal_electron_power); comparing the two characterizes the non-thermal efficiency of a given wave-heating scheme.

Together with [thermal_electron_power](name:thermal_electron_power) and [fast_ion_power](name:fast_ion_power), this quantity contributes to [absorbed_power](name:absorbed_power) — the total wave energy transferred to the plasma per unit time. It enters the electron energy balance as a suprathermal source term within [electron_power](name:electron_power), the all-channel electron energy-balance quantity.

NAMES.name: per_toroidal_mode_fast_electron_power
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Wave power absorbed by the fast (non-thermal) electron population from a coherent wave, attributed to a single toroidal Fourier harmonic identified by mode number $n_\phi$.
NAMES.long:
This quantity gives the contribution to the total absorbed fast-electron wave power from a single toroidal Fourier harmonic of a coherent wave, identified by toroidal mode number $n_\phi$. It decomposes [fast_electron_power](name:fast_electron_power) — the volume-integrated power absorbed by the non-thermal electron population — into individual harmonic contributions.

The summation closure relation is:

$$
P_{\rm fast,e} = \sum_{n_\phi} P_{\rm fast,e}(n_\phi)
$$

where $P_{\rm fast,e}(n_\phi)$ is the power absorbed by fast electrons from the harmonic with toroidal mode number $n_\phi$.

In wave-modeling calculations, the electromagnetic fields of a coherent wave are expanded as a Fourier series in the toroidal angle $\phi$, and the contribution from each harmonic to the fast-electron power balance is evaluated separately using quasilinear diffusion theory applied to the non-thermal electron distribution. Resonant absorption mechanisms — such as electron cyclotron or lower-hybrid resonances — accelerate electrons to suprathermal energies, and the harmonic decomposition reveals which modes dominate this energy transfer. The radially cumulative (inside-flux-surface) variant is [fast_electron_power_at_inside_flux_surface](name:fast_electron_power_at_inside_flux_surface), while the local power-density analog per mode is [per_toroidal_mode_fast_electron_power_density](name:per_toroidal_mode_fast_electron_power_density). The equivalent decomposition for the thermal electron population is [per_toroidal_mode_thermal_electron_power](name:per_toroidal_mode_thermal_electron_power), and the fast-ion counterpart is [per_toroidal_mode_fast_ion_power](name:per_toroidal_mode_fast_ion_power).

NAMES.name: fast_electron_power_density
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: RF wave energy absorption rate per unit volume by the fast, suprathermal electron population. It represents the non-thermal electron channel of wave power deposition.
NAMES.long:
Fast electron power density is the rate per unit volume at which an RF wave deposits energy in the suprathermal electron population. It is a volumetric source term for the fast-electron energy balance; fast denotes the modeled non-thermal part of the electron distribution rather than a universal sharp energy threshold.

For a local point $\mathbf{x}$, a kinetic definition is obtained by taking the particle-energy moment of the wave-driven part of the fast-electron distribution evolution:

$$
p_\mathrm{fast}(\mathbf{x}) = \int \frac{1}{2} m_e v^2 \, \mathcal{C}_\mathrm{wave}[f_\mathrm{fast}](\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v}) \, d^3v
$$

where $m_e$ is the electron mass, $v$ is particle speed, $f_\mathrm{fast}$ is the fast-electron distribution function with units $s^3 m^{-6}$, $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element with units $m^3 s^{-3}$, and $\mathcal{C}_\mathrm{wave}[f_\mathrm{fast}]$ is the wave-driven contribution to $\partial f_\mathrm{fast}/\partial t$ with units $s^2 m^{-6}$. When the quantity is associated with a flux coordinate $\rho$ such as normalized toroidal flux radius, it denotes the flux-surface average of this local volumetric density, not the cumulative power. The cumulative fast-electron power inside a surface labeled by $\rho$ is related by $P_\mathrm{fast}(<\rho)=\int_{V(\rho)} p_\mathrm{fast}\,dV$, and the corresponding differential volume density is $dP_\mathrm{fast}/dV=(dP_\mathrm{fast}/d\rho)/(dV/d\rho)$.

In practice this quantity is usually inferred from wave-particle absorption calculations constrained by launched RF power, antenna or launcher configuration, magnetic equilibrium, and plasma profiles. Experimental checks can come from global power balance and from diagnostics sensitive to suprathermal electrons, such as non-thermal radiation or energetic-electron emission, but the local partition between thermal and fast-electron channels is generally model dependent.

Representative magnitudes span a wide range because RF deposition can be broad or highly localized. Core values of about $10^3-10^7$ W m$^{-3}$ are typical order-of-magnitude levels for auxiliary heating, with smaller values in weakly absorbing regions and larger peaks possible for strongly localized absorption.
NAMES.sign: Positive when RF wave energy is transferred from the wave field to the fast electron population.

NAMES.name: per_toroidal_mode_fast_electron_power_density
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: RF wave energy deposition rate per unit volume into the suprathermal electron population, resolved per toroidal mode number, such that summing over all modes recovers the total fast electron power density.
NAMES.long:
Fast electron power density per toroidal mode is the volumetric rate at which a coherent RF wave deposits energy into the suprathermal (non-thermal) electron population attributed to a single toroidal harmonic of the wave field. The fast electrons are those resonantly accelerated above the bulk thermal velocity through wave-particle interaction, forming a non-Maxwellian energetic tail in the electron distribution function.

The total [fast electron power density](name:fast_electron_power_density) is recovered by summing over all toroidal mode numbers:

$$
P_\mathrm{fast,e}(r) = \sum_{n_\phi} p_\mathrm{fast,e}(r,\, n_\phi)
$$

where $p_\mathrm{fast,e}(r, n_\phi)$ is the power density contribution from toroidal mode number $n_\phi$ and $r$ is the radial coordinate.

The mode-resolved deposition is computed by wave-propagation models — ray-tracing or full-wave solvers equipped with quasilinear diffusion operators — that decompose the RF electric field into toroidal harmonics and evaluate the mode-dependent damping on the fast electron component of the distribution function.

The harmonic structure of fast-electron absorption depends on wave type: electron cyclotron heating concentrates deposition near the fundamental or harmonic cyclotron resonance in a narrow toroidal mode range, while lower-hybrid and ICRH Landau and transit-time damping distribute absorption across a broader toroidal mode spectrum. The fast-ion counterpart is [per_toroidal_mode_fast_ion_power_density](name:per_toroidal_mode_fast_ion_power_density), the thermal electron counterpart is [per_toroidal_mode_thermal_electron_power_density](name:per_toroidal_mode_thermal_electron_power_density), and the mode-resolved total absorbed power density summed over all populations is given by per_toroidal_mode_absorbed_power_density.

NAMES.name: fast_ion_power_density
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Volumetric rate at which RF waves transfer energy to the nonthermal fast ion population. It represents deposited wave power per unit plasma volume, summed over the relevant fast-ion species and charge states.
NAMES.long:
Fast-ion power density is the volumetric source term for energy deposited by radio-frequency (RF) waves into the nonthermal ion distribution. It is the state-aggregated counterpart of [fast_ion_state_power_density](name:fast_ion_state_power_density) and excludes deposition to thermal ions or fast electrons. Its volume integral gives [fast_ion_power](name:fast_ion_power), while integration inside a chosen flux surface gives [fast_ion_power_at_inside_flux_surface](name:fast_ion_power_at_inside_flux_surface).

For RF absorption, the local source can be written as the cycle-averaged work done by the RF electric field on the fast-ion current response:

$$
p_{\mathrm{fi}}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{a,q} \left\langle \mathbf{J}^{\mathrm{RF}}_{\mathrm{fi},a q}(\mathbf{x},t) \cdot \mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{RF}}(\mathbf{x},t) \right\rangle_t
$$

where $p_{\mathrm{fi}}$ is the fast-ion power density, $a$ labels ion species, $q$ labels charge state, $\mathbf{J}^{\mathrm{RF}}_{\mathrm{fi},a q}$ is the RF current response associated with that fast-ion component, $\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{RF}}$ is the RF electric field, and $\langle\cdot\rangle_t$ denotes averaging over the RF period.

In practice this quantity is inferred from wave propagation and quasilinear absorption calculations constrained by magnetic equilibrium, antenna or launcher parameters, and measurements sensitive to the fast-ion distribution. It may also be cross-checked against changes in stored fast-ion energy, neutron or gamma-ray emission, neutral-particle measurements, and global RF power balance.

Representative magnitudes are strongly scenario dependent. A useful scale is the absorbed RF power divided by the effective deposition volume: 1 MW deposited over 0.1-10 m$^3$ corresponds to 10$^5$-10$^7$ W m$^{-3}$, while values are near zero where no resonant wave-particle interaction occurs.
NAMES.sign: Positive when energy is transferred from the RF wave field to the fast-ion population.

NAMES.name: per_toroidal_mode_fast_ion_power_density
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Absorbed coherent-wave power density deposited in the fast, non-thermal ion population, resolved by toroidal mode number and summed over fast-ion charge states. It quantifies each toroidal harmonic's contribution to volumetric energy transfer from the wave to energetic ions.
NAMES.long:
Absorbed coherent-wave power density per toroidal mode is the rate per unit plasma volume at which one toroidal Fourier harmonic transfers energy to the fast, non-thermal ion population. It is summed over fast-ion charge states; the charge-state-resolved counterpart is [per_toroidal_mode_fast_ion_state_power_density](name:per_toroidal_mode_fast_ion_state_power_density).

The corresponding volume-integrated per-mode fast-ion power is obtained from the volumetric density:

$$
P_\mathrm{fast}(n_\phi) = \int_V p_\mathrm{fast}(n_\phi, \mathbf{x})\,dV
$$

where $p_\mathrm{fast}(n_\phi, \mathbf{x})$ is this power density in W m^-3, $P_\mathrm{fast}(n_\phi)$ is [per_toroidal_mode_fast_ion_power](name:per_toroidal_mode_fast_ion_power), $n_\phi$ is the toroidal mode number, $\mathbf{x}$ is spatial position, and $V$ is the plasma volume considered. If expressed on a magnetic surface labeled by the flux coordinate $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$, the quantity denotes the flux-surface average of the local volumetric density, still in W m^-3, not a volume-integrated power.

In coherent-wave heating calculations, the wave field is decomposed into toroidal Fourier harmonics and the resonant wave-particle power transfer is evaluated against the fast-ion distribution. The total [fast_ion_power_density](name:fast_ion_power_density) is recovered by summing $p_\mathrm{fast}(n_\phi, \mathbf{x})$ over toroidal mode numbers, while $p_\mathrm{fast}(n_\phi, \mathbf{x}) = \sum_q p_{\mathrm{fast},q}(n_\phi, \mathbf{x})$ relates it to the charge-state-resolved density over fast-ion charge states $q$. Integrating the state-resolved densities gives [per_toroidal_mode_fast_ion_state_power](name:per_toroidal_mode_fast_ion_state_power).

Large values occur where a toroidal harmonic has strong wave amplitude, satisfies the relevant resonance condition, and overlaps a substantial fast-ion phase-space density. The absolute scale is highly scenario dependent, so interpretation is usually made by comparing the integrated per-mode power, the absorbing volume, and the distribution of launched toroidal harmonics rather than by using a universal numerical range.
NAMES.sign: Positive when coherent-wave energy is transferred to the fast, non-thermal ion population.

NAMES.name: fast_ion_state_power
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Total RF wave power absorbed by the fast (suprathermal) ion population of a specified charge state, volume-integrated over the entire plasma and excluding collisional energy exchange between populations.
NAMES.long:
Fast-ion-state power is the total electromagnetic-wave energy per unit time deposited into the fast (suprathermal) ion component of a single, specified ion charge state, integrated over the entire plasma volume. It is the charge-state-resolved fast-ion contribution to [ion_state_power](name:ion_state_power), which also includes the thermal population's absorbed wave power; collisional energy exchange between the fast and thermal ion populations is excluded by definition. Fast ions typically absorb RF energy through direct wave-particle resonance mechanisms such as minority-species fundamental resonance or second-harmonic absorption in ion cyclotron resonance heating schemes.

The quantity is the volume integral of the fast-ion absorbed power density $p_{\mathrm{fast},s}(\mathbf{r})$ for charge state $s$:

$$
P_{\mathrm{fast},s} = \int_V p_{\mathrm{fast},s}(\mathbf{r}) \, dV
$$

where $V$ is the total plasma volume and $p_{\mathrm{fast},s}$ is the local deposition rate given by [fast_ion_state_power_density](name:fast_ion_state_power_density).

In RF wave modeling, the local deposition profile is obtained from quasi-linear wave-particle interaction calculations, then integrated over all flux surfaces. Summing over all charge states of a given ion species recovers [fast_ion_power](name:fast_ion_power), the total fast-ion absorbed wave power without charge-state resolution. The toroidal-mode-resolved cumulative variant is available via [per_toroidal_mode_fast_ion_state_power](name:per_toroidal_mode_fast_ion_state_power).

NAMES.name: fast_ion_state_power_density
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Absorbed wave power density deposited on fast (non-thermal) ions in a specified charge state, expressed per unit plasma volume. When averaged over a magnetic flux surface, it is the local radial source whose volume integral gives the cumulative absorbed power for that state.
NAMES.long:
Fast-ion state power density is the volumetric rate at which wave energy is transferred to the non-thermal ion population in a specified charge state. It is a charge-state-resolved component of [fast_ion_power_density](name:fast_ion_power_density) and is distinct from heating of the thermal-ion population represented by [thermal_ion_power_density](name:thermal_ion_power_density).

For nested magnetic flux surfaces labeled by a dimensionless radial label $\rho$, the flux-surface-averaged density is

$$
p_{\mathrm{fast},c}(\rho) = \frac{1}{V'(\rho)} \int_{S(\rho)} \frac{q_{\mathrm{fast},c}(\mathbf{x})}{|\nabla \rho|} \, dA
$$

where $p_{\mathrm{fast},c}$ is this power density in W m^-3, $c$ denotes the charge state, $q_{\mathrm{fast},c}$ is the local wave-to-fast-ion energy-transfer density in W m^-3, $S(\rho)$ is the magnetic flux surface, $dA$ is the area element in m^2, $|\nabla\rho|$ has units m^-1, and $V'(\rho)$ is the differential volume in m^3 per unit $\rho$. Integrating $p_{\mathrm{fast},c}(\rho)V'(\rho)$ from the magnetic axis to a chosen surface gives [fast_ion_state_power_at_inside_flux_surface](name:fast_ion_state_power_at_inside_flux_surface) in W.

In practice, this quantity is computed from wave absorption or energy-balance modeling that partitions deposited wave power among ion species, charge states, and thermal or fast components. Inputs typically include wave fields, resonance physics, the fast-ion distribution, charge-state populations, equilibrium geometry, and collisional energy exchange; no particular reconstruction or heating code is implied.

Typical flux-surface-averaged magnitudes are 10^3-10^6 W m^-3 for charge-state-resolved fast-ion wave heating in present tokamaks. Strongly localized resonant absorption can approach 10^7 W m^-3, while regions with little matching fast-ion population are near 0 W m^-3.
NAMES.sign: Positive when energy is transferred from the wave field to fast ions in the specified charge state.

NAMES.name: per_toroidal_mode_right_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field
NAMES.short: Amplitude of the right-hand circularly polarized E-minus component of a radio-frequency wave electric field for one toroidal Fourier mode. It is a local electric-field amplitude used to characterize polarization-dependent wave coupling and absorption.
NAMES.long:
Per-toroidal-mode right-hand circularly polarized wave electric field is the local amplitude of the $E^-$ component of an oscillatory electromagnetic wave for a single toroidal Fourier harmonic. It isolates the transverse wave-field component with right-hand circular polarization about the equilibrium magnetic-field direction. The quantity is local in the poloidal plane and is not a flux-surface average.

Let the toroidal dependence be expanded in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius in meters, $\phi$ is toroidal angle in radians, and $Z$ is vertical height in meters. For harmonic $n$, use a local right-handed field-aligned basis $(\hat{e}_1, \hat{e}_2, \hat{b})$ with $\hat{b}=\mathbf{B}_0/|\mathbf{B}_0|$ and $\hat{e}_1\times\hat{e}_2=\hat{b}$; with wave phasors proportional to $e^{i n\phi-i\omega t}$, the $E^-$ amplitude is:

$$
E_{-,n}(R,Z)=\left|\frac{E_{1,n}(R,Z)-iE_{2,n}(R,Z)}{\sqrt{2}}\right|
$$

where $E_{1,n}$ and $E_{2,n}$ are the complex transverse electric-field components of harmonic $n$, each in V m$^{-1}$; $n$ is the dimensionless toroidal mode number; $\omega$ is angular frequency in rad s$^{-1}$; and $E_{-,n}$ has units V m$^{-1}$. The minus projection $(E_{1,n}-iE_{2,n})/\sqrt{2}$ defines the right-hand circular $E^-$ basis convention, and this quantity is the magnitude of that complex component, not its phase.

In practice, $E_{-,n}$ is usually obtained from frequency-domain wave calculations of the launched antenna spectrum using the equilibrium magnetic field, plasma density, temperature, and species composition. Experimental constraints are indirect and can come from radio-frequency field probes, antenna loading, deposited-power estimates, fast-ion response, and comparison with inferred absorption patterns.

Typical amplitudes in ion-cyclotron-range heating are 10^2-10^4 V m^-1 in the confined plasma and 10^3-10^5 V m^-1 near antennas, edge evanescence regions, or strong resonance layers. Values scale approximately with the square root of launched power for fixed plasma conditions and depend strongly on the toroidal mode spectrum and polarization.

NAMES.name: perpendicular_fast_particle_energy
NAMES.subject: particle
NAMES.short: Perpendicular fast-particle energy is the non-negative kinetic energy content of the suprathermal particle population associated with motion perpendicular to the local magnetic field. For a gyrotropic fast-particle pressure tensor, it equals the plasma-volume integral of the perpendicular fast-particle pressure.
NAMES.long:
Perpendicular fast-particle energy is the volume-integrated kinetic energy of the fast, suprathermal particle population associated with velocity components perpendicular to the local magnetic field. It includes the two perpendicular velocity-space degrees of freedom and excludes the kinetic energy associated with motion parallel to the magnetic field. The value is non-negative and is zero when the plasma volume contains no perpendicular fast-particle pressure.

For a gyrotropic fast-particle pressure tensor, the perpendicular energy is defined by the volume integral of the perpendicular pressure component:

$$
W_{\perp,\mathrm{fast}} = \int_V p_{\perp,\mathrm{fast}}(\mathbf{x})\, dV
$$

where $W_{\perp,\mathrm{fast}}$ is in J, $p_{\perp,\mathrm{fast}}$ is the [perpendicular fast-particle pressure](name:perpendicular_fast_particle_pressure) in Pa ($\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$), $dV$ is a volume element in $\mathrm{m^3}$, and $V$ is the plasma volume considered. For the pressure tensor $\mathbf{P}_\mathrm{fast}=p_{\perp,\mathrm{fast}}(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{b}\mathbf{b})+p_{\parallel,\mathrm{fast}}\mathbf{b}\mathbf{b}$, the total fast-particle energy is $W_\mathrm{fast}=W_{\perp,\mathrm{fast}}+W_{\parallel,\mathrm{fast}}$, with $W_{\parallel,\mathrm{fast}}=\frac{1}{2}\int_V p_{\parallel,\mathrm{fast}}\,dV$. Thus the isotropic relation $3p/2$ applies to total scalar-pressure energy density, not to the perpendicular component alone.

In practice this quantity is computed from modeled or reconstructed fast-particle distribution functions by taking the perpendicular kinetic-energy moment to obtain $p_{\perp,\mathrm{fast}}$ and integrating it over the plasma volume. It may include contributions from neutral-beam ions, radio-frequency-heated ions, fusion alpha particles, or other suprathermal species, constrained by fast-particle diagnostics, neutron emission, diamagnetic measurements, and equilibrium pressure balance.

Typical values range from $10^3$-$10^5$ J in low- to moderate-power heated plasmas and $10^5$-$10^7$ J in strongly heated or reactor-scale plasmas. For an isotropic fast-particle distribution, the perpendicular part is about two thirds of the total fast-particle kinetic energy; pitch-angle anisotropy can make this fraction larger or smaller.

NAMES.name: thermal_electron_power
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Thermal electron power is the total coherent-wave power absorbed by the bulk thermal electron population, integrated over the plasma volume. It excludes power deposited in fast electrons, ions, or other channels.
NAMES.long:
Thermal electron power is the volume-integrated rate at which a coherent electromagnetic wave transfers energy to the bulk thermal electron population. It represents the thermal-electron heating channel of wave absorption and excludes absorption assigned to fast electrons, ions, or other particle populations.

The quantity is defined as the volume integral of the local thermal-electron wave power density:

$$
P_{e,\mathrm{th}} = \int_V p_{e,\mathrm{th}}(\mathbf{x}) \, dV
$$

where $P_{e,\mathrm{th}}$ is the total thermal electron power in W, $p_{e,\mathrm{th}}$ is the local power density in W m$^{-3}$, $\mathbf{x}$ is position in m, $dV$ is the volume element in m$^3$, and $V$ is the plasma volume over which absorption is evaluated.

In practice this power is inferred from wave-heating power balance, electron energy balance, heating modulation, or wave-absorption calculations constrained by launched power, transmission, reflection, and measured plasma conditions. It is a channel-resolved absorbed power, so consistency with the total absorbed wave power requires summing over all absorbing populations and accounting for unabsorbed or lost wave power.

Typical values range from near 0 W when thermal-electron absorption is weak to 10^4-10^7 W in many wave-heated tokamak plasmas, with values of several 10^7 W possible in high-power heating scenarios. The value depends on launched wave power, coupling efficiency, wave frequency, plasma density and temperature, magnetic configuration, and competing absorption by ions or fast particles.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the coherent wave transfers net energy to the bulk thermal electron population.

NAMES.name: per_toroidal_mode_thermal_electron_power
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Cumulative wave power absorbed by the thermal electron population from a coherent wave inside a flux surface, resolved per toroidal mode number.
NAMES.long:
The thermal electron power per toroidal mode number quantifies the wave energy deposition rate into the bulk Maxwellian electron population attributed to a single toroidal harmonic $n_\phi$ of a coherent wave's spectrum. When evaluated as a cumulative (volume-integrated) quantity inside a given flux surface, it reveals the radial deposition profile contributed by each toroidal harmonic to thermal electron heating.

The cumulative absorbed power from toroidal mode $n_\phi$ inside the flux surface at normalized radial coordinate $\rho$ is:

$$
P_{\rm th,e}(n_\phi, \rho) = \int_0^\rho p_{\rm th,e}(n_\phi, \rho') \, dV'
$$

where $p_{\rm th,e}(n_\phi, \rho')$ is the [per_toroidal_mode_thermal_electron_power_density](name:per_toroidal_mode_thermal_electron_power_density) and $dV'$ is the differential plasma volume element.

Summing over all toroidal mode numbers $n_\phi$ recovers the total [thermal_electron_power_at_inside_flux_surface](name:thermal_electron_power_at_inside_flux_surface), whose global limit is the parent quantity [thermal_electron_power](name:thermal_electron_power). This quantity is computed from full-wave or ray/beam-tracing models of RF wave propagation and absorption, where quasilinear wave–particle interaction determines how each toroidal harmonic deposits power into the thermal electrons. The analogous mode-resolved quantities for other species are [per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_power](name:per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_power) and [per_toroidal_mode_fast_electron_power](name:per_toroidal_mode_fast_electron_power).
NAMES.sign: Positive when net wave power flows from the coherent wave field into the thermal electron population.

NAMES.name: thermal_electron_power_density
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Volumetric coherent-wave power density absorbed by the thermal (bulk) electron population. It is the local rate of wave energy deposition into bulk electrons per unit plasma volume.
NAMES.long:
Thermal electron power density is the time-averaged volumetric rate at which a coherent wave transfers energy to the bulk thermal electron population. It represents electron heating by wave absorption, distinct from power deposited directly into ions, fast particles, or other nonthermal populations.

For a monochromatic wave, with physical fields written using peak-amplitude phasors as $\mathbf{E}(t)=\mathrm{Re}[\tilde{\mathbf{E}}e^{-i\omega t}]$ and $\mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{th},e}(t)=\mathrm{Re}[\tilde{\mathbf{J}}_{\mathrm{th},e}e^{-i\omega t}]$, the cycle-averaged absorbed power density is

$$
p_{\mathrm{th},e}=\left\langle \mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{th},e}(t)\cdot\mathbf{E}(t)\right\rangle_t = \frac{1}{2}\,\mathrm{Re}\!\left[\tilde{\mathbf{J}}_{\mathrm{th},e}\cdot\tilde{\mathbf{E}}^{*}\right]
$$

where $p_{\mathrm{th},e}$ is in W m$^{-3}$, $\mathbf{E}$ is the wave electric field in V m$^{-1}$, $\mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{th},e}$ is the induced current density associated with thermal electrons in A m$^{-2}$, $\omega$ is the angular frequency, $\langle\cdot\rangle_t$ denotes an average over a wave period, and $^{*}$ denotes complex conjugation. If rms phasor amplitudes are used instead of peak amplitudes, the factor $1/2$ is omitted.

The cumulative thermal-electron wave power inside a plasma volume is the volume integral of this local density, $P_{\mathrm{th},e}(V)=\int_V p_{\mathrm{th},e}\,dV$. For a volume bounded by a flux surface, this relation connects the local deposition density to [thermal_electron_power_at_inside_flux_surface](name:thermal_electron_power_at_inside_flux_surface).

In practice this quantity is computed from wave-field solutions and the electron response used to evaluate absorption, or inferred indirectly by constraining heating models with electron temperature, density, radiated-power, and power-balance measurements. Its spatial distribution depends on wave frequency, polarization, propagation, resonance or damping conditions, and the local electron distribution.

Typical magnitudes are strongly scenario dependent. Volume-averaged auxiliary wave heating is often of order $10^{4}$-$10^{6}$ W m$^{-3}$, while localized deposition regions can reach $10^{6}$-$10^{8}$ W m$^{-3}$ in high-power heating scenarios.
NAMES.sign: Positive when wave energy is transferred from the coherent wave field to the thermal (bulk) electron population.

NAMES.name: thermal_ion_power
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Total RF wave power absorbed by the bulk Maxwellian (thermal) ion population from a coherent wave, volume-integrated over the entire plasma.
NAMES.long:
Thermal ion power is the net rate at which a coherent RF wave deposits energy into the bulk Maxwellian ion distribution, integrated over the entire plasma volume. As the thermal ion-channel component of [ion_power](name:ion_power), it isolates wave energy transferred directly to the thermal bulk, distinct from absorption by suprathermal populations captured by [fast_ion_power](name:fast_ion_power).

The absorbed power follows from the volume integral of the wave–plasma energy coupling:

$$
P_{\rm th,i} = \frac{1}{2} \int_V \mathrm{Re}\!\left(\mathbf{J}_{\rm th,i}^* \cdot \mathbf{E}\right) dV
$$

where $\mathbf{J}_{\rm th,i}$ is the thermal ion current density driven by the coherent wave electric field $\mathbf{E}$, and $V$ is the plasma volume.

Full-wave or ray-tracing codes that incorporate the Maxwellian ion dielectric response (via the plasma dispersion function) are used to evaluate this quantity. Together with [thermal_electron_power](name:thermal_electron_power), [fast_ion_power](name:fast_ion_power), and [fast_electron_power](name:fast_electron_power), it partitions [absorbed_power](name:absorbed_power) across all plasma populations. In ion cyclotron resonance heating, the fraction directed to the thermal bulk versus fast minority ions depends on the resonance harmonic, minority concentration, and wave polarization at the resonance layer. The spatially resolved volumetric deposition per toroidal mode is described by [per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_power_density](name:per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_power_density).

NAMES.name: per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_power
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Cumulative coherent-wave power absorbed by bulk thermal ions inside a flux surface, resolved by toroidal mode number. It is the toroidal-mode spectrum of thermal-ion heating.
NAMES.long:
Per-toroidal-mode thermal-ion power is the cumulative rate at which a coherent wave transfers energy to the bulk thermal ion population for a single toroidal Fourier mode. The toroidal mode number labels Fourier structure in the toroidal angle $\phi$ of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height; it is not a cyclotron resonance harmonic order.

For a closed flux surface labeled by a radial surface label $\rho$, the cumulative power for ion species $i$ and toroidal mode $n$ is the volume integral of the corresponding local absorbed power density:

$$
P_{i,n}(\rho) = \int_{V(\rho)} p_{i,n}(\mathbf{x})\, dV
$$

where $P_{i,n}$ is the cumulative absorbed power in W, $p_{i,n}$ is the [per-toroidal-mode thermal-ion power density](name:per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_power_density) in W m$^{-3}$, $dV$ is a volume element in m$^3$, and $V(\rho)$ is the plasma volume enclosed by the selected flux surface. Summing $P_{i,n}$ over toroidal mode number gives the corresponding [thermal-ion power inside the flux surface](name:thermal_ion_power_at_inside_flux_surface) in W.

This quantity is usually computed from coherent-wave heating calculations by decomposing the wave field or absorbed power density into toroidal Fourier modes and integrating the wave-particle energy transfer over the chosen plasma volume. Experimentally it is inferred indirectly through consistency between wave coupling, ion heating, power balance, and equilibrium or transport analysis rather than measured as a separate direct observable.

Typical per-mode values range from near 0 W for weakly coupled modes to $10^3$-$10^7$ W for strongly absorbed radio-frequency heating in medium and large tokamaks. The sum over modes is bounded by the absorbed wave power available to thermal ions and can vary strongly with species composition, resonance location, wave spectrum, and plasma temperature.
NAMES.sign: Positive when electromagnetic wave energy is absorbed by the bulk thermal ion population.

NAMES.name: thermal_ion_power_density
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Volumetric absorbed wave power density deposited into the bulk Maxwellian ion population by coherent wave-particle interaction, summed over toroidal modes unless a mode-resolved quantity is specified.
NAMES.long:
Thermal ion power density is the local rate per unit volume at which a coherent electromagnetic wave transfers energy to the bulk Maxwellian ion population. It excludes energy deposited directly into fast ions or electrons and represents the total thermal-ion absorption associated with the wave; for a toroidal-mode decomposition, summing the mode-resolved contributions gives this quantity.

The local time-averaged absorption can be written in a quasi-linear Poynting-theorem form as

$$
p_{\mathrm{th},i}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_n \frac{1}{2}\,\mathrm{Re}\!\left[\mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{th},i,n}(\mathbf{x}) \cdot \mathbf{E}_n^*(\mathbf{x})\right]
$$

where $p_{\mathrm{th},i}$ is the thermal ion power density, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $n$ is the toroidal Fourier mode index in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, $\mathbf{E}_n$ is the complex wave electric-field amplitude, $\mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{th},i,n}$ is the induced current associated with the thermal ion response, $^*$ denotes complex conjugation, and $\mathrm{Re}$ denotes the real part. A positive value corresponds to conversion of wave energy into thermal ion internal energy.

In practice it is computed from coherent-wave fields and the thermal ion dielectric or damping response, including resonant wave-particle interactions, finite-Larmor-radius effects, and the relevant ion composition. Integrating this density over a plasma volume gives the corresponding [thermal_ion_power](name:thermal_ion_power), while integration inside a magnetic flux surface gives [thermal_ion_power_at_inside_flux_surface](name:thermal_ion_power_at_inside_flux_surface). Charge-state-resolved deposition is represented by [thermal_ion_state_power_density](name:thermal_ion_state_power_density), and toroidal-mode-resolved deposition by [per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_power_density](name:per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_power_density).

Typical values in RF-heated tokamak plasmas are about $10^3$-$10^6$ W m$^{-3}$ for broadly distributed thermal-ion absorption, with localized ion-cyclotron resonance layers or strong single-pass damping reaching $10^6$-$10^8$ W m$^{-3}$. Values can be much smaller away from resonant layers or when most wave power is absorbed by electrons or fast ions.

NAMES.name: per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_power_density
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Absorbed coherent-wave power density deposited in bulk thermal ions, resolved by toroidal mode number. It may be local or magnetic-surface averaged under the stated spatial convention; summing modes gives the total thermal-ion absorbed power density.
NAMES.long:
Per-toroidal-mode thermal-ion power density is the volumetric rate at which one toroidal Fourier component of a coherent wave deposits energy in the bulk thermal ion population. The mode number $n_\phi$ labels variation with toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle increasing counter-clockwise when viewed from $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height. The quantity can represent either a pointwise deposition density or a flux-surface-averaged density over a thin magnetic-surface shell.

The density is defined as the differential absorbed modal power per unit plasma volume:

$$
p_{\mathrm{th},i,n_\phi}(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{dP_{\mathrm{th},i,n_\phi}}{dV}(\mathbf{x})
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{th},i,n_\phi}$ is the coherent-wave power absorbed by bulk thermal ions from toroidal mode $n_\phi$, $dV$ is a plasma volume element, and $\mathbf{x}$ denotes either a spatial position or the magnetic-surface label after averaging. Thus $p_{\mathrm{th},i,n_\phi}$ has units W m$^{-3}$; integrating it over a chosen plasma volume gives [per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_power](name:per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_power), while summing over toroidal modes gives [thermal_ion_power_density](name:thermal_ion_power_density).

In practice this quantity is computed from the mode-resolved wave field and the thermal-ion part of the wave-particle energy balance or dielectric response. For a local convention, the value applies at the specified point; for a flux-surface-averaged convention, it is the shell-volume average whose product with shell volume gives the shell contribution to the absorbed power. The corresponding electron quantities are [per_toroidal_mode_thermal_electron_power_density](name:per_toroidal_mode_thermal_electron_power_density) and, after volume integration, [per_toroidal_mode_thermal_electron_power](name:per_toroidal_mode_thermal_electron_power); ion-state resolution is represented by [per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_state_power_density](name:per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_state_power_density).

Typical magnitudes range from $10^3$-$10^6$ W m$^{-3}$ in heated plasma cores, with localized resonance or damping regions reaching about $10^7$ W m$^{-3}$ in high-power scenarios and values near zero where the selected toroidal mode is weakly absorbed.
NAMES.sign: Positive when net coherent-wave energy is transferred to the bulk thermal ion population.

NAMES.name: thermal_ion_state_power
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Total power from a coherent electromagnetic wave absorbed by the thermal bulk ion population in a specified charge state, integrated over the plasma volume and summed over all toroidal mode numbers.
NAMES.long:
Thermal ion state power is the net rate at which a coherent electromagnetic wave transfers energy to the thermal, or bulk, ions of one specified ion charge state. It excludes power absorbed by electrons, other ion charge states, and non-thermal energetic-ion populations, and represents the sum over all toroidal mode numbers.

For a mode-decomposed wave field, the total thermal ion state power is defined by the mode-sum volume integral:

$$
P_{\mathrm{th},i}^{q} = \sum_n \int_V p_{\mathrm{th},i}^{q,n}(\mathbf{x})\, dV
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{th},i}^{q}$ is the total absorbed power for ion species $i$ in charge state $q$, $p_{\mathrm{th},i}^{q,n}$ is the local power-density transfer from toroidal mode number $n$ to that thermal ion state, and $V$ is the plasma volume over which absorption is evaluated. The single-mode contribution corresponds to [per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_state_power](name:per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_state_power).

In practice this quantity is computed from wave-field and plasma-response calculations by integrating the deposited power density for the selected ion charge state and summing the mode contributions. It may be constrained experimentally by total launched and coupled wave power, calorimetry or power-balance analysis, and changes in ion temperature, but the charge-state-resolved partition is generally model dependent.

Typical magnitudes for an actively heated thermal ion charge state range from 10^3-10^7 W in present magnetic-confinement experiments, with weakly coupled charge states near 0 W and high-power scenarios reaching 10^7-10^8 W.
NAMES.sign: Positive when energy is transferred from the coherent electromagnetic wave to the thermal ion population of the specified charge state.

NAMES.name: per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_state_power
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Wave power absorbed by a specified thermal ion species and charge state from one toroidal Fourier harmonic of a coherent wave. It is volume-integrated over the region enclosed by a magnetic flux surface; at the outer boundary it is the global contribution of that mode to charge-state-resolved ion heating.
NAMES.long:
Per-toroidal-mode thermal ion state power is the coherent-wave power absorbed by the thermal population of a specified ion species and charge state for one toroidal mode number. For an interior magnetic flux surface, it is a cumulative volume integral over the plasma region enclosed by that surface; at the outer boundary it is the total absorbed power for that charge state and mode. The toroidal mode number is the integer harmonic in a Fourier decomposition with respect to the toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

For a magnetic flux surface $S$, the cumulative contribution of mode $n$ can be written as

$$
P^{\mathrm{th}}_{a,z,n}(S) = \int_{V(S)} p^{\mathrm{th}}_{a,z,n}(\mathbf{x})\, dV
$$

where $P^{\mathrm{th}}_{a,z,n}$ is the absorbed power in W, $p^{\mathrm{th}}_{a,z,n}$ is the local absorbed power density in W m$^{-3}$, $dV$ is the volume element in m$^3$, $V(S)$ is the volume enclosed by $S$, $a$ labels the ion species, $z$ labels the charge state, and $n$ is dimensionless. Summing over toroidal mode numbers gives the total charge-state-resolved thermal ion power, $P^{\mathrm{th}}_{a,z}(S)=\sum_n P^{\mathrm{th}}_{a,z,n}(S)$, while summing over the relevant ion species and charge states gives the aggregate per-mode thermal ion power, $P^{\mathrm{th}}_{\mathrm{i},n}(S)=\sum_{a,z} P^{\mathrm{th}}_{a,z,n}(S)$.

In practice this quantity is obtained from coherent-wave absorption calculations, using local wave fields and thermal ion distribution functions to evaluate the absorbed power density before integrating over the enclosed volume. It may be constrained or checked against global power balance, charge-state composition, and diagnostics sensitive to ion heating, but it is fundamentally a mode-resolved deposition quantity rather than a directly local thermodynamic state variable.

Typical values for an individual charge-state and toroidal-mode contribution range from near 0 W for weakly coupled modes or nonresonant charge states to $10^3$-$10^7$ W in strongly heated plasmas. The sum over modes and charge states is bounded by the coherent-wave power coupled to the plasma and by losses to other particle populations or damping channels.
NAMES.sign: Positive when net wave energy is transferred from the coherent wave field to the specified thermal ion charge state.

NAMES.name: thermal_ion_state_power_density
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Volumetric coherent-wave power density absorbed by the thermal (bulk) ion population of a specified charge state, distinguishing bulk-ion heating from fast-particle wave absorption at the same charge state.
NAMES.long:
This quantity gives the local rate of wave energy deposition per unit plasma volume into the thermal ion population of one specified charge state from a coherent electromagnetic wave, such as an ion cyclotron resonance heating (ICRH) wave. It is the thermal-ion, charge-state-resolved component of the total ion-state power density, separating bulk-ion absorption from the suprathermal contribution captured by [fast_ion_state_power_density](name:fast_ion_state_power_density).

The local absorbed power density for thermal ions in charge state $q$ is:

$$
p_{\mathrm{th},q} = \frac{1}{2} \, \mathrm{Re}\!\left(\mathbf{E} \cdot \mathbf{J}^{*}_{\mathrm{th},q}\right)
$$

where $\mathbf{E}$ is the complex wave electric field amplitude and $\mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{th},q}$ is the complex current density response of the thermal ions in charge state $q$.

Summing over all charge states of a given species yields the species-level quantity [thermal_ion_power_density](name:thermal_ion_power_density). Volume-integrating over the region enclosed by a given flux surface gives the cumulative absorbed power [thermal_ion_state_power_at_inside_flux_surface](name:thermal_ion_state_power_at_inside_flux_surface), and the toroidal-mode-resolved form is available as [per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_state_power_density](name:per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_state_power_density). The quantity is computed from full-wave or ray-tracing wave propagation solvers coupled to a kinetic description of the bulk ion distribution.

In ICRH scenarios, bulk thermal-ion absorption power densities near the fundamental or harmonic cyclotron resonance layer reach 0.1–10 MW m$^{-3}$, with the partition between thermal and fast ions depending on the minority heating scheme and local ion temperature.

NAMES.name: wave_driven_current_density
NAMES.short: Local electric current density vector generated by directed momentum transfer from resonant electromagnetic waves to charged particles. It is the wave-driven contribution to the total current density, distinct from Ohmic and bootstrap currents.
NAMES.long:
Wave-driven current density is the local vector current carried by charged particles whose distribution functions are altered by resonant electromagnetic waves. It represents the current-drive contribution of auxiliary heating waves to the total [current_density](name:current_density), distinct from Ohmic, inductive, and bootstrap current. It is not a flux-surface average, volume average, or integrated current; those operations produce derived quantities such as [parallel_wave_driven_current_density](name:parallel_wave_driven_current_density) or contributions to [toroidal_plasma_current](name:toroidal_plasma_current).

In quasilinear kinetic descriptions, the wave-driven contribution is the first velocity moment of the wave-induced perturbation to the distribution function:

$$
\mathbf{j}_\mathrm{wave}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_s q_s \int \mathbf{v}\,\delta f_s^\mathrm{wave}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $s$ labels particle species, $q_s$ is the species charge in C, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element, and $\delta f_s^\mathrm{wave}$ is the wave-induced perturbation to the distribution function in $\mathrm{s^3\,m^{-6}}$. The sign of $q_s$ makes electron current opposite to the resonant electron drift velocity.

In practice, wave-driven current density is computed from injected wave spectra and polarization, wave propagation and absorption, quasilinear diffusion, and collisional relaxation of the resonant distribution function. It is constrained experimentally by magnetic equilibrium reconstruction, loop-voltage balance, current-drive efficiency estimates, and wave or emission diagnostics, but direct point measurements are uncommon. Integrating or projecting this vector over space and over launched modes yields mode-resolved or global current-drive quantities such as [per_toroidal_mode_current_due_to_wave_driven_current_drive](name:per_toroidal_mode_current_due_to_wave_driven_current_drive).

Typical local magnitudes in auxiliary-heated tokamaks are $10^3$-$10^5$ A.m^-2 over broad wave-absorption regions and can reach $10^5$-$10^6$ A.m^-2 in strongly localized current-drive regions. Flux-surface-averaged parallel values and volume-averaged values are generally smaller because regions of weak or oppositely directed drive contribute to the average.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the conventional-current component of $\mathbf{j}_\mathrm{wave}$ points in the positive direction of its stated basis vector; in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, a positive toroidal component flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: parallel_wave_driven_current_density
NAMES.short: Flux-surface-averaged parallel current density produced by resonant wave-particle interactions, giving the net RF-driven current per unit area along the magnetic field direction.
NAMES.long:
The parallel wave-driven current density is the flux-surface average of the wave-driven current projected along the equilibrium magnetic field, capturing the RF current-drive contribution to the parallel current profile from a single coherent wave. Resonant electromagnetic waves transfer directed momentum to the plasma, altering the particle velocity distribution in a way that produces a net current preferentially aligned with the magnetic field direction.

The defining relation is:

$$
j_{\parallel,\mathrm{wave}} = \frac{\langle \mathbf{j}_\mathrm{wave} \cdot \mathbf{B} \rangle}{B_0}
$$

where $\langle \cdots \rangle$ denotes the flux-surface average, $\mathbf{j}_\mathrm{wave}$ is the local wave-driven current density vector of the parent [wave_driven_current_density](name:wave_driven_current_density), $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field, and $B_0$ is the on-axis reference magnetic field magnitude.

This quantity is computed by quasi-linear or wave-kinetic RF solvers that determine the non-Maxwellian perturbation to the particle distribution induced by resonant wave absorption, then flux-surface-average the resulting driven current. The per-toroidal-mode resolved version is [parallel_per_toroidal_mode_wave_driven_current_density](name:parallel_per_toroidal_mode_wave_driven_current_density). Summed over all wave contributions, this quantity constitutes the wave-current-drive component of [parallel_non_inductive_current_density](name:parallel_non_inductive_current_density), alongside parallel_current_density_due_to_bootstrap and in contrast to the resistively driven [parallel_ohmic_current_density](name:parallel_ohmic_current_density).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the wave-driven parallel current flows in the direction of the equilibrium magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$.

NAMES.name: beryllium_density_at_divertor_target
NAMES.subject: beryllium
NAMES.short: Local non-negative number density of beryllium ions at the divertor target, summed over Be1+ through Be4+ charge states and excluding neutral beryllium atoms.
NAMES.long:
Beryllium density at the divertor target is the local number of beryllium ions per unit volume in the plasma adjacent to the divertor target surface. It is a species-resolved, non-negative scalar density for atomic number 4 and excludes neutral beryllium unless a separate neutral-density quantity is specified.

When individual charge states are not represented separately, the ion density is the sum over the bound-electron charge states of beryllium ions:

$$
n_{\mathrm{Be},\mathrm{tgt}} = \sum_{q=1}^{4} n_{\mathrm{Be}^{q+},\mathrm{tgt}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{Be},\mathrm{tgt}}$ is the beryllium ion number density at the divertor target, $n_{\mathrm{Be}^{q+},\mathrm{tgt}}$ is the partial number density in m$^{-3}$ of ions in charge state Be$^{q+}$, and $q$ is the charge-state index; an ion in charge state $q$ carries charge $+q e$, with $e$ the elementary charge. The neutral state Be$^{0}$ is not included in this sum.

In practice this quantity is inferred from beryllium line emission together with atomic population modeling, from impurity transport modeling constrained by edge and divertor measurements, or from edge-plasma simulations that evolve species-resolved ion densities. It is a beryllium-specific component of the local divertor-target ion population and should be interpreted relative to [total_ion_density_at_divertor_target](name:total_ion_density_at_divertor_target) when assessing impurity concentration.

Typical absolute values are strongly dependent on wall material, erosion and recycling conditions, ionization balance, and divertor plasma state, so no device-independent numerical range is implied by the definition. Under trace-impurity conditions $n_{\mathrm{Be},\mathrm{tgt}}$ is much smaller than the total target ion density; in all cases it is constrained to be non-negative and not larger than the local total ion density. Related beryllium-density quantities include [beryllium_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:beryllium_density_at_plasma_boundary), [beryllium_density_at_limiter](name:beryllium_density_at_limiter), [volume_averaged_beryllium_density](name:volume_averaged_beryllium_density), and [line_averaged_beryllium_density](name:line_averaged_beryllium_density).

NAMES.name: carbon_density_at_divertor_target
NAMES.subject: carbon
NAMES.short: Number density of carbon ions in the plasma immediately adjacent to a divertor target surface, summed over charge states C+ through C6+. Neutral carbon atoms and molecules are excluded unless a neutral-inclusive quantity is explicitly specified.
NAMES.long:
Carbon density at a divertor target is the local number density of carbon ions in the plasma immediately adjacent to a divertor target surface. It is a charge-state-summed impurity ion density, so neutral carbon atoms and molecules are treated as separate species and are not included.

The charge-state-summed carbon ion density is obtained by summing over the ionization stages of carbon:

$$
n_{C,\mathrm{ion}} = \sum_{q=1}^{6} n_{C^{q+}}
$$

where $n_{C,\mathrm{ion}}$ is the total carbon ion density in m^-3, $n_{C^{q+}}$ is the density of carbon ions in charge state $q$ in m^-3, and $q$ is the dimensionless positive ion charge state ranging from $1$ up to the nuclear charge $6$.

This density is commonly inferred from divertor spectroscopy of carbon emission lines combined with local electron density and temperature estimates and a collisional-radiative model, or evolved per charge state in edge-plasma transport calculations and then summed.

Typical values near divertor targets span a wide range depending on plasma-facing material composition, recycling regime, and detachment state, and are generally a fraction of the local total ion density.

NAMES.name: current_of_divertor
NAMES.short: Total net electric current carried by charged particles striking the divertor assembly, summed over all divertor target surfaces. It is positive for conventional current into the material and can be negative when the electron contribution dominates.
NAMES.long:
Current of a divertor is the net electric current delivered to the divertor by incident charged particles. It represents the charge transport associated with ions and electrons striking the plasma-facing divertor targets, summed over all relevant target surfaces.

The net incident current can be expressed as a surface integral of the signed particle charge flux:

$$
I_\mathrm{div} = \int_{A_\mathrm{div}} \sum_s q_s\,\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_s \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}_\mathrm{mat}\, dA
$$

where $A_\mathrm{div}$ is the union of divertor target surfaces, $q_s$ is the signed charge of species $s$, $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_s$ is the incident particle flux density of that species, and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}_\mathrm{mat}$ is the local unit normal directed from the plasma-facing side into the material.

In practice this current may be inferred from embedded target current sensors, biased divertor circuits, Langmuir-probe measurements combined with sheath models, or plasma-edge simulations that integrate ion and electron fluxes over the target surfaces. Care is needed to distinguish the net signed current from separate ion and electron current components, which can be much larger before cancelation.

Typical net summed currents are often near 0 A for electrically floating, quasi-ambipolar target conditions. During biased operation, strong sheath asymmetry, detachment transients, or disruption-related wall loading, absolute values from 1-10000 A can occur, with larger values possible in large devices or off-normal events.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the net conventional current carried by incident charged particles is directed from the plasma into the divertor material.

NAMES.name: current_of_divertor_tile
NAMES.short: Net electric current flowing from the plasma across the electrostatic sheath onto the plasma-facing surface of an individual divertor tile.
NAMES.long:
The current of a divertor tile is the net electric current flowing from the plasma across the electrostatic sheath onto the plasma-facing surface of a single tile. It provides tile-resolved resolution of the current distribution across the divertor strike zone, complementing the target-integrated quantity [current_at_divertor_target](name:current_at_divertor_target).

The tile current integrates the local net sheath current density $j_s$ over the plasma-facing tile area $A_\mathrm{tile}$:

$$
I_\mathrm{tile} = \int_{A_\mathrm{tile}} j_s \, dA
$$

where $j_s$ depends on the local ion saturation current density, the tile-to-plasma sheath potential, and the local [electron temperature at the divertor target](name:electron_temperature_at_divertor_target). Dividing by the tile area, available from [surface_area_of_divertor_tile](name:surface_area_of_divertor_tile), converts this quantity to a mean incident current density.

Tile currents are measured using isolated tile circuits or embedded Langmuir probes whose signals are routed through the mechanical tile support structure, enabling time-resolved acquisition during plasma operation including transient ELM events.

Summing contributions from all tiles on a given target recovers [current_at_divertor_target](name:current_at_divertor_target), and summing over all targets gives [current_of_divertor](name:current_of_divertor). Tile-level current data are used to diagnose thermoelectric current loops, local erosion hot spots, and strike-zone asymmetries driven by 3D magnetic perturbations.
NAMES.sign: Positive when net electric current flows from the plasma onto the tile surface.

NAMES.name: deuterium_density_at_divertor_target
NAMES.subject: deuterium
NAMES.short: Number density of deuterium ions in the plasma immediately adjacent to a divertor target. It is the species-resolved fuel-ion population at the plasma-material interface in deuterium-fueled operation.
NAMES.long:
Deuterium density at the divertor target is the local number density of deuterium ions, usually singly ionized $D^+$, in the plasma next to a divertor target surface. It is a species-resolved ion density, distinct from the species-agnostic [density at divertor target](name:density_at_divertor_target) and from [total ion density at divertor target](name:total_ion_density_at_divertor_target), which sums over all ion species present.

For a small volume element adjacent to the target, the deuterium ion density is defined by the local particle population per unit volume:

$$
n_D = \frac{dN_D}{dV}
$$

where $N_D$ is the number of deuterium ions in the volume element $dV$ and $n_D$ is the corresponding number density.

In practice, this quantity is inferred from local divertor plasma measurements and modeling, such as target-region probe analysis, spectroscopic interpretation of deuterium emission, or divertor Thomson scattering when available. The inferred value depends strongly on recycling, ionization balance, cross-field transport, sheath-edge conditions, and whether the divertor is attached, partially detached, or detached.

Typical values are about $10^{18}-10^{20}$ m^-3 in attached divertor conditions and can reach $10^{20}-10^{21}$ m^-3 in high-recycling or detached divertor conditions, depending on fueling, target heat flux, and divertor geometry.

NAMES.name: effective_charge_at_divertor_target
NAMES.short: Effective charge (Zeff) of the plasma evaluated at the divertor target, a dimensionless composite indicator of impurity content equal to unity for a pure hydrogen plasma and rising above unity as high-charge impurity species accumulate.
NAMES.long:
The effective charge $Z_\text{eff}$ characterizes the multi-species ion composition at the divertor target by weighting each ion species by the square of its charge number, normalized to the electron density. It reflects the local impurity content arising from sputtering of plasma-facing components, deliberate impurity seeding for power exhaust control, and recycling processes at the divertor surface.

The quantity is defined under quasi-neutrality by:

$$
Z_\text{eff} = \frac{\sum_s n_s Z_s^2}{n_e}
$$

where $n_s$ is the number density of ion species $s$ with charge number $Z_s$, and $n_e = \sum_s n_s Z_s$ is the electron number density enforced by quasi-neutrality. High-$Z$ impurities contribute disproportionately: a trace fraction of [iron_density_at_divertor_target](name:iron_density_at_divertor_target) or [argon_density_at_divertor_target](name:argon_density_at_divertor_target) raises $Z_\text{eff}$ far more than an equivalent density of [hydrogen_density_at_divertor_target](name:hydrogen_density_at_divertor_target).

$Z_\text{eff}$ at the divertor is inferred from spectroscopic impurity line emission or from the Bremsstrahlung continuum, whose volumetric emissivity scales as $n_e^2 Z_\text{eff}$. Impurity seeding enhances radiative power dissipation in detachment scenarios, thereby reducing the [peak_power_density_at_divertor_target](name:peak_power_density_at_divertor_target). This is the effective-charge component of the [charge_at_divertor_target](name:charge_at_divertor_target) family.

Typical values range from 1 for a pure hydrogen plasma to 2–8 in seeded or erosion-dominated divertor conditions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when at least one ion species with nonzero charge number is present in the plasma, as the numerator $\sum_s n_s Z_s^2$ and denominator $n_e$ are both positive under quasi-neutrality, ensuring $Z_\text{eff} \geq 1$.

NAMES.name: electron_density_at_divertor_target
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Electron number density in the plasma immediately adjacent to the divertor target surface. It is the downstream scrape-off-layer electron density at the target and is distinct from the electron density at the plasma boundary or separatrix.
NAMES.long:
Electron density at the divertor target is the local number of free electrons per unit volume in the plasma adjacent to the plasma-facing target, usually interpreted as a sheath-entrance or near-target plasma density rather than a property inside the solid surface. It characterizes downstream scrape-off-layer conditions at the material boundary and should not be identified with the separatrix value [electron_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:electron_density_at_plasma_boundary), which is evaluated upstream at the plasma boundary.

As a local number density it is defined by

$$
n_{e,t} = \left.\frac{dN_e}{dV}\right|_{\mathrm{target}}
$$

where $N_e$ is the number of free electrons in a small plasma volume $V$ adjacent to the target and $n_{e,t}$ is expressed in m$^{-3}$.

In practice, $n_{e,t}$ is obtained from near-target diagnostics and edge-plasma modeling. Flush or embedded Langmuir probes infer it from ion-saturation current using sheath assumptions, effective ion mass, and local electron and ion temperatures; divertor Thomson scattering and spectroscopic analysis can provide independent constraints where available. Reduced two-point scrape-off-layer estimates may infer $n_{e,t}$ from upstream or separatrix conditions and target temperature using quasineutrality and parallel pressure or momentum balance, but the coefficient relating upstream and target quantities depends on ion temperature, Mach number, sheath boundary conditions, volumetric momentum losses, radiation, recycling, and detachment state. Therefore a fixed electron-only pressure-balance factor is not a general definition; in such formulas both $n_{e,t}$ and any upstream density $n_{e,u}$ are electron number densities in m$^{-3}$.

Typical values are about $10^{18}$-$10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$ in sheath-limited or attached divertor conditions and $10^{20}$-$10^{21}$ m$^{-3}$ in high-recycling conditions. During detachment, the near-target density may rise before rollover and then decrease as the ionization front moves away from the target, so the range is strongly dependent on fueling, magnetic geometry, and power exhaust regime.

NAMES.name: electron_power_at_inner_divertor_target
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Electron thermal power deposited on the inner divertor target.
NAMES.long:
Electron power at the inner divertor target is the total rate at which electron thermal energy is deposited on the inner, high-field-side divertor target surface. It is the electron contribution to the deposited target power and is distinct from ion, neutral, radiative, or electromagnetic power contributions.

The deposited electron power is the surface integral of the electron heat-flux density normal to the target and directed into the material:

$$
P_{e,\mathrm{inner}} = \int_{A_\mathrm{inner}} q_{e,n}^{\mathrm{dep}} \, dA
$$

where $A_\mathrm{inner}$ is the inner target surface area over which electron heat is deposited, $dA$ is an element of target area in m$^2$, and $q_{e,n}^{\mathrm{dep}}$ is the deposited electron heat-flux density in W m$^{-2}$. If a vector electron heat flux is used, $q_{e,n}^{\mathrm{dep}}$ is its projection onto the unit normal pointing into the target material; only the into-surface electron thermal component is included.

In practice this quantity is obtained by integrating local electron heat-flux estimates over the inner target. Those estimates may come from Langmuir probe measurements with a sheath heat-transmission model, from surface calorimetry or infrared thermography combined with a model that separates the electron channel, or from edge-plasma simulations constrained by divertor diagnostics.

As a deposited power it is reported as a non-negative scalar; 0 W means that no resolved electron thermal power reaches the inner target. Values are strongly device- and scenario-dependent, ranging from near 0 W during highly detached or low-power phases to kilowatt or megawatt scales in powered divertor plasmas. The corresponding outer-target quantity is [electron_power_at_outer_divertor_target](name:electron_power_at_outer_divertor_target), while integrated divertor power balances are described by [thermal_power_of_divertor](name:thermal_power_of_divertor) and power_of_divertor.

NAMES.name: hydrogen_density_at_divertor_target
NAMES.subject: hydrogen
NAMES.short: Number density of hydrogen ions evaluated locally in the plasma adjacent to the divertor target surface.
NAMES.long:
Hydrogen density at the divertor target is the local number density of hydrogen ions in the plasma immediately adjacent to the target surface. It represents the hydrogen contribution to the ion population that enters the divertor sheath and participates in recycling, ionization balance, and target particle loading.

For an attached sheath-limited target, the hydrogen ion particle flux to the surface is often related to the local density by the Bohm sheath estimate:

$$
\Gamma_H \simeq n_H c_s
$$

where $n_H$ is the hydrogen ion density in m$^{-3}$, $\Gamma_H$ is the hydrogen ion particle flux density in m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$, and $c_s$ is the ion sound speed at the sheath entrance in m s$^{-1}$. In collisional or detached conditions, the same density may require a more detailed treatment of ionization, recombination, charge exchange, and flow between the plasma and the material surface.

This quantity is usually inferred rather than measured directly. Langmuir probes can constrain local electron density and ion saturation current, spectroscopy can constrain hydrogen emission and ionization sources through collisional-radiative analysis, and edge plasma modeling combines these observations with particle-balance assumptions to separate the hydrogen ion contribution from other ion species.

A universal numerical range is not intrinsic to the quantity because divertor target density varies strongly with machine size, fueling, detachment state, impurity seeding, and isotope mix. In hydrogen-dominated, singly ionized target plasma, $n_H$ is typically of the same order as the local [electron density](name:electron_density_at_divertor_target); in mixed-species plasmas it is the hydrogen component of the local [ion density](name:ion_density_at_divertor_target) and is reduced by deuterium, tritium, helium, or impurity dilution.

NAMES.name: iron_density_at_divertor_target
NAMES.subject: iron
NAMES.short: Number density of iron ions at the divertor target, summed over all ionization stages, providing a local measure of this high-Z metallic impurity from erosion of iron-containing plasma-facing and structural materials.
NAMES.long:
Iron is a high-Z metallic impurity in fusion plasmas, originating from sputtering and erosion of iron-containing structural components and plasma-facing materials. The iron number density at the divertor target represents the total number of iron ions per unit volume at the divertor target location, aggregated over all ionization states $z = 1, \ldots, 26$.

The combined iron density is defined as:

$$
n_\text{Fe} = \sum_{z=1}^{26} n_{\text{Fe}^{z+}}
$$

where $n_{\text{Fe}^{z+}}$ is the local density of iron ions in charge state $z$, in m$^{-3}$.
