where $n_\mathrm{B}$ is the local boron ion density in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$ summed over all charge states, $\psi_b$ is the flux value at the last closed flux surface, and $J$ (in $\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{T}$ for $(\psi, \theta)$) is the coordinate-space Jacobian that supplies the flux-surface-average weighting measure rather than a simple arithmetic average over poloidal angle. Near an X point the separatrix value is interpreted as a limit from neighboring closed flux surfaces.

The quantity is inferred from edge impurity emission spectroscopy combined with charge-state-resolved collisional-radiative and impurity-transport modeling, mapped to the plasma boundary through equilibrium reconstruction. Because each boron ion is counted once regardless of charge state, this is a particle density and carries no charge-squared weighting; charge-state populations are required separately to evaluate charge density, radiated power, or effective-charge contributions.

Unlike the present quantity, [volume_averaged_boron_density](name:volume_averaged_boron_density) averages over the entire confined plasma volume and, depending on definition, may include neutral boron. Boundary boron densities depend strongly on wall conditioning, boronization, and edge transport, and are typically small relative to the boundary total ion density.

NAMES.name: flux_surface_averaged_carbon_density
NAMES.subject: carbon
NAMES.short: Flux-surface average of the total elemental carbon number density on a closed magnetic surface. The local carbon density is summed over all charge states from neutral carbon to fully stripped carbon before averaging.
NAMES.long:
Flux-surface-averaged carbon density is the mean total elemental carbon number density on a closed magnetic flux surface. The local carbon density is summed over all charge states from neutral carbon through fully stripped carbon before averaging, matching the charge-state scope of [volume_averaged_carbon_density](name:volume_averaged_carbon_density) and [line_averaged_carbon_density](name:line_averaged_carbon_density) while using a magnetic-surface average.

For an axisymmetric closed surface labeled by the poloidal magnetic flux $\psi$, the flux-surface average over the closed poloidal contour is

$$
\langle n_C \rangle_\psi = \frac{\oint_\psi n_C(R,Z)\, R\, dl / |\nabla\psi|}{\oint_\psi R\, dl / |\nabla\psi|}
$$

where $n_C = \sum_{q=0}^{6} n_{\mathrm{C},q}$ is the total carbon density, $n_{\mathrm{C},0}$ is neutral carbon, and $n_{\mathrm{C},6}$ is fully stripped carbon. The contour lies in a poloidal cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, with $R$ the major radius, $\phi$ the toroidal angle, and $Z$ the vertical height; $dl$ is the arc-length element in meters, $\psi$ is in webers, and $|\nabla\psi|$ is in Wb m$^{-1}$. The denominator normalizes the geometric weighting so the result retains units of m$^{-3}$.

In practice, local charge-state densities are estimated from impurity spectroscopy, charge-exchange recombination measurements when available, collisional-radiative modeling, and particle-balance constraints for weakly observed charge states. A magnetic equilibrium maps those local estimates to the same closed flux surfaces used for [flux_surface_averaged_total_ion_density](name:flux_surface_averaged_total_ion_density), and the charge-state sum is formed consistently before applying the average.

Representative edge-plasma values are commonly $10^{16}-10^{18}\ \mathrm{m}^{-3}$ in carbon-wall or carbon-seeded conditions, with smaller values possible in low-carbon metal-wall plasmas and larger transient values during sputtering or injection events. Comparison with [ratio_of_carbon_density_to_electron_density](name:ratio_of_carbon_density_to_electron_density) expresses the carbon burden relative to electrons, while [carbon_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:carbon_density_at_magnetic_axis) gives the corresponding central local value. The analogous [flux_surface_averaged_iron_density](name:flux_surface_averaged_iron_density) applies the same magnetic-surface average to iron.

NAMES.name: flux_surface_averaged_iron_density
NAMES.subject: iron
NAMES.short: Flux-surface average of the total iron impurity ion number density, summed over all iron ionization states. It represents the density assigned to a magnetic flux surface after averaging local variation around that surface, not a statement that iron is spatially uniform there.
NAMES.long:
Flux-surface-averaged iron density is the average of the total iron impurity ion number density on a magnetic flux surface. The total iron density is summed over all iron ionization states. It is a representative density for the surface and does not imply that the local iron density is uniform on that surface.

The flux-surface average can be written using a poloidal magnetic flux label $\psi$:

$$
\langle n_{\mathrm{Fe}}\rangle_{\psi} = \frac{\int_{\psi=\mathrm{const}} n_{\mathrm{Fe}}\, dA/|\nabla\psi|}{\int_{\psi=\mathrm{const}} dA/|\nabla\psi|}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{Fe}}$ is the local total iron ion density in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, $n_{\mathrm{Fe}}=\sum_q n_{\mathrm{Fe}^{q+}}$ over iron ionization states $q$, $dA$ is a surface-area element in $\mathrm{m}^2$, and $|\nabla\psi|$ is in $\mathrm{Wb}\,\mathrm{m}^{-1}$ when $\psi$ is in $\mathrm{Wb}$. The weighting corresponds to averaging over the thin volume between neighboring flux surfaces.

In practice, this quantity is obtained by combining an equilibrium reconstruction that supplies the magnetic flux surfaces with local or modeled iron charge-state densities. These densities may be inferred from extreme-ultraviolet, x-ray, or visible line emission with collisional-radiative modeling, and may be constrained by impurity transport, radiation, electron density, and electron temperature measurements. Strong edge gradients and localized sources can make the local iron density vary strongly on a surface, so the flux-surface average should be interpreted as an averaged abundance rather than a local value.

Typical values for trace iron contamination are $10^{12}-10^{16}\ \mathrm{m}^{-3}$ in confined plasmas. During strong wall influx, impurity accumulation, disruptions, or deliberate impurity injection, edge or separatrix averages can reach $10^{17}\ \mathrm{m}^{-3}$ or higher.

NAMES.name: flux_surface_averaged_magnetic_shear
NAMES.short: Flux-surface value of magnetic shear, describing how the safety factor changes with normalized toroidal flux radius on a magnetic flux surface. When the safety factor is a flux function, it is the representative surface value, not an independent average of a local pointwise shear.
NAMES.long:
Flux-surface-averaged magnetic shear is the magnetic shear assigned to an entire magnetic flux surface, quantifying the radial variation of field-line pitch through the safety factor. It is the flux-surface counterpart of [magnetic_shear](name:magnetic_shear_at_pedestal); when the safety factor is constant on a flux surface, no separate local-shear averaging model is implied.

The value on a surface labeled by normalized toroidal flux radius $\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is defined by:

$$
s_{\mathrm{fs}}(\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}) = \frac{\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}}{q(\rho_{\mathrm{tor}})} \frac{d q}{d \rho_{\mathrm{tor}}}
$$

where $s_{\mathrm{fs}}$ is the flux-surface value of magnetic shear, $q$ is the [safety factor](name:safety_factor), and $\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}$ labels the flux surface, with $\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}=0$ at the magnetic axis and $\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}=1$ at the last-closed flux surface.

In practice, this quantity is inferred from an equilibrium description by evaluating the radial derivative of $q(\rho_{\mathrm{tor}})$ at the chosen surface, such as a separatrix, pedestal, or internal-transport-barrier location. It is sensitive to the local radial variation of $q$, so uncertainty is largest where the safety-factor variation is weakly constrained or changes rapidly.

Typical dimensionless values are of order unity to several in many tokamak equilibria. Values near zero indicate a locally flat safety-factor variation, negative values indicate reversed magnetic shear, and larger positive values can occur in steep-gradient edge or separatrix regions.

NAMES.name: helium_3_density_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.subject: helium_3
NAMES.short: Number density of helium-3 ions (the stable helium isotope with mass number 3) evaluated at the plasma boundary, the last closed flux surface separating the magnetically confined plasma from the scrape-off layer.
NAMES.long:
Helium-3 ($^3$He) is the stable helium isotope with two protons and one neutron (mass number 3, charge number 2). This quantity gives the number of $^3$He ions per unit volume evaluated at the plasma boundary, defined as the last closed flux surface (separatrix) that divides the closed-field-line confined region from the open-field-line scrape-off layer. It is the helium-3 specialization of [density_at_plasma_boundary](name:density_at_plasma_boundary).

Helium-3 enters tokamak plasmas either as a minority heating species in ion cyclotron resonance heating schemes, where a small $^3$He fraction resonates efficiently with the ICRH wave, or as a fuel ion in D-$^3$He burn scenarios. In both cases, the boundary density is a key parameter for edge particle balance and fuel-purity assessment. Boundary values are inferred from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy using $^3$He spectral lines or from edge transport modeling constrained by particle flux boundary conditions.

Typical $^3$He boundary densities in minority-heating scenarios lie in the range $10^{16}$–$10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$, well below the separatrix electron density of $10^{19}$–$10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$. The corresponding core value is captured by [helium_3_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:helium_3_density_at_magnetic_axis), the pedestal-top value by [helium_3_density_at_pedestal](name:helium_3_density_at_pedestal), and the downstream target value by [helium_3_density_at_divertor_target](name:helium_3_density_at_divertor_target), together forming a complete radial survey of $^3$He ion density from core to divertor.

NAMES.name: helium_4_density_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.subject: helium_4
NAMES.short: Number density of helium-4 ions evaluated on the plasma boundary, the last closed flux surface separating the magnetically confined plasma from the scrape-off layer.
NAMES.long:
Helium-4 density at the plasma boundary is the number density of ions whose nuclei are the isotope $^{4}\mathrm{He}$, evaluated on the last closed flux surface. The plasma boundary is the separatrix between the closed-field-line region and the scrape-off layer. The quantity is non-negative and is a species density, not a charge density.

Using a flux-coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$ with normalized radial label $\rho$ chosen so that the plasma boundary is at $\rho=1$, the local boundary value is

$$
n_{^{4}\mathrm{He},b} = n_{^{4}\mathrm{He}}(\rho=1)
$$

where $n_{^{4}\mathrm{He}}$ is the helium-4 ion number density field and the subscript $b$ denotes evaluation at the boundary. This definition specifies boundary evaluation only; it does not by itself imply a flux-surface average over $(\theta,\phi)$. If an averaged boundary value is used, that averaging is an additional reduction of the local boundary density.

In practice the value is obtained by evaluating a species-resolved edge plasma model or reconstruction at the separatrix, often constrained by spectroscopic, charge-exchange, divertor, or edge-profile measurements when available. In a fully ionized plasma, helium-4 is typically present as $\mathrm{He}^{2+}$, so its electron-density contribution is $2 n_{^{4}\mathrm{He}}$; charge-state effects should be treated consistently when partial ionization is important near the edge.

Typical values can range from near 0 m^-3 when helium-4 is absent or weakly retained to about $10^{16}$-$10^{19}$ m^-3 in plasmas with helium ash, helium fueling, or dedicated helium operation. The upper range is limited by the local edge electron density and the helium concentration.

NAMES.name: hydrogen_density_at_pedestal
NAMES.subject: hydrogen
NAMES.short: Hydrogen (protium) ion number density evaluated at the H-mode pedestal top.
NAMES.long:
Hydrogen density at pedestal is the local number density of protium ions at the pedestal top of an H-mode plasma. The pedestal top is the inner edge of the steep-gradient edge transport barrier, where the edge density gradient relaxes toward the core plasma behavior.

In practice, this quantity is inferred from edge density measurements together with ion-species composition information and an identification of the pedestal-top location. It represents the protium ion contribution only; deuterium, tritium, and impurity ions are separate species contributions to the total ion population.

Representative values are scenario dependent. In majority-hydrogen H-mode plasmas, pedestal-top protium ion densities are commonly of order $1-10 \times 10^{19}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$; in mixed-isotope or trace-hydrogen plasmas they can be substantially lower depending on fueling, isotope mix, and edge transport.

NAMES.name: hydrogen_density_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.subject: hydrogen
NAMES.short: Number density of hydrogen (protium) ions at the plasma boundary, the last closed flux surface separating the magnetically confined plasma from the open-field-line scrape-off layer.
NAMES.long:
Hydrogen ion number density at the plasma boundary is the count of protium (H+) ions per unit volume at the separatrix, the last closed flux surface (LCFS) that bounds magnetically confined plasma against the open-field-line scrape-off layer. As the hydrogen-specific instance of [density_at_plasma_boundary](name:density_at_plasma_boundary), it characterizes the local protium population at the edge transport boundary, governing ionization balance, recycling flux, and neutral penetration depth.

The boundary value is obtained as the flux-surface average of the local hydrogen ion density over the LCFS:

$$
n_H^{\rm sep} = \frac{1}{S_{\rm LCFS}} \oint_{\rm LCFS} n_H \, dS
$$

where $S_{\rm LCFS}$ is the total area of the last closed flux surface and $n_H$ is the local hydrogen ion number density on the surface.

This quantity is inferred from edge Thomson scattering, Balmer-series hydrogen spectroscopy (H$\alpha$ emission), or Langmuir-probe measurements combined with ionization-balance modeling in edge fluid codes.

In deuterium-dominated discharges, protium (hydrogen-1) is a minority main-ion species due to wall outgassing; separatrix hydrogen ion densities lie in the range $10^{17}$–$10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$, rising toward $10^{19}$ m$^{-3}$ in hydrogen-fueled or heavy-recycling scenarios. The analogous density for the dominant fuel isotope is [deuterium_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:deuterium_density_at_plasma_boundary), while heavier impurity boundary densities include [carbon_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:carbon_density_at_plasma_boundary) and [helium_4_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:helium_4_density_at_plasma_boundary).

NAMES.name: ion_average_temperature_at_pedestal_top
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Ion average temperature at the pedestal top is the density-weighted temperature of all ion species and charge states evaluated at the core-side shoulder of the H-mode pedestal. The pedestal top is distinct from the pedestal foot near the separatrix and scrape-off layer.
NAMES.long:
Ion average temperature at the pedestal top is the ion_average_temperature evaluated at the core-side shoulder of the H-mode edge transport barrier. Moving outward from the plasma center, this location marks the transition from the central plasma to the steep-gradient pedestal region; it is distinct from the pedestal foot on the separatrix and scrape-off-layer side.

For ion populations indexed by $j$, where each population corresponds to a species and charge state, the pedestal-top average is commonly defined as a density-weighted mean:

$$
\langle T_i \rangle_{\mathrm{top}} = \frac{\sum_j n_{j,\mathrm{top}} T_{j,\mathrm{top}}}{\sum_j n_{j,\mathrm{top}}}
$$

where $T_{j,\mathrm{top}}$ is the temperature of ion population $j$ in eV, $n_{j,\mathrm{top}}$ is its number density in m^-3, and the subscript $\mathrm{top}$ denotes evaluation at the pedestal-top radial location. If the value is used to estimate SI ion thermal pressure, the eV-valued temperature must be converted by the elementary charge: $p_i = e\,n_i\langle T_i\rangle_{\mathrm{top}}$, with $n_i = \sum_j n_{j,\mathrm{top}}$.

In practice, this quantity is inferred from edge ion-temperature measurements such as charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, neutral-particle analysis, or integrated kinetic analysis, combined with an identification of the pedestal-top location from the measured radial variation of temperature, density, or pressure. When only impurity-ion temperatures are measured, main-ion temperature estimates require collisional equilibration or transport assumptions.

Typical pedestal-top ion average temperatures range from 100-1000 eV in smaller or moderate-performance H-mode plasmas and from 1000-5000 eV in large, high-performance H-mode plasmas. The value varies with heating power, pedestal density, isotope mix, collisionality, and edge-localized-mode phase.

NAMES.name: ion_heat_decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Radial e-folding decay length of the ion heat flux in the scrape-off layer, equal to the inverse magnitude of its outward logarithmic radial gradient. It is non-negative by definition and characterizes how rapidly ion heat exhaust falls away from the separatrix.
NAMES.long:
The ion heat decay length over the scrape-off layer is the radial e-folding scale over which the ion heat flux decreases outside the confined plasma. It characterizes the width of the ion heat exhaust channel and complements the electron-channel quantity [electron_heat_decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer](name:electron_heat_decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer) in determining the overall heat-exhaust fall-off described by [heat_decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer](name:heat_decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer).

The local decay length is the inverse magnitude of the outward logarithmic gradient of the ion heat flux:

$$
\lambda_{q_i} = \left|\frac{\partial \ln q_i}{\partial r_\perp}\right|^{-1}
$$

where $q_i(r_\perp)$ is the positive ion heat-flux density in W m^-2, $r_\perp$ is distance in meters measured locally outward from the separatrix approximately normal to magnetic flux surfaces, and $\lambda_{q_i}$ is in meters. For an exponential dependence $q_i \propto \exp(-r_\perp/\lambda_{q_i})$, the ion heat flux decreases by a factor $e$ over one decay length.

In practice, this quantity is inferred by fitting or differentiating the radial dependence of ion heat-flux estimates in the scrape-off layer. Those estimates may come from target heat measurements, probe-based ion energy and particle flux measurements, edge power balance, or transport modeling with magnetic mapping between divertor and upstream locations. It is distinct from ion temperature decay lengths such as [radial_average_ion_temperature_decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer](name:radial_average_ion_temperature_decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer) and ion_average_decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer, because it describes heat-flux fall-off rather than temperature fall-off.

Typical magnitudes in present tokamak scrape-off layers are on the order of 0.001-0.03 m, ranging from millimeter-scale widths in narrow high-confinement conditions to centimeter-scale widths in broader low-confinement or high-collisionality conditions. The value depends on plasma density, power crossing the separatrix, magnetic geometry, collisionality, and whether the quoted location is upstream or mapped to the divertor target.

NAMES.name: iron_density_at_pedestal
NAMES.subject: iron
NAMES.short: Charge-state-summed number density of iron impurity ions at the H-mode pedestal top, where the steep edge transport barrier joins the flatter confined plasma.
NAMES.long:
Iron density at the pedestal is the total number density of iron impurity ions on the pedestal-top flux surface. It is summed over all ionized charge states of iron and is non-negative as a particle number density. The pedestal top is the shoulder of the H-mode edge transport barrier, often identified consistently with quantities such as [density_at_pedestal](name:density_at_pedestal), electron_density_at_pedestal_top, and [electron_temperature_at_pedestal_top](name:electron_temperature_at_pedestal_top).

The charge-state-summed pedestal density is defined by

$$
n_{\mathrm{Fe,ped}} = \sum_{q=1}^{26} n_{\mathrm{Fe}^{q+}}(\rho_\mathrm{ped})
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{Fe,ped}}$ is the total iron ion density at the pedestal top in m$^{-3}$, $n_{\mathrm{Fe}^{q+}}$ is the density of iron ions with charge state $q+$ in m$^{-3}$, and $\rho_\mathrm{ped}$ denotes the pedestal-top flux surface.

Iron is a high-Z metallic impurity commonly produced by sputtering or erosion of steel components, ferritic materials, and other iron-containing plasma-facing structures. At the pedestal, iron can contribute strongly to line radiation and bremsstrahlung losses, so this local density is important for interpreting pedestal energy balance, impurity screening, and edge confinement degradation. It complements [volume_averaged_iron_density](name:volume_averaged_iron_density), [iron_density_at_divertor_target](name:iron_density_at_divertor_target), and [iron_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:iron_density_at_internal_transport_barrier).

In practice, the pedestal iron density is inferred from spectroscopic measurements of selected iron emission lines, typically in the vacuum ultraviolet, soft X-ray, or charge-exchange wavelength ranges, together with collisional-radiative or ionization-balance modeling to recover the total charge-state-summed density. The pedestal-top location is usually obtained from fitted edge profiles, commonly near the transition between the steepest-gradient pedestal region and the flatter core plasma.

Representative pedestal values are highly device-, wall-condition-, and scenario-dependent: clean discharges may have about $10^{12}$-$10^{14}$ m$^{-3}$, while stronger metallic source conditions or impurity-accumulation phases can reach $10^{15}$-$10^{16}$ m$^{-3}$. Related seeded-impurity pedestal densities include [nitrogen_density_at_pedestal](name:nitrogen_density_at_pedestal) and [argon_density_at_pedestal](name:argon_density_at_pedestal).

NAMES.name: lithium_density_at_pedestal
NAMES.subject: lithium
NAMES.short: Number density of ionized lithium at the H-mode pedestal top, equal to the local sum over Li+, Li2+, and Li3+ charge states. Neutral lithium atoms are excluded, so the quantity is non-negative and expressed per cubic meter.
NAMES.long:
Lithium density at the pedestal is the local number density of ionized lithium evaluated at the H-mode pedestal top, where the steep-gradient edge transport barrier transitions toward the flatter core plasma. It includes the lithium ion charge states Li$^+$, Li$^{2+}$, and Li$^{3+}$, and excludes neutral lithium atoms, lithium molecules, and wall-bound lithium. The value is a local pedestal-top density, not an average over the pedestal region.

The pedestal-top lithium-ion density is defined by the charge-state sum:

$$
n_{\mathrm{Li,ped}} = \sum_{q=1}^{3} n_{\mathrm{Li}^{q+}}\big|_{\mathrm{ped}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{Li}^{q+}}\big|_{\mathrm{ped}}$ is the local number density of lithium ions with charge state $q+$ at the pedestal top. The neutral density $n_{\mathrm{Li}^0}$ is not included in this sum.

In practice, this quantity is inferred from lithium-sensitive spectroscopy, charge-exchange or emission analysis where available, and impurity transport or collisional-radiative modeling constrained by local electron density and temperature. The pedestal-top location is usually identified from steep-gradient-region structure in measured or reconstructed edge plasma quantities, then the lithium charge-state densities are evaluated at that location.

Typical values are strongly scenario dependent. In plasmas without an active lithium source the value may be zero or below diagnostic detectability, while lithium-conditioned or lithium-injected plasmas often remain in a trace-impurity range of about $10^{14}$-$10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$ at the pedestal top; higher local values can occur during strong transient injection.

NAMES.name: lithium_density_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.subject: lithium
NAMES.short: Number density of ionized lithium impurity at the plasma boundary, identified with the separatrix. It is summed over Li+, Li2+, and Li3+ charge states, excludes neutral lithium, and is a non-negative scalar in m^-3.
NAMES.long:
Lithium density at the plasma boundary is the number density of ionized lithium impurity at the separatrix, the interface between closed magnetic flux surfaces and open scrape-off-layer field lines. It includes all ionized lithium charge states, Li$^+$ through Li$^{3+}$, and excludes neutral lithium. As a particle number density, it is non-negative and has unit m$^{-3}$.

The charge-state-summed lithium ion density is defined by:

$$
n_\mathrm{Li} = \sum_{q=1}^{3} n_{\mathrm{Li}^{q+}}
$$

where $n_\mathrm{Li}$ is the total ionized lithium number density in m$^{-3}$, $n_{\mathrm{Li}^{q+}}$ is the number density in m$^{-3}$ of lithium ions with charge state $q$, and $q=1,2,3$ for lithium. Neutral lithium, $\mathrm{Li}^0$, is not included.

Boundary lithium ion density is inferred from edge impurity spectroscopy, charge-exchange measurements when available, atomic-physics modeling, and consistency with separatrix electron density and temperature. When represented as a single boundary scalar, it denotes a representative separatrix value; it should not be interpreted as necessarily flux-surface averaged unless the quantity is explicitly identified as flux-surface averaged, as in [flux_surface_averaged_electron_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:flux_surface_averaged_electron_density_at_plasma_boundary).

Typical separatrix lithium ion densities are often trace levels of about $10^{14}$-$10^{17}$ m$^{-3}$, but active lithium injection, evaporation, or strong lithium wall sources can raise values toward $10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$. These values are usually small compared with [total_ion_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:total_ion_density_at_plasma_boundary) and the corresponding electron density, but they can still affect edge radiation and [effective_charge_at_plasma_boundary](name:effective_charge_at_plasma_boundary). The concept is analogous to other impurity boundary densities such as [carbon_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:carbon_density_at_plasma_boundary).

NAMES.name: magnetic_shear_at_pedestal
NAMES.short: Dimensionless magnetic shear — the normalized logarithmic derivative of the safety factor with respect to normalized toroidal flux radius — evaluated at the H-mode pedestal transport barrier.
NAMES.long:
Magnetic shear quantifies the spatial variation of field-line helicity across nested flux surfaces, controlling the stability of MHD and drift-wave modes. Evaluated at the pedestal — the steep pressure-gradient transport barrier characteristic of H-mode confinement — it enters directly into peeling-ballooning stability criteria governing edge-localized modes and sets constraints on the maximum achievable pedestal pressure.

The pedestal magnetic shear is defined as:

$$
s = \frac{\rho_\mathrm{tor}}{q} \frac{dq}{d\rho_\mathrm{tor}}
$$

where $q$ is the local safety factor and $\rho_\mathrm{tor}$ is the normalized toroidal flux radius, equal to 0 at the magnetic axis and 1 at the separatrix. This is the scalar pedestal-locus counterpart of the radial profile [magnetic_shear](name:magnetic_shear_at_pedestal), and is analogous in structure to [magnetic_shear_at_magnetic_axis](name:magnetic_shear_at_magnetic_axis) evaluated on axis and [magnetic_shear_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:magnetic_shear_at_internal_transport_barrier) evaluated at internal barriers.

Pedestal magnetic shear is inferred from equilibrium reconstruction, combining external magnetic measurements with internal profile constraints such as motional Stark effect polarimetry or pressure-profile data. In conventional H-mode pedestals, $s$ spans 1–5, reflecting the rapid increase in $q$ across the narrow pedestal width; reversed-shear configurations can yield negative values near the pedestal foot.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $q$ increases with increasing $\rho_\mathrm{tor}$, corresponding to outward-increasing field-line helicity toward the plasma edge.

NAMES.name: neon_density_at_pedestal
NAMES.subject: neon
NAMES.short: Neon ion number density at the H-mode pedestal top, summed over all ionization charge states of the neon element. It is a non-negative elemental impurity density at the transition from the steep edge transport barrier to the flatter core plasma.
NAMES.long:
The neon density at the pedestal is the total number density of neon ions at the H-mode pedestal top, where the steep-gradient edge transport barrier joins the more weakly varying confined plasma. It is an elemental impurity density: ions in different neon charge states contribute to the same total. As a number density, it is non-negative and has units of $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$.

The charge-state-summed elemental density is defined by

$$
n_{\mathrm{Ne,ped}} = \sum_{q=1}^{Z_\mathrm{Ne}} n_{\mathrm{Ne}^{q+},\mathrm{ped}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{Ne,ped}}$ is the neon ion number density at the pedestal top in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, $n_{\mathrm{Ne}^{q+},\mathrm{ped}}$ is the number density in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$ of neon ions with charge state $q+$ at the pedestal top, and $Z_\mathrm{Ne}=10$ is the nuclear charge of neon.

In practice, this quantity is obtained by summing resolved charge-state densities, or by inferring the elemental neon content from impurity measurements together with a pedestal-top location determined from plasma profiles and equilibrium information. It is commonly interpreted relative to [electron_density_at_pedestal](name:electron_density_at_pedestal) or main_ion_density_at_pedestal, for example through the concentration $n_{\mathrm{Ne,ped}}/n_{e,\mathrm{ped}}$, because neon is usually a trace or minor impurity rather than the dominant ion species.

Typical values are strongly scenario-dependent, especially in plasmas with deliberate neon seeding for edge radiation control. No device-independent absolute range is implied by the definition; the physically useful scale is usually the neon concentration relative to the local pedestal electron or main-ion density.

This quantity is the neon counterpart of pedestal impurity densities such as [nitrogen_density_at_pedestal](name:nitrogen_density_at_pedestal), [oxygen_density_at_pedestal](name:oxygen_density_at_pedestal), and [xenon_density_at_pedestal](name:xenon_density_at_pedestal). The same elemental neon density evaluated at an internal transport barrier is represented by [neon_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:neon_density_at_internal_transport_barrier).

NAMES.name: neon_density_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.subject: neon
NAMES.short: Number density of neon ions at the plasma boundary (separatrix), the last closed flux surface separating the magnetically confined plasma from the open-field-line scrape-off layer.
NAMES.long:
The neon impurity density at the plasma boundary quantifies the concentration of neon ions at the separatrix, which marks the transition between the nested closed flux surfaces of the confined plasma and the open-field-line scrape-off layer. Neon (atomic number $Z = 10$) is a widely used medium-Z seeding species whose partially stripped ionization states radiate efficiently in the edge region and divertor, contributing to radiative power exhaust and reducing peak heat loads on plasma-facing components.

The separatrix neon density $n_\mathrm{Ne}$ provides a key boundary condition for impurity transport models linking the core plasma to the exhaust region. It complements [neon_density_at_divertor_target](name:neon_density_at_divertor_target) in constraining the neon distribution between the separatrix and the divertor target, and belongs to the same species-resolved family as [nitrogen_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:nitrogen_density_at_plasma_boundary), [xenon_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:xenon_density_at_plasma_boundary), and [deuterium_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:deuterium_density_at_plasma_boundary), all components of [density_at_plasma_boundary](name:density_at_plasma_boundary).

Boundary neon density is measured or inferred through charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, emission spectroscopy from helium-like or hydrogen-like neon charge states, or estimated from integrated power balance coupled with edge transport modeling. The reported value is often a flux-surface average over the separatrix contour.

In neon-seeded experiments, separatrix densities range from roughly $10^{17}$ to $10^{19}$ m$^{-3}$, scaling with the gas injection throughput and local edge transport properties.
NAMES.sign: Positive when neon ions are present at a nonzero concentration at the plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: neutral_state_effective_momentum_convection_velocity
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: Effective velocity vector used in a fluid closure for convective momentum transport of one resolved neutral state. It sets the transport direction and speed multiplying the neutral momentum density in the convective momentum-flux tensor.
NAMES.long:
The neutral state effective momentum convection velocity is the vector velocity assigned to the convective transport of momentum for a single resolved neutral population state. It is a closure quantity: it need not be identical to the bulk neutral flow velocity, but it has the same physical dimensions and determines how that state's momentum is carried through space in the model.

A common dyadic closure for the convective momentum-flux tensor is

$$
\Pi^{(a)}_{\mathrm{conv},ij} = m_a n_a v^{(a)}_{\mathrm{mom},i} u^{(a)}_j
$$

where $a$ labels the resolved neutral state, $\Pi^{(a)}_{\mathrm{conv},ij}$ is the convective flux of the $j$-th momentum component across a surface normal to the $i$ direction in kg.m^-1.s^-2, $m_a$ is the neutral particle mass in kg, $n_a$ is the neutral number density in m^-3, $v^{(a)}_{\mathrm{mom},i}$ is the $i$-th component of this effective momentum convection velocity in m.s^-1, and $u^{(a)}_j$ is the $j$-th component of the neutral fluid velocity in m.s^-1. With this convention the dyadic product orders the transport direction first and the transported momentum component second.

This quantity is generally obtained from a neutral-fluid or coupled edge-plasma transport closure rather than measured directly. The relation between this state-resolved velocity and an aggregate neutral effective momentum convection velocity is model-dependent; the aggregate represents a population-combined momentum-transport closure and is not necessarily a simple arithmetic average of the state-resolved values.

No universal numerical range exists because the value depends on the neutral-state definition, collision rates, recycling source, and closure assumptions. In edge-plasma and divertor fluid modeling, component magnitudes are often of order 10^2-10^4 m.s^-1, with larger values possible when the effective transport follows faster neutral drift or thermal motion.
NAMES.sign: Positive when a component points along the positive basis direction used for that component; in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, positive components point toward increasing $R$, increasing toroidal angle $\phi$, or increasing $Z$, respectively.

NAMES.name: nitrogen_density_at_pedestal
NAMES.subject: nitrogen
NAMES.short: Number density of nitrogen impurity ions at the H-mode pedestal top, where the steep-gradient edge transport barrier transitions to the flatter core plasma.
NAMES.long:
Nitrogen density at the pedestal is the total number density of nitrogen impurity ions at the pedestal top of an H-mode plasma. Unless a charge state is specified separately, it represents the sum over all nitrogen ionization states at the location where the steep edge transport barrier joins the core plasma.

The density is the zeroth velocity moment of the nitrogen ion distribution functions at the pedestal-top position:

$$
n_{\mathrm{N,ped}} = \sum_q \int f_{\mathrm{N}^{q+}}(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{ped}},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{N,ped}}$ is in m^-3, $q$ indexes nitrogen ionization charge states, $f_{\mathrm{N}^{q+}}$ is the phase-space distribution function with units m^-6 s^3, $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{ped}}$ is the pedestal-top position, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity in m/s, and $d^3v$ has units m^3 s^-3. For a single resolved charge state, the summation is omitted.

In practice this quantity is inferred from impurity spectroscopy, charge-exchange recombination measurements when available, and collisional-radiative modeling, often constrained by local electron density and temperature at the pedestal top. The pedestal top is identified from the transition between the steep edge gradient region and the core plasma, commonly using fitted electron pressure, density, or temperature behavior.

Representative pedestal nitrogen densities span roughly 10^16-10^19 m^-3, depending strongly on nitrogen seeding level, edge transport, ionization balance, and plasma size. Trace or unseeded conditions are usually toward the lower end, while actively seeded H-mode plasmas can reach the upper part of this range locally.

NAMES.name: nitrogen_density_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.subject: nitrogen
NAMES.short: Number density of nitrogen impurity ions evaluated at the plasma boundary (separatrix), representing the impurity concentration at the last closed flux surface separating confined plasma from the scrape-off layer.
NAMES.long:
Nitrogen ion number density at the plasma boundary quantifies the concentration of nitrogen impurity ions at the separatrix — the last closed flux surface demarcating the magnetically confined plasma from the open-field-line scrape-off layer. This is the nitrogen-species instantiation of [density_at_plasma_boundary](name:density_at_plasma_boundary). Nitrogen is routinely injected into tokamaks as a controlled impurity to enhance radiative dissipation of exhaust power and reduce peak heat loads at divertor targets.

The boundary value reflects the balance between impurity sources (gas injection, ionization of recycled neutrals) and outward transport through the scrape-off layer. Its magnitude relative to the main-ion density influences the effective charge $Z_\mathrm{eff}$ and the radiated power fraction at the plasma edge. The toroidal flow of nitrogen at the same location is separately captured by [toroidal_nitrogen_velocity_at_plasma_boundary](name:toroidal_nitrogen_velocity_at_plasma_boundary).

The quantity is inferred from spectroscopic measurements of nitrogen line emission in the edge and divertor regions combined with collisional-radiative modeling, or from fluid impurity transport simulations constrained by bolometric data. Typical values range from $10^{16}$ to $10^{19}$ m$^{-3}$, depending on the nitrogen injection rate and edge plasma density. Analogous separatrix densities for other impurity species include [neon_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:neon_density_at_plasma_boundary), [carbon_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:carbon_density_at_plasma_boundary), and [oxygen_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:oxygen_density_at_plasma_boundary).
NAMES.sign: Positive definite, as number density is a particle count per unit volume and does not change sign under any coordinate transformation.

NAMES.name: normalized_poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_pedestal
NAMES.short: Dimensionless radial coordinate of the H-mode pedestal, defined as the normalized poloidal magnetic flux evaluated at the pedestal's flux surface.
NAMES.long:
The normalized poloidal magnetic flux coordinate $\psi_N$ maps the equilibrium poloidal flux function $\psi$ to the interval $[0, 1]$ by subtracting the on-axis value and dividing by the flux range from axis to boundary. Evaluated at the pedestal, it provides a dimensionless, device-independent label for the radial location of the H-mode edge transport barrier.

The defining relation is:

$$
\psi_N = \frac{\psi - \psi_0}{\psi_b - \psi_0}
$$

where $\psi_0$ is [the poloidal flux at the magnetic axis](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis), $\psi_b$ is its value at the last closed flux surface, and $\psi$ is the flux at the flux surface of interest. The pedestal center in this coordinate marks the inflection point of the steep-gradient region; combined with the pedestal [full width], it fully characterizes the radial extent and location of the barrier.

In H-mode operation, the pedestal position is found in the range $\psi_N \approx 0.88$–$0.99$, with the exact value depending on plasma shaping, current, and heating power. It is extracted from analytic fits to edge profiles of electron density, temperature, or pressure using methods such as modified hyperbolic-tangent or piecewise-linear models. The companion quantity [poloidal magnetic flux at the pedestal](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_pedestal) gives the corresponding absolute flux value without normalization.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the pedestal flux surface lies outside the magnetic axis, so that $\psi > \psi_0$.

NAMES.name: oxygen_density_at_pedestal
NAMES.subject: oxygen
NAMES.short: Oxygen impurity ion number density at the H-mode pedestal top, where the steep-gradient edge transport barrier meets the flatter core profile.
NAMES.long:
The oxygen ion number density at the pedestal top characterizes the volumetric concentration of oxygen impurities within the H-mode edge transport barrier. Oxygen (atomic number $Z = 8$) enters tokamak plasmas primarily through plasma-wall interactions and recycling; at the pedestal, its local density contributes to fuel dilution, radiative heat losses, and the effective charge $Z_\mathrm{eff}$.

The quantity $n_\mathrm{O}$ represents the total oxygen ion number density summed over all ionization charge states at the pedestal-top flux surface. At pedestal electron temperatures of 0.3–1 keV, oxygen approaches full ionization, predominantly occupying the $\mathrm{O}^{7+}$ and $\mathrm{O}^{8+}$ charge states. This is the oxygen-specific member of the [density_at_pedestal](name:density_at_pedestal) family, using the same pedestal-top evaluation convention as [neon_density_at_pedestal](name:neon_density_at_pedestal), [carbon_density_at_pedestal](name:carbon_density_at_pedestal), and [nitrogen_density_at_pedestal](name:nitrogen_density_at_pedestal).

Oxygen pedestal density is inferred from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy or from impurity transport modeling constrained by soft X-ray and visible spectroscopy data. Typical values in current tokamak experiments range from $10^{16}$ to $10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$, representing a trace level relative to the main ion pedestal density. The associated fluid velocity at the pedestal is captured by [toroidal_oxygen_velocity_at_pedestal](name:toroidal_oxygen_velocity_at_pedestal).
NAMES.sign: Positive when oxygen ions are present at the pedestal location.

NAMES.name: oxygen_density_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.subject: oxygen
NAMES.short: Flux-surface-averaged number density of oxygen impurity ions at the plasma boundary, defined by the last closed flux surface separating the confined plasma from the scrape-off layer. It represents the sum over oxygen ion charge states, not neutral oxygen.
NAMES.long:
Oxygen density at the plasma boundary is the elemental number density of ionized oxygen on the last closed flux surface, taken as a flux-surface average over that boundary. It is one impurity-species contribution to [total_ion_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:total_ion_density_at_plasma_boundary); the quantity counts oxygen ions as particles and is not charge-weighted.

The total oxygen ion density at the boundary is obtained by summing charge-state-resolved oxygen ion densities and applying the boundary flux-surface average:

$$
n_{\mathrm{O},b} = \left\langle \sum_{q=1}^{8} n_{\mathrm{O}^{q+}} \right\rangle_{\mathrm{LCFS}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{O}^{q+}}$ is the number density of oxygen ions with charge $q e$, $q=1$ to $8$ spans singly ionized through fully stripped oxygen, and $\langle\cdot\rangle_{\mathrm{LCFS}}$ denotes the flux-surface average over the last closed flux surface, normally understood as the closed-surface limit approaching the separatrix.

In practice this density is inferred from impurity spectroscopy combined with electron temperature, electron density, ionization balance, and impurity transport modeling. Line emission constrains charge states with bound electrons, while the fully stripped contribution is inferred indirectly from ionization balance or recombination-related information.

Typical boundary oxygen ion densities are highly scenario dependent. In tokamak edge analyzes oxygen is usually a trace impurity, with representative values around 10^14-10^18 m^-3, and should be interpreted relative to the local total ion and electron densities.

NAMES.name: parallel_ion_heat_convection_velocity
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: The effective velocity at which bulk ion thermal energy is advected along magnetic field lines in the edge plasma, used as a transport coefficient in the parallel ion energy equation.
NAMES.long:
The parallel ion heat convection velocity is the field-aligned component of the effective velocity governing convective ion thermal-energy transport in the edge plasma. It represents the aggregate ion population over all charge states, in contrast to the per-charge-state quantity parallel_effective_ion_state_energy_convection_velocity, which resolves a single ionization level.

In the ion energy equation, the parallel convective heat flux density is:

$$
q_{\parallel,i}^{\text{conv}} = \frac{5}{2}\, n_i T_i\, v_{\parallel,\text{heat}}^{i}
$$

where $n_i$ is the total ion number density, $T_i$ is the ion temperature, and $v_{\parallel,\text{heat}}^{i}$ is this convection velocity. The prefactor $5/2$ reflects the enthalpy content per particle for a monatomic ideal gas.

This quantity is computed from edge plasma fluid transport models solving the ion energy equation in the scrape-off layer and divertor regions. Values range from order $10^2$ m/s in low-density far-SOL regions to near the ion acoustic speed ($\sim 10^4$–$10^5$ m/s) approaching divertor target plates, depending on local ion density and temperature.

The parent quantity [ion_heat_convection_velocity](name:ion_heat_convection_velocity) defines the full vector; the parallel component dominates along open field lines where parallel transport greatly exceeds cross-field transport. The analogous transport coefficient for parallel momentum is [parallel_momentum_effective_convection_velocity](name:parallel_momentum_effective_convection_velocity).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the ion heat convection is directed along the local magnetic field unit vector $\hat{b} = \mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$.

NAMES.name: parallel_plasma_momentum_flux
NAMES.short: Parallel plasma momentum flux is the double projection of the charged-plasma momentum-flux tensor along the local magnetic-field direction. It includes bulk-flow transport of parallel momentum, isotropic pressure, and parallel viscous or anisotropic stress.
NAMES.long:
Parallel plasma momentum flux is the component of the charged-plasma momentum-flux tensor obtained by projecting both tensor indices along the local magnetic-field direction. It represents the effective pressure-like transport of parallel momentum through a surface normal to the field, including streaming inertia, thermodynamic pressure, and parallel viscous stress. Because it is a double projection, it is unchanged by reversing the sign chosen for the magnetic-field unit vector and should not be interpreted as a one-way directed flux.

For charged species $s$, the total parallel component is

$$
\Phi_{\parallel,\mathrm{plasma}} = \hat{\mathbf{b}}\cdot\left[\sum_{s\in\mathrm{charged}}\left(\rho_s\mathbf{u}_s\mathbf{u}_s + p_s\mathbf{I} + \boldsymbol{\pi}_s\right)\right]\cdot\hat{\mathbf{b}} = \sum_{s\in\mathrm{charged}}\left(\rho_s u_{\parallel s}^2 + p_s + \pi_{\parallel\parallel s}\right)
$$

where $\hat{\mathbf{b}}=\mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$ is dimensionless, $\rho_s$ is mass density in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, $\mathbf{u}_s\mathbf{u}_s$ is the dyadic product of the flow velocity with itself, $\mathbf{u}_s$ is in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $u_{\parallel s}=\mathbf{u}_s\cdot\hat{\mathbf{b}}$, $p_s$ is scalar pressure in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$, $\mathbf{I}$ is the identity tensor, $\boldsymbol{\pi}_s$ is the viscous or anisotropic stress tensor in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$, and $\pi_{\parallel\parallel s}=\hat{\mathbf{b}}\cdot\boldsymbol{\pi}_s\cdot\hat{\mathbf{b}}$. The $\rho_s u_{\parallel s}^2$ term is mean-flow advective transport; a Reynolds-stress contribution from turbulent velocity fluctuations would be a separate modeled closure.

In edge-plasma modeling this quantity is computed from charged-species density, parallel flow, scalar pressure, and a closure or kinetic evaluation of the parallel stress. Experimentally, its components are constrained by density and temperature measurements, spectroscopic flow measurements, probes where applicable, and momentum-balance analysis; the viscous or anisotropic stress contribution is often inferred rather than directly measured. The neutral counterpart resolved by neutral state is [parallel_neutral_state_momentum_flux](name:parallel_neutral_state_momentum_flux).

Typical magnitudes in scrape-off-layer and divertor plasmas are 0.1-10^4 kg m^-1 s^-2. Attached edge conditions commonly give 10-10^3 kg m^-1 s^-2, while cold detached regions can be below 10 kg m^-1 s^-2 and short transients or high-recycling divertor conditions can reach 10^4 kg m^-1 s^-2 or more.

NAMES.name: poloidal_flux_surface_averaged_electron_beta_at_pedestal_top
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Dimensionless ratio of electron kinetic pressure to flux-surface-averaged poloidal magnetic pressure, evaluated at the H-mode pedestal top.
NAMES.long:
The poloidal electron beta using the flux-surface-averaged poloidal field quantifies the electron pressure balance against the poloidal confining field at the outer edge of the H-mode transport barrier. Using the flux-surface average of the poloidal magnetic field removes the poloidally asymmetric variation between the high-field and low-field sides, providing a single representative value per flux surface at the pedestal top.

The defining relation is:

$$
\beta_{p,e}^{\mathrm{avg}} = \frac{2\mu_0 \, p_e}{\langle B_\theta \rangle_{\mathrm{fs}}^2}
$$

where $p_e$ is the electron kinetic pressure at the pedestal top, $\langle B_\theta \rangle_{\mathrm{fs}}$ is the flux-surface-averaged poloidal magnetic field at the same flux surface — see poloidal_flux_surface_averaged_magnetic_field_at_pedestal_top — and $\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}$ H m$^{-1}$ is the permeability of free space.

Values are inferred from pedestal profile analysis, combining electron temperature and density fits (modified hyperbolic tangent or linear functions applied to Thomson scattering data) with equilibrium magnetic field reconstruction for the poloidal field. Typical values in H-mode pedestals range from 0.05 to 0.5 across current tokamaks.

The flux-surface-average normalization distinguishes this quantity from [poloidal_electron_beta_at_pedestal_top_high_field_side](name:poloidal_electron_beta_at_pedestal_top_high_field_side), which evaluates $B_\theta$ at the high-field-side midplane, and from [poloidal_electron_beta_at_pedestal_top](name:poloidal_electron_beta_at_pedestal_top_high_field_side), which uses the poloidal field at a specific poloidal location. The total-species analog is [beta_at_pedestal_top](name:beta_at_pedestal_top).

NAMES.name: radial_plasma_momentum_diffusion_coefficient
NAMES.short: Effective radial diffusion coefficient for cross-field transport of ion-fluid momentum in the edge plasma. It aggregates the momentum carried by all ion species and charge states into a single transport parameter, rather than resolving it per species or charge state.
NAMES.long:
Radial plasma momentum diffusion coefficient is the scalar coefficient that relates the radial (cross-field) diffusive flux of ion-fluid momentum to the radial gradient of momentum density in the edge plasma. It is an aggregate quantity summed over all ion species and charge states; electron inertial momentum is usually negligible in these ion-dominated edge regimes and is not included. It complements the species- and charge-state-resolved [radial_ion_state_momentum_diffusivity](name:radial_ion_state_momentum_diffusivity).

In a Fickian transport closure, the radial diffusive flux of a momentum component is proportional to the radial gradient of the corresponding aggregate momentum density:

$$
\Gamma_j = -D \, \frac{\partial \mathcal{P}_j}{\partial r_\perp}
$$

where $D$ is the radial plasma momentum diffusion coefficient, $\Gamma_j$ is the radial flux of the $j$-th momentum component in kg m^-1 s^-2, $r_\perp$ is the distance measured outward normal to flux surfaces in m, and $\mathcal{P}_j = \sum_{a,z} m_a\, n_{a,z}\, u_{a,z,j}$ is the aggregate ion momentum density in kg m^-2 s^-1, with $m_a$ the ion mass in kg, $n_{a,z}$ the number density of charge state $z$ of species $a$ in m^-3, and $u_{a,z,j}$ the corresponding fluid-velocity component in m s^-1. The leading minus sign means a positive coefficient drives momentum down its gradient, from regions of higher toward lower momentum density.

The coefficient is typically inferred as an effective transport parameter from edge momentum-balance analysis, measured ion flows and rotation shear, and comparisons with collisional, neoclassical, or turbulence-based transport estimates. It is the aggregate momentum counterpart to the aggregate energy and particle transport coefficients radial_total_energy_diffusion_coefficient and [radial_diffusion_coefficient](name:radial_ion_particle_diffusivity), and pairs with the convective term radial_ion_effective_momentum_convection_velocity in diffusion-convection closures.

Representative effective edge-plasma values used in transport modeling are of order 0.01-10 m^2 s^-1, with smaller values where diffusive coupling is weak and larger values in regions of strong turbulent or externally driven momentum redistribution. This range is indicative and not a physical bound.

NAMES.name: toroidal_argon_velocity_at_pedestal
NAMES.subject: argon
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of argon impurity bulk flow velocity evaluated at the H-mode pedestal top, a key quantity for determining the pedestal radial electric field through the impurity force balance.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal velocity of argon ions at the pedestal top quantifies the $\hat{\phi}$-directed bulk flow of this impurity species within the steep-gradient edge transport barrier of H-mode plasmas. Alongside [toroidal nitrogen velocity at the pedestal](name:toroidal_nitrogen_velocity_at_pedestal) and [toroidal tungsten velocity at the pedestal](name:toroidal_tungsten_velocity_at_pedestal), it enables species-resolved comparison of impurity momentum transport in the pedestal region.

The toroidal velocity component $v_\phi^{\rm Ar}$ enters the radial force balance for argon ions:

$$
E_r = v_\phi^{\rm Ar} B_\theta - v_\theta^{\rm Ar} B_\phi + \frac{1}{Z_{\rm Ar} e n_{\rm Ar}} \frac{dp_{\rm Ar}}{dr}
$$

where $E_r$ is the radial electric field, $B_\theta$ and $B_\phi$ are the poloidal and toroidal magnetic field components, $v_\theta^{\rm Ar}$ is the argon poloidal velocity, $Z_{\rm Ar}$ is the mean ionization state of argon, $n_{\rm Ar}$ is the argon number density (see [argon density at the pedestal](name:argon_density_at_pedestal)), and $p_{\rm Ar}$ is the argon pressure.

Argon toroidal velocity at the pedestal is measured by charge exchange recombination spectroscopy (CXRS), which detects the Doppler shift of argon emission lines excited by neutral beam injection in the pedestal region. The full radial profile of argon rotation is built from this pedestal value together with the counterpart quantities [at the magnetic axis](name:toroidal_argon_velocity_at_magnetic_axis), [at the internal transport barrier](name:toroidal_argon_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier), and [at the plasma boundary](name:toroidal_argon_velocity_at_plasma_boundary).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the argon flow points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_beryllium_velocity_at_pedestal
NAMES.subject: beryllium
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of beryllium impurity ion velocity at the H-mode pedestal, where the steep electron pressure gradient defines the edge transport barrier.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal velocity of beryllium ions at the pedestal is the projection of the beryllium impurity ion fluid velocity onto the toroidal direction $\hat{\phi}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, evaluated at the pedestal location.

The defining projection is:

$$
v_{\phi}^{\rm Be} = \mathbf{v}_{\rm Be} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_{\rm Be}$ is the beryllium ion fluid velocity and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

Toroidal impurity rotation is measured by charge exchange recombination spectroscopy (CXRS), in which the Doppler shift of Be emission lines at the pedestal chord positions yields the local toroidal velocity. The pedestal's steep pressure gradient and associated radial electric field well can drive strong toroidal velocity shear, contributing to turbulence suppression at the edge transport barrier. Toroidal velocities at the pedestal range from near-zero in low-momentum-input plasmas to tens of km/s in discharges with strong neutral-beam injection. Position-resolved analogs are available via [toroidal_beryllium_velocity_at_plasma_boundary](name:toroidal_beryllium_velocity_at_plasma_boundary) and [toroidal_beryllium_velocity_at_magnetic_axis](name:toroidal_beryllium_velocity_at_magnetic_axis); the analogous quantity for tritium at the same location is [toroidal_tritium_velocity_at_pedestal](name:toroidal_tritium_velocity_at_pedestal).
NAMES.sign: Positive when $v_{\phi}^{\rm Be}$ is directed in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$).

NAMES.name: toroidal_carbon_velocity_at_pedestal_top
NAMES.subject: carbon
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the carbon impurity ion fluid velocity evaluated at the pedestal top, the steep-gradient transport barrier just inside the separatrix in H-mode plasmas.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal carbon velocity at the pedestal top quantifies the $\phi$-component of the carbon impurity ion fluid velocity at the top of the H-mode transport barrier, where the steep pressure-gradient region transitions to the flatter core profile. Carbon (typically fully stripped C$^{6+}$ in hot plasmas) provides a widely used spectroscopic tracer for plasma toroidal rotation because inter-species Coulomb collisions couple impurity and main-ion momenta on the neoclassical timescale.

The toroidal velocity component is defined as:

$$
v_\phi = \mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{C}} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{C}}$ is the carbon ion fluid velocity and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

This quantity is measured by charge exchange recombination spectroscopy (CXRS): a neutral beam excites carbon ions in the pedestal region, and the resulting Doppler-shifted C VI emission line encodes the line-of-sight velocity component. Spatial resolution is set by the beam geometry and viewing configuration. Typical pedestal-top values range from a few km/s up to tens of km/s depending on plasma current, heating scheme, and device size. The analogous carbon velocity at other radial locations includes [toroidal carbon velocity at the magnetic axis](name:toroidal_carbon_velocity_at_magnetic_axis), [at the internal transport barrier](name:toroidal_carbon_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier), and [at the plasma boundary](name:toroidal_carbon_velocity_at_plasma_boundary). The hydrogen-isotope counterpart in the pedestal region is [toroidal hydrogen velocity at the pedestal](name:toroidal_hydrogen_velocity_at_pedestal).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the carbon ion flow is in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$).

NAMES.name: toroidal_carbon_velocity_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.subject: carbon
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the carbon impurity ion bulk flow velocity at the plasma boundary, resolved in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It is the local value at the last-closed flux surface, not a flux-surface average.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal carbon velocity at the plasma boundary is the component of the carbon impurity ion bulk flow along the toroidal direction at the last-closed flux surface or separatrix. The toroidal direction is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. This quantity denotes a local boundary value; the corresponding flux-surface-averaged quantity is [toroidal_flux_surface_averaged_carbon_velocity_at_plasma_boundary](name:toroidal_flux_surface_averaged_carbon_velocity_at_plasma_boundary).

The local toroidal component is defined by projecting the carbon bulk velocity onto the toroidal unit vector:

$$
v_{\phi}^{\mathrm{C}} = \mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{C}} \cdot \hat{\phi} = R\Omega_{\mathrm{C}}
$$

where $v_{\phi}^{\mathrm{C}}$ is the carbon toroidal velocity in m.s^-1, $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{C}}$ is the carbon ion bulk velocity in m.s^-1, $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$, $R$ is the major radius in m, and $\Omega_{\mathrm{C}}$ is the carbon toroidal angular rotation frequency in s^-1.

In practice, this velocity is commonly inferred from Doppler shifts of carbon spectral lines, often using charge-exchange or passive edge spectroscopy, after correcting for viewing geometry and projecting the measured line-of-sight velocity onto the toroidal direction. The plasma boundary location is usually supplied by magnetic equilibrium reconstruction, and the measured or modeled velocity is mapped to the last-closed flux surface. When only an average over the boundary flux surface is intended, the flux-surface-averaged standard name should be used instead.

Typical absolute values at the plasma boundary are of order $10^3-5 \times 10^4$ m.s^-1 in tokamak edge plasmas. Values can be close to zero in weakly rotating conditions and can approach $10^5$ m.s^-1 in plasmas with strong external torque or steep edge rotation gradients.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the carbon ion flow is in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_deuterium_tritium_velocity_at_pedestal
NAMES.subject: deuterium_tritium
NAMES.short: Toroidal velocity of the fictitious DT single-species (atomic mass 2.5 amu) at the H-mode pedestal, used in simulations treating the deuterium-tritium fuel as a single ion fluid.
NAMES.long:
The fictitious DT species is a single-fluid representation of the deuterium-tritium fuel mixture, assigned an atomic mass of 2.5 amu (the arithmetic mean of deuterium mass 2 and tritium mass 3), and treated as a single ion population in transport and gyrokinetic simulations. The toroidal velocity of this species at the pedestal quantifies the bulk toroidal rotation of the fuel ions within the steep-gradient edge transport barrier characteristic of H-mode plasmas.

The toroidal component is the projection of the DT ion fluid velocity onto the toroidal unit vector $\hat{\phi}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame:

$$
v_\phi = \mathbf{v}_\mathrm{DT} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_\mathrm{DT}$ is the DT ion fluid velocity vector.

Toroidal rotation at the pedestal contributes to the $E \times B$ shear layer that suppresses turbulent transport and sustains the H-mode confinement barrier. Ion toroidal velocities are inferred from Doppler shifts in charge exchange recombination spectroscopy (CXRS) emission lines on trace impurity species and corrected to the DT fuel population via neoclassical offsets. This pedestal evaluation belongs to a spatial family that includes [toroidal_deuterium_tritium_velocity_at_magnetic_axis](name:toroidal_deuterium_tritium_velocity_at_magnetic_axis) and [toroidal_deuterium_tritium_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:toroidal_deuterium_tritium_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier); the resolved deuterium counterpart at the same location is [toroidal_deuterium_velocity_at_pedestal](name:toroidal_deuterium_velocity_at_pedestal).
NAMES.sign: Positive when $v_\phi$ points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$).

NAMES.name: toroidal_deuterium_velocity_at_pedestal
NAMES.subject: deuterium
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the deuterium ion fluid velocity evaluated at the H-mode pedestal, defined as the projection of the deuterium flow along increasing toroidal angle phi in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal deuterium velocity at the pedestal is the toroidal component of the deuterium ion fluid velocity evaluated in the steep-gradient edge region that forms the H-mode pedestal. It represents the projection of the species flow along the toroidal basis direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The component is defined by projecting the local deuterium fluid velocity onto the toroidal unit vector:

$$
v_{\phi,D,\mathrm{ped}} = \mathbf{v}_{D,\mathrm{ped}} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_{D,\mathrm{ped}}$ is the deuterium ion fluid velocity at the pedestal in m.s^-1, $\hat{\phi}$ is the dimensionless unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$, and $v_{\phi,D,\mathrm{ped}}$ is the toroidal component in m.s^-1.

In practice this quantity is inferred from spectroscopic ion Doppler measurements, momentum-balance analysis, or edge transport interpretation. Measurements often involve impurity-ion rotation and require physics assumptions to relate the observed species to deuterium, including collisional coupling, neoclassical effects, and radial electric-field constraints; the pedestal location is identified from the local steep-gradient edge region.

Typical pedestal toroidal deuterium velocities are strongly scenario dependent. Many edge analyzes find values from near 0 to several $10^4$ m.s^-1 in magnitude, while plasmas with strong external torque or large intrinsic rotation can approach order $10^5$ m.s^-1; either sign is possible depending on the rotation direction.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the deuterium ion fluid velocity at the pedestal points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_deuterium_velocity_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.subject: deuterium
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the deuterium ion bulk flow velocity at the last closed flux surface. It is the projection along increasing toroidal angle phi in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal deuterium velocity at the plasma boundary is the toroidal component of the bulk flow velocity of deuterium ions evaluated on the last closed flux surface. The toroidal direction is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The boundary value is the projection of the deuterium bulk velocity onto the local toroidal unit vector:

$$
v_{D,\phi,b} = \mathbf{v}_D(\mathbf{x}_b,t) \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $v_{D,\phi,b}$ is the toroidal deuterium velocity at the boundary in m s$^{-1}$, $\mathbf{v}_D$ is the deuterium ion bulk velocity in m s$^{-1}$, $\mathbf{x}_b$ is a point on the last closed flux surface with $R$ and $Z$ in meters and $\phi$ in radians, $t$ is time, and $\hat{\phi}$ is the dimensionless unit vector in the direction of increasing $\phi$.

In practice this quantity is inferred by evaluating or reconstructing the deuterium flow field at the plasma boundary and projecting it onto $\hat{\phi}$. It may be constrained by ion-flow spectroscopy, edge diagnostics where applicable, and equilibrium or transport interpretation that maps measured velocities to the last closed flux surface; it is a boundary toroidal component and is distinct from a flux-surface average.

Typical boundary toroidal deuterium velocities in tokamak plasmas are often within $-5\times10^4$ to $5\times10^4$ m s$^{-1}$, with magnitudes approaching $1\times10^5$ m s$^{-1}$ in strongly momentum-driven or rapidly rotating edge conditions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the deuterium bulk flow at the plasma boundary has a toroidal component in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_flux_surface_averaged_deuterium_velocity_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.subject: deuterium
NAMES.short: Flux-surface-averaged toroidal component of deuterium ion bulk-flow velocity at the plasma boundary in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, where R is major radius and Z is vertical height.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the flux-surface average, on the plasma boundary or separatrix, of the deuterium ion bulk-flow velocity component in the toroidal direction. The toroidal component is the projection of the deuterium flow velocity onto $\hat{\phi}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It represents the net boundary toroidal rotation of the deuterium ion population after poloidal variation around the boundary surface has been averaged out.

A compact definition is:

$$
V_{\phi,D}^{\mathrm{FS},b} = \left\langle v_{\phi,D} \right\rangle_{\psi=\psi_b}
$$

where $V_{\phi,D}^{\mathrm{FS},b}$ is the boundary flux-surface-averaged deuterium toroidal velocity in m.s^-1, $v_{\phi,D}$ is the local deuterium toroidal bulk-flow velocity in m.s^-1, $\psi_b$ is the poloidal magnetic-flux value at the plasma boundary, and $\langle\cdot\rangle_{\psi=\psi_b}$ denotes the flux-surface average over that boundary surface.

Experimentally, this quantity may be inferred from spectroscopic measurements of deuterium flow near the separatrix, combined with magnetic-equilibrium geometry to map local measurements to the boundary surface. In transport modeling it is the boundary-surface representative value of deuterium toroidal rotation, distinct from the local [toroidal_deuterium_velocity_at_plasma_boundary](name:toroidal_deuterium_velocity_at_plasma_boundary). It is directly comparable with species analogs such as [toroidal_flux_surface_averaged_helium_3_velocity_at_plasma_boundary](name:toroidal_helium_3_velocity_at_plasma_boundary), [toroidal_flux_surface_averaged_neon_velocity_at_plasma_boundary](name:toroidal_flux_surface_averaged_neon_velocity_at_plasma_boundary), and [toroidal_flux_surface_averaged_oxygen_velocity_at_plasma_boundary](name:toroidal_flux_surface_averaged_oxygen_velocity_at_plasma_boundary).

Representative edge values are strongly discharge-dependent and are often near zero to a few $10^4$ m.s^-1 in magnitude; stronger external momentum input or edge radial-electric-field shear can produce values of order $10^5$ m.s^-1. The signed value can be positive or negative depending on the direction of toroidal deuterium flow.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the deuterium ion bulk flow is directed along $+\hat{\phi}$, the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$, in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_flux_surface_averaged_oxygen_velocity_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.subject: oxygen
NAMES.short: Flux-surface-averaged toroidal bulk flow velocity of oxygen ions evaluated at the plasma boundary (last closed flux surface).
NAMES.long:
The flux-surface-averaged toroidal velocity of oxygen ions at the plasma boundary quantifies the net toroidal bulk flow of oxygen impurities along the last closed flux surface (separatrix), collapsing the poloidal variation into a single representative scalar for the toroidal rotation state of oxygen at the plasma edge.

The flux-surface average is defined as a poloidal-contour integral weighted by the inverse of the poloidal magnetic field magnitude $B_p$:

$$
\langle v_{\phi,\mathrm{O}} \rangle = \frac{\oint v_{\phi,\mathrm{O}} \, dl / B_p}{\oint dl / B_p}
$$

where $v_{\phi,\mathrm{O}}$ is the local toroidal oxygen ion velocity at poloidal arc-length position $l$ along the flux contour.

Oxygen toroidal rotation is measured by charge exchange recombination spectroscopy (CXRS) using the Doppler shift of oxygen emission lines; combining measurements at multiple poloidal locations allows construction of the flux-surface average. The non-averaged local boundary value is given by [toroidal_oxygen_velocity_at_plasma_boundary](name:toroidal_oxygen_velocity_at_plasma_boundary), while analogous flux-surface-averaged toroidal velocities for other impurity species are given by [toroidal_flux_surface_averaged_carbon_velocity_at_plasma_boundary](name:toroidal_flux_surface_averaged_carbon_velocity_at_plasma_boundary), [toroidal_flux_surface_averaged_neon_velocity_at_plasma_boundary](name:toroidal_flux_surface_averaged_neon_velocity_at_plasma_boundary), and [toroidal_flux_surface_averaged_tungsten_velocity_at_plasma_boundary](name:toroidal_flux_surface_averaged_tungsten_velocity_at_plasma_boundary).

Typical edge toroidal velocities for light impurities such as oxygen range from approximately $-2 \times 10^4$ to $+2 \times 10^4$ m/s, with sign and magnitude depending on plasma current direction, auxiliary heating power, and confinement mode.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the oxygen ion bulk flow is directed in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_flux_surface_averaged_tungsten_velocity_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.subject: tungsten
NAMES.short: Flux-surface-averaged toroidal component of the tungsten impurity ion bulk flow velocity evaluated at the plasma boundary (last closed flux surface / separatrix).
NAMES.long:
The flux-surface-averaged toroidal velocity of tungsten ions at the plasma boundary quantifies the mean toroidal rotation of the tungsten impurity species on the last closed flux surface, averaging out poloidal asymmetries that arise from neoclassical effects and centrifugal trapping. It differs from the local [toroidal tungsten velocity at the plasma boundary](name:toroidal_tungsten_velocity_at_plasma_boundary) by applying the flux-surface average operator, yielding a single representative scalar per flux surface rather than a position-dependent field along the separatrix.

The flux-surface-averaged toroidal velocity is defined as:

$$
\langle v_\phi \rangle = \frac{\oint v_\phi \, dl / B_p}{\oint dl / B_p}
$$

where $v_\phi$ is the local toroidal component of the tungsten ion bulk flow, $B_p$ is the poloidal magnetic field magnitude, and the line integral runs along the plasma boundary flux surface in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

Tungsten boundary rotation is primarily inferred from charge exchange recombination spectroscopy (CXRS) using Doppler-shifted tungsten emission lines; local velocity measurements at multiple poloidal positions are then combined with magnetic geometry to evaluate the flux-surface average. The same averaging convention is applied consistently across impurity species, as in [toroidal flux-surface-averaged carbon velocity at the plasma boundary](name:toroidal_flux_surface_averaged_carbon_velocity_at_plasma_boundary) and [toroidal flux-surface-averaged neon velocity at the plasma boundary](name:toroidal_flux_surface_averaged_neon_velocity_at_plasma_boundary). Typical boundary toroidal impurity rotation magnitudes range from $10^3$ to $10^5$ m/s depending on heating power and toroidal momentum injection.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the tungsten ion bulk flow is directed in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_helium_3_velocity_at_pedestal
NAMES.subject: helium_3
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the bulk helium-3 ion flow velocity at the H-mode pressure pedestal, resolved along the toroidal direction in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal helium-3 velocity at the pedestal is the component of the bulk flow velocity of $^3\mathrm{He}$ ions along the toroidal basis direction at the H-mode pressure pedestal. The pedestal denotes the steep-gradient edge region just inside the last-closed flux surface, where flows strongly affect radial electric field balance, impurity and isotope transport, and edge stability.

The toroidal component is the projection of the helium-3 bulk velocity onto the toroidal unit vector in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame:

$$
v_{\phi,^3\mathrm{He}} = \mathbf{v}_{^3\mathrm{He}} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_{^3\mathrm{He}}$ is the bulk helium-3 ion flow velocity and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

In practice this quantity is inferred from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, passive spectroscopy when applicable, or edge-plasma modeling constrained by diagnostics. The pedestal value is obtained by evaluating the reconstructed helium-3 toroidal flow at the pedestal location, commonly identified from the steep-gradient region of pressure, density, or temperature.

Typical pedestal toroidal ion velocities range from about $-1\times10^5$ to $1\times10^5$ m.s^-1 in tokamak H-mode plasmas, with isotope-specific values depending on neutral-beam momentum input, collisional coupling, radial electric field shear, and edge rotation damping.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the helium-3 bulk flow is in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_helium_3_velocity_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.subject: helium_3
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the helium-3 ion bulk flow velocity at the plasma boundary, resolved along the phi direction in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It characterizes rotation or flow of helium-3 ions where closed magnetic flux surfaces meet the scrape-off layer.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal helium-3 velocity at the plasma boundary is the toroidal component of the bulk flow velocity of $^3\mathrm{He}$ ions evaluated on the last closed flux surface. It describes the directed motion of the helium-3 ion population around the torus at the interface between confined plasma and the open-field-line scrape-off layer.

The component is defined by projecting the helium-3 ion bulk velocity onto the toroidal basis direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame:

$$
v_{\phi,^3\mathrm{He}} = \mathbf{v}_{^3\mathrm{He}} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_{^3\mathrm{He}}$ is the helium-3 ion bulk velocity and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.
