In practice, this quantity may be inferred from Doppler shifts of helium spectral lines, charge-exchange measurements when suitable active neutrals are available, or from edge plasma modeling constrained by spectroscopy and equilibrium reconstruction. The boundary value is obtained by evaluating or interpolating the helium-3 flow to the last closed flux surface.

Typical boundary values are often in the range $-5 \times 10^4$ to $5 \times 10^4$ m.s^-1, with larger magnitudes approaching $1 \times 10^5$ m.s^-1 possible when strong momentum input, edge electric fields, or ion-temperature-gradient-driven flows are present.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the helium-3 ion bulk flow is in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_helium_4_velocity_at_pedestal
NAMES.subject: helium_4
NAMES.short: Toroidal velocity of helium-4 ions at the pedestal.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal helium-4 velocity at the pedestal is the toroidal component of the bulk flow velocity of helium-4 ions evaluated in the edge transport-barrier region. The component is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The signed toroidal component is the projection of the helium-4 ion flow velocity onto the toroidal basis direction:

$$
v_{\phi,\mathrm{He4,ped}} = \mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{He4,ped}} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $v_{\phi,\mathrm{He4,ped}}$ is the pedestal toroidal helium-4 velocity in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{He4,ped}}$ is the bulk helium-4 ion flow velocity at the pedestal in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, and $\hat{\phi}$ is the dimensionless unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle.

In practice this quantity is obtained from measurements or modeling that resolve ion flow in the pedestal region. Spectroscopic Doppler measurements of suitable helium emission, combined with viewing geometry and equilibrium information, can constrain the toroidal component when the relevant charge-state emission is available; otherwise it may be inferred from transport or momentum-balance analysis.

Representative signed pedestal toroidal velocities may range from near 0 to several $10^4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, with values of either sign depending on the rotation direction and discharge conditions. The magnitude should be interpreted relative to local edge thermal speeds and collisional coupling to other ion species.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the helium-4 ion bulk flow is in the $+\hat{\phi}$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_helium_4_velocity_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.subject: helium_4
NAMES.short: Toroidal velocity of helium-4 ions at the plasma boundary.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal helium-4 velocity at the plasma boundary is the local toroidal component of the helium-4 ion bulk flow evaluated on the last closed flux surface. It is a local boundary value at the evaluation point, not a flux-surface average; by contrast, [toroidal_flux_surface_averaged_helium_3_velocity_at_plasma_boundary](name:toroidal_helium_3_velocity_at_plasma_boundary) represents a boundary value averaged over a flux surface for helium-3.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, the quantity is the projection of the helium-4 bulk velocity onto the toroidal basis direction:

$$
v_{\phi,{}^{4}\mathrm{He}}(\mathbf{x}_b) = \mathbf{u}_{{}^{4}\mathrm{He}}(\mathbf{x}_b) \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{x}_b$ is a point on the plasma boundary, $\mathbf{u}_{{}^{4}\mathrm{He}}$ is the helium-4 ion bulk velocity in m.s^-1, $\hat{\phi}$ is the dimensionless unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle, and $v_{\phi,{}^{4}\mathrm{He}}$ is in m.s^-1.

In practice this velocity is obtained from local edge ion-flow measurements, such as Doppler shifts of helium emission where available, or from edge plasma modeling and interpolation to the last closed flux surface. The value may vary around the boundary, so it should not be interpreted as a flux-surface-averaged toroidal flow unless that averaging is explicitly part of the named quantity.

Typical edge helium-ion toroidal velocities are often of order 10^3-10^5 m.s^-1, with values near 0 possible at flow reversal or stagnation points. The magnitude and sign depend on momentum input, collisional coupling to other ion species, neoclassical effects, and edge electric fields.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the helium-4 ion bulk flow is in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_hydrogen_velocity_at_pedestal
NAMES.subject: hydrogen
NAMES.short: Local toroidal component of the hydrogen ion fluid velocity at the pedestal reference location, not a pedestal-region average, resolved along increasing toroidal angle phi in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame where R is major radius and Z is vertical height.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal hydrogen velocity at the pedestal is the scalar toroidal component of the hydrogen ion fluid velocity evaluated at a single local pedestal reference location. That reference location is set by the pedestal characterization used for the discharge, for example a fitted pedestal-top point or another declared point within the steep-gradient pedestal, so this quantity is not an average over the whole pedestal region. Comparisons with [toroidal deuterium velocity at the pedestal](name:toroidal_deuterium_velocity_at_pedestal) and [toroidal nitrogen velocity at the pedestal](name:toroidal_nitrogen_velocity_at_pedestal) should use the same local pedestal reference location.

The projection onto the toroidal basis direction is

$$
v_{\phi,\mathrm{H}} = \mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{H}} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $v_{\phi,\mathrm{H}}$ is the toroidal hydrogen velocity in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{H}}$ is the hydrogen ion fluid velocity in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector along increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, with $R$ the major radius, $\phi$ increasing counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ the vertical height.

The local value is obtained by evaluating a measured or modeled hydrogen flow at the chosen pedestal reference location. Experimental determinations generally use Doppler-shift information from hydrogen emission or other edge-flow constraints together with viewing geometry and magnetic-equilibrium geometry; modeling obtains the quantity from the hydrogen species momentum balance and samples the same pedestal point. The companion [hydrogen density at the pedestal](name:hydrogen_density_at_pedestal) is often needed to interpret the corresponding hydrogen momentum density and particle flow.

Typical pedestal hydrogen toroidal velocities are signed and strongly scenario dependent: weakly rotating edges may be close to 0 m.s^-1, while rotating pedestal plasmas often have magnitudes of order 10^3-10^4 m.s^-1 and can be larger under strong momentum input. The value should be compared across species only when the same pedestal reference location and the same right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame are used.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the hydrogen ion fluid velocity has a component in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_hydrogen_velocity_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.subject: hydrogen
NAMES.short: Local toroidal component of the hydrogen species bulk-flow velocity evaluated at a point on the plasma boundary, meaning the last-closed flux surface or separatrix. It is not a flux-surface average and is signed in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal hydrogen velocity at the plasma boundary is the local component of the hydrogen species bulk-flow velocity tangent to the toroidal direction at a specified point on the last-closed flux surface or separatrix. The component is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It is distinct from flux-surface-averaged boundary quantities such as [toroidal_flux_surface_averaged_deuterium_velocity_at_plasma_boundary](name:toroidal_flux_surface_averaged_deuterium_velocity_at_plasma_boundary) and [toroidal_flux_surface_averaged_carbon_velocity_at_plasma_boundary](name:toroidal_flux_surface_averaged_carbon_velocity_at_plasma_boundary), which average around the boundary rather than retaining the local value.

The local projection is

$$
v_{\phi,\mathrm{H}}(\mathbf{x}_b) = \mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{H}}(\mathbf{x}_b) \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{x}_b$ is the selected boundary position, specified by $R$ and $Z$ in meters and $\phi$ in radians; $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{H}}$ is the hydrogen bulk velocity in m.s^-1; $\hat{\phi}$ is the dimensionless toroidal unit vector; and $v_{\phi,\mathrm{H}}$ is the toroidal component in m.s^-1.

In practice this quantity may be inferred from edge flow diagnostics, spectroscopic velocity measurements when applicable, or transport calculations constrained by edge plasma observations. Because it is local, it can vary with poloidal position along the separatrix and should not be substituted for a flux-surface average without an explicit averaging operation.

No universal numerical range applies at the separatrix because the value depends strongly on plasma current, toroidal field, collisionality, rotation sources, and edge momentum transport. Representative edge main-species toroidal speeds are often of order 10^3-10^4 m.s^-1, with values that may be near zero or may reverse sign locally.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the hydrogen bulk flow has a component in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_krypton_velocity_at_pedestal
NAMES.subject: krypton
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the krypton ion bulk flow velocity at the H-mode pedestal top, resolved along the direction of increasing phi in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, where R is major radius, phi is toroidal angle, and Z is vertical height.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal krypton velocity at the pedestal is the signed toroidal component of the bulk-flow velocity of krypton ions evaluated at the H-mode pedestal top. The toroidal direction is the $\hat{\phi}$ basis direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It is the krypton-specific pedestal quantity corresponding to the more general [toroidal ion velocity](name:toroidal_ion_velocity) and can be compared with [toroidal krypton velocity at the internal transport barrier](name:toroidal_krypton_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier).

The scalar toroidal component is defined by projection of the krypton ion velocity vector onto the toroidal unit vector:

$$
v_\phi^{\mathrm{Kr}} = \mathbf{v}^{\mathrm{Kr}} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $v_\phi^{\mathrm{Kr}}$ is the signed toroidal scalar velocity in m.s$^{-1}$, $\mathbf{v}^{\mathrm{Kr}}$ is the krypton ion bulk-flow velocity vector in m.s$^{-1}$, and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle.

In practice this quantity is inferred from impurity-velocity measurements or calculations localized to the pedestal top. Spectroscopic determinations use Doppler shifts of krypton emission and viewing-geometry corrections to isolate the toroidal component; modeled values are obtained from impurity momentum balance or transport calculations constrained by edge plasma conditions.

No device-independent krypton-specific range is universal. Representative signed pedestal impurity toroidal velocities are often of order $10^3$-$10^5$ m.s$^{-1}$ in either toroidal direction, with values near zero indicating little resolved toroidal bulk flow.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the krypton ion bulk flow at the pedestal is along $+\hat{\phi}$, the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_lithium_velocity_at_pedestal
NAMES.subject: lithium
NAMES.short: Signed toroidal component of the lithium ion fluid velocity at the H-mode pedestal top in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It represents the local azimuthal rotation of lithium impurity ions at the steep-gradient edge transport barrier, not a pedestal average.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal lithium velocity at the pedestal is the local toroidal component of the lithium ion fluid velocity at the pedestal-top reference location, near the inner edge of the steep-gradient H-mode edge transport barrier. It is a signed component in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height; it is not a radial integral, volume average, or average over the full pedestal width.

The component is defined by projecting the lithium ion fluid velocity onto the toroidal unit vector:

$$
v_{\phi}^{\mathrm{Li}} = \mathbf{v}^{\mathrm{Li}} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $v_{\phi}^{\mathrm{Li}}$ is the toroidal lithium velocity in m.s^-1, $\mathbf{v}^{\mathrm{Li}}$ is the lithium ion fluid velocity in m.s^-1, and $\hat{\phi}$ is the dimensionless unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

In practice, this quantity is commonly inferred from Doppler shifts of localized lithium line emission or charge-exchange emission, with corrections for viewing geometry, instrumental wavelength calibration, and the projection of the measured line-of-sight velocity onto $\hat{\phi}$. The pedestal-top reference location is determined from edge profile analysis, typically using the radial position at the top of the steep gradient region rather than a flux-surface average over the pedestal.

Representative pedestal impurity toroidal velocities are device- and scenario-dependent and may be near zero or of order $10^3-10^5$ m.s^-1 in tokamak H-mode plasmas. The value can change sign with the direction of toroidal rotation and may differ from main-ion rotation because lithium is an impurity species with its own charge state, source distribution, and collisional coupling.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the lithium ion fluid velocity component is in the $+\hat{\phi}$ direction, the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$, in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_neon_velocity_at_pedestal
NAMES.subject: neon
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the neon ion fluid velocity in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, evaluated at the H-mode pedestal.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal neon velocity at the pedestal is the component of the neon ion fluid velocity along the toroidal direction, evaluated in the steep-gradient edge region characteristic of H-mode confinement. The pedestal lies near the outer edge of the confined plasma and is defined by strong radial gradients in quantities such as temperature, density, or pressure.

The toroidal component is the projection of the neon ion fluid velocity onto the toroidal basis direction:

$$
v_{\phi,\mathrm{Ne}} = \mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{Ne}} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{Ne}}$ is the neon ion fluid velocity in m.s^-1, $v_{\phi,\mathrm{Ne}}$ is its toroidal component in m.s^-1, and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

In practice, the pedestal location is identified from edge-gradient structure, and the neon toroidal flow is evaluated at that location from impurity-flow measurements or from impurity momentum-balance calculations. The value represents directed rotation of the neon impurity population rather than a thermal speed.

Typical absolute magnitudes for impurity toroidal flow at the pedestal are of order 10^3-10^5 m.s^-1 in tokamak edge plasmas, with the sign and magnitude depending on torque input, radial electric field, collisional coupling, and neoclassical transport.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the neon ion fluid velocity component points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_neutral_momentum_coefficient
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Dimensionless factor applied to the toroidal component of neutral-particle momentum flux density in edge-plasma transport closures. It scales the component along increasing toroidal angle in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame without defining the sign of that flux.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal neutral momentum coefficient is a dimensionless flux-limiter factor for the toroidal component of neutral-particle momentum transport. It is associated with momentum carried by neutral atoms or molecules along the $\phi$ direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The coefficient represents closure-model scaling of a signed toroidal momentum-flux density; it does not by itself define the direction or sign of that flux.

When used as a multiplicative limiter, its role can be written as:

$$
\Pi_{\phi,n}^{\mathrm{lim}} = C_{\phi,n}\,\Pi_{\phi,n}^{\mathrm{ref}}
$$

where $C_{\phi,n}$ is the dimensionless toroidal neutral momentum coefficient, $\Pi_{\phi,n}^{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the reference or unmodified toroidal neutral momentum-flux density, and $\Pi_{\phi,n}^{\mathrm{lim}}$ is the limited or effective toroidal neutral momentum-flux density. Both flux-density variables have units of $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$, equivalently $\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$. The sign of the associated flux component is the sign of [toroidal_neutral_momentum_flux](name:toroidal_neutral_momentum_flux), while this coefficient only scales that component.

The coefficient is specified or computed within a neutral momentum-transport closure, for example from local collisionality, neutral mean free path, gradients, or a prescribed flux-limiting rule. It is not normally a directly measured observable; experimental information constrains it indirectly through comparisons between modeled and observed edge-plasma and neutral behavior.

Typical values are closure-specific dimensionless factors of order unity. In a purely attenuating limiter, $C_{\phi,n}=1$ leaves the reference toroidal momentum flux unchanged and $0 \le C_{\phi,n} \le 1$ reduces its magnitude; more general calibrated closures may define a different admissible interval, so the valid numerical range is part of the closure definition rather than a universal neutral-physics constant.

NAMES.name: toroidal_nitrogen_velocity_at_pedestal
NAMES.subject: nitrogen
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the nitrogen impurity ion fluid velocity evaluated at the H-mode pedestal reference location.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal velocity $v_{\phi,\mathrm{N}}$ of nitrogen impurity ions at the pedestal quantifies their rotation along the toroidal direction within the steep-gradient edge transport barrier characteristic of H-mode plasmas. Nitrogen is a low-Z impurity frequently injected into fusion devices for radiative power exhaust management, and its toroidal velocity at the pedestal reflects the combined influence of neoclassical impurity transport, momentum input from external heating, and ion-impurity friction.

The quantity is defined as the projection of the nitrogen ion fluid velocity vector onto the toroidal unit vector in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame:

$$
v_{\phi,\mathrm{N}} = \mathbf{v}_\mathrm{N} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_\mathrm{N}$ is the nitrogen ion fluid velocity vector and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

This velocity component is commonly measured by charge exchange recombination spectroscopy (CXRS), in which the Doppler shift of nitrogen emission lines arising from charge-exchange reactions with an injected neutral beam gives the local ion flow velocity projected onto the toroidal direction. The pedestal value is a local evaluation at the reference flux surface of the H-mode pedestal, not a region average, consistent with the analogous quantities [toroidal_neon_velocity_at_pedestal](name:toroidal_neon_velocity_at_pedestal) and [toroidal_hydrogen_velocity_at_pedestal](name:toroidal_hydrogen_velocity_at_pedestal). Radial profiles of nitrogen toroidal flow connect this pedestal value to [toroidal_nitrogen_velocity_at_magnetic_axis](name:toroidal_nitrogen_velocity_at_magnetic_axis) and [toroidal_nitrogen_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:toroidal_nitrogen_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the nitrogen ion flow is in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise when viewed from above in the $+\hat{Z}$ direction).

NAMES.name: toroidal_nitrogen_velocity_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.subject: nitrogen
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the nitrogen impurity ion velocity evaluated at the last closed flux surface (plasma boundary), characterizing edge impurity rotation at the separatrix.
NAMES.long:
Nitrogen ($\mathrm{N}$) is a seeding impurity used in tokamak edge plasmas for radiative cooling and divertor heat-load mitigation. The toroidal velocity of nitrogen ions at the plasma boundary (last closed flux surface) characterizes edge impurity rotation and enters momentum-balance models for the scrape-off layer boundary condition.

The quantity is defined as the projection of the nitrogen impurity ion fluid velocity onto the toroidal unit vector $\hat{\phi}$ at the separatrix:

$$
v_\phi^{\mathrm{N}} = \mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{N}} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{N}}$ is the nitrogen impurity ion fluid velocity and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

Measurement is typically performed by charge exchange recombination spectroscopy (CXRS), in which the Doppler shift of nitrogen emission lines yields the local toroidal velocity component; the separatrix position is determined by equilibrium reconstruction. The corresponding on-axis quantity is [toroidal nitrogen velocity at the magnetic axis](name:toroidal_nitrogen_velocity_at_magnetic_axis); analogous boundary-velocity quantities for other seeding impurities include [toroidal_neon_velocity_at_plasma_boundary](name:toroidal_neon_velocity_at_plasma_boundary) and [toroidal_xenon_velocity_at_plasma_boundary](name:toroidal_xenon_velocity_at_plasma_boundary).
NAMES.sign: Positive when $v_\phi^{\mathrm{N}}$ points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_oxygen_velocity_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.subject: oxygen
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the oxygen impurity ion bulk flow velocity evaluated at the plasma boundary (last closed flux surface).
NAMES.long:
The toroidal velocity of oxygen impurity ions at the plasma boundary quantifies the toroidal momentum carried by the oxygen ion population at the last closed flux surface, which separates the magnetically confined plasma from the open-field-line scrape-off layer. This local point value is distinct from the flux-surface-averaged quantity [toroidal_flux_surface_averaged_oxygen_velocity_at_plasma_boundary](name:toroidal_flux_surface_averaged_oxygen_velocity_at_plasma_boundary), which integrates the velocity weighted by the boundary flux-surface geometry.

The toroidal component $v_\phi$ is the projection of the oxygen bulk flow velocity onto the toroidal direction:

$$
v_\phi = \mathbf{v}_\mathrm{O} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_\mathrm{O}$ is the oxygen ion bulk flow velocity and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

Oxygen toroidal velocity at the boundary is primarily measured by charge exchange recombination spectroscopy (CXRS), exploiting the Doppler shift of oxygen emission lines to extract the ion flow velocity component along $\hat{\phi}$. Analogous boundary velocities for other impurity species include [toroidal_carbon_velocity_at_plasma_boundary](name:toroidal_carbon_velocity_at_plasma_boundary) and [toroidal_neon_velocity_at_plasma_boundary](name:toroidal_neon_velocity_at_plasma_boundary).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the oxygen ion flow is directed in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise when viewed from above in the $+\hat{Z}$ direction).

NAMES.name: toroidal_tritium_velocity_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.subject: tritium
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the tritium ion fluid velocity evaluated at the plasma boundary, the last closed flux surface separating the magnetically confined plasma from the open-field-line scrape-off layer.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal tritium velocity at the plasma boundary gives the bulk rotational flow of tritium ions projected onto the toroidal direction $\hat{\phi}$, evaluated at the last closed flux surface where the confined plasma meets the scrape-off layer. This boundary value constrains the outer edge of the radial tritium rotation profile and reflects the balance between momentum injection, viscous transport across the pedestal, and ion-neutral friction at the plasma edge.

The defining relation is the projection of the tritium ion fluid velocity vector $\mathbf{v}_T$ onto $\hat{\phi}$ at the last closed flux surface:

$$
v_{\phi,T}^{\rm b} = \mathbf{v}_T \cdot \hat{\phi}\Big|_{\rm LCFS}
$$

where $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, with $R$ the major radius and $Z$ the vertical height.

The toroidal ion velocity at the boundary is measured by charge exchange recombination spectroscopy (CXRS), inferring the flow from Doppler shifts of charge-exchange emission lines in the steep-gradient edge region. For tritium-containing plasmas, measurements carry additional constraints due to the radioactive nature of the fuel species. Edge toroidal ion velocities in tokamak plasmas range from ~1 km/s in L-mode to ~100 km/s in strongly heated H-mode discharges. Comparing this quantity with [toroidal tritium velocity at the pedestal](name:toroidal_tritium_velocity_at_pedestal) and [toroidal tritium velocity at the magnetic axis](name:toroidal_tritium_velocity_at_magnetic_axis) characterizes the full radial rotation profile; [toroidal helium-3 velocity at the plasma boundary](name:toroidal_helium_3_velocity_at_plasma_boundary) provides the analogous boundary quantity for the helium-3 species.
NAMES.sign: Positive when tritium ions flow in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise when viewed from the $+\hat{Z}$ direction).

NAMES.name: toroidal_tungsten_velocity_at_pedestal
NAMES.subject: tungsten
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the flow velocity of tungsten impurity ions evaluated at the H-mode pedestal top.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal velocity of tungsten impurity ions at the pedestal top characterizes the $\hat{\phi}$-direction rotation of this high-Z impurity species at the steep-gradient edge transport barrier. Tungsten enters the confined plasma primarily through erosion of plasma-facing components in metal-wall devices, and its toroidal rotation at the pedestal reflects neoclassical impurity transport, ion–impurity friction, and externally applied toroidal momentum.

The radial force balance for the tungsten ion population links the toroidal velocity to the local radial electric field $E_r$:

$$
E_r = \frac{1}{Z_W e n_W} \frac{\partial p_W}{\partial r} + v_{\phi,W} B_\theta - v_{\theta,W} B_\phi
$$

where $Z_W$ is the mean tungsten charge state, $e$ is the elementary charge, $n_W$ is the tungsten number density (see [tungsten density at the pedestal](name:tungsten_density_at_pedestal)), $p_W$ is the tungsten pressure, $B_\theta$ and $B_\phi$ are the poloidal and toroidal magnetic field components, and $v_{\theta,W}$ is the poloidal tungsten velocity.

This quantity is measured by charge exchange recombination spectroscopy (CXRS) from Doppler shifts of tungsten emission lines localized to the pedestal region. Toroidal impurity rotation at the pedestal in H-mode plasmas reaches magnitudes of order $10^3$–$10^4$ m/s, with sign and magnitude determined by the momentum input scenario. The same species velocity at other radial locations is given by [toroidal tungsten velocity at the magnetic axis](name:toroidal_tungsten_velocity_at_magnetic_axis) and [at the plasma boundary](name:toroidal_tungsten_velocity_at_plasma_boundary); the analogous quantity for xenon is [toroidal xenon velocity at the pedestal](name:toroidal_xenon_velocity_at_pedestal).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the tungsten ion flow is directed in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_tungsten_velocity_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.subject: tungsten
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the tungsten impurity ion fluid velocity in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, evaluated at the last closed flux surface separating confined plasma from the scrape-off layer.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal tungsten velocity at the plasma boundary is the component of the tungsten impurity ion fluid velocity along the toroidal direction at the last closed flux surface, the surface separating confined plasma from the scrape-off layer. The component is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle increasing counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The defining projection is:

$$
v_{\phi,W}^{\mathrm{LCFS}} = \left.\mathbf{v}_W \cdot \hat{\phi}\right|_{\mathrm{LCFS}}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_W$ is the tungsten ion fluid velocity, $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle, and LCFS denotes the last closed flux surface.

Experimentally, this velocity is commonly inferred from Doppler shifts of tungsten spectral lines using edge spectroscopy or charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy when suitable tungsten emission is available. In modeling and equilibrium-coupled transport analysis, it is obtained by projecting the impurity fluid velocity onto $\hat{\phi}$ or by solving an impurity momentum balance including electric-field forces, pressure-gradient effects, collisional friction with the main ions, and momentum sources.

Typical tokamak edge values are about $10^3-5 \times 10^4$ m.s^-1, with the sign and magnitude depending on bulk plasma rotation, radial electric field, collisionality, charge-state distribution, and pedestal conditions. This pointwise boundary quantity is distinguished from the flux-surface average [toroidal_flux_surface_averaged_tungsten_velocity_at_plasma_boundary](name:toroidal_flux_surface_averaged_tungsten_velocity_at_plasma_boundary), and it uses the same toroidal-component convention as related species velocities such as [toroidal_deuterium_velocity_at_plasma_boundary](name:toroidal_deuterium_velocity_at_plasma_boundary), [toroidal_nitrogen_velocity_at_plasma_boundary](name:toroidal_nitrogen_velocity_at_plasma_boundary), and [toroidal_electron_velocity](name:toroidal_electron_velocity).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the tungsten ion fluid velocity points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_xenon_velocity_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.subject: xenon
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the xenon ion bulk flow velocity at the plasma boundary, the last closed flux surface separating the confined plasma from the open-field-line scrape-off layer.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal xenon velocity at the plasma boundary is the $\hat{\phi}$-component of the xenon impurity ion fluid velocity, evaluated as a flux-surface average on the last closed flux surface (separatrix). It quantifies the net toroidal rotation of the xenon ion population at the transition between the closed-field-line confined region and the open-field-line scrape-off layer.

The toroidal velocity component is defined as:

$$
v_\phi^{\rm Xe} = \mathbf{v}_{\rm Xe} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_{\rm Xe}$ is the xenon ion fluid velocity and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

Xenon impurity ion velocities at the plasma boundary are typically inferred from the Doppler shift of charge exchange recombination spectroscopy lines, or from passive spectroscopy of xenon ion emission at the plasma edge. Xenon is a heavy noble-gas impurity with atomic number $Z = 54$, used for radiative plasma cooling and seeding; its large mass and high charge states make the toroidal velocity measurement sensitive to local momentum balance and neoclassical transport at the separatrix. Analogous boundary toroidal velocities for other impurity species include [toroidal krypton velocity](name:toroidal_krypton_velocity_at_plasma_boundary), [toroidal neon velocity](name:toroidal_neon_velocity_at_plasma_boundary), and [toroidal carbon velocity](name:toroidal_carbon_velocity_at_plasma_boundary).
NAMES.sign: Positive when xenon ions flow in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$).

NAMES.name: tritium_density_at_pedestal
NAMES.subject: tritium
NAMES.short: Tritium ion number density evaluated at the H-mode pedestal top.
NAMES.long:
Tritium density at the pedestal is the local number density of ionized tritium at the H-mode pedestal top. The pedestal top is the radial location where the steep-gradient edge transport barrier transitions to the flatter core density distribution, so this value characterizes the tritium content just inside the barrier.

The local number-density definition evaluated at that location is:

$$
n_{T,\mathrm{ped}} = \left.\frac{dN_T}{dV}\right|_{\mathrm{ped}}
$$

where $dN_T$ is the number of tritium ions in the infinitesimal volume $dV$, $dV$ is measured in $\mathrm{m}^3$, and the subscript $\mathrm{ped}$ means that the limit is taken at the pedestal-top location.

In practice, this value is obtained by identifying the pedestal top from the edge density or pressure structure and evaluating the tritium ion density there. If the tritium component is not resolved independently, it may be inferred from the total ion density together with the local isotopic fraction, so $n_{T,\mathrm{ped}}$ reflects both the pedestal density and the fuel mix.

Typical values are zero in plasmas without tritium fueling or with negligible tritium inventory. In deuterium-tritium H-mode operation, representative pedestal-top tritium densities are about $10^{18}-5 \times 10^{19}\ \mathrm{m}^{-3}$, depending on total pedestal density, dilution by impurities and other fuel ions, and the tritium fraction.

NAMES.name: tritium_density_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.subject: tritium
NAMES.short: Number density of tritium ions at the plasma boundary (separatrix), the last closed magnetic flux surface separating the confined plasma from the scrape-off layer.
NAMES.long:
Tritium density at the plasma boundary is the local number density of tritium ions evaluated on the separatrix. It characterizes the tritium component of the ion population at the outer edge of the closed-field-line plasma and is non-negative by definition.

Using the normalized poloidal flux coordinate $\psi_N$, with $\psi_N=0$ at the magnetic axis and $\psi_N=1$ at the separatrix, the boundary value is

$$
n_{\mathrm{T},b} = n_{\mathrm{T}}(\psi_N=1)
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{T},b}$ is the tritium ion density at the plasma boundary in m^-3 and $n_{\mathrm{T}}$ is the tritium ion density as a function of $\psi_N$, also in m^-3.

In practice this quantity is obtained by identifying the separatrix from magnetic-equilibrium reconstruction and evaluating or extrapolating the tritium ion density to that surface. The isotope-resolved value is commonly constrained from the total edge density together with an assumed, modeled, or independently inferred tritium fraction, rather than from the separatrix location alone.

Typical values range from 0 m^-3 in plasmas without tritium to about 10^18-10^20 m^-3 in deuterium-tritium edge plasmas, depending on the total separatrix density and isotope mix. Values below zero are unphysical for a number density.

NAMES.name: xenon_density_at_pedestal
NAMES.subject: xenon
NAMES.short: Xenon ion number density evaluated at the H-mode pedestal top, where the steep-gradient edge transport barrier meets the flatter core pressure profile.
NAMES.long:
Xenon impurity ion number density at the pedestal top characterizes the local concentration of xenon at the shoulder of the H-mode edge transport barrier. As a heavy noble gas with atomic number $Z = 54$, xenon contributes substantially to the effective charge $Z_\mathrm{eff}$ and radiative power losses even at trace concentrations, making its pedestal value a key diagnostic of impurity accumulation, pedestal stability, and impurity transport modeling.

The pedestal top is the radial location $\rho_\mathrm{ped}$ at which the steep-gradient barrier region joins the gentler core density profile. The xenon pedestal density $n_\mathrm{Xe,ped}$ is the value of the ion number density profile at that reference position:

$$
n_\mathrm{Xe,ped} = n_\mathrm{Xe}(\rho_\mathrm{ped})
$$

where $\rho_\mathrm{ped}$ is determined from the electron temperature or pressure profile pedestal fit, and $n_\mathrm{Xe}$ is the total xenon ion density summed over all ionization stages unless individual charge states are specified separately.

Xenon is introduced into fusion plasmas for controlled radiative seeding to reduce divertor heat loads, for ELM suppression, and in disruption mitigation scenarios. Pedestal xenon density is typically inferred from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy or soft X-ray emission spectroscopy, with the pedestal location identified from Thomson scattering or reflectometry profiles. This quantity is part of the [density_at_pedestal](name:density_at_pedestal) family; analogous pedestal densities for lighter noble gas seeding species include [neon_density_at_pedestal](name:neon_density_at_pedestal) and [argon_density_at_pedestal](name:argon_density_at_pedestal). For xenon density at other plasma reference locations see [xenon_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:xenon_density_at_plasma_boundary) and [xenon_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:xenon_density_at_magnetic_axis).
NAMES.sign: Positive when xenon ions are present at the pedestal top.

NAMES.name: xenon_density_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.subject: xenon
NAMES.short: Number density of xenon ions at the plasma boundary (last closed flux surface), setting the outer boundary condition for xenon impurity transport between the confined plasma and the scrape-off layer.
NAMES.long:
Xenon ($Z = 54$) is a heavy noble-gas impurity that is either deliberately seeded into the edge plasma for radiative power exhaust mitigation or present as a trace contaminant. The xenon ion number density at the plasma boundary is the local ion number density $n_{\rm Xe}$ evaluated at the last closed flux surface — the magnetic separatrix separating field-line-closed confinement from the open-field-line scrape-off layer — constituting the outer boundary condition for core impurity transport calculations. Unless a specific ionization stage is resolved separately, it is summed over all charge states Xe$^{1+}$ through Xe$^{54+}$.

This boundary value connects the core inventory, quantified by [volume_averaged_xenon_density](name:volume_averaged_xenon_density) and [line_averaged_xenon_density](name:line_averaged_xenon_density), to scrape-off-layer impurity balance. The analogous on-axis value is [xenon_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:xenon_density_at_magnetic_axis), while xenon_fraction expresses the xenon ion content relative to electrons. The boundary density is inferred from passive spectroscopy of high-charge-state line emission near the separatrix or from two-dimensional edge transport modeling benchmarked to spectroscopic line-ratios. The parent quantity [density_at_plasma_boundary](name:density_at_plasma_boundary) defines the general species-agnostic framework.

Typical separatrix xenon densities in seeded tokamak discharges range from $10^{16}$ to $10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$, depending on seeding rate and plasma conditions; trace-impurity backgrounds may be two to three orders of magnitude lower.
NAMES.sign: Positive when xenon ions are present at the last closed flux surface.

NAMES.name: gradient_of_electron_pressure
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Signed derivative of electron pressure with respect to normalized poloidal magnetic flux, evaluated at the H-mode pedestal location of greatest absolute pressure steepness. The selection uses the largest magnitude of the derivative, while the reported value retains its algebraic sign.
NAMES.long:
The gradient of electron pressure is the signed slope of [electron_pressure](name:electron_pressure) with respect to the normalized poloidal magnetic flux coordinate $\psi_N$ in the H-mode pedestal. It is evaluated at the pedestal location where the absolute value of that slope is greatest, so a steep outward pressure drop is selected by magnitude but reported with its negative sign.

The defining value is

$$
G_{p_e} = \left.\frac{d p_e}{d\psi_N}\right|_{\psi_N=\psi_*}, \qquad \psi_* = \operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\psi_N \in \mathrm{pedestal}} \left|\frac{d p_e}{d\psi_N}\right|
$$

where $p_e$ is electron pressure, $\psi_N$ is normalized poloidal magnetic flux increasing from 0 at the magnetic axis to 1 at the last closed flux surface, and $\psi_*$ is the pedestal location of maximum absolute slope. Electron pressure is $p_e=n_e k_B T_e$ when $T_e$ is thermodynamic temperature in K, equivalently $p_e=n_e e T_e$ when $T_e$ is reported in eV; $n_e$ is electron density in m$^{-3}$, $k_B$ is the Boltzmann constant, and $e$ is the elementary charge.

In practice this quantity is obtained by fitting the radial dependence of electron pressure across the pedestal, often from electron density and temperature measurements such as Thomson scattering, and then differentiating the fitted function with respect to $\psi_N$. Modified hyperbolic-tangent and piecewise-linear fits are common ways to locate the steepest pedestal segment. This normalized-flux derivative complements [gradient_of_electron_temperature](name:gradient_of_electron_temperature) and [gradient_of_electron_density](name:gradient_of_electron_density), and differs from [gradient_of_radial_electron_pressure](name:derivative_with_respect_to_normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_of_electron_pressure_at_pedestal), which is a spatial derivative requiring a local conversion between $\psi_N$ and a chosen radial distance.

Typical signed values are usually negative in ordinary H-mode pedestals. Absolute magnitudes are about $10^4$-$10^6$ Pa in present tokamaks; small or low-pressure pedestals can be near $10^3$ Pa, while high-performance pedestals can reach several $10^6$ Pa.
NAMES.sign: Positive when electron pressure increases as the normalized poloidal magnetic flux coordinate $\psi_N$ increases from the magnetic axis toward the last closed flux surface.

NAMES.name: parallel_diamagnetic_current_density
NAMES.short: Field-aligned component of the diamagnetic current density, projected onto the local magnetic field direction in the edge plasma.
NAMES.long:
The parallel diamagnetic current density is the projection of the total [diamagnetic_current_density](name:diamagnetic_current_density) onto the local magnetic field direction at each point in the edge plasma. The diamagnetic current arises from the gyration of magnetized particles in a pressure-gradient field; in an isotropic ideal plasma, $\mathbf{j}_\mathrm{dia} = (\mathbf{B} \times \nabla p)/B^2$ is purely perpendicular to $\mathbf{B}$, so its parallel component vanishes in that limit. In more complete descriptions including pressure anisotropy, finite Larmor radius corrections, or the inhomogeneous magnetic geometry of the tokamak edge, a field-aligned component emerges and must be tracked separately.

The parallel projection is defined as:

$$
j_{\parallel,\mathrm{dia}} = \mathbf{j}_\mathrm{dia} \cdot \hat{b}
$$

where $\mathbf{j}_\mathrm{dia}$ is the diamagnetic current density vector and $\hat{b} = \mathbf{B}/B$ is the unit vector along the magnetic field of magnitude $B$.

In edge plasma current decompositions, this component is closely related to [parallel_current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:parallel_current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift), which encodes the same physical mechanism through the explicit drift formalism. The toroidal_diamagnetic_current_density provides the complementary geometric projection of the same vector field onto the toroidal direction.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the current flows in the direction of the local magnetic field unit vector $\hat{b} = \mathbf{B}/B$.

NAMES.name: parallel_ion_state_convection_velocity
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Parallel component of the effective convective velocity used for particle transport of a specified ion charge state in the edge plasma. It is a transport coefficient along the local magnetic-field direction and need not equal the bulk ion fluid velocity.
NAMES.long:
The parallel ion-state convection velocity is the coefficient multiplying the density of one ion charge state in the convective part of its parallel particle transport. It describes transport along the local magnetic-field direction in the edge plasma and is an effective balance-equation coefficient, not necessarily the literal mean fluid velocity of that ion state.

A common particle-flux decomposition defines the named quantity as:

$$
\Gamma_{\parallel,s} = n_s v_{\parallel,s}^{\mathrm{conv}} + \Gamma_{\parallel,s}^{\mathrm{nonconv}}
$$

where $\Gamma_{\parallel,s}$ is the total parallel particle flux of charge state $s$ along $\hat{b}=\mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$, $n_s$ is the charge-state density, $v_{\parallel,s}^{\mathrm{conv}}$ is this effective convection velocity, and $\Gamma_{\parallel,s}^{\mathrm{nonconv}}$ contains diffusive, drift-ordering, turbulent, and source-related contributions that are not represented as density times a convective coefficient. Equivalently, where $n_s$ is nonzero, the effective coefficient is the residual parallel flux per particle after those nonconvective contributions have been separated; it can differ from the bulk ion fluid parallel velocity.

In practice it is obtained from charge-state particle-balance analysis or transport modeling using density evolution, parallel flux constraints, and atomic source terms such as ionization, recombination, charge exchange, neutral fueling, and recycling. Direct charge-state-resolved parallel flux measurements are uncommon, so the coefficient is usually constrained by a combination of spectroscopy, edge or divertor probes, and consistency with modeled sources and sinks. The same effective-coefficient interpretation underlies related radial convection-velocity quantities such as [radial_ion_convection_velocity](name:radial_ion_convection_velocity) and [radial_ion_state_effective_momentum_convection_velocity](name:radial_ion_state_momentum_convection_velocity).

Typical signed values in the confined edge are about $-10^4$ to $10^4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, while scrape-off-layer and divertor values often reach $-10^5$ to $10^5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Magnitudes comparable to a fraction of the local ion sound speed are common near material boundaries or strong source regions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the effective convective particle flux for the ion charge state is directed along the local magnetic-field unit vector $\hat{b}$.

NAMES.name: parallel_ion_state_momentum
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Parallel ion state momentum is the component, along the local magnetic-field direction, of the momentum source term for a specified ion species and charge state in an edge plasma. It has unit kg m^-1 s^-2 and represents addition or removal of that state's parallel momentum.
NAMES.long:
Parallel ion state momentum is the signed projection of a charge-state-resolved ion momentum source term along the local magnetic-field direction. It applies to one ion species and one ion charge state, and has unit $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$, the same dimensional unit as pressure or momentum flux.

The signed parallel projection is defined by:

$$
S_{p,\parallel}^{(a,q)} = \mathbf{S}_p^{(a,q)} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{b}}
$$

where $S_{p,\parallel}^{(a,q)}$ is the parallel momentum source term for ion species $a$ and charge state $q$ with unit $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$, $\mathbf{S}_p^{(a,q)}$ is the corresponding vector momentum source term with the same unit, $\hat{\mathbf{b}} = \mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$ is the dimensionless unit vector along the local magnetic field, and $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field measured in tesla.

In practice this quantity is usually inferred or computed as part of a momentum balance for the selected ion state rather than measured directly. Contributing mechanisms can include ion-neutral momentum exchange, charge exchange, ionization and recombination momentum transfer, collisional friction, and externally applied momentum sources. Complementary projections of the same charge-state-resolved ion momentum source are represented by [poloidal_ion_state_momentum](name:poloidal_ion_state_momentum), [toroidal_ion_state_momentum](name:toroidal_ion_state_momentum), and radial_ion_state_momentum.

Typical absolute magnitudes are strongly case dependent: they range from near $0\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$ where net parallel momentum transfer cancels to values comparable with local edge ion pressure $p_i$ or dynamic momentum-flux scales such as $m_i n_i u_\parallel^2$, where $m_i$, $n_i$, and $u_\parallel$ are ion mass, ion density, and parallel flow speed. The relevant scale can vary by orders of magnitude between weak-source edge regions and localized divertor or recycling regions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the momentum source acts in the direction of the local magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$.

NAMES.name: parallel_total_ion_energy_convection_velocity
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Parallel effective convection velocity for total ion energy transport in edge plasma. It is the signed field-aligned speed associated with the convective part of the total ion energy flux.
NAMES.long:
Parallel total ion energy convection velocity is the signed effective field-aligned speed that multiplies a total ion energy density to give the convective part of the parallel ion-energy flux density. It represents advection of the ion energy variable used in an edge-plasma transport model and need not be identical to the bulk ion particle velocity.

The defining relation is the flux-density ratio:

$$
v_{\parallel,E_i}^{\mathrm{conv}} = \frac{q_{\parallel,E_i}^{\mathrm{conv}}}{\mathcal{E}_i}
$$

where $q_{\parallel,E_i}^{\mathrm{conv}}$ is the signed parallel convective flux density of total ion energy in W.m^-2 and $\mathcal{E}_i$ is the total ion energy density in J.m^-3, so the ratio has units m.s^-1. The denominator must be consistent with the energy variable used by the transport model; for a thermal-ion contribution, $T_i$ is treated as energy per ion, so $3 n_i T_i/2$ is in J.m^-3 when $T_i$ is in joules, while $3 n_i e T_i/2$ is used when the numerical temperature is in eV.

In practice, this velocity is specified by a transport closure or recovered from modeled energy flux density and energy density. It is the field-aligned analog of [radial_total_ion_effective_energy_convection_velocity](name:radial_ion_energy_convection_velocity), with the direction taken along magnetic field lines rather than across magnetic surfaces. Because enthalpy factors, species sums, or other closure choices may be included in either the flux or energy variable, values should be compared only when the same total-ion-energy definition is used.

Typical values are model dependent rather than universal. Magnitudes may be near 0 m.s^-1 when explicit parallel energy convection is absent and can range up to the local field-aligned transport-speed scale, often order 10^2-10^5 m.s^-1 in edge-plasma modeling; the chosen value should be interpreted with the same energy-density convention used in the defining ratio.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the effective convection of total ion energy is along the local magnetic-field direction $\hat{b}=\mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_ion_energy_diffusivity
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Effective scalar diffusion coefficient for poloidal transport of ion thermal energy. In a diffusive closure, it multiplies the poloidal gradient of ion energy density to give the down-gradient ion energy flux.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal ion energy diffusivity is an effective scalar transport coefficient for diffusive redistribution of ion thermal energy along the poloidal direction. The poloidal direction is tangent to increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ at fixed radial flux coordinate $\rho$ and toroidal angle $\phi$ in a flux-coordinate representation $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$. It characterizes the ion energy channel and should be distinguished from aggregate total-ion or total-plasma energy transport coefficients when those channels are defined separately.

A common local down-gradient closure for the diffusive poloidal ion energy flux is:

$$
q_{\theta,i}^{E,\mathrm{diff}} = -D_{\theta,i}^{E}\,\frac{\partial \varepsilon_i}{\partial l_\theta}
$$

where $q_{\theta,i}^{E,\mathrm{diff}}$ is the poloidal diffusive ion energy flux density in W.m^-2, $D_{\theta,i}^{E}$ is the poloidal ion energy diffusivity in m^2.s^-1, $\varepsilon_i$ is the ion thermal energy density in J.m^-3, and $l_\theta$ is poloidal arclength in meters. For a Maxwellian ion population, $\varepsilon_i = 3p_i/2$, where $p_i$ is ion pressure; equivalently, $\varepsilon_i = 3n_iT_i/2$ when $T_i$ is expressed as energy per particle. The minus sign means that a positive diffusivity drives the diffusive contribution from higher toward lower ion thermal energy density.

In practice this coefficient is usually specified, fitted, or inferred within edge-plasma transport modeling from ion temperature, density, pressure, and heat-flux constraints rather than measured directly as a material property. It is the poloidal ion-energy analog of radial transport quantities such as radial_total_energy_diffusion_coefficient, [radial_ion_state_energy_diffusivity](name:radial_ion_state_energy_diffusivity), and [radial_diffusion_coefficient](name:radial_ion_particle_diffusivity), and it is related to [poloidal_ion_diffusivity](name:poloidal_ion_diffusivity) and [poloidal_ion_momentum_diffusivity](name:poloidal_ion_momentum_diffusivity) for particle and momentum transport in the same direction. Use [poloidal_total_ion_energy_diffusivity](name:poloidal_ion_energy_diffusivity) when the modeled coefficient applies to an aggregate total-ion energy channel.

Typical effective values are strongly model and region dependent, with no universal range. Edge transport studies commonly explore broad values such as 0.01-100 m^2.s^-1; values near zero suppress modeled poloidal energy diffusion, while larger values more rapidly smooth poloidal variations of ion energy density.

NAMES.name: poloidal_ion_state_diffusivity
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Poloidal ion-state diffusivity is the scalar diagonal transport coefficient for diffusive particle transport of a specified ion charge state along increasing poloidal angle in a chosen flux-coordinate system (rho, theta, phi). It multiplies the charge-state density gradient to give the down-gradient poloidal particle flux.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal ion-state diffusivity is the scalar diagonal component of charge-state-resolved ion particle diffusion in the physical poloidal direction associated with increasing $\theta$ in a specified flux-coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$. It applies to one ionization state $z$ and is the charge-state-resolved counterpart of [poloidal_ion_diffusivity](name:poloidal_ion_diffusivity), with analogous role to momentum transport coefficients such as [poloidal_ion_state_momentum_diffusivity](name:poloidal_ion_state_momentum_diffusivity).

The local down-gradient closure for the poloidal particle flux component is

$$
\Gamma_{\mathrm{pol},z} = -D_{\mathrm{pol},z}\,\nabla_{\mathrm{pol}} n_z
$$

where $\Gamma_{\mathrm{pol},z}$ is the charge-state particle flux density along the poloidal direction in $m^{-2}\,s^{-1}$, $D_{\mathrm{pol},z}$ is the poloidal ion-state diffusivity in $m^2\,s^{-1}$, $n_z$ is the ion number density for charge state $z$ in $m^{-3}$, and $\nabla_{\mathrm{pol}} n_z$ is the physical poloidal component of the density gradient in $m^{-4}$. The minus sign means that, for $D_{\mathrm{pol},z}>0$, the diffusive flux is opposite to the density gradient; if density increases along increasing $\theta$, the diffusive flux component points toward decreasing $\theta$.

In edge plasma particle-balance modeling, this coefficient is used when ionization states are evolved separately and poloidal redistribution of each charge-state population must be represented. It may be prescribed as an effective transport parameter or constrained by comparisons with charge-state-sensitive density measurements, together with ionization, recombination, parallel losses, and boundary conditions.

There is no device-independent numerical range fixed by the definition. In a purely diffusive closure it is normally treated as non-negative: $D_{\mathrm{pol},z}=0$ removes this diffusive channel, while larger values more strongly smooth poloidal variations of the charge-state density.

NAMES.name: poloidal_neutral_energy_diffusivity
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Effective diagonal diffusivity for neutral-particle energy transport in the poloidal direction of flux coordinates (rho, theta, phi), tangent to a flux surface at fixed rho and phi. It relates the length-normalized poloidal gradient of neutral energy density to the diffusive poloidal energy flux.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal neutral energy diffusivity is the effective diagonal diffusion coefficient for transport of neutral-particle energy along the poloidal direction in flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$. The direction is tangent to a flux surface at fixed $\rho$ and $\phi$, and the coefficient represents how rapidly neutral thermal or internal energy is smoothed along that direction.

A Fick-law closure for the poloidal neutral energy flux density is

$$
q_\theta^{\mathrm{n},E} = -D_\theta^{\mathrm{n},E}\,\frac{1}{h_\theta}\,\frac{\partial u_n}{\partial \theta}
$$

where $q_\theta^{\mathrm{n},E}$ is the neutral energy flux density taken positive in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$, $D_\theta^{\mathrm{n},E}$ is the poloidal neutral energy diffusivity, $u_n$ is the neutral energy density in $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$, and $h_\theta$ is the poloidal metric scale factor in meters so that $(1/h_\theta)\partial u_n/\partial\theta$ is a length-normalized gradient in $\mathrm{J\,m^{-4}}$. For a Maxwellian neutral population, $u_n$ is commonly evaluated from the neutral density and temperature; for example, $u_n=3 n_n T_n/2$ when $T_n$ is expressed as energy per particle.

This coefficient is used in reduced neutral-fluid or transport closures for edge and scrape-off-layer plasmas when the full neutral energy transport tensor is represented by direction-resolved effective diffusivities. Its value may represent collisional scattering, charge-exchange mediated redistribution, atomic and molecular processes, and unresolved turbulent or kinetic effects. It is the energy-transport analog of [poloidal neutral momentum diffusivity](name:poloidal_neutral_momentum_diffusivity), and it complements orthogonal-direction quantities such as [radial neutral energy diffusion coefficient](name:radial_neutral_energy_diffusion_coefficient).

Typical effective values range from $0.1-10^4\ \mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$. Smaller values are expected for cold, dense, highly collisional divertor neutrals, while larger effective values can occur in hotter or more rarefied edge regions, or when unresolved kinetic transport is represented by an enhanced diffusive closure. A true diffusive coefficient is expected to be non-negative; negative fitted values indicate an anti-diffusive effective closure or a convention-dependent model artifact rather than ordinary diffusion.

NAMES.name: poloidal_neutral_momentum_diffusivity
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Poloidal component of the effective neutral-particle momentum diffusivity tensor in flux coordinates (rho, theta, phi), governing diffusive redistribution of neutral momentum along increasing poloidal angle theta.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal neutral momentum diffusivity is the diagonal poloidal component of an effective neutral-particle momentum diffusivity tensor. It parameterizes how neutral momentum density is smoothed along the poloidal direction, tangent to increasing $\theta$ at fixed $\rho$ and $\phi$ in flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, locally lying in a meridional plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

In a local Fick-type closure, the poloidal diffusive flux of neutral poloidal momentum is written as:

$$
\Pi_{\theta,n} = -D_\theta\,\frac{\partial}{\partial l_\theta}\left(m_n n_n u_{\theta,n}\right)
$$

where $\Pi_{\theta,n}$ is the poloidal neutral-momentum flux in kg m$^{-1}$ s$^{-2}$, taken positive in the direction of increasing $\theta$; $D_\theta$ is the poloidal neutral momentum diffusivity in m$^2$ s$^{-1}$; $m_n$ is neutral particle mass in kg; $n_n$ is neutral number density in m$^{-3}$; and $u_{\theta,n}$ is the neutral fluid velocity component along increasing $\theta$ in m s$^{-1}$. The poloidal arclength $l_\theta$ follows the coordinate line of increasing $\theta$, with metric relation $dl_\theta=h_\theta d\theta$ and $h_\theta=|\partial\mathbf{x}/\partial\theta|_{\rho,\phi}$ in meters when $\theta$ is dimensionless; the minus sign means that positive diffusivity drives neutral poloidal momentum down its arclength gradient.

This coefficient is usually obtained indirectly from neutral-transport modeling, reduced fluid closures, or interpretation of edge and divertor measurements sensitive to neutral flow and momentum exchange. As an effective coefficient, it may include neutral-neutral collisions, charge-exchange coupling to ions, and unresolved kinetic or geometric effects represented in a diffusive approximation.

Typical effective values in tokamak edge and divertor neutral-momentum closures are about 0.01-10 m$^2$ s$^{-1}$, with values up to roughly 100 m$^2$ s$^{-1}$ possible in highly diffusive reduced descriptions or regions where long neutral mean-free paths are represented by an effective fluid diffusivity.

NAMES.name: poloidal_particle_diffusivity
NAMES.subject: particle
NAMES.short: Effective particle diffusion coefficient for transport along the poloidal direction in flux coordinates (rho, theta, phi). It relates particle flux in the direction of increasing poloidal angle to the metric-scaled gradient of particle number density for a generic particle population.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal particle diffusivity $D_\mathrm{pol}$ is an effective scalar transport coefficient for particle mixing along the poloidal direction in a flux-coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, where $\rho$ labels flux surfaces, $\theta$ is poloidal angle, and $\phi$ is toroidal angle. It applies to a generic particle population and represents the net effect of collisional, turbulent, or modeled unresolved transport along increasing or decreasing $\theta$.

The local Fick-law closure for the poloidal particle flux density is

$$
\Gamma_\theta = -D_\mathrm{pol}\,\nabla_\theta n
$$

where $\Gamma_\theta$ is the particle flux density along increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in $\mathrm{m}^{-2}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, $D_\mathrm{pol}$ is in $\mathrm{m}^2\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, $n$ is the particle number density in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, and $\nabla_\theta n$ is the physical component of $\nabla n$ along increasing $\theta$ at fixed $\rho$ and $\phi$. For an orthogonal metric this component is $h_\theta^{-1}\partial n/\partial\theta$, where $h_\theta$ is the poloidal arc-length scale factor. For $D_\mathrm{pol} > 0$, the minus sign gives down-gradient transport: flux in the direction of increasing $\theta$ occurs when density decreases with increasing $\theta$.

This coefficient is usually prescribed or inferred in edge particle-balance and transport calculations rather than measured directly. It may be adjusted to reproduce measured density evolution, particle balance, or poloidal density asymmetries, and its interpretation should follow the particle population being modeled; species-resolved counterparts are used when electron, ion, or ion-state transport must be distinguished.

Typical prescribed edge-plasma values are model-dependent and are commonly of order 0.01-10 m^2.s^-1 for anomalous particle mixing. Reduced closures or effective neutral-particle treatments may use values up to about 100 m^2.s^-1, while values near zero represent negligible poloidal diffusive mixing. A passive diffusion coefficient is normally non-negative; negative values would represent an anti-diffusive closure rather than ordinary diffusion.

NAMES.name: radial_current_density_due_to_viscosity
NAMES.short: Radial component of the viscosity-driven current density in the edge plasma, formed from viscous stress contributions and directed along the major-radius direction of the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Radial current density due to viscosity is the major-radius component of the electric current density produced by viscous momentum transport in the edge plasma. It represents the part of the current associated with viscous stress closures, including perpendicular, parallel, and heat-viscous contributions, projected onto the $\hat{R}$ direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

A useful defining relation is the projection of the aggregate viscosity-driven current density onto the major-radius basis vector:

$$
j_R^{\mathrm{visc}} = \left(\mathbf{j}_{\perp}^{\mathrm{visc}} + \mathbf{j}_{\parallel}^{\mathrm{visc}} + \mathbf{j}_{q}^{\mathrm{visc}}\right) \cdot \hat{R}
$$

where $j_R^{\mathrm{visc}}$ is the radial viscosity-driven current density, $\mathbf{j}_{\perp}^{\mathrm{visc}}$ is the contribution associated with perpendicular viscous stress, $\mathbf{j}_{\parallel}^{\mathrm{visc}}$ is the contribution associated with parallel viscous stress, $\mathbf{j}_{q}^{\mathrm{visc}}$ is the heat-viscous contribution, and $\hat{R}$ is the outward major-radius unit vector.

This quantity is usually computed from edge fluid, gyrofluid, or kinetic transport models rather than measured directly. It depends on plasma collisionality, magnetization, density and temperature gradients, flow shear, magnetic geometry, and the closure used for the viscous stress tensor; it contributes to cross-field current closure and to the evolution of electric fields in the edge and scrape-off layer.

Typical magnitudes are often about 0.01-100 A.m^-2 in quiescent edge conditions, with localized or transient values reaching 1000 A.m^-2 when gradients, flows, or turbulent structures are strong.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the viscosity-driven current density points in the direction of increasing major radius $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: radial_electron_convection_velocity
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Effective radial convection velocity for electron particle transport. It is the advective coefficient multiplying electron density in a radial particle-flux closure at the plasma edge.
NAMES.long:
Radial electron convection velocity is the effective advective speed associated with cross-field electron particle transport at the plasma edge. It represents the convective, or pinch, part of the radial electron particle flux after diffusive transport has been separated from the closure.

A common particle-flux closure writes the radial electron particle flux as:

$$
\Gamma_{e,r} = -D_{e,r}\,\frac{\partial n_e}{\partial r} + v_{e,r}\,n_e
$$

where $\Gamma_{e,r}$ is the radial electron particle flux in $\mathrm{m^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$, $D_{e,r}$ is an effective radial diffusivity in $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$, $n_e$ is the electron density in $\mathrm{m^{-3}}$, $r$ is an outward radial coordinate in meters, and $v_{e,r}$ is the radial electron convection velocity.

This quantity is usually inferred from edge transport analysis, reduced transport modeling, or fits to electron-density evolution using sources, sinks, and radial gradients. It is an effective closure coefficient: it need not identify a single microscopic drift mechanism and may summarize turbulence, neoclassical effects, and geometry-dependent transport into one advective term.

Typical effective values in the confined edge are from about -50 to 50 m.s^-1. Larger apparent values, up to several hundred m.s^-1, can occur in the scrape-off layer or during strong transient edge transport, depending on the chosen transport closure and averaging interval.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the effective electron particle convection is directed outward across magnetic flux surfaces from the confined plasma toward the plasma-facing material surfaces.

NAMES.name: radial_ion_convection_velocity
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Effective radial convection velocity for ion particle transport in the edge plasma. It is the coefficient multiplying ion density in the cross-field ion particle flux, not necessarily a literal ion fluid velocity.
NAMES.long:
The radial ion convection velocity $v_{r,i}$ is the effective advective coefficient for ion particle transport across magnetic flux surfaces in the edge plasma. The radial direction is the outward normal direction associated with an increasing radial flux label $\rho$ in a flux-surface coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, where $\theta$ is poloidal angle and $\phi$ is toroidal angle. This quantity represents the particle-transport channel and need not equal the radial component of the ion bulk flow.

The convective contribution to the radial ion particle flux density is defined by:

$$
\Gamma_{r,i}^{\mathrm{conv}} = n_i v_{r,i}
$$

where $\Gamma_{r,i}^{\mathrm{conv}}$ is the convective radial ion particle flux density in m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$, $n_i$ is the local ion number density in m$^{-3}$, and $v_{r,i}$ is the radial ion convection velocity in m s$^{-1}$. In a full transport model this term is commonly combined with diffusive and source terms; the convection velocity is the coefficient of the density-proportional part of the cross-field particle flux.

In edge-plasma modeling, $v_{r,i}$ is obtained from transport closures, reduced fluid or kinetic models, or inference from particle balance after separating density-gradient-driven diffusion from density-proportional advection. It may represent the net effect of mean drifts, turbulent transport, intermittent filament motion, ion-neutral coupling, and other unresolved processes. Analogous effective convection velocities are used for ion energy and momentum channels, including charge-state-resolved variants.

Typical absolute values for background effective radial convection in scrape-off-layer and divertor transport studies are about 0.1-100 m s$^{-1}$, depending strongly on plasma regime, collisionality, turbulence level, and proximity to material surfaces. Local transient or filament-associated effective radial speeds can be larger, often 10-1000 m s$^{-1}$, but these may not correspond to a steady flux-surface-averaged coefficient.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $v_{r,i}$ is directed outward across magnetic flux surfaces, toward increasing radial flux label $\rho$ in the flux-surface coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$.

NAMES.name: radial_ion_energy_convection_velocity
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Effective radial convection velocity for the convective part of ion energy transport in the edge plasma. It is an energy-transport coefficient, not necessarily the ion particle flow velocity.
NAMES.long:
Radial ion energy convection velocity is the signed transport coefficient that multiplies the ion pressure or thermal-energy scale in the convective radial ion energy flux. It characterizes advective transport of ion thermal energy across magnetic flux surfaces in the edge plasma, separate from diffusive or conductive transport driven by gradients.

The defining transport relation can be written as:

$$
q^{\mathrm{conv}}_{i,E,r} = p_i v_r
$$

where $q^{\mathrm{conv}}_{i,E,r}$ is the convective radial ion energy flux density in W m$^{-2}$, $p_i$ is the ion pressure or energy-density scale in J m$^{-3}$, and $v_r$ is this velocity in m s$^{-1}$. When $p_i=n_i T_i$ is used, $n_i$ is in m$^{-3}$ and $T_i$ must be in joules; if $T_i$ is represented in eV, it is converted using the elementary charge.

In practice, $v_r$ is inferred from edge transport analysis by separating the convective part of the ion energy flux from conductive or diffusive terms and from local sources and sinks. It differs from [radial_ion_convection_velocity](name:radial_ion_convection_velocity), which refers to particle advection, and from [radial_ion_effective_energy_convection_velocity](name:radial_ion_energy_convection_velocity) when additional non-convective mechanisms are intentionally absorbed into a model-equivalent velocity.

Typical edge-plasma values are often of order -10-50 m s$^{-1}$ on closed edge flux surfaces, with larger effective values of order 100 m s$^{-1}$ possible near strong pedestal gradients or in scrape-off-layer transport analyzes. Values near zero indicate little convective contribution compared with diffusion or conduction.
NAMES.sign: Positive when directed outward across magnetic flux surfaces, from the confined plasma toward the scrape-off layer and wall.

NAMES.name: radial_ion_state_diffusivity
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Radial particle diffusion coefficient for a specific ion charge state, relating the cross-field diffusive particle flux to the radial gradient of that charge-state's number density in the edge plasma.
NAMES.long:
The radial ion state diffusivity $D_r^{(z)}$ quantifies cross-field particle diffusion for ions in a specific ionization stage $z$ in the edge plasma. It is the radial projection of the full [ion_state_diffusivity](name:ion_state_diffusivity) tensor, representing how efficiently that charge state diffuses across magnetic flux surfaces perpendicular to the field.

The quantity enters the charge-state continuity equation through Fick's law:

$$
\Gamma_r^{(z)} = -D_r^{(z)} \nabla_r n_z
$$

where $\Gamma_r^{(z)}$ is the radial diffusive particle flux density of the charge state (in m$^{-2}$s$^{-1}$) and $\nabla_r n_z$ is the radial component of the number density gradient of that charge state (in m$^{-4}$).

In practice, $D_r^{(z)}$ is either prescribed from turbulent-transport models or fitted to experimental edge density profiles by matching computed and measured charge-state distributions. It may vary spatially across the edge grid depending on local turbulence and plasma conditions.

Cross-field particle diffusivities in edge plasmas are anomalously enhanced above neoclassical levels by turbulence, with values commonly in the range $10^{-2}$ to $10^1$ m$^2$s$^{-1}$ in the scrape-off layer and pedestal region. The companion coefficients [radial_ion_state_energy_diffusivity](name:radial_ion_state_energy_diffusivity) and [radial_ion_state_momentum_diffusivity](name:radial_ion_state_momentum_diffusivity) govern radial energy and momentum transport for the same charge state, while [parallel_ion_charge_state_diffusivity](name:parallel_ion_charge_state_diffusivity) captures diffusion along the magnetic field.

NAMES.name: ratio_of_vertical_vorticity_to_major_radius
NAMES.short: The vertical component of the plasma vorticity vector divided by the local major radius. It is the major-radius-scaled form of vertical vorticity used in toroidal edge-fluid operators and has units of inverse meter-second.
NAMES.long:
Ratio of vertical vorticity to major radius is the vertical projection of plasma vorticity divided by the local major radius. Vorticity is the curl of the plasma flow velocity, and its vertical component measures signed local rotation in planes perpendicular to the vertical direction. Dividing by $R$ gives the major-radius-scaled form of the unscaled [vertical vorticity](name:vertical_vorticity).

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height, the quantity is defined by:

$$
\frac{\omega_Z}{R} = \frac{(\nabla \times \mathbf{v}) \cdot \hat{Z}}{R}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}$ is the plasma flow velocity, $\boldsymbol{\omega}=\nabla\times\mathbf{v}$ is the vorticity, $\omega_Z=\boldsymbol{\omega}\cdot\hat{Z}$ is the vertical vorticity component, and $R>0$ is the local major radius.

In practice this quantity is computed from measured, reconstructed, or modeled velocity fields by evaluating the vertical component of the curl and dividing pointwise by $R$. In toroidal edge-fluid and turbulence formulations it may appear when divergence, polarization, or curvature-related operators are written with major-radius metric factors; this use does not change its definition as scaled vertical vorticity.

Representative edge-plasma magnitudes depend on flow shear, turbulent length scale, and machine size. Vorticity magnitudes of about $10^4-10^7$ s$^{-1}$ at major radii of $0.5-3$ m correspond to roughly $10^4-10^7$ m$^{-1}$ s$^{-1}$, with intermittent turbulent structures sometimes outside this range.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the vertical component of the vorticity vector points in the $+\hat{Z}$ direction, since $R$ is positive.

NAMES.name: thermal_plasma_pressure
NAMES.short: Total kinetic pressure of the bulk thermal plasma, equal to the sum of electron and bulk-ion thermal pressure contributions and excluding fast, suprathermal, or runaway populations.
NAMES.long:
Thermal plasma pressure is the isotropic kinetic pressure associated with particle populations close to local thermodynamic equilibrium. It includes the thermal electron contribution and the contributions from bulk thermal ion species, but excludes nonthermal populations such as fast ions, suprathermal tails, and runaway electrons. It is the thermal component of the more general [plasma_pressure](name:plasma_pressure) and is closely related to thermal_pressure, [total_electron_pressure](name:total_electron_pressure), and [total_ion_pressure](name:total_ion_pressure).

For Maxwellian or near-Maxwellian thermal species, the pressure is defined by the species density-temperature sum:

$$
p_\mathrm{th} = n_e k_B T_e + \sum_i n_i k_B T_i
$$

where $n_e$ and $n_i$ are electron and bulk-ion number densities in m$^{-3}$, $T_e$ and $T_i$ are thermodynamic temperatures in K, $k_B$ is Boltzmann's constant, and the sum is over thermal ion species. When temperatures are tabulated in eV, the equivalent SI pressure is obtained by replacing $k_B T_s$ with $e T_s$, where $e$ is the elementary charge and $T_s$ is the temperature value in eV; this gives $p_\mathrm{th}$ in Pa.
