Ferritic elements are ferromagnetic inserts employed in some fusion devices to reduce toroidal magnetic-field ripple; each element is modeled as an axisymmetric body whose cross-section is an annulus centered at a reference point $(R_0, Z_0)$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius from the toroidal symmetry axis and $Z$ is the vertical height.

For an annular cross-section with inner radius $r_\mathrm{in}$ and outer radius $r_\mathrm{out}$, the enclosed area is

$$
A = \pi\bigl(r_\mathrm{out}^2 - r_\mathrm{in}^2\bigr)
$$

with the geometric constraint $0 \leq r_\mathrm{in} < r_\mathrm{out}$. The inner radius is a design parameter supplied directly to the geometry model and is not inferred from in-situ measurements. Together with [outer_radius_of_ferritic_element](name:outer_radius_of_ferritic_element), it fully characterizes the radial extent of the annular cross-section, while the overall radial placement of the element is given by [radius_of_ferritic_element](name:radius_of_ferritic_element). The analogous quantity for iron core segments is [inner_radius_of_iron_core_segment](name:inner_radius_of_iron_core_segment).
NAMES.sign: Positive as a non-negative radial distance from the annulus center to the inner surface in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame where $R \geq 0$.

NAMES.name: outer_radius_of_ferritic_element
NAMES.short: Outer major-radius boundary of an annular representation of a ferritic element in an axisymmetric equivalent geometry. It is the maximum R extent of the ferritic annulus in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The outer radius of a ferritic element is the largest major-radius coordinate occupied by the annular cross-section used to represent magnetically permeable material in an axisymmetric equivalent geometry. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $R$ is distance from the toroidal symmetry axis and $Z$ is vertical height; this quantity defines the radially outward boundary of the annulus.

For an annular ferritic region $\Omega_f$ represented in the poloidal $(R,Z)$ plane, the outer radius is

$$
R_{\mathrm{outer}} = \max_{(R,Z)\in\Omega_f} R
$$

where $\Omega_f$ is the cross-section assigned to the ferritic material and $R$ is the major-radius coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

The value is usually obtained from engineering geometry, computer-aided design models, or simplified axisymmetric models of ferritic inserts, cores, shields, or other magnetic structures. Together with the corresponding inner radius, it sets the radial thickness and placement of the annular magnetic material used in equilibrium and magnetic-field calculations.

Typical values are device- and component-dependent: compact ferritic inserts may have outer radii of 0.2-2 m, while larger ferritic structures in medium to large tokamaks may extend to 2-10 m. The value is non-negative by geometry and must exceed the corresponding inner radius for a finite annular thickness.

NAMES.name: radius_of_passive_structure
NAMES.short: Curvature radius of each arc-of-circle segment approximating the cross-sectional contour of a passive conducting structure element in a piecewise boundary representation.
NAMES.long:
The curvature radius parametrizes individual arc segments in the piecewise arc-of-circle description of a passive conducting structure element's cross-sectional boundary in the poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius and $Z$ is the vertical height. The full cross-sectional contour is assembled from a sequence of such arcs sharing consecutive endpoint vertices to form a closed boundary curve.

Each arc is the locus of points at distance $\rho$ from the arc's center of curvature $(R_c, Z_c)$ in the poloidal plane:

$$
\sqrt{(R - R_c)^2 + (Z - Z_c)^2} = \rho
$$

where $(R_c, Z_c)$ are in meters. Specifying the starting vertex coordinates and $\rho$ for each successive arc fully determines the conductor cross-section shape; the straight-line limit is approached as $\rho \to \infty$.

This arc-of-circle convention is shared across conductor geometries in the machine: [radius_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:radius_of_poloidal_field_coil) applies the same representation to active coil elements, and [radius_of_iron_core_segment](name:radius_of_iron_core_segment) applies it to transformer core cross-sections. For passive structures with annular cross-sections, [inner_radius_of_passive_structure](name:inner_radius_of_passive_loop) defines the bore radius, while [width_of_passive_structure](name:width_of_passive_structure) and [height_of_passive_structure](name:height_of_passive_structure) characterize rectangular cross-section geometries. Values typically range from centimeters for tightly curved conductor corners to larger values for gently curving contour segments.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the arc center of curvature lies at a finite distance from the boundary arc in the poloidal $(R, Z)$ plane; the curvature radius is non-negative by geometric construction.

NAMES.name: radius_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Non-negative curvature radius of one arc-of-circle segment used to approximate the cross-sectional contour of a poloidal field coil. The contour lies in a poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, where R is major radius and Z is vertical height.
NAMES.long:
Radius of a poloidal-field-coil arc is the non-negative circle radius of a single circular segment of the coil cross-sectional contour, taken in a poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height. The conductor or winding-pack boundary is approximated by connected circular arcs, and this quantity sets the local radius of curvature of one such arc.

For a circular contour segment, the curvature radius $\rho$ (in m) is the inverse magnitude of the planar curvature $\kappa$ (in m$^{-1}$) of the boundary curve in the $(R, Z)$ cross-section:

$$
\rho = \frac{1}{|\kappa|}
$$

where a finite physical arc has $\rho > 0$, and as $\rho$ grows the segment approaches a straight line ($\kappa \to 0$). Each arc is anchored by a start point in the poloidal plane: its major-radius coordinate is given by [major_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:major_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil) and its vertical coordinate by [height_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:height_of_poloidal_field_coil); both together with $\rho$ are needed to locate and shape one arc, with the end of each arc coinciding with the start of the next.

The value is determined from the designed circular-arc contour, from CAD geometry, or by fitting circular arcs to surveyed boundary points. Small radii represent tightly rounded corners and compact winding-pack features, while larger radii represent gently curved coil sides; the magnitude scales with coil aperture, winding-pack dimensions, and mechanical-clearance requirements. An analogous arc-of-circle convention applies to iron core segment boundaries via [radius_of_iron_core_segment](name:radius_of_iron_core_segment).

NAMES.name: inner_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Inner radius of the annular cross-section of a poloidal field coil, defining the size of the conductor bore in the poloidal plane.
NAMES.long:
The inner radius is the smaller of the two radial dimensions characterizing the annular conductor cross-section of a poloidal field coil, measured from the center of the annulus to its inner conducting boundary in a poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius and $Z$ is the vertical height.

Together with [outer_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:outer_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil) and the annulus center position, the inner radius completely specifies the annular cross-section geometry required for electromagnetic calculations including inductance and field-map computations. The annular cross-sectional area relates to both radii via:

$$
A = \pi \left( r_\mathrm{out}^2 - r_\mathrm{in}^2 \right)
$$

where $r_\mathrm{in}$ is the inner radius and $r_\mathrm{out}$ is the outer radius; this area corresponds to [area_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:area_of_poloidal_field_coil). The physical constraint $0 \le r_\mathrm{in} < r_\mathrm{out}$ must hold; when $r_\mathrm{in} = 0$ the annular cross-section degenerates to a solid disk.

The inner radius is taken directly from engineering design specifications and serves as a geometric input to electromagnetic and structural modeling of PF coil systems. The analogous quantity for non-axisymmetric correction coils is [inner_radius_of_correction_coil](name:inner_radius_of_correction_coil).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the inner conductor boundary is displaced radially outward from the annulus center, as measured in the poloidal cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: major_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Major radius coordinate of an arc-of-circle defining point for a poloidal field coil conductor, equal to the radial distance in meters from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Major radius for a poloidal field coil is the $R$ coordinate of a point on the conductor contour in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is distance from the toroidal symmetry axis, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. For an arc-of-circle contour, this quantity locates each arc-defining point radially and complements the associated [vertical coordinate of the poloidal field coil].

The relation to horizontal Cartesian coordinates of the same point is:

$$
R = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}
$$

where $R$, $x$, $y$, and the associated $Z$ coordinate are all lengths in meters. The coordinates $x$ and $y$ are measured in a right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$ frame with $x=y=0$ on the toroidal symmetry axis and $\hat{z}$ parallel to the vertical $+\hat{Z}$ direction.

The value is determined from engineering geometry, CAD models, or mechanical survey of the coil conductor. In an arc-of-circle representation, the radial coordinate of each defining point and its associated vertical coordinate determine the arc segments that form the conductor cross-section; it is a geometric quantity rather than a magnetic field or current.

Typical values are device-scale non-negative distances in meters. Central-solenoid conductors generally have smaller $R$ than outboard poloidal-field coils, but the admissible range is machine-specific and no universal numerical interval is implied by the quantity definition.

NAMES.name: outer_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Outer radius of the annular cross-section of a poloidal field coil conductor element, defining the radial outer boundary of the conductor geometry.
NAMES.long:
The outer radius defines the outward radial extent of the annular cross-section used to model a poloidal field coil conductor element. Together with the [inner_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:inner_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil) and the coil center position in the poloidal $(R, Z)$ plane, it fully specifies the annular geometry required for electromagnetic calculations such as mutual inductance and Biot-Savart field evaluation.

The annular cross-sectional area $A$ is:

$$
A = \pi \left( r_\mathrm{out}^2 - r_\mathrm{in}^2 \right)
$$

where $r_\mathrm{out}$ is the outer radius and $r_\mathrm{in}$ is the [inner_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:inner_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil). This [area_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:area_of_poloidal_field_coil) enters directly into current density and inductance calculations.

For PF coil conductors in medium-to-large fusion devices, outer radii range from a few centimeters to approximately 0.3-0.5 m, depending on the conductor bundle size and design current.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the outer boundary lies at a greater radial distance from the annulus center than the inner boundary, as required for a physically valid annular cross-section.

NAMES.name: resistance_of_correction_coil
NAMES.short: Electrical resistance of a non-axisymmetric correction coil conductor, determining the ohmic power dissipation and static voltage drop across the coil terminals.
NAMES.long:
The resistance of a correction coil characterizes the DC ohmic resistance of the conductor winding, governing resistive power dissipation and the steady-state voltage-current relationship in the coil circuit. Correction coils are non-axisymmetric coils that apply three-dimensional magnetic perturbations for ELM suppression, error field correction, or resonant magnetic perturbation experiments.

The ohmic power dissipated in the coil is:

$$
P_{\rm ohm} = I^2 R
$$

where $I$ is the [current through the coil](name:current_of_correction_coil) and $R$ is the resistance. The corresponding [terminal voltage](name:voltage_of_correction_coil) satisfies $V = IR$ under DC conditions; at finite frequency an inductive contribution adds to the impedance, but the resistive component captured here determines steady-state dissipation and thermal loading on the coil support structure.

Resistance is determined from conductor material resistivity (which varies with temperature), conductor cross-sectional area, and total winding path length, or measured directly by a DC voltage-current sweep at the coil terminals.

Values for correction coils in large tokamaks range from a few milliohms to several ohms, depending on conductor dimensions and winding geometry. The analogous quantity for toroidal field coils is [resistance_of_toroidal_field_coil](name:resistance_of_toroidal_field_coil).

NAMES.name: resistance_of_passive_loop
NAMES.short: Ohmic electrical resistance of a passive conducting loop, which together with its self-inductance sets the L/R time constant governing eddy-current decay during plasma transients.
NAMES.long:
The resistance of a passive conducting loop quantifies the ohmic opposition to current flow in an axisymmetric conductor that is inductively coupled to the plasma but not connected to an external power supply. Passive loops carry eddy currents induced by changes in plasma current or equilibrium position, and their resistance governs how quickly those induced currents decay.

The resistance $R$ and self-inductance $L$ together determine the characteristic decay time constant:

$$
\tau = \frac{L}{R}
$$

where $\tau$ is the e-folding time for eddy-current decay, $L$ is the self-inductance, and $R$ is this resistance. A smaller resistance extends $\tau$, prolonging the stabilizing influence of the eddy currents during vertical displacement events or plasma disruptions.

For a loop of uniform cross-section, $R = \rho \ell / A$, where $\rho$ is the material resistivity (see [resistivity_of_passive_structure](name:resistivity_of_passive_structure)), $\ell$ is the mean conductor path length, and $A$ is the cross-sectional area determined by [inner_radius_of_passive_loop](name:inner_radius_of_passive_loop) and [outer_radius_of_passive_loop](name:outer_radius_of_passive_loop). Values range from sub-milliohm for low-resistivity conductors to tens of milliohms for higher-resistivity materials, depending on geometry. This quantity follows the established resistance-of-object pattern alongside [resistance_of_toroidal_field_coil](name:resistance_of_toroidal_field_coil) and [resistance_of_correction_coil](name:resistance_of_correction_coil).

NAMES.name: resistance_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Ohmic electrical resistance of a poloidal field coil winding. It relates coil current to resistive voltage drop and Joule heating at the specified operating state.
NAMES.long:
Resistance of a poloidal field coil is the effective series ohmic resistance of the coil winding at its operating state. It represents conversion of electrical energy into heat in the conductor, joints, and other series elements included in the coil definition, and it sets the resistive part of the terminal voltage demand.

In a lumped circuit model for coil $k$, the terminal-voltage balance is commonly written after choosing branch-current and terminal-voltage reference directions:

$$
V_k = R_k I_k + L_k \frac{dI_k}{dt} + \sum_{j \ne k} \epsilon_{kj} M_{kj} \frac{dI_j}{dt}
$$

where $V_k$ is the terminal voltage in V, $R_k$ is the coil resistance in ohm, $I_k$ and $I_j$ are currents in A, $L_k$ is self-inductance in H, $M_{kj}$ is mutual inductance in H, $dI/dt$ is in A/s, $j$ labels coupled circuits or conductors, and $\epsilon_{kj}$ is a dimensionless factor equal to $+1$ or $-1$ for the chosen mutual-reference orientation. The equation assumes the passive reference for the resistive drop, with $V_k$ positive as a voltage drop along the chosen positive $I_k$ direction; reversing a current reference or terminal-voltage polarity changes the algebraic signs of the inductive and mutual terms consistently, but does not change the non-negative value of $R_k$.

The value is computed from conductor material resistivity, winding length, cross-sectional area, cooling state, and the temperature distribution of the winding. It may be measured by four-terminal DC injection or inferred from slow current ramps after subtracting inductive and mutual voltage contributions. For normal-conducting coils the resistance increases with temperature; for superconducting coils the effective series resistance depends on whether joints, current-sharing regions, or quench behavior are included in the coil model.

Typical effective resistances are $10^{-4}$-$10^{-1}$ ohm for large normal-conducting poloidal field coils and $10^{-3}$-1 ohm for smaller shaping or laboratory coils. Superconducting poloidal field windings in steady superconducting operation are often represented as 0-$10^{-6}$ ohm effective series resistance when only persistent or joint losses are included; during current sharing or a quench, the apparent resistance can rise to $10^{-4}$-1 ohm and becomes strongly time dependent.

NAMES.name: resistance_of_toroidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Ohmic electrical resistance of a toroidal field coil conductor, determining resistive power dissipation and voltage drop during coil operation.
NAMES.long:
The resistance of a toroidal field coil is the ohmic impedance of its conductor winding at a given temperature and operational state, governing how the coil dissipates energy and sustains a voltage drop when carrying current.

The resistive power deposited in the coil is defined by:

$$
P_\mathrm{ohm} = I^2 R_\mathrm{TF}
$$

where $I$ is the coil current and $R_\mathrm{TF}$ is the coil resistance. The resistance depends on conductor geometry and material electrical resistivity $\rho_e$ through $R_\mathrm{TF} = \rho_e L / A_c$, where $L$ is the total conductor length and $A_c$ is the conductor cross-sectional area.

Coil resistance is determined by direct four-wire (Kelvin) electrical measurements or from conductor material properties and geometry as a function of temperature. For superconducting TF coils operated below the critical temperature, the effective resistance is negligible; for normal-conducting (resistive) TF coils, values range from a few milliohms to tens of milliohms depending on device scale and conductor material.

The resistive voltage drop $V_R = I \cdot R_\mathrm{TF}$ contributes to the total terminal voltage captured by [voltage_of_toroidal_field_coil](name:voltage_of_toroidal_field_coil). Analogous quantities for other coil systems include [resistance_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:resistance_of_poloidal_field_coil) and [resistance_of_correction_coil](name:resistance_of_correction_coil).

NAMES.name: thickness_of_iron_core_segment
NAMES.short: Face-to-face distance across an iron-core segment measured normal to its centerline; a non-negative transverse size of the segment cross-section.
NAMES.long:
Thickness of an iron-core segment is the face-to-face distance across the segment measured along the local normal to its centerline; it is a non-negative geometric length. In a local right-handed segment basis $(\hat{s}, \hat{n}, \hat{b})$, $\hat{s}$ is tangent to the centerline, $\hat{n}$ is the transverse thickness direction, and $\hat{b}$ completes the triad. For axisymmetric poloidal-plane descriptions, $\hat{s}$ and $\hat{n}$ lie in the $(R,Z)$ plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise when viewed from above, and $Z$ is vertical height.

For a rectangular cross-section normal to the centerline, the thickness sets the area together with the segment width:

$$
A_\perp = t\,w
$$

where $A_\perp$ is the cross-sectional area in m^2, $t$ is the segment thickness in m, and $w$ is the [width of the iron-core segment](name:width_of_iron_core_segment) in m.

Thickness is obtained from engineering drawings, surveys, or magnetic-circuit geometry by taking the separation of the two bounding faces along $\hat{n}$. In electromagnetic calculations, increasing thickness increases cross-sectional area, reduces magnetic reluctance, and lowers the magnetic flux density for a given total flux, helping to avoid iron saturation.

Typical values are about 0.05-0.5 m for small pole-piece or local insert segments, 0.5-2 m for medium transformer-core limbs or return-yoke pieces, and 2-5 m for very large iron-core sectors. The selected value depends on required flux, allowable saturation, mechanical clearance, and segmentation.

NAMES.name: thickness_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Thickness of a poloidal field coil is the full conductor-package cross-sectional extent measured normal to the coil reference centerline in a poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, where R is major radius, phi is toroidal angle, and Z is vertical height. It is distinct from radial width and vertical height.
NAMES.long:
Thickness of a poloidal field coil is the face-to-face size of the coil conductor package measured along the direction normal to the coil reference centerline in a poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It is a local transverse dimension of the winding pack or conductor envelope, not necessarily the same as the radial width along $R$ or the vertical height along $Z$.

For a coil cross-section with boundary points $\mathbf{x}$ and a unit normal $\hat{n}$ in the poloidal plane, the thickness $t$ may be written as the full projected extent of the cross-section:

$$
t = \max_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{x}\cdot\hat{n}) - \min_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{x}\cdot\hat{n})
$$

where $\hat{n}$ is perpendicular to the local coil reference centerline and the extrema are taken over the gross conductor-package cross-section.

The value is obtained from the engineering geometry of the poloidal field coil winding pack or conductor package. Unless a more specific quantity states otherwise, it denotes the gross physical envelope assigned to the coil package, including insulation, stabilizer, casing, or internal voids that are part of that envelope; it is not the net area of electrically conducting material alone. Together with complementary dimensions such as [width_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:width_of_poloidal_field_coil) and [height_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:height_of_poloidal_field_coil), it determines the geometric cross-section used to compute quantities such as [area_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:area_of_poloidal_field_coil).

Typical values range from 0.05-0.5 m for small or medium experimental coils and about 0.2-1.5 m for large tokamak poloidal-field winding packs; very large superconducting coil packages can have thicknesses of order 2 m or more.

NAMES.name: toroidal_angle_of_toroidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Toroidal angle coordinate of a toroidal-field-coil conductor cross-section contour point, expressed relative to the cross-section reference point in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It is used with major radius and vertical height to locate the contour point.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal angle of a toroidal-field-coil conductor cross section is the angular coordinate of a conductor-contour point measured relative to a designated reference point on that cross section. It is the toroidal component of the point location in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height.

For contour point $i$, the relative toroidal angle is defined as the difference between the point and reference toroidal coordinates:

$$
\phi_{\mathrm{rel},i} = \phi_i - \phi_{\mathrm{ref}}
$$

where $\phi_i$ is the toroidal coordinate of the contour point, $\phi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the toroidal coordinate of the reference point, and $\phi_{\mathrm{rel},i}$ is expressed in radians. Because toroidal angle is periodic, values that differ by $2\pi n$, with integer $n$, represent the same toroidal direction; the physical definition does not impose a device-independent wrapping interval.

In practice, this coordinate is computed from the engineered conductor geometry by evaluating the toroidal coordinate of each contour point and subtracting the reference-point toroidal coordinate. Together with the radial coordinate [major_radius_of_toroidal_field_coil](name:major_radius_of_toroidal_field_coil) and vertical height [height_of_toroidal_field_coil](name:height_of_toroidal_field_coil), it locates the contour point in the cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The corresponding generic conductor quantity is [toroidal_angle_of_conductor_cross_section](name:toroidal_angle_of_conductor_cross_section).

Typical numerical values are design-specific and depend on the chosen reference point and conductor cross-section geometry. The relevant universal scale is the angular periodicity $2\pi$ rad, so the values should be interpreted as relative toroidal coordinates rather than as absolute toroidal positions of the coil.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the contour point is displaced from the reference point in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_magnetic_field_at_ferritic_element_centroid
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the magnetic field evaluated at the geometric centroid of each ferritic in-vessel element, giving the local phi-direction field strength experienced by the ferromagnetic material.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal magnetic field at a ferritic element centroid is the projection of the total magnetic field vector onto the toroidal direction $\hat{\phi}$ at the geometric center of a ferromagnetic in-vessel structural component. Ferritic elements are ferromagnetic inserts installed inside the vacuum vessel; the field value at their centroid provides a representative local field for each discrete element in thin-shell or equivalent-circuit magnetic models of ferromagnetic in-vessel hardware.

The toroidal component is defined by:

$$
B_\phi = \mathbf{B} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, with $R$ the major radius and $Z$ the vertical coordinate.

In magnetostatic models of ferromagnetic in-vessel components, $B_\phi$ at the centroid enters the material's $B$–$H$ constitutive relation to determine the element's toroidal magnetization state, captured by [toroidal magnetization](name:toroidal_magnetization_of_ferritic_element). Together with [radial_magnetic_field_at_ferritic_element_centroid](name:radial_magnetic_field_at_ferritic_element_centroid) and [vertical_magnetic_field_at_ferritic_element_centroid](name:vertical_magnetic_field_at_ferritic_element_centroid), it reconstructs the full field vector at each ferritic centroid, enabling assessment of the element's magnetization state under operational conditions. In tokamak configurations the toroidal field dominates, with values of order 1–6 T near in-vessel components depending on the device and radial position.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $B_\phi$ points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: vertical_angle_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Inclination angle beta of the second oblique side of a poloidal field coil parallelogram cross-section, measured counter-clockwise from the vertically upward direction in the poloidal plane.
NAMES.long:
The vertical angle $\beta$ parameterizes the tilt of the second inclined side of the oblique parallelogram cross-section of a poloidal field coil conductor element, specified in the poloidal $R$-$Z$ plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. Together with the [radial angle $\alpha$](name:radial_angle_of_poloidal_field_coil) (measured counter-clockwise from the outward $\hat{R}$ direction), $\beta$ fully defines the oblique orientation of the non-rectangular conductor winding-pack geometry.

The angle is defined by the dot-product relation:

$$
\hat{e}_{\beta} \cdot \hat{Z} = \cos\beta
$$

where $\hat{e}_{\beta}$ is the unit vector along the beta-side inclined edge and $\hat{Z}$ is the vertically upward unit vector; the signed direction is determined by measuring $\beta$ counter-clockwise from $+\hat{Z}$ in the poloidal $R$-$Z$ plane.

This geometric parameter is derived from engineering design data for the coil winding pack and is used in electromagnetic analysis to compute conductor self- and mutual inductances and Lorentz forces on the cross-section. The extent of the beta-side edge is given by [length_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:length_of_poloidal_field_coil), while [major_length_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:major_length_of_poloidal_field_coil) gives the alpha-side edge extent.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the beta-side edge direction $\hat{e}_{\beta}$ is rotated counter-clockwise from $+\hat{Z}$ in the poloidal $R$-$Z$ plane.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_conductor_cross_section
NAMES.short: Vertical Z-coordinate of the geometric center of a conductor cross-section in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate of a conductor cross-section is the $Z$ location of the geometric center, or centroid, of the cross-sectional shape in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. In this frame, $R$ is major radius in meters, $\phi$ is toroidal angle in radians, and $Z$ is vertical height in meters.

For a finite cross-sectional area, the centroid coordinate is defined by the area average of the vertical position:

$$
Z_c = \frac{1}{A}\int_A Z\,dA
$$

where $Z_c$ is the conductor cross-section center coordinate in meters, $A$ is the cross-sectional area in square meters, and $Z$ is the vertical coordinate in meters over that area.

This quantity is determined from the conductor geometry, for example from engineering design data, survey geometry, or a geometric model used for magnetic-field calculations. Together with the companion major-radius coordinate major_radius_of_conductor_cross_section, it locates the conductor cross-section center in the poloidal $(R, Z)$ plane.

Values are reported in meters and depend on the chosen vertical origin and the size and layout of the magnetic-field system; no universal numerical range applies across devices. Components centered above the vertical origin have positive $Z_c$, while those centered below it have negative $Z_c$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the conductor cross-section center is displaced in the $+Z$ direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_ferritic_element_centroid
NAMES.short: Vertical Z coordinate of the geometric centroid of a ferritic element in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, where Z increases upward from the machine midplane.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate $Z$ locates the geometric centroid of a ferritic element along the machine vertical axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius from the toroidal symmetry axis and $Z$ is measured from the machine midplane, increasing upward.

Ferritic elements are passive ferromagnetic components — typically ferritic steel tiles or inserts — installed within the vacuum vessel to reduce toroidal magnetic field ripple and improve single-particle confinement. Accurate centroid positions are required for electromagnetic modeling of ripple fields and for equilibrium reconstruction codes that account for the perturbed toroidal field.

Together with the corresponding radial position [major_radius_of_ferritic_element](name:major_radius_of_ferritic_element), this quantity fully specifies the centroid location in the poloidal cross-section for axisymmetric geometric representations. The equivalent Cartesian description uses [x_coordinate_of_ferritic_element_centroid](name:x_coordinate_of_ferritic_element_centroid) and [y_centroid_of_ferritic_element](name:y_coordinate_of_ferritic_element_centroid) for three-dimensional positioning. Centroid coordinates are typically derived from engineering drawings or CAD geometry of the as-built device.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the centroid lies above the machine midplane in the direction of increasing $Z$.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_passive_structure
NAMES.short: Vertical Z-coordinate of a geometric reference point on the cross-section of a passive conducting structure, measured in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame from the machine midplane.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate $Z$ locates a geometric point defining the cross-sectional shape of a passive conducting structure element in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle increasing counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is the height above the machine midplane. Passive structures are unpowered conducting elements — such as stabilizing loops, conducting shells, or vacuum vessel segments — that respond to time-varying magnetic fields through induced eddy currents, influencing plasma vertical stability and equilibrium evolution.

Cross-sections of passive elements are described by parametric shapes: polygon outlines (sequences of vertices), arcs of circles, oblique trapezoids, or thick-line segments defined by two endpoint coordinates. This $Z$ coordinate specifies one such geometric vertex or endpoint, and must be paired with the corresponding major-radius coordinate to fully define a point in the poloidal plane. Geometry is typically specified from engineering drawings or as-built surveys of the device. Analogous coordinates for active coil elements are given by [vertical_coordinate_of_coil_conductor](name:vertical_coordinate_of_coil_conductor) and [vertical_coordinate_of_conductor_cross_section](name:vertical_coordinate_of_conductor_cross_section).

Typical values span the vertical extent of the machine, ranging from approximately $-2$ to $+2$ m in medium-sized tokamaks and up to $\pm 4$ m in larger devices.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the point lies above the machine midplane in the $+Z$ direction.

NAMES.name: vertical_force_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Vertical electromagnetic force acting on an individual poloidal field coil, positive when directed upward along the machine symmetry axis.
NAMES.long:
The vertical force on a poloidal field coil is the net Lorentz body force integrated over the full coil conductor volume in the direction parallel to the machine symmetry axis $\hat{Z}$ of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It arises from the interaction of the coil current with the combined magnetic field produced by the plasma current, all active poloidal field coils, and any passive conducting structures present in the device.

The defining integral is:

$$
F_Z = \int_V (\mathbf{J} \times \mathbf{B}) \cdot \hat{Z} \, dV
$$

where $\mathbf{J}$ is the coil current density, $\mathbf{B}$ is the total local magnetic flux density, and the integral is taken over the coil conductor volume $V$.

In practice this force is computed from electromagnetic equilibrium models using the coil geometry and reconstructed current distribution rather than measured directly on the conductor. It is a key input for structural analysis of coil support systems, as large vertical forces develop during plasma current ramp-up, steady-state operation, and especially at disruptions.

The orthogonal in-plane component is given by [radial_force_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:radial_force_of_poloidal_field_coil), while the system-level sum over all PF coils is captured by vertical_force. Operating bounds on the aggregate system are characterized by [vertical_minimum_force](name:vertical_minimum_force).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the net force is directed in the $+Z$ direction (upward along the machine symmetry axis).

NAMES.name: vertical_magnetic_field_at_ferritic_element_centroid
NAMES.short: Vertical component of the magnetic field at the centroid of a ferritic element, measuring the Z-directed field contribution to the local magnetic state of the ferromagnetic in-vessel component.
NAMES.long:
Ferritic elements are ferromagnetic in-vessel components, such as ferritic steel inserts, installed in some tokamaks to reduce toroidal field ripple and manage magnetic loads. The magnetic field sampled at each element's centroid serves as the representative local field vector used to evaluate the element's magnetization state and compute its back-reaction on the global equilibrium.

The vertical component $B_Z = \mathbf{B} \cdot \hat{Z}$ is the projection of the total magnetic field onto the $\hat{Z}$ axis of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $Z$ is the vertical height measured from the device midplane. Together with the [radial component](name:radial_magnetic_field_at_ferritic_element_centroid) $B_R$ and the [toroidal component](name:toroidal_magnetic_field_at_ferritic_element_centroid) $B_\phi$, it fully specifies the local field vector that drives the element's [vertical magnetization](name:vertical_magnetization_of_ferritic_element) $M_Z$.

In magnetostatic modeling, the centroid field is obtained from the self-consistent equilibrium solution or from a reduced thick-line approximation of the ferromagnetic element, where the centroid value represents the spatially averaged field over the element's cross-section.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $B_Z$ points in the $+Z$ direction (upward along the machine symmetry axis).

NAMES.name: vertical_maximum_force
NAMES.short: Vertical maximum force is the upper allowable value of the net electromagnetic force component along Z in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame acting on an axisymmetric poloidal-field coil system. It is a design-defined hard constraint for coil-current scenario optimization.
NAMES.long:
Vertical maximum force is the upper structural limit on the net electromagnetic force component in the $Z$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $Z$ is vertical height, acting on the complete axisymmetric poloidal-field coil system. It defines the positive side of the vertical force envelope: admissible operating points require the instantaneous vertical_force to satisfy $F_Z \le F_{Z,\max}$ while also respecting [vertical_minimum_force](name:vertical_minimum_force).

The instantaneous force constrained by this limit is the sum of Lorentz forces on the coil conductors:

$$
F_Z = \sum_k I_k \oint_{\mathcal{C}_k} \left(d\boldsymbol{\ell}_k \times \mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{ext},k}\right) \cdot \hat{Z}
$$

where $F_Z$ is the net vertical force in N, $k$ indexes coil windings or current circuits, $I_k$ is the circuit current in A, $d\boldsymbol{\ell}_k$ is the conductor line element in m oriented with the current, and $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{ext},k}$ is the magnetic field in T at that conductor due to sources external to the same current element.

The limit value is a design and structural-analysis quantity, not a scenario-dependent response. It is set from support loads, stress allowables, load combinations, margins, and protection requirements; scenario optimization treats it as a fixed upper bound while the actual $F_Z$ varies with coil currents, plasma current, equilibrium shape, and induced currents in nearby conductors.

Typical upper limits range from $10^5$-$10^7$ N for small and medium devices and from $10^7$-$10^8$ N or more for large high-field devices, depending on coil size, field strength, support stiffness, and allowable mechanical stress.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the net vertical electromagnetic force on the coil system points in the $+Z$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_minimum_force
NAMES.short: Minimum allowable net vertical electromagnetic force on the axisymmetric PF coil system, defining the lower bound of the structural force envelope within which plasma operations must remain.
NAMES.long:
The vertical minimum force is the lower structural limit on the combined net vertical electromagnetic force that the axisymmetric poloidal field coil system can safely sustain. This limit, together with [vertical_maximum_force](name:vertical_maximum_force), defines the allowable force window that the mechanical support structure must accommodate across all plasma scenarios without mechanical failure or loss of coil positional stability.

The net vertical electromagnetic force on the coil assembly is the $Z$-component of the Lorentz body force integrated over all coil volumes:

$$
F_z = \sum_k \int_{V_k} (\mathbf{J}_k \times \mathbf{B}) \cdot \hat{Z} \, dV
$$

where $\mathbf{J}_k$ is the current density in the $k$-th coil, $\mathbf{B}$ is the total magnetic field, and $\hat{Z}$ is the vertical unit vector of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

The instantaneous vertical_force must remain between this lower limit and [vertical_maximum_force](name:vertical_maximum_force) throughout operation. The analogous lower radial limit is provided by [radial_total_minimum_force_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:radial_minimum_force_of_poloidal_field_coil). These limits are determined from structural analysis of the coil support system and are specified as design constraints for the tokamak electromagnetic load envelope.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the net vertical force acts in the $+Z$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_vacuum_magnetic_vector_potential
NAMES.short: Vertical Z component of the vacuum magnetic vector potential produced by toroidal-field coil currents, evaluated in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The vertical vacuum magnetic vector potential is the $Z$ component $A_Z$ of the magnetic vector potential $\mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{vac}}$ produced by toroidal-field coil currents with plasma-current and material-response currents excluded. It is evaluated along $\hat{Z}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The associated vacuum magnetic field satisfies $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{vac}} = \nabla \times \mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{vac}}$.

In the Coulomb gage with reference $\mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{vac}} \to 0$ far from localized coils, the Biot-Savart definition of the component is:

$$
A_Z(R, \phi, Z) = \hat{Z}\cdot\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int_{\Omega_{\mathrm{TF}}}\frac{\mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{TF}}(\mathbf{r}')}{|\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}'|}\,d^3r'
$$

where $\mathbf{r}$ is the field point with cylindrical coordinates $(R, \phi, Z)$ in meters, $\mathbf{r}'$ is a source point in meters, $\Omega_{\mathrm{TF}}$ is the toroidal-field-coil conductor volume, $\mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{TF}}$ is the coil current density in A m$^{-2}$, $d^3r'$ is the source volume element in m$^3$, $\mu_0$ is the vacuum permeability in N A$^{-2}$, and $A_Z$ is in T m.

It is normally computed from coil geometry and currents using Biot-Savart quadrature or a magnetostatic vector-potential solver. Together with the radial and toroidal components of $\mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{vac}}$, it determines associated vacuum-field components through the cylindrical curl, including [toroidal_vacuum_magnetic_field](name:toroidal_vacuum_magnetic_field) and non-axisymmetric field components such as [vertical_non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field](name:vertical_non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field).

Typical magnitudes in the plasma region are about $10^{-3}$-$10$ T m for medium to large tokamaks, with larger local values possible near high-current coil conductors. The value depends on coil current, conductor geometry, distance from the coils, and the specified gage reference.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the gage-fixed vacuum magnetic vector potential has a component in the $+Z$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: voltage_of_correction_coil
NAMES.short: Terminal voltage of a non-axisymmetric correction coil is the signed electric potential difference between its two electrical terminals. It includes the resistive drop and the self- and mutual-inductive voltage associated with changing currents.
NAMES.long:
Voltage of a correction coil is the signed terminal electric potential difference across a coil or conductor that is used to compensate field errors or impose controlled non-axisymmetric magnetic perturbations. It is a circuit quantity, not a magnetic-field amplitude, and represents the voltage applied to or absorbed at the coil terminals.

For a lumped coupled-circuit model using a passive terminal polarity, the terminal voltage of coil $k$ can be written as:

$$
V_k = R_k I_k + L_k \frac{d I_k}{dt} + \sum_{j \ne k} M_{kj} \frac{d I_j}{dt}
$$

where $V_k$ is the terminal voltage in volts, $R_k$ is the coil resistance in ohms, $I_k$ and $I_j$ are currents in amperes, $L_k$ is the self-inductance in henries, $M_{kj}$ is the mutual inductance from circuit $j$ to coil $k$ in henries, and $t$ is time in seconds. The sign of each $M_{kj}$ is the sign of the flux linkage in coil $k$ produced by positive $I_j$, so mutual coupling contributes as a signed voltage term.

The voltage is measured with terminal voltage taps, isolation amplifiers, or calibrated power-supply monitors. For analysis it can be computed from measured current waveforms together with the coil resistance and the self- and mutual-inductance matrix; cable drops, feedthroughs, and power-supply output filters are treated separately when the reference terminals do not coincide with the coil terminals.

Typical values are 1-100 V for slowly varying error-field correction and 100-5000 V during fast current ramps, resonant magnetic perturbation pulses, or rapid feedback action. Steady operation is dominated by $R_k I_k$, while transient operation is dominated by $L_k dI_k/dt$ and coupled-current terms.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the electric potential at the terminal where positive current enters the coil in the chosen winding orientation is greater than the electric potential at the terminal where it leaves.

NAMES.name: voltage_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Terminal voltage across a poloidal field coil winding, equal to the sum of the resistive drop and inductive back-EMF presented to the power supply circuit.
NAMES.long:
The voltage of a poloidal field coil is the electric potential difference measured across the coil terminals, combining the ohmic drop through the winding resistance and the inductive back-EMF arising from changes in coil current and mutual coupling with neighboring coils.

The terminal voltage is governed by the coil circuit equation:

$$
V = R \, I + L \frac{dI}{dt} + \sum_j M_j \frac{dI_j}{dt}
$$

where $R$ is the winding resistance, $I$ is the coil current (see [current_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:current_of_poloidal_field_coil)), $L$ is the self-inductance, and $M_j$ is the mutual inductance with the $j$-th neighboring coil carrying current $I_j$.

In plasma shape and position control, the power supply imposes this voltage as the primary actuator to ramp, sustain, or reduce the coil current, thereby shaping the poloidal field and controlling plasma boundaries. Terminal voltage is measured directly by transducers at the power supply output or coil junction and is monitored continuously for control and protection. Typical values range from near zero during steady-state flat-top operation to several kilovolts during fast current transients. The analogous quantity for the toroidal system is [voltage_of_toroidal_field_coil](name:voltage_of_toroidal_field_coil), and three-dimensional correction coil voltages are described by [voltage_of_correction_coil](name:voltage_of_correction_coil).

NAMES.name: voltage_of_toroidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Terminal voltage of a toroidal field coil, including the resistive voltage drop and the inductive voltage associated with changes in coil current.
NAMES.long:
Voltage of a toroidal field coil is the electrical potential difference between the two coil terminals for a specified terminal polarity. It represents the terminal voltage required to drive the toroidal-field-coil current and the voltage developed by the coil circuit during current transients.

For a lumped circuit representation in which mutual-coupling terms are absent or treated separately, the principal passive-sign terminal-voltage relation is:

$$
V_{\mathrm{TF}} = R_{\mathrm{TF}} I_{\mathrm{TF}} + L_{\mathrm{TF}} \frac{d I_{\mathrm{TF}}}{dt}
$$

where $V_{\mathrm{TF}}$ is the terminal voltage in V, $R_{\mathrm{TF}}$ is the effective series resistance in ohms, $I_{\mathrm{TF}}$ is the [toroidal-field-coil current](name:current_of_toroidal_field_coil) in A, $L_{\mathrm{TF}}$ is the effective self-inductance in H, and $t$ is time in s. The $R_{\mathrm{TF}} I_{\mathrm{TF}}$ term is the ohmic voltage drop, while the $L_{\mathrm{TF}} dI_{\mathrm{TF}}/dt$ term is the self-inductive terminal voltage associated with changing the magnetic energy stored by the coil.

The quantity is obtained from calibrated voltage measurement across the coil terminals or from a circuit calculation using the measured coil current and effective circuit parameters. In a more complete coupled-circuit model, additional mutually induced voltage terms may be included, but the terminal voltage remains the signed potential difference between the same two connection points.

Typical magnitudes are strongly machine and operating-mode dependent. During steady-current operation they may be near 0 V for superconducting coils or from tens to thousands of volts for resistive coils; during ramping or other current transients they can range from a few volts to many kilovolts depending on coil inductance and $dI_{\mathrm{TF}}/dt$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the terminal at which positive toroidal-field-coil current enters the coil conductor is at higher electric potential than the terminal from which it leaves.

NAMES.name: width_of_correction_coil
NAMES.short: Full transverse dimension of a non-axisymmetric correction-coil conductor cross-section, measured along the local normal axis; for circular or annular sections it equals the outer diameter.
NAMES.long:
Width of a correction coil is the full transverse extent of its conductor cross-section measured along the local normal axis, in the plane perpendicular to the conductor centerline. In the local right-handed conductor frame $(\hat{t}, \hat{n}, \hat{b})$, $\hat{t}$ is tangent to the conductor centerline, $\hat{n}$ is the normal direction that defines the width, and $\hat{b}=\hat{t}\times\hat{n}$ is the binormal direction that defines the complementary height.

For a cross-section $C$ taken at centerline point $\mathbf{r}_0$, the width is the full outer extent along $\hat{n}$:

$$
w \equiv \max_{\mathbf{r}\in C} \left[(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}_0)\cdot\hat{n}\right] - \min_{\mathbf{r}\in C} \left[(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}_0)\cdot\hat{n}\right]
=\begin{cases}
a_n, & \text{rectangular or square conductor},\\
D, & \text{solid circular conductor},\\
D_{\mathrm{out}}, & \text{annular conductor},
\end{cases}
$$

where $a_n$ is the outer rectangular dimension along $\hat{n}$, $D$ is the diameter of a solid circular conductor, and $D_{\mathrm{out}}$ is the outer diameter of an annular conductor. This quantity is the direct analog, for non-axisymmetric error-field and edge-localized-mode control coils, of [width_of_toroidal_field_coil](name:width_of_toroidal_field_coil), and is complementary to the binormal-direction [height_of_correction_coil](name:height_of_correction_coil).

The value is taken from the conductor engineering geometry, the manufacturing drawing, or dimensional inspection of the outer conductor envelope. It is a gross outer-envelope dimension that bounds the full conductor footprint, including any jacket, insulation, or cooling channel; it is therefore generally larger than the net current-carrying region implied by the conductor [area_of_correction_coil](name:area_of_correction_coil). Width should be used consistently with the binormal height: solid circular conductors have equal width and height, whereas annular conductors use the outer diameter here rather than the bore diameter set by [inner_radius_of_correction_coil](name:inner_radius_of_correction_coil).

Representative correction-coil conductor widths are design dependent, commonly about 0.005-0.1 m for individual conductors and up to roughly 0.2-0.3 m for large external conductor assemblies. The chosen width is governed by required current capacity, cooling channel layout, structural support, and the space available around the coil path.

NAMES.name: width_of_passive_structure
NAMES.short: Full horizontal width of a rectangular passive conducting structure element, measured along R in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Width of a passive structure is the full horizontal size of a rectangular conducting cross-section in the poloidal plane. In the conductor-local rectangular cross-section, the horizontal axis is parallel to $\hat{R}$ and the vertical axis is parallel to $\hat{Z}$ of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height.

The width is the separation between the two radial faces of the rectangular element:

$$
w = R_{\max} - R_{\min}
$$

where $R_{\min}$ and $R_{\max}$ are the smaller and larger major radii of those faces in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

The value is obtained from the engineering geometry of the passive conductor. Together with [height_of_passive_structure](name:height_of_passive_structure), it defines the rectangular cross-section used to compute geometric area, resistance, inductance, and electromagnetic coupling to coils and plasma currents.

Typical values are 0.01-0.5 m for individual passive conductor elements, and can exceed 1 m for coarse vessel, shell, or stabilizing-structure segments depending on the engineering model.

NAMES.name: width_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Width of a poloidal field coil is the non-negative scalar full radial extent of a rectangular conductor cross-section. It is a length measured along the major-radius direction, not a directed displacement.
NAMES.long:
Width of a poloidal field coil is the full radial extent of a rectangular conductor cross-section. It is a non-negative scalar length in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

For a rectangular cross-section with radial bounds $R_\mathrm{in}$ and $R_\mathrm{out}$, the width is

$$
w = R_\mathrm{out} - R_\mathrm{in} = \max(R) - \min(R)
$$

where $w$ is the coil width, $R_\mathrm{out}$ and $R_\mathrm{in}$ are the larger and smaller radial bounds of the conductor cross-section, and all lengths are measured in meters.

The width is determined from the conductor geometry, for example from the radial bounds represented by the [radial_outline_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:radial_outline_of_poloidal_field_coil). Together with the [height_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:height_of_poloidal_field_coil), it defines the rectangular cross-section used in electromagnetic and structural calculations; for a rectangle, the [area_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:area_of_poloidal_field_coil) satisfies the inline relation $A = w h$, where $h$ is in meters and $A$ is in square meters.

Valid values satisfy $w \ge 0$. A strictly positive value represents a finite conductor cross-section, while $w = 0$ is a degenerate geometric limit rather than a physical coil width.

NAMES.name: width_of_toroidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Non-negative transverse width of a toroidal field coil conductor cross-section, measured in the local normal direction of the conductor frame and perpendicular to the conductor path. It is the full normal-direction extent for rectangular or square sections and the outer diameter for circular or annular sections.
NAMES.long:
The width of a toroidal field coil conductor is the non-negative length describing the normal-direction size of the conductor cross-section. At each point on the conductor centerline, use the local right-handed conductor frame $(\hat{t}, \hat{n}, \hat{b})$, where $\hat{t}$ follows the conductor path, $\hat{n}$ is the cross-section normal direction, and $\hat{b}=\hat{t}\times\hat{n}$ is the binormal; the width is measured along $\hat{n}$, while [height_of_toroidal_field_coil](name:height_of_toroidal_field_coil) is measured along $\hat{b}$. For rectangular or square conductors it is the full extent along $\hat{n}$; for circular sections it is the diameter, and for annular sections it is the outer diameter.

For a rectangular conductor cross-section, the width and height determine the geometric cross-sectional area:

$$
A = w h
$$

where $A$ is the [area_of_toroidal_field_coil](name:area_of_toroidal_field_coil) in m^2, $w$ is the width in m, and $h$ is the [height_of_toroidal_field_coil](name:height_of_toroidal_field_coil) in m.

In practice, the width is taken from the coil conductor design definition, manufacturing survey, or a reconstructed conductor outline in the local cross-section plane $(\hat{n}, \hat{b})$. For an outline-based description, it corresponds to the full projected extent of the conductor boundary along $\hat{n}$, with the geometric model determining whether the same parameter represents a rectangular width, a circular diameter, or an annular outer diameter.

Typical toroidal field coil conductor widths in medium-to-large tokamaks are about 0.01-0.10 m, with larger values possible for heavily reinforced cases or winding packs in high-field devices.

NAMES.name: x_coordinate_of_ferritic_element_centroid
NAMES.short: Signed x position of the geometric centroid of a ferritic element in the right-handed Cartesian (x, y, z) frame, with z along the vertical toroidal symmetry axis.
NAMES.long:
The x coordinate of a ferritic element centroid is the signed Cartesian position of the element's geometric center along the $\hat{x}$ direction. It is defined in the right-handed Cartesian $(x, y, z)$ coordinate frame with basis $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$, where $\hat{z}$ is vertical and coincides with $\hat{Z}$ of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, and $x=y=0$ lies on the toroidal symmetry axis.

For a centroid with cylindrical position $(R_c, \phi_c, Z_c)$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, the Cartesian coordinate is

$$
x_c = R_c \cos \phi_c
$$

where $x_c$ is the centroid x coordinate, $R_c$ is the major radius of the centroid, and $\phi_c$ is its toroidal angle measured from the $+\hat{x}$ radial half-plane.

The coordinate is obtained from the component geometry or metrology after fixing the machine Cartesian axes. Together with [y_centroid_of_ferritic_element](name:y_coordinate_of_ferritic_element_centroid) and [vertical_coordinate_of_ferritic_element](name:vertical_coordinate_of_ferritic_element_centroid), it specifies the centroid position used to describe the placement of passive ferritic structures in magnetic-field calculations.

Typical values are set by the machine radius: compact devices commonly have centroid x coordinates from -1 m to +1 m, medium-sized tokamaks from -4 m to +4 m, and large devices can approach -10 m to +10 m.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the centroid lies on the $+\hat{x}$ side of the $y$-$z$ plane in the right-handed Cartesian $(x, y, z)$ coordinate frame, toward the $\phi=0$ radial half-plane.

NAMES.name: alfven_frequency
NAMES.short: Complex frequency of the local shear Alfvén continuum for a single toroidal mode number, whose real part is the oscillation frequency and imaginary part the damping or growth rate.
NAMES.long:
The shear Alfvén continuum collects the frequencies at which shear Alfvén waves resonate on each flux surface for a chosen toroidal mode number $n$. A linear MHD calculation returns the complex frequency $\omega_A = \omega_r + i\omega_i$ for every root of the local continuum equation, resolving both the oscillation frequency and its damping or growth rate as continuous functions of minor radius. The local continuum frequency follows

$$
\omega_A = k_\parallel v_A
$$

with parallel wavenumber $k_\parallel = (nq - m)/(qR_0)$ for poloidal harmonic $m$, safety factor $q$, and major radius $R_0$, and Alfvén speed $v_A = B/\sqrt{\mu_0 \rho}$ for total field magnitude $B$ and mass density $\rho$. Under the $e^{-i\omega t}$ convention a positive $\omega_i$ grows and a negative $\omega_i$ damps; the continuum is purely real in ideal MHD, with finite $\omega_i$ arising from resistive, kinetic, or energetic-particle effects. The separate parts are the [alfven_frequency_real_part](name:alfven_frequency_real_part) and [alfven_frequency_imaginary_part](name:alfven_frequency_imaginary_part), discrete Alfvén eigenmodes form in the gaps the continuum leaves open, and the characteristic timescale is the [alfven_time](name:alfven_time).

NAMES.name: alfven_frequency_imaginary_part
NAMES.short: Damping rate when negative or growth rate when positive, the imaginary part of the complex shear Alfvén continuum frequency, for a single toroidal mode number at a given radial position.
NAMES.long:
The imaginary part of the complex shear Alfvén continuum frequency, $\gamma = \operatorname{Im}(\omega_A)$, sets how fast a shear Alfvén perturbation grows or decays at a given radial position for a chosen toroidal mode number $n$. Together with the oscillation frequency [alfven_frequency_real_part](name:alfven_frequency_real_part) it fixes the full time dependence, which under the $e^{-i\omega_A t}$ convention evolves as

$$
\delta f(t) \propto e^{\gamma t}\, e^{-i\omega_r t}
$$

so a positive $\gamma$ marks an unstable, growing response and a negative $\gamma$ a linearly damped one. A linear MHD calculation resolves $\gamma$ as a function of minor radius and toroidal mode number. The continuum is purely real in ideal MHD, and a finite $\gamma$ arises from resistive, kinetic, or energetic-particle effects, the same drives that excite the discrete Alfvén eigenmodes occupying the continuum gaps. The full complex value is the [alfven_frequency](name:alfven_frequency).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the mode amplitude grows exponentially in time under the $e^{-i\omega_A t}$ convention.

NAMES.name: alfven_frequency_real_part
NAMES.short: Oscillation frequency, the real part of the complex frequency, of the local shear Alfvén continuum at a given radial position for a single toroidal mode number.
NAMES.long:
The shear Alfvén continuum is the set of frequencies at which shear Alfvén waves resonate on each flux surface, and its real part gives the local oscillation frequency for a chosen toroidal mode number $n$. A linear MHD calculation returns one frequency for every root of the local continuum equation at each radial position, so the spectrum varies continuously with minor radius. In the cylindrical limit the continuum frequency for poloidal harmonic $m$ is

$$
\operatorname{Re}(\omega_A) = \frac{|n - m/q|}{R}\, v_A
$$

where $q$ is the safety factor, $R$ the major radius in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, and $v_A = B/\sqrt{\mu_0 \rho}$ the Alfvén speed for total field magnitude $B$ and mass density $\rho$. Toroidal coupling of neighboring poloidal harmonics opens frequency gaps in which discrete Alfvén eigenmodes, such as the toroidicity-induced and reversed-shear modes, can form. The companion damping or growth rate is the [alfven_frequency_imaginary_part](name:alfven_frequency_imaginary_part), the two together forming the complex [alfven_frequency](name:alfven_frequency), and the associated timescale is the [alfven_time](name:alfven_time).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the wave phase advances in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: alfven_time
NAMES.short: Alfvén time is the non-negative shear-Alfvén transit time used to normalize ideal-MHD dynamics. It is the magnetic-axis major radius divided by the local Alfvén speed, using the on-axis toroidal magnetic-field magnitude and the local ion mass density at the flux surface of interest.
NAMES.long:
Alfvén time $\tau_A$ is a characteristic MHD timescale for shear Alfvén-wave propagation across a tokamak plasma, with the transit length set by the magnetic-axis major radius. It is a non-negative duration and provides the inverse frequency scale commonly used to normalize ideal-MHD oscillation frequencies and instability growth rates.

Using the magnetic-axis major radius as the characteristic length and the local Alfvén speed from the on-axis toroidal magnetic-field magnitude and local ion mass density, the Alfvén time is defined by:

$$
\tau_A(\rho_f) = \frac{R_0}{v_A(\rho_f)} = \frac{R_0 \sqrt{\mu_0\,m_i\,n_i(\rho_f)}}{B_0}
$$

where $\rho_f$ is the flux-surface label used to localize the density, such as the normalized toroidal-flux radius $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$; $R_0$ is the magnetic-axis major radius in m; $v_A$ is the Alfvén speed in m s$^{-1}$; $\mu_0$ is the permeability of free space in H m$^{-1}$; $m_i$ is the ion mass in kg; $n_i$ is the ion number density in m$^{-3}$; and $B_0$ is the magnitude of the toroidal magnetic-field component at the magnetic axis in T. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, $B_0$ denotes a magnitude, so reversal of toroidal-field direction does not change $\tau_A$.

In practice, $\tau_A$ is computed from an equilibrium magnetic-axis position, an on-axis toroidal-field magnitude, and ion density and composition at the flux surface of interest. For multi-ion plasmas, the product $m_i n_i$ is commonly replaced by the total ion mass density $\sum_s m_s n_s$, with electron mass usually negligible for this MHD normalization. Frequencies such as the real part of an Alfvén eigenmode frequency and linear growth rates are often compared with or normalized by $\tau_A^{-1}$.

For tokamak parameters $R_0 \sim 1-6$ m, $B_0 \sim 1-8$ T, and deuterium ion density $n_i \sim 10^{19}-10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$, representative values are typically of order $10^{-7}-10^{-6}$ s. The timescale increases with major radius and with the square root of ion mass density, and decreases in inverse proportion to the magnetic-field magnitude.

NAMES.name: critical_momentum_due_to_avalanche
NAMES.short: Scalar threshold momentum separating drag-dominated electrons from electrons that can run away under electric-field acceleration in avalanche modeling. It is a momentum-space boundary used when evaluating avalanche multiplication and Compton or tritium beta-decay seed contributions, not a source rate.
NAMES.long:
Critical momentum due to avalanche is the scalar electron momentum threshold at which electric-field acceleration just balances collisional slowing-down in the runaway-electron kinetic equation. Above this boundary an electron is in the runaway region; below it Coulomb drag dominates. It is a momentum magnitude and does not encode the direction of motion along the magnetic field.

A common relativistic Coulomb-drag approximation for field-aligned motion gives

$$
p_{c,\mathrm{av}} = m_e c \left(\frac{|E_\parallel|}{E_c} - 1\right)^{-1/2}
$$

where $p_{c,\mathrm{av}}$ is the critical momentum, $m_e$ is the electron rest mass in kg, $c$ is the speed of light in m s^-1, $E_\parallel$ is the electric-field component parallel to the magnetic field in V m^-1, and $E_c$ is the Connor-Hastie critical electric field in V m^-1. The expression is valid for $|E_\parallel| > E_c$ and follows from the force balance $e|E_\parallel|=F_\mathrm{drag}$ with high-energy Coulomb drag $F_\mathrm{drag}\simeq eE_c[1+(m_ec/p)^2]$ in N; $E_c$ is often approximated by $n_e e^3\ln\Lambda/(4\pi\epsilon_0^2m_ec^2)$, with $n_e$ in m^-3 and $\ln\Lambda$ dimensionless.

In practice, the threshold is computed from the local parallel electric field, electron density and temperature, effective charge, Coulomb logarithm, and any model corrections for partial screening, radiation reaction, or pitch-angle dynamics. Avalanche multiplication, Compton scattering, and tritium beta decay provide source terms for the runaway population; this critical momentum supplies the drag-versus-acceleration boundary used to decide whether those electrons enter the runaway region.

Typical thresholds are most transparent in normalized form $\bar p_c=p_{c,\mathrm{av}}/(m_ec)$. For $|E_\parallel|/E_c$ of about 1.1-10, $\bar p_c$ is about 0.3-3, corresponding to roughly 1e-22-1e-21 kg m s^-1; very near $E_c$ the threshold can be much larger, while for $|E_\parallel|\le E_c$ this simple balance gives no finite runaway threshold.

NAMES.name: effective_charge
NAMES.short: Effective ionic charge Z_eff of the plasma, equal to the density-weighted mean-squared ion charge normalized to electron density, governing resistivity, bremsstrahlung emission, and neoclassical transport coefficients.
NAMES.long:
The effective charge $Z_\text{eff}$ characterizes the net ionic charge state of the full plasma mixture, replacing the multi-species ion distribution with a single equivalent charge that reproduces the electron–ion collision frequency. It is dimensionless and always at least unity for any quasi-neutral plasma, with values exceeding 1 indicating the presence of impurity species.

The defining relation is:

$$
Z_\text{eff} = \frac{\sum_i n_i Z_i^2}{n_e}
$$

where $n_i$ is the number density of ion species $i$, $Z_i$ is the charge number of species $i$, and $n_e = \sum_i n_i Z_i$ is the electron density obtained from quasi-neutrality. For a pure hydrogen plasma $Z_\text{eff} = 1$; high-$Z$ impurities drive it substantially above unity.

$Z_\text{eff}$ enters the Spitzer resistivity $\eta \propto Z_\text{eff} \ln\Lambda / T_e^{3/2}$, the bremsstrahlung radiation power $P_\text{brem} \propto n_e^2 Z_\text{eff} T_e^{1/2}$, and neoclassical transport coefficients. It is most commonly inferred from visible or near-infrared bremsstrahlung continuum emissivity, which scales as $n_e^2 Z_\text{eff}$, or estimated from resistive flux consumption during the ohmic heating phase.

Typical values range from 1 in clean hydrogen plasmas to 2–5 in H-mode discharges with moderate impurity seeding, and can exceed 5 near the plasma edge in impurity-rich regimes. The [line-averaged effective charge](name:line_averaged_effective_charge) is obtained from a spectroscopic chord integral, while the [volume-averaged effective charge](name:volume_averaged_effective_charge) provides a single global impurity metric; radial profiles capture the local $Z_\text{eff}$ variation across the plasma.
NAMES.sign: Positive for all physically realizable plasmas, since $Z_\text{eff} \geq 1$ follows from quasi-neutrality and the positivity of all ion charge-state densities.

NAMES.name: electron_temperature
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Thermal energy of the bulk electron population expressed as a kinetic temperature, equal to two-thirds of the mean electron kinetic energy per particle.
NAMES.long:
The electron temperature $T_e$ quantifies the mean thermal kinetic energy of the electron population, parameterizing the second moment of the electron velocity distribution under the Maxwellian approximation. It is the primary scalar measure of the electron thermal state at a given spatial point.

The defining relation connects $T_e$ to the mean electron kinetic energy per particle $\langle E_e \rangle$:

$$
T_e = \frac{2}{3} \langle E_e \rangle
$$

where both $T_e$ and $\langle E_e \rangle$ are in eV, and the conversion to absolute temperature is $1\;\text{eV} = 11605\;\text{K}$.

Thomson scattering measures $T_e$ from the spectral width of scattered laser light and is the gold-standard profile diagnostic from the plasma core to the edge. Electron cyclotron emission resolves $T_e$ with high temporal resolution in optically thick core regions. Langmuir probes extract $T_e$ from the exponential slope or multi-temperature fits to the probe I-V characteristic near plasma-facing surfaces, providing point measurements such as [electron temperature at the wall](name:electron_temperature_at_wall) and [at the outboard midplane](name:electron_temperature_at_midplane).

Typical values span 1-20 keV in the plasma core during H-mode operation, decreasing to 10-200 eV in the pedestal and scrape-off layer, and 1-30 eV near plasma-facing surfaces.

NAMES.name: electrostatic_potential
NAMES.short: Scalar electric potential of the plasma, equal to the electrostatic work per unit positive charge relative to a grounded reference, whose negative gradient defines the radial electric field and drives E×B plasma rotation.
NAMES.long:
The electrostatic potential $\phi$ is the scalar electric potential of the plasma, quantifying the electrostatic work per unit positive charge measured relative to a reference surface (conventionally the grounded vacuum vessel). It encodes the large-scale electrostatic structure governing cross-field transport and $E \times B$ rotation in both the core and edge regions.

The electrostatic contribution to the electric field is defined by:

$$
\mathbf{E}_{\rm es} = -\nabla\phi
$$

where $\phi$ is measured in V. The radial component $E_r = -\partial\phi/\partial r$ enters the neoclassical radial force balance for ion species and drives $E \times B$ rotation at velocity $\mathbf{v}_{E\times B} = (-\nabla\phi) \times \mathbf{B}/B^2$, where $\mathbf{B}$ is the total magnetic field vector and $B = |\mathbf{B}|$.

In the plasma core, $\phi$ is inferred from spectroscopic measurements of impurity rotation combined with pressure-gradient data via the radial ion momentum balance. In the edge plasma and scrape-off layer, Langmuir probes and emissive probes measure the plasma potential directly relative to the vessel wall; location-specific quantities are described by [electrostatic_potential_at_wall](name:electrostatic_potential_at_wall) and [electrostatic_potential_at_midplane](name:electrostatic_potential_at_midplane).

Typical scrape-off layer values are of order a few $T_e/e$ above the vessel potential, where $T_e$ is the local electron temperature; core values in high-performance discharges may reach hundreds of volts as the potential integrates over a large radial extent.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the local plasma potential exceeds the grounded vacuum vessel reference potential.

NAMES.name: energy_upper_fraction_due_to_disruption
NAMES.short: Dimensionless upper fractional threshold (commonly labeled X2) for the custom linear thermal-energy decay time during a disruption, marking the higher of two crossing levels of the normalized thermal energy.
NAMES.long:
The energy upper fractional threshold X2 is the higher of two user-specified dimensionless levels of the normalized thermal energy $W_\mathrm{th}/W_\mathrm{th,0}$ used to bracket the thermal-energy quench interval during a disruption. It marks the point in the decay sequence that the thermal energy crosses first, and is paired with [energy_lower_fraction_due_to_disruption](name:energy_lower_fraction_due_to_disruption) (X1, where $X_1 < X_2 \leq 1$) to define the decay-time window.

The two thresholds jointly define the custom linear thermal-energy decay time $\tau_\mathrm{th,lin}$:

$$
\tau_\mathrm{th,lin} = \frac{t(X_2) - t(X_1)}{X_1 - X_2}
$$

where $t(X_i)$ is the time at which the normalized thermal energy $W_\mathrm{th}(t)/W_\mathrm{th,0}$ passes through level $X_i$ and $W_\mathrm{th,0}$ is the pre-disruption reference energy. Because thermal energy decays monotonically during a quench, $t(X_2) < t(X_1)$, so both numerator and denominator are negative and $\tau_\mathrm{th,lin}$ is positive. The resulting decay time is reported as [thermal_decay_time](name:thermal_energy_decay_time_due_to_disruption). This quantity is the energy-specific instance of the general [upper_fraction_due_to_disruption](name:upper_fraction_due_to_disruption) concept, which applies analogously to plasma-current metrics as in plasma_linear_decay_time.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the upper threshold level X2 is set to a nonzero fraction of the pre-disruption thermal energy and above the lower threshold X1, corresponding to a physically valid downward-crossing decay interval.

NAMES.name: normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_sawtooth_inversion_radius
NAMES.short: Value of the normalized toroidal flux radius rho_tor_norm at the sawtooth inversion surface. This surface is identified by the sign change of the electron-temperature perturbation during a sawtooth crash and is often close to the q=1 rational surface.
NAMES.long:
The normalized toroidal flux coordinate at the sawtooth inversion radius is the value of the flux coordinate $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ on the surface where the electron-temperature perturbation changes sign during a sawtooth crash. The inversion surface is a marker of the radial extent of the sawtooth crash and is commonly associated with the $q=1$ rational surface.

The normalized toroidal flux radius on a magnetic flux surface is defined by

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}} = \left(\frac{\Phi - \Phi_0}{\Phi_b - \Phi_0}\right)^{1/2}
$$

where $\Phi$ is the toroidal magnetic flux enclosed by the surface in Wb, $\Phi_0$ is the magnetic-axis value in Wb, and $\Phi_b$ is the boundary value in Wb. For this quantity, the expression is evaluated on the sawtooth inversion surface.

In practice, the inversion radius is inferred from time-resolved electron-temperature or emissivity measurements by locating the radial position where the crash-induced perturbation changes sign, then mapping that position to the reconstructed flux coordinate $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$. When direct inversion-surface localization is limited, the nearby $q=1$ rational surface may be used as a physics reference, often together with quantities such as [magnetic_shear_at_sawtooth_inversion_radius](name:magnetic_shear_at_sawtooth_inversion_radius). The inversion radius is typically inside or comparable to the sawtooth mixing radius, described by [normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_sawtooth_mixing_radius](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_sawtooth_mixing_radius).

Values are dimensionless and lie between 0 at the magnetic axis and 1 at the plasma boundary for closed-flux-surface normalization. Sawtooth inversion surfaces are usually in the plasma core, commonly around 0.2-0.6, with the exact value depending on the current profile, pressure profile, and sawtooth dynamics.

NAMES.name: normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_sawtooth_mixing_radius
NAMES.short: Value of rho_tor_norm at the sawtooth mixing radius, the flux surface marking the outer boundary of the plasma region homogenized during a sawtooth crash.
NAMES.long:
