The coolant inlet temperature is the absolute temperature of the working fluid measured at the inlet port of a cooling circuit, before traversing the component and absorbing heat. It establishes the upstream thermal boundary condition for thermodynamic analysis of the cooling loop and is a primary input to heat load calculations.

Combined with [coolant_temperature_at_outlet](name:coolant_temperature_at_outlet) and the coolant mass flow rate from [coolant_flow](name:coolant_flow), the deposited thermal power $P$ is determined by:

$$
P = \dot{m} \, c_p \, (T_\mathrm{out} - T_\mathrm{in})
$$

where $\dot{m}$ is the mass flow rate in kg s$^{-1}$, $c_p$ is the specific heat capacity of the coolant in J kg$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$, $T_\mathrm{in}$ is the inlet temperature, and $T_\mathrm{out}$ is the outlet temperature.

Measured using calibrated resistance temperature detectors (RTDs) or thermocouples mounted at the inlet manifold of the cooling circuit. It applies to calorimetry components, cooling loops, and breeding blanket module circuits.

Typical inlet temperatures in water-cooled tokamak circuits range from 290-330 K; helium-cooled blanket systems may operate at inlet temperatures up to 550 K or higher depending on the thermal design point. The temperature difference $(T_\mathrm{out} - T_\mathrm{in})$ is the key diagnostic observable for computing [thermal_power_of_plant_component_port](name:thermal_power_of_plant_component_port).

NAMES.name: coolant_temperature_at_outlet
NAMES.short: Absolute temperature of the cooling fluid at the exit port of a cooling loop or calorimetry component, serving as the downstream thermal boundary condition in calorimetric heat-load assessment.
NAMES.long:
The coolant outlet temperature is the absolute thermodynamic temperature of the working fluid leaving a cooling-loop channel or calorimetry component. Paired with [coolant_temperature_at_inlet](name:coolant_temperature_at_inlet) and the [coolant mass flow rate](name:coolant_flow), it supplies the thermodynamic data needed to close the first-law calorimetric enthalpy balance.

The deposited thermal power $P_{th}$ is defined by:

$$
P_{th} = \dot{m} \, c_p \, (T_{\mathrm{out}} - T_{\mathrm{in}})
$$

where $\dot{m}$ is the coolant mass flow rate, $c_p$ is the specific heat capacity of the coolant at constant pressure (approximately 4180 J kg$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$ for water), $T_{\mathrm{out}}$ is this outlet temperature, and $T_{\mathrm{in}}$ is the [inlet temperature](name:coolant_temperature_at_inlet). The resulting [deposited thermal power](name:thermal_power_of_plant_component_port) and [cumulative thermal energy](name:thermal_energy_of_plant_component_port) are derived from this relation.

Outlet temperature is measured by resistance temperature detectors (RTDs) or calibrated thermocouples mounted at the component exit manifold. For water-cooled plasma-facing and structural components, outlet temperatures range from 300 to 400 K, with temperature rises of a few to tens of kelvins depending on the incident heat load.

NAMES.name: effective_area_of_langmuir_probe
NAMES.short: Effective ion collection area of a Langmuir probe, equal to the plasma-facing surface area projected onto the plane perpendicular to the local magnetic field.
NAMES.long:
Effective area of a Langmuir probe is the collecting area presented to ions streaming along the local magnetic field. It is the projected part of the plasma-facing surface that intercepts field-aligned particle flux, and is smaller than the geometric area when the magnetic field strikes the surface obliquely.

For a locally planar collector, the effective collection area is defined by the field-surface incidence angle:

$$
A_\mathrm{eff} = A \sin\alpha = A\,|\hat{\mathbf{b}}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}}|
$$

where $A_\mathrm{eff}$ is the effective collection area in m^2, $A$ is the geometric plasma-facing area in m^2, $\alpha$ is the [angle_of_langmuir_probe](name:angle_of_langmuir_probe) in radians measured between the local magnetic field line direction and the plasma-facing surface, $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$ is the dimensionless unit vector along the magnetic field, and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is the dimensionless unit normal to the collector surface. Thus $\alpha=0$ gives zero effective area for a field line tangent to the surface, while $\alpha=\pi/2$ gives the full geometric area for normal incidence. For a curved or segmented collector, the same projection is applied locally and summed over the exposed plasma-facing surface.

In practice, this quantity is computed from the known exposed probe geometry and the local magnetic-field direction at the probe position. It is used when converting measured ion saturation current to [parallel_ion_current_density](name:parallel_ion_current_density), because that current density is defined per unit area perpendicular to the magnetic field.

Typical effective areas for small embedded or flush-mounted Langmuir probes are about 10^-8-10^-5 m^2. Larger protruding tips or collector plates may reach about 10^-4 m^2, while very grazing magnetic-field incidence can reduce the effective area by orders of magnitude relative to the geometric surface area.

NAMES.name: electron_average_temperature_at_midplane
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Electron temperature averaged along a magnetic field line connecting the upstream midplane crossing to a downstream divertor target in the scrape-off layer. It is a parallel field-line mean, distinct from the local electron temperature at the midplane.
NAMES.long:
Electron average temperature at midplane is the path-length-weighted mean electron temperature along a scrape-off-layer magnetic field line, assigned to the field line's upstream midplane crossing. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, the upstream endpoint is the intersection of the field line with the device midplane $Z=Z_\mathrm{mid}$; the downstream endpoint is the connected divertor target reached by following the same field line.

With $l_\parallel$ the distance measured along the magnetic field line from the upstream midplane endpoint to the target, the average is defined by:

$$
\langle T_e \rangle_\parallel = \frac{1}{L_\parallel}\int_0^{L_\parallel} T_e(l_\parallel)\,dl_\parallel
$$

where $T_e(l_\parallel)$ is the local electron temperature in eV, $l_\parallel$ and the connection length $L_\parallel$ are in meters, and $\langle T_e \rangle_\parallel$ is in eV.

In practice, this quantity is computed by tracing the magnetic field line and integrating an inferred or modeled electron-temperature distribution along it. A reciprocating Langmuir probe near the midplane can constrain the local upstream value, but it does not by itself measure the full upstream-to-target average unless combined with information or assumptions about the temperature variation along the connected field line. This quantity is therefore distinct from the local [electron_temperature_at_midplane](name:electron_temperature_at_midplane), from a volume mean such as [volume_averaged_electron_temperature](name:volume_averaged_electron_temperature), and from radial scrape-off-layer scale lengths such as [thermal_electron_decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer](name:thermal_electron_decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer).

Representative scrape-off-layer field-line averages are regime dependent and should be interpreted with the endpoint definition and diagnostic constraints in mind. Values are often a few eV to 100 eV: detached or cold-divertor conditions can give averages near 1-10 eV, while attached, hotter upstream conditions near the separatrix can give 10-100 eV or higher.

NAMES.name: electron_temperature_at_midplane
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Local electron temperature at the outboard, low-field-side midplane in the scrape-off-layer plasma. It is the thermodynamic electron energy scale there, distinct from a flux-surface average or a field-line average.
NAMES.long:
Electron temperature at the midplane is the local electron temperature at the outboard, low-field-side intersection of the plasma midplane with the scrape-off layer. It characterizes the thermal spread of the electron velocity distribution at that location, rather than a [flux-surface-averaged electron temperature](name:flux_surface_averaged_electron_temperature) or a field-line average such as [electron average temperature at midplane](name:electron_average_temperature_at_midplane).

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, the local evaluation can be written as:

$$
T_{e,\mathrm{mid}} = T_e(R_{\mathrm{OMP}}, \phi_0, Z_{\mathrm{mid}})
$$

where $T_e$ is the local electron temperature, $R_{\mathrm{OMP}}$ is the major radius of the outboard midplane point in the scrape-off layer, $\phi_0$ is the toroidal angle of that point, and $Z_{\mathrm{mid}}$ is the vertical height of the plasma midplane. Expressed in eV, $T_e$ is the electron thermal energy scale; for a Maxwellian distribution, the mean random thermal kinetic energy per electron is $\langle E_e\rangle = 3T_e/2$ when both are expressed as energies.

It is commonly inferred from local edge measurements such as Langmuir-probe current-voltage characteristics, with interpretation depending on sheath physics, plasma potential, secondary emission, magnetization, and non-Maxwellian effects. Local sampling makes this quantity sensitive to radial position relative to the separatrix, turbulent fluctuations, and toroidal or poloidal asymmetries; separate measures such as [thermal electron decay length over the scrape-off layer](name:thermal_electron_decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer) describe radial falloff rather than this single local value.

Typical values in tokamak scrape-off layers are 5-100 eV near the outboard midplane, with lower values common farther from the separatrix and higher values possible close to the separatrix in strongly heated plasmas. The value is governed by parallel heat conduction, sheath heat transmission, cross-field transport, ionization and radiation losses, and upstream power flow.

NAMES.name: ion_current_of_mass_spectrometer_channel
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Electrical current collected at a single mass-discriminated detector channel of a mass spectrometer, quantifying the ion abundance for the atomic mass species assigned to that channel.
NAMES.long:
In a mass spectrometer, each channel selects ions of a fixed mass-to-charge ratio $m/z$ from an ionized sample of the plasma exhaust or vessel atmosphere. When these ions strike the detector — a Faraday cup for higher-abundance species or an electron multiplier for trace signals — they produce a measurable electrical current that is directly proportional to the ion arrival rate at that mass channel.

The collected current $I_\text{ch}$ is related to the ion arrival rate $\dot{N}$ by:

$$
I_\text{ch} = Z_i \, e \, \dot{N}
$$

where $Z_i$ is the ion charge state (typically unity for singly ionized atoms or molecules), $e = 1.602 \times 10^{-19}$ C is the elementary charge, and $\dot{N}$ is the number of ions collected per second.

The ion current signal is subsequently converted to a partial pressure via the spectrometer's sensitivity factor, which encodes the ionization cross-section, ion transmission efficiency, and detector gain for each species; the resulting partial pressure for the same channel is [neutral_pressure_of_mass_spectrometer_channel](name:neutral_pressure_of_mass_spectrometer_channel). The detector bias voltage governing amplification efficiency is given by [voltage_of_mass_spectrometer_channel](name:voltage_of_mass_spectrometer_channel).

Typical collected ion currents range from $10^{-12}$ A to $10^{-7}$ A depending on the vessel gas composition, partial pressure level, and detector type. Faraday cups are suitable for dominant fuel species such as hydrogen isotopes, while electron multipliers extend sensitivity to low-abundance impurity or noble-gas species.

NAMES.name: ion_saturated_current_density
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Ion saturation current density collected by a Langmuir probe when biased sufficiently negative to repel all electrons; a primary diagnostic for local plasma density and particle flux in the scrape-off layer.
NAMES.long:
The ion saturation current density $j_{i,sat}$ is the maximum ion current per unit area collected at a probe surface when the probe potential is driven sufficiently negative that the electron current is completely suppressed. This saturation regime corresponds to the flat portion of the probe current–voltage (I–V) characteristic at large negative bias, where all ions entering the presheath are accelerated through the sheath and collected regardless of further reduction in probe potential.

In the Bohm approximation, the ion saturation current density is:

$$
j_{i,sat} = \frac{1}{2} n_e e c_s
$$

where $n_e$ is the electron density, $e$ is the elementary charge, and $c_s = \sqrt{e T_e / m_i}$ is the Bohm velocity with $T_e$ the electron temperature (in eV) and $m_i$ the ion mass. Inverting this relation to obtain $n_e$ requires independent knowledge of $T_e$ and the [effective_area_of_langmuir_probe](name:effective_area_of_langmuir_probe).

This quantity is routinely measured by both embedded probes fixed in divertor tiles or first-wall plasma-facing components and by reciprocating probes that traverse the scrape-off layer to build radial profiles. Multiplying $j_{i,sat}$ by the effective collection area yields the total [ion_saturated_current](name:ion_saturated_current), while turbulent fluctuations in this quantity are characterized by [ion_saturated_fluctuating_current_density](name:ion_saturated_fluctuating_current_density).

Typical values range from ~10–100 A/m² in the far scrape-off layer to ~1–50 kA/m² near divertor strike points during attached plasma operation.
NAMES.sign: Positive when ions flow from the plasma toward the probe collector surface.

NAMES.name: ion_saturated_fluctuating_current_density
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Standard deviation of the ion saturation current density collected at a Langmuir-probe surface, representing the fluctuation amplitude of the ion-saturation signal.
NAMES.long:
Ion saturated fluctuating current density is the root-mean-square amplitude of departures of ion saturation current density from its mean over a specified averaging interval. The underlying ion saturation current density is the current collected per effective collecting area when the probe is biased sufficiently negative to measure the ion-saturation branch. This quantity describes the fluctuation amplitude, not the signed mean current density.

For a continuous time series, the fluctuation amplitude over an interval from $t_1$ to $t_2$ is defined by

$$
\sigma_{j_{i,\mathrm{sat}}} = \left[\frac{1}{t_2-t_1}\int_{t_1}^{t_2}\left(j_{i,\mathrm{sat}}(t)-\bar{j}_{i,\mathrm{sat}}\right)^2\,dt\right]^{1/2}
$$

where $\sigma_{j_{i,\mathrm{sat}}}$ is the ion saturated fluctuating current density, $j_{i,\mathrm{sat}}(t)$ is the instantaneous ion saturation current density in A m^-2, $\bar{j}_{i,\mathrm{sat}}$ is its mean over the same interval in A m^-2, and $t$, $t_1$, and $t_2$ are times in seconds. For sampled data, the integral is replaced by the corresponding average over the selected samples.

It is obtained from fast Langmuir-probe current measurements after choosing an averaging interval, applying the relevant bandwidth or filtering, and dividing the measured current by the effective ion-collecting area. The underlying current density is evaluated along the local collector normal; reversing the arbitrary sign of the raw current time series does not change this standard deviation. In sheath interpretation, the mean ion saturation current density is approximately proportional to local plasma density and ion sound speed, so the fluctuation level is mainly sensitive to density turbulence, with additional dependence on electron and ion temperature, plasma potential, sheath expansion, magnetic-field incidence angle, and probe geometry.

The quantity is non-negative and is zero only for a perfectly steady ion saturation current density over the averaging interval, apart from instrumental noise. Typical edge and scrape-off-layer values are about 10^2-10^5 A m^-2, often 0.05-1 times the local mean ion saturation current density; intermittent events, high-density conditions, or short averaging intervals can give larger values.

NAMES.name: parallel_ion_current_density
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Parallel ion current density is the projection of the total ion electric-current density onto the local magnetic-field direction. It is a charge-weighted sum over ion species and charge states, so each ion particle flux contributes in proportion to its charge state rather than as an unweighted particle count.
NAMES.long:
Parallel ion current density is the component of ion electric-current density flowing along the local magnetic field. For an ion population with multiple species or charge states, the unqualified quantity represents the total ion contribution, obtained by charge-weighting and summing the parallel particle fluxes of the contributing ion populations.

The projection and charge-weighted aggregation are

$$
j_{\parallel i} = \mathbf{j}_i \cdot \hat{\mathbf{b}} = e \sum_s Z_s \, \Gamma_{\parallel s}
$$

where $j_{\parallel i}$ is the parallel ion current density in A m$^{-2}$, $\mathbf{j}_i$ is the total ion current-density vector in A m$^{-2}$, $\hat{\mathbf{b}}=\mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$ is the unit vector along the local magnetic field, $e$ is the elementary charge in C, $s$ indexes ion species and charge states, $Z_s$ is the ion charge state, and $\Gamma_{\parallel s}$ is the signed parallel particle flux of population $s$ in m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$. This distinguishes the current density from an unweighted ion particle flux: highly charged ions contribute proportionally more electric current for the same particle flux.

In practice, this quantity may be inferred from charged-particle collection by Langmuir probes or other plasma-facing collectors using a sheath and collection-area model, local magnetic-field direction, and surface geometry. It may also be computed from kinetic or fluid descriptions by taking the first velocity moment of the ion distribution for each species and charge state, multiplying by charge, summing, and projecting along $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$.

Representative boundary-plasma magnitudes vary strongly with density, temperature, magnetic-field incidence angle, and proximity to material surfaces. Edge and divertor measurements commonly span order-of-magnitude ranges such as $10^2$-$10^5$ A m$^{-2}$, with larger transient or near-sheath values possible in high-flux conditions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the net ion charge flux is in the local magnetic-field direction $\hat{\mathbf{b}}=\mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$.

NAMES.name: parallel_ion_fluctuating_current_density
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Standard deviation of the ion current density component parallel to the local magnetic field, expressed per unit effective collection area perpendicular to that field. It is a non-negative fluctuation amplitude of the signed parallel ion current density.
NAMES.long:
Parallel ion fluctuating current density is the standard deviation of the signed ion current density component along the local magnetic field. The current density is defined per unit effective collection area perpendicular to the local magnetic field, so it represents fluctuations of parallel ion flux density rather than fluctuations of total collected current.

For a time series or ensemble of instantaneous parallel ion current density, the fluctuation amplitude is defined as the root-mean-square departure from the mean:

$$
j_{i\parallel,\sigma} = \sqrt{\left\langle \left(j_{i\parallel} - \left\langle j_{i\parallel}\right\rangle\right)^2 \right\rangle}
$$

where $j_{i\parallel,\sigma}$ and $j_{i\parallel}$ are in A m$^{-2}$, and $\langle\cdot\rangle$ denotes the chosen time average, ensemble average, or analysis-window average.

In collecting-surface measurements, the signed density is obtained from a collected ion current using $j_{i\parallel}=I_i/A_\mathrm{eff}$, where $I_i$ is in A and $A_\mathrm{eff}$ is the effective collection area in m$^2$ for ions moving along the local magnetic field. The same [effective collection area](name:effective_area_of_langmuir_probe) convention used for [parallel ion current density](name:parallel_ion_current_density) must be used for its fluctuation amplitude. Practical estimates also depend on the averaging interval, sampling bandwidth, detrending, and separation of slow changes from turbulent fluctuations.

No universal absolute range in A m$^{-2}$ is intrinsic to this quantity, because it scales with local plasma density, ion sound speed, magnetic incidence angle, surface collection model, and analysis bandwidth. Comparisons are most meaningful when the effective-area convention and averaging window are stated, or when the amplitude is normalized to the local mean parallel ion current density.

Because this quantity is a standard deviation, it is non-negative and does not retain the sign of the underlying instantaneous parallel ion current density.

NAMES.name: thermal_energy_of_plant_component_port
NAMES.short: Cumulative thermal energy extracted through a cooling-loop port on a plant component since the start of the plasma pulse, obtained by time-integrating the measured coolant enthalpy balance.
NAMES.long:
The thermal energy of a plant component port is the total heat removed by the cooling loop of that component, accumulated from pulse start to the current measurement time. It is the time-integral of the instantaneous [thermal power extracted at the port](name:thermal_power_of_plant_component_port), making it a running calorimetric total rather than a rate quantity.

The defining relation is:

$$
E_\text{th}(t) = \int_0^t P_\text{th}(t') \, dt'
$$

where $P_\text{th}$ is the instantaneous extracted thermal power (in W) and the lower integration limit is the start of the pulse.

The integrand $P_\text{th}$ is itself derived from the coolant enthalpy balance $P_\text{th} = \dot{m} c_p (T_\text{out} - T_\text{in})$, where $\dot{m}$ is the coolant mass flow rate, $c_p$ is the specific heat capacity of the coolant, and $T_\text{out}$ and $T_\text{in}$ are the [outlet](name:coolant_temperature_at_outlet) and [inlet](name:coolant_temperature_at_inlet) coolant temperatures. This cumulative measure is used in pulse-integrated heat load accounting for plasma-facing components and cooling circuits, complementing the instantaneous power signal for assessing total energy deposition over a discharge.

NAMES.name: vertical_angle_of_camera
NAMES.short: Vertical angular field of view of the camera, defined as the total angular span covered along the detector-plane vertical direction.
NAMES.long:
Vertical angle of a camera is the vertical field-of-view width: the total angular span imaged between the lower and upper edges of the active detector area along the detector-plane vertical direction. It is an angular aperture, not a signed pointing or elevation angle, so it is reported as a non-negative value in radians.

For an ideal rectilinear optical model with an effective focal length, the vertical field of view is commonly approximated by:

$$
\theta_v = 2\arctan\left(\frac{h}{2 f_\mathrm{eff}}\right)
$$

where $\theta_v$ is the vertical angular field of view, $h$ is the active detector height in meters, and $f_\mathrm{eff}$ is the effective focal length in meters. This relation assumes a rectilinear projection and an effective focal length that already includes the relevant optical configuration.

In practice, the value is obtained from optical design parameters, laboratory calibration, or a ray-tracing model of the camera and its lenses. For distorted, telecentric, or otherwise non-rectilinear optics, the field of view is better determined from the calibrated viewing rays at the vertical detector edges, or equivalently from the difference between the upper and lower vertical viewing-angle bounds of the detector pixels.

Typical values for diagnostic cameras range from about 0.05-1 rad, with narrow views used for localized high-resolution imaging and wider views used to cover larger plasma-facing regions.

NAMES.name: x_coordinate_of_sensor_attachment_point
NAMES.short: X coordinate of the point where a sensor is mechanically attached to a device component, expressed in the right-handed Cartesian (x, y, z) frame. It is signed relative to the Cartesian origin and +x direction.
NAMES.long:
The $x$ coordinate of a sensor attachment point is the signed horizontal position component of the mechanical point at which a sensor or its mount is fixed to a device component. It is defined in a right-handed Cartesian $(x, y, z)$ frame with basis $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$; $+\hat{z}$ is vertical and parallel to $+\hat{Z}$ of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The origin lies on the toroidal symmetry axis at the machine midplane, so $z=0$ and $Z=0$ denote the midplane.

Relative to the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, the horizontal Cartesian component is

$$
x = R \cos\phi
$$

where $R$ is major radius in meters and $\phi$ is toroidal angle in radians; $\phi=0$ lies along $+\hat{x}$ and increasing $\phi$ points toward $+\hat{y}$ when viewed from $+\hat{z}$.

Together with the [y coordinate of the sensor attachment point](name:y_coordinate_of_sensor_attachment_point) and the [vertical coordinate of the sensor attachment point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_sensor_attachment_point), this quantity specifies the mechanical attachment location. In practice it is obtained from engineering design geometry or from alignment surveys using coordinate-measuring equipment, laser trackers, photogrammetry, or optical metrology of the installed sensor and mount. The attachment point is a mechanical reference point, not necessarily the sensitive volume, viewing aperture, or line-of-sight origin of the sensor.

Typical values are set by device size and by whether the sensor is mounted inside the vessel, on the vessel wall, or on external support structures. Compact devices often fall within $\pm 2$ m, medium-sized devices within $\pm 5$ m, and large devices or external diagnostic supports can reach $\pm 15$ m.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the attachment point is displaced from the Cartesian origin in the $+\hat{x}$ direction.

NAMES.name: x_direction_unit_vector
NAMES.short: X-axis projection of a direction unit vector encoding the spatial orientation of a device or sensor in the right-handed Cartesian (x, y, z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The x component of the [direction_unit_vector](name:direction_unit_vector) gives the projection of a hardware device's pointing direction onto the $\hat{x}$ axis of the right-handed Cartesian $(x, y, z)$ frame, where $\hat{z}$ coincides with the vertical $+Z$ direction and the azimuthal origin $\phi = 0$ is defined by facility convention.

For a unit vector $\hat{d}$ specifying device orientation, the three Cartesian components satisfy the unit-norm identity:

$$
d_x^2 + d_y^2 + d_z^2 = 1
$$

where $d_x$ is this quantity, $d_y$ is the [y_direction_unit_vector](name:y_direction_unit_vector_of_strain_gauge_sensor), and $d_z$ is the [vertical_direction_unit_vector](name:vertical_direction_unit_vector). This constraint restricts the valid range to $d_x \in [-1, 1]$, with $|d_x| = 1$ only when the device points purely along the $\pm x$ axis.

This component is determined from mechanical installation geometry — precision survey measurements or engineering alignment procedures — rather than from plasma diagnostics. It applies to a broad class of hardware components including sensors, cameras, injector nozzles, and launcher mirrors whose spatial pointing must be registered in a common Cartesian frame.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the direction vector has a component in the $+x$ direction of the right-handed Cartesian $(x, y, z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: y_coordinate_of_sensor_attachment_point
NAMES.short: Y coordinate of the point where a sensor is physically attached to a device component, in the right-handed Cartesian (x, y, z) machine frame.
NAMES.long:
The $y$ coordinate of a sensor attachment point specifies the location along the $y$ axis of the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ machine frame at which a sensor is physically mounted to a structural component, where $\hat{z}$ is the vertical axis and $\phi = 0$ is defined by the facility convention.

Together with [x_coordinate_of_sensor_attachment_point](name:x_coordinate_of_sensor_attachment_point) and [vertical_coordinate_of_sensor_attachment_point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_sensor_attachment_point), this coordinate fully determines the three-dimensional position of the mechanical attachment point in the machine reference frame. Attachment point coordinates are established from engineering drawings or direct metrology surveys of the as-built device; accurate knowledge of these positions is essential for relating sensor signals to plasma geometry and for alignment corrections in field or current reconstructions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the attachment point lies in the $+\hat{y}$ direction from the machine Cartesian origin.

NAMES.name: diameter_of_diagnostic_aperture
NAMES.short: Full linear width of a circular diagnostic aperture at the entrance pupil, equal to twice the aperture radius and determining the solid-angle light-collection acceptance of the diagnostic channel.
NAMES.long:
The diameter of a diagnostic aperture is the full chord across the circular opening at the entrance pupil of the optical collection system. It is geometrically related to the [radius_of_diagnostic_aperture](name:radius_of_diagnostic_aperture) by $d = 2r$, and it directly governs the solid angle subtended at a given distance from the plasma emission region, setting the total light throughput and therefore the signal-to-noise balance of the diagnostic.

The solid angle $\Omega$ subtended by a circular aperture of diameter $d$ at perpendicular distance $L$ from the emission region is:

$$
\Omega \approx \frac{\pi d^2}{4 L^2}
$$

where $d$ is the aperture diameter and $L$ is the line-of-sight distance from the plasma to the aperture plane.

This geometric parameter characterizes the entrance cone of spectroscopic diagnostics, including charge exchange recombination spectroscopy channels where the aperture diameter limits angular acceptance and spatial resolution. Typical values in fusion diagnostic systems range from a few millimeters to several centimeters depending on the required étendue and spatial selectivity of the measurement.
NAMES.sign: Positive when measured as the full chord through the aperture center in the plane of the entrance pupil.

NAMES.name: height_of_neutron_detector
NAMES.short: Full extent of the neutron detector aperture in the second local coordinate direction (X2), specifying one transverse dimension of a rectangular detector opening.
NAMES.long:
The height of a neutron detector specifies the aperture dimension along the second axis of the detector-local Cartesian $(X1, X2)$ coordinate frame, where $X2$ is oriented perpendicular to both the line-of-sight direction and the $X1$ axis. This quantity applies to rectangular aperture geometries and, paired with [width_of_neutron_detector](name:width_of_neutron_detector) measured along the $X1$ axis, fully defines the two-dimensional rectangular aperture opening.

The aperture height enters the computation of geometric detector acceptance: for a rectangular aperture the effective acceptance area is the product of the height ($X2$) and width ($X1$) dimensions, which scales the solid angle subtended by the detector and directly affects the inferred [neutron_flux_of_neutron_detector](name:neutron_flux_of_neutron_detector). The aggregate quantity [surface_area_of_neutron_detector](name:surface_area_of_neutron_detector) is derived from these geometric parameters.

In fusion neutron diagnostics, detector aperture heights range from a few millimeters to a few centimeters, chosen to balance spatial resolution against counting-rate requirements.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the aperture height is measured in the positive $X2$ direction of the detector-local coordinate frame.

NAMES.name: helium_4_density
NAMES.subject: helium_4
NAMES.short: Local number density of helium-4 ions per unit plasma volume, the principal measure of fusion ash concentration in deuterium-tritium burning plasmas.
NAMES.long:
The helium-4 ion number density $n_{{}^4\text{He}}$ quantifies the local concentration of ${}^4\text{He}$ nuclei at a given point in the plasma. At fusion-relevant temperatures (several keV), helium-4 is fully stripped to He$^{2+}$, and in deuterium-tritium burning plasmas it accumulates as the primary fusion ash product of the reaction ${}^2\text{H} + {}^3\text{H} \rightarrow {}^4\text{He} + n$; its buildup dilutes the fuel and reduces the fusion reaction rate if not exhausted by the divertor system.

The time evolution of $n_{{}^4\text{He}}$ is governed by the particle continuity equation

$$
\frac{\partial n_{{}^4\text{He}}}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{{}^4\text{He}} = S_{{}^4\text{He}}
$$

where $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{{}^4\text{He}}$ is the helium-4 particle flux and $S_{{}^4\text{He}}$ is the volumetric source rate from fusion reactions and ionization of recycled helium neutrals at the plasma edge.

The helium-4 density is measured primarily via charge exchange recombination spectroscopy, where injected neutral beam atoms undergo charge exchange with He$^{2+}$ ions to produce line emission from excited helium atoms; passive spectroscopy of edge recycling emission provides a complementary approach. Chord-averaged and volume-averaged forms are provided by [line_averaged_helium_4_density](name:line_averaged_helium_4_density) and [volume_averaged_helium_4_density](name:volume_averaged_helium_4_density) respectively, while [helium_4_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:helium_4_density_at_plasma_boundary) gives the boundary value.

In D-T burning plasmas, central He-4 densities are in the range $10^{18}$-$10^{19}$ m$^{-3}$, with the helium-to-electron density ratio — captured by [fraction](name:fraction) — kept below approximately 5-10% in steady state to avoid excessive fuel dilution.

NAMES.name: krypton_density
NAMES.subject: krypton
NAMES.short: Local number density of krypton impurity summed over all ionization states, giving the total krypton particle concentration per unit plasma volume.
NAMES.long:
The krypton number density is the volumetric concentration of krypton impurity at a given point in the plasma, encompassing all ionization states from neutral krypton Kr$^0$ through fully stripped Kr$^{36+}$. It is the primary local measure of krypton seeding level and the parent quantity from which spatially averaged forms are derived.

The total krypton particle density $n_\mathrm{Kr}$ at a given location is defined as:

$$
n_\mathrm{Kr} = \sum_{q=0}^{36} n_\mathrm{Kr}^{(q)}
$$

where $n_\mathrm{Kr}^{(q)}$ is the number density of krypton ions in charge state $q$. The [chord-averaged form](name:line_averaged_krypton_density) integrates this local quantity along a line of sight, while [volume_averaged_krypton_density](name:volume_averaged_krypton_density) provides a global mean. The concentration relative to electron density is tracked by krypton_fraction, and the pedestal-region value by [krypton_density_at_pedestal](name:krypton_density_at_pedestal).

Krypton (atomic number $Z=36$) is injected as a high-$Z$ seeding gas for radiative power exhaust and divertor detachment control. Its local density is inferred from passive spectroscopy of charge-state emission lines, active charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, or tomographic inversion of multi-chord line-integrated measurements. Typical seeded-discharge values in tokamak edge and divertor regions range from $10^{16}$ to $10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$, corresponding to 0.01–1% of the local electron density.
NAMES.sign: Positive when krypton particles are present in the plasma volume element.

NAMES.name: line_averaged_beryllium_density
NAMES.subject: beryllium
NAMES.short: Chord-average of the beryllium ion number density along a diagnostic line of sight, equal to the path integral of the local beryllium density divided by the chord length.
NAMES.long:
The line-averaged beryllium ion number density quantifies the mean beryllium ion content along a plasma diagnostic chord, normalized by chord length. It is the chord-integrated analog of the local [beryllium_density](name:beryllium_density) and is the most directly accessible measure of beryllium impurity concentration from line-of-sight diagnostics.

The quantity is defined as:

$$
\bar{n}_{Be} = \frac{1}{L} \int_0^L n_{Be}(l) \, dl
$$

where $n_{Be}(l)$ is the local beryllium ion number density at path coordinate $l$ along the chord and $L$ is the total chord length.

Inferred from passive spectroscopy of beryllium emission lines by inverting chord-integrated emission intensities using atomic emissivity coefficients; the result aggregates contributions from all beryllium ionization states present along the chord. The [volume_averaged_beryllium_density](name:volume_averaged_beryllium_density) provides a complementary global volume average, while [beryllium_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:beryllium_density_at_magnetic_axis) gives the local on-axis value.
NAMES.sign: Positive when beryllium ions populate the measurement chord.

NAMES.name: line_averaged_helium_4_density
NAMES.subject: helium_4
NAMES.short: Chord-averaged helium-4 ion number density, equal to the path integral of the local helium-4 density divided by the measurement chord length.
NAMES.long:
The line-averaged helium-4 density gives the spatial mean of the local [helium_4_density](name:helium_4_density) along a diagnostic chord through the plasma. As the principal ash product of deuterium-tritium fusion, helium-4 accumulates in the plasma core and its line-integrated concentration must be monitored to prevent fuel dilution and degradation of energy confinement.

The chord average is defined as:

$$
\bar{n}_{\mathrm{He4}} = \frac{1}{L} \int_0^L n_{\mathrm{He4}}(\ell) \, d\ell
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{He4}}(\ell)$ is the local helium-4 ion number density at position $\ell$ along the chord (in m$^{-3}$) and $L$ is the total chord length in m.

This quantity is a natural output of line-integrated optical diagnostics such as charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy and helium spectral-line emission measurements, prior to any spatial inversion. It complements [volume_averaged_helium_4_density](name:volume_averaged_helium_4_density), which integrates over the full plasma volume, and is directly analogous to [line_averaged_helium_3_density](name:line_averaged_helium_3_density) for the lighter helium isotope. Typical values in deuterium-tritium burning plasmas range from $10^{17}$ to $10^{19}$ m$^{-3}$, depending on fusion power and helium exhaust efficiency.
NAMES.sign: Positive when helium-4 ions occupy the measurement chord at finite density; number density is orientation-independent and cannot take negative values.

NAMES.name: line_averaged_krypton_density
NAMES.subject: krypton
NAMES.short: Chord-average of the krypton number density, equal to the path integral of the local krypton particle density divided by the measurement chord length.
NAMES.long:
Krypton ($Z = 36$) is a noble-gas impurity that may be seeded into fusion plasmas for edge radiative cooling and power exhaust control. The line-averaged krypton density $\bar{n}_\mathrm{Kr}$ gives the krypton particle concentration averaged along a measurement chord, providing a line-of-sight integrated measure of impurity content rather than a local point value.

The defining relation is:

$$
\bar{n}_\mathrm{Kr} = \frac{1}{L} \int_0^L n_\mathrm{Kr}(\ell) \, d\ell
$$

where $n_\mathrm{Kr}(\ell)$ is the local krypton number density at position $\ell$ along the chord and $L$ is the total chord length in meters.

This quantity is typically inferred from chord-integrated optical or vacuum-ultraviolet emission spectroscopy of krypton line radiation, combined with emissivity modeling along the line of sight. It provides a path-integrated measure complementary to the local [krypton_density](name:krypton_density) and to the global [volume_averaged_krypton_density](name:volume_averaged_krypton_density). For comparison, [line_averaged_argon_density](name:line_averaged_argon_density) follows the same chord-average definition for argon seeding. Local concentrations at specific plasma regions are captured by [krypton_density_at_pedestal](name:krypton_density_at_pedestal) and [krypton_density_at_limiter](name:krypton_density_at_limiter).

Typical line-averaged krypton densities in power-exhaust seeding scenarios range from $10^{16}$ to $10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$, depending on seeding rate and plasma confinement regime.
NAMES.sign: Positive when krypton particles are present along the measurement chord, consistent with the intrinsically non-negative character of particle number density.

NAMES.name: line_averaged_lithium_density
NAMES.subject: lithium
NAMES.short: Path-length average of the lithium impurity ion number density along a diagnostic line of sight. It sums all ionized lithium charge states and excludes neutral lithium.
NAMES.long:
Line-averaged lithium density is the path-length average of the lithium impurity ion number density along a specified line of sight. The local lithium ion density is the sum over ionized lithium charge states, $n_{\mathrm{Li,ion}} = n_{\mathrm{Li}^+} + n_{\mathrm{Li}^{2+}} + n_{\mathrm{Li}^{3+}}$, and excludes neutral lithium atoms.

For a chord of length $L$, the line average is defined by

$$
\langle n_{\mathrm{Li}} \rangle_{\mathrm{line}} = \frac{1}{L}\int_0^L n_{\mathrm{Li,ion}}(\ell)\,d\ell
$$

where $\ell$ is distance along the line of sight in meters, $L$ is the chord length in meters, $n_{\mathrm{Li,ion}}$ is the local summed ionized-lithium density in m^-3, and $\langle n_{\mathrm{Li}} \rangle_{\mathrm{line}}$ is in m^-3.

In practice, this quantity may be inferred from a line-integrated lithium-sensitive measurement divided by the relevant chord length, or computed by integrating a reconstructed local lithium ion density along the same path. It provides a bulk chord measure of lithium impurity content and does not by itself resolve where along the line of sight the lithium ions are located.

The value is non-negative and is typically interpreted relative to electron density or to other impurity densities, because lithium content depends strongly on wall conditioning, fueling, transport, and plasma scenario. No universal numerical range is implied by the definition.

NAMES.name: neutron_rate_of_neutron_detector
NAMES.subject: neutron
NAMES.short: Number of individual neutron detection events registered per unit time by a neutron detector operating in pulse-counting mode.
NAMES.long:
Neutron rate of a neutron detector is the count rate of resolved neutron-induced pulses recorded by the detector. It is a detector response quantity, not the total neutron emission rate of the plasma source and not the incident neutron flux at the detector location.

The rate is defined from the cumulative number of accepted neutron detection events:

$$
R_n(t) = \frac{dN_\mathrm{det}(t)}{dt}
$$

where $R_n(t)$ is the neutron detection rate and $N_\mathrm{det}(t)$ is the cumulative number of neutron events that pass the detector pulse-height, timing, and discrimination criteria.

In practice, the rate is obtained by counting pulses in a finite time bin and dividing by the bin duration, with corrections as needed for dead time, background, pile-up, and neutron-gamma discrimination. For a given neutron field it depends on detector efficiency, active area or volume, shielding, collimation, and the neutron energy and angular response; at high rates, unresolved pile-up can make pulse counting unreliable and motivate current-mode or other integrating operation.

Typical pulse-counting rates range from about 10^0-10^7 s^-1, depending on detector type, distance from the plasma, shielding, and fusion power. Rates above roughly 10^6-10^7 s^-1 often require careful dead-time correction or a change of operating mode.

NAMES.name: nitrogen_density
NAMES.subject: nitrogen
NAMES.short: Local number density of all nitrogen nuclei per unit plasma volume, summed over all ionization states from neutral nitrogen through fully stripped ions.
NAMES.long:
Local number density of all nitrogen nuclei per unit plasma volume, totaling contributions from every ionization state of the species.

The total nitrogen density is the sum over all charge states:

$$
n_N = \sum_{z=0}^{7} n_{N^{z+}}
$$

where $n_{N^{z+}}$ is the number density of nitrogen ions in charge state $z+$, with $z = 0$ for neutral nitrogen and $z = 7$ for fully stripped N$^{7+}$ (atomic number $Z_N = 7$).

Nitrogen is commonly seeded into fusion plasmas as a radiative impurity to dissipate excess divertor heat flux; the local $n_N$ directly determines the radiative cooling power and the nitrogen contribution to the effective charge $Z_\mathrm{eff}$. It is inferred from vacuum-ultraviolet or extreme-ultraviolet emission spectroscopy analyzed with collisional-radiative models, or from active charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy.

During active nitrogen seeding, core concentrations in present-day tokamaks range from $10^{17}$ to $5 \times 10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$, with elevated values near the plasma edge. The [line-averaged nitrogen density](name:line_averaged_nitrogen_density) and [volume-averaged nitrogen density](name:volume_averaged_nitrogen_density) provide chord-integrated and globally averaged measures of the nitrogen particle inventory; [nitrogen_fraction](name:nitrogen_fraction) normalizes $n_N$ to the electron density.
NAMES.sign: Positive when nitrogen nuclei are present in the plasma volume.

NAMES.name: line_averaged_nitrogen_density
NAMES.subject: nitrogen
NAMES.short: Line-averaged number density of nitrogen nuclei along a plasma diagnostic chord, summed over all ionization states. It equals the path integral of the local nitrogen density divided by the chord length.
NAMES.long:
Line-averaged nitrogen density is the chord-average of the local nitrogen number density sampled along a diagnostic line of sight. The nitrogen density includes nitrogen nuclei in all ionization states, so different charge states contribute according to their local abundance along the chord.

For a chord path $\Gamma$, the line-averaged nitrogen density is defined by:

$$
\langle n_N \rangle_L = \frac{1}{L}\int_{\Gamma} n_N(\ell)\,d\ell
$$

where $n_N(\ell)$ is the local nitrogen number density in m^-3, summed over all ionization states, $\ell$ is arclength along the chord in meters, and $L=\int_{\Gamma}d\ell$ is the chord length in meters over the sampled plasma region.

In practice this quantity is inferred from diagnostics and analysis methods that constrain nitrogen content along a line of sight, often using spectroscopic signals, atomic physics modeling, plasma background parameters, and the known viewing geometry. Because many measurements are sensitive to emissivity or to particular charge-state populations rather than directly to total nitrogen density, the conversion to all-ionization-state nitrogen density is model dependent and is not simply a geometric division of a raw signal by chord length.

Typical line-averaged nitrogen densities in tokamak plasmas range from about 1e15-1e18 m^-3 for trace-seeded conditions and can reach 1e19 m^-3 in strongly seeded or detached-edge regimes, depending on fueling, impurity seeding rate, transport, and ionization balance.

NAMES.name: nuclear_density_of_neutron_detector_converter
NAMES.short: Number density of target nuclei in a neutron detector converter material for the nuclear species involved in the neutron-induced detection reaction.
NAMES.long:
Nuclear density of a neutron detector converter is the number of target atomic nuclei per unit volume of converter material for the nuclear species that participates in the neutron-induced detection reaction. It is a material-and-composition property, distinct from converter volume or neutron flux, and sets the number of reaction centers available to incident neutrons.

For a converter made from one or more compounds or phases $c$, the target-nucleus density can be computed from the bulk material density and composition as:

$$
n_i = \rho_m N_A \sum_c f_c \frac{\nu_{i,c} a_{i,c}}{M_c}
$$

where $n_i$ is the target nuclear density in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, $\rho_m$ is the bulk mass density of the converter material in $\mathrm{kg\,m}^{-3}$, $N_A$ is Avogadro's constant in $\mathrm{mol}^{-1}$, $f_c$ is the dimensionless mass fraction of compound or phase $c$, $M_c$ is its molar mass in $\mathrm{kg\,mol}^{-1}$, $\nu_{i,c}$ is the number of atoms of the relevant parent element per formula unit, and $a_{i,c}$ is the dimensionless isotopic abundance or enrichment of target isotope $i$. For a pure elemental or pure isotopic converter this reduces to the familiar single-component density relation.

In practice this quantity is derived from material specifications, density measurements, stoichiometry, isotopic assay, enrichment certificates, and corrections for porosity or inactive binder fraction when those affect the active converter volume. In response calculations it is combined with the microscopic reaction cross section and the converter-level neutron flux, such as [neutron_flux_of_neutron_detector_converter](name:incident_neutron_fluence_of_neutron_detector_converter); this is the flux at or within the converter and is distinct from a detector-level incident or averaged [neutron_flux_of_neutron_detector](name:neutron_flux_of_neutron_detector).

Typical dense solid converter materials have total atomic densities of about $10^{28}-10^{29}\ \mathrm{m}^{-3}$. Target isotope densities are commonly $10^{26}-10^{29}\ \mathrm{m}^{-3}$ depending on stoichiometry, enrichment, and loading, while gas or low-density converter media can be much lower, around $10^{20}-10^{25}\ \mathrm{m}^{-3}$.

NAMES.name: nuclear_target_atomic_fraction_of_neutron_detector_converter
NAMES.short: Fraction of atoms in the neutron detector converter material that belong to the nuclear target species responsible for the primary neutron-induced detection reaction.
NAMES.long:
The nuclear target atomic fraction specifies what proportion of the total atoms present in the neutron detector converter are of the isotopic species that participates in the primary neutron detection reaction (for example, neutron capture or fission). Converter materials exploit specific target nuclei that interact with incident neutrons to produce detectable secondary charged particles; the converter's intrinsic efficiency and absolute response are set directly by how many such target atoms exist within the active volume.

The fraction is defined as:

$$
f_{\rm target} = \frac{N_{\rm target}}{N_{\rm total}}
$$

where $N_{\rm target}$ is the number of target nuclear species atoms and $N_{\rm total}$ is the total atom count in the converter.

This fraction enters the calculation of the total reactive nucleus inventory together with the [nuclear number density](name:nuclear_density_of_neutron_detector_converter) and the [converter volume](name:volume_of_neutron_detector_converter), and it scales the [nuclear reaction rate per unit volume](name:nuclear_rate_of_neutron_detector_converter) proportionally. Converters fabricated from isotopically enriched materials have values approaching 1, while natural-abundance converter materials may exhibit significantly lower fractions depending on the isotope's natural abundance. The [normalized atomic count](name:nuclear_target_atomic_fraction_of_neutron_detector_converter) provides a complementary dimensionless measure of the reactive nucleus inventory integrated over the full detector assembly.

NAMES.name: oxygen_density
NAMES.subject: oxygen
NAMES.short: Total number density of oxygen atoms and ions across all charge states, from neutral to fully stripped, giving the local oxygen impurity concentration at a point in the plasma.
NAMES.long:
The local oxygen number density $n_\mathrm{O}$ quantifies the total concentration of oxygen impurity per unit plasma volume, encompassing neutral atomic oxygen and all ionic charge states up to fully stripped O$^{8+}$. Oxygen is a ubiquitous low-Z impurity in fusion devices, entering through wall outgassing and vessel conditioning; it contributes to radiative power losses and dilutes the hydrogenic fuel inventory.

The total oxygen density is defined as the sum over all ionization states:

$$
n_\mathrm{O} = \sum_{Z=0}^{8} n_{\mathrm{O}^{Z+}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{O}^{Z+}}$ is the number density of oxygen in charge state $Z^+$, with $Z$ ranging from 0 (neutral) to 8 (fully stripped).

The local density is inferred from passive extreme-ultraviolet spectroscopy, charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, and soft X-ray emission tomography. Spatially averaged forms include [line_averaged_oxygen_density](name:line_averaged_oxygen_density) (chord integral divided by chord length) and [volume_averaged_oxygen_density](name:volume_averaged_oxygen_density) (integral over the plasma volume). The dimensionless [oxygen_fraction](name:ratio_of_volume_averaged_oxygen_ion_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density) relates this local density to the electron density as an impurity concentration measure.

In well-conditioned fusion plasmas the core oxygen density is a small fraction of the electron density; edge concentrations of $10^{15}$–$10^{17}$ m$^{-3}$ are representative of limiter and divertor configurations.
NAMES.sign: Positive when oxygen atoms or ions are present in the plasma volume element.

NAMES.name: line_averaged_oxygen_density
NAMES.subject: oxygen
NAMES.short: Line-of-sight average of the total oxygen impurity number density, encompassing all charge states from neutral to fully stripped, divided by the chord length.
NAMES.long:
The line-averaged oxygen density is the chord-mean of the local oxygen number density—summed over all charge states from neutral O$^0$ through fully stripped O$^{8+}$—along a measurement path through the plasma. It characterizes the mean impurity concentration of oxygen along a given line of sight and is directly related to the local [oxygen_density](name:oxygen_density) integrated along the chord.

The defining relation is:

$$
\langle n_O \rangle_\ell = \frac{1}{L} \int_0^L n_O(\ell) \, d\ell
$$

where $n_O(\ell)$ is the local oxygen number density at position $\ell$ along the chord and $L$ is the chord length in m.

Line-averaged impurity densities are extracted from chord-integrated spectroscopic measurements of oxygen emission lines combined with ionization balance models. Passive spectroscopy of ultraviolet oxygen transitions or charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy of helium-like and hydrogen-like oxygen lines provides the chord-integrated signal from which the line-averaged density is inferred. As a chord-averaged observable, spatial resolution is inherently limited, and tomographic inversion or profile modeling is required to recover local distributions.

Oxygen is a low-concentration impurity in fusion plasmas under normal operating conditions; line-averaged values fall several orders of magnitude below the electron density, with representative ranges of $10^{15}$–$10^{17}$ m$^{-3}$ depending on wall conditioning and impurity seeding. The [volume_averaged_oxygen_density](name:volume_averaged_oxygen_density) provides the plasma-volume–weighted counterpart, while analogous chord-averaged densities for other impurity species include [line_averaged_nitrogen_density](name:line_averaged_nitrogen_density) and [line_averaged_carbon_density](name:line_averaged_carbon_density).
NAMES.sign: Positive when oxygen impurity particles are present along the measurement chord at nonzero concentration.

NAMES.name: requested_lower_voltage_of_neutron_detector
NAMES.short: Requested low-voltage supply setpoint for a neutron detector module. It is the commanded target potential difference for detector electronics operation, not a measured detector signal.
NAMES.long:
The requested low-voltage supply setpoint is the target electrical potential difference commanded for the low-voltage power supply associated with a neutron detector module. It represents the intended operating point of the detector electronics supply rather than the voltage actually delivered at the terminals.

The setpoint is defined as the commanded potential difference between the regulated low-voltage output and its electrical reference:

$$
V_{\mathrm{LV,set}} = \Phi_{\mathrm{out,set}} - \Phi_{\mathrm{ref}}
$$

where $V_{\mathrm{LV,set}}$ is the requested low-voltage setpoint in volts (V), $\Phi_{\mathrm{out,set}}$ is the commanded output-terminal electric potential in volts (V), and $\Phi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the associated supply return or electrical reference potential in volts (V).

This quantity is produced by the detector control or configuration system as the target for a regulated low-voltage supply. It should be distinguished from the high-voltage bias command represented by [requested upper voltage of neutron detector](name:requested_upper_voltage_of_neutron_detector) and from detector signal voltages such as [voltage of neutron detector](name:voltage_of_neutron_detector). When an actual low-voltage monitor is available, this setpoint is the reference value against which the achieved supply voltage is assessed.

Typical values are device-specific and set by the detector electronics design. Low-voltage detector supplies are commonly commanded to nominal service rails of a few V to a few tens of V; allowable zero, standby, bipolar, or negative-rail commands depend on the particular supply and detector module.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the commanded low-voltage supply output terminal is at higher electric potential than its associated supply return or electrical reference terminal.

NAMES.name: requested_upper_voltage_of_neutron_detector
NAMES.short: Commanded target potential difference for the upper high-voltage bias connection of a neutron detector, referenced to the detector high-voltage return or electronics common. It specifies the requested operating bias for detector electronics, not a measured supply output or detector signal.
NAMES.long:
Requested upper voltage of a neutron detector is the commanded potential difference assigned to the detector's upper high-voltage bias connection relative to the detector high-voltage return or electronics reference. It sets the intended operating bias for charge collection, gas multiplication, scintillator photodetector gain, or related detector-electronics behavior. This quantity is a setpoint, not a measured high-voltage readback and not the radiation-induced detector signal voltage.

The reference polarity is defined by the potential difference between the commanded upper bias potential and the chosen detector reference potential:

$$
V_{\mathrm{upper,req}} = \Phi_{\mathrm{upper,req}} - \Phi_{\mathrm{ref}}
$$

where $\Phi_{\mathrm{upper,req}}$ is the commanded electric potential of the upper high-voltage bias connection and $\Phi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the detector high-voltage return, electronics common, or other explicitly defined bias reference.

In practice the value is prescribed from the detector operating point and may be held constant, ramped during conditioning, or changed between acquisition phases. The realized voltage, if monitored, is a separate supply readback; detector pulse or current signals are also separate physical quantities produced by neutron interactions and the associated electronics chain.

Typical commanded magnitudes range from about 100-3000 V for many gas-filled neutron detectors, fission chambers, ionization chambers, and photodetector-based systems, with lower or higher values possible depending on detector type, pressure, electrode spacing, insulation limits, and required gain.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the commanded potential of the upper high-voltage bias connection is greater than the detector high-voltage return or electronics reference potential.

NAMES.name: temperature_of_neutron_detector
NAMES.short: Calibrated thermodynamic temperature, in kelvin, representing the thermal state of a neutron detector assembly or its neutron-conversion element. It is the temperature used to characterize detector response, not the raw temperature-sensor voltage.
NAMES.long:
Temperature of a neutron detector is the calibrated thermodynamic temperature representing the thermal state of the detector assembly, housing, electronics-adjacent sensor location, or neutron-to-charged-particle converter element. The reported quantity is an absolute temperature in kelvin and is therefore non-negative; it is distinct from a raw sensor output such as [voltage_of_temperature_sensor](name:voltage_of_temperature_sensor).

When the detector temperature is spatially non-uniform or measured by several sensors, the scalar value should represent the location or thermal component most relevant to the detector response, such as the converter material or the sensor thermally coupled to the active detector module. If several readings are combined, the value is normally a calibrated representative temperature, for example an average or response-weighted estimate, with the choice determined by the detector calibration model.

In practice the temperature is obtained from thermistors, resistance temperature detectors, thermocouples, semiconductor sensors, or similar devices attached to the detector body, converter, or local electronics package. The calibrated temperature is used to monitor gain stability, temperature-dependent efficiency, electronic noise, and time-dependent corrections applied to neutron count-rate or signal measurements such as [voltage_of_neutron_detector](name:voltage_of_neutron_detector) and [neutron_flux_of_neutron_detector](name:neutron_flux_of_neutron_detector).

Representative operating values for room-temperature neutron detector systems are often about 280-330 K. Detectors with active heating, cooling, in-vessel placement, or thermally isolated converter elements may operate outside this range, and transient heating during a discharge can produce smaller time-dependent excursions around the local baseline.

NAMES.name: voltage_of_neutron_detector
NAMES.short: Instantaneous or sampled raw electrical output voltage of a neutron detector module, measured relative to its electronics reference or baseline before pulse extraction, filtering, calibration, or conversion to neutron rate.
NAMES.long:
Voltage of a neutron detector is the signed electrical potential difference produced at the detector output at a specified instant or sample of the raw waveform. It represents the direct analog signal relative to an electronics reference level or baseline, not a calibrated neutron flux, count rate, pulse height, or integrated charge.

For an output node with electric potential $\Phi_\mathrm{out}(t)$ and a reference or baseline potential $\Phi_\mathrm{ref}(t)$, the raw detector voltage is defined by:

$$
V_\mathrm{raw}(t) = \Phi_\mathrm{out}(t) - \Phi_\mathrm{ref}(t)
$$

where $t$ is the sampling time, $\Phi_\mathrm{out}$ is the detector or front-end electronics output potential, and $\Phi_\mathrm{ref}$ is the chosen electronics ground, bias reference, or estimated baseline.

In practice this quantity is obtained from the uncalibrated detector readout before pulse finding, shaping correction, pile-up rejection, energy calibration, efficiency correction, or conversion to neutron rate. For pulsed detectors it is the waveform sample value; derived quantities such as pulse maximum, pulse integral, or discriminator counts should be treated separately.

Typical raw amplitudes range from 1e-3-10 V depending on detector type, biasing, preamplifier gain, termination, and neutron intensity. Baseline fluctuations and electronic noise are often in the 1e-4-1e-2 V range, while large pulses may approach the dynamic range or saturation limit of the acquisition electronics.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the detector output potential is above the chosen electronics reference or baseline potential.

NAMES.name: peak_voltage_of_neutron_detector
NAMES.short: Peak voltage of a neutron detector is the baseline-referenced pulse height of the processed detector signal, evaluated at the pulse extremum after applying the channel pulse-polarity convention. It represents the voltage amplitude assigned to an individual detector response.
NAMES.long:
Peak voltage of a neutron detector is the pulse height assigned to the processed voltage waveform from a detector module. It is referenced to the local pre-pulse baseline and uses the channel pulse-polarity convention, so it is not simply the raw algebraic maximum of the unprocessed waveform or an absolute value over the full record.

For a pulse-search window, the baseline-referenced peak voltage can be written as the maximum polarity-corrected excursion:

$$
V_{\mathrm{peak}} = \max_{t \in W}\left[p\left(V_{\mathrm{proc}}(t)-V_{\mathrm{base}}\right)\right]
$$

where $V_{\mathrm{peak}}$, $V_{\mathrm{proc}}(t)$, and $V_{\mathrm{base}}$ are in volts, $W$ is the time window associated with the pulse, and $p$ is the pulse-polarity factor: $p=+1$ for positive-going processed pulses and $p=-1$ for negative-going processed pulses.

In practice, the digitized detector output is conditioned by shaping, filtering, or other signal-processing steps before the peak is found. The baseline is usually estimated from pre-pulse samples or a nearby quiet interval, and pulse pileup, saturation, and electronic noise determine whether the extracted peak is reliable. This quantity is distinct from the instantaneous [detector voltage](name:voltage_of_neutron_detector), which denotes the voltage signal itself before the peak-height reduction.

Representative processed pulse heights are strongly instrument-dependent, but neutron detector electronics commonly report values from about 0.001-5 V for resolved pulses. Values near the noise floor are threshold-dependent, while values approaching the acquisition full scale may indicate saturation rather than a proportional neutron response.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the pulse excursion is in the channel's configured pulse-polarity direction relative to the local baseline; for a positive-going channel this means the processed voltage at the pulse peak exceeds the baseline, and for a negative-going channel it means it is below the baseline before polarity correction.

NAMES.name: voltage_of_temperature_sensor
NAMES.short: Electrical potential difference output by a temperature sensor that monitors the thermal environment of a neutron detector module. It is the sensor signal measured relative to a designated electronics reference, normally before conversion to calibrated temperature.
NAMES.long:
Voltage of a temperature sensor is the electrical potential difference generated by, or produced from, the sensor element and read by the acquisition electronics as the thermal-monitor signal for a neutron detector module. It is an electrical signal in volts, not a temperature; conversion to detector or sensor temperature requires the applicable calibration, baseline, and electronics gain information.

The temperature calibration is commonly represented as a mapping from the corrected sensor voltage:

$$
T_s = f_\mathrm{cal}\!\left(\frac{V_s - V_0}{G}\right)
$$

where $T_s$ is the inferred sensor temperature, $V_s$ is this measured voltage, $V_0$ is the voltage offset or baseline associated with the reference condition and readout chain, $G$ is the dimensionless electronics gain, and $f_\mathrm{cal}$ is the calibration function for the sensor type. For a locally linear calibration, the sensitivity $S_T = dV/dT$ has units of V/K and is distinct from the voltage value $V_s$ itself.

In practice the voltage is obtained by digitizing the potential difference between the sensor signal terminal and the electronics reference or return terminal. The sensor may be a thermocouple, resistance thermometer, thermistor, or integrated temperature monitor, with appropriate excitation, cold-junction compensation, amplification, filtering, and offset correction applied according to the measurement chain.

Typical recorded voltages depend strongly on sensor type and conditioning. Unamplified thermocouple signals are commonly in the $10^{-4}$-$10^{-2}$ V range over practical temperature excursions, with sensitivities of order $10^{-5}$-$10^{-4}$ V/K; conditioned resistive or semiconductor temperature channels are often scaled to about $0$-$5$ V or $-10$-$10$ V. These voltage ranges should not be interpreted as temperature sensitivities unless a calibration slope in V/K is specified.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the sensor signal terminal is at higher electric potential than the designated electronics reference or return terminal.

NAMES.name: volume_of_neutron_detector_converter
NAMES.short: Physical volume occupied by the converter material in a neutron detector. It excludes inactive supports, housings, and voids unless they are part of the neutron-converting medium.
NAMES.long:
Converter volume is the physical volume occupied by material that produces the detectable secondary signal from incident neutrons, such as a gas fill, scintillator, fission deposit, or neutron-converting coating. It is a geometrical property of the active converter medium, distinct from its nuclear number density or reaction rate per unit volume.

The converter volume is defined by integrating over the region occupied by the active converter material:

$$
V_\mathrm{conv} = \int_{\Omega_\mathrm{conv}} d^3x
$$

where $\Omega_\mathrm{conv}$ is the physical region containing converter material and $d^3x$ is the local volume element.

In practice, $V_\mathrm{conv}$ is obtained from the detector geometry: the measured or specified dimensions of gas cells, scintillator blocks, converter foils, coatings, or deposits. For segmented or multilayer converters, the total volume is the sum over active converter regions; for porous, patterned, or partially filled media, only the fraction actually occupied by converter material is included. For thin coatings, the volume is often computed as active coated area times effective converter thickness.

Representative values are highly detector-dependent: thin fission or boron/lithium coatings can be about $10^{-11}$-$10^{-7}$ m$^3$, compact solid scintillator converters about $10^{-7}$-$10^{-4}$ m$^3$, and gas-filled converter regions about $10^{-5}$-$10^{-2}$ m$^3$. The detection probability also depends on the [nuclear number density](name:nuclear_density_of_neutron_detector_converter) and microscopic cross sections, while the local conversion rate is represented by the [nuclear reaction rate per unit volume](name:nuclear_rate_of_neutron_detector_converter).

NAMES.name: width_of_neutron_detector
NAMES.short: Full width of a rectangular neutron detector aperture along the first local coordinate direction (X1), defining the collimation boundary on that transverse axis.
NAMES.long:
The width of a neutron detector specifies the full linear extent of its rectangular aperture along the first transverse local coordinate direction, X1, of the detector assembly. This geometric parameter governs the collimation acceptance in the X1 direction and is defined only when the aperture cross-section is rectangular.

Together with [height_of_neutron_detector](name:height_of_neutron_detector), which gives the corresponding aperture extent along the orthogonal X2 local coordinate, these two dimensions fully characterize the rectangular aperture geometry. Their product yields the total aperture area captured by [surface_area_of_neutron_detector](name:surface_area_of_neutron_detector), which enters the solid-angle computation and flux normalization underpinning the measured [neutron_flux_of_neutron_detector](name:neutron_flux_of_neutron_detector). The spatial location of the detector in the machine frame is described by [major_radius_of_neutron_detector](name:major_radius_of_neutron_detector) and [vertical_coordinate_of_neutron_detector](name:vertical_coordinate_of_neutron_detector).

Typical aperture widths in tokamak neutron diagnostics range from a few millimeters to several centimeters, balancing spatial resolution against counting-rate requirements and detection efficiency.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the aperture extent is measured from the lower X1 boundary to the upper X1 boundary of the detector geometry.

NAMES.name: x2_coordinate_of_neutron_detector
NAMES.short: Signed coordinate along the X2 axis of a vertex on the neutron detector boundary in the detector-local Cartesian (X1, X2) frame, defining the detector's cross-sectional outline.
NAMES.long: The X2 coordinate, together with [x1_coordinate_of_neutron_detector](name:x1_coordinate_of_neutron_detector), traces the irregular polygonal boundary of the neutron detector element in its detector-local planar Cartesian $(X1, X2)$ frame. This local frame is rigidly attached to the detector's physical orientation and position, and is distinct from the machine cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame; the relationship between the two frames is determined by the detector mounting geometry. The complete ordered sequence of $(X1, X2)$ vertex pairs defines the detector's active area or aperture cross-section, which enters computations of detection solid angle, geometric efficiency, and neutron-emission synthetic diagnostics. The analogous coordinate for hard X-ray detectors follows the same convention as [x2_coordinate_of_hard_xray_detector](name:x2_coordinate_of_hard_xray_detector), and the soft X-ray analog is [x2_coordinate_of_soft_xray_detector](name:x2_coordinate_of_soft_xray_detector).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the vertex lies in the positive X2 direction of the detector-local Cartesian $(X1, X2)$ frame.

NAMES.name: xenon_density
NAMES.subject: xenon
NAMES.short: Number density of xenon ions at a given point in the plasma, summed over all ionization states from singly ionized through fully stripped xenon, excluding neutral xenon atoms.
NAMES.long:
Xenon is a high-$Z$ noble-gas impurity (atomic number $Z_\mathrm{Xe} = 54$) introduced into fusion plasmas for radiative-mantle experiments, impurity-transport studies, and disruption mitigation. The xenon ion number density $n_\mathrm{Xe}$ quantifies the local concentration of all charged xenon species and enters the plasma effective charge through $Z_\mathrm{eff} = \sum_i Z_i^2 n_i / n_e$, where $n_i$ is the partial density of ion species $i$ and $n_e$ is the electron density.

The total xenon ion density is the sum over all ionic charge states:

$$
n_\mathrm{Xe} = \sum_{z=1}^{54} n_{\mathrm{Xe}^{z+}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{Xe}^{z+}}$ is the partial number density of xenon ions carrying charge $ze$. The charge-state distribution is determined by coronal equilibrium or collisional-radiative modeling at the local electron temperature and density.

The xenon density profile is inferred from vacuum-ultraviolet or soft-X-ray line emission via spectroscopy and tomographic inversion, or from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy using neutral-beam injection. Spatially resolved forms include [xenon_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:xenon_density_at_magnetic_axis) at the innermost flux surface and [xenon_density_at_pedestal](name:xenon_density_at_pedestal) in the edge transport barrier, while [volume_averaged_xenon_density](name:volume_averaged_xenon_density) provides the global impurity content figure of merit. The dimensionless impurity fraction relative to electron density is given by xenon_fraction.
NAMES.sign: Positive when ionized xenon is present in the plasma.

NAMES.name: line_averaged_xenon_density
NAMES.subject: xenon
NAMES.short: Line-averaged number density of xenon ions along a chord through the plasma, obtained by dividing the path integral of the local xenon ion density by the chord length.
NAMES.long:
The line-averaged xenon ion number density is the chord-path mean of the local [xenon_density](name:xenon_density), which sums all charged xenon ionization states from Xe$^{1+}$ through Xe$^{54+}$, normalized by the measurement chord length through the plasma.

The defining relation is:

$$
\bar{n}_\mathrm{Xe} = \frac{1}{L} \int_0^L n_\mathrm{Xe}(\ell) \, d\ell
$$

where $n_\mathrm{Xe}(\ell)$ is the local xenon ion number density at arc-length position $\ell$ along the chord and $L$ is the total chord length.

This quantity is inferred from line-integrated emission diagnostics sensitive to xenon spectral lines — including soft X-ray arrays and visible-range spectrometers — combined with knowledge of the chord geometry. The [volume_averaged_xenon_density](name:volume_averaged_xenon_density) provides the spatial mean over the full plasma volume, and [xenon_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:xenon_density_at_magnetic_axis) captures the on-axis value. The analogous chord-averaged quantity for argon is documented as [line_averaged_argon_density](name:line_averaged_argon_density).

In trace impurity transport experiments, xenon concentrations yield $\bar{n}_\mathrm{Xe} \sim 10^{14}$–$10^{16}$ m$^{-3}$; during disruption-mitigation massive gas injection or shattered-pellet scenarios, values can reach $10^{17}$–$10^{19}$ m$^{-3}$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when xenon ions are present along the measurement chord.

NAMES.name: fast_ion_atomic_number
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Nuclear proton count of the fast ion species detected in charge exchange spectroscopy, uniquely identifying the element independently of its ionization state.
NAMES.long:
The fast ion atomic number $Z_n$ is the number of protons in the nucleus of the energetic (non-thermal) ion species observed via Fast Ion Charge eXchange (FICX) spectroscopy. As an intrinsic nuclear property, $Z_n$ is invariant with respect to ionization state and unambiguously identifies the element: $Z_n = 1$ for hydrogen isotopes (deuterium, tritium), $Z_n = 2$ for helium (alpha particles), $Z_n = 6$ for carbon, and $Z_n = 74$ for tungsten.

This quantity is the fast-ion-population counterpart of [ion_atomic_number](name:ion_atomic_number), which gives the same nuclear property for a general ion species. It is physically distinct from [fast_ion_charge](name:fast_ion_atomic_number), which specifies the ionic charge state $Z_\text{ion}$ — the net charge arising from electron removal — and which can vary for the same element at different ionization conditions. Together with [fast_ion_mass](name:ion_atomic_mass), the atomic number fully characterizes the fast ion species entering the spectral interpretation of FICX emission.

In charge exchange diagnostics, the fast ion species is identified prior to line inversion; $Z_n$ is an integer-valued input parameter rather than a derived measurement, taking values from 1 (hydrogenic fast ions in D-T plasmas) to the atomic number of the heaviest injected impurity species.

NAMES.name: line_averaged_argon_density
NAMES.subject: argon
NAMES.short: Line-averaged number density of argon ions along a chord through the plasma, obtained by dividing the path integral of the local argon ion density by the chord length.
NAMES.long:
