where $v_R$ is the radial velocity in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $\mathbf{v}_\mathrm{cm}$ is the pellet center-of-mass velocity with components in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, and $\hat{R}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing $R$. Together with [toroidal_velocity_of_pellet](name:toroidal_velocity_of_pellet) and [vertical_velocity_of_pellet](name:vertical_velocity_of_pellet), it specifies the pellet velocity components in the same right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

In practice, $v_R$ is computed from the time derivative of the pellet center-of-mass position, or from a specified launch speed and injection direction, followed by projection onto $\hat{R}$. For shattered-pellet applications, the same definition applies when the tracked center of mass represents the pellet material after fragmentation.

Typical pellet injection speeds in magnetic-confinement devices are about 100-1000 m s^-1. The radial component may be near 0 m s^-1 for nearly toroidal or vertical launch and may reach magnitudes of 100-1000 m s^-1 for predominantly radial launch; signed values depend on whether the motion is inward or outward in major radius.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the pellet center of mass moves in the $+\hat{R}$ direction, toward increasing major radius $R$ and away from the machine symmetry axis.

NAMES.name: silane_source_rate
NAMES.subject: silane
NAMES.short: Instantaneous injection rate of silane (SiH4) gas into the plasma vessel, expressed in equivalent electrons per second.
NAMES.long:
Silane ($\mathrm{SiH_4}$, silicon tetrahydride) is a silicon-bearing compound injected as a controlled impurity source in plasma experiments. The source rate quantifies the instantaneous rate of silane introduction expressed as an equivalent-electron flux, where each $\mathrm{SiH_4}$ molecule contributes the combined atomic numbers of its constituent atoms.

Each silane molecule carries $Z_\mathrm{Si} + 4\,Z_\mathrm{H} = 14 + 4 = 18$ equivalent electrons. The equivalent-electron rate $\dot{N}_\mathrm{eq}$ relates to the molecular injection flux $\dot{N}_{\mathrm{SiH_4}}$ by:

$$
\dot{N}_\mathrm{eq} = 18 \, \dot{N}_{\mathrm{SiH_4}}
$$

where $Z_\mathrm{Si} = 14$ is the atomic number of silicon, $Z_\mathrm{H} = 1$ is the atomic number of hydrogen, and $\dot{N}_{\mathrm{SiH_4}}$ is the molecular injection rate in molecules per second.

The instantaneous rate is inferred from calibrated gas-valve systems monitoring flow at the injection manifold. Integrating this rate over the plasma discharge from breakdown gives the [accumulated silane count](name:accumulated_silane_count), which tracks the total equivalent-electron inventory of silane introduced during a discharge. Analogous rate quantities for other injected species include [xenon_source_rate](name:xenon_source_rate) and [nitrogen_source_rate](name:nitrogen_source_rate).
NAMES.sign: Positive when silane gas is being injected into the plasma vessel.

NAMES.name: total_power_of_plant_system
NAMES.short: Aggregate electrical power consumed by all plant systems during operation. It represents the total auxiliary electrical load of the plant, summed over individual plant-system consumption terms.
NAMES.long:
Total plant-system power is the aggregate electrical load required to operate all auxiliary plant systems. It includes electrical consumption by systems such as pumps, cryogenics, heating and current-drive auxiliaries, tritium processing, cooling, control, and other balance-of-plant services when those systems are drawing power.

The total is defined as the sum of the consumed electrical power of each plant system:

$$
P_{\mathrm{plant,total}} = \sum_i P_{\mathrm{plant},i}
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{plant,total}}$ is the total plant-system electrical consumption in W, $P_{\mathrm{plant},i}$ is the electrical power consumed by plant system $i$ in W, and the sum extends over all plant systems included in the plant operating boundary. Each term is treated as a positive electrical load; this quantity is not a signed net export or generation term.

In practice, the quantity is computed from electrical metering, plant control signals, or design-point power budgets for the contributing systems. Time averaging should be chosen consistently with the plant operating state being represented, because pulsed operation, recirculating power, standby loads, and transient actuator demands can change the aggregate load substantially.

Typical values range from 1-100 MW for large experimental facilities and from 100-1000 MW for power-plant studies, depending strongly on heating and current-drive demand, cryogenic load, coolant pumping power, and balance-of-plant design.

NAMES.name: total_thermal_power_at_inlet
NAMES.short: Gross thermal power delivered to the heat-input side of a power conversion cycle in a fusion power plant. It is the total recoverable heat entering the cycle before thermal-to-electric conversion, as opposed to the rejected heat or the net electrical output.
NAMES.long:
Total thermal power at the inlet is the gross heat rate carried into the power conversion cycle by the working and coolant fluids, before any thermal-to-electric conversion. It is the heat-input reference against which rejected heat and thermal conversion efficiency are balanced, and is the counterpart of the [total thermal power at the outlet](name:total_thermal_power_at_outlet), which carries the rejected heat to the cold sink.

The inlet thermal power is the sum, over all coolant and working-fluid streams feeding the cycle, of mass flow rate multiplied by the enthalpy rise relative to the cycle's cold-return state:

$$
P_\mathrm{th,in} = \sum_i \dot{m}_i \left( h_{i,\mathrm{in}} - h_{i,\mathrm{ref}} \right)
$$

where $\dot{m}_i$ is the mass flow rate of stream $i$ in kg/s, $h_{i,\mathrm{in}}$ is its specific enthalpy at the cycle inlet in J/kg, and $h_{i,\mathrm{ref}}$ is the specific enthalpy of the corresponding cold return state in J/kg. The thermal conversion efficiency follows inline as $\eta_\mathrm{th} = (P_\mathrm{th,in} - P_\mathrm{th,out})/P_\mathrm{th,in}$, where $P_\mathrm{th,out}$ is the heat rejected from the cycle.

In practice this quantity is obtained from a steady-state plant heat balance or calorimetrically from measured coolant mass flow rates and enthalpy changes across the heat exchangers that feed the conversion cycle. The per-stream contributions correspond to the [thermal power of plant component ports](name:thermal_power_of_plant_component_port) summed over the inlet ports of the conversion cycle.

For reactor-scale plants the inlet thermal power is of the order of one to several gigawatts, with the precise value set by the heat sources coupled to the cycle and the plant design.
NAMES.sign: Positive when net heat flows into the power conversion cycle.

NAMES.name: tritium_prefill_count
NAMES.subject: tritium
NAMES.short: Accumulated number of tritium atoms injected as gas during the plasma prefill phase, expressed in equivalent electrons.
NAMES.long:
The tritium prefill count records the total number of tritium atoms ($^3_1\text{H}$, charge number $Z = 1$) delivered to the vessel as neutral gas during the prefill phase — the period from the start of gas injection up to plasma breakdown. Because tritium is a hydrogen isotope with $Z = 1$, the equivalent-electron count equals the raw atom count directly.

The prefill phase establishes the initial neutral gas background required for reproducible plasma initiation; the tritium component is particularly relevant in deuterium-tritium operations, where it contributes to the initial fuel mix and breakdown conditions. The count is accumulated from calibrated gas injection valve signals integrated over the duration of the prefill phase. For multi-species prefill scenarios, the total electron-equivalent inventory is $\sum_s Z_s N_s$, where $Z_s$ is the charge number and $N_s$ the atom count for species $s$.

This quantity complements [deuterium_prefill_count](name:deuterium_prefill_count), [neon_prefill_count](name:neon_prefill_count), and [krypton_prefill_count](name:krypton_prefill_count), which together with this name characterize the full multi-species neutral gas inventory available at breakdown; the aggregate is captured by [prefill_count](name:accumulated_lithium_prefill_count_due_to_gas_injection).
NAMES.sign: Positive when tritium atoms have been injected into the vessel during the prefill phase.

NAMES.name: vertical_velocity_of_pellet
NAMES.short: Z component of the shattered pellet center-of-mass velocity in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The vertical velocity of a pellet is the $Z$ component $v_Z$ of the center-of-mass velocity of a shattered pellet or its fragment cloud. It describes motion parallel to the vertical direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. Together with [radial velocity of the pellet](name:radial_velocity_of_pellet) and [toroidal velocity of the pellet](name:toroidal_velocity_of_pellet), it forms the cylindrical component representation of the pellet translational velocity.

The pellet center-of-mass velocity decomposes in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame as:

$$
\mathbf{v}_\mathrm{pellet} = v_R \hat{R} + v_\phi \hat{\phi} + v_Z \hat{Z}
$$

where $v_R$, $v_\phi$, and $v_Z$ are the radial, toroidal, and vertical velocity components, all in m.s^-1, and $\hat{R}$, $\hat{\phi}$, and $\hat{Z}$ are the corresponding unit vectors.

In practice, $v_Z$ is obtained from the time derivative of the pellet or fragment-cloud center-of-mass position, or from a reconstructed trajectory and launch geometry. For a fragment cloud, the center-of-mass velocity represents the mass-weighted translational motion of the cloud rather than the motion of any individual fragment.

Typical values are configuration- and trajectory-dependent and are reported in m.s^-1. For a given pellet speed $|\mathbf{v}_\mathrm{pellet}|$, the component satisfies $-|\mathbf{v}_\mathrm{pellet}| \le v_Z \le |\mathbf{v}_\mathrm{pellet}|$; it may be near zero for nearly horizontal trajectories or comparable to the total speed for strongly inclined trajectories.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the pellet center of mass moves in the direction of increasing $Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: thermal_power_of_divertor
NAMES.short: Total heat-exhaust power deposited on the plasma-facing surfaces of the divertor system. It is the surface integral of the local thermal heat flux over divertor targets and included divertor components, excluding main-wall loads and distinct electrical-current power.
NAMES.long:
Thermal power of the divertor is the total rate at which plasma exhaust energy is deposited as heat on the divertor system. The relevant integration surface is the plasma-facing boundary of the divertor system, including divertor targets and any other divertor components included in the thermal-load definition, but excluding main-wall surfaces. This quantity represents the thermal heat-exhaust load; it is distinct from divertor power associated specifically with electric currents.

For a specified divertor surface set, the total thermal power is the surface integral of the deposited thermal heat-flux density:

$$
P_{\mathrm{th,div}} = \int_{S_{\mathrm{div}}} q_{\mathrm{th}}(\mathbf{x}) \, dA
$$

where $S_{\mathrm{div}}$ is the selected plasma-facing divertor surface, $q_{\mathrm{th}}$ is the local thermal heat-flux density deposited into that surface in W m$^{-2}$, $dA$ is the surface element in m$^2$, and $P_{\mathrm{th,div}}$ is in W. If the divertor is treated as a set of components or targets, the same quantity is the sum of this integral over those components.

In practice it is inferred by integrating mapped divertor heat-flux measurements from infrared thermography, embedded calorimetry, thermocouples, probes, or radiation and neutral-exhaust analysis, often constrained by global power balance. Modeling estimates compute the same surface-integrated thermal deposition from parallel transport, cross-field spreading, volumetric radiation, charge-exchange neutrals, and plasma-surface interaction physics.

Typical values are strongly device and scenario dependent: small or medium experiments may deposit about $10^5$-$10^7$ W on the divertor, large tokamak scenarios about $10^7$-$10^8$ W, and reactor or power-plant designs can require exhaust handling at about $10^8$-$10^9$ W. The distribution over the wetted area is often as important as the total, because material limits are governed by local heat flux as well as integrated power.
NAMES.sign: Positive when thermal energy is deposited into the divertor system from the plasma.

NAMES.name: poloidal_angle_at_plasma_boundary_gap_reference_point
NAMES.short: Angle in the poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame that specifies the direction used for a plasma boundary gap distance from its reference point. It is measured clockwise from the outward radial (+R) direction.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal angle at a plasma boundary gap reference point is the orientation of the line along which the associated [plasma boundary gap distance] is evaluated. The angle lies in the poloidal $(R,Z)$ plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height; $\alpha_\mathrm{gap}=0$ points in the outward radial $+\hat{R}$ direction.

The reported angle $\alpha_\mathrm{gap}$, in radians, defines the unit direction vector for the gap measurement as

$$
\hat{\mathbf{g}} = \cos(\alpha_\mathrm{gap})\,\hat{R} - \sin(\alpha_\mathrm{gap})\,\hat{Z}
$$

where $\hat{\mathbf{g}}$ is the unit vector along the specified gap direction, and $\hat{R}$ and $\hat{Z}$ are the local radial and vertical basis vectors of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

In practice this angle is chosen from the position-control geometry or computed from the direction vector between the gap reference point and the intended boundary-intersection direction in the poloidal cross-section. It specifies only the direction; the companion gap quantity gives the distance along that direction from the reference point.

Typical values may be represented over $-\pi$ to $\pi$ rad or equivalently over $0$ to $2\pi$ rad, with angles differing by $2\pi$ rad describing the same direction. Common reference directions include $0$ rad for outward radial, $\pi/2$ rad for downward, $\pi$ rad for inward radial, and $3\pi/2$ rad or $-\pi/2$ rad for upward.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the gap direction is rotated clockwise from $+\hat{R}$ toward $-\hat{Z}$ in the poloidal $(R,Z)$ plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: argon_density_at_limiter
NAMES.subject: argon
NAMES.short: Argon ion number density immediately adjacent to a limiter material surface, evaluated in the boundary plasma at the plasma-limiter contact. It represents the local concentration of ionized argon impurity at the plasma-wall interface.
NAMES.long:
Argon density at the limiter is the number density of ionized argon in the boundary plasma immediately adjacent to a material limiter surface. The evaluation point is the plasma-facing sheath-edge region at the plasma-limiter contact, not inside the solid limiter and not a core, pedestal, or flux-surface-averaged value.

For an argon impurity population resolved by charge state, the local ion density is

$$
n_{\mathrm{Ar,lim}} = \lim_{\Delta V \to 0} \frac{1}{\Delta V}\sum_{q=1}^{18} \Delta N_{\mathrm{Ar}^{q+}}
$$

where $q$ is the argon charge state, $\Delta N_{\mathrm{Ar}^{q+}}$ is the number of argon ions in charge state $q$ within a small plasma sampling volume adjacent to the limiter, and $\Delta V$ is that volume in m$^3$, giving $n_{\mathrm{Ar,lim}}$ in m$^{-3}$. Neutral argon atoms are not included in this ion density.

In practice this quantity is obtained from boundary-plasma and impurity-transport modeling, or inferred from argon line emission using collisional-radiative modeling together with local electron density and temperature. It is governed by parallel transport to the limiter, ionization and recombination balance, recycling and impurity source rates, and radiative cooling in the scrape-off-layer plasma near the limiter.

Typical values for trace argon seeding near limiter contact are about $10^{14}$-$10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$. Strong local impurity sources or highly radiating edge conditions can produce values approaching $10^{19}$ m$^{-3}$, while unseeded plasmas may be below spectroscopic detectability.

NAMES.name: boron_density_at_limiter
NAMES.subject: boron
NAMES.short: Charge-state-summed boron ion number density immediately adjacent to a plasma-facing limiter surface.
NAMES.long:
Boron density at the limiter is the local number density of boron ions in the plasma volume immediately adjacent to a plasma-facing limiter, where open scrape-off-layer field lines intersect a material boundary. Unless a single charge state is specified, it is the charge-state-summed boron ion population and is the boron-resolved component of [density_at_limiter](name:density_at_limiter).

For a representative small plasma volume next to the limiter, the localized density $n_{B,\mathrm{lim}}$ is the boron ion count per unit volume:

$$
n_{B,\mathrm{lim}} = \frac{N_B}{V}
$$

where $N_B$ is the number of boron ions in the sampled volume and $V$ is that volume in m$^3$, giving $n_{B,\mathrm{lim}}$ in m$^{-3}$. Because fully stripped boron carries charge $Z_B = 5$, its contribution to the effective charge $Z_\mathrm{eff} = \sum_k n_k Z_k^2 / n_e$ is large relative to its number fraction, so even sub-percent boron concentrations affect plasma resistivity and the radiated power budget.

This quantity is inferred from edge impurity emission spectroscopy combined with collisional-radiative or atomic-rate modeling, from active charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, or from scrape-off-layer transport calculations constrained by limiter source estimates. The limiter value refers to the plasma-side impurity density adjacent to the material surface, not to boron bound within the solid limiter material.

Typical limiter-adjacent boron densities depend strongly on wall conditioning, limiter material history, plasma density, erosion source strength, and ionization balance. Trace impurity values in edge modeling are often roughly $10^{14}$-$10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$, while localized transient sources, boron injection, or freshly boronized surfaces can produce values outside this range.

NAMES.name: deuterium_density_at_limiter
NAMES.subject: deuterium
NAMES.short: Number density of deuterium ions in the plasma-side boundary layer immediately adjacent to a plasma-facing limiter surface, evaluated near the plasma-sheath interface.
NAMES.long:
Deuterium density at a limiter is the local number density of deuterium ions, usually $D^+$, on the plasma side of the sheath adjacent to a limiter surface. It is the species-resolved deuterium contribution to the edge ion population, not necessarily the total ion density when several ion species are present.

For sheath-limited contact, a common boundary estimate relates the partial deuterium ion flux to the sheath-edge density through the Bohm relation:

$$
\Gamma_D \simeq n_D c_s
$$

where $n_D$ is this density in $\mathrm{m^{-3}}$, $\Gamma_D$ is the species-resolved deuterium particle flux to the limiter in $\mathrm{m^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$, and $c_s$ is the ion-acoustic speed in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. For singly ionized deuterium, $c_s$ is commonly estimated from local electron and ion temperatures, for example $c_s \approx [e(T_e+\gamma_i T_i)/m_D]^{1/2}$ when $T_e$ and $T_i$ are in eV; $e$ is the elementary charge, $m_D$ is the deuterium ion mass, and $\gamma_i$ is an ion heat-capacity factor.

In practice this quantity is inferred from edge diagnostics near the limiter, such as probe measurements combined with sheath models, spectroscopic analysis with collisional-radiative modeling, or edge plasma simulations constrained by density and recycling measurements. Its value is sensitive to parallel transport along open field lines, local ionization and recombination, neutral recycling from the limiter surface, and the degree to which deuterium is diluted by other ion species.

Typical limiter-adjacent deuterium ion densities are about $10^{18}-10^{19}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$ in many tokamak scrape-off-layer conditions, with broader operating ranges of roughly $10^{17}-10^{20}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$ depending on plasma current, fueling, recycling, and proximity to high-density or detached boundary regimes.

NAMES.name: deuterium_tritium_density_at_limiter
NAMES.subject: deuterium_tritium
NAMES.short: Number density of the fictitious deuterium-tritium fuel pseudo-species in the plasma immediately adjacent to a limiter surface. The pseudo-species represents an equimolar DT mixture as one ion constituent with effective mass about 2.5 atomic mass units.
NAMES.long:
Deuterium-tritium density at a limiter is the local number density of the fictitious DT fuel pseudo-species on the plasma side of a plasma-facing limiter surface. The pseudo-species represents an equimolar mixture of deuterium and tritium as one ion constituent with effective mass about 2.5 atomic mass units, distinct from separately tracked deuterium or tritium densities.

The local limiter value is defined by evaluating the DT pseudo-species density at the plasma-facing limiter boundary:

$$
n_{\mathrm{DT,lim}} = \left. n_{\mathrm{DT}} \right|_{\text{plasma side of limiter}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{DT}}$ is the local pseudo-species number density and the vertical bar denotes evaluation immediately outside the limiter material, normally near the sheath entrance. Both quantities have unit m^-3. When comparing with a resolved-isotope description, the equimolar pseudo-species corresponds to the total fuel-ion density $n_D+n_T$ with $n_D \simeq n_T$.

This quantity is the DT-fuel component of [density_at_limiter](name:density_at_limiter). It may be inferred from edge density measurements combined with species-fraction information, or computed from edge, scrape-off-layer, and plasma-wall interaction models at the limiter contact region. In limiter-bounded plasmas it is closely related to [deuterium_tritium_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:deuterium_tritium_density_at_plasma_boundary), while [deuterium_tritium_density_at_divertor_target](name:deuterium_tritium_density_at_divertor_target) describes the analogous pseudo-species density at a divertor target.

Representative near-limiter DT pseudo-species densities in tokamak edge plasmas are often about 10^17-10^19 m^-3, varying strongly with fueling, recycling, edge temperature, confinement regime, and whether the plasma boundary is limiter- or divertor-defined.

NAMES.name: effective_charge_at_limiter
NAMES.short: Effective charge number of the ion mixture in the boundary plasma at the limiter, quantifying the degree of impurity contamination at this plasma-facing surface.
NAMES.long:
The effective charge $Z_\text{eff}$ at the limiter is the charge-squared-weighted average ion charge of the plasma species in the scrape-off layer immediately adjacent to the limiter surface. It captures the aggregate effect of all impurity species on plasma resistivity and radiation behavior without resolving individual impurity charge states.

The quantity is defined by

$$
Z_\text{eff} = \frac{\sum_i n_i Z_i^2}{n_e}
$$

where $n_i$ is the number density of ion species $i$ with integer charge number $Z_i$, and $n_e = \sum_i n_i Z_i$ is the electron density enforced by quasi-neutrality. For a pure hydrogen-isotope plasma, $Z_\text{eff} = 1$; impurity ions with $Z_i > 1$ raise the value above unity.

At the limiter, $Z_\text{eff}$ is typically elevated compared to the core because sputtered wall material and recycled impurities concentrate near the plasma-facing surface. Typical values range from 1.5 to 4 in limiter-configuration plasmas, depending on the wall material (beryllium, carbon, or tungsten) and fueling conditions. This local value complements [effective_charge_at_plasma_boundary](name:effective_charge_at_plasma_boundary) and [effective_charge_at_divertor_target](name:effective_charge_at_divertor_target), which quantify $Z_\text{eff}$ at other boundary reference locations. It is inferred from the ratio of total Bremsstrahlung emissivity to the square of the electron density integrated along lines of sight through the boundary plasma, or from spectroscopic resolution of individual impurity charge states.
NAMES.sign: Positive for any plasma consisting of positively charged ions and electrons satisfying quasi-neutral balance.

NAMES.name: electron_particle_flux_at_wall
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Incident electron particle flux density at a plasma-facing wall, equal to the number of electrons arriving from the plasma side per unit wall area per unit time.
NAMES.long:
Electron particle flux at a wall is the one-way incident number flux density of electrons crossing from the plasma into a material surface. It counts arriving electrons per unit wall area and per unit time; electrons emitted, reflected, or backscattered from the surface are not included.

For a wall point $\mathbf r_w$, the incident flux is the velocity-space moment over particles moving into the wall:

$$
\Gamma_e^\mathrm{inc}(\mathbf r_w) = \int_{\mathbf v \cdot \hat{\mathbf n}_w > 0} (\mathbf v \cdot \hat{\mathbf n}_w)\, f_e(\mathbf r_w,\mathbf v)\, d^3v
$$

where $\hat{\mathbf n}_w$ is the dimensionless unit normal pointing from the plasma into the wall material, $\mathbf v$ is electron velocity in m.s^-1, and $f_e$ is the electron velocity distribution with units m^-3 (m.s^-1)^-3. The result has units m^-2.s^-1 and is a one-way arrival flux, not the signed normal component of the electron fluid particle flux.

For a finite wall region $A$, the associated total incident electron arrival rate is $\dot N_e^\mathrm{inc}(A)=\int_A \Gamma_e^\mathrm{inc}(\mathbf r_w)\,dA$, where $dA$ is a surface element in m^2 and $\dot N_e^\mathrm{inc}$ has units s^-1; this is the area-integrated quantity related to electron_source_rate_at_wall. In practice the flux is estimated from sheath or edge-plasma modeling, kinetic simulations, probe current measurements, retarding-field or surface diagnostics, and particle-balance analysis, with corrections for local sheath potential, magnetic incidence angle, and emitted-electron contributions when those affect the inferred incident population.

Typical time-averaged values range from 10^20-10^23 m^-2.s^-1 on main-chamber plasma-facing surfaces and 10^22-10^24 m^-2.s^-1 in attached divertor strike-point regions. Detached, shadowed, or remote wall areas can be orders of magnitude lower, while transient events can briefly exceed steady-state levels.

NAMES.name: energy_flux_at_wall_due_to_eddy_current
NAMES.short: Energy flux density crossing the plasma-facing wall surface due to Joule heating by eddy currents induced in conducting structures. It represents the portion of internally deposited Ohmic power that is transported back to the surface and emitted toward the plasma.
NAMES.long:
Energy flux at the wall due to eddy current is the thermal power per unit wall area that reaches the plasma-facing surface after eddy-current Joule heating inside conducting wall material. Time-varying magnetic fields induce currents in the wall; their Ohmic dissipation deposits power within the solid, while this quantity describes only the emitted surface flux directed toward the plasma.

The volumetric source that feeds this surface emission is the local Ohmic dissipation from the induced current density:

$$
p_\mathrm{eddy} = \frac{|\mathbf{J}_\mathrm{eddy}|^2}{\sigma_w}
$$

where $p_\mathrm{eddy}$ is the volumetric power density in W m$^{-3}$, $\mathbf{J}_\mathrm{eddy}$ is the eddy-current density in A m$^{-2}$, and $\sigma_w$ is the wall electrical conductivity in S m$^{-1}$. The corresponding surface energy flux density depends on the spatial distribution of this source, the wall geometry, thermal conductivity, heat capacity, and the timescale over which heat diffuses to the plasma-facing surface.

In practice, the quantity is computed from electromagnetic and thermal analyzes of conducting wall structures during magnetic transients such as disruptions, current quenches, vertical displacement events, or rapid control-coil field changes. It may be inferred by combining reconstructed or modeled eddy-current distributions with a heat-transfer calculation that maps internal Ohmic deposition to heat flux at the surface.

Typical values are near zero during steady conditions when magnetic fields vary slowly. During fast transients, localized emitted fluxes can be 10^3-10^6 W m$^{-2}$, with higher short-duration peaks possible near highly conducting structures or geometric current-concentration regions.

This quantity is part of the wall energy balance together with radiative loading, particle energy fluxes, and total Ohmic dissipation in wall structures. It is distinct from the total [power_at_wall_due_to_ohmic_dissipation](name:power_at_wall_due_to_ohmic_dissipation), because only the portion transported to and emitted from the plasma-facing surface contributes to this surface flux density.
NAMES.sign: Positive when thermal energy is emitted from the wall surface toward the plasma.

NAMES.name: hydrogen_density_at_limiter
NAMES.subject: hydrogen
NAMES.short: Number density of hydrogen (protium) ions in the boundary plasma adjacent to a limiter surface. It characterizes the local ion population interacting with the plasma-facing limiter material.
NAMES.long:
Hydrogen density at a limiter is the local number density of hydrogen ions in the boundary plasma next to a limiter surface. It describes the plasma population available for particle flux, recycling, charge exchange, and plasma-material interaction at the limiter location, without implying a universal relation to upstream or pedestal densities.

As a number density, it is defined by the local particle content per unit volume:

$$
n_{\mathrm{H}^+} = \frac{dN_{\mathrm{H}^+}}{dV}
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{H}^+}$ is the number of hydrogen ions in a small plasma volume $V$ near the limiter. The value is non-negative and is expressed in $m^{-3}$.

In practice this quantity is inferred from boundary-plasma diagnostics and modeling, such as Langmuir probes, spectroscopic measurements combined with collisional-radiative interpretation, or edge plasma simulations constrained by measurements. Its value depends on local ionization, recycling from the limiter, cross-field transport, magnetic connection length, plasma fueling, and the limiter geometry.

Typical values in tokamak boundary plasmas are about $10^{17}$-$10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$, with lower values in tenuous scrape-off-layer conditions and higher values near dense, strongly recycling limiter plasmas.

NAMES.name: ion_kinetic_energy_flux_at_wall
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Incident kinetic energy flux per unit wall area carried by plasma ions, summed over ion species and charge states, as they strike the plasma-facing wall.
NAMES.long:
Ion kinetic energy flux at the wall is the incident component of kinetic power carried by ions crossing a plasma-facing material surface per unit area. It includes the translational kinetic energy of ions at impact, summed over all ion species and charge states, and is the ionic contribution to the total [kinetic_energy_flux_at_wall](name:kinetic_energy_flux_at_wall). It excludes ion potential energy, radiation, and energy transported by particles emitted or reflected from the wall.

For a kinetic ion distribution evaluated at a wall point, the local incident flux can be written as:

$$
Q_{i,\mathrm{kin}}^{\mathrm{inc}}(\mathbf{x}_w) = \sum_{s,z} \int_{\mathbf{v}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}}_w < 0} \frac{1}{2} m_s |\mathbf{v}|^2 |\mathbf{v}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}}_w| f_{s,z}(\mathbf{x}_w,\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $Q_{i,\mathrm{kin}}^{\mathrm{inc}}$ is in W m^-2, $\mathbf{x}_w$ is the wall-surface position in meters, $s$ labels ion species, $z$ labels charge state, $m_s$ is the ion mass in kg, $\mathbf{v}$ is ion velocity in m s^-1, $\hat{\mathbf{n}}_w$ is the unit normal directed from the wall material into the plasma, and $f_{s,z}$ is the ion distribution function in m^-3 (m s^-1)^-3. The integration domain selects ions moving toward the wall.

In practice this quantity is estimated from ion particle fluxes and impact energies using boundary plasma diagnostics, sheath or edge-plasma modeling, kinetic simulations, or wall heat-flux measurements combined with a decomposition of the total heat load. Separating the ion kinetic contribution from electron heat flux, neutral heat flux, potential-energy terms, radiation, and emitted-particle losses generally requires model assumptions.

Typical magnitudes are strongly dependent on wall location and plasma regime. Main-chamber surfaces may receive values from about 10^2-10^5 W m^-2, while divertor or limiter strike regions in attached or partially detached operation can reach about 10^5-10^7 W m^-2; short transient events can be substantially larger.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the wall-normal ion kinetic energy flux is directed from the plasma into the wall material.

NAMES.name: ion_kinetic_energy_flux_at_wall_due_to_surface_emission
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Kinetic energy flux density carried by ions leaving the plasma-facing wall through surface emission processes such as physical sputtering and ion backscattering.
NAMES.long:
The kinetic energy flux density at the plasma-facing wall surface carried by ions emitted outward via surface emission — the family of plasma–wall interaction processes, including physical sputtering, chemical sputtering, and ion backscattering, that return ionic species from the wall to the plasma. The `kinetic` qualifier restricts this to translational kinetic energy of the emitted ion velocity distribution, excluding potential energy stored in electronic excitation or residual ionization charge, which is captured separately by [energy_flux_at_wall_due_to_recombination](name:energy_flux_at_wall_due_to_recombination).

The emitted kinetic energy flux $\Phi_{\mathrm{kin,emit}}$ sums over all emitted ion species $s$:

$$
\Phi_{\mathrm{kin,emit}} = \sum_s \int_{v_n > 0} \tfrac{1}{2} m_s v^2 \, v_n \, f_{s,\mathrm{emit}}(\mathbf{v}) \, d^3v
$$

where $m_s$ is the ion mass of species $s$, $v = |\mathbf{v}|$ is the ion speed, $v_n > 0$ is the outward surface-normal velocity component at the wall, and $f_{s,\mathrm{emit}}(\mathbf{v})$ is the velocity distribution function of emitted ions.

In plasma–surface interaction modeling, this flux is evaluated by convolving incident plasma conditions with energy-resolved surface emission yields and backscattering coefficients from binary-collision approximation databases. It is the mechanism-attributed form of [ion_energy_flux_at_wall](name:ion_kinetic_energy_flux_at_wall_due_to_surface_emission) and the emitted counterpart to [ion_kinetic_energy_flux_at_wall](name:ion_kinetic_energy_flux_at_wall), which captures the incident kinetic flux. Charge-state-resolved contributions are tracked by ion_state_energy_flux_at_wall, and the electron analog is [electron_energy_flux_at_wall](name:electron_energy_flux_at_wall).

NAMES.name: ion_particle_flux_at_wall
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Aggregate incident particle flux of ions, summed over all charge states, arriving at the plasma-facing wall surface.
NAMES.long:
The ion particle flux at the wall is the aggregate rate at which ions from the plasma impinge on a unit area of plasma-facing material, summed over all ion charge states. As the ion-species component of the total [particle_flux_at_wall](name:particle_flux_at_wall), it does not include contributions from neutral particles (see [neutral_particle_flux_at_wall](name:neutral_particle_flux_at_wall)) or electrons.

In fluid plasma models, the incident flux $\Gamma_i^{\rm wall}$ at a wall surface element with inward surface normal $\hat{n}$ is:

$$
\Gamma_i^{\rm wall} = \sum_z n_{i,z} \, \mathbf{u}_{i,z} \cdot \hat{n}
$$

where $n_{i,z}$ is the number density of ions in charge state $z$ and $\mathbf{u}_{i,z}$ is the corresponding bulk ion flow velocity, with the summation running over all charge states $z$. The charge-state-resolved analog is given by [ion_state_particle_flux_at_wall](name:ion_state_particle_flux_at_wall).

This flux is computed as a surface boundary output of edge plasma fluid simulations or estimated from experimental ion saturation current density measurements via the Bohm sheath criterion. Together with [ion_kinetic_energy_flux_at_wall](name:ion_kinetic_energy_flux_at_wall), it characterizes the particle and energy loading on plasma-facing components and serves as a key input to sputtering yield and fuel-retention models.

NAMES.name: ion_state_energy_flux_at_wall_due_to_recombination
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Energy flux density emitted from a plasma-facing wall by recombination of a specified ion charge state. It gives the charge-state-resolved contribution to the recombination energy released per unit wall area.
NAMES.long:
Ion-state recombination energy flux at the wall is the power per unit plasma-facing surface area emitted at the surface when ions of a specified species and charge state recombine. It represents only that initial charge-state contribution; summing over charge states for one ion species gives [ion_energy_flux_at_wall_due_to_recombination](name:ion_energy_flux_at_wall_due_to_recombination), and summing over ion species gives [energy_flux_at_wall_due_to_recombination](name:energy_flux_at_wall_due_to_recombination). This quantity refers to recombination energy release, not to the incident ion kinetic or thermal energy flux.

For ions of species $s$ arriving in charge state $z$, a local estimate is the recombining particle flux multiplied by the total ionization energy recovered during neutralization:

$$
q^{\mathrm{rec}}_{s,z} = \Gamma_{s,z} \, e \sum_{k=1}^{z} I_{s,k}
$$

where $q^{\mathrm{rec}}_{s,z}$ is the recombination energy flux density in W m$^{-2}$, $\Gamma_{s,z}$ is the flux of recombining ions of species $s$ and charge state $z$ to the wall in m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$, $I_{s,k}$ is the $k$th ionization potential of species $s$ in eV, and $e$ converts eV to joule. More detailed surface models may partition this released energy among photons, emitted neutrals, electrons, and solid-surface heating, but the charge-state-resolved energy scale is set by the sum of ionization potentials.

In practice this quantity is computed from charge-state-resolved ion fluxes to plasma-facing components together with atomic ionization energies and surface recombination or neutralization models. It may also be constrained indirectly by combining particle-flux estimates from probes, spectroscopy, or particle balance with atomic data, while keeping it separate from incident kinetic heat flux, radiation absorbed at the wall, and chemical or sputtering energy terms.

Typical charge-state-resolved values range from less than 10$^{2}$ W m$^{-2}$ on weakly wetted wall regions to 10$^{4}$-10$^{6}$ W m$^{-2}$ in recycling divertor or limiter regions. Local values can approach 10$^{6}$-10$^{7}$ W m$^{-2}$ for very large particle fluxes or high charge states, but the summed recombination contribution is usually below the total plasma heat load.
NAMES.sign: Positive when recombination energy is emitted from the wall surface into the adjacent plasma or vacuum.

NAMES.name: ion_state_particle_flux_at_wall
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Incident particle flux of ions in a specific charge state at the plasma-facing wall surface.
NAMES.long:
Ions bombarding plasma-facing surfaces arrive in a range of charge states whose individual contributions govern sputtering thresholds, energy deposition, and fuel recycling. This quantity gives the local incident particle flux from ions in a single specified charge state $z$, the charge-state-resolved building block of the total ion bombardment.

The incident flux from ions in charge state $z$ is:

$$
\Gamma_{\mathrm{ion},z} = n_{\mathrm{ion},z} \, v_{\perp,z}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{ion},z}$ is the local number density of ions in charge state $z$ (m$^{-3}$) and $v_{\perp,z}$ is their mean velocity component directed toward the wall surface (m s$^{-1}$).

Summing over all charge states recovers [ion_particle_flux_at_wall](name:ion_particle_flux_at_wall); including all particle species (neutrals, electrons) gives [particle_flux_at_wall](name:particle_flux_at_wall). The structurally analogous quantity for neutral particles resolved by quantum state is [neutral_state_particle_flux_at_wall](name:neutral_state_particle_flux_at_wall). Charge-state resolution is essential for computing state-dependent sputtering yields and surface chemistry reactions in plasma-wall interaction models.

Typical incident ion fluxes in tokamak boundary plasmas range from $10^{19}$ to $10^{22}$ m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$, with peak values near divertor strike points on plasma-facing components.

NAMES.name: iron_density_at_limiter
NAMES.subject: iron
NAMES.short: Number density of iron (Fe) impurity ions in the plasma immediately adjacent to a limiter surface, excluding neutral iron atoms.
NAMES.long:
Iron density at the limiter is the local number density of ionized iron in the plasma-side region next to a limiter surface. It represents iron impurity ions only; neutral Fe atoms are excluded from this quantity.

When charge states are resolved, the total iron ion density is the sum over all positive ionization states:

$$
n_{\mathrm{Fe}} = \sum_{q=1}^{26} n_{\mathrm{Fe}^{q+}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{Fe}}$ is the total iron ion number density in m$^{-3}$, $q$ is the ion charge state, and $n_{\mathrm{Fe}^{q+}}$ is the number density in m$^{-3}$ of iron ions with charge $+q e$. The sum starts at $q=1$, so neutral iron, $\mathrm{Fe}^0$, is not included.

In practice this quantity is obtained from local or modeled impurity-ion densities evaluated at the plasma-facing limiter boundary. If only charge-state-resolved densities are available, they are summed over ionized charge states; if a total iron ion density is available directly, it should correspond to the same ion-only definition.

Typical values are highly device-, discharge-, material-, and plasma-edge dependent, and no universal range is implied by the definition. The value is non-negative and is expressed in m$^{-3}$.

NAMES.name: krypton_density_at_limiter
NAMES.subject: krypton
NAMES.short: Local krypton ion number density evaluated at the plasma-facing limiter surface, where impurity sputtering and recycling connect edge plasma composition to the wall material.
NAMES.long:
The krypton number density at the limiter is the local volumetric count of krypton ions per unit volume at the plasma-side limiter contact point, near the sheath entrance of this plasma-facing component. It is the krypton-species-resolved component of the total [density_at_limiter](name:density_at_limiter). When individual ionization stages are resolved, this quantity equals their sum:

$$
n_\mathrm{Kr}(x_\mathrm{lim}) = \sum_{q=1}^{36} n_{\mathrm{Kr}^{q+}}(x_\mathrm{lim})
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{Kr}^{q+}}$ is the number density of krypton ions in charge state $q+$ at the limiter evaluation point $x_\mathrm{lim}$; when charge states are not individually resolved, this sum is implicit.

Krypton ($Z = 36$) is a high-atomic-number noble gas that can be seeded into the edge plasma for radiative cooling of the scrape-off layer, disruption mitigation studies, or impurity transport experiments near plasma-facing components. Its local concentration at the limiter is governed by sputtering sources, charge-exchange recycling, and cross-field impurity transport from the confined region. Spatial counterparts at other poloidal positions include [krypton_density_at_pedestal](name:krypton_density_at_pedestal), [krypton_density_at_divertor_target](name:krypton_density_at_divertor_target), and [krypton_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:krypton_density_at_magnetic_axis); the [volume_averaged_krypton_density](name:volume_averaged_krypton_density) characterizes the global impurity inventory.
NAMES.sign: Positive when krypton ions are present at the limiter location, consistent with particle number density being a non-negative definite quantity.

NAMES.name: lithium_density_at_limiter
NAMES.subject: lithium
NAMES.short: Lithium ion number density in the plasma immediately adjacent to the limiter surface, where lithium impurities originate from wall conditioning, sputtering, or deliberate injection.
NAMES.long:
Lithium ion number density at the limiter quantifies the local concentration of lithium ions in the plasma at the limiter contact region, evaluated near the sheath entrance on the plasma side rather than within the solid wall material. It is the lithium-species contribution to the total [density_at_limiter](name:density_at_limiter), isolating lithium impurities arising from sputtering, desorption, or intentional wall conditioning from contributions by other ion species present at the same location.

The number density is defined as the lithium ion count per unit volume adjacent to the limiter surface, $n_{\mathrm{Li}} = N_{\mathrm{Li}} / V$, where $N_{\mathrm{Li}}$ is the number of lithium ions within the volume element $V$.

Measurement relies on passive or active optical emission spectroscopy detecting characteristic lithium line emission from the plasma edge, or on edge transport models constrained by spectroscopic observations of the limiter vicinity. In lithium wall-conditioning experiments, elevated values at the limiter reflect recycled and re-ionized lithium returning from the plasma-facing surface. Typical edge lithium densities in conditioning regimes range from $10^{15}$ to $10^{18}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$, depending on conditioning intensity and plasma parameters.

For the same species at other spatial locations, [lithium_density_at_pedestal](name:lithium_density_at_pedestal) and [lithium_density_at_divertor_target](name:lithium_density_at_divertor_target) provide analogous localized quantities, while [line_averaged_lithium_density](name:line_averaged_lithium_density) gives the chord-integrated complement useful for global impurity inventory estimates.
NAMES.sign: Positive for any finite concentration of lithium ions at the limiter position, consistent with number density being a non-negative particle count per unit volume.

NAMES.name: neon_density_at_limiter
NAMES.subject: neon
NAMES.short: Neon ion number density in the boundary plasma immediately adjacent to a limiter surface, evaluated at the plasma-side sheath entrance. It is summed over neon ionization stages unless a charge-state-resolved quantity is specified.
NAMES.long:
Neon density at the limiter is the local number density of neon ions in the boundary plasma just outside a limiter surface, at the plasma-side sheath entrance. It is the limiter-surface analog of [neon_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:neon_density_at_plasma_boundary), restricted to the plasma-wall interaction region rather than the global plasma boundary.

For a small plasma volume adjacent to the limiter, the charge-state-summed neon ion density is the count of neon ions per unit volume:

$$
n_\mathrm{Ne} = \frac{N_\mathrm{Ne}}{V}
$$

where $N_\mathrm{Ne}=\sum_z N_{\mathrm{Ne}^{z+}}$ is the total number of neon ions over all included ionization stages and $V$ is the sampled plasma volume in m^3, giving $n_\mathrm{Ne}$ in m^-3.

In practice this quantity is inferred from limiter-viewing spectroscopy with collisional-radiative modeling, from edge impurity transport analysis constrained by local electron density and temperature, or from plasma-wall interaction simulations. It counts neon ions in the plasma, not neutral neon at the wall and not a charge-weighted quantity such as an effective charge contribution.

Typical limiter-adjacent neon ion densities are about 10^14-10^18 m^-3 in trace to moderately seeded boundary plasmas, with local values approaching 10^19 m^-3 during strong neon puffing or very dense, cool edge conditions.

NAMES.name: neutral_energy_flux_at_wall
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Incident wall-normal arrival flux density of neutral atoms and molecules in the kinetic-energy channel reaching a plasma-facing wall, summed over neutral species and internal quantum states. It counts particle arrivals per unit wall area and time, expressed in arrivals per square meter per second, and is not a heat flux in watts per square meter.
NAMES.long:
Neutral energy flux at the wall is the incident arrival flux density of neutral atoms and molecules associated with the kinetic-energy channel at a plasma-facing surface, summed over all neutral species and internal quantum states. Despite the term "energy flux" in the name, its canonical unit is particle arrivals per square meter per second, so it is a particle-rate quantity and not an energy-weighted heat flux in watts per square meter.

For a point on the wall it is defined from the inward-directed part of the neutral velocity distribution as the wall-normal arrival rate per unit area:

$$
\Gamma^{\mathrm{inc}} = \sum_{\alpha} \int_{\mathbf{v}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}}_p<0} \left(-\mathbf{v}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}}_p\right) f_{\alpha}^{0}(\mathbf{x}_w,\mathbf{v})\, d^3v
$$

where $\Gamma^{\mathrm{inc}}$ has units $\mathrm{m^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$, $\alpha$ labels neutral species and internal states, $\hat{\mathbf{n}}_p$ is the unit normal pointing from the material wall toward the plasma, $\mathbf{x}_w$ is the wall position in meters, $\mathbf{v}$ is the neutral velocity in meters per second, and $f_{\alpha}^{0}$ is the neutral distribution function with units $\mathrm{s^3\,m^{-6}}$. No factor of kinetic energy multiplies the integrand: an energy-weighted neutral heat flux would require weighting by $E_k = m_{\alpha} v^2 / 2$ and would instead carry units $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$.

This quantity is obtained from neutral transport modeling and kinetic wall tallies that accumulate inward-crossing neutral trajectories, with contributions summed over atomic, molecular, and excited populations. It is the species- and state-summed counterpart of [neutral_state_energy_flux_at_wall](name:neutral_state_energy_flux_at_wall); the analogous quantity without the kinetic-channel qualifier is [neutral_particle_flux_at_wall](name:neutral_particle_flux_at_wall), whose state-resolved form is [neutral_state_particle_flux_at_wall](name:neutral_state_particle_flux_at_wall). It should be distinguished from [energy_flux_at_wall](name:energy_flux_at_wall_due_to_eddy_current), which is an energy-weighted wall loading rather than a particle-rate flux.

Typical values are about $10^{18}-10^{21}\ \mathrm{m^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$ on main-chamber surfaces and $10^{21}-10^{24}\ \mathrm{m^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$ in strongly recycling divertor or limiter regions, depending on plasma density, recycling coefficient, fueling rate, and wall geometry.
NAMES.sign: Positive when neutral particles cross the wall surface from the plasma side toward the material wall.

NAMES.name: neutral_particle_flux_at_wall
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Incident flux of neutral particles (atoms and molecules) arriving at the plasma-facing wall per unit area per unit time, summed over all quantum states of the neutral species.
NAMES.long:
The neutral particle flux at the wall is the local rate per unit area at which neutral atoms and molecules impinge on plasma-facing material from the plasma-boundary region. It is the total neutral contribution to [particle_flux_at_wall](name:particle_flux_at_wall), summed over all quantum states of the neutral species. Neutrals reaching the wall arrive primarily through charge-exchange reactions and recombination in the scrape-off layer, gas injection, and desorption from the surface.

The incident neutral flux density is defined by integrating the wall-directed component of the neutral velocity distribution:

$$
\Gamma_n = \int_{v_\perp > 0} v_\perp \, f_n(\mathbf{v}) \, d^3v
$$

where $v_\perp$ is the velocity component directed toward the wall surface and $f_n(\mathbf{v})$ is the neutral particle velocity distribution function.

This flux is a primary driver of fuel recycling, hydrogenic implantation, and physical sputtering of plasma-facing components. The quantum-state-resolved analog [neutral_state_particle_flux_at_wall](name:neutral_state_particle_flux_at_wall) decomposes this total by individual electronic excitation state, while [neutral_energy_flux_at_wall](name:neutral_energy_flux_at_wall) gives the associated kinetic energy carried by the same neutral population. The species counterparts [ion_particle_flux_at_wall](name:ion_particle_flux_at_wall) and [electron_particle_flux_at_wall](name:electron_particle_flux_at_wall) complete the particle-species decomposition of the total wall loading.

NAMES.name: neutral_state_energy_flux_due_to_recombination
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: Incident energy-resolved flux density of neutral particles in a specified quantum state produced by recombination and directed toward a plasma-facing wall surface.
NAMES.long:
Neutral state energy flux due to recombination is the incident, energy-resolved flux density of neutral particles in a specified quantum state that are produced by recombination and cross a plasma-facing surface toward the material. It counts the neutral particle flow associated with a kinetic-energy channel and internal state, so its canonical unit is m^-2 s^-1 rather than power per unit area.

For a surface element with unit normal $\hat{\mathbf n}_w$ directed from the material toward the plasma, the incident flux in state $q$ and energy interval $\Delta E$ may be written as

$$
\Gamma_{q,\Delta E}^{\mathrm{rec,inc}} = \int_{\mathbf v\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}_w < 0,\ E(\mathbf v)\in\Delta E} \left(-\mathbf v\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}_w\right) f_q^{\mathrm{rec}}(\mathbf x_w,\mathbf v)\,d^3v
$$

where $f_q^{\mathrm{rec}}$ is the velocity distribution of recombination-produced neutrals in quantum state $q$ at wall position $\mathbf x_w$, $E(\mathbf v)$ is their kinetic energy, and $-\mathbf v\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}_w$ is the positive speed component into the wall. Integrating over energy intervals and summing over neutral states gives the corresponding total recombination-produced incident neutral flux.

In practice this quantity is obtained from edge-plasma and plasma-wall interaction modeling, neutral transport calculations, or diagnostics combined with a collisional-radiative model that resolves recombination channels and neutral-state populations. It is non-negative because only particles crossing toward the surface are included; neutrals moving away from the surface are part of the outgoing flux, not the incident flux.

Typical values depend strongly on plasma density, electron temperature near the surface, recycling, and detached-divertor conditions. Representative incident state-resolved recombination fluxes can range from 10^16-10^22 m^-2 s^-1, with the largest values usually occurring in cold, dense recombining boundary plasmas.

NAMES.name: neutral_state_particle_flux_at_wall
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: Incident particle flux at the plasma-facing wall for neutral particles in a specified quantum state, such as a particular electronic energy level or molecular internal state.
NAMES.long:
The particle flux at the wall for a neutral species in a given quantum state quantifies the local arrival rate of neutrals — carrying a specific electronic excitation level, charge state, or internal molecular state — per unit area of plasma-facing material. It provides finer resolution than [neutral_particle_flux_at_wall](name:neutral_particle_flux_at_wall), which sums over all neutral states, enabling plasma-wall interaction models to track contributions from individual neutral populations such as ground-state atoms, excited neutrals, or molecular dissociation products.

The incident flux in quantum state $s$ is defined as:

$$
\Gamma_{\rm wall}^{(s)} = \int_{v_n > 0} v_n \, f_s(\mathbf{v}) \, d^3v
$$

where $f_s(\mathbf{v})$ is the velocity distribution function of neutrals in state $s$ and $v_n$ is the component of particle velocity normal to the wall surface, with the integral restricted to particles directed toward the wall.

This quantity is evaluated in plasma-edge neutral-transport codes that resolve neutral populations by quantum state using collisional-radiative models describing excitation, ionization, and recombination transitions. Summing over all neutral quantum states yields [neutral_particle_flux_at_wall](name:neutral_particle_flux_at_wall), while including all particle species gives the total incident loading captured in [particle_flux_at_wall](name:particle_flux_at_wall). The corresponding kinetic energy flux for the same quantum state is given by [neutral_state_energy_flux_at_wall](name:neutral_state_energy_flux_at_wall).

NAMES.name: nitrogen_density_at_limiter
NAMES.subject: nitrogen
NAMES.short: Number density of ionized nitrogen in the boundary plasma immediately adjacent to a limiter. It represents the local nitrogen impurity ion population, normally summed over ion charge states.
NAMES.long:
Ionized nitrogen density at a limiter is the local number of nitrogen impurity ions per unit volume in the boundary plasma immediately adjacent to a limiter surface. Unless a charge-state-specific quantity is named, it denotes the sum over all ionized nitrogen charge states $N^{q+}$ with $q=1,\ldots,7$ and excludes neutral nitrogen atoms or molecules.

The charge-state-summed density is the zeroth velocity-space moment of the nitrogen ion distribution functions:

$$
n_N^{\mathrm{ion}} = \sum_{q=1}^{7} n_{N^{q+}} = \sum_{q=1}^{7} \int f_{N^{q+}}(\mathbf{v}) \, d^3v
$$

where $n_N^{\mathrm{ion}}$ is the total ionized nitrogen number density in m^-3, $n_{N^{q+}}$ is the number density of charge state $q$ in m^-3, $f_{N^{q+}}(\mathbf{v})$ is the velocity-space distribution function with units s^3 m^-6, and $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element with units m^3 s^-3.

In experiments, this quantity is typically inferred from impurity spectroscopy together with atomic data, local electron density and temperature constraints, and edge plasma modeling. In simulations or reconstructions that resolve nitrogen charge states, the limiter value is obtained by summing the local ionized charge-state densities adjacent to the limiter; neutral nitrogen is treated separately.

Typical summed ionized nitrogen densities near limiters are about $10^{14}$-$10^{17}$ m^-3 for trace or weakly seeded nitrogen and can reach $10^{17}$-$10^{19}$ m^-3 during strong nitrogen seeding or local nitrogen release. The value depends on the limiter source rate, ionization balance, recombination, and transport along the boundary plasma.

NAMES.name: oxygen_density_at_limiter
NAMES.subject: oxygen
NAMES.short: Charge-state-summed number density of ionized oxygen impurity immediately adjacent to a limiter surface at the plasma-wall interface.
NAMES.long:
Oxygen density at a limiter is the local number density of ionized oxygen impurity in the plasma immediately adjacent to the limiter surface. It is species-specific and charge-state-summed, so it represents oxygen ions only, not neutral oxygen or electrons.

For oxygen ion charge states from singly ionized to fully stripped, the charge-state-summed limiter density is defined as:

$$
n_{\mathrm{O,lim}} = \sum_{q=1}^{8} n_{\mathrm{O}^{q+},\mathrm{lim}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{O,lim}}$ and each charge-state density $n_{\mathrm{O}^{q+},\mathrm{lim}}$ are number densities in m^-3, $q$ is the dimensionless ion charge state, and the upper limit 8 is the nuclear charge of oxygen. The neutral state $q=0$ is excluded.

In practice, this quantity is estimated from oxygen spectral line emission together with collisional-radiative or ionization-balance modeling, or from edge plasma and impurity-transport calculations constrained by local plasma conditions and wall-interaction source terms. It is the limiter-local counterpart of [oxygen_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:oxygen_density_at_plasma_boundary) and is interpreted alongside limiter plasma quantities such as [electron_density_at_limiter](name:electron_density_at_limiter).

Typical limiter-adjacent oxygen ion densities are strongly device- and scenario-dependent and are usually trace impurity values relative to the local electron density. Representative order-of-magnitude values can range from 10^14-10^18 m^-3 in clean or moderately conditioned edge plasmas, with larger transient values possible during enhanced oxygen influx or strong plasma-wall interaction.

NAMES.name: peak_power_density_at_first_wall
NAMES.short: Spatial maximum of the incident heat flux density deposited on first-wall plasma-facing surfaces.
NAMES.long:
Peak power density at the first wall is the largest local incident thermal power per unit area deposited on first-wall plasma-facing surfaces. It is the first-wall-specific form of a wall peak-load metric, distinct from peaks evaluated over all wall elements, limiter surfaces, or divertor targets.

For a first-wall surface $S_\mathrm{FW}$, it is defined as the maximum positive projection of the local power-flow vector onto the surface normal pointing from the plasma-facing surface into the solid wall:

$$
q_{\mathrm{FW}}^{\mathrm{peak}} = \max_{\mathbf{x} \in S_\mathrm{FW}} \max\left(0, \boldsymbol{q}(\mathbf{x}) \cdot \hat{\boldsymbol{n}}_w(\mathbf{x})\right)
$$

where $q_{\mathrm{FW}}^{\mathrm{peak}}$ is the peak first-wall power density in W m^-2, $\boldsymbol{q}(\mathbf{x})$ is the local energy flux density vector in W m^-2, and $\hat{\boldsymbol{n}}_w(\mathbf{x})$ is a dimensionless unit normal directed into the wall material at surface location $\mathbf{x}$. The inner maximum retains only incident heating and excludes outward or cooling fluxes.

In practice, this quantity is obtained from infrared thermography and inverse heat-conduction analysis, embedded thermocouples, calorimetric measurements, or modeled combinations of plasma particle bombardment, charge-exchange neutral loading, and radiative heat deposition. Surface geometry, material properties, viewing factors, and time response are important when converting measured temperature or radiation signals into local incident heat flux.

Representative steady or quasi-steady first-wall peak loads are typically about 0.1-5 MW m^-2, depending on device size, plasma scenario, wall material, and active cooling. Short transients such as edge-localized modes, runaway-electron impacts, or disruptions can produce substantially larger instantaneous local peaks over shorter durations. Related quantities include [power_density_at_wall](name:power_density_at_wall) for a local wall heat-flux density, [peak_power_density_at_wall](name:peak_power_density_at_wall) for the maximum over wall surfaces more generally, [peak_power_density_at_limiter](name:peak_power_density_at_limiter) for limiter elements, and [peak_power_density_at_divertor_target](name:peak_power_density_at_divertor_target) for divertor target plates.

NAMES.name: peak_power_density_at_limiter
NAMES.short: Spatial maximum of the heat flux per unit surface area deposited by scrape-off-layer plasma on the limiter surface.
NAMES.long:
Peak power density at a limiter is the spatial maximum of the local heat flux density deposited on the wetted limiter surface by scrape-off-layer plasma. It is the limiting local thermal load for limiter plasma-facing material, distinct from total limiter power because it depends on how narrowly the heat is distributed over the contact area.

The peak limiter heat-flux density is defined as the maximum of the local deposited normal heat flux over the wetted limiter surface:

$$
q_{\mathrm{peak,lim}} = \max_{\mathbf{x} \in A_{\mathrm{lim}}} q_\perp(\mathbf{x})
$$

where $q_{\mathrm{peak,lim}}$ and $q_\perp$ have units W m^-2, $\mathbf{x}$ is a point on the limiter surface, and $A_{\mathrm{lim}}$ is the wetted limiter surface area in m^2. For attached scrape-off-layer transport, the geometric projection is often approximated by $q_\perp \approx q_\parallel \sin\alpha$, where $q_\parallel$ is the parallel heat flux in W m^-2 and $\alpha$ is the dimensionless grazing angle between the magnetic field line and the surface; sheath heat-transmission factors, particle recycling, radiation, and surface incidence effects can modify this simple projection.

In practice this quantity is inferred from infrared thermography, calorimetry, embedded temperature sensors, or probes, often combined with surface thermal modeling and magnetic field-line tracing to identify the wetted region. Equilibrium geometry and limiter alignment are important because small changes in strike location or grazing angle can strongly change the local maximum.

Typical steady attached limiter loads in medium-size tokamaks are about 1-10 MW m^-2, with lower values in low-power or strongly radiating plasmas and substantially higher short-lived peaks possible during transients or localized contact events.

NAMES.name: power_density_at_wall
NAMES.short: Power flux density deposited on plasma-facing wall surfaces by all incident particle and radiation channels from the boundary plasma.
NAMES.long:
Power density at the wall quantifies the total thermal energy load per unit surface area delivered to plasma-facing components, aggregating contributions from charged particle impact, neutral atom bombardment, charge-exchange flux, and photon irradiation. It provides a spatially distributed measure of wall heating across the full plasma-facing geometry, in contrast to extremal statistics such as [peak_power_density_at_first_wall](name:peak_power_density_at_first_wall) or [peak_power_density_at_divertor_target](name:peak_power_density_at_divertor_target).

The local wall power density $q_w$ sums over all incident energy channels:

$$
q_w = \sum_s \Gamma_s \, E_s + q_{\mathrm{rad}}
$$

where $\Gamma_s$ is the incident particle flux density of species $s$, $E_s$ is the mean energy deposited per particle, and $q_{\mathrm{rad}}$ is the radiative contribution represented by [energy_flux_at_wall_due_to_radiation](name:energy_flux_at_wall_due_to_radiation).

Spatially resolved wall heat loads are measured via calibrated infrared thermography or derived from boundary plasma transport simulations validated against bolometric total-power measurements. The [electron_energy_flux_at_wall](name:electron_energy_flux_at_wall) and ion contributions can be tracked separately as components of this total.

Typical steady-state values range from 0.1–1 MW/m² on the main first wall to 5–20 MW/m² at actively loaded divertor strike zones; transient power loads during edge-localized modes can transiently exceed these by an order of magnitude.

NAMES.name: radiated_power_at_wall
NAMES.short: Net photon power deposited on plasma-facing first-wall surfaces by radiation emitted from the plasma. It is the surface-integrated incident radiative power intercepted by the wall minus the power carried away by reflected photons.
NAMES.long:
Radiated power at the wall is the net radiative heating power delivered to plasma-facing first-wall surfaces by photons originating in the plasma. It is the radiation-only contribution to the wall heat-load budget, distinct from conductive, convective, neutral-particle, and charge-exchange energy channels, and it complements the total wall load described by thermal_power_at_wall.

The net deposited radiative power is defined by the incident photon power on the wall minus the reflected photon power:

$$
P_\mathrm{rad,wall} = P_\mathrm{inc} - P_\mathrm{ref} = (1 - \mathcal{R}_\mathrm{eff}) P_\mathrm{inc}
$$

where $P_\mathrm{inc}$ is the photon power incident on all relevant first-wall surfaces, $P_\mathrm{ref}$ is the photon power reflected from those surfaces, and $\mathcal{R}_\mathrm{eff}$ is an effective wall reflectivity averaged over surface material, spectrum, angle of incidence, and illuminated area.

This quantity is usually estimated from bolometric measurements of plasma radiation combined with geometric view-factor or ray-tracing calculations that determine how much photon power reaches the first wall. It may also be inferred from infrared thermography or surface calorimetry when the radiative component can be separated from other heat-load channels. It is related to [radiated_power_at_inside_flux_surface](name:total_plasma_radiated_power), but represents only the photon power that escapes the plasma region and is absorbed at the wall; the analogous divertor-target radiation load is [power_at_divertor_target_due_to_radiation](name:power_at_divertor_target_due_to_radiation).

Typical values range from $10^3$-$10^5$ W in small experiments to $10^6$-$10^8$ W in large tokamaks during high-density, impurity-seeded, or detached-plasma operation. The value increases with total plasma radiation, wall view factor, and wall absorptivity, and decreases when a larger fraction of photons is intercepted by divertor targets or reflected by plasma-facing materials.

NAMES.name: surface_emissivity
NAMES.short: Surface emissivity is the dimensionless effective thermal emissivity of a plasma-facing surface: the ratio of its emitted thermal radiance or radiative exitance to that of a blackbody at the same surface temperature. As a scalar, it represents the stated spectral band and angular averaging rather than a wavelength- and direction-resolved emissivity.
NAMES.long:
Surface emissivity is a dimensionless measure of how efficiently a real surface emits thermal radiation compared with a blackbody at the same surface temperature. For a scalar value, it is an effective emissivity averaged over the relevant wavelength band and angular domain, not the full spectral, directional, or polarization-dependent emissivity function.

The effective value can be defined as a weighted ratio of emitted spectral radiance to blackbody spectral radiance:

$$
\epsilon_\mathrm{eff}(T_s) = \frac{\int_{\lambda}\int_{\Omega} W(\lambda,\Omega)\,L_\lambda^\mathrm{surf}(T_s,\Omega)\,d\Omega\,d\lambda}{\int_{\lambda}\int_{\Omega} W(\lambda,\Omega)\,L_\lambda^\mathrm{bb}(T_s)\,d\Omega\,d\lambda}
$$

where $T_s$ is the surface temperature, $L_\lambda^\mathrm{surf}$ is the emitted spectral radiance of the real surface, $L_\lambda^\mathrm{bb}$ is the blackbody spectral radiance at the same temperature, $\Omega$ is the selected angular domain, and $W(\lambda,\Omega)$ specifies the spectral response and angular weighting. For a broadband hemispherical thermal model, the angular domain is the outward hemisphere and the associated emitted heat-flux density is $q_\mathrm{rad}=\epsilon_\mathrm{eff}\sigma T_s^4$; total radiated power is obtained by integrating that flux density over surface area.

In practice, surface emissivity is obtained from material data, laboratory calibration, in-situ calibration, or fitting of thermal-radiation measurements together with an independent temperature estimate. It is strongly affected by material composition, roughness, oxidation, deposited layers, erosion, temperature, wavelength band, and viewing angle, so the averaging convention should match the radiation model or infrared measurement being interpreted.

Typical values range from 0.02-0.2 for clean polished metals, 0.3-0.9 for oxidized or rough metals, 0.7-0.95 for graphite and many carbon-rich surfaces, and about 0.1-0.6 for tungsten plasma-facing components depending on wavelength and surface condition. For an opaque passive surface the physical range is normally $0 \le \epsilon_\mathrm{eff} \le 1$; apparent values outside this range usually indicate calibration, reflection, background-subtraction, or model-assumption errors.

NAMES.name: surface_temperature
NAMES.short: Thermodynamic temperature of the exposed material surface of a plasma-facing component at a specified surface location and time. It is a local surface state variable, distinct from a surface average or a maximum over an area.
NAMES.long:
Surface temperature is the thermodynamic temperature of the outermost exposed material surface at a specified location and time. It is a local material property of a plasma-facing component; surface averages, area-integrated quantities, and peak values are different quantities and should not be inferred from this name alone.

The temperature controls thermal emission from the surface. For an opaque gray surface, the hemispherical radiant exitance may be approximated by the Stefan-Boltzmann relation:

$$
M = \varepsilon \sigma T_s^4
$$

where $M$ is the emitted radiant power per unit surface area, $\varepsilon$ is the surface emissivity, $\sigma$ is the Stefan-Boltzmann constant, and $T_s$ is the surface temperature.

In practice, surface temperature may be obtained from infrared thermography, pyrometry, embedded temperature sensors, thermocouples, or heat-transfer modeling. Thermal-emission methods require knowledge of emissivity, optical transmission, viewing geometry, reflected radiation, and calibration. The referenced location is the material point on the exposed surface, which may be parameterized by surface coordinates or by its position in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

Typical values are 290-320 K for components near room temperature before operation, 500-1500 K for heated first-wall or divertor surfaces during plasma exposure, and 1500-3000 K for localized hot spots or transient heat loads. Values approaching material limits, such as about 3683 K for tungsten melting, are critical for component lifetime and machine protection.

NAMES.name: maximum_surface_temperature
NAMES.short: Highest apparent surface temperature among the valid points in a defined infrared camera region of interest. It is a temperature maximum, not a heat flux or power-density measure.
NAMES.long:
Maximum surface temperature is the largest apparent temperature assigned to an observed plasma-facing surface within a defined region of interest at a given observation time. The word apparent indicates the radiance-derived temperature after the assumed emissivity, optical transmission, calibration, and background corrections have been applied; it may differ from the true thermodynamic surface temperature if those assumptions are inaccurate. This quantity identifies the hottest inferred point in the region, but it does not by itself quantify deposited heat flux.

For a region of interest $\Omega_\mathrm{ROI}$, the maximum is defined as the maximum over all valid temperature samples in that region:

$$
T_\mathrm{max} = \max_{p \in \Omega_\mathrm{ROI}} T_\mathrm{app}(p)
$$

where $T_\mathrm{max}$ and $T_\mathrm{app}(p)$ are temperatures in kelvin, $p$ labels a valid surface sample or camera pixel associated with the region of interest, and $\Omega_\mathrm{ROI}$ is the selected set of samples. Invalid, masked, saturated, or uncalibrated samples are excluded before taking the maximum; the result is a pointwise maximum, not an average, percentile, or time maximum unless an additional processing definition states otherwise.

In practice, infrared thermography infers $T_\mathrm{app}$ from measured thermal radiance using camera calibration, spectral response, surface emissivity, optical transmission, and reflected-background corrections. A common calibration model is based on Planck spectral radiance, with $L_\lambda(T) = \epsilon(\lambda,T)\,2hc^2/\lambda^5[\exp(hc/(\lambda k_B T))-1]^{-1}$ integrated over the camera bandpass, where $L_\lambda$ is spectral radiance in W m^-3 sr^-1, $\epsilon$ is dimensionless emissivity, $\lambda$ is wavelength in meters, $h$ is Planck's constant in J s, $c$ is the speed of light in m s^-1, $k_B$ is Boltzmann's constant in J K^-1, and $T$ is temperature in kelvin.

Typical values are about 290-350 K for surfaces near room temperature before plasma exposure, several hundred to 1500 K during moderate heating, and above 2000 K for localized hot spots in high-power operation. Allowable maxima depend strongly on surface material, coatings, pulse duration, and machine-protection limits.

This quantity should be distinguished from heat-flux or power-density quantities such as peak power density at a divertor target or limiter. Temperature is the surface thermal state, whereas heat flux depends on deposited power, material thermal properties, geometry, cooling, and the time history of the exposure.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_divertor_target
NAMES.short: Vertical Z coordinate of the divertor target surface center in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, where Z is vertical height.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate of the divertor target is the $Z$ component of the geometric center of the target surface in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It locates the hardware surface as a geometric reference and is distinct from the vertical position of a plasma strike point on that surface.

For a finite divertor target surface $S_t$, the surface-center coordinate is the area centroid of that surface:

$$
Z_t = \frac{1}{A_t}\int_{S_t} Z(\mathbf{x})\,dA, \qquad A_t = \int_{S_t} dA
$$

where $Z_t$ is the target-center vertical coordinate, $A_t$ is the target-surface area, $dA$ is the surface area element, and $Z(\mathbf{x})$ is the vertical height of point $\mathbf{x}$ on the target surface.

In practice this coordinate is computed from the defined target geometry, for example from an engineering surface model, metrology description, or calibrated diagnostic geometry. For a mesh representation, the integral is evaluated as an area-weighted average of the mesh-element center $Z$ coordinates. The corresponding horizontal or transverse coordinates are described by [x_coordinate_of_divertor_target](name:x_coordinate_of_divertor_target) and [y_coordinate_of_divertor_target](name:y_coordinate_of_divertor_target), while inner and outer strike-location quantities refer to different physical points on the divertor.

Typical values are machine-size and vertical-origin dependent. In lower-single-null tokamaks the target surface center commonly has $Z<0$, often about 0.5-3 m below the magnetic-axis or midplane region in medium to large devices; upper-divertor targets have comparable positive values, and compact devices can have magnitudes of about 0.1-1 m.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the divertor target surface center lies in the $+Z$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: y_coordinate_of_divertor_target
NAMES.short: Cartesian Y coordinate of the divertor target surface center in the right-handed (x, y, z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The Y coordinate locates the center of the divertor target surface along the $\hat{y}$ axis of the right-handed Cartesian $(x, y, z)$ frame, where $\hat{z} = \hat{Z}$ is vertical and $\hat{x}$ is aligned with $\phi = 0$, with the toroidal angle $\phi$ increasing counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$. This coordinate relates to the cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ description of the same point by the standard transformation $y = R\sin\phi$, where $R$ is the major radius from the toroidal symmetry axis and $\phi$ is the toroidal angle.
