This coordinate is used alongside [x_coordinate_of_divertor_target](name:x_coordinate_of_divertor_target) and [vertical_coordinate_of_divertor_target](name:vertical_coordinate_of_divertor_target) to fully specify the three-dimensional Cartesian position of the divertor target center in plasma-wall interaction modeling. It is obtained from engineering drawings of the divertor geometry or from geometric calibration of diagnostics such as infrared cameras that image the target surface.

The magnitude of $y$ is bounded by the major radius of the machine; for a target segment at toroidal angle $\phi$ and radial distance $R$ from the symmetry axis, $|y|$ spans zero to approximately $R$ depending on the toroidal location of the target.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the divertor target center is displaced in the $+\hat{y}$ direction of the right-handed Cartesian $(x, y, z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: power_at_wall_due_to_conduction
NAMES.short: Conductive component of plasma power deposited on first-wall and divertor material surfaces. It represents heat carried by thermal conduction and excludes convected, radiated, recombination, and neutral-particle power channels.
NAMES.long:
Power at wall due to conduction is the component of the wall-deposited plasma energy flux carried by thermal conduction, primarily electron heat conduction along magnetic field lines in the scrape-off-layer and divertor plasma. It is distinct from particle enthalpy convection, radiation, recombination energy, and neutral-particle energy deposition.

The scalar power is defined by integrating the deposited conductive heat-flux density over the plasma-facing material surface:

$$
P_{\mathrm{wall,cond}} = \int_{A_{\mathrm{wall}}} q_{n,\mathrm{cond}}^{\mathrm{dep}} \, dA
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{wall,cond}}$ is the conducted wall power, $A_{\mathrm{wall}}$ is the wetted first-wall and divertor material surface, $dA$ is a surface element in $\mathrm{m^2}$, and $q_{n,\mathrm{cond}}^{\mathrm{dep}}$ is the local conductive heat-flux density into the material in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$. The upstream parallel conductive heat flux is often modeled as $q_{\parallel,\mathrm{cond}} = -\kappa_\parallel \nabla_\parallel T_e$, where $q_{\parallel,\mathrm{cond}}$ is in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$, $\kappa_\parallel$ is in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,eV^{-1}}$ when $T_e$ is expressed in eV, and $\nabla_\parallel T_e$ is in $\mathrm{eV\,m^{-1}}$. Mapping this upstream flux to $q_{n,\mathrm{cond}}^{\mathrm{dep}}$ includes magnetic incidence on the surface and may include a sheath heat-transmission factor, so the deposited conductive power is not simply the bare upstream parallel flux integrated over geometric wall area.

In practice this quantity is inferred from wall heat-flux measurements and edge-plasma modeling. Infrared thermography, calorimetry, embedded temperature sensors, Langmuir probes, and edge Thomson scattering can constrain the deposited heat flux, electron temperature gradients, and the partition between conductive and convective channels. Together with [power_at_wall_due_to_convection](name:power_at_wall_due_to_convection), this quantity forms the main kinetic thermal contribution to plasma_power_at_wall; it is also part of thermal_power_at_wall and the divertor-local thermal load described by [thermal_power_of_divertor](name:thermal_power_of_divertor).

Typical magnitudes range from $10^5-10^7$ W in medium-size tokamak plasmas, can fall near zero in strongly detached or highly radiative conditions, and can reach $10^7-10^8$ W or more in high-power devices if a large fraction of scrape-off-layer power reaches material surfaces conductively.
NAMES.sign: Positive when conductive thermal energy is deposited from the plasma into first-wall or divertor material surfaces.

NAMES.name: power_at_wall_due_to_ohmic_dissipation
NAMES.short: Total resistive Joule power converted to heat within conducting wall, plasma-facing, and vessel structures by induced, halo, or other plasma-wall currents.
NAMES.long:
Power at the wall due to ohmic dissipation is the total rate at which electrical energy is converted into heat inside conducting wall, plasma-facing, and vessel structures by currents associated with plasma-wall interaction. It includes resistive dissipation from eddy currents induced by changing magnetic fields and from halo or shared currents that pass through conducting structures.

The instantaneous Joule-heating power over the conducting material volume is

$$
P_\mathrm{ohm} = \int_V \eta(\mathbf{x},T)\, |\mathbf{j}(\mathbf{x})|^2 \, dV
$$

where $V$ is the conducting material volume, $\eta(\mathbf{x},T)$ is the electrical resistivity at position $\mathbf{x}$ and material temperature $T$ in $\Omega\,\mathrm{m}$, $\mathbf{j}$ is the local current density in $\mathrm{A}\,\mathrm{m}^{-2}$, and $dV$ is a differential volume element in $\mathrm{m}^3$. For passive resistive materials, $\eta \ge 0$ and $|\mathbf{j}|^2 \ge 0$, so the integral is non-negative and represents heat production rather than a signed electromagnetic power flow.

This quantity is computed from electromagnetic circuit or field models of the conducting structures, often constrained by magnetic sensors, wall-current measurements, halo-current measurements, and material resistivity data. Thermal analysis or calorimetry can provide an independent constraint when other heat sources, such as particle impact, radiation, and recombination, are separated. The related [energy flux at wall due to eddy current](name:energy_flux_at_wall_due_to_eddy_current) describes a local surface heat flux from eddy-current dissipation only; this quantity is a volume-integrated power and may also include halo-current dissipation.

Typical values are about 10^3-10^6 W during routine operation with slowly varying fields, and about 10^6-10^9 W during disruptions, vertical displacement events, or rapid current quenches in large devices. The magnitude depends on plasma current, magnetic-field ramp rate, wall geometry, material resistivity, and the electrical circuit paths that connect the plasma to surrounding conducting structures.

NAMES.name: ratio_of_beryllium_density_to_electron_density
NAMES.short: Dimensionless ratio of total beryllium ion number density to electron number density. It measures beryllium impurity abundance relative to the plasma electron population, with the beryllium ion density summed over charged ionization states.
NAMES.long:
The ratio of beryllium density to electron density is a dimensionless impurity abundance measuring how much beryllium ion population is present relative to the free electron population. The beryllium numerator is the total beryllium ion number density, summed over charged ionization states, and does not by itself weight the ions by charge.

The defining relation is:

$$
f_\mathrm{Be} = \frac{n_\mathrm{Be}}{n_e} = \frac{\sum_{q=1}^{4} n_{\mathrm{Be}^{q+}}}{n_e}
$$

where $n_\mathrm{Be}$ is the total beryllium ion number density, $n_{\mathrm{Be}^{q+}}$ is the number density of beryllium ions in charge state $q$, and $n_e$ is the electron number density; all densities in the ratio have units of m$^{-3}$. In a quasi-neutral plasma, the charge-weighted impurity contribution enters the electron balance through terms of the form $q n_{\mathrm{Be}^{q+}}$, so this ratio is closely related to fuel dilution but is not itself the charge fraction.

Beryllium impurities are commonly produced by plasma-wall interaction processes such as sputtering of beryllium-containing plasma-facing components, followed by transport and ionization in the edge and confined plasma. The ratio is inferred by combining beryllium spectroscopic measurements and collisional-radiative modeling with electron density measurements from diagnostics such as interferometry and Thomson scattering. Related beryllium density quantities include [volume_averaged_beryllium_density](name:volume_averaged_beryllium_density), [beryllium_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:beryllium_density_at_magnetic_axis), [beryllium_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:beryllium_density_at_plasma_boundary), and [beryllium_density_at_limiter](name:beryllium_density_at_limiter).

Typical values in well-conditioned plasmas with beryllium plasma-facing surfaces are about $10^{-4}$-$10^{-2}$, with many H-mode conditions lying near $10^{-3}$-$5 \times 10^{-3}$. Values can rise to several percent during strong wall source events, early conditioning phases, or after disruptions.

NAMES.name: reference_wavelength_of_filter
NAMES.short: Reference wavelength of an optical filter is the nominal center or peak wavelength of its passband, usually the wavelength at which the nominal transmission is maximal. It identifies the spectral location of the filter response, not the full passband shape or width.
NAMES.long:
Reference wavelength of a filter, $\lambda_\mathrm{ref}$, is the nominal spectral position assigned to an optical bandpass filter. For a single-peaked bandpass it is normally the wavelength at which the nominal spectral transmittance is largest; for asymmetric or structured responses it is a manufacturer- or calibration-defined reference point for the passband center.

For a peak-defined filter reference, the defining relation is

$$
\lambda_\mathrm{ref} = \operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\lambda} T_\mathrm{nom}(\lambda)
$$

where $T_\mathrm{nom}(\lambda)$ is the nominal spectral transmittance as a function of wavelength $\lambda$.

The value is obtained from the filter specification or from laboratory spectral-transmission calibration. It is used together with the passband width and, when available, lower and upper wavelength bounds to describe the spectral region transmitted by the filter; the reference wavelength alone does not fully determine the filter response.

Typical values for visible and infrared plasma diagnostics are about $4\times10^{-7}$-$1.5\times10^{-5}$ m, with narrow line filters often centered near specific atomic or molecular emission wavelengths and thermal-infrared filters commonly in the micrometer range.

NAMES.name: back_surface_curvature_of_optical_element
NAMES.short: Radius of curvature of the rear surface of a diagnostic optical element along the local X1 axis, applicable to spherical, cylindrical, and toroidal surface geometries.
NAMES.long:
The back-surface X1 radius of curvature $R_{\mathrm{back},X1}$ describes the curvature of the exit face of a diagnostic optical element in the X1 direction of the local surface frame $(X1, X2, X3)$, where $X1$ and $X2$ span the optical surface and $X3$ is the outward surface normal. This parameter is required by ray-tracing and Gaussian-optics models to compute the wavefront transformation induced by the rear surface of lenses, windows, and mirrors used in visible and infrared camera systems and visible spectrometer diagnostics. A finite value applies only when the surface curvature type permits non-planar geometry in X1: specifically, spherical (type 2), cylindrical along X1 (type 4), and toroidal (type 5) surface types.

For a thick lens in air, the paraxial focal length $f$ is related to the front and back radii by the Lensmaker's equation:

$$
\frac{1}{f} = (n-1)\left[\frac{1}{R_{\mathrm{front},X1}} - \frac{1}{R_{\mathrm{back},X1}} + \frac{(n-1)d}{n\,R_{\mathrm{front},X1}\,R_{\mathrm{back},X1}}\right]
$$

where $n$ is the refractive index of the element material, $d$ is the axial thickness, and $R_{\mathrm{front},X1}$ is the front-surface radius of curvature given by front_surface_curvature_of_optical_element. For toroidal or cylindrical elements the orthogonal principal curvature in X2 is an independent parameter given by [vertical_back_surface_curvature_of_optical_element](name:vertical_back_surface_curvature_of_optical_element); for a spherical surface both principal radii are equal.

Absolute values range from a few millimeters for tightly curved condenser elements to hundreds of meters for near-flat windows and beam-splitters; a zero value conventionally represents an infinite radius (planar surface).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the center of curvature of the back surface lies on the exit (transmitted-beam) side of the optical element.

NAMES.name: bragg_crystal_width
NAMES.short: Full width of the Bragg crystal in an X-ray crystal spectrometer along the first transverse (X1) axis, applicable only for rectangular crystal geometry.
NAMES.long:
The Bragg crystal width specifies the physical extent of the diffracting crystal element along its first transverse coordinate axis (X1) in an X-ray crystal spectrometer channel. This dimension is only defined for rectangular crystal geometry; together with bragg_crystal_height along the orthogonal X2 axis and [thickness_of_bragg_crystal](name:thickness_of_bragg_crystal) through the crystal body, it fully parameterizes the three-dimensional rectangular crystal geometry required for solid-angle and acceptance calculations.

The X1 width governs the acceptance aperture along the meridional or sagittal direction depending on the crystal mount orientation. A larger width intercepts a greater solid angle of X-ray emission from the plasma source, increasing photon throughput, but can introduce geometric aberrations in curved-crystal focusing arrangements such as Johann or Johansson geometries. The bragg_wavelength separately characterizes the diffraction condition, linking crystal orientation to the photon energies that satisfy Bragg's law.

Typical crystal widths for fusion-diagnostic X-ray spectrometers range from a few millimeters to a few tens of millimeters, depending on crystal material and spectrometer geometry.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the extent is measured as a physical length from one edge of the crystal to the other along the X1 transverse axis of the crystal coordinate frame.

NAMES.name: brightness_of_visible_camera
NAMES.short: Photon radiance measured by a visible-band camera channel, giving the number of photons collected per unit detector area, per unit time, and per unit solid angle along a line of sight.
NAMES.long:
Brightness of a visible camera is the photon radiance reaching the camera within its visible passband along a line of sight. It counts photons rather than radiant energy, normalized by collection area, observation time, and accepted solid angle, with the viewing-angle projection treated explicitly.

The photon radiance can be defined from the photons collected by a small detector element viewing a small solid angle:

$$
B_\mathrm{vis} = \frac{dN_\gamma}{dt\,dA\,\cos\alpha\,d\Omega}
$$

where $B_\mathrm{vis}$ has unit m^-2.s^-1.sr^-1, $dN_\gamma$ is the photon count with unit 1, $dt$ is the exposure or integration time in s, $dA$ is the unprojected physical detector area in m^2, $\alpha$ is the [alpha angle] in rad between the detector surface normal and the incoming ray, and $d\Omega$ is the accepted solid angle in sr. The factor $dA\cos\alpha$ is the projected detector area normal to the ray.

In practice this quantity is obtained from calibrated camera counts after dark-offset subtraction, flat-field and gain correction, detector quantum-efficiency calibration, exposure-time normalization, optical-transmission correction, and geometric calibration of the viewed solid angle. It can include visible line radiation, continuum bremsstrahlung, molecular-band emission, impurity radiation, and light from plasma-wall interactions within the camera response band.

Typical magnitudes vary widely with wavelength band, viewing geometry, and plasma conditions. Faint continuum or wall-background signals may be about 10^15-10^18 m^-2.s^-1.sr^-1, while bright edge or divertor line emission is often 10^18-10^22 m^-2.s^-1.sr^-1; intense transient or saturated views can exceed 10^22 m^-2.s^-1.sr^-1.

NAMES.name: deuterium_deuterium_power_density_due_to_fusion
NAMES.subject: deuterium_deuterium
NAMES.short: Local fusion energy release rate per unit volume from deuterium-deuterium reactions. It includes energy released through the neutron-emitting and proton-emitting D-D branches, expressed as a volumetric power density.
NAMES.long:
Deuterium-deuterium fusion power density is the local rate at which nuclear binding energy is released per unit plasma volume by reactions between deuterium ions. It is a source term for fusion product energy before any subsequent transport, slowing down, or wall losses. The quantity includes energy released in both principal D-D branches, not only the neutron-emitting branch.

Using a total D-D reactivity summed over the neutron-emitting and proton-emitting branches, the local power density is

$$
p_{DD} = \frac{1}{2} n_D^2 \langle\sigma v\rangle_{DD} E_{DD} = \epsilon_{n,DD}\frac{E_{DD}}{f_n}
$$

where $n_D$ is deuterium ion density in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, $\langle\sigma v\rangle_{DD}$ is the velocity-distribution-averaged total D-D reactivity in $\mathrm{m}^3\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, and $E_{DD}$ is the branch-weighted reaction energy in joules. The factor $1/2$ avoids double counting pairs of identical deuterons. $\epsilon_{n,DD}$ is the neutron emissivity from the D-D neutron branch in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ and $f_n$ is that branch's fraction of all D-D reactions, so neutron-branch emissivity is converted to total D-D power density by multiplying by $E_{DD}/f_n$. For nearly equal branch probabilities, $f_n \approx 0.5$; with branch energies of 3.27 MeV and 4.03 MeV, $E_{DD} \approx 3.65$ MeV = $5.85\times10^{-13}$ J per total D-D reaction, and $E_{DD}/f_n \approx 7.30$ MeV = $1.17\times10^{-12}$ J per emitted D-D neutron.

In practice, this quantity may be computed from deuterium density, ion velocity distributions, and nuclear reactivity data, or inferred from neutron measurements. Tomographic inversion estimates the local D-D neutron emissivity, after which branch fractions and reaction energies provide the conversion to total fusion power density. Absolute calibration, scattered-neutron corrections, viewing geometry, fuel dilution, and nonthermal deuterium populations can all affect the inferred value.

Typical core values in present deuterium plasmas range from 10-10^4 W m^-3 for thermal ion temperatures of a few to about 15 keV. Hotter plasmas or plasmas with strong fast-ion populations can reach 10^5-10^6 W m^-3 locally, while values near the cool plasma edge are often much smaller.

NAMES.name: deuterium_tritium_power_density_due_to_fusion
NAMES.subject: deuterium_tritium
NAMES.short: Local volumetric power density from deuterium-tritium thermonuclear reactions, with each reaction yielding 17.6 MeV distributed between the alpha particle (3.5 MeV) and the neutron (14.1 MeV).
NAMES.long:
The D-T fusion power density is the local rate at which deuterium-tritium reactions $D + T \rightarrow {}^4\mathrm{He} + n$ deposit energy per unit plasma volume, with each event releasing $Q_\mathrm{DT} = 17.6\,\mathrm{MeV}$, partitioned as 3.5 MeV to the alpha particle and 14.1 MeV to the 14.1 MeV neutron.

The volumetric power density is defined by:

$$
P_\mathrm{DT} = n_D \, n_T \, \langle \sigma v \rangle_\mathrm{DT} \, Q_\mathrm{DT}
$$

where $n_D$ and $n_T$ are the local deuterium and tritium number densities, $\langle \sigma v \rangle_\mathrm{DT}$ is the velocity-averaged D-T fusion reactivity (maximized near ion temperature $T_i \approx 65\,\mathrm{keV}$), and $Q_\mathrm{DT} = 17.6\,\mathrm{MeV}$ is the total energy released per reaction.

The spatial distribution of $P_\mathrm{DT}$ is inferred from neutron emissivity tomography: multi-channel neutron detector signals are tomographically inverted to yield the [deuterium_tritium_emissivity_due_to_fusion](name:deuterium_tritium_emissivity_due_to_fusion) (volumetric reaction rate), which is then scaled by $Q_\mathrm{DT}$ to obtain the power density. In a balanced D-T fuel mixture at reactor-relevant temperatures of 10–20 keV, the D-T channel dominates the total [power_density_due_to_fusion](name:power_density_due_to_fusion), exceeding the [deuterium_deuterium_power_density_due_to_fusion](name:deuterium_deuterium_power_density_due_to_fusion) by roughly two orders of magnitude due to the much larger D-T reactivity at these temperatures. Peak on-axis values in near-ignition plasmas are expected to reach several MW m$^{-3}$.

NAMES.name: energy_of_detector_pixel
NAMES.short: Characteristic photon energy assigned to a detector pixel in an X-ray crystal spectrometer from the pixel's Bragg diffraction geometry.
NAMES.long:
The energy of a detector pixel is the central photon energy represented by that pixel's spectral channel in an X-ray crystal spectrometer. It is set by the pixel position relative to the diffracting crystal and detector surface, and is the energy counterpart of the pixel Bragg wavelength [wavelength_of_detector_pixel](name:wavelength_of_detector_pixel). The finite spectral acceptance of the pixel is bracketed by [lower_bound_energy_of_detector_pixel](name:lower_bound_energy_of_detector_pixel) and [upper_bound_energy_of_detector_pixel](name:upper_bound_energy_of_detector_pixel).

For diffraction order $n$, the central pixel energy follows from Bragg's law and the photon relation $E = hc/\lambda$:

$$
E_\mathrm{pix} = \frac{n h c}{2 e d \sin\theta_\mathrm{pix}}
$$

where $E_\mathrm{pix}$ is the photon energy in eV, $n$ is the dimensionless positive integer diffraction order, $h$ is Planck's constant in J s, $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum in m s^-1, $e$ is the elementary charge used to convert joules to electronvolts, $d$ is the crystal-plane spacing in meters, and $\theta_\mathrm{pix}$ is the Bragg angle for the pixel in radians.

The energy-to-pixel mapping is obtained from the spectrometer geometry by ray tracing, from an optical model of the crystal and detector, or by calibration against emission lines with well-known photon energies. In fusion applications these lines often come from highly ionized impurities, such as He-like or H-like argon, krypton, or other injected species.

Typical photon energies range from a few hundred eV for soft X-ray instruments to 5-20 keV for harder X-ray crystal spectrometers, depending on the chosen crystal spacing, diffraction order, viewing geometry, and target spectral lines.

NAMES.name: hard_xray_outer_width
NAMES.subject: hard_xray
NAMES.short: Outer half-width of the hard X-ray emissivity peak in normalized toroidal flux coordinate, defined as the radial distance from the peak to the half-maximum point on the separatrix-facing side.
NAMES.long:
The outer half-width of the hard X-ray emissivity peak measures the radial distance in normalized toroidal flux coordinate $\rho_{tor,norm}$ from the emissivity maximum to its half-maximum point on the side facing the separatrix. Hard X-ray emission in magnetized plasmas originates from bremsstrahlung of energetic non-thermal electrons — runaway and fast electrons — as they scatter off background plasma ions; a spatially localized emissivity peak therefore reflects a confined population of such electrons, and the outer half-width characterizes how far that population extends radially toward the plasma edge.

The outer half-width $\Delta\rho_{ext}$ is defined by:

$$
\Delta\rho_{ext} = \rho_{1/2,ext} - \rho_{peak}
$$

where $\rho_{peak}$ is the $\rho_{tor,norm}$ coordinate of the emissivity maximum, $\rho_{1/2,ext}$ is the outboard coordinate at which the emissivity falls to half its peak value, and $\rho_{tor,norm} = \sqrt{\Phi_{tor}/\Phi_{tor,\mathrm{LCFS}}}$ with $\Phi_{tor,\mathrm{LCFS}}$ the toroidal magnetic flux enclosed by the last-closed flux surface.

The emissivity radial distribution is inferred from multi-chord hard X-ray camera brightnesses via tomographic inversion under the assumption of toroidal symmetry. Comparing the outer half-width with the complementary [hard_xray_inner_width](name:hard_xray_inner_width) reveals radial asymmetry in the non-thermal electron population; a larger outer value relative to the inner indicates that the fast electron distribution extends further toward the separatrix than toward the magnetic axis. Both quantities are expressed on the [normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate) scale.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the outer half-maximum boundary lies at greater $\rho_{tor,norm}$ than the emissivity peak, in the direction of increasing normalized toroidal flux toward the separatrix.

NAMES.name: lower_bound_energy_of_detector_pixel
NAMES.short: Minimum photon energy accepted by a detector pixel in an X-ray crystal spectrometer. It is the low-energy edge of that pixel's photon-energy bandpass.
NAMES.long:
The lower bound energy of a detector pixel is the minimum photon energy in the spectral interval accepted by that pixel. Together with the corresponding upper bound, it defines the pixel bandpass around the calibrated photon_energy coordinate.

For a crystal spectrometer calibrated by Bragg diffraction, the lower bound for pixel $p$ can be written as the minimum energy over the Bragg-angle interval accepted by that pixel:

$$
E_{\mathrm{lower},p} = \min_{\theta \in \Omega_p} \frac{n h c}{2 d \sin\theta\, e}
$$

where $\Omega_p$ is the accepted Bragg-angle interval of pixel $p$, $n$ is the positive integer diffraction order for the calibrated spectral branch, $d$ is the crystal lattice-plane spacing, $h$ is Planck's constant, $c$ is the speed of light, and $e$ is the elementary charge converting joules to electronvolts. Equivalently, if $d$ is expressed in nm, $hc/e = 1239.841984\ \mathrm{eV\,nm}$ gives $E$ directly in eV.

In practice this bound is obtained from the spectrometer geometry, crystal spacing and orientation, detector position, pixel aperture, and a wavelength or line-emission calibration. The finite pixel size and optical response determine the accepted angular interval, so the lower bound is the low-energy edge of the pixel response rather than merely the energy at its center.

Typical lower bounds for fusion X-ray crystal spectrometers are 500-20000 eV, with common impurity-line measurements in the 3000-8000 eV range and harder spectral branches extending to 10000-50000 eV. Adjacent-pixel energy intervals are often a few eV to tens of eV, depending on dispersion and pixel size.

NAMES.name: lower_photon_energy
NAMES.short: Minimum photon energy defining the low-energy edge of an X-ray detector, camera pixel, or energy-resolved emission band. Incident photons below this cutoff are rejected, not counted, or excluded from the corresponding photon-energy window.
NAMES.long:
Lower photon energy is the minimum photon energy admitted by a photon-counting or energy-selective X-ray measurement. Together with an upper cutoff such as [upper_photon_energy](name:upper_photon_energy), it defines the accepted photon-energy interval; for pixel-specific thresholds it is the lower-edge counterpart of [lower_bound_energy_of_detector_pixel](name:lower_bound_energy_of_detector_pixel) and is paired with [upper_bound_energy_of_detector_pixel](name:upper_bound_energy_of_detector_pixel).

Photon energy is related to radiation frequency and wavelength by:

$$
E_\gamma = h\nu = \frac{hc}{\lambda}
$$

where $E_\gamma$ is photon energy, $h$ is Planck's constant, $\nu$ is photon frequency, $c$ is the speed of light, and $\lambda$ is wavelength. The lower threshold $E_\mathrm{lower}$ selects photons satisfying $E_\gamma \ge E_\mathrm{lower}$, usually in combination with an upper threshold $E_\mathrm{upper}$.

In practice this threshold is set by detector absorption filters, scintillator or semiconductor response, electronic discrimination levels, pulse-height analysis, or analysis choices used to isolate an energy band for emissivity inference. Calibration with known radiation sources or modeled detector response functions is used to relate the threshold setting to photon energy.

Typical lower thresholds are about 100-1000 eV for soft X-ray measurements and about 1e3-1e5 eV for hard X-ray measurements, depending on detector material, filter stack, electronic noise floor, and the intended spectral band.

NAMES.name: major_radius_of_detector_pixel
NAMES.short: Major radius coordinate of the center of a detector pixel in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Major radius of a detector pixel is the cylindrical $R$ coordinate of the pixel center. It is the perpendicular distance from the machine toroidal symmetry axis to the point representing the center of the pixel's active area in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height.

When the same point is represented in a right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ basis with origin on the toroidal symmetry axis and $\hat{z}=\hat{Z}$, the major radius is

$$
R = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}
$$

where $x$ and $y$ are the horizontal Cartesian coordinates of the pixel center in m, and $R$ is the major radius in m.

In practice this coordinate is obtained from the diagnostic geometry, survey information, optical design, or alignment model that maps each detector pixel into machine coordinates. Together with the corresponding toroidal angle and vertical position, it fixes the spatial location used to determine viewing geometry, lines of sight, and spatial calibration for pixel-resolved radiation measurements.

Typical values are set by the diagnostic location and device size: detector pixels in compact tokamaks may have major radii of about 0.3-2 m, while pixels associated with cameras or spectrometers on larger devices may lie at about 2-10 m from the toroidal symmetry axis.

NAMES.name: neutron_energy
NAMES.subject: neutron
NAMES.short: Kinetic energy of a fusion-born neutron, used as the energy variable for neutron emission spectra, transport, and detector response calculations.
NAMES.long:
Neutron energy $E_n$ is the kinetic energy carried by a neutron emitted or transported in a fusion plasma. It is the spectral variable for neutron emission spectra and detector response functions, and it separates reaction channels such as DD and DT fusion by their characteristic birth energies. Broad distributions arise from ion thermal motion, energetic-ion reactions, scattering, and transport effects.

Detector response calculations often fold an incident neutron spectrum with an energy-dependent response over $E_n$:

$$
C_k = \int R_k(E_n)\, \frac{d\Phi_n}{dE_n}(E_n)\, dE_n
$$

where $C_k$ is the predicted signal in detector channel $k$, in counts for a fluence calculation or counts s$^{-1}$ for a flux calculation; $R_k(E_n)$ is the channel response, with units counts m$^2$ for this normalization; and $d\Phi_n/dE_n$ is the incident differential fluence spectrum in m$^{-2}$ eV$^{-1}$ or differential flux spectrum in m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$ eV$^{-1}$.

The birth spectrum is computed from two-body fusion kinematics folded with reactant velocity distributions, then modified by scattering and transport before detection. Measurements infer the spectrum using time-of-flight systems, recoil-particle spectrometers, scintillators, activation thresholds, or other energy-sensitive diagnostics together with response-function unfolding. Energy-resolved neutron emission is represented by neutron_energy_spectrum, with reaction-specific fluxes such as [deuterium_deuterium_flux_due_to_thermal_fusion](name:deuterium_deuterium_flux_due_to_thermal_fusion), deuterium_tritium_flux_due_to_thermal_fusion, and [deuterium_tritium_flux_due_to_beam_beam_fusion](name:deuterium_tritium_flux_due_to_beam_beam_fusion).

Typical diagnostic coverage is $1 \times 10^3$-$2 \times 10^7$ eV. Primary thermal DD neutrons occur near $2.45 \times 10^6$ eV, and primary thermal DT neutrons near $1.41 \times 10^7$ eV; thermal broadening is often $10^4$-$10^5$ eV, while energetic-ion populations can produce broader asymmetric tails.

NAMES.name: nitrogen_fraction
NAMES.subject: nitrogen
NAMES.short: Volume-averaged nitrogen concentration: the total nitrogen-particle density over all charge states divided by electron density.
NAMES.long:
Nitrogen fraction is the dimensionless volume-averaged abundance of nitrogen relative to electrons in a plasma. It counts nitrogen nuclei in all ionization states, from neutral $\mathrm{N}^{0}$ through fully stripped $\mathrm{N}^{7+}$, and normalizes their total number density by the local electron density.

Using a volume average over the plasma volume, the fraction is defined as:

$$
f_\mathrm{N} = \left\langle \frac{\sum_{q=0}^{7} n_{\mathrm{N}^{q+}}}{n_e} \right\rangle_V
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{N}^{q+}}$ is the number density of nitrogen with charge state $q$, $q=0$ denotes neutral nitrogen, $q=7$ denotes fully stripped nitrogen, $n_e$ is electron density, and $\langle\cdot\rangle_V$ denotes volume averaging. Fully stripped nitrogen is $\mathrm{N}^{7+}$; there is no $\mathrm{N}^{8+}$ charge state for nitrogen.

In practice, this quantity is inferred from a combination of impurity spectroscopy, charge-exchange recombination measurements when available, bolometric radiation constraints, electron-density measurements, and collisional-radiative or transport modeling to complete the charge-state distribution. Neutral and fully stripped populations can be difficult to observe directly, so their contributions are often inferred from ionization-balance modeling rather than measured as isolated emission features.

Typical values are $10^{-4}$-$10^{-3}$ for trace background nitrogen and $10^{-3}$-$5\times10^{-2}$ during deliberate nitrogen seeding for radiative divertor or edge-cooling control. Larger fractions increase radiated power and fuel dilution and therefore strongly affect plasma performance.

NAMES.name: radiance_at_spectral_line
NAMES.short: Photon radiance of an identified spectral emission line: photon rate per unit area perpendicular to the viewing direction and per unit solid angle, integrated over the wavelength interval assigned to the line.
NAMES.long:
Radiance at a spectral line is the wavelength-integrated spectral photon radiance associated with one identified emission line. It characterizes photon number reaching an observer per unit area perpendicular to the viewing direction and per unit solid angle, not total emitted power or energy radiance.

Let $I_\lambda(\lambda)$ be the calibrated spectral photon radiance. The line radiance $L_\mathrm{line}$ is defined by integrating the continuum-subtracted spectral radiance over the wavelength window assigned to the line:

$$
L_\mathrm{line} = \int_{\lambda_1}^{\lambda_2} \left[I_\lambda(\lambda) - I_{\lambda,\mathrm{bg}}(\lambda)\right] \, d\lambda
$$

where $L_\mathrm{line}$ has units m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$ sr$^{-1}$, $\lambda$ is wavelength in meters, $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$ are the endpoints of the integration window with $\Delta\lambda=\lambda_2-\lambda_1$ in meters, and $I_\lambda$ and $I_{\lambda,\mathrm{bg}}$ have units m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$ sr$^{-1}$ m$^{-1}$. The window is chosen to contain the instrumental and physical line shape while excluding neighboring lines as far as possible; the background term represents continuum emission, stray light, dark signal, or other slowly varying contributions estimated from adjacent wavelengths or from a simultaneous fit. For a gross line integral, the same expression applies with $I_{\lambda,\mathrm{bg}}=0$.

In practice, line radiance is obtained from calibrated spectroscopic measurements. A [spectral calibration factor](name:spectral_calibration_factor_of_spectrometer) $K_\lambda(\lambda)$ converts wavelength-resolved detector signal $C_\lambda(\lambda)$, after subtraction of detector background $C_{\lambda,\mathrm{bg}}(\lambda)$, to spectral photon radiance; the corresponding practical relation is $L_\mathrm{line}=\int_{\lambda_1}^{\lambda_2} K_\lambda(\lambda)[C_\lambda(\lambda)-C_{\lambda,\mathrm{bg}}(\lambda)]\,d\lambda$ over the same line window. Grating spectrometers, filter spectrometers, and charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy systems use this quantity for emission-line strengths; inference of densities, effective charge, or radiated power requires additional atomic-physics and viewing-geometry modeling.

The wavelength-resolved quantity underlying the integral is related to [spectral flux], while [flux at spectral line](name:spectral_flux_of_spectrometer_channel) is the corresponding line-integrated photon-flux analog before radiance normalization or absolute radiance calibration. [Brightness of visible camera](name:brightness_of_visible_camera) is a broadband radiance analog integrated over a camera passband rather than over a single identified line.

Typical visible and near-ultraviolet line radiances in magnetically confined plasmas span about $10^{16}$-$10^{21}$ m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$ sr$^{-1}$ for weak-to-strong steady emission. Bright edge events or active beam and charge-exchange lines can approach $10^{22}$ m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$ sr$^{-1}$, with values depending strongly on species, charge state, electron temperature and density, path length, neutral-beam density for active measurements, and optical passband.

NAMES.name: radiated_power_density
NAMES.short: Local non-negative volumetric rate at which plasma emits electromagnetic radiation, representing radiated power per unit volume.
NAMES.long:
Radiated power density is the local, non-negative volumetric rate at which plasma thermal energy is converted to electromagnetic radiation. It includes continuum, line, recombination, and other photon emission processes that contribute to bolometric radiated power.

The total radiated power associated with a plasma volume is the volume integral of the local emission density:

$$
P_\mathrm{rad} = \int_V p_\mathrm{rad}(\mathbf{x})\,dV
$$

where $P_\mathrm{rad}$ is total radiated power in W, $p_\mathrm{rad}$ is radiated power density in W m$^{-3}$, $\mathbf{x}$ denotes spatial position, and $dV$ is a volume element in m$^3$. For an axisymmetric reconstruction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise when viewed from above, and $Z$ is vertical height, the poloidal-plane volume element is $dV = 2\pi R\,dR\,dZ$; this reduction assumes toroidal symmetry of $p_\mathrm{rad}$.

Bolometer measurements infer this quantity from calibrated line-of-sight signals through an optically thin plasma. For channel $i$, the measured signal is commonly modeled as a path integral, $b_i \approx \int_{\ell_i} G_i(\mathbf{x})\,p_\mathrm{rad}(\mathbf{x})\,dl$, where $b_i$ is the calibrated channel response, $G_i$ is the geometric and instrumental response kernel, $\ell_i$ is the viewing chord, and $dl$ is path length in meters. Tomographic inversion combines many such chords, with regularization and uncertainty estimates, to recover the spatial emission distribution.

Typical local values are about $10^3$-$10^6$ W m$^{-3}$ in relatively low-radiation core plasmas, $10^6$-$10^8$ W m$^{-3}$ in strongly radiating edge, divertor, or impurity-accumulation regions, and near zero outside the emitting plasma within measurement uncertainty.

NAMES.name: radius_of_diagnostic_aperture
NAMES.short: Radius of a circular diagnostic aperture, defined as the distance from the aperture center to its circular edge. It characterizes the opening size used to compute the corresponding aperture area.
NAMES.long:
The radius of a circular diagnostic aperture is the distance from the center of an idealized circular opening to its edge. It is the appropriate size parameter when the entrance aperture, collimating aperture, or sensitive circular region is modeled as a circle; non-circular apertures are characterized by quantities such as [width_of_diagnostic_aperture](name:width_of_diagnostic_aperture).

For an ideal circular aperture, the associated aperture area is

$$
A = \pi r^2
$$

where $r$ is the aperture radius in meters and $A$ is the area_of_diagnostic_aperture in square meters. The corresponding [diameter_of_diagnostic_aperture](name:diameter_of_diagnostic_aperture) is $d = 2r$, where $d$ is the full edge-to-edge distance through the aperture center.

The radius is obtained from mechanical drawings, dimensional metrology, optical inspection, or calibration of the fabricated diagnostic component. For a non-ideal or partially obscured circular opening, an effective radius may be chosen so that the ideal circular area matches the usable open area. The radius contributes to geometric throughput and solid-angle calculations together with the aperture position, orientation, and viewing geometry, but it does not by itself determine the full acceptance.

Representative engineering scales are device- and diagnostic-dependent. Small pinholes or tightly collimated openings may have radii of about 0.0001-0.001 m, while many optical, fiber, or detector apertures use millimeter- to centimeter-scale radii of about 0.001-0.01 m; larger values can occur in wide-aperture systems.

NAMES.name: reference_wavelength_of_spectrometer_channel
NAMES.short: Reference wavelength of a spectrometer channel is the wavelength at which that channel's spectral instrument function has maximum response. It is a peak-position parameter of the channel response, distinct from a calibration reference wavelength and from the wavelength of a physical spectral line.
NAMES.long:
Reference wavelength of a spectrometer channel is the wavelength coordinate at which that channel's spectral instrument function reaches its maximum response. It is an instrument-response property for the channel, not the wavelength of an observed spectral line and not the reference wavelength used to define or check a wavelength calibration. As a wavelength, it is a non-negative spectral coordinate rather than a signed direction-dependent quantity.

Let $G_c(\lambda)$ denote the spectral instrument function of channel $c$ as a function of wavelength $\lambda$. The reference wavelength $\lambda_{\mathrm{ref},c}$ is the peak location:

$$
\lambda_{\mathrm{ref},c} = \operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\lambda} G_c(\lambda)
$$

where $G_c$ may be normalized or unnormalized, because the peak position is unchanged by an overall response scaling. If the response model has multiple local maxima, the reference wavelength denotes the designated principal response peak used to define the channel center.

In practice, $\lambda_{\mathrm{ref},c}$ is obtained from wavelength calibration measurements, an optical or diffraction geometry model, or spectral fitting of known features to a channel response model. For crystal X-ray spectrometers, the nominal wavelength is constrained by the Bragg relation $n\lambda = 2d\sin\theta_B$, where $d$ is the lattice-plane spacing, $\theta_B$ is the Bragg angle, and $n$ is the diffraction order. The related [spectral_width_of_spectrometer_channel](name:spectral_width_of_spectrometer_channel) describes response broadening, while spectral_instrument_function_of_spectrometer_channel describes the full wavelength-dependent response shape.

This quantity should be distinguished from [reference_calibration_wavelength](name:reference_calibration_wavelength_of_spectrometer_channel), which is a fiducial wavelength used to establish or validate a wavelength scale, and from [wavelength_of_spectral_line](name:wavelength_of_spectral_line), which is a physical photon wavelength associated with an atomic, molecular, or ionic transition.

Typical values depend on the spectral band: crystal X-ray spectrometer channels commonly lie in the range $10^{-11}$-$10^{-9}$ m, with many impurity-line measurements near $10^{-10}$-$10^{-9}$ m, while ultraviolet and visible spectrometer channels are typically about $10^{-7}$-$10^{-6}$ m.

NAMES.name: spectral_absorptivity_of_filter
NAMES.short: Dimensionless wavelength-dependent probability that an incident photon is absorbed in a diagnostic filter material rather than transmitted or redirected by other loss channels. It ranges from 0 for no absorption to 1 for complete absorption at the specified wavelength.
NAMES.long:
Spectral absorptivity of a filter is the fraction of incident photons at wavelength $\lambda$ that are absorbed within the filter material. It is dimensionless, bounded by $0 \le A_\lambda \le 1$, and describes the wavelength dependence of filter attenuation rather than a wavelength-integrated response.

For a monochromatic photon population, the absorptivity can be written as a photon balance:

$$
A_\lambda = \frac{N_\mathrm{abs}(\lambda)}{N_\mathrm{inc}(\lambda)} = 1 - T_\lambda - R_\lambda - S_\lambda
$$

where $\lambda$ is wavelength in meters, $N_\mathrm{inc}$ and $N_\mathrm{abs}$ are the incident and absorbed photon counts, $T_\lambda$ is the transmitted photon fraction, $R_\lambda$ is the reflected fraction, and $S_\lambda$ represents other nonabsorbed losses such as scattering out of the accepted beam or escaping fluorescence. For a homogeneous slab of thickness $d$ in meters with linear attenuation coefficient $\mu(\lambda)$ in m$^{-1}$, the unscattered transmitted fraction is often approximated by $T_\lambda \simeq \exp[-\mu(\lambda)d]$; then $A_\lambda \simeq 1-\exp[-\mu(\lambda)d]$ only when reflection, scattering, and escaping secondary radiation are negligible or are intentionally included in the lost-photon category.

Spectral absorptivity is obtained from tabulated or measured optical constants, mass attenuation coefficients, material composition, layer thicknesses, and surface coatings, and may be verified by calibration with known photon spectra. It is defined only over the wavelength interval for which those material properties and calibration data are valid; outside that interval, extrapolated values should be treated as model assumptions rather than measured filter behavior. The corresponding transmission relation is $T_\lambda = 1 - A_\lambda - R_\lambda - S_\lambda$, reducing to $T_\lambda \simeq 1-A_\lambda$ only when the additional nonabsorbed loss channels are negligible.

Typical values span nearly the full range 0-1: thin filters may have absorptivity below 0.01 in their pass band, intermediate attenuation often gives 0.1-0.9, and wavelengths near strong absorption edges or below the filter cutoff can approach 1. Sharp spectral structure can occur near material absorption edges, so neighboring wavelengths may have substantially different absorptivity.

NAMES.name: spectral_refractive_index_of_optical_element
NAMES.short: Wavelength-resolved ratio of the vacuum speed of light to the phase velocity in a diagnostic optical element material, capturing the spectral dispersion required for chromatic transmission and reflection modeling.
NAMES.long:
The spectral refractive index $n(\lambda)$ of an optical element quantifies how the phase velocity of light is reduced relative to vacuum as a function of wavelength $\lambda$. Its wavelength dependence, known as dispersion, governs chromatic aberration, wavelength-dependent Fresnel reflection coefficients, and the focusing and transmission characteristics of lenses, windows, and filters across a diagnostic spectral range.

The defining relation is:

$$
n(\lambda) = \frac{c}{v_\phi(\lambda)}
$$

where $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum and $v_\phi(\lambda)$ is the phase velocity at wavelength $\lambda$. In practice, $n(\lambda)$ is well described by a Sellmeier dispersion relation, $n^2(\lambda) = 1 + \sum_i B_i \lambda^2 / (\lambda^2 - C_i)$, with empirically determined material coefficients $B_i$ and $C_i$ specific to the optical glass or crystal.

The spectral refractive index is evaluated on the same wavelength axis defined by [spectral_wavelength](name:spectral_wavelength_of_optical_element) and is typically sourced from manufacturer material specifications or measured by prism minimum-deviation refractometry or spectroscopic ellipsometry. For infrared optical elements, $n(\lambda)$ is paired with the extinction coefficient to fully characterize the complex optical response governing transmission and reflection. The full dispersion curve constitutes the spectral resolution of the broadband [refractive_index_of_optical_element](name:refractive_index_of_optical_element).

Typical values span $n \approx 1.45$–$1.47$ for fused silica in the UV-visible range, $n \approx 1.5$ for BK7 optical glass, and $n \approx 2.4$ for ZnSe at mid-infrared wavelengths. Compare with [parallel_refractive_index](name:parallel_refractive_index), which describes the refractive index projected along a wave beam directional axis in plasma wave-propagation contexts.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the phase velocity of light in the material is less than the speed of light in vacuum, as holds for all conventional dielectric and metallic optical elements used in fusion plasma diagnostics.

NAMES.name: spectral_wavelength_of_optical_element
NAMES.short: Wavelength coordinate axis defining the spectral sampling grid at which the optical properties or instrument response of a diagnostic optical element are characterized.
NAMES.long:
This quantity specifies the set of photon wavelength values constituting the spectral axis used to sample the wavelength-resolved properties of a diagnostic optical element, such as its transmission, reflectivity, absorption, refractive index, or instrument response function. It applies across a wide range of diagnostic types, from crystal X-ray spectrometers and soft or hard X-ray filter windows to visible-band filter spectrometers, wherever the element's spectral behavior must be characterized on a defined wavelength grid.

The photon wavelength $\lambda$ relates to photon energy $E$ by

$$
\lambda = \frac{hc}{E}
$$

where $h$ is Planck's constant and $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum. For hard X-ray filter materials the grid spans roughly 0.001–0.1 nm; for soft X-ray diagnostics, 0.1–50 nm; for visible-band spectrometers, 380–780 nm.

This spectral coordinate is the companion axis to wavelength-resolved material properties such as [spectral_refractive_index_of_optical_element](name:spectral_refractive_index_of_optical_element) and feeds into the derivation of quantities like [effective_spectral_width_of_spectrometer_channel](name:effective_spectral_width_of_spectrometer_channel). For identifying individual spectral features resolved within this grid, the central rest-frame vacuum wavelength of a transition is given by [wavelength_of_spectral_line](name:wavelength_of_spectral_line).

NAMES.name: spectral_width_of_spectrometer_channel
NAMES.short: Spectral width of a spectrometer channel is the Gaussian standard deviation, expressed as a wavelength interval, of the channel response to monochromatic radiation. It describes instrumental broadening about the channel reference wavelength.
NAMES.long:
Spectral width of a spectrometer channel is the wavelength standard deviation of a Gaussian component of the channel response to monochromatic radiation. It represents the instrumental contribution to line-shape broadening about the [reference wavelength](name:reference_wavelength_of_spectrometer_channel), separate from physical broadening in the emitting plasma. The valid physical domain is $\sigma_\lambda \ge 0$; $\sigma_\lambda = 0$ is the ideal limit of no spectral broadening by that component.

For a Gaussian component $G(\lambda)$ centered at $\lambda_0$, the width is equivalently the square root of the second central moment:

$$
\sigma_\lambda^2 = \frac{\int (\lambda - \lambda_0)^2 G(\lambda)\, d\lambda}{\int G(\lambda)\, d\lambda}
$$

where $\lambda$ and $\lambda_0$ are wavelengths in meters, $\lambda_0$ is the channel reference wavelength, and $G(\lambda)$ is the Gaussian response component expressed with the same amplitude units as the corresponding spectral instrument function. The normalization of $G$ cancels in the ratio, so $\sigma_\lambda$ has units of meters; the Gaussian full width at half maximum is $2\sqrt{2\ln 2}\,\sigma_\lambda$.

In practice, this width is estimated from calibration measurements with narrow spectral lines, from optical response modeling, or by fitting measured spectra while separating source broadening from instrumental broadening. Contributions can include crystal rocking curve, detector spatial resolution mapped into wavelength, aperture geometry, finite source extent, and alignment tolerances. Together with component amplitudes represented by the spectral_factor_of_spectrometer_channel and centers such as the reference wavelength, the widths define Gaussian terms that compose the spectral_instrument_function_of_spectrometer_channel or channel-level [instrument_function_of_spectrometer_channel](name:spectral_width_of_spectrometer_channel).

Typical values range from $10^{-14}$-$10^{-12}$ m for high-resolution x-ray crystal spectrometer channels and $10^{-12}$-$10^{-10}$ m for lower-resolution optical or ultraviolet spectrometer channels. Values should be interpreted relative to the channel reference wavelength and the intrinsic source line width; instrumental widths comparable to or larger than the physical width dominate the measured broadening.

NAMES.name: surface_area_of_filter
NAMES.short: Total true geometric area of the filter window surface that intercepts incoming radiation. For curved windows, this is the material surface area, not merely the planar projected aperture.
NAMES.long:
Surface area of a filter is the true geometric area of the filter-window face exposed to the accepted radiation beam. It describes the size of the intercepting surface and is distinct from [thickness_of_filter](name:thickness_of_filter), which governs attenuation through the material.

For an arbitrarily shaped or curved window, the surface area can be defined by integrating over the exposed surface:

$$
A = \int_U \left| \frac{\partial \mathbf{r}}{\partial u} \times \frac{\partial \mathbf{r}}{\partial v} \right|\,du\,dv
$$

where $A$ is the surface area in m^2, $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ is the position vector of the window surface in meters, and $u$ and $v$ are dimensionless surface parameters spanning the exposed region $U$. For a flat window this reduces to the planar aperture area; for a rectangular clear aperture with side lengths $a$ and $b$ in meters, the area is $ab$.

In practice, the value is obtained from mechanical design dimensions, aperture-mask geometry, optical or mechanical metrology, or a surface model of the installed window. For curved filter windows, the true surface area should be computed from the measured or specified curvature rather than from the projected outline alone. The area scales the intercepted photon rate for a given incident flux density, while the energy-dependent transmission is set primarily by material composition and filter thickness.

Typical values range from 10^{-6}-10^{-4} m^2 for small channel filters and from 10^{-4}-10^{-2} m^2 for larger camera or spectrometer filter windows.

NAMES.name: thickness_of_filter
NAMES.short: Physical thickness of a diagnostic filter window material, which governs the energy-dependent photon attenuation and the effective spectral passband of X-ray detector channels.
NAMES.long:
The filter window thickness is the geometric extent of the absorbing filter material measured along the direction normal to the filter surface, coinciding with the photon beam propagation path. Together with the material composition, it sets the Beer-Lambert transmission spectrum of the filter, controlling the low-energy photon cutoff and shaping the spectral sensitivity of the detector channel.

The photon transmission through a filter of thickness $d$ at photon energy $E$ follows:

$$
T(E) = \exp(-\mu(E)\, d)
$$

where $\mu(E)$ is the energy-dependent linear attenuation coefficient of the filter material in m$^{-1}$ and $d$ is the filter thickness. Increasing $d$ suppresses low-energy photons more strongly, raising the effective energy cutoff of the diagnostic.

The thickness is a fixed hardware parameter established at instrument construction and determined by the required spectral selection. In soft X-ray diagnostics, filter foils span from tens of nanometers to tens of micrometers; hard X-ray diagnostics may use material layers from tens of micrometers to millimeters. The wavelength-resolved photon absorption that results from this thickness is captured by [spectral absorptivity of the filter](name:spectral_absorptivity_of_filter), while the lateral extent of the filter opening is characterized by [radius_of_filter](name:radius_of_filter). The analogous geometric parameter for the dispersing element is [thickness_of_bragg_crystal](name:thickness_of_bragg_crystal).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the filter material thickness is measured from the beam-entry face to the beam-exit face along the direction of photon propagation.

NAMES.name: total_plasma_radiated_power
NAMES.short: Total radiated power from the entire plasma volume, integrated over all photon energies and emission mechanisms, representing the global electromagnetic radiative loss from the plasma.
NAMES.long:
Total plasma radiated power is the aggregate electromagnetic power emitted by the plasma and carried away by photons. It includes continuum and line radiation from all plasma regions included in the physical volume being considered, and is a global loss term in the plasma power balance.

If $\epsilon_\mathrm{rad}(\mathbf{r})$ is the spectral-integrated volumetric radiative emissivity, the total radiated power is

$$
P_\mathrm{rad} = \int_V \epsilon_\mathrm{rad}(\mathbf{r})\, dV
$$

where $V$ is the plasma volume, $\epsilon_\mathrm{rad}$ has units W m$^{-3}$, and $dV$ has units m$^3$.

In experiments, this quantity is commonly inferred from bolometric measurements by reconstructing the spatial emissivity distribution and integrating it over the plasma volume. It may also be computed from radiation models that combine impurity line radiation, recombination radiation, bremsstrahlung, and other relevant photon-emission processes. Related quantities may restrict the integration region, for example to the plasma inside the last closed flux surface, or isolate a specific contribution such as [bremsstrahlung_power](name:bremsstrahlung_power).

Typical values range from $10^4$-$10^6$ W in small or moderate plasmas and from $10^6$-$5 \times 10^7$ W in high-power tokamak plasmas. The radiated fraction of the injected or conducted heating power is often 20-80%, depending strongly on density, impurity content, edge conditions, and detachment state.

NAMES.name: upper_bound_energy_of_detector_pixel
NAMES.short: High-energy edge of the photon spectral acceptance interval for a detector pixel in an X-ray crystal spectrometer. It is the maximum photon energy included in that pixel's bandpass.
NAMES.long:
The upper bound energy of a detector pixel is the largest photon energy accepted within that pixel's spectral bandpass. In a dispersive X-ray crystal spectrometer it marks the high-energy edge of the interval over which photons diffracted by the crystal are assigned to that pixel, complementing the lower bound and bracketing the representative pixel energy.

For a crystal reflection, the high-energy edge is related to the Bragg angle at the corresponding edge of the pixel acceptance:

$$
E_{\mathrm{upper}} = \frac{n h c}{2 d \sin\theta_{\mathrm{upper}}}
$$

where $E_{\mathrm{upper}}$ is in eV, $n$ is the dimensionless diffraction order, $h$ is Planck's constant in eV s, $c$ is the speed of light in $m\,s^{-1}$, $d$ is the lattice-plane spacing in meters, and $\theta_{\mathrm{upper}}$ is the Bragg angle in radians. Equivalently, $n\lambda_{\mathrm{upper}} = 2d\sin\theta_{\mathrm{upper}}$ with photon wavelength $\lambda_{\mathrm{upper}}$ in meters and $E_{\mathrm{upper}} = hc/\lambda_{\mathrm{upper}}$.

In practice this quantity is obtained from the calibrated mapping between detector position and photon energy, using the crystal spacing, diffraction order, spectrometer geometry, and detector pixel extent. Calibration may be refined with known spectral lines, and the resulting bound can include effects from finite pixel size, crystal rocking curve, source extent, alignment uncertainty, and the chosen definition of the pixel response threshold.

Typical upper-bound energies for fusion X-ray crystal spectrometers are 1000-20000 eV. The separation from the corresponding lower bound is often 1-50 eV in high-resolution line spectroscopy and can be larger for broad-band or lower-dispersion configurations.

NAMES.name: upper_photon_energy
NAMES.short: Upper photon energy bound defining the high-energy threshold of an X-ray detector channel spectral sensitivity window.
NAMES.long:
The upper photon energy bound marks the maximum photon energy at which a detector channel registers photon counts, defining the high-energy edge of the band over which photon flux is integrated. Together with [lower_photon_energy](name:lower_photon_energy), it fully specifies the energy band used for spectrally resolved X-ray bremsstrahlung measurements in both soft and hard X-ray diagnostics.

The photon energy $E_\gamma$ relates to radiation frequency $\nu$ and wavelength $\lambda$ through:

$$
E_\gamma = h\nu = \frac{hc}{\lambda}
$$

where $h \approx 4.136 \times 10^{-15}$ eV·s is Planck's constant and $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum.

The upper energy limit is set by detector material properties, filter transmittance, and electronic discriminator thresholds in the pulse-height analyzer. Soft X-ray channel upper bounds span roughly 0.1–10 keV; hard X-ray diagnostic channels extend to tens to hundreds of keV depending on detector type. The analogous threshold for crystal spectrometer cameras is [upper_bound_energy_of_detector_pixel](name:upper_bound_energy_of_detector_pixel).
NAMES.sign: Positive for all physical photon energies, as $E_\gamma = h\nu > 0$ for any non-zero photon frequency.

NAMES.name: upper_wavelength_of_filter
NAMES.short: Upper wavelength limit of the passband transmitted by a diagnostic filter window. It is the long-wavelength, low-photon-energy cutoff of the filter-window transmission band.
NAMES.long:
The upper wavelength of a filter is the long-wavelength boundary of the passband transmitted by a filter window. It is the largest wavelength included by the filter-window transmission criterion and therefore corresponds to the lowest photon energy admitted by that filter passband. Together with [lower_wavelength_of_filter](name:lower_wavelength_of_filter), it defines the wavelength interval of the transmitted band, normally with $\lambda_{\mathrm{lower}} \le \lambda_{\max}$.

The corresponding minimum photon energy is related to the cutoff wavelength by

$$
E_{\min} = \frac{hc}{\lambda_{\max}}
$$

where $\lambda_{\max}$ is the upper wavelength cutoff in meters, $E_{\min}$ is the corresponding photon energy in joules, $h$ is Planck's constant in joule seconds, and $c$ is the speed of light in meters per second.

For a real filter window the spectral transmission edge is gradual rather than perfectly sharp, so the upper wavelength should be interpreted using the stated passband criterion, such as a specified transmission threshold or calibrated edge definition. It is obtained from the filter-window transmission curve, computed from material optical properties and thickness or measured by spectral transmission calibration.

Representative X-ray and soft-X-ray filter-window upper cutoffs are commonly in the range $10^{-11}$-$10^{-8}$ m, depending on filter material, thickness, and the selected transmission criterion. The wavelength-dependent attenuation within and outside the passband is described by [spectral_absorptivity_of_filter](name:spectral_absorptivity_of_filter).

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_bolometer
NAMES.short: Vertical (Z) coordinate of the center of a bolometer detector in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, where R is major radius, phi is toroidal angle, and Z is vertical height.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate of a bolometer is the $Z$ position of the detector center in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The coordinate value is measured in meters relative to the device coordinate origin and locates the detector center above or below the reference midplane.

This coordinate is determined from the diagnostic geometry, typically using mechanical design data, metrology surveys, or alignment calibration. Together with the detector radial coordinate, toroidal angle, aperture position, and viewing direction, it contributes to the geometric definition of a bolometer line of sight or viewing cone, but does not by itself define the full chord geometry.

Typical values are device dependent. Detector centers are commonly near diagnostic ports or the vessel periphery, with $Z$ values of about -2 to 2 m in medium-sized tokamaks and up to roughly -10 to 10 m in large devices.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the detector center lies in the $+Z$ direction, vertically above the coordinate origin.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_camera
NAMES.short: Vertical (Z) coordinate of the center of a camera in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate $Z$ locates the geometric center of a camera — encompassing visible, X-ray, and UV imaging instruments — along the machine symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius from the symmetry axis, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle, and $Z$ is the height measured from the machine midplane with $Z$ increasing upward.

This coordinate is obtained from mechanical survey, laser tracker measurements, or design models of the diagnostic installation referenced to the machine coordinate origin. Together with $R$ and $\phi$, it fully specifies the three-dimensional position of the camera center in the tokamak geometry. The analogous vertical coordinate for general optical elements is given by [vertical_coordinate_of_optical_element](name:vertical_coordinate_of_optical_element), and for diagnostic apertures by [vertical_coordinate_of_diagnostic_aperture](name:vertical_coordinate_of_diagnostic_aperture).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the camera center lies above the machine midplane in the direction of increasing $Z$.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_detector_pixel
NAMES.short: Vertical height Z of the center of a detector pixel in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, where R is major radius and Z is vertical height. It is an absolute machine-geometry coordinate of the pixel center, not a detector-local row index or the active-height span across pixels.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate of a detector pixel is the $Z$ coordinate of the geometric center of an individual pixel of a radiation-imaging detector (such as an X-ray camera or crystal spectrometer) in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle increasing counter-clockwise viewed from above, and $Z$ is vertical height. It is an absolute machine-geometry coordinate measured from the $Z=0$ reference plane, distinct from any detector-local active-height coordinate, row index, or the full vertical extent of the pixel.

Together with the corresponding radial and toroidal coordinates of the same pixel center, this quantity fixes the spatial location of each sensing element, which in turn defines the viewing geometry used to relate detected radiation to its plasma source region.

Typical absolute values are set by the diagnostic installation height and commonly lie within $-2$ to $2$ m for medium-sized tokamaks, extending to several meters in larger devices. Differences in $Z$ between neighboring pixel centers are much smaller, of order $0.001$ to $0.1$ m, set by pixel pitch and detector orientation.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the pixel center lies above the $Z=0$ reference plane, displaced in the $+\hat{Z}$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: wavelength_of_detector_pixel
NAMES.short: Photon wavelength assigned to each detector pixel of an X-ray crystal spectrometer by the Bragg diffraction geometry of the dispersing crystal.
NAMES.long:
In an X-ray crystal spectrometer, each detector pixel intercepts photons diffracted at a specific angle by the Bragg crystal, and this angle uniquely determines the photon wavelength. The wavelength varies primarily along the principal dispersion direction of the detector, with a secondary dependence across the orthogonal direction arising from the elliptical curvature of iso-wavelength surfaces produced by curved-crystal geometry.

The per-pixel wavelength follows Bragg's law:

$$
\lambda = \frac{2d\sin\theta}{n}
$$

where $d$ is the interplanar spacing of the diffracting crystal planes, $\theta$ is the local Bragg angle at the pixel position in the spectrometer focal plane, and $n$ is the integer diffraction order.

The wavelength map is computed from the spectrometer geometry — crystal curvature, crystal-to-detector distance, and pixel coordinates — and calibrated against known spectral emission lines; the reference diffraction wavelength at the nominal crystal orientation is described by bragg_wavelength. Pixel-by-pixel energy bounds on the spectral acceptance window are provided by [lower_bound_energy_of_detector_pixel](name:lower_bound_energy_of_detector_pixel) and [upper_bound_energy_of_detector_pixel](name:upper_bound_energy_of_detector_pixel). Typical wavelengths for fusion-relevant X-ray impurity emission lines (helium-like argon, titanium, or iron charge states) fall in the range 0.1–1 nm.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the wavelength is assigned at a positive Bragg diffraction angle from the crystal surface, which is satisfied for all physically detected photons.

NAMES.name: wavelength_of_spectral_line
NAMES.short: Central rest-frame vacuum wavelength of an atomic, ionic, molecular, or nuclear spectral emission or absorption line. It is set by the transition energy between quantum states and identifies the unshifted physical line.
NAMES.long:
Wavelength of a spectral line is the central vacuum wavelength $\lambda_0$ of the photon associated with a transition between two quantum states, evaluated in the rest frame of the emitting or absorbing species. It is a property of the transition itself, separate from observed wavelength shifts, broadening, field-induced splitting, and instrumental response.

The rest wavelength is set by the transition energy:

$$
\lambda_0 = \frac{h c}{|E_u - E_l|}
$$

where $\lambda_0$ is the vacuum wavelength in meters, $h$ is the Planck constant in joule seconds, $c$ is the speed of light in meters per second, and $E_u$ and $E_l$ are the upper- and lower-state energies in joules.

In spectroscopy, $\lambda_0$ is usually taken from evaluated atomic, molecular, or nuclear transition data, or from fitted line centers after wavelength calibration and correction to vacuum wavelength. For an observed line center $\lambda_{\mathrm{obs}}$ in meters, the non-relativistic Doppler relation is $(\lambda_{\mathrm{obs}}-\lambda_0)/\lambda_0 \approx v_{\mathrm{los}}/c$ for $|v_{\mathrm{los}}| \ll c$, where $v_{\mathrm{los}}$ is in meters per second and is positive when the source recedes from the observer, increasing the observed wavelength. Thermal Doppler Gaussian width scales as $\sigma_\lambda/\lambda_0 \approx \sqrt{k_B T_s/(m_s c^2)}$, where $\sigma_\lambda$ is in meters, $T_s$ is the species temperature in kelvin, and $m_s$ is the particle mass in kilograms; equivalently use $\sqrt{T_s/(m_s c^2)}$ when $T_s$ is expressed as an energy.

The quantity is not limited to a particular spectral band. Lines used in plasma spectroscopy commonly span about $1\times10^{-11}$-$1\times10^{-5}$ m, including soft-x-ray lines near $1\times10^{-10}$-$1\times10^{-9}$ m, extreme-ultraviolet and ultraviolet lines near $1\times10^{-8}$-$4\times10^{-7}$ m, visible lines near $4\times10^{-7}$-$7\times10^{-7}$ m, and near-infrared lines near $7\times10^{-7}$-$1\times10^{-5}$ m; other atomic, molecular, or nuclear transitions can lie outside these ranges.

NAMES.name: width_of_hard_xray_detector
NAMES.short: Full physical width of a hard X-ray detector aperture measured along the local X1 direction of the detector frame (X1, X2, X3). It is one rectangular-aperture dimension used with the orthogonal height.
NAMES.long:
Width of a hard X-ray detector is the full clear aperture extent along the local detector-frame axis $\hat{X}_1$ in the detector frame $(\hat{X}_1, \hat{X}_2, \hat{X}_3)$. Together with the orthogonal height along $\hat{X}_2$, it defines the rectangular detector opening used in geometric acceptance calculations. As a length, it is a non-negative scalar and does not encode the orientation sign of the local axis.

For two small, planar, mutually visible rectangular apertures separated in free space, the detector width enters the usual small-aperture etendue approximation through the detector area:

$$
G \simeq \frac{(w_\mathrm{det} h_\mathrm{det})(w_\mathrm{ap} h_\mathrm{ap})}{L^2}\cos\alpha_\mathrm{det}\cos\alpha_\mathrm{ap}
$$

where $G$ is the geometric etendue in m$^2$ sr, $w_\mathrm{det}$ is this detector width in m, $h_\mathrm{det}$ is the detector height in m, $w_\mathrm{ap}$ and $h_\mathrm{ap}$ are the corresponding opposing-aperture dimensions in m, $L$ is the center-to-center separation in m, and $\alpha_\mathrm{det}$ and $\alpha_\mathrm{ap}$ are the angles between each aperture normal and the connecting ray in radians. The approximation assumes aperture dimensions are small compared with $L$, the apertures are approximately planar, the centers and normals are sufficiently aligned that one representative separation and angle can be used, and vignetting or other obstructions are negligible.

In practice the value is taken from the mechanical design, metrology, or detector calibration geometry as the distance between the clear inner aperture edges projected onto $\hat{X}_1$. If edge chamfers, masks, or partial obstructions are present, the relevant value is the effective clear width used by the line-of-sight or acceptance model.

Typical hard-X-ray detector aperture widths are 0.001-0.05 m, with millimeter-scale values common for tightly collimated channels and centimeter-scale values used for larger scintillator or camera openings.

NAMES.name: x1_coordinate_of_bragg_crystal
NAMES.short: X1 coordinate of a Bragg-crystal outline vertex, measured along the first axis of the crystal-local Cartesian (X1, X2) frame. Together with the corresponding X2 coordinate, it defines the crystal cross-section boundary used in diffraction geometry.
NAMES.long:
The $x_1$ coordinate of a Bragg crystal is the signed scalar position of an outline vertex along the first axis of the crystal-local Cartesian $(X_1, X_2)$ frame. Paired with the corresponding [x2 coordinate of a Bragg crystal](name:x2_coordinate_of_bragg_crystal), it identifies one vertex of the crystal cross-section boundary; consecutive paired vertices define the ordered polygonal outline of the crystal aperture.

For a vertex with position vector $\mathbf{r}$ in the crystal-local Cartesian $(X_1, X_2)$ frame, the coordinate is the projection of the displacement from the local origin onto the positive $X_1$ axis:

$$
x_1 = (\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}_0) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}_{X_1}
$$

where $\mathbf{r}_0$ is the local-frame origin and $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{X_1}$ is the unit vector along the positive $X_1$ direction.

Crystal outline coordinates are usually obtained from mechanical design drawings, manufacturer specifications, or optical and coordinate-measuring metrology of the mounted crystal. The outline specifies the physical aperture and illuminated crystal extent in ray tracing or spectrometer geometry models, but it does not by itself determine whether the Bragg condition is satisfied; diffraction also depends on lattice spacing, incidence angle, diffraction order, and X-ray wavelength.

Typical coordinate magnitudes for Bragg-crystal spectrometers range from 0.001-0.10 m, with millimeter-scale values for small crystals and centimeter-scale values for larger analyzer crystals or extended mounts.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the vertex displacement from the local origin has a component along the positive $X_1$ axis of the crystal-local Cartesian $(X_1, X_2)$ frame.

NAMES.name: x1_coordinate_of_filter
NAMES.short: X1 coordinate of a vertex or sampled point on a diagnostic filter boundary in the local planar (X1, X2) frame. It gives the projection of that boundary point along the first in-plane basis direction and is distinct from quantities that specifically name a separate filter-window component.
NAMES.long:
The $x_1$ coordinate of a filter is the signed in-plane position of a point on the boundary of the filtering element or its transmissive footprint, expressed in a local planar $(X_1, X_2)$ frame with basis $(\hat{X}_1, \hat{X}_2)$. It describes the filter boundary itself; [x1_coordinate_of_filter_window](name:x1_coordinate_of_filter_window) should be used when the intended object is a separately identified filter-window component.

For a boundary point at position $\mathbf{r}_v$ and a filter-frame origin at $\mathbf{r}_0$, the coordinate is the projection onto the first local basis direction:

$$
x_1 = (\mathbf{r}_v - \mathbf{r}_0) \cdot \hat{X}_1
$$

where $\hat{X}_1$ is the first in-plane unit vector of the local planar $(X_1, X_2)$ frame. The origin is normally a defined reference point of the filter plane, such as a geometric center or mechanical fiducial, while $\hat{X}_1$ and $\hat{X}_2$ span the plane and are fixed by the diagnostic mechanical definition or calibration fiducials.

The coordinate is obtained from mechanical drawings, CAD geometry, survey metrology, or calibration of the filter aperture used in the X-ray diagnostic line of sight. Together with the corresponding [x2_coordinate_of_filter](name:x2_coordinate_of_filter), it defines a polygonal or sampled boundary used to compute geometric transmission, vignetting, and ray intersections through the filter.

Typical absolute coordinate excursions are about $10^{-4}$-$10^{-2}$ m for compact soft-X-ray filter apertures and can reach a few $10^{-2}$ m for larger spectrometer filter openings.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the boundary point lies in the $+\hat{X}_1$ direction from the origin of the local planar $(X_1, X_2)$ frame.

NAMES.name: x1_coordinate_of_optical_element
NAMES.short: X1 coordinate of an optical element's outline vertices or fiber-center positions in the element-local two-dimensional Cartesian (X1, X2) frame.
NAMES.long:
The X1 coordinate locates a point — such as an aperture outline vertex, a detector-face boundary vertex, or an optical fiber center — along the first axis of the element-local two-dimensional Cartesian (X1, X2) frame. This local frame is defined independently for each optical element, with its origin placed at a reference feature of the component (for example, a grating summit, a detector center, or a fiber bundle centroid) and its axes aligned with the element's principal directions.

Together with the companion X2 coordinate, the (X1, X2) pair describes the planar geometry of optical elements such as aperture boundaries, detector active areas, grating outlines, or fiber spatial layouts. Closed polygons formed from ordered (X1, X2) vertex pairs define the collimating or sensitive area used in etendue calculations and line-of-sight reconstruction. Analogous coordinates for other diagnostic components follow the same convention: [x1_coordinate_of_aperture](name:x1_coordinate_of_aperture) and [x1_coordinate_of_diagnostic_aperture](name:x1_coordinate_of_filter) describe collimating aperture outlines, while [x1_coordinate_of_soft_xray_detector](name:x1_coordinate_of_soft_xray_detector) covers detector-face vertices.
