Typical values span the physical dimensions of the optical element, ranging from fractions of a millimeter for individual optical fiber cores to several centimeters for large detector faces or diffraction grating surfaces.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the point lies in the positive X1 direction from the origin of the element-local (X1, X2) coordinate frame.

NAMES.name: x1_coordinate_of_soft_xray_detector
NAMES.short: X1 coordinate of the soft X-ray detector outline vertices in the detector-local Cartesian (X1, X2) frame, used to define the polygonal detector boundary for etendue and line-of-sight calculations.
NAMES.long:
The X1 coordinate specifies the position of each vertex of the soft X-ray detector's polygonal outline along the first axis of the detector-local Cartesian (X1, X2) frame. Together with the companion [X2 coordinate](name:x2_coordinate_of_soft_xray_detector), these vertex coordinates fully define the cross-sectional shape of the detector aperture. The complete outline is required to compute the etendue — the geometric throughput governing the detector's luminous acceptance — and to trace the lines of sight that determine what fraction of plasma soft X-ray emission reaches the channel.

For a polygonal detector with $N$ vertices, the outline is the ordered sequence of $(X1_i,\,X2_i)$ pairs for $i = 1,\ldots,N$, with the polygon closed by returning to the first vertex. The detector-local (X1, X2) axes are attached to the detector face; their orientation relative to the machine cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame is defined by the detector's mounting geometry. Typical soft X-ray detector face dimensions range from a few millimeters to several centimeters. The analogous first-axis coordinate for a neutron detector is [x1_coordinate_of_neutron_detector](name:x1_coordinate_of_neutron_detector).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the vertex is displaced in the positive X1 direction from the origin of the detector-local Cartesian (X1, X2) frame.

NAMES.name: x2_coordinate_of_diagnostic_aperture
NAMES.short: X2 coordinate of a diagnostic aperture outline vertex in the local aperture-plane (X1, X2) frame. Together with the X1 coordinate, it defines the transverse boundary used in sight-line, acceptance, and etendue geometry.
NAMES.long:
The $x_2$ coordinate of a diagnostic aperture is the signed position of an outline vertex along the second axis of the local aperture-plane $(X_1, X_2)$ frame. Paired with the corresponding $x_1$ coordinate, it specifies the transverse polygon or curved boundary that limits the rays accepted by an aperture, fiber entrance, detector face, or similar diagnostic opening.

For a polygonal aperture outline, the paired vertex coordinates determine the enclosed geometric area through the shoelace relation:

$$
A = \frac{1}{2}\left|\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left(x_{1,i}x_{2,i+1} - x_{1,i+1}x_{2,i}\right)\right|
$$

where $N$ is the number of outline vertices, cyclic indexing is used so vertex $N+1$ is vertex $1$, and $x_{1,i}$ and $x_{2,i}$ are measured in meters. The resulting area $A$ is in square meters and is one input to aperture acceptance and etendue calculations.

In practice, $x_2$ values are obtained from mechanical drawings, optical design models, metrology of aperture plates or fiber bundles, or calibration of detector geometry. The coordinate is interpreted only relative to the local aperture-plane $(X_1, X_2)$ frame, whose origin and axis directions are defined by the diagnostic geometry.

Typical magnitudes range from $10^{-5}$-$10^{-1}$ m, from tens of micrometers for small fiber cores to millimeters or centimeters for pinholes, slits, detector faces, and camera apertures.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the vertex is displaced in the $+X_2$ direction of the local aperture-plane $(X_1, X_2)$ frame.

NAMES.name: x2_coordinate_of_filter
NAMES.short: X2 coordinate of filter window outline vertices in the local orthogonal (X1, X2) plane frame, giving the second-axis positions that jointly define the filter aperture boundary shape.
NAMES.long:
The filter aperture boundary is represented as a closed polygon of vertices whose positions are specified in a local orthogonal 2D coordinate system $(X_1, X_2)$ attached to the filter element. The X2 coordinate provides the second-axis component of each boundary vertex, and together with [x1_coordinate_of_filter](name:x1_coordinate_of_filter), fully defines the transverse cross-sectional outline of the filter window. This planar boundary geometry is used to compute the étendue, solid angle, and angular acceptance of the associated X-ray diagnostic channel.

The local $(X_1, X_2)$ frame is defined in the plane of the filter element; both axes form a right-handed orthogonal pair with the origin fixed to the filter element mounting reference. Filter windows in X-ray diagnostics span dimensions from roughly 0.001–0.05 m, so outline vertex coordinates lie within that range of the local frame origin. The identical coordinate convention governs the aperture outline described by [x2_coordinate_of_diagnostic_aperture](name:x2_coordinate_of_diagnostic_aperture), while the closely related [x2_coordinate_of_filter_window](name:x2_coordinate_of_filter_window) applies the same scheme to a more narrowly scoped filter-window object.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the vertex position lies in the positive $X_2$ direction from the local frame origin.

NAMES.name: x2_coordinate_of_filter_window
NAMES.short: X2 coordinate of the filter window outline vertices in the local (X1, X2) frame, jointly defining the aperture boundary shape with the paired X1 vertex positions.
NAMES.long:
The X2 coordinate gives the positions of the filter window outline vertices along the second axis of the local two-dimensional $(X_1, X_2)$ coordinate frame attached to the filter window assembly. Together with the [X1 coordinate](name:x1_coordinate_of_filter_window), these vertex positions jointly specify the full irregular polygonal boundary of the filter aperture.

The outline is constructed from a set of $N$ vertex pairs $(x_{1,i},\, x_{2,i})$, $i = 1, \ldots, N$, connected sequentially to close the boundary polygon:

$$
\partial A = \{(x_{1,i},\, x_{2,i}) : i = 1, \ldots, N\}
$$

where each $(x_{1,i}, x_{2,i})$ is a vertex of the closed outline and $\partial A$ denotes the filter aperture boundary. This representation applies when the window shape is described as an irregular polygon; simpler geometries such as rectangles or circles may instead be parameterized by scalar width or radius descriptors.

The filter window geometry is characterized during instrument fabrication or calibration by direct dimensional measurement of the filter frame. For X-ray cameras and crystal spectrometers, the precise aperture shape determines the acceptance solid angle and enters etendue calculations that link measured count rates to source brightness, making accurate vertex coordinates essential for absolute photometric calibration. The analogous role for collimating apertures is served by [x2_coordinate_of_diagnostic_aperture](name:x2_coordinate_of_diagnostic_aperture).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the outline vertex lies in the positive $X_2$ direction from the local coordinate origin of the filter window frame.

NAMES.name: x2_coordinate_of_hard_xray_detector
NAMES.short: Signed coordinate of a hard X-ray detector outline vertex along the X2 axis in the detector-local Cartesian (X1, X2) frame.
NAMES.long:
The X2 coordinate of a hard X-ray detector is the signed position of a detector-outline vertex along the second axis of the detector-local Cartesian $(X_1, X_2)$ frame. Together with the companion x1_coordinate_of_hard_xray_detector, it defines the detector outline in the local plane; the value is relative to the detector-local origin and axis orientation, not to an absolute machine position.

For a vertex displacement from the detector-local origin, the coordinate is the scalar projection onto the local X2 direction:

$$
x_2 = \Delta \mathbf{r}_v \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}_2
$$

where $x_2$ is the X2 coordinate in meters, $\Delta \mathbf{r}_v$ is the vector from the detector-local origin to the vertex in meters, and $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_2$ is the dimensionless unit vector along the positive X2 axis of the detector-local Cartesian $(X_1, X_2)$ frame.

In practice, X2 vertex coordinates are obtained from the detector mechanical design, survey information, or geometry model. Paired with X1 coordinates, they specify the polygonal detector outline used in geometric area, etendue, and sight-line acceptance calculations. The same local-outline concept is used for related diagnostic aperture and detector coordinates such as [x2_coordinate_of_diagnostic_aperture](name:x2_coordinate_of_diagnostic_aperture) and [x2_coordinate_of_soft_xray_detector](name:x2_coordinate_of_soft_xray_detector).

Typical magnitudes are set by the physical detector face and the chosen local origin. Compact hard-X-ray detector outlines are often millimeter-to-centimeter scale, with representative coordinate magnitudes around 0.001-0.1 m; exact values are device-specific and may be positive or negative within the local outline.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the vertex displacement from the detector-local origin has a component in the positive X2 direction of the detector-local Cartesian $(X_1, X_2)$ frame.

NAMES.name: x2_coordinate_of_optical_element
NAMES.short: Coordinate of a point on an optical element measured along the second axis of the element's local planar (X1, X2) frame. It is the signed in-plane displacement from the local origin resolved on the X2 basis direction.
NAMES.long:
The x2 coordinate of an optical element is the signed distance, within the element's local plane, from the element's local origin to a specified point resolved along the second local in-plane axis. The coordinate is defined in a local planar $(X_1,X_2)$ frame with origin $O$ and basis $(\hat{\mathbf{X}}_1,\hat{\mathbf{X}}_2)$ attached to the optical element, rather than in a global laboratory frame.

For an orthonormal local planar basis, the coordinate is the projection of the point displacement onto the second basis direction:

$$
x_2 = (\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}_O) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{X}}_2
$$

where $\mathbf{r}$ is the position vector of the point, $\mathbf{r}_O$ is the position vector of the local origin, and $\hat{\mathbf{X}}_2$ is the unit vector along the local $X_2$ axis.

In practice, this coordinate is obtained from mechanical drawings, optical metrology, or calibration fits by expressing measured point positions in the element's local planar $(X_1,X_2)$ frame. The same definition applies whether the point represents a fiber center, an aperture-outline vertex, a detector-face point, or another geometrical feature of an optical component.

There is no universal physical range because the value is set by the transverse size of the particular optical element and by the chosen local origin. Meaningful values normally lie within the element's active or mechanical aperture; compact diagnostic optics may have absolute coordinates of order $10^{-4}$-$10^{-1}$ m, while larger optical elements can extend beyond this range.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the displacement from the local origin to the point has a component in the $+\hat{\mathbf{X}}_2$ direction of the optical element's local planar $(\hat{\mathbf{X}}_1,\hat{\mathbf{X}}_2)$ basis.

NAMES.name: x2_coordinate_of_soft_xray_detector
NAMES.short: Signed coordinate along the X2 axis of a vertex on the soft X-ray detector boundary in the detector-local Cartesian (X1, X2) frame. Together with the X1 coordinate, it defines the detector boundary used for line-of-sight acceptance and etendue calculations, distinct from any diagnostic aperture.
NAMES.long:
The $x_2$ coordinate of a soft X-ray detector is the signed in-plane position of a point on the detector boundary in the detector-local Cartesian $(X_1, X_2)$ frame with orthonormal basis $(\hat{\mathbf{X}}_1, \hat{\mathbf{X}}_2)$. Together with the [soft-X-ray detector $x_1$ coordinate](name:x1_coordinate_of_soft_xray_detector), it specifies the detector boundary; this detector surface is distinct from the diagnostic aperture boundary described, for example, by the [diagnostic-aperture $x_2$ coordinate](name:x2_coordinate_of_diagnostic_aperture).

The coordinate is the scalar projection of the detector-boundary point relative to the detector-local origin onto the local $X_2$ direction:

$$
x_2 = (\mathbf{r}_d - \mathbf{r}_{d,0}) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{X}}_2
$$

where $\mathbf{r}_d$ is the detector-boundary point position vector in m, $\mathbf{r}_{d,0}$ is the detector-local origin position vector in m, and $\hat{\mathbf{X}}_2$ is a dimensionless unit vector.

Detector boundary coordinates are obtained from mechanical design, survey metrology, CAD models, or alignment calibration of the diagnostic head. In ray tracing and etendue calculations, the detector boundary defines the detector integration surface $A_d$, while the diagnostic aperture defines a separate aperture integration surface $A_a$; a common geometric etendue relation is $G = \int_{A_d}\int_{A_a} \cos\alpha_d\cos\alpha_a\, |\mathbf{r}_d-\mathbf{r}_a|^{-2}\, dA_d\, dA_a$, where $\mathbf{r}_d$ and $\mathbf{r}_a$ are detector and aperture surface-point position vectors in m, $dA_d$ and $dA_a$ are differential surface elements in m^2, and the cosine factors are dimensionless projections onto the two surface normals.

Typical signed coordinate values are about -0.01-0.01 m for compact diode or chip-scale soft X-ray detector elements and can extend to about -0.05-0.05 m for larger detector assemblies, depending on the chosen detector-local origin.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the detector-boundary point is displaced in the $+\hat{\mathbf{X}}_2$ direction of the detector-local Cartesian $(X_1, X_2)$ frame.

NAMES.name: cold_neutral_temperature
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Translational kinetic temperature of the low-energy neutral atom component, represented by the narrow Doppler-broadened contribution to visible spectral emission. It characterizes the cold population separately from hotter charge-exchange or beam-related neutrals.
NAMES.long:
Cold neutral temperature is the translational kinetic temperature of the low-energy neutral atom population contributing to an observed emission line. In two-component Doppler models it corresponds to the narrow Gaussian component, while the broad component is associated with hotter neutrals described by [hot_neutral_temperature](name:hot_neutral_temperature). It is a component-resolved quantity and is distinct from a state- or population-averaged [neutral_state_temperature](name:neutral_state_temperature).

For a non-relativistic Maxwellian neutral distribution with isotropic velocity spread along the line of sight, the Doppler full width at half maximum of a spectral line is related to the cold neutral temperature by:

$$
T_\mathrm{cold} = \frac{m c^2}{8 \ln 2\, e}\left(\frac{\Delta\lambda_\mathrm{D,FWHM}}{\lambda_0}\right)^2
$$

where $m$ is the neutral atom mass, $c$ is the speed of light, $e$ is the elementary charge, $\lambda_0$ is the rest wavelength, and $\Delta\lambda_\mathrm{D,FWHM}$ is the Doppler contribution to the fitted narrow-line full width after other broadening mechanisms have been accounted for. The result is expressed in eV.

In practice this quantity is inferred by fitting visible emission-line shapes with one or more components. Instrumental resolution, fine-structure effects, Zeeman or Stark broadening, and line blending must be modeled or deconvolved so that the remaining narrow width represents neutral thermal motion. If the neutral distribution is non-Maxwellian, strongly anisotropic, or sufficiently energetic for relativistic corrections to matter, the fitted value should be interpreted as an effective cold-component temperature rather than a true thermodynamic temperature.

Typical cold neutral temperatures in edge and divertor spectroscopy are of order 0.1-10 eV, depending on recycling conditions, isotope mass, ionization mean free path, and local coupling to the plasma. Values much smaller than the associated [hot_neutral_temperature](name:hot_neutral_temperature) indicate a clear separation between recycled thermal neutrals and hotter charge-exchange or beam-related populations.

NAMES.name: cold_neutral_velocity
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Line-of-sight projected velocity of the cold neutral atom population inferred from an emission-line Doppler shift.
NAMES.long:
Cold neutral velocity is the scalar projection of the mean velocity of the cold neutral atom population along a specified spectrometer line of sight. The cold component is the relatively narrow, low-energy neutral emission component, complementary to [hot_neutral_velocity](name:hot_neutral_velocity), with the corresponding thermal width characterized by [cold_neutral_temperature](name:cold_neutral_temperature).

For nonrelativistic Doppler shifts, the line-of-sight velocity is determined from the signed centroid shift of the cold spectral component:

$$
v_\mathrm{los} = c\,\frac{\Delta\lambda_\mathrm{los}}{\lambda_0}
$$

where $v_\mathrm{los}$ is the line-of-sight velocity in m.s^-1, $\Delta\lambda_\mathrm{los}$ is the signed wavelength shift in meters after applying the line-of-sight orientation convention, $\lambda_0$ is the rest or central [wavelength_of_spectral_line](name:wavelength_of_spectral_line) in meters, and $c$ is the speed of light in m.s^-1. With this definition, $\Delta\lambda_\mathrm{los}>0$ corresponds to motion from the first line-of-sight point toward the second; depending on viewing geometry, this may correspond to either the measured redshift or its negative.

In practice this quantity is obtained from the calibrated centroid of the cold component of an atomic emission line. Spectral modeling separates this centroid shift from instrumental calibration offsets, line blending, thermal broadening, and any broader hot-neutral contribution; the result is only the velocity component projected along the observed line of sight, not the full neutral flow vector.

Typical magnitudes in edge and divertor neutral spectroscopy are of order 1,000-30,000 m.s^-1, with signed values near zero possible when the neutral flow is weak or nearly perpendicular to the line of sight.
NAMES.sign: Positive when cold neutral atoms move from the first defining point of the line of sight toward the second defining point.

NAMES.name: hot_neutral_temperature
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Kinetic temperature of the energetic (hot) component of the neutral atom population, inferred from the broad Doppler profile of visible spectral line emission.
NAMES.long:
The hot neutral temperature characterizes the energetic component of the neutral atom population in the plasma edge and scrape-off layer, distinguished from the thermal bulk described by [cold_neutral_temperature](name:cold_neutral_temperature). Hot neutrals arise primarily from charge exchange reactions between thermal ions and cold neutrals, or from energetic recycling at plasma-facing surfaces, producing a fast atom population carrying significantly more kinetic energy than the bulk.

The temperature is inferred by fitting the observed spectral emission line profile to a two-Gaussian model. The broad Gaussian component corresponds to the hot neutral sub-population, with its half-width governed by the Doppler broadening relation:

$$
\Delta\lambda_D = \frac{\lambda_0}{c}\sqrt{\frac{8\ln 2 \, k_B T_{\rm hot}}{m_n}}
$$

where $\lambda_0$ is the rest-frame line center wavelength of the emission transition, $c$ is the speed of light, $k_B$ is the Boltzmann constant, $T_{\rm hot}$ is the hot neutral temperature, and $m_n$ is the neutral atom mass.

Measurements are obtained from visible spectrometer channels recording hydrogen isotope Balmer series emission, where spectral line fitting resolves the hot and cold sub-populations simultaneously. Polarization spectroscopy channels provide access to both the temperature and the line-of-sight Doppler shift, the latter captured in [hot_neutral_velocity](name:hot_neutral_velocity).

Typical values for the hot component span a few eV to approximately 50 eV in edge and scrape-off layer plasmas, substantially above the cold bulk neutral temperature of approximately 0.1–1 eV, and bounded above by the local ion temperature.

NAMES.name: hot_neutral_velocity
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Line-of-sight projected velocity of the energetic (hot) neutral atom population, inferred from the Doppler centroid shift of the broad emission component in visible polarization spectroscopy.
NAMES.long:
The hot neutral population consists of energetic neutral atoms — produced primarily by charge-exchange reactions between fast ions and cold neutrals or by beam-neutral interactions — whose velocity distribution yields a broad Doppler profile overlaid on the narrower thermal (cold) component. The line-of-sight component $v_\mathrm{hot}$ represents the bulk flow of this energetic neutral ensemble along the diagnostic chord, distinguishing it from [cold_neutral_velocity](name:cold_neutral_velocity) for the thermal population; the associated kinetic spread is captured by [hot_neutral_temperature](name:hot_neutral_temperature).

The centroid velocity is extracted from the observed wavelength shift of the emission line:

$$
v_\mathrm{hot} = c \, \frac{\lambda_\mathrm{obs} - \lambda_0}{\lambda_0}
$$

where $c$ is the speed of light, $\lambda_\mathrm{obs}$ is the centroid wavelength of the hot neutral spectral component, and $\lambda_0$ is the rest wavelength of the observed line.

Measurement requires fitting the observed line profile from a visible polarization spectrometer with a multi-Gaussian model that separates the broad hot and narrow cold neutral contributions; the centroid shift of the broad component yields $v_\mathrm{hot}$. Hot neutrals sourced from fast-ion charge exchange carry line-of-sight velocities spanning tens to hundreds of km/s, substantially exceeding those of cold recycled neutrals.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the hot neutral atoms are moving from the first to the second point along the line of sight.

NAMES.name: neutron_flux_due_to_beam_thermal_fusion
NAMES.subject: neutron
NAMES.short: Beam-thermal neutron emission rate from fusion reactions between injected fast ions and thermal plasma ions, summed over DD, DT, and TT channels.
NAMES.long:
Neutron flux due to beam-thermal fusion is the volume-integrated neutron emission rate produced when fast neutral-beam ions fuse with thermal ions in the plasma. It excludes purely thermal-thermal and beam-beam reactions, and counts emitted neutrons rather than fusion events, so DD branching and TT neutron multiplicity are included.

A channel-resolved expression for the rate is:

$$
\Phi_n^{\mathrm{BT}} = \sum_{a,b\in\{D,T\}} \int_V dV \int d^3 v_a \int d^3 v_b\, f_a^{\mathrm{beam}}(\mathbf r,\mathbf v_a) f_b^{\mathrm{th}}(\mathbf r,\mathbf v_b)\, \sigma_{ab}(v_{\mathrm{rel}})\, v_{\mathrm{rel}}\, Y_{ab}(v_{\mathrm{rel}})
$$

where $\Phi_n^{\mathrm{BT}}$ is the neutron emission rate in s$^{-1}$, equivalent to Hz; $a$ is the fast beam isotope and $b$ is the thermal target isotope; $f_a^{\mathrm{beam}}$ and $f_b^{\mathrm{th}}$ are velocity-space densities normalized to number density in m$^{-3}$; $\sigma_{ab}$ is the fusion cross-section in m$^2$; $v_{\mathrm{rel}}=|\mathbf v_a-\mathbf v_b|$ is the relative speed in m s$^{-1}$; and $Y_{ab}$ is the neutron yield per reaction. For DT, $Y_{DT}=1$; for TT, $Y_{TT}=2$ because two neutrons are emitted per reaction; for DD, $Y_{DD}$ is the energy-dependent branching fraction of the neutron-producing branch.

In practice this rate is computed from fast-ion distributions, thermal ion densities and temperatures, isotope composition, and fusion reactivity data. It is constrained experimentally by neutron monitors, activation systems, neutron cameras, and neutron spectroscopy, often using beam modulation or transport modeling to separate beam-thermal emission from [thermal_neutron_flux](name:total_neutron_source_rate_due_to_thermal_fusion) and other neutron-producing components. The channel-resolved components include [deuterium_deuterium_flux_due_to_beam_thermal_fusion](name:deuterium_deuterium_flux_due_to_beam_thermal_fusion), [deuterium_tritium_flux_due_to_beam_thermal_fusion](name:deuterium_tritium_flux_due_to_beam_thermal_fusion), and the TT beam-thermal contribution; their sum contributes to total_neutron_flux.

Typical beam-thermal neutron emission rates are about $10^{12}$-$10^{16}$ Hz in deuterium neutral-beam plasmas, $10^{16}$-$10^{19}$ Hz in high-power mixed deuterium-tritium operation, and can approach $10^{20}$ Hz in large burning-plasma scenarios with strong auxiliary beams. Values scale strongly with injected power, fast-ion confinement, target density, isotope mix, and ion temperature.

NAMES.name: incident_radiated_power_of_breeder_blanket_module
NAMES.short: Total electromagnetic radiative power from the plasma arriving at the outer surface of a breeding blanket module, including bremsstrahlung and line radiation contributions, before accounting for surface reflection losses.
NAMES.long:
The incident radiated power of a breeding blanket module is the total electromagnetic power from the surrounding plasma that arrives at the module's outer surface, integrated over that surface per unit time. Plasma radiation sources contributing to this load include bremsstrahlung from electron-ion Coulomb collisions, impurity line radiation, and synchrotron emission, all transported across the scrape-off layer to the first-wall and blanket boundary.

The incident radiative load is defined as:

$$
P_\mathrm{inc,rad} = \int_S \mathbf{q}_\mathrm{rad} \cdot \hat{n} \, dA
$$

where $\mathbf{q}_\mathrm{rad}$ is the local incident radiative heat-flux vector, $\hat{n}$ is the inward surface unit normal, and the integral extends over the total module surface area $A$.

This quantity represents the gross radiative power before surface reflection; the net thermally retained fraction is captured by [absorbed_radiated_power_of_breeder_blanket_module](name:absorbed_radiated_power_of_breeder_blanket_module), which subtracts the reflected component. Together with nuclear heating quantified by [total_neutron_power_of_breeder_blanket_module](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_module), this term enters the full surface thermal balance of the blanket and is a key input for coolant circuit design and blanket lifetime assessment.

NAMES.name: neutron_maximum_back_surface_energy_flux_of_breeder_blanket_module
NAMES.subject: neutron
NAMES.short: Peak neutron energy flux density escaping through the plasma-distal rear face of a breeding blanket module, serving as the primary figure of merit for blanket shielding effectiveness against the fusion neutron field.
NAMES.long:
The back surface of a breeding blanket module is its plasma-distal face, which interfaces with the vacuum vessel and structural components located behind the blanket. The maximum neutron energy flux at this surface quantifies the spatial peak of the neutron energy current per unit area escaping through the rear face after the neutron population has traversed the full blanket material stack, including breeding, multiplying, and structural layers.

The local neutron energy flux at a point $\mathbf{r}$ on the back surface is:

$$
\Phi_n(\mathbf{r}) = \int_0^\infty \int_{\hat{\Omega}\cdot\hat{n}\,>\,0} E\,\psi(\mathbf{r},\hat{\Omega},E)\,(\hat{\Omega}\cdot\hat{n})\,d\hat{\Omega}\,dE
$$

where $\psi$ is the neutron angular flux (neutrons per unit area per unit time per unit solid angle per unit energy), $E$ is neutron energy, $\hat{\Omega}$ is the particle direction unit vector, and $\hat{n}$ is the outward surface normal at the back face. The standard name records the maximum of $\Phi_n$ over all back-surface area elements of the module.

This quantity is evaluated through neutron transport calculations applied to the three-dimensional blanket geometry. For reactor-scale designs, the incoming neutron energy flux at the first wall is of order 2 MW m$^{-2}$; shielding requirements typically demand that back-surface values be reduced by three or more orders of magnitude to protect superconducting coils and other sensitive components. Compare with [neutron_maximum_energy_flux_at_first_wall](name:neutron_maximum_energy_flux_at_first_wall), which characterizes the peak incoming flux at the plasma-facing surface, and [nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_module](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_module) for the corresponding volumetrically integrated nuclear energy deposition.

NAMES.name: neutron_maximum_energy_flux_at_first_wall
NAMES.subject: neutron
NAMES.short: Maximum over the plasma-facing first-wall surface of the incoming neutron energy current per unit area for a breeding blanket module. It counts neutrons crossing into the wall from the plasma side, not rear-surface or outgoing crossings.
NAMES.long:
Neutron maximum energy flux at the first wall is the largest local incident neutron power per unit area on the plasma-facing surface of a breeding blanket module. It is a surface-crossing quantity: only the incoming component of the neutron angular current through the first-wall surface is included, and the reported value is the maximum over that surface.

For a first-wall surface $S_{fw}$ with unit normal $\hat{n}$ pointing from the blanket material toward the plasma, the local incident neutron energy flux can be defined from the neutron angular flux $\Phi_n(\mathbf{r},E,\hat{\Omega})$ as:

$$
q_n^{inc}(\mathbf{r}) = \int_0^\infty \int_{\hat{\Omega}\cdot\hat{n}<0} E\,\Phi_n(\mathbf{r},E,\hat{\Omega})\,|\hat{\Omega}\cdot\hat{n}|\,d\hat{\Omega}\,dE, \qquad q_{n,max}^{inc}=\max_{\mathbf{r}\in S_{fw}} q_n^{inc}(\mathbf{r})
$$

where $E$ is neutron kinetic energy, $\hat{\Omega}$ is the neutron flight direction, and the condition $\hat{\Omega}\cdot\hat{n}<0$ selects neutrons traveling from the plasma side into the first wall. The absolute projected factor makes the incident flux non-negative and excludes neutrons leaving the material surface.

In practice this quantity is computed with neutron transport calculations using the fusion neutron source, detailed blanket and vessel geometry, material compositions, and local surface normals. Experimental constraints may come from activation foils, fission chambers, or other neutron monitors, but the local maximum on the first-wall surface is usually obtained from a validated neutronics model rather than direct point measurement.

Typical peak values are about $10^5$-$10^6$ W m$^{-2}$ in lower-power experimental blanket environments and $10^6$-$10^7$ W m$^{-2}$ in reactor-class deuterium-tritium blanket designs. The corresponding surface integral over the first wall gives an integrated neutron power, while back-surface neutron energy flux characterizes neutrons crossing the opposite side of the module.

NAMES.name: nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_module
NAMES.short: Total nuclear heating power deposited in a single breeder blanket module by neutron scattering, neutron capture, and secondary gamma radiation interactions with the module's structural and functional materials.
NAMES.long:
Nuclear heating power of a breeder blanket module is the total rate at which neutron and photon radiation transfer energy to the structural and functional materials comprising that module. The dominant mechanisms are neutron elastic and inelastic scattering, exothermic neutron capture reactions (including lithium reactions that also breed tritium), and absorption of secondary gamma rays produced throughout the module volume.

The module-level heating power is the volume integral of the local nuclear heating power density $q_\text{nuc}(\mathbf{r})$ over the module volume $V$:

$$
P_\text{nuc} = \int_V q_\text{nuc}(\mathbf{r}) \, dV
$$

where $q_\text{nuc}$ is the volumetric energy deposition rate in W m$^{-3}$, as described by [nuclear_power_density_of_breeder_blanket_module](name:nuclear_power_density_of_breeder_blanket_module).

This quantity is obtained from neutron and photon transport simulations and feeds directly into thermal-hydraulic analyzes for coolant sizing and material temperature verification. It is more spatially resolved than [nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket), which aggregates over all modules, and complements [nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_layer](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_layer), which further resolves heating by material layer within the module. Unlike [total_neutron_power_of_breeder_blanket_module](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_module), this quantity includes gamma-ray heating contributions and accounts only for energy absorbed rather than that generated within the module.

NAMES.name: nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_shield
NAMES.short: Nuclear heating power deposited in the breeding blanket shield by neutron and gamma radiation interactions with shield structural materials.
NAMES.long:
The breeder blanket shield absorbs residual neutron and gamma radiation that penetrates the breeding zone, converting particle energy to heat through neutron scattering, capture reactions, and Compton scattering of secondary photons. This thermal load determines the cooling circuit requirements for the shield structure and is a principal design constraint for protecting superconducting magnets from radiation-induced heating.

The total nuclear heating power is the volume integral of the local nuclear power density $q'''(\mathbf{r})$ over the shield volume $V_\mathrm{shield}$:

$$
P_\mathrm{shield} = \int_{V_\mathrm{shield}} q'''(\mathbf{r}) \, dV
$$

where $q'''(\mathbf{r})$ is in W m$^{-3}$ and sums contributions from both neutron and secondary gamma interactions throughout the shield material.

This quantity is evaluated via neutron transport analysis using validated nuclear cross-section libraries for the shield material composition, benchmarked against integral activation experiments. It is the shield-level analog of the layer-resolved [nuclear heating power of a breeder blanket layer](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_layer) and the blanket-wide integral [nuclear heating power of the full breeding blanket](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket); the volumetric counterpart [nuclear power density of a breeder blanket module](name:nuclear_power_density_of_breeder_blanket_module) provides the spatially resolved distribution used in detailed thermal-hydraulic analyzes.

NAMES.name: nuclear_power_density_of_limiter_tile
NAMES.short: Local volumetric heating rate in a limiter tile due to neutron scattering, neutron capture, and secondary gamma radiation interactions with the tile material.
NAMES.long:
Nuclear power density in a limiter tile is the volumetric rate of energy deposition arising from nuclear interactions between the fusion neutron field and the tile material, including fast neutron elastic and inelastic scattering, radiative capture, and secondary gamma heating. It characterizes how the total nuclear heat load is distributed spatially within the tile volume.

The nuclear power density $q'''_\mathrm{nuc}(\mathbf{r})$ at a point $\mathbf{r}$ within the tile is:

$$
q'''_\mathrm{nuc}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum_r \Sigma_r(\mathbf{r})\,\phi(\mathbf{r})\,Q_r
$$

where $\Sigma_r(\mathbf{r})$ is the macroscopic cross section for reaction $r$, $\phi(\mathbf{r})$ is the local neutron flux, and $Q_r$ is the energy deposited per reaction. Integrating $q'''_\mathrm{nuc}$ over the tile volume yields the total nuclear power deposited in the tile, as given by [nuclear_power_of_limiter_tile](name:nuclear_power_of_limiter_tile).

This quantity is computed from neutronics transport calculations using the fusion neutron source spectrum and material-specific nuclear cross-section libraries, with the spatial distribution depending on local material composition and tile geometry. Analogous volumetric nuclear heating quantities for breeding blanket structures are given by [nuclear_power_density_of_breeder_blanket_module](name:nuclear_power_density_of_breeder_blanket_module) and [nuclear_power_density_of_breeder_blanket_layer](name:nuclear_power_density_of_breeder_blanket_layer), where nuclear deposition additionally drives tritium breeding.

NAMES.name: resistance_of_cryostat
NAMES.short: Electrical resistance of a discrete block element of the cryostat passive conductor structure, covering both the structural vessel and thermal shield segments, used in eddy current and electromagnetic analyzes.
NAMES.long:
The electrical resistance of a discrete cryostat element quantifies its opposition to current flow, characterizing the ohmic property of a localized conducting segment within the passive cryostat structure. The cryostat passive structure encompasses both the structural vessel body and the thermal shield; in lumped-circuit electromagnetic models each is discretized into finite block elements, each assigned a resistance value.

For a homogeneous element, the resistance relates to the bulk material resistivity $\rho$ (see [resistivity_of_cryostat](name:resistivity_of_cryostat)) through:

$$
R = \frac{\rho \, \ell}{A}
$$

where $\ell$ is the current-path length through the element and $A$ is the cross-sectional area perpendicular to current flow.

During plasma disruptions, halo events, or fast field transients, time-varying magnetic fluxes induce eddy currents in the passive cryostat structure; the per-element resistance governs both the magnitude of the [toroidal current of the cryostat](name:toroidal_current_of_cryostat) and the Joule dissipation rate $P = I^2 R$ in each segment. The analogous quantity for the vacuum vessel passive structure is [resistance_of_vacuum_vessel](name:resistance_of_vacuum_vessel), which follows the same discrete-element methodology. For large fusion-device cryostats fabricated from austenitic stainless steel or Inconel, individual block-element resistances typically fall in the micro-ohm to milli-ohm range, depending on element geometry and alloy composition.

NAMES.name: resistivity_of_cryostat
NAMES.short: Electrical resistivity of the cryostat structural material, encompassing both the vessel body and the thermal shield, used as the primary electromagnetic material property in eddy-current analyzes.
NAMES.long:
Electrical resistivity is an intrinsic material property quantifying resistance to electrical current flow per unit length and unit cross-sectional area of a conducting medium. For the cryostat — which comprises the main structural vessel and the surrounding thermal shield — this property governs the amplitude of eddy currents induced during transient plasma events such as disruptions and vertical displacement events, and the resulting ohmic heating and electromagnetic forces on the structure.

The resistance $R$ of a cryostat structural element is related to its resistivity $\rho$ through element geometry:

$$
R = \rho \frac{L}{A}
$$

where $L$ is the element length along the current path and $A$ is its cross-sectional area perpendicular to current flow.

This material constant is applied in electromagnetic finite-element analyzes to model induced current distributions and compute $\mathbf{J} \times \mathbf{B}$ forces and ohmic power deposition during disruptions. Metallic cryostat materials span a wide range: austenitic stainless steel yields roughly $7 \times 10^{-7}$ Ω·m, while aluminum alloys are lower at approximately $3 \times 10^{-8}$ Ω·m at ambient temperature; both values increase with temperature. The companion [resistance_of_cryostat](name:resistance_of_cryostat) gives the total resistance of a discrete structural element, while [resistivity_of_vacuum_vessel](name:resistivity_of_vacuum_vessel) is the analogous property for the vacuum vessel wall.

NAMES.name: thickness_of_breeder_blanket_layer
NAMES.short: Layer-normal distance between the inner and outer material interfaces of a breeder blanket layer at the equatorial midplane of a module. For radially stacked layers in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, it coincides with the midplane radial build.
NAMES.long:
The thickness of a breeder blanket layer is the local separation between the layer's two bounding material interfaces at the equatorial midplane of a blanket module. It is a layer-normal through-thickness, not the toroidal width, poloidal height, or a volume-equivalent thickness. For radially stacked layers it is the radial build in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ system, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

A local midplane thickness for layer $i$ can be defined from the interface positions and the local layer normal:

$$
d_i = \left|\left(\mathbf{x}_{i,\mathrm{out}} - \mathbf{x}_{i,\mathrm{in}}\right) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}_i\right|
$$

where $d_i$ is the layer thickness in m, $\mathbf{x}_{i,\mathrm{in}}$ and $\mathbf{x}_{i,\mathrm{out}}$ are points on the inner and outer bounding interfaces at the midplane in m, and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}_i$ is the unit normal through the layer. When the interfaces are locally normal to the major-radius direction, this reduces to the absolute midplane difference in $R$. The total build along the same normal may be written inline as $D=\sum_i d_i$, with each $d_i$ and the total $D$ in m.

In practice this quantity is obtained from engineering geometry or a neutronics model by intersecting the blanket module with the equatorial midplane, identifying consecutive material interfaces, and measuring their spacing along the layer-normal direction. When combined with [nuclear_power_density_of_breeder_blanket_layer](name:nuclear_power_density_of_breeder_blanket_layer), the product of local nuclear power density and thickness gives an areal power contribution in W/m^2 for approximately uniform heating along the normal; total power requires integration over the layer volume.

Typical individual layer thicknesses range from 0.001-0.01 m for thin coatings or liners, 0.01-0.10 m for coolant, structural, multiplier, or breeder sublayers, and 0.1-0.6 m for large breeding or shielding regions. Complete blanket radial builds are commonly of order 0.5-1.5 m, depending on device size and shielding requirements.

NAMES.name: thickness_of_breeder_blanket_module
NAMES.short: Normal distance through the side-wall material of a breeding blanket module, measured between the inner face bounding the module interior and the outer side-wall face. It is the structural side-wall extent of the module as a whole, distinct from the thickness of an individual breeder layer within the module.
NAMES.long:
Thickness of a breeder blanket module is the through-wall distance across the module side wall, taken normal to the wall between its inner face (bounding the module interior) and its outer face. It quantifies the lateral structural material enclosing the module and is distinct from the thickness of an individual breeder layer in the internal stack.

The local wall-normal thickness is the projection of the separation between opposing wall faces onto the unit normal of the reference wall surface:

$$
t = \left|\left(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{out}} - \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{in}}\right) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}\right|
$$

where $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{in}}$ and $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{out}}$ are corresponding points on the inner and outer side-wall faces, $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is the local unit normal directed through the wall, and $t$ is in meters. As a magnitude it is non-negative by construction. For curved or tapered walls this is a local or nominal engineering thickness and is not in general a simple difference in major radius $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

The value is obtained from the module envelope or detailed engineering geometry at the specified side-wall reference section. Together with material composition, layer thicknesses, and the poloidal cap thicknesses it governs mechanical stiffness, thermal conduction paths, neutron attenuation, and the volume available for tritium breeding material, without itself defining the internal layer arrangement.

Typical values are design dependent and lie on the centimeter-to-decimeter scale, roughly 0.01-0.3 m across common blanket module concepts, with the appropriate value set by module size, structural material, coolant and breeder arrangement, neutron shielding requirements, and mechanical load margins.

NAMES.name: lower_thickness_of_breeder_blanket_module
NAMES.short: Physical extent of the lower cap of a breeder blanket module, measured through the cap between its lower exterior boundary surface and its interface with the main module body along the local surface normal. It is a non-negative geometric length in meters, not a signed coordinate displacement.
NAMES.long:
Lower thickness of a breeder blanket module is the non-negative length variable that describes the physical extent of the module's lower cap. It is measured through the cap from the lower exterior boundary surface to the interface where the cap joins the main module body, along the local normal to the lower cap surface. The word lower identifies the lower poloidal end of the module; the quantity is not an overall module dimension or a signed vertical position.

For a locally smooth cap, the thickness can be represented as the projected separation between the two reference surfaces:

$$
t_{\mathrm{lower}} = \left|\left(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{int}} - \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{ext}}\right) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}_{\mathrm{lower}}\right|
$$

where $t_{\mathrm{lower}}$ is the lower cap thickness in m, $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{ext}}$ is a point on the lower exterior boundary surface in m, $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{int}}$ is the corresponding point on the interface with the main module body in m, and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{\mathrm{lower}}$ is the dimensionless unit normal pointing from the exterior boundary toward that interface. The absolute value expresses that this is a length. The measurement direction is a local surface-normal direction, not a projection along $R$ or $Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

In practice the value is taken from the engineering geometry or design definition of the blanket module. If the lower cap is curved, tapered, or has nonparallel reference surfaces, local projected separations can vary; this scalar should denote the nominal design thickness specified for the lower cap. Minimum, maximum, average, or location-specific lower-cap thicknesses should be defined explicitly rather than substituted for this quantity unless the design definition states that the nominal scalar is one of those values.

Typical values are design-dependent and should be checked against the surrounding module geometry. Conceptual breeder blanket cap dimensions are commonly centimeter- to decimeter-scale engineering lengths, roughly 0.01-0.3 m, and should remain consistent with related dimensions such as [thickness_of_breeder_blanket_module](name:thickness_of_breeder_blanket_module), [thickness_of_breeder_blanket_layer](name:thickness_of_breeder_blanket_layer), and radial_distance_at_midplane.

NAMES.name: thickness_of_cryostat
NAMES.short: Physical wall thickness of the cryostat structural vessel, measured as the through-wall distance between its inner and outer faces along the local wall normal. For an annular layer this is perpendicular to the vessel centerline; for a block element it is evaluated along the wall-normal line through the element midplane.
NAMES.long:
Thickness of the cryostat is the local through-wall extent of the load-bearing cryostat vessel material between its inner and outer faces. It is a structural geometry parameter for the cryostat wall and is distinct from the effective thermal shielding thickness represented by [thermal_thickness_of_cryostat](name:thickness_of_cryostat).

The general wall-normal definition is the absolute projection of the separation between corresponding inner and outer surface points onto the local unit normal:

$$
t_c = \left|\left(\mathbf{x}_\mathrm{out} - \mathbf{x}_\mathrm{in}\right) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}\right|
$$

where $t_c$ is the cryostat thickness, $\mathbf{x}_\mathrm{in}$ and $\mathbf{x}_\mathrm{out}$ are the inner- and outer-face position vectors in meters, and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is the local unit normal to the wall. For an annular layer this reduces to the radial span $R_\mathrm{out}-R_\mathrm{in}$, with $R_\mathrm{in}$ and $R_\mathrm{out}$ in meters in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height. For a block element the same through-wall distance is taken along the wall-normal line passing through the element midplane. The absolute value expresses that thickness is non-negative.

The thickness is obtained from engineering geometry, design drawings, or surveyed vessel dimensions and is used in structural stiffness, vacuum-load, thermal-mass, and electromagnetic response estimates. The related [thickness_of_vacuum_vessel](name:thickness_of_vacuum_vessel) applies the same wall-normal concept to the vacuum vessel, while [resistivity_of_cryostat](name:resistivity_of_cryostat) is a material property used with the cryostat geometry in electromagnetic calculations.

Representative cryostat wall or layer thicknesses are typically about 0.02-0.2 m for shell panels and local annular layers, with reinforced regions, flanges, or block-like structural elements sometimes reaching about 0.5 m. Actual values depend on vessel size, pressure loading, support layout, penetrations, and reinforcement strategy.

NAMES.name: tritium_breeding_ratio_of_breeder_blanket_module
NAMES.short: Per-module contribution to blanket tritium breeding ratio: tritium atoms produced in a breeder blanket module divided by the common incident fusion-neutron count used for the blanket normalization. It is dimensionless and additive across modules when all modules use that same denominator.
NAMES.long:
The tritium breeding ratio of a breeder blanket module is the module-resolved contribution to blanket tritium production. It counts tritium atoms generated in one module per incident fusion neutron used for the overall blanket normalization, so it is not normalized separately to the neutrons entering only that module.

The module contribution can be written using particle rates over a common time basis:

$$
\mathrm{TBR}_m = \frac{\dot{N}_{T,m}}{\dot{N}_{n,\mathrm{inc}}}
$$

where $\dot{N}_{T,m}$ is the tritium-atom production rate in module $m$, in s^-1, and $\dot{N}_{n,\mathrm{inc}}$ is the common incident fusion-neutron rate used to normalize the blanket tritium breeding ratio, in s^-1. Equivalent particle counts over the same time interval may be used instead; the numerator and denominator are then both counts, and the ratio has unit 1.

In practice, $\dot{N}_{T,m}$ is obtained from neutronics transport and nuclear-response calculations by integrating tritium-producing reaction-rate densities over the breeder regions of the module. The same denominator must be used for every module, so summing module values gives the corresponding contribution to the overall [tritium_breeding_ratio](name:tritium_breeding_ratio). The value is commonly interpreted together with module nuclear-load quantities such as [total_neutron_power_of_breeder_blanket_module](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_module), because neutron power indicates source strength while material composition and neutron spectrum determine how effectively that source breeds tritium.

Typical additive module values depend strongly on how the blanket is subdivided. Small replaceable modules may contribute about 10^-4-10^-2, larger sector-scale modules about 0.01-0.5, and the sum over a full breeding blanket is generally of order 1 in reactor design studies. Values are dimensionless and vary with module solid angle coverage, lithium enrichment, multiplier content, structural fraction, coolant, and neutron leakage.

NAMES.name: upper_thickness_of_breeder_blanket_module
NAMES.short: Upper thickness of a breeder blanket module is the non-negative projected separation between the module's upper exterior end boundary and the interface where the upper cap joins the main module body, measured along the specified upper-cap thickness direction. It characterizes the geometric thickness of the upper end cap.
NAMES.long:
Upper thickness of a breeder blanket module is the geometric thickness of the upper cap that closes the module at its upper end. The reference surfaces are the upper exterior end boundary of the cap and the cap-to-module interface where the cap joins the main blanket body; the thickness is measured as a projected separation along the specified upper-cap thickness direction, not as an arbitrary point-to-point distance between inner and outer surfaces.

For a local cap-thickness direction $\hat{\mathbf{n}}_\mathrm{u}$, the projected thickness is

$$
t_\mathrm{u} = \left|\left(\mathbf{x}_\mathrm{end} - \mathbf{x}_\mathrm{int}\right) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}_\mathrm{u}\right|
$$

where $t_\mathrm{u}$ is the upper cap thickness, $\mathbf{x}_\mathrm{end}$ is a point on the upper exterior end boundary, $\mathbf{x}_\mathrm{int}$ is the corresponding point on the cap-to-module interface, and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}_\mathrm{u}$ is the unit direction used to define the upper-cap thickness. The absolute value reflects that this scalar is a non-negative length.

In engineering definitions the value is taken from the module geometry or design specification. For a tapered or spatially varying upper cap, the scalar denotes the specified nominal projected thickness, commonly the representative average over the cap region or the value at the design reference section; local maxima, minima, and detailed shape variations are separate geometric information.

This quantity is related to the overall [breeder blanket module thickness](name:thickness_of_breeder_blanket_module), to the analogous [lower cap thickness](name:lower_thickness_of_breeder_blanket_module), and to individual [breeder blanket layer thicknesses](name:thickness_of_breeder_blanket_layer). It is reported in meters and is design-specific; no universal device-independent numerical range is implied.

NAMES.name: vertical_outline_of_limiter_tile
NAMES.short: Vertical (Z) coordinate of the contour points tracing the poloidal cross-sectional outline of a limiter tile.
NAMES.long:
The vertical outline of a limiter tile provides the ordered set of $Z$ coordinates that, paired with the corresponding radial coordinates, trace the poloidal cross-sectional boundary of an individual limiter tile. Limiter tiles are plasma-facing solid components that can establish the last-closed flux surface in limited plasma configurations, physically protecting the first wall from direct high-heat-flux plasma contact.

The outline is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius measured from the machine symmetry axis and $Z$ is the vertical height relative to the device midplane. Each point in the outline array corresponds to a vertex on the tile boundary contour in the poloidal plane, and the complete set of $(R, Z)$ pairs fully specifies the tile cross-section geometry.

These coordinates are obtained from engineering drawings, CAD models, or in-vessel metrology, and are applied in heat load mapping, plasma-wall gap analysis, and geometric boundary modeling. The analogous outline coordinates for divertor components follow the same convention as [vertical_outline_of_divertor_tile](name:vertical_outline_of_divertor_tile), and the equivalent representation for mobile wall components is [vertical_outline_of_wall_material](name:vertical_outline_of_wall_material). The active contact point of a limited plasma with the limiter surface is tracked separately by [vertical_coordinate_of_active_limiter_point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_active_limiter_point).

Typical $Z$ values for limiter tiles range from approximately $-3$ m to $+3$ m depending on the tile's poloidal location and the machine size.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $Z$ points upward in the $+\hat{Z}$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_outline_of_wall_material
NAMES.short: Vertical Z-coordinate of the outline polygon that defines the poloidal cross-sectional boundary of a mobile wall material component.
NAMES.long: The vertical $Z$-coordinate locates each vertex of the polygon that traces the cross-sectional shape of a mobile wall material element in the poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius measured from the symmetry axis and $Z$ is the vertical height. The complete poloidal outline is formed by a sequence of $(R, Z)$ vertex pairs; this quantity captures the $Z$ component of those vertices, complementing the corresponding major-radius component of the same outline. Mobile wall components are plasma-facing structural elements — such as retractable limiters or adjustable tiles — whose positions may vary, making accurate outline tracking essential for equilibrium reconstruction and plasma-wall gap analysis. For fixed structural elements, analogous $Z$ outline coordinates are provided by [vertical_outline_of_limiter_tile](name:vertical_outline_of_limiter_tile), [vertical_outline_of_vacuum_vessel](name:vertical_outline_of_vacuum_vessel), and [vertical_outline_of_divertor_tile](name:vertical_outline_of_divertor_tile). Typical values span the vertical extent of the vacuum vessel, generally within $\pm 3$ m for medium-sized tokamaks.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the outline vertex lies above the geometric midplane in the $+Z$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: volumetric_force
NAMES.short: Net force per unit volume acting at each point of a current-carrying conductor or plasma element, resolved as a vector in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Volumetric force is the local force density vector, expressing the net mechanical load per unit volume at each point in a material or plasma region. In electromagnetic contexts — the primary application in tokamak structural engineering — it is the Lorentz body-force density exerted on a current-carrying element by the surrounding magnetic field.

The defining relation is:

$$
\mathbf{f} = \mathbf{J} \times \mathbf{B}
$$

where $\mathbf{J}$ is the current density and $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic flux density. The vector is decomposed into cylindrical components [radial_volumetric_force](name:radial_volumetric_force), [toroidal_volumetric_force](name:toroidal_volumetric_force), and [vertical_volumetric_force](name:vertical_volumetric_force) in the right-handed $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. Integrating over the volume of a structural element recovers the total [force](name:force) acting on that element.

This quantity is used in magnetomechanical and structural integrity analyzes of plasma-facing components, breeding blanket modules, and coil structures, particularly during disruption events when rapidly changing currents induce large transient body forces on conducting structures.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the force component points in the $+\hat{R}$ direction (outward from the symmetry axis), in the $+\hat{\phi}$ direction (direction of increasing toroidal angle), or in the $+\hat{Z}$ direction (upward) in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: radial_volumetric_force
NAMES.short: Radial component of the electromagnetic body-force density vector, projected onto the direction of increasing major radius R in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The radial volumetric force is the $\hat{R}$-projection of the local electromagnetic body-force density $\mathbf{f} = \mathbf{J} \times \mathbf{B}$ acting on plasma volumes or conducting wall and structural elements. It characterizes the net radial push or pull arising from the interaction of local current density with the magnetic field, driving stress and displacement in the major-radial direction.

The defining relation is the radial projection of the Lorentz force density in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame with basis $(\hat{R}, \hat{\phi}, \hat{Z})$:

$$
f_R = (\mathbf{J} \times \mathbf{B}) \cdot \hat{R} = J_\phi B_Z - J_Z B_\phi
$$

where $\mathbf{J}$ is the current density vector, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field, and $J_\phi$, $J_Z$, $B_\phi$, $B_Z$ are the toroidal and vertical components respectively.

This component is computed in magnetohydrodynamic equilibrium analyzes and disruption-load assessments to quantify radial electromagnetic stresses on plasma-facing components, wall tiles, and blanket structures. Together with [toroidal_volumetric_force](name:toroidal_volumetric_force) and [vertical_volumetric_force](name:vertical_volumetric_force), it resolves the complete local electromagnetic body-force density vector described by [volumetric_force](name:volumetric_force).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the electromagnetic force points in the direction of increasing major radius $R$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_volumetric_force
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the local electromagnetic force per unit volume acting on plasma or material, projected onto the direction of increasing toroidal angle phi in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal volumetric force is the signed component of force per unit volume projected onto the $\hat{\phi}$ direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It represents the local body-force density that tends to accelerate plasma or load material in the toroidal direction.

For electromagnetic loading, the toroidal component is the projection of the Lorentz force density onto $\hat{\phi}$:

$$
f_\phi = \mathbf{f}\cdot\hat{\phi} = (\mathbf{J}\times\mathbf{B})\cdot\hat{\phi} = J_Z B_R - J_R B_Z
$$

where $f_\phi$ is the toroidal volumetric force in $N\,m^{-3}$, $\mathbf{f}$ is the force density in $N\,m^{-3}$, $\mathbf{J}$ is current density in $A\,m^{-2}$, and $\mathbf{B}$ is magnetic field in $T$. The component labels $R$ and $Z$ denote projections onto the radial and vertical basis directions of the same right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

This quantity is usually computed from reconstructed or simulated current-density and magnetic-field distributions, and may be integrated over a plasma or material volume to obtain a net toroidal load. Direct measurement is uncommon; practical estimates generally combine magnetic diagnostics, current models, and electromagnetic or magnetohydrodynamic force calculations.

Typical magnitudes are near zero in quiescent regions, about $10^3$-$10^7\ N\,m^{-3}$ in conducting structures during electromagnetic transients, and can reach $10^8\ N\,m^{-3}$ or higher in localized disruption, halo-current, or fast current-quench conditions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the force density is projected in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: argon_density
NAMES.subject: argon
NAMES.short: Local number density of argon ions at a given plasma position, summed over all ionization stages.
NAMES.long:
The argon ion number density $n_\mathrm{Ar}$ is the number of argon ions per unit volume at a specified location in the plasma, with contributions from all ionization stages $q = 1, \ldots, 18$ included unless a charge-state-resolved quantity is explicitly indicated. Argon is a mid-$Z$ noble-gas impurity injected into magnetically confined fusion plasmas primarily for radiative divertor cooling and plasma-facing-component protection, and its local density profile governs impurity transport, radiated power distribution, and fuel dilution.

The total argon density at position $\mathbf{r}$ is given by the charge-state sum:

$$
n_\mathrm{Ar}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum_{q=1}^{18} n_{\mathrm{Ar},q}(\mathbf{r})
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{Ar},q}$ denotes the number density of argon ions in charge state $q$.

Local argon density is inferred from soft X-ray tomography, vacuum-ultraviolet line emission spectroscopy, or charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, typically combined with ionization-equilibrium modeling to resolve individual charge-state contributions. Spatial aggregates derived from this quantity include [volume_averaged_argon_density](name:volume_averaged_argon_density) and [line_averaged_argon_density](name:line_averaged_argon_density), while point evaluations at reference locations are given by [argon_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:argon_density_at_magnetic_axis) and [argon_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:argon_density_at_plasma_boundary). Core argon densities in H-mode discharges with divertor seeding are typically $10^{15}$–$10^{16}$ m$^{-3}$, while edge values during strong argon injection can reach $10^{17}$–$10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$.

NAMES.name: argon_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: argon
NAMES.short: Number density of argon ions at the magnetic axis, the innermost point of the confined plasma where the gradient of the poloidal magnetic flux vanishes.
NAMES.long:
The argon ion number density at the magnetic axis gives the on-axis concentration of argon impurity ions, the species-specific realization of [density_at_magnetic_axis](name:density_at_magnetic_axis), evaluated at the point where $\nabla\psi = 0$ (with $\psi$ the poloidal magnetic flux) at coordinates $(R_\mathrm{axis}, Z_\mathrm{axis})$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. Neoclassical impurity transport tends to drive high-$Z$ species inward under collisional H-mode conditions, making this on-axis value a sensitive indicator of core argon accumulation relative to outer radii, distinct from the boundary concentration captured by [argon_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:argon_density_at_plasma_boundary).

Argon is introduced into fusion plasmas for radiative power balance experiments, edge cooling, and disruption mitigation; the on-axis density reflects both the seeded impurity inventory and any neoclassical inward pinch, with the peaking factor $n_\mathrm{Ar}(0)/\langle n_\mathrm{Ar}\rangle$ serving as a quantitative measure of core accumulation. On-axis impurity concentrations are typically orders of magnitude below the bulk ion density under trace-seeding conditions, increasing substantially during massive-injection disruption mitigation.

This quantity is commonly inferred from charge exchange recombination spectroscopy of argon charge-state line emission or from soft X-ray tomography, with the magnetic axis position supplied by equilibrium reconstruction. Comparing this value with [argon_density_at_pedestal](name:argon_density_at_pedestal) characterizes the radial impurity gradient between the core and the transport barrier. The analogous on-axis density for neon is [neon_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:neon_density_at_magnetic_axis), governed by the same neoclassical transport physics but with different charge-dependent accumulation rates.

NAMES.name: beryllium_density_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: beryllium
NAMES.short: Local number density of beryllium ions at the internal transport barrier reference radius, where reduced cross-field transport can produce steep impurity density gradients.
NAMES.long:
Beryllium density at an internal transport barrier is the local number density of beryllium ions on the flux surface selected as the barrier reference location. Unless a charge state is specified separately, it is an elemental impurity ion density summed over beryllium ionization states.

The local number density is defined as the differential beryllium ion count per plasma volume evaluated at the barrier location:

$$
n_{\mathrm{Be}}(r_{\mathrm{ITB}}) = \left.\frac{dN_{\mathrm{Be}}}{dV}\right|_{r=r_{\mathrm{ITB}}}
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{Be}}$ is the number of beryllium ions in a small plasma volume $V$, and $r_{\mathrm{ITB}}$ denotes the flux-surface label of the internal transport barrier reference radius.

In practice this quantity is inferred from impurity spectroscopy, charge-exchange measurements when available, and collisional-radiative modeling, often constrained by equilibrium and transport analysis. The barrier location is identified from the region of reduced turbulent transport or steep gradients, and the beryllium density is evaluated or interpolated on that flux surface.

Typical values are trace-impurity densities compared with the bulk ion density. In plasmas with beryllium plasma-facing components or measurable beryllium influx, representative internal-transport-barrier values are often about $10^{16}$-$10^{18}$ m^-3, depending on wall source strength, confinement, ionization balance, and impurity screening.

NAMES.name: boron_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: boron
NAMES.short: Number density of boron ions at the magnetic axis, the innermost flux-surface singular point of the confined plasma, summed over all boron ionization states.
NAMES.long:
Boron density at the magnetic axis is the local number density of boron ions on the innermost flux-surface singular point of a magnetically confined plasma. It is a charge-state-summed impurity density, representing the total population of ionized boron regardless of ionization stage.

The on-axis boron density can be written as the sum over boron ion charge states evaluated at the magnetic axis:

$$
n_{\mathrm{B,axis}} = \sum_q n_{\mathrm{B}^{q+}}(R_{\mathrm{axis}}, Z_{\mathrm{axis}})
$$

where $q$ indexes boron ion charge states, $n_{\mathrm{B}^{q+}}$ is the number density of charge state $q$, and $(R_{\mathrm{axis}}, Z_{\mathrm{axis}})$ locates the magnetic axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, with $R$ the major radius and $Z$ the vertical height. For an axisymmetric plasma the value is independent of toroidal angle $\phi$; in three-dimensional equilibria it refers to the value on the magnetic-axis curve.

In practice, the magnetic-axis location is obtained from an equilibrium reconstruction, while boron densities are inferred from spectroscopic measurements, charge-exchange or line-emission analysis, and impurity transport or collisional-radiative modeling. Because different boron charge states radiate most strongly in different temperature ranges, the charge-state-summed density generally requires a model-based reconstruction rather than a single spectral line.

Typical on-axis boron densities in tokamak core plasmas are about $10^{15}$-$10^{18}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$. Values near the upper end can occur after boronization, boron injection, or strong plasma-wall interaction, and often correspond to roughly $10^{-5}$-$10^{-2}$ of the local electron density.

NAMES.name: carbon_density_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: carbon
NAMES.short: Unweighted local number density of carbon ions at the internal-transport-barrier reference radius. It counts carbon ion particles per unit volume, summed over ionization states when charge-state-resolved densities are combined, and excludes neutral carbon and charge weighting.
NAMES.long:
Carbon density at an internal transport barrier is the local unweighted number density of carbon ions on the radial surface selected as the barrier reference. It counts ion particles per unit volume and excludes neutral carbon; it is not an electric charge density or an effective-charge weighting. It is the carbon-species counterpart of [total_ion_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:total_ion_density_at_internal_transport_barrier) and can be compared with other impurity densities at the same location.

With a dimensional radial coordinate $r$ measured in meters, the compact definition is the carbon-ion density field evaluated at the prescribed internal-transport-barrier reference radius:

$$
n_{\mathrm{C,ion}}(r_{\mathrm{ITB}}) = \sum_{q=1}^{6} n_{\mathrm{C}^{q+}}(r_{\mathrm{ITB}})
$$

where $q$ is the carbon ion charge state, $n_{\mathrm{C}^{q+}}$ is the number density of carbon ions in that charge state, and $r_{\mathrm{ITB}}$ is the value of the same radial coordinate at the selected ITB reference surface. All number densities in this expression are particle number densities with unit m^-3; if carbon is represented as a single elemental ion species, $n_{\mathrm{C,ion}}$ denotes the same charge-state-summed carbon ion density.

In practice, the ITB reference surface is identified from measured or reconstructed kinetic and transport behavior, and the carbon-ion density is evaluated locally on that surface rather than averaged over the full barrier width. Carbon abundance may be inferred from impurity spectroscopy together with atomic population modeling or transport analysis, with the charge-state sum made explicitly when charge-state-resolved information is available.

Typical values are highly scenario dependent. For trace-carbon conditions in confined tokamak plasmas, ITB-local carbon ion densities are often of order $10^{16}-10^{18}$ m^-3; carbon-rich wall sources, impurity injection, or strong accumulation can move the value outside this range.

NAMES.name: carbon_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: carbon
NAMES.short: Local number density of carbon ions at the magnetic axis, summed over carbon ion charge states rather than tied to a single ionization state. It is a point value at the plasma center, not a flux-surface, line, or volume average.
NAMES.long:
Carbon density at the magnetic axis is the local elemental number density of the carbon ion population evaluated at the magnetic axis, the center of the nested closed magnetic flux surfaces. Because no charge state is specified, it denotes the sum over carbon ion charge states and is not the density of a single state such as fully stripped carbon unless all carbon ions are in that state.

The charge-state sum defining the local elemental carbon ion density is

$$
n_{\mathrm{C,axis}} = \sum_{q \in \mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{C}}} n_{\mathrm{C}^{q+}}(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{axis}})
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{C}^{q+}}$ is the local number density of carbon ions in charge state $q$ in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{C}}$ is the set of carbon ion charge states included in the ion population, and $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{axis}}$ is the magnetic-axis position.

In practice this quantity is obtained by evaluating a reconstructed or modeled carbon density distribution at the magnetic axis. Spectroscopic constraints, charge-state balance, collisional-radiative modeling, and impurity transport calculations may all contribute to the inferred elemental density, but the standard name denotes the local axis value itself, not a flux-surface average, line-integrated value, or volume-averaged impurity content.

Typical values depend strongly on wall material, impurity sources, and plasma conditions. Core carbon densities of $10^{16}-10^{18}\ \mathrm{m}^{-3}$ are common in low-impurity plasmas, while carbon-wall operation or enhanced impurity influx can produce values approaching $10^{19}\ \mathrm{m}^{-3}$.

NAMES.name: co_passing_fast_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Local volumetric Coulomb collisional energy transfer rate to fast ions belonging to the co-passing orbit class, which circulate poloidally in the same direction as the plasma current.
NAMES.long:
The co-passing orbit class consists of fast ions whose guiding-center trajectories complete full poloidal circuits in the same direction as the plasma current, as opposed to trapped particles (which bounce between magnetic mirror points) and counter-passing ions. This quantity isolates the co-passing contribution to the total fast-ion collisional power density, enabling orbit-resolved energy-balance analysis of suprathermal ion populations.

The collisional power density is the energy moment of the Coulomb collision operator restricted to the co-passing velocity-space domain:

$$
P_{\mathrm{cp}} = \int_{\mathrm{co\text{-}passing}} \tfrac{1}{2} m_i v^2 \, C[f_{\mathrm{fast}}^{\mathrm{cp}}] \, d^3v
$$

where $m_i$ is the fast-ion mass in kg, $v$ is the particle speed in m s$^{-1}$, and $C[f_{\mathrm{fast}}^{\mathrm{cp}}]$ is the Coulomb collision operator acting on the co-passing portion of the fast-ion distribution function.

Orbit-resolving Fokker-Planck or Monte Carlo kinetic codes evaluate this quantity by partitioning velocity space into co-passing, counter-passing, and trapped regions. Summing these three orbit-class components recovers [fast_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:fast_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions), the total fast-ion collisional power density. The symmetric companion for the counter-circulating population is [counter_passing_fast_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:counter_passing_fast_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions); asymmetry between the two arises from anisotropic fast-ion sources such as co-injected neutral beams.
NAMES.sign: Positive when co-passing fast ions gain kinetic energy through Coulomb collisions with background plasma species.

NAMES.name: co_passing_fast_particle_density
NAMES.subject: particle
NAMES.short: Number density of suprathermal particles in the co-passing orbit class, from the fast-particle distribution function restricted to the co-passing region of velocity space.
NAMES.long:
Co-passing fast particle density is the number of non-thermal particles per unit physical volume whose guiding-center orbits are passing and belong to the co-passing branch. It is a partial zeroth moment of the fast-particle distribution function, complementary to the counter-passing and trapped fast-particle contributions.

The density at position $\mathbf{x}$ is defined by integrating the fast-particle distribution over the co-passing velocity-space domain:

$$
n_{\mathrm{fast}}^{\mathrm{co}}(\mathbf{x}) = \int_{\Omega_{\mathrm{co}}(\mathbf{x})} f_{\mathrm{fast}}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $f_{\mathrm{fast}}$ is the suprathermal distribution function with units $\mathrm{s^3\,m^{-6}}$, $\mathbf{x}$ is position in m, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity in m s$^{-1}$, $d^3v$ has units m$^3$ s$^{-3}$, and $\Omega_{\mathrm{co}}(\mathbf{x})$ is the subset of velocity space corresponding to co-passing orbits. The trapped-passing boundary is set by magnetic geometry and particle invariants such as energy and magnetic moment; in pitch coordinates it should be treated as the local trapped-passing separatrix rather than a universal pitch cutoff.

In practice, this quantity is computed by applying an orbit-classification operator to a kinetic fast-particle distribution and taking the partial zeroth moment over the co-passing domain. The same definition applies whether the distribution is expressed in Cartesian velocity, energy-pitch, or guiding-center variables, provided the appropriate velocity-space Jacobian is included. When the orbit classes form a complete disjoint partition, the total fast-particle density is the sum of the co-passing, counter-passing, and trapped contributions.

Typical values are strongly scenario dependent because fast-particle populations are set by sources, slowing-down, redistribution, and loss processes. Representative values can range from below $10^{14}$ m$^{-3}$ in weak suprathermal populations to $10^{17}$-$10^{19}$ m$^{-3}$ in strongly heated or fusion-product-rich plasmas, usually remaining below the bulk thermal particle density.

NAMES.name: co_passing_fast_particle_pressure
NAMES.subject: particle
