NAMES.short: Total pressure of the suprathermal co-passing particle population, obtained by integrating both parallel and perpendicular kinetic energy contributions of the fast-particle distribution function over the co-passing velocity-space domain.
NAMES.long:
Co-passing fast particles are suprathermal guiding-center orbits that circulate toroidally in the same direction as the plasma current, covering the velocity-space region where the pitch-angle cosine $\xi = v_\parallel/v$ exceeds the magnetic trapping boundary. This quantity is the orbit-class-resolved scalar pressure component of the total fast_particle_pressure, complementing the [counter_passing_fast_particle_pressure](name:counter_passing_fast_particle_pressure) and [trapped_fast_particle_pressure](name:trapped_fast_particle_pressure) contributions that together partition the full fast-particle pressure.

The co-passing fast-particle pressure is defined as the second velocity moment of the fast-particle distribution function $f_\mathrm{fast}$ restricted to the co-passing domain $\Omega_\mathrm{co}$:

$$
P_\mathrm{co} = \frac{m}{3} \int_{\Omega_\mathrm{co}} v^2 \, f_\mathrm{fast}(\mathbf{v}) \, d^3v
$$

where $m$ is the particle mass, $v = |\mathbf{v}|$ is the speed, and $\Omega_\mathrm{co}$ denotes the co-passing region ($\xi > \xi_\mathrm{trap}$, with $\xi_\mathrm{trap}$ the trapping-boundary cosine). Equivalently, $P_\mathrm{co} = \tfrac{1}{3}(P_{\parallel,\mathrm{co}} + 2P_{\perp,\mathrm{co}})$, decomposing into the [parallel component](name:parallel_co_passing_fast_particle_pressure) and the [perpendicular component](name:perpendicular_co_passing_fast_particle_pressure).

This quantity is computed from kinetic distribution-function solvers or Monte Carlo transport codes that resolve velocity-space orbit classes. Tangential neutral beam injection preferentially populates the co-passing orbit class, making this pressure component particularly prominent in NBI-heated plasmas where beam geometry and injection energy determine the co-passing fraction.
NAMES.sign: Positive when suprathermal particles occupy the co-passing orbit class with finite kinetic energy density.

NAMES.name: co_passing_power_density
NAMES.short: Flux-surface-averaged volumetric rate at which kinetic energy is added to or removed from the co-passing orbit population. It is the energy moment of the source term for passing particles moving on the co-current branch.
NAMES.long:
Co-passing power density is the flux-surface-averaged volumetric source rate of kinetic energy for passing particles whose parallel motion is on the co-current orbit branch. It separates energy exchange with the co-passing population from corresponding exchange with counter-passing and trapped particles.

The local energy moment of the phase-space source term gives the flux-surface-averaged power density:

$$
p_{\mathrm{co}}(\rho) = \left\langle \int_{\Omega_{\mathrm{co}}} \frac{1}{2} m v^2\, S_f(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\, d^3v \right\rangle_{\rho}
$$

where $p_{\mathrm{co}}$ is the co-passing power density, $\rho$ labels the magnetic flux surface, $\langle\cdot\rangle_{\rho}$ is the flux-surface average, $\Omega_{\mathrm{co}}$ is the co-passing region of velocity or invariant space, $m$ is particle mass, $v$ is speed, $S_f$ is the source contribution to the distribution-function evolution per unit spatial volume and per unit time, and $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element.

In practice this quantity is computed by orbit-classifying the kinetic distribution and integrating the energy moment of source operators over the co-passing domain. The source term may come from wave-particle interactions, neutral-particle injection, external fueling, collisional operators, or modeled loss mechanisms; constraints from global power balance and fast-particle or radiation diagnostics are often used to validate the inferred deposition or removal.

Typical magnitudes are $10^3-10^6\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-3}}$ in auxiliary-heated tokamak plasmas, with strongly localized wave or neutral-beam deposition reaching $10^7\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-3}}$. Values close to zero indicate weak net coupling to the co-passing population, while negative values of comparable magnitude occur where the modeled process removes kinetic energy.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the modeled source process increases the kinetic energy of the co-passing orbit population per unit volume.

NAMES.name: coulomb_logarithm
NAMES.short: Dimensionless logarithm of the ratio of the Debye screening length to the minimum Coulomb impact parameter, appearing as a multiplicative factor in all classical collision frequencies and resistivity expressions.
NAMES.long:
The Coulomb logarithm $\ln \Lambda$ is a dimensionless factor encoding the effective range of impact parameters that contribute to cumulative small-angle Coulomb scattering in a plasma. It arises because the Debye-shielded potential introduces a maximum effective impact parameter $b_{\max}$, while quantum or classical mechanics sets a minimum $b_{\min}$, producing a well-defined logarithmic ratio.

The defining expression is

$$
\ln \Lambda = \ln\!\left(\frac{b_{\max}}{b_{\min}}\right)
$$

where $b_{\max} = \lambda_D$ is the Debye screening length, and $b_{\min}$ is the larger of the classical distance of closest approach $e^2/(m_e v_e^2)$ and the thermal de Broglie wavelength $\hbar/(m_e v_e)$, with $e$ the elementary charge, $m_e$ the electron mass, and $v_e$ the electron thermal speed.

The collision frequency scales as $\nu \propto \ln \Lambda$ and the Spitzer resistivity as $\eta \propto \ln \Lambda \, T_e^{-3/2}$, where $T_e$ is the electron temperature. In tokamak core conditions ($T_e \sim 5$–$10$ keV, $n_e \sim 10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$), $\ln \Lambda \approx 17$–$19$; in the cooler edge ($T_e \sim 10$–$100$ eV), values fall to approximately $10$–$14$. The pedestal-localized value is captured by [coulomb_logarithm_at_pedestal_top](name:coulomb_logarithm_at_pedestal_top).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the Debye length exceeds the minimum Coulomb impact parameter, a condition satisfied in all weakly coupled plasmas where $\Lambda > 1$.

NAMES.name: counter_passing_density
NAMES.short: Total number density of counter-passing particles — those whose guiding-center parallel velocity is directed opposite to the plasma current — including both thermal and suprathermal contributions from the distribution function.
NAMES.long:
Counter-passing particles are those whose guiding-center parallel velocity is directed opposite to the local plasma current direction, giving them sufficient parallel energy to complete full poloidal orbits around the torus without being reflected by the magnetic mirror force. This density integrates both the thermal bulk and any suprathermal population over the counter-passing region of phase space, weighted solely by orbit topology.

The counter-passing number density is defined by the velocity-space integral of the guiding-center distribution function restricted to the counter-passing domain:

$$
n_\text{cpass}(\mathbf{r}) = \int_{\text{cpass}} f(\mathbf{r}, v_\parallel, v_\perp) \, 2\pi v_\perp \, dv_\parallel \, dv_\perp
$$

where $f(\mathbf{r}, v_\parallel, v_\perp)$ is the guiding-center distribution function and the integral extends over the phase-space region of particles that circulate counter to the plasma current without magnetic trapping.

This quantity is computed by kinetic Fokker-Planck solvers that evolve the guiding-center distribution function and classify phase-space trajectories by orbit topology. Together with [co-passing density](name:total_co_passing_particle_density) and [trapped density](name:total_trapped_particle_density), it provides a complete orbit-class decomposition of the total local particle number density; summing all three classes recovers the full population. The suprathermal subset of this orbit class is resolved separately by [counter_passing_fast_particle_density](name:counter_passing_fast_particle_density), and the pressure moment of the same orbit class is given by counter_passing_pressure. Asymmetry between the co-passing and counter-passing densities reflects net parallel momentum injection, for example from directed neutral beam injection.
NAMES.sign: Positive when counter-passing particles are present in the distribution function; particle number density is intrinsically non-negative.

NAMES.name: counter_passing_fast_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Local volumetric rate at which Coulomb collisions transfer kinetic energy to fast ions on counter-passing guiding-center orbits. Counter-passing ions move parallel to the magnetic field opposite to the plasma-current direction.
NAMES.long:
Counter-passing fast-ion power density due to collisions is the local rate per unit volume at which Coulomb collisions transfer kinetic energy to the counter-passing part of the fast-ion distribution. Counter-passing refers to passing guiding-center orbits whose parallel velocity is opposite to the plasma-current direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

It is the energy moment of the collision operator restricted to the counter-passing region of velocity space:

$$
P_{\mathrm{cp}}^{\mathrm{coll}}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{s,b} \int_{\Omega_{\mathrm{cp}}} \frac{1}{2} m_s v^2\, C_{sb}[f_s,f_b](\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\, d^3v
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{cp}}^{\mathrm{coll}}$ is the counter-passing fast-ion collisional power density at spatial position $\mathbf{x}$, $s$ indexes fast-ion species or charge states, $b$ indexes background plasma species, $m_s$ is the fast-ion mass, $v=|\mathbf{v}|$, $f_s$ and $f_b$ are distribution functions, $C_{sb}$ is the collision operator acting on fast ions of class $s$ due to collisions with species $b$, $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element, and $\Omega_{\mathrm{cp}}$ is the counter-passing domain. With a pitch variable $\xi=v_\parallel/v$ and positive $v_\parallel$ chosen along the plasma current, $\Omega_{\mathrm{cp}}$ corresponds to $\xi<0$. The resulting unit is W m$^{-3}$.

This quantity is usually obtained from kinetic fast-ion calculations, Fokker-Planck or Monte Carlo collision operators, or reduced transport models using the reconstructed magnetic geometry and fast-ion distribution. For suprathermal fast ions in a cooler plasma it is often negative because Coulomb drag removes kinetic energy from the fast-ion population; it can be positive where collisions heat the selected counter-passing fast ions.

Typical magnitudes are $10^2$-$10^6$ W m$^{-3}$ in regions with appreciable fast-ion pressure and can reach about $10^7$ W m$^{-3}$ in strongly heated cores. Values approach zero where the counter-passing fast-ion density is small or collisional energy exchange is weak.
NAMES.sign: Positive when Coulomb collisions increase the kinetic energy of the counter-passing fast-ion population.

NAMES.name: counter_passing_fast_particle_density
NAMES.subject: particle
NAMES.short: Number density of fast (suprathermal) particles in the counter-passing orbit class, where guiding-center parallel velocity is directed opposite to the bulk plasma current.
NAMES.long:
Counter-passing fast particles are suprathermal ions or electrons whose guiding-center parallel velocity is anti-parallel to the bulk plasma current, executing closed toroidal orbits without magnetic mirror reflection. They are distinct from trapped particles, which undergo mirror reflection on the low-field side of the torus, and from [co_passing_fast_particle_density](name:co_passing_fast_particle_density) particles, which travel parallel to the current.

The counter-passing fast-particle density is the velocity-space integral of the fast-particle distribution function $f_\text{fast}$ restricted to counter-passing orbits:

$$
n_\text{fast,cp}(\mathbf{r}) = \int_{v_\parallel < 0} f_\text{fast}(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{v}) \, d^3v
$$

where $v_\parallel$ is the guiding-center parallel velocity and the integration domain covers orbits with $v_\parallel$ anti-parallel to the plasma current direction.

Together with [co_passing_fast_particle_density](name:co_passing_fast_particle_density), this quantity partitions the passing component of [fast_particle_density](name:fast_particle_density) by orbit class. The counter-passing population has opposite radial drift-orbit displacement from co-passing particles due to gradient and curvature drifts in the inhomogeneous tokamak field, making this decomposition essential for toroidal momentum balance, fast-particle orbit-loss studies, and neoclassical transport analyzes. The related [counter_passing_density](name:counter_passing_density) covers both thermal and suprathermal counter-passing particles.
NAMES.sign: Positive when counter-passing fast particles are present, with counter-passing defined as guiding-center parallel velocity anti-parallel to the plasma current direction.

NAMES.name: counter_passing_fast_particle_pressure
NAMES.subject: particle
NAMES.short: Scalar kinetic pressure moment of the suprathermal particle distribution restricted to counter-passing guiding-center orbits. It represents the counter-passing fast-particle contribution to pressure, evaluated locally or as a flux-surface average of the same orbit-selected moment.
NAMES.long:
Counter-passing fast-particle pressure is the scalar trace pressure carried by suprathermal particles on passing guiding-center orbits whose transit direction is opposite to the plasma current. It is the fast-particle contribution to [counter-passing total particle pressure](name:flux_surface_average_counter_passing_total_particle_pressure), complementary to [co-passing fast-particle pressure](name:co_passing_fast_particle_pressure) and [trapped fast-particle pressure](name:trapped_fast_particle_pressure). As a trace quantity it is consistent with the parallel and perpendicular tensor components for the same orbit class.

The local scalar trace pressure is defined by the second velocity moment over the counter-passing part of phase space:

$$
P_{\mathrm{cp,fast}}(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{3}\sum_s m_s \int_{\Omega_{\mathrm{cp},s}(\mathbf{x})} v^2 f_{\mathrm{fast},s}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $s$ labels fast-particle species, $m_s$ is the particle mass in kg, $v=|\mathbf{v}|$ is the particle speed in m s$^{-1}$, $f_{\mathrm{fast},s}$ is the fast-particle distribution function, and $\Omega_{\mathrm{cp},s}$ contains only passing orbits with parallel transit opposite to the plasma current. The result has units of Pa. The tensor trace relation is $P_{\mathrm{cp,fast}}=(P_{\parallel,\mathrm{cp,fast}}+2P_{\perp,\mathrm{cp,fast}})/3$ when [parallel](name:parallel_counter_passing_fast_particle_pressure) and [perpendicular](name:perpendicular_counter_passing_fast_particle_pressure) components use the same orbit selection.

In practice this pressure is computed from fast-particle distribution functions obtained from orbit-following, Fokker-Planck, or Monte Carlo modeling, often constrained by energetic-particle diagnostics such as neutron emission, gamma emission, neutral-particle analysis, or fast-ion light emission. A flux-surface-averaged value is obtained by first forming the local orbit-selected pressure moment and then averaging that scalar over a surface of constant magnetic flux; the averaging does not change the counter-passing orbit definition or the pressure-tensor trace relation.

Typical magnitudes are strongly scenario dependent. Values may be near 0 Pa where the counter-passing fast population is absent, around 10^2-10^4 Pa in modest auxiliary-heated plasmas, and up to order 10^5 Pa in strongly beam-heated or fusion-alpha-heated cores; the counter-passing subset is usually a fraction of the total fast-particle pressure.

NAMES.name: counter_passing_power_density
NAMES.short: Flux-surface-averaged volumetric energy source rate for the counter-passing orbit population. It is the local power density transferred to or from that population by wave-particle interactions, collisions, or particle sources.
NAMES.long:
Counter-passing power density is the flux-surface-averaged rate at which kinetic energy is added to the counter-passing orbit population per unit physical volume. Counter-passing refers to the passing part of velocity space whose guiding-center motion is opposite to the co-passing direction; it excludes trapped orbits.

A kinetic definition is the energy moment of the net source operator over the counter-passing velocity-space domain, followed by a flux-surface average:

$$
S_{\mathrm{cp}}^{\varepsilon}(\rho,t) = \left\langle \int_{\Omega_{\mathrm{cp}}} \frac{1}{2} m_s v^2\, \mathcal{S}_s(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v},t)\, d^3v \right\rangle_{\rho}
$$

where $S_{\mathrm{cp}}^{\varepsilon}$ has units W m$^{-3}$, $\rho$ is a radial flux-surface label in flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, $\Omega_{\mathrm{cp}}$ is the counter-passing velocity-space domain, $m_s$ is the species mass in kg, $v=|\mathbf{v}|$ is speed in m s$^{-1}$, and $d^3v$ has units m$^3$ s$^{-3}$. The operator $\mathcal{S}_s$ is the net time rate of change of the distribution function from sources, collisions, and wave interactions; if $\int f_s d^3v$ is a number density in m$^{-3}$, then $\mathcal{S}_s$ has units s$^2$ m$^{-6}$. The notation $\langle A\rangle_{\rho}$ denotes the flux-surface average at fixed $\rho$, equivalently the surface integral of $A$ weighted by $1/|\nabla\rho|$ divided by the corresponding weighted surface area.

In practice this quantity is computed from kinetic or Fokker-Planck models by taking the velocity-space energy moment of the relevant collision, external source, and wave-particle operators over the counter-passing domain. It is constrained indirectly by deposited heating, fast-particle measurements, loss measurements, and power-balance analysis. Together with [co_passing_power_density](name:co_passing_power_density) and [trapped_power_density](name:trapped_power_density), it partitions the orbit-integrated [power_density](name:electron_power_density).

Typical magnitudes are 10$^3$-10$^6$ W m$^{-3}$ in auxiliary-heated tokamak plasmas, with localized radio-frequency or neutral-beam deposition reaching about 10$^7$ W m$^{-3}$. Weakly driven regions can be near zero, and collisional drag or loss terms can give negative values with comparable magnitudes.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the counter-passing orbit population gains kinetic energy from the net source operator.

NAMES.name: current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift
NAMES.short: Vector current density produced by diamagnetic drift in a magnetized plasma, directed by the right-handed cross product of the magnetic field with the plasma pressure gradient and scaled by the squared magnetic-field magnitude. It is perpendicular to both the magnetic field and the pressure gradient.
NAMES.long:
Diamagnetic-drift current density is the perpendicular current produced by pressure gradients in a magnetized plasma. For an isotropic scalar pressure, it is directed along the ordered cross product of the magnetic field with the plasma pressure gradient, so that it contributes to the perpendicular current required for magnetohydrodynamic pressure balance.

For scalar pressure $p$, the diamagnetic current density is defined by

$$
\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{dia}} = \frac{\mathbf{B} \times \nabla p}{B^2}
$$

where $\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{dia}}$ is the diamagnetic current density, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field in T, $B^2=\mathbf{B}\cdot\mathbf{B}$, and $\nabla p$ is the plasma pressure gradient in Pa m^-1. With this ordering, $\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{dia}} \times \mathbf{B}=\nabla p_\perp$ when the pressure gradient is perpendicular to the magnetic field, consistent with perpendicular force balance.

In practice this quantity is computed from reconstructed or modeled magnetic fields together with pressure gradients inferred from density and temperature measurements or transport calculations. Its radial and vertical projections in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame are related to [radial_diamagnetic_current_density](name:radial_diamagnetic_current_density) and [vertical_diamagnetic_current_density](name:vertical_diamagnetic_current_density).

Typical magnitudes in magnetically confined fusion plasmas are about 10^2-10^5 A m^-2 in the core and edge pedestal, with larger values occurring where pressure gradients are steep and the magnetic field is comparatively weak.
NAMES.sign: Positive when conventional positive charge flow is along $\mathbf{B} \times \nabla p$.

NAMES.name: current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity
NAMES.short: Full current density vector produced by the divergence of the field-aligned component of the plasma viscous stress tensor. It is the viscous drift current required to balance the parallel-viscous force density against the magnetic field.
NAMES.long:
Current density due to parallel viscosity is the vector current associated with the force density produced by spatial variation of the field-aligned part of the plasma viscous stress tensor. It is a viscous drift-current contribution to momentum balance, distinct from currents driven by pressure gradients, inertia, resistivity, or perpendicular viscous stress.

The defining force-balance form for this contribution is:

$$
\mathbf{J}_{\Pi_\parallel} = \frac{(\nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\Pi}_\parallel) \times \mathbf{B}}{B^2}
$$

where $\mathbf{J}_{\Pi_\parallel}$ is the current density due to parallel viscosity, $\boldsymbol{\Pi}_\parallel$ is the parallel viscous stress tensor in Pa, $\nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\Pi}_\parallel$ is the corresponding viscous force density in N m$^{-3}$, equivalently Pa m$^{-1}$, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field in T, and $B=|\mathbf{B}|$. The cross product makes this contribution locally perpendicular to $\mathbf{B}$.

This current is generally inferred rather than measured directly. It is evaluated from a magnetic-field estimate and a closure or model for the field-aligned viscous stress, with the divergence capturing spatial variation of parallel viscous momentum transport. When resolved in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, its projections include [radial_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity](name:radial_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity) and [toroidal_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity](name:toroidal_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity). The total radial and toroidal viscous-current components combine these with perpendicular-viscosity contributions in [radial_current_density_due_to_viscosity](name:radial_current_density_due_to_viscosity) and [toroidal_current_density_due_to_viscosity](name:toroidal_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity); [parallel_current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity](name:parallel_current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity) is the complementary field-aligned contribution driven by perpendicular viscous stress.

Typical magnitudes are closure- and regime-dependent. Components are often 10^-2-10^2 A.m^-2 in weakly viscous core regions and can reach 10^3-10^4 A.m^-2 in steep-gradient, strong-flow-shear, or edge regions, usually remaining below the main equilibrium current density.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the current density vector is directed as $(\nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\Pi}_\parallel) \times \mathbf{B}$ according to the right-hand rule.

NAMES.name: current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity
NAMES.short: Full current density vector arising from the divergence of the perpendicular viscous stress tensor in magnetized plasma, driving drift currents transverse to the local magnetic field.
NAMES.long:
The current density vector $\mathbf{J}_{\pi_\perp}$ quantifies the electromagnetic current generated when the divergence of the perpendicular viscous stress tensor acts on the charged-particle fluid in a magnetized plasma. Perpendicular viscosity encompasses the components of the viscous stress tensor that act transverse to the local magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$, coupling cross-field velocity shear to momentum transport across flux surfaces and producing a drift current that enters the overall current balance.

The defining relation follows from the perpendicular projection of the two-fluid momentum equation:

$$
\mathbf{J}_{\pi_\perp} = \frac{\mathbf{B} \times (\nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\pi}_\perp)}{B^2}
$$

where $\boldsymbol{\pi}_\perp$ is the perpendicular viscous stress tensor and $B = |\mathbf{B}|$ is the local magnetic field magnitude. This full vector subsumes the [diamagnetic-direction projection](name:diamagnetic_current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity) and all cylindrical components resolved in the right-handed $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

This current is most significant in the edge and scrape-off layer where velocity shear and density gradients are steep. It is computed from two-fluid transport models that carry the full viscous stress tensor and contributes, alongside [bootstrap current density](name:bootstrap_current_density), to non-inductive current closure in the plasma momentum balance.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the radial component points in the $+R$ direction away from the symmetry axis, the toroidal component points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$, and the vertical component points in the $+Z$ direction, all defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: deuterium_density_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: deuterium
NAMES.short: Number density of deuterium ions evaluated at the radial position of the internal transport barrier, the flux surface where turbulent cross-field transport is locally suppressed and steep radial gradients can form.
NAMES.long:
The deuterium ion number density at the internal transport barrier (ITB) characterizes the local fuel-ion concentration at the barrier's reference flux surface, where cross-field turbulent diffusion is suppressed and steep radial density gradients can persist. Internal transport barriers form when $E \times B$ velocity shear or reversed magnetic shear quenches dominant drift-wave turbulence, creating a region of locally enhanced particle confinement.

The quantity is the deuterium ion density profile $n_D(\rho)$ evaluated at the ITB reference radius $\rho_\mathrm{ITB}$:

$$
n_D^\mathrm{ITB} = n_D(\rho_\mathrm{ITB})
$$

where $\rho_\mathrm{ITB}$ is the ITB position in the chosen radial coordinate, such as the normalized toroidal flux radius, and corresponds to the surface where the transport suppression is most pronounced.

In practice, this value is inferred from Thomson scattering, charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, or reflectometry measurements resolved at the barrier location, combined with equilibrium reconstruction to map measurement positions to flux-surface coordinates.

The parent quantity [density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:density_at_internal_transport_barrier) covers all constituent species using the same locus convention. The analogous fuel-ion siblings for hydrogen and tritium are [hydrogen_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:hydrogen_density_at_internal_transport_barrier) and [tritium_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:tritium_density_at_internal_transport_barrier). The pedestal counterpart for deuterium is [deuterium_density_at_pedestal](name:deuterium_density_at_pedestal).
NAMES.sign: Positive when deuterium ions are present; particle number density is an intrinsically non-negative quantity.

NAMES.name: deuterium_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: deuterium
NAMES.short: Number density of deuterium ions at the magnetic axis, the innermost point of the confined plasma where the gradient of the poloidal magnetic flux vanishes.
NAMES.long:
Deuterium density at the magnetic axis is the local number density of ionized deuterium fuel at the center of the nested closed flux surfaces. It counts deuterium ions, normally fully ionized $D^+$ in the hot core, and excludes neutral deuterium atoms.

The quantity is the deuterium number-density field evaluated at the magnetic-axis point:

$$
n_{D,\mathrm{axis}} = n_D(\mathbf{x}_\mathrm{axis}) = \left.\frac{dN_D}{dV}\right|_{\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{x}_\mathrm{axis}}
$$

where $n_D$ is the deuterium ion number density, $N_D$ is the number of deuterium ions in an infinitesimal volume $V$, and $\mathbf{x}_\mathrm{axis}$ is the point where $\nabla\psi=0$ for the poloidal magnetic flux $\psi$.

In practice this value is obtained by evaluating the deuterium density at the reconstructed magnetic axis. It may be constrained by isotope-resolved density measurements, neutron emission, particle-balance modeling, and quasineutrality using electron density, impurity content, and other ion-species densities. It is closely related to the full deuterium density distribution [deuterium_density](name:deuterium_density), the electron density on axis [electron_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:electron_density_at_magnetic_axis), and the summed ion density on axis [total_ion_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:total_ion_density_at_magnetic_axis).

Typical on-axis values in tokamak plasmas are $0.1-5 \times 10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$, with lower values in low-density or weakly fueled discharges and higher values in dense deuterium or deuterium-tritium scenarios.

NAMES.name: deuterium_deuterium_flux
NAMES.subject: deuterium_deuterium
NAMES.short: Total neutron emission rate from deuterium-deuterium fusion through the neutron-producing D(d,n)He-3 branch. It includes thermal, beam-thermal, and beam-beam deuteron reactions; each counted reaction emits one 2.45 MeV neutron.
NAMES.long:
The deuterium-deuterium neutron flux is the global rate at which neutrons are produced by the neutron branch of DD fusion, $\mathrm{D(d,n)^3He}$. It counts neutron-producing reactions from all relevant deuteron populations, including thermal bulk ions, beam ions reacting with thermal deuterons, and beam ions reacting with other fast deuterons.

The total DD neutron emission rate can be written as the sum of thermal, beam-thermal, and beam-beam contributions:

$$
S_{\mathrm{DD},n} = S_{\mathrm{th},n} + S_{\mathrm{bt},n} + S_{\mathrm{bb},n} = \int_V \left[\frac{1}{2} n_{\mathrm{D,th}}^2 \langle \sigma v \rangle_{\mathrm{DD},n}^{\mathrm{th}} + R_{\mathrm{bt},n} + R_{\mathrm{bb},n}\right] dV
$$

where $S_{\mathrm{DD},n}$ is the total neutron rate in Hz, $S_{\mathrm{th},n}$, $S_{\mathrm{bt},n}$, and $S_{\mathrm{bb},n}$ are the thermal, beam-thermal, and beam-beam parts, $n_{\mathrm{D,th}}$ is the thermal deuterium density, $\langle \sigma v \rangle_{\mathrm{DD},n}^{\mathrm{th}}$ is the branch reactivity for $\mathrm{D(d,n)^3He}$, and $R_{\mathrm{bt},n}$ and $R_{\mathrm{bb},n}$ are local volumetric neutron production rates from beam-thermal and beam-beam reactions. The factor $1/2$ avoids double counting identical thermal deuteron pairs.

Experimentally, this rate is inferred from absolutely calibrated neutron diagnostics such as fission chambers, activation systems, scintillators, or proportional counters, with corrections for detector efficiency, geometry, attenuation, and neutron energy response. In modeling and transport analysis, the thermal part corresponds to [deuterium_deuterium_flux_due_to_thermal_fusion](name:deuterium_deuterium_flux_due_to_thermal_fusion), the beam-thermal part to [deuterium_deuterium_flux_due_to_beam_thermal_fusion](name:deuterium_deuterium_flux_due_to_beam_thermal_fusion), and the beam-beam part to [deuterium_deuterium_flux_due_to_beam_beam_fusion](name:deuterium_deuterium_flux_due_to_beam_beam_fusion).

Typical DD neutron rates range from about $10^{10}$-$10^{14}$ Hz in low-power or ohmic deuterium plasmas, $10^{14}$-$10^{16}$ Hz in hotter medium-sized tokamak plasmas, and up to $10^{17}$-$10^{18}$ Hz when strong neutral-beam heating produces a large fast-deuteron population.

NAMES.name: deuterium_deuterium_flux_due_to_beam_beam_fusion
NAMES.subject: deuterium_deuterium
NAMES.short: Rate of neutron production from deuterium-deuterium fusion reactions in which both reacting deuterons are energetic fast ions from neutral beam injection, before thermalization with the background plasma.
NAMES.long:
The D-D beam-beam neutron flux counts the rate at which 2.45 MeV neutrons are emitted via the $D + D \rightarrow {}^3\text{He} + n$ branch of D-D fusion, where both interacting deuterium nuclei are fast ions from neutral beam injection that have not yet thermalized with the background plasma. This is a component of [flux_due_to_beam_beam_fusion](name:flux_due_to_beam_beam_fusion), which sums beam-beam neutron rates over all reaction channels, and is distinguished from [deuterium_deuterium_flux_due_to_beam_thermal_fusion](name:deuterium_deuterium_flux_due_to_beam_thermal_fusion), where only one reactant is a beam ion.

The total rate integrates over beam fast-ion pairs across the plasma volume:

$$
\Phi_{DD}^{bb} = \frac{1}{2} \int_V \int \int \sigma_{DD}(g)\, g\, f_b(\mathbf{v}_1)\, f_b(\mathbf{v}_2)\, d^3v_1\, d^3v_2\, dV
$$

where $\sigma_{DD}(g)$ is the D-D cross section for the neutron-producing branch, $g = |\mathbf{v}_1 - \mathbf{v}_2|$ is the relative speed of the two fast ions, $f_b$ is the beam deuterium fast-ion phase-space distribution, and $V$ is the plasma volume. The factor of $\frac{1}{2}$ prevents double-counting identical-species pairs.

Because beam ion densities are much lower than bulk plasma densities, this contribution is generally smaller than [deuterium_deuterium_flux_due_to_beam_thermal_fusion](name:deuterium_deuterium_flux_due_to_beam_thermal_fusion); in D-T plasmas, [deuterium_tritium_flux_due_to_beam_beam_fusion](name:deuterium_tritium_flux_due_to_beam_beam_fusion) typically dominates the beam-beam neutron budget owing to the larger D-T cross section at NBI energies. The rate is computed from fast-ion distribution models constrained by neutron spectrometry, activation measurements, or fission-chamber data.
NAMES.sign: Positive when D-D beam-beam fusion reactions emit neutrons from the plasma.

NAMES.name: deuterium_tritium_density
NAMES.subject: deuterium_tritium
NAMES.short: Ion number density of the fictitious combined deuterium-tritium fuel pseudo-species, equal to the sum of the local deuterium and tritium ion densities in transport models treating both isotopes as one effective ion.
NAMES.long:
The deuterium-tritium density is the local ion count per unit volume belonging to the fictitious combined fuel pseudo-species formed by merging the deuterium and tritium populations into a single effective ion. This simplification reduces the fuel ion description to a single continuity equation and is employed in transport simulations that do not resolve D and T as separately evolved species.

The DT pseudo-species density $n_{DT}$ equals the sum of the individual isotope number densities:

$$
n_{DT} = n_D + n_T
$$

where $n_D$ is the deuterium ion number density and $n_T$ is the tritium ion number density.

The local density is inferred from neutron emission profiles, hydrogen isotope spectroscopy, or charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy combined with charge-state balance. In integrated modeling, it is evolved by a continuity equation incorporating ionization, recombination, and transport source terms. The volume average of this quantity is [volume_averaged_deuterium_tritium_density](name:volume_averaged_deuterium_tritium_density), and the on-axis value is [deuterium_tritium_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:deuterium_tritium_density_at_magnetic_axis). When D and T are resolved as separate species, the individual isotope densities are tracked by [volume_averaged_deuterium_density](name:volume_averaged_deuterium_density) and [volume_averaged_tritium_density](name:volume_averaged_tritium_density).

Typical core values in DT burning plasmas range from $10^{19}$ to $10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$, decreasing toward the edge and scrape-off layer.

NAMES.name: diamagnetic_momentum_effective_convection_velocity
NAMES.short: Charge-state-aggregated diamagnetic effective convection velocity for radial ion momentum transport. It is the velocity coefficient that, multiplied by the total ion momentum density, reproduces the summed charge-state diamagnetic convective momentum flux across magnetic flux surfaces.
NAMES.long:
Diamagnetic momentum effective convection velocity is the scalar velocity coefficient that condenses the charge-state-aggregated diamagnetic convective contribution to radial ion momentum transport into a single effective velocity. It multiplies the total ion momentum density to reproduce the summed diamagnetic convective momentum flux from all ion charge states.

For ion charge states indexed by $z$, it is defined as the ratio of the summed diamagnetic momentum flux to the summed momentum density on a magnetic flux surface:

$$
V_{\pi,\mathrm{eff}}^{\mathrm{dia}} = \frac{\sum_z \langle \Gamma_{\pi,z}^{\mathrm{dia}} \rangle}{\sum_z \langle \pi_z \rangle}
$$

where $\Gamma_{\pi,z}^{\mathrm{dia}}$ is the radial diamagnetic flux of ion momentum for charge state $z$ (units of momentum density times m.s^-1, i.e. kg.m^-1.s^-2 or Pa for linear momentum density), $\pi_z$ is the corresponding momentum density, and $\langle A \rangle$ denotes the average of $A$ over a magnetic flux surface labeled by the normalized toroidal flux radius $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$. Equivalently, given charge-state velocities $V_{\pi,z}^{\mathrm{dia}}$ with a common convention, $V_{\pi,\mathrm{eff}}^{\mathrm{dia}} = \sum_z \langle \pi_z \rangle V_{\pi,z}^{\mathrm{dia}} / \sum_z \langle \pi_z \rangle$, provided the denominator is nonzero.

This is the charge-state-aggregated counterpart of the ion-resolved ion_diamagnetic_momentum_convection_velocity and the per-state [ion_state_diamagnetic_momentum_convection_velocity](name:ion_state_diamagnetic_momentum_convection_velocity); it carries the effective qualifier relative to [diamagnetic_momentum_convection_velocity](name:diamagnetic_momentum_convection_velocity) to indicate the density-weighted aggregation over charge states. It is not usually a directly measured velocity but is inferred from reconstructed equilibrium geometry, kinetic profiles, rotation measurements, and the transport model used to separate the diamagnetic component from other momentum-flux channels.

Typical magnitudes are 0.1-10 m.s^-1 in core transport analyzes and can reach 10-100 m.s^-1 in steep-gradient regions or during strong momentum redistribution. The value may be either inward or outward and should be interpreted together with the chosen momentum density and the full momentum-flux decomposition.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the charge-state-aggregated diamagnetic convective flux of ion momentum is directed toward increasing normalized toroidal flux radius $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$, from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: effective_charge_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.short: Effective charge Zeff of the plasma ion mixture evaluated at the internal transport barrier, defined as the charge-squared-weighted mean charge number over all ion species.
NAMES.long:
The effective charge $Z_\text{eff}$ characterizes the ionic composition of a magnetically confined plasma by weighting each ion species by the square of its charge number relative to the first charge moment, yielding a single dimensionless index of impurity content.

The defining relation is

$$
Z_\text{eff} = \frac{\sum_s n_s Z_s^2}{\sum_s n_s Z_s}
$$

where $n_s$ is the number density of ion species $s$ (summed over all charge states) and $Z_s$ is its charge number. A pure single-species hydrogenic plasma gives $Z_\text{eff} = 1$; the presence of higher-$Z$ impurities always raises $Z_\text{eff}$ above unity.

Evaluated at the internal transport barrier (ITB), this quantity captures the local effective charge where turbulent transport is suppressed and kinetic profile gradients are steep — the same reference location used by [electron density at the ITB](name:electron_density_at_internal_transport_barrier) and [electron temperature at the ITB](name:electron_temperature_at_internal_transport_barrier). Local impurity accumulation or expulsion near the ITB can shift the local $Z_\text{eff}$ considerably from its volume-averaged value.

The effective charge is inferred spectroscopically from the free-free bremsstrahlung continuum, whose radiated intensity scales as $n_e^2 Z_\text{eff} T_e^{-1/2}$ where $n_e$ is the electron number density and $T_e$ is the electron temperature, or from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy summed over resolved ion species. In clean deuterium discharges $Z_\text{eff}$ approaches 1.0, rising to 3–5 in high-impurity or metallic-wall scenarios.
NAMES.sign: Positive when any ionized species populate the plasma, which is always the case in a magnetically confined discharge; the lower bound $Z_\text{eff} = 1$ is attained only for a hypothetically impurity-free single-species plasma.

NAMES.name: effective_charge_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.short: Effective charge at the magnetic axis is the local density-weighted mean of squared ion charge numbers, summed over ion species or charge states and normalized by electron density. It quantifies how on-axis impurities increase collisionality relative to a pure hydrogen-isotope plasma.
NAMES.long:
Effective charge at the magnetic axis is the local value of [effective_charge](name:effective_charge) evaluated on the magnetic axis, the center of the nested magnetic flux surfaces. It is not the arithmetic mean ion charge; because the charge number is squared, highly charged impurity ions contribute disproportionately even at small density fractions.

For a plasma with local electron density and ion species or charge-state densities, the on-axis effective charge is defined as:

$$
Z_{\mathrm{eff,axis}} = \frac{\sum_s n_s(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{axis}}) Z_s^2}{n_e(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{axis}})}
$$

where $s$ indexes ion species or ionization states present at the magnetic axis, $n_s$ is the corresponding ion density in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, $Z_s$ is the positive ion charge number in units of the elementary charge, $n_e$ is the electron density in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, and $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{axis}}$ denotes the magnetic-axis location. For a quasineutral plasma, $n_e = \sum_s n_s Z_s$ locally, so the ratio has unit 1.

In practice the quantity is computed from a local estimate of plasma composition at the magnetic axis. That composition may be inferred from a combination of electron-density information, impurity measurements, radiation constraints, and transport or atomic-physics modeling; no single diagnostic defines it universally.

Representative on-axis values are $Z_{\mathrm{eff,axis}}=1$ for a pure hydrogen-isotope plasma and about 1-3 for many low-to-moderate impurity tokamak cores. Larger values indicate a stronger contribution from high-charge impurity ions or unusually impurity-rich conditions.

NAMES.name: electron_density_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Number density of electrons at the radial location of an internal transport barrier, where reduced turbulent cross-field transport permits steep electron-density gradients to form.
NAMES.long:
The electron density at the internal transport barrier is the local electron number density $n_e$ at the single flux-surface radius assigned to the barrier in the chosen radial coordinate. An internal transport barrier is a localized plasma region where anomalous cross-field particle transport is suppressed, enabling sustained steep radial density gradients; this value characterizes particle confinement within the barrier and serves as a key local constraint on transport modeling.

The quantity is a point evaluation on the electron continuity equation:

$$
\frac{\partial n_e}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \Gamma_e = S_e
$$

where $\Gamma_e$ is the electron particle flux and $S_e$ is the electron particle source rate. At the ITB radius the reduction in anomalous $\Gamma_e$ permits a steep $n_e$ gradient to develop and be sustained against diffusion.

The value is extracted from measured electron-density radial profiles obtained by Thomson scattering, microwave reflectometry, or far-infrared interferometry, with the ITB radius identified from characteristic features such as a sharp peak or inflection in the $n_e$ gradient profile.

Typical values in ITB discharges range from $5 \times 10^{18}$ to $2 \times 10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$, depending on plasma current, heating power, and fueling scenario. The companion quantity [electron_temperature_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:electron_temperature_at_internal_transport_barrier) combines with this density to yield the local electron pressure. Impurity densities at the same location, such as [neon_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:neon_density_at_internal_transport_barrier) and [argon_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:argon_density_at_internal_transport_barrier), characterize impurity enrichment within the barrier; the general species-agnostic form is given by [density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:density_at_internal_transport_barrier).

NAMES.name: electron_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: On-axis electron number density at the innermost point of the confined plasma where the gradient of poloidal magnetic flux vanishes.
NAMES.long:
The electron density at the magnetic axis is the local free-electron number density per unit volume evaluated at the point $(R_\mathrm{axis}, Z_\mathrm{axis})$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame — where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height — at which $\nabla\psi = 0$, identifying the center of the nested flux-surface family. As the on-axis value of the electron density radial profile, it represents the profile peak in centrally-heated plasmas and serves as the normalization reference for the density peaking factor.

The on-axis electron density $n_{e,0}$ is linked to companion on-axis ion densities through the quasineutrality condition:

$$
n_{e,0} = \sum_i Z_i \, n_{i,0}
$$

where $Z_i$ is the charge number and $n_{i,0}$ is the on-axis number density of ion species $i$. This connects $n_{e,0}$ to quantities such as [total_ion_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:total_ion_density_at_magnetic_axis), [hydrogen_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:hydrogen_density_at_magnetic_axis), and impurity species like [carbon_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:carbon_density_at_magnetic_axis) and [argon_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:argon_density_at_magnetic_axis).

The on-axis value is measured by Thomson scattering, which provides spatially localized electron density and temperature simultaneously, or inferred from line-integrated interferometry combined with profile inversion. Typical on-axis values in current medium-sized tokamaks range from $2 \times 10^{19}$ to $1 \times 10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$, approaching the Greenwald limit at high plasma current. It also enters collisionality estimates as $\nu_* \propto n_{e,0} / T_{e,0}^2$, where $T_{e,0}$ is the on-axis electron temperature. See [density_at_magnetic_axis](name:density_at_magnetic_axis) for the species-agnostic parent definition.

NAMES.name: electron_energy_diffusivity
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Effective Fickian diffusivity for electron thermal energy transport across magnetic flux surfaces, multiplying the electron-temperature gradient to give the conductive electron heat flux.
NAMES.long:
Electron energy diffusivity, usually denoted $\chi_e$, is the effective Fickian transport coefficient for conductive transport of electron thermal energy. It represents the part of the electron heat flux driven by gradients of electron temperature, distinct from convective transport of electron energy by a pinch or flow velocity.

For a radial flux-surface label $\rho$ increasing from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary, with outward unit normal $\hat{n}_\rho$, the conductive electron heat-flux projection is commonly written as:

$$
q_{e,\rho}^{\mathrm{cond}} = - n_e \chi_e \, \nabla T_e \cdot \hat{n}_\rho
$$

where $q_{e,\rho}^{\mathrm{cond}}$ is positive toward increasing $\rho$ and has units W m$^{-2}$, $n_e$ is the electron density in m$^{-3}$, $\chi_e$ is the electron energy diffusivity in m$^2$ s$^{-1}$, and $T_e$ is the electron temperature expressed as an energy per particle in joules. If $T_e$ is expressed in eV, the right-hand side must be multiplied by the elementary charge to obtain W m$^{-2}$. The minus sign means that a temperature decreasing outward gives an outward conductive heat flux.

This quantity is not measured directly. It is inferred from the electron energy balance using measured electron density and temperature, estimates of heating, radiation, particle, and exchange terms, and a reconstruction or model of the heat-flux divergence; it may also be predicted by neoclassical or turbulent transport models. In reduced transport descriptions it is often used together with an electron energy convection velocity to separate diffusive and convective contributions.

Representative inferred values in magnetically confined plasmas are about 0.1-10 m^2.s^-1 in the confined core, with values reaching several tens of m^2.s^-1 in strongly turbulent or edge regions. The effective value can vary strongly with radius, collisionality, magnetic shear, turbulence regime, and applied heating.

NAMES.name: electron_energy_implicit_source_rate
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Implicit rate coefficient for the stiff part of an electron energy source term. Multiplying it by the local electron energy density gives the contribution treated implicitly in an electron energy balance or transport solver.
NAMES.long:
The electron energy implicit source rate is the linear coefficient used to represent the stiff part of an electron energy source or sink. It separates a source term into a part evaluated explicitly and a part proportional to the local electron energy density, improving numerical stability for rapidly responding physics.

A common local decomposition of the electron energy source is:

$$
Q_e = Q_{e,\mathrm{expl}} + S_{e,\mathrm{impl}}\,u_e
$$

where $Q_e$ is the total volumetric electron energy source, $Q_{e,\mathrm{expl}}$ is the explicit contribution, $S_{e,\mathrm{impl}}$ is the electron energy implicit source rate, and $u_e$ is the electron energy density. The product $S_{e,\mathrm{impl}}u_e$ has units of volumetric power density.

This coefficient is usually obtained from the linearization of heating, radiation, equilibration, ionization, recombination, or other source models with respect to the evolved electron energy variable. It is a numerical representation of local stiffness rather than a directly measured physical observable; experiments constrain it through the underlying source models and reconstructed electron density, temperature, and radiation or heating power.

Typical magnitudes are highly model dependent. Slowly varying heating or loss terms may have effective rates below 1 s^-1, while stiff collisional, atomic, or radiation terms commonly fall in the range 1-10^4 s^-1 and can be larger in cold or dense edge conditions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the implicit contribution adds energy to the electron population.

NAMES.name: electron_implicit_source_rate
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Implicit (stiff) rate coefficient for the electron particle source in transport equations, multiplied by the local electron density to give the source contribution treated implicitly.
NAMES.long:
Electron implicit source rate is the coefficient that represents the stiff, density-proportional part of the electron particle source in a particle-balance transport equation. It converts the local electron density into an implicit source-density contribution, so its dimensions are inverse time rather than particles per volume per time.

The source decomposition can be written in unit-balanced form as:

$$
S_e = S_{e,\mathrm{exp}} + \gamma_{e,\mathrm{imp}} n_e
$$

where $S_e$ is the total electron particle source density, $S_{e,\mathrm{exp}}$ is the part advanced explicitly, $\gamma_{e,\mathrm{imp}}$ is the electron implicit source rate, and $n_e$ is the local electron density; $S_e$ and $S_{e,\mathrm{exp}}$ have units of m^-3 s^-1 when $n_e$ is in m^-3.

It is usually computed rather than measured directly. Atomic and molecular processes such as electron-impact ionization contribute positive density-proportional terms, while radiative and three-body recombination contribute negative terms; transport models may also include linearized fueling, recycling, or other external particle sources according to the numerical implicit-explicit split. It is the electron-particle counterpart of [electron_energy_implicit_source_rate](name:electron_energy_implicit_source_rate) and is coupled to ion source coefficients through ionization balance and quasineutrality.

Typical values are near zero for weakly sourced core regions, about 10^-3-10 s^-1 for particle replacement on confinement-time scales, and can reach 10^2-10^5 s^-1 in cold edge, recycling, or localized strong-source regions where atomic timescales are short. Negative values of similar magnitude can occur where recombination or net particle removal dominates.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the implicit term $\gamma_{e,\mathrm{imp}} n_e$ increases the electron number density.

NAMES.name: electron_particle_flux
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Electron particle flux is the signed number of electrons crossing a unit area per unit time through an oriented surface. It is the surface-normal component of electron particle transport due to flow, drifts, diffusion, or turbulence.
NAMES.long:
Electron particle flux is the signed rate at which electrons cross unit area of an oriented surface. It is the surface-normal component of the electron particle-flux density vector, combining transport from bulk motion, drifts, collisional diffusion, and turbulent fluctuations.

The flux through a surface with unit normal $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is commonly decomposed into convective and nonconvective contributions:

$$
\Gamma_e = \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_e \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} = \left(n_e \mathbf{u}_e + \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{e,\mathrm{diff}} + \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{e,\mathrm{drift}} + \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{e,\mathrm{turb}}\right)\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}}
$$

where $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_e$ is the electron particle-flux density vector, $n_e$ is electron density, $\mathbf{u}_e$ is the mean electron velocity, and the remaining terms represent diffusive, drift, and turbulent particle transport contributions.

In practice, electron particle flux is obtained from particle balance, kinetic or fluid transport calculations, or experimental inference using density, flow, and particle-source measurements. Diffusive closures often make the diffusive contribution proportional to $-\nabla n_e$, while turbulent transport is usually inferred from fluctuation measurements or from balance between sources, sinks, and changes in density.

Typical magnitudes range from $10^{18}$-$10^{21}$ m^-2.s^-1 for cross-field transport in confined or scrape-off-layer plasmas, and can reach $10^{22}$-$10^{24}$ m^-2.s^-1 for strong parallel flows to material surfaces in high-density divertor conditions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the net electron particle flow crosses the oriented surface in the direction of its positive normal.

NAMES.name: electron_power_density
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Signed volumetric source term in the electron energy transport equation that captures net power deposition into or removal from the electron population per unit plasma volume.
NAMES.long:
The electron power density $Q_e$ is the aggregate signed volumetric source in the electron energy balance, capturing all mechanisms that exchange power with the electron population — including ohmic heating, wave absorption, collisional energy exchange with ions and neutrals, ionization, and radiation losses — per unit plasma volume.

The principal defining relation is the electron energy transport equation:

$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\!\left(\frac{3}{2} n_e T_e\right) + \nabla \cdot \mathbf{q}_e = Q_e
$$

where $n_e$ is the electron number density, $T_e$ is the electron temperature in energy units, and $\mathbf{q}_e$ is the electron heat flux vector.

The total $Q_e$ aggregates all power channels acting on electrons. It can be decomposed into sub-contributions such as [fast_electron_power_density](name:fast_electron_power_density) for the suprathermal electron component and [thermal_electron_power_density](name:thermal_electron_power_density) for the bulk electron channel. The complementary species-level source terms are [ion_power_density](name:total_ion_power_density) and [neutral_power_density](name:neutral_state_power_density). Core heating sources typically fall in the range $10^4$–$10^7$ W m$^{-3}$; negative values arise when electrons transfer energy to ions via Coulomb collisions or lose energy through radiation.
NAMES.sign: Positive when energy is deposited into the electron population (net electron heating); negative when the electron channel is a net donor of energy to other populations or loss mechanisms.

NAMES.name: electron_pressure
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Kinetic pressure of the electron population, defined for an isotropic Maxwellian as the product of electron number density and thermal energy per particle.
NAMES.long:
The electron pressure quantifies the isotropic mechanical stress exerted by the electron population and enters the plasma momentum equation through the pressure-gradient force $-\nabla p_e$, driving both parallel and cross-field transport. It encompasses contributions from the thermal bulk and suprathermal fast-electron populations.

For an isotropic distribution function $f_e(\mathbf{v})$, the scalar pressure is the second velocity-moment:

$$
p_e = \frac{m_e}{3} \int v^2 \, f_e(\mathbf{v}) \, d^3v
$$

where $m_e$ is the electron mass and $v = |\mathbf{v}|$. For a Maxwellian distribution this reduces to $p_e = n_e T_e$, where $n_e$ is the electron number density and $T_e$ is the electron temperature expressed in joules.

The electron pressure profile is inferred from Thomson scattering, which yields simultaneous $n_e$ and $T_e$ measurements, or from independent diagnostics combining interferometry for density with electron cyclotron emission for temperature. Decomposing by population yields [thermal_electron_pressure](name:thermal_electron_pressure_at_post_sawtooth_crash) and [fast_electron_pressure](name:fast_electron_pressure), whose sum is the [total_electron_pressure](name:total_electron_pressure); adding ion contributions gives the [bulk thermal plasma pressure]. Typical core values in H-mode discharges range from $10^3$–$10^4$ Pa, falling to $1$–$100$ Pa in the scrape-off layer.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the electron population carries finite kinetic energy, which holds for all physical plasmas at nonzero temperature.

NAMES.name: electron_source_rate
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Particle source rate for electrons in the electron number-density transport equation, representing the net local production or loss of free electrons per unit volume.
NAMES.long:
Electron source rate is the local net rate at which free electrons are created or removed by particle processes. It is the particle source term for the electron number-density balance, with source and sink contributions combined into one signed volumetric rate.

The source term enters the electron continuity equation as the non-transport contribution to the density evolution:

$$
\frac{\partial n_e}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \Gamma_e = S_e = S_{e,\mathrm{exp}} + \nu_{e,\mathrm{imp}} n_e
$$

where $n_e$ is the electron density, $\Gamma_e$ is the electron particle flux, $S_e$ is the electron source rate, $S_{e,\mathrm{exp}}$ is an explicit source contribution with units m$^{-3}$ s$^{-1}$, and $\nu_{e,\mathrm{imp}}$ is the [electron_implicit_source_rate](name:electron_implicit_source_rate), a density-dependent coefficient with units s$^{-1}$ that multiplies $n_e$.

In practice, this rate is obtained from particle-balance analysis or transport modeling. Important contributors include ionization of neutrals and impurities, recombination of ions and electrons, externally supplied fueling after ionization, and other modeled processes that change the number of free electrons; processes that only exchange charge between heavy particles without changing the free-electron count do not directly contribute.

Typical magnitudes are about $10^{18}$-$10^{21}$ m$^{-3}$ s$^{-1}$ in the confined plasma and can reach $10^{20}$-$10^{23}$ m$^{-3}$ s$^{-1}$ in strongly fueled or recycling edge regions. Net negative values occur where electron-loss processes such as recombination exceed local production.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the local net effect of particle processes increases the free-electron number density.

NAMES.name: electron_temperature_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Kinetic temperature of the electron population evaluated at the single flux-surface radius assigned to the internal transport barrier, a core region where turbulent transport is locally suppressed and steep profile gradients develop.
NAMES.long:
The electron temperature at the internal transport barrier (ITB) location quantifies the local thermal energy of the electron population at the specific radial position identifying the barrier, a region inside the last-closed flux surface where turbulent cross-field transport is reduced and steep gradients steepen. It is the electron-species component of [temperature_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:temperature_at_internal_transport_barrier), evaluated for the electron population specifically rather than for ions or a bulk-average.

Under the Maxwellian approximation, $T_e$ is the second-velocity-moment quantity:

$$
T_e = \frac{m_e}{3 n_e} \int |\mathbf{v}|^2 f_e(\mathbf{v}) \, d^3v
$$

where $m_e$ is the electron mass, $n_e$ is the local electron number density, and $f_e(\mathbf{v})$ is the electron velocity distribution function normalized so that $\int f_e \, d^3v = n_e$.

The electron temperature profile is routinely measured by Thomson scattering or electron cyclotron emission diagnostics; the ITB value is extracted by evaluating the measured radial profile at the flux-surface radius assigned to the barrier, typically identified by local extrema in the pressure or temperature gradient scale length. Together with [electron_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:electron_density_at_internal_transport_barrier) and [effective_charge_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:effective_charge_at_internal_transport_barrier), $T_e$ at the ITB characterizes local electron pressure and collisionality at the transport transition. In high-power tokamak discharges with well-developed ITBs, electron temperatures at the barrier radius span approximately 1–8 keV depending on heating power and barrier strength.

NAMES.name: electron_temperature_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Thermal energy per particle of the electron population evaluated at the magnetic axis, the innermost point of the confined plasma where the poloidal magnetic flux gradient vanishes.
NAMES.long:
The electron temperature at the magnetic axis is the local kinetic temperature of the electron population at the center of the nested flux-surface topology, where $\nabla\psi = 0$ for the poloidal magnetic flux $\psi$. In standard plasma operation this is the peak of the core electron thermal profile and a primary diagnostic indicator of core heating efficiency and energy confinement quality.

$$
T_{e,0} = T_e\bigl|_{\rho = 0}
$$

where $\rho$ is any normalized radial flux coordinate and $\rho = 0$ identifies the magnetic axis; $T_{e,0}$ serves as the innermost boundary condition on the electron temperature profile in core transport modeling.

On-axis electron temperature is routinely obtained from electron cyclotron emission using the spectral channel positioned closest to the magnetic axis, from Thomson scattering profiles spatially interpolated to $\rho = 0$, or from soft X-ray emissivity ratios across photon-energy bands. Typical values range from 1–3 keV in purely ohmic discharges to 5–20 keV with strong auxiliary heating in large devices.

Comparing $T_{e,0}$ with [electron_temperature_at_pedestal_top](name:electron_temperature_at_pedestal_top) quantifies the peaking of the electron thermal profile across the confined region. The corresponding ion quantity is [ion_average_temperature_at_magnetic_axis](name:ion_average_temperature_at_magnetic_axis), and [electron_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:electron_density_at_magnetic_axis) together with $T_{e,0}$ determines the central electron pressure.

NAMES.name: electron_velocity
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Bulk mean flow velocity vector of the electron fluid, equal to the first velocity-space moment of the electron distribution divided by electron density. It represents advective electron motion, not the much larger random thermal speed of individual electrons.
NAMES.long:
Electron velocity is the bulk, advective flow velocity of the electron fluid. It is the mean velocity of the electron distribution and is the velocity that enters electron continuity, momentum balance, generalized Ohm's law, current drive, and convective particle and energy transport.

The electron fluid velocity is defined by the first velocity-space moment of the electron distribution function:

$$
\mathbf{v}_e(\mathbf{x}, t) = \frac{1}{n_e(\mathbf{x}, t)} \int \mathbf{c}\, f_e(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{c}, t)\, d^3 c
$$

where $f_e$ is the electron distribution function, $\mathbf{c}$ is particle velocity, $n_e$ is the electron number density, and the integral is over all velocity space. The electron contribution to the current density is $-e n_e \mathbf{v}_e$, so the total current density may be written inline as $\mathbf{j} = -e n_e \mathbf{v}_e + \sum_i Z_i e n_i \mathbf{v}_i$ for ion species $i$ with charge number $Z_i$, density $n_i$, and bulk velocity $\mathbf{v}_i$.

In magnetized fusion plasmas, electron velocity is often decomposed into physically meaningful components such as [parallel_electron_velocity](name:parallel_electron_velocity) along the magnetic field, [toroidal_electron_velocity](name:toroidal_electron_velocity) around the torus, [poloidal_electron_velocity](name:poloidal_electron_velocity) in the short way around the plasma cross-section, and [radial_electron_velocity](name:radial_electron_velocity) across flux surfaces. It is computed from kinetic or fluid moments and can be inferred experimentally from current density constraints, Langmuir-probe measurements in the edge, Doppler spectroscopy where electron-flow information is accessible, and combined equilibrium or transport analysis.

Typical bulk electron velocities are much smaller than electron thermal speeds. Parallel or toroidal flow associated with plasma current is commonly 10^3-10^5 m.s^-1 in tokamak plasmas, while mean cross-field transport velocities are often 0.1-10^2 m.s^-1; localized drift or edge flows can reach 10^4-10^5 m.s^-1.
NAMES.sign: Positive when a resolved component of $\mathbf{v}_e$ points along its positive coordinate basis direction; for components in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, these directions are increasing major radius $R$, increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ counter-clockwise viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and increasing vertical height $Z$.

NAMES.name: fast_electron_power_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Coulomb-collisional power density received by the fast electron population. It is the volumetric rate of kinetic-energy exchange between suprathermal electrons and other plasma species.
NAMES.long:
Fast-electron collisional power density is the local rate per unit volume at which Coulomb collisions transfer kinetic energy to the suprathermal electron population. It represents the fast-electron channel of electron collisional energy exchange; together with the thermal-electron channel it forms the total electron collisional power density.

The quantity is the kinetic-energy moment of the Fokker-Planck collision operator for the fast-electron distribution:

$$
P_{e,\mathrm{fast}}^{\mathrm{coll}} = \sum_s \int \frac{1}{2} m_e v^2\, C_{es}[f_{e,\mathrm{fast}}, f_s](\mathbf{v})\, d^3v
$$

where the sum is over collision partners $s$, $f_{e,\mathrm{fast}}$ is normalized so that $\int f_{e,\mathrm{fast}}\,d^3v$ gives the fast-electron density, $f_s$ is the distribution of species $s$, $m_e$ is the electron mass in kg, $v=|\mathbf{v}|$ is speed in m/s, and $C_{es}$ has units of $f_{e,\mathrm{fast}}$ per second. With these definitions the integral has units of W m^-3. For relativistic fast electrons, the kinetic-energy weight is replaced by the appropriate relativistic kinetic energy.

In practice this quantity is computed by applying a Coulomb collision operator to a modeled or reconstructed fast-electron distribution and integrating over velocity space. If the fast population is partitioned by orbit class, the co-passing, counter-passing, and trapped components sum to this quantity when the same collision model and phase-space partition are used.

Typical local absolute magnitudes are scenario dependent: about 10^2-10^5 W m^-3 for weak suprathermal tails, 10^5-10^7 W m^-3 in strongly driven electron-heating or current-drive cases, and up to 10^8 W m^-3 or more in localized runaway-electron regimes. During ordinary slowing down, the value is often negative because fast electrons transfer energy to the thermal plasma.
NAMES.sign: Positive when Coulomb collisions transfer kinetic energy to the fast electron population.

NAMES.name: fast_electron_source_rate
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Total volumetric generation rate of fast, suprathermal electrons, summed over all relevant production mechanisms. It counts creation into the fast-electron population and excludes transport losses or explicit sink terms in the number-density balance.
NAMES.long:
The fast-electron source rate $S_\mathrm{fast}$ is the local volumetric rate at which electrons enter the fast, suprathermal population. It measures how rapidly the population is created before transport, slowing-down, or other sink processes are applied. It is the sum of production mechanisms such as Dreicer acceleration, avalanche multiplication, hot-tail survival after rapid cooling, Compton scattering, and tritium beta-decay injection.

In a local fast-electron number-density balance, the production role of $S_\mathrm{fast}$ can be written as

$$
\frac{\partial n_\mathrm{fast}}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_\mathrm{fast} = S_\mathrm{fast} - L_\mathrm{fast}
$$

where $n_\mathrm{fast}$ is the [fast_electron_density](name:fast_electron_density) in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_\mathrm{fast}$ is the fast-electron particle flux in $\mathrm{m}^{-2}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, $S_\mathrm{fast}$ is this production rate in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, and $L_\mathrm{fast}$ represents explicit loss, slowing-down, or reclassification terms in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$. A signed production-minus-removal residual is therefore a net balance term, not this source rate.

The rate is usually obtained from kinetic or integrated transport modeling by summing mechanism-specific contributions, including quantities such as [fast_electron_source_rate_due_to_hot_tail](name:fast_electron_source_rate_due_to_hot_tail). It can also be constrained indirectly by combining time-resolved estimates of fast-electron density or current with transport and loss models, using diagnostics sensitive to suprathermal electrons such as hard-x-ray emission, synchrotron radiation, electron-cyclotron emission, and current evolution. The closely related [runaway_electron_source_rate](name:runaway_electron_source_rate) applies the same aggregate-production concept to the runaway-electron subset.

Representative magnitudes are highly scenario-dependent and should be interpreted as order-of-magnitude scales rather than universal constants. With no active accelerating or seed mechanism the rate is effectively $0\ \mathrm{m}^{-3}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$; creating $10^{14}$-$10^{18}\ \mathrm{m}^{-3}$ fast electrons over $1\ \mathrm{ms}$-$1\ \mathrm{s}$ corresponds to an average source-rate scale of about $10^{14}$-$10^{21}\ \mathrm{m}^{-3}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, with stronger disruption or avalanche phases potentially exceeding this scale.

NAMES.name: fast_electron_source_rate_due_to_compton_scattering
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Volumetric production rate of fast electrons generated when high-energy gamma-ray photons Compton-scatter from thermal plasma electrons. Only scattering events that transfer enough energy for the electron to join the fast-electron population are counted; losses and subsequent evolution are excluded.
NAMES.long:
Fast electron source rate due to Compton scattering is the local volumetric production rate of electrons added to the [fast-electron density](name:fast_electron_density) by gamma-ray Compton scattering. It counts only scattering events in which a thermal electron receives enough kinetic energy to enter the fast-electron population; thermalization, transport losses, and avalanche multiplication are separate processes.

A representative local source expression is obtained by folding the gamma-ray photon flux with the Compton differential cross-section over the scattering angles that exceed the fast-electron energy threshold:

$$
S_\mathrm{C} = n_e \int \Phi_\gamma(E_\gamma) \left[ \int_{\Omega_\mathrm{fast}} \frac{d\sigma_\mathrm{C}}{d\Omega}(E_\gamma, \Omega)\, d\Omega \right] dE_\gamma
$$

where $S_\mathrm{C}$ is the source rate in m^-3.s^-1, $n_e$ is the thermal electron density in m^-3, $E_\gamma$ is the gamma-ray photon energy in J, $\Phi_\gamma(E_\gamma)$ is the differential photon flux in m^-2.s^-1.J^-1, $d\sigma_\mathrm{C}/d\Omega$ is the Compton differential cross-section in m^2.sr^-1, $d\Omega$ is a solid-angle element in sr, and $\Omega_\mathrm{fast}$ denotes scattering angles for which the recoil-electron kinetic energy $K_e$ exceeds the fast-electron threshold $K_\mathrm{fast}$, both in J.

In practice this source is computed from the local electron density, the gamma-ray radiation field, and the chosen fast-electron threshold, often using gamma diagnostics or radiation-transport estimates to constrain the photon spectrum. It enters transport models as an additive production term for the fast-electron population and should not include later acceleration, pitch-angle scattering, or loss of those electrons.

Typical values are strongly scenario dependent. In plasmas with little MeV gamma radiation the rate is effectively 0 m^-3.s^-1; in intense gamma fields, modeled local values can span roughly 10^6-10^12 m^-3.s^-1, depending on photon flux, electron density, and the fast-electron threshold.

This is a production-only source term and is therefore non-negative: counted Compton events increase the fast-electron population, while removal or relaxation terms are represented separately.

NAMES.name: fast_electron_source_rate_due_to_dreicer
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Density source rate of fast electrons due to the Dreicer generation mechanism, in which a parallel electric field accelerates high-energy tail electrons faster than Coulomb collisions slow them. It refers to the fast-electron population; the analogous runaway-electron term uses runaway-electron nomenclature.
NAMES.long:
Fast-electron source rate due to Dreicer generation is the local volumetric production rate of fast electrons created when the parallel electric field accelerates suprathermal tail electrons through collisional drag. It is a contribution to the total [fast_electron_source_rate](name:fast_electron_source_rate) and describes the same primary electric-field generation channel as [runaway_electron_source_rate_due_to_dreicer](name:runaway_electron_source_rate_due_to_dreicer), with the population labeled as fast electrons rather than specifically runaway electrons. It is distinct from avalanche multiplication and from hot-tail generation.

The model-independent definition is the Dreicer contribution to the fast-electron density balance:

$$
S_\mathrm{D} = \left.\frac{\partial n_\mathrm{fast}}{\partial t}\right|_\mathrm{Dreicer}
$$

where $S_\mathrm{D}$ is the fast-electron source rate due to Dreicer generation in $\mathrm{m^{-3}\,s^{-1}}$, $n_\mathrm{fast}$ is the fast-electron number density in $\mathrm{m^{-3}}$, $t$ is time in $\mathrm{s}$, and the subscript denotes the part of the density time derivative caused by the Dreicer mechanism alone.

The rate is usually inferred from analytic runaway-source formulas or kinetic Fokker-Planck modeling rather than measured as an isolated observable. Inputs typically include electron density $n_e$ in $\mathrm{m^{-3}}$, electron temperature $T_e$ in eV or J, effective charge $Z_\mathrm{eff}$ with unit 1, Coulomb logarithm $\ln\Lambda$ with unit 1, and the parallel electric field $E_\parallel$ in $\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$. The dependence is very sensitive to $E_\parallel/E_D$, where $E_D$ is the electric_field_due_to_dreicer, while critical_electric_field sets the lower electric-field scale for sustained runaway acceleration.

The quantity denotes a local scalar rate density. If used in a radial transport reduction with the flux coordinate $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$, the corresponding value is the flux-surface average of the local $S_\mathrm{D}$ over that magnetic surface and retains the unit $\mathrm{m^{-3}\,s^{-1}}$. No component of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ system is selected by the scalar rate itself; only $E_\parallel$ in the generation model refers to the local magnetic-field direction.

Typical modeled values range from effectively 0 in weak-electric-field conditions to $10^{17}$-$10^{22}$ $\mathrm{m^{-3}\,s^{-1}}$ in strong-electric-field transients, with intermediate seed-production values spanning many orders of magnitude. Because Dreicer generation depends steeply on plasma temperature, density, collisionality, and electric field, quoted ranges are scenario and model dependent.
NAMES.sign: Positive when Dreicer generation increases the fast-electron number density.

NAMES.name: fast_ion_density
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Number density of fast (non-thermal) ions of a given species, summed over all ionic charge states.
NAMES.long:
Fast (non-thermal) ions constitute the suprathermal tail of the ion velocity distribution, with energies substantially exceeding the local thermal energy $k_B T_i$. This quantity is obtained by integrating the fast-ion distribution function over the suprathermal region of velocity space and summing over all ionization states of the given species, yielding the local concentration of energetic ions per unit volume. It forms the fast-ion component of [ion_density](name:ion_density), complementary to the thermal population described by [thermal_ion_density](name:thermal_ion_density).

The fast-ion number density is defined as:

$$
n_\mathrm{fast} = \int f_\mathrm{fast}(\mathbf{v}) \, d^3v
$$

where $f_\mathrm{fast}(\mathbf{v})$ is the fast-ion distribution function restricted to the suprathermal velocity domain and $\mathbf{v}$ is the ion velocity. The charge-state-resolved counterpart [fast_ion_state_density](name:fast_ion_state_density) sums to $n_\mathrm{fast}$ over all ionization states $z$.
