NAMES.short: Total net volumetric power source for a specified ion charge state, giving the local rate at which that population gains or loses energy through non-transport interactions.
NAMES.long:
Ion-state power density is the signed local rate of energy gain per unit plasma volume for ions belonging to one specified species and charge state. It is the total non-transport source term for that charge-state population, including effects such as external heating, atomic energy exchange, charge exchange with neutrals, and Coulomb energy exchange with electrons or other ion populations.

The local definition is the source part of the energy-density balance:

$$
P_{a\zeta} = \left.\frac{\partial \mathcal{E}_{a\zeta}}{\partial t}\right|_{\mathrm{sources}}
$$

where $P_{a\zeta}$ is the ion-state power density for ion species $a$ and charge state $\zeta$, in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-3}}$; $\mathcal{E}_{a\zeta}$ is the corresponding energy density, in $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$; and the subscript indicates that only local source and sink processes are included, not advective or conductive energy transport. Integrating $P_{a\zeta}$ over a plasma volume gives the net power delivered to that charge-state population in that volume.

In practice, this quantity is computed from a combination of heating deposition, atomic and molecular rate coefficients, neutral and impurity populations, charge-exchange rates, and Coulomb collisional energy-exchange rates. It may also be inferred indirectly by balancing the measured or reconstructed time evolution of charge-state-resolved energy density against transport and known external power inputs.

Typical absolute magnitudes are about $10^3$-$10^6\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-3}}$ in the main confined plasma. Localized heating regions, dense edge plasma, or divertor plasma can reach $10^6$-$10^8\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-3}}$, while weak trace charge states may have much smaller values.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the specified ion charge state gains energy.

NAMES.name: ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Local volumetric rate of Coulomb-collisional energy exchange for a specified ion charge state, positive for net energy gain and negative for net energy loss to other plasma populations.
NAMES.long:
Ion-state collisional power density is the net volumetric power deposited into or extracted from a single ionic charge state by Coulomb collisions with all other plasma populations — electrons, bulk ions of other charge states, and fast particles. It is the charge-state-resolved component of [power_density_due_to_collisions](name:power_density_due_to_collisions) in the plasma energy balance, and being pairwise-conservative, power removed from one charge state appears as a gain for its collision partner, so the sum over all populations vanishes identically.

The quantity is defined as the energy moment of the Coulomb collision operator for charge state $z$:

$$
P_\mathrm{coll}^{(z)} = \int \frac{m v^2}{2} \, \mathcal{C}^{(z)}\!\left[f^{(z)}\right] d^3v
$$

where $m$ is the ion mass, $v$ is particle speed, and $\mathcal{C}^{(z)}$ is the Coulomb collision operator acting on the distribution function $f^{(z)}$ of charge state $z$. Summing over all charge states of a species recovers the total ion collisional power density.

This term enters as a source or sink in the charge-state energy equation and is evaluated in kinetic or fluid transport codes from the second velocity moment of the collision operator. No direct experimental diagnostic resolves it per charge state; values are inferred from impurity transport modeling constrained by spectroscopic line-emission measurements.

Orbit-class-resolved subsets are tracked separately as [fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions) for suprathermal ions and [thermal_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:thermal_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions) for bulk thermal ions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when Coulomb collisions transfer net energy into the specified ion charge state.

NAMES.name: fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Coulomb collisional power density for fast ions in a specified charge state, giving the local energy exchange rate per volume between that fast-ion population and the background plasma. It is positive when collisions add kinetic energy to the selected fast-ion state and negative when they remove it.
NAMES.long:
Fast-ion state collisional power density is the local kinetic-energy exchange rate per unit volume between fast ions in a specified charge state and the surrounding plasma due to Coulomb collisions. It is a signed scalar source term in the fast-ion energy balance, resolved by charge state rather than summed over all charge states.

The quantity is defined as the kinetic-energy moment of the Coulomb Fokker-Planck collision operator acting on the fast-ion distribution for charge state $q$:

$$
p_{\mathrm{fast},q}^{\mathrm{coll}}(\mathbf{x}) = \int \frac{1}{2} m_q v^2\, C_q^{\mathrm{coll}}[f_{\mathrm{fast},q}, f_{\mathrm{bg}}](\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\, d^3v
$$

where $p_{\mathrm{fast},q}^{\mathrm{coll}}$ has units of W m$^{-3}$, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $\mathbf{v}$ is velocity, $v=|\mathbf{v}|$ in m s$^{-1}$, $m_q$ is the ion mass in kg, $f_{\mathrm{fast},q}$ is the fast-ion velocity distribution for charge state $q$, $f_{\mathrm{bg}}$ represents the background electron and ion distributions, and $C_q^{\mathrm{coll}}$ is the Coulomb Fokker-Planck collision operator with units of distribution function per second. For fast-ion slowing-down calculations this operator is commonly treated as a linearized test-particle operator with drag and diffusion coefficients expressible through Rosenbluth potentials.

In practice this term is inferred from kinetic modeling constrained by measurements of the fast-ion population and by background density, temperature, and composition, which determine the Coulomb collision frequencies. Volume integration gives [fast_ion_state_power_due_to_collisions](name:fast_ion_state_power_due_to_collisions), summing over charge states gives [fast_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:fast_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions), and orbit-topology partitions give [co_passing_fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:co_passing_fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions), [counter_passing_fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:counter_passing_fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions), and [trapped_fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:trapped_fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions).

Typical absolute magnitudes are about 10$^{3}$-10$^{7}$ W m$^{-3}$ in beam-heated, radio-frequency-heated, or fusion-alpha-heated tokamak plasmas. Values can be much smaller in weak-source or edge regions and larger locally in compact, high-power deposition regions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when Coulomb collisions transfer kinetic energy to the selected fast-ion charge-state population.

NAMES.name: co_passing_fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Volumetric Coulomb-collisional kinetic-energy transfer rate for a specified fast-ion charge state, restricted to co-passing particles that circulate poloidally in the same direction as the plasma current.
NAMES.long:
The co-passing fast-ion-state collisional power density is the local volumetric rate of kinetic-energy exchange between fast ions of a specified charge state in the co-passing orbit class and the surrounding plasma, driven by Coulomb collisions. Co-passing particles follow closed toroidal orbits and circulate poloidally in the same sense as the plasma current, occupying a distinct region of velocity space that is separate from the trapped and counter-passing populations.

The quantity is computed as the velocity-space integral of the Coulomb collision operator weighted by kinetic energy, restricted to the co-passing velocity-space domain for a single ion charge state $s$:

$$
P_\text{co-pass}^{\text{fast},s} = \int_{\Omega_\text{co-pass}} \frac{m_i v^2}{2} \, C[f_\text{fast}^s] \, d^3v
$$

where $m_i$ is the ion mass, $v$ is the particle speed, $C[f_\text{fast}^s]$ is the Fokker-Planck collision operator for the fast-ion distribution function $f_\text{fast}^s$ of charge state $s$, and $\Omega_\text{co-pass}$ denotes the co-passing region of velocity space.

This quantity is obtained from kinetic transport simulations that resolve the full distribution function over orbit class, such as Fokker-Planck or Monte Carlo codes, where velocity-space integrals are performed separately over co-passing trajectories for each ion charge state. Summing co-passing and [counter-passing](name:counter_passing_fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions) contributions recovers the orbit-class-integrated quantity [fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions). The charge-state-summed co-passing analog is [co_passing_fast_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:co_passing_fast_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions).
NAMES.sign: Positive when Coulomb collisions deliver net kinetic energy to the co-passing fast ions of the specified charge state.

NAMES.name: counter_passing_fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Volumetric Coulomb-collisional kinetic-energy transfer rate for a specified fast-ion charge state, restricted to counter-passing particles. Positive values mean that charge state gains kinetic energy from collisions; negative values mean it loses kinetic energy.
NAMES.long:
Counter-passing fast ion state power density due to collisions is the local collisional source term in the kinetic-energy balance of a specified fast-ion charge state, evaluated only over the counter-passing part of velocity space. Counter-passing fast ions have guiding-center parallel motion whose toroidal circulation is opposite to the plasma-current direction. The charge-state label denotes one resolved ionization state of the fast-ion species.

The quantity is the kinetic-energy moment of the Coulomb collision operator over the counter-passing velocity-space domain:

$$
P_{\mathrm{fast},z}^{\mathrm{counter}} = \int_{\Omega_{\mathrm{counter}}} \mathcal{E}_z(\mathbf{v})\, C_z[f_{\mathrm{fast},z}](\mathbf{v})\, d^3v
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{fast},z}^{\mathrm{counter}}$ is the counter-passing collisional power density for charge state $z$, $\Omega_{\mathrm{counter}}$ is the counter-passing region of velocity space, $\mathcal{E}_z$ is the particle kinetic energy in joules, and $C_z[f_{\mathrm{fast},z}]$ is the collisional part of the time derivative of the local fast-ion distribution function for that charge state. If $f_{\mathrm{fast},z}$ is normalized so that $\int f_{\mathrm{fast},z}\,d^3v$ is the number density, then $C_z[f_{\mathrm{fast},z}]$ has units of number density per time per velocity-space volume, and $d^3v$ has units $(\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1})^3$, giving $P_{\mathrm{fast},z}^{\mathrm{counter}}$ in W m$^{-3}$.

In practice this quantity is computed from a kinetic fast-ion distribution and a Coulomb collision operator, often constrained by measurements such as neutron emission, neutral-particle analysis, fast-ion loss signals, charge-exchange spectroscopy, or gamma-ray diagnostics. Orbit classification partitions the distribution into trapped, co-passing, and counter-passing domains; summing the orbit components gives [fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions), while summing over charge states gives [counter_passing_fast_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:counter_passing_fast_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions). The complementary counter-current decomposition is [co_passing_fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:co_passing_fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions), and a thermal-ion analog is [counter_passing_thermal_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:counter_passing_thermal_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions).

Typical magnitudes are highly regime dependent: orbit- and charge-state-resolved values can be below 1 W m$^{-3}$ in weakly populated regions, 10$^2$-10$^6$ W m$^{-3}$ in auxiliary-heated core plasmas, and locally approach 10$^7$ W m$^{-3}$ in strongly driven fast-ion populations. Negative values occur where collisions remove kinetic energy from the specified fast-ion charge state and transfer it to other species or charge states.
NAMES.sign: Positive when Coulomb collisions increase the kinetic energy density of the specified fast-ion charge state.

NAMES.name: ion_state_source_rate
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Net volumetric particle source rate for a specific ion charge state, entering the charge-state-resolved continuity equation as a creation or destruction term.
NAMES.long:
The ion-state source rate is the net volumetric rate at which particles of a specified ionic charge state are created or destroyed within a plasma volume element, serving as the source term in the charge-state-resolved particle continuity equation. Processes contributing to this rate include electron-impact ionization, radiative and dielectronic recombination, and charge exchange with neutral species.

The governing charge-state continuity equation is:

$$
\frac{\partial n_z}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_z = S_z
$$

where $n_z$ is the number density of charge state $z$ in m$^{-3}$, $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_z$ is the associated particle flux in m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$, and $S_z$ is this source rate. Transport solvers may decompose $S_z$ into an explicit part added directly to the right-hand side and an implicit part proportional to $n_z$; the latter is captured separately as the [implicit ion particle source rate].

This quantity is computed by coupling atomic physics rate coefficients for ionization and recombination to local electron temperature and density profiles, and may incorporate contributions from neutral beam injection or pellet injection. Summing over all ionization states yields the total [ion source rate]; the analogous quantity for neutral charge states is the [neutral state source rate](name:neutral_state_source_rate).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the specified charge state experiences a net local particle gain; negative when ionization from below or recombination from above causes a net depletion of that state.

NAMES.name: ion_state_upper_bound_charge
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Maximum ionization charge number (Z_max) of an ion charge-state bundle; equals the lower-bound charge when the bundle contains only a single resolved charge state.
NAMES.long:
The upper-bound charge number specifies the highest ionization state included in an ion charge-state bundle, where the ionization charge $Z$ counts the number of electrons removed from the neutral atom. In multi-fluid plasma models, consecutive ionization states of the same ion species are often grouped into bundles to reduce computational expense; this quantity gives the ceiling $Z_\mathrm{max}$ of the charge range $[Z_\mathrm{min}, Z_\mathrm{max}]$ spanned by the bundle.

When a bundle encloses only a single charge state, $Z_\mathrm{max}$ equals the corresponding [lower-bound charge]. For multi-state bundles the interval width $Z_\mathrm{max} - Z_\mathrm{min} \geq 1$, and the [concentration-weighted average charge] or [mean charge] provides a representative effective charge for transport and source-term calculations.

Charge-state values are non-negative integers bounded above by the nuclear charge number $Z_n$ of the species: for hydrogen $Z_\mathrm{max} \leq 1$, for carbon $Z_\mathrm{max} \leq 6$, and for heavy impurities such as tungsten $Z_\mathrm{max} \leq 74$. The bundle definition is set at model initialization and does not vary with plasma conditions at a given time step.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the ion carries net positive charge, corresponding to the removal of one or more electrons from the neutral atom.

NAMES.name: ion_state_velocity
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Bulk fluid velocity vector of an ion species in a specified ionization charge state, defined as the first velocity moment of the charge-state distribution function normalized by the local charge-state number density.
NAMES.long:
The ion-state velocity is the mean flow velocity of ions belonging to a single resolved ionization charge state, representing the hydrodynamic drift of that charge-state fluid within the plasma. In a multi-fluid treatment, each charge state $z$ of a given ion species carries its own velocity field, which couples to neighboring charge states through ionization, recombination, and Coulomb friction between the constituent fluids.

The velocity vector is the first moment of the charge-state-resolved distribution function $f_z(\mathbf{v})$:

$$
\mathbf{u}_z = \frac{1}{n_z} \int \mathbf{v} \, f_z(\mathbf{v}) \, d^3v
$$

where $n_z = \int f_z(\mathbf{v}) \, d^3v$ is the number density of ions in charge state $z$ (in m$^{-3}$) and $\mathbf{v}$ is the particle velocity.

The vector components are defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle increasing counter-clockwise when viewed from above, and $Z$ is the vertical height. The magnetic-field-aligned projection is [parallel_ion_state_velocity](name:parallel_ion_state_velocity), which is experimentally accessible via Doppler shifts from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy. The charge-state-averaged parallel flow is captured by [parallel_ion_velocity](name:parallel_ion_velocity), while [parallel_electron_velocity](name:parallel_electron_velocity) provides the electron-fluid counterpart entering Ohm's law. Full vector components are computed self-consistently in multi-fluid edge transport codes that evolve separate momentum equations per charge state.

Typical parallel ion-state flow speeds range from sub-km/s in the low-flow core to near-sonic values of order $10^4$ m/s approaching the divertor target.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the flow is directed in the positive direction of the respective basis vectors $+\hat{R}$, $+\hat{\phi}$, or $+\hat{Z}$ of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: ion_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Scalar diamagnetic component of the drift velocity for a specified ion charge state, driven by the cross-product of that state's partial pressure gradient with the local magnetic field, perpendicular to both.
NAMES.long:
The diamagnetic drift arises in a magnetized plasma when a pressure gradient causes a systematic imbalance between contributions from opposing sides of ion gyro-orbits, producing a net bulk fluid flow perpendicular to both $\mathbf{B}$ and $\nabla p_s$ without requiring net particle displacement across field lines. For an ion charge state $s$ with charge $q_s = Z_s e$, number density $n_s$, and partial pressure $p_s = n_s k_B T_s$, the defining drift vector is:

$$
\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{dia},s} = \frac{\mathbf{B} \times \nabla p_s}{q_s \, n_s \, B^2}
$$

where $B = |\mathbf{B}|$ is the local magnetic-field magnitude. This scalar quantity gives the projection of $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{dia},s}$ onto the local diamagnetic direction $\hat{\mathbf{b}} \times \widehat{\nabla p_s}$, where $\hat{\mathbf{b}} = \mathbf{B}/B$. Diamagnetic flows contribute to bulk poloidal plasma motion, pressure-driven currents, and poloidal asymmetries in particle and heat transport in edge and scrape-off-layer regions. Directional projections are available as [radial_ion_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:radial_ion_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift), [poloidal_ion_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:poloidal_ion_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift), [toroidal_ion_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:toroidal_ion_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift), and [vertical_ion_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:vertical_ion_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift). The bulk-plasma scalar analog is [plasma_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:plasma_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift) and the neutral-particle counterpart is [neutral_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:neutral_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift); the species-general parent quantity is [velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the drift is aligned with $\mathbf{B} \times \nabla p_s$, where $\mathbf{B}$ is the local magnetic field vector and $\nabla p_s$ is the partial pressure gradient of the ion charge state.

NAMES.name: ion_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Full vector E×B drift velocity for a specified ion charge state, perpendicular to both the local electric and magnetic fields and independent of the ion's mass and charge value.
NAMES.long:
The E×B drift velocity of a specified ion charge state is the guiding-center drift arising when a magnetized charged particle experiences an electric field perpendicular to the confining magnetic field. Because the drift depends only on the local ratio of fields and not on particle mass, charge sign, or ionization degree, this quantity resolved per ion charge state is numerically identical to the same drift for any other species; tracking it per charge state enables charge-state-resolved transport modeling in edge plasma simulations.

The defining expression is:

$$
\mathbf{v}_{E\times B} = \frac{\mathbf{E} \times \mathbf{B}}{B^2}
$$

where $\mathbf{E}$ is the local electric field in V m$^{-1}$, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field in T, and $B = |\mathbf{B}|$, yielding a velocity directed perpendicular to both fields. Scalar projections of this vector are provided by [radial_ion_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift](name:radial_ion_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift), [toroidal_ion_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift](name:toroidal_ion_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift), and [parallel_ion_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift](name:parallel_ion_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift). The parent quantity [velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift](name:velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift) gives the species-independent drift for the bulk plasma.

In tokamak edge and pedestal plasmas, E×B drift speeds range from $10^3$ to $10^5$ m s$^{-1}$, set primarily by the magnitude of the radial electric field relative to the local magnetic field strength. This drift is computed from equilibrium or fluid-model electric and magnetic field profiles and drives cross-field convective particle and momentum transport.
NAMES.sign: Positive when each cylindrical vector component points in the direction of increasing $R$, increasing toroidal angle $\phi$, or increasing $Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius measured from the symmetry axis and $Z$ is the vertical coordinate.

NAMES.name: iron_density_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: iron
NAMES.short: Number density of iron ions at the radial location of the internal transport barrier, where suppressed turbulent transport enables steep impurity density gradients to develop.
NAMES.long:
Iron (Fe, atomic number $Z = 26$) is a high-Z metallic impurity that enters fusion plasmas through sputtering or erosion of plasma-facing components. An internal transport barrier (ITB) is a radially localized region where turbulent cross-field transport is strongly suppressed, enabling steep radial gradients in density and temperature to develop and persist. This quantity is the total iron ion number density — summed over all ionization charge states — evaluated at the single reference radius assigned to the ITB in the chosen flux coordinate.

The ITB-local iron density is defined as:

$$
n_{\rm Fe}^{\rm ITB} = \sum_{z=1}^{26} n_{{\rm Fe},z}(r_{\rm ITB})
$$

where $n_{{\rm Fe},z}$ is the number density of iron ions in charge state $z$ and $r_{\rm ITB}$ is the ITB reference radius in the chosen flux coordinate.

This quantity is inferred from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy targeting iron spectral lines, or from impurity transport modeling constrained by soft X-ray tomography and bolometry data. The ITB reference radius is identified from regions of steep gradient in the ion or electron temperature profile, as described under [density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:density_at_internal_transport_barrier). Analogous quantities for other impurity species include [carbon_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:carbon_density_at_internal_transport_barrier), [argon_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:argon_density_at_internal_transport_barrier), and [oxygen_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:oxygen_density_at_internal_transport_barrier); the companion electron density is [electron_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:electron_density_at_internal_transport_barrier).
NAMES.sign: Positive when iron ions are present at the internal transport barrier location.

NAMES.name: iron_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: iron
NAMES.short: Number density of iron ions at the magnetic axis, the innermost point of the confined plasma where the gradient of the poloidal magnetic flux vanishes.
NAMES.long:
Iron ($\mathrm{Fe}$, atomic number 26) is a high-$Z$ metallic impurity that enters the plasma primarily through physical sputtering of iron-containing plasma-facing components. At the magnetic axis — the point $(R_\mathrm{axis}, Z_\mathrm{axis})$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame where $\nabla\psi = 0$ — this density gives the on-axis value of the iron impurity radial profile and is the primary indicator of core impurity accumulation.

The total iron number density summed over all ionization states is:

$$
n_\mathrm{Fe}(R_\mathrm{axis}) = \sum_{z=1}^{26} n_{\mathrm{Fe}^{z+}}(R_\mathrm{axis})
$$

where $z$ is the charge state ranging from singly-ionized $\mathrm{Fe}^{1+}$ to fully-stripped $\mathrm{Fe}^{26+}$, and $n_{\mathrm{Fe}^{z+}}$ is the partial density in m$^{-3}$.

Elevated on-axis values signal core impurity accumulation, which develops when the neoclassical inward pinch of high-$Z$ impurities exceeds outward turbulent transport. This quantity is inferred by combining line-integrated spectroscopic measurements — soft X-ray tomography, vacuum ultraviolet spectroscopy, or charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy — with Abel inversion or impurity transport modeling. Core iron concentrations $n_\mathrm{Fe}/n_e$ typically span $10^{-5}$–$10^{-3}$ in tokamaks with iron-containing plasma-facing components. The [iron_density_at_pedestal](name:iron_density_at_pedestal) and [volume_averaged_iron_density](name:volume_averaged_iron_density) provide complementary pedestal-top and global characterizations of the same species; [nitrogen_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:nitrogen_density_at_magnetic_axis) is the analogous on-axis density for nitrogen and follows the same localized [density_at_magnetic_axis](name:density_at_magnetic_axis) structure.
NAMES.sign: Positive when iron ions are present; the number density is zero only in the complete absence of iron impurities and otherwise strictly positive.

NAMES.name: krypton_density_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: krypton
NAMES.short: Number density of krypton ions evaluated at the radial position of the internal transport barrier, where locally reduced cross-field turbulent transport sustains steep impurity density gradients within the confined plasma.
NAMES.long:
Krypton (atomic number $Z = 36$) is a noble-gas impurity that is seeded into fusion plasmas for divertor heat-load mitigation and radiative power exhaust control. This quantity is the total number of krypton particles per unit volume, aggregated over all charge states present, evaluated at the radial location of the internal transport barrier (ITB) — a localized zone where cross-field turbulent transport is strongly suppressed, allowing steep radial gradients in both temperature and impurity density to persist.

The krypton density at the ITB reflects the competition between the neoclassical inward pinch, which tends to accumulate impurities in the plasma core, and turbulent outward diffusion, which is reduced at the barrier; the resulting impurity peaking makes this quantity a sensitive indicator of barrier strength and confinement quality. It is a species-specific instance of [density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:density_at_internal_transport_barrier), directly analogous to [xenon_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:xenon_density_at_internal_transport_barrier) and [argon_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:argon_density_at_internal_transport_barrier) for heavier and lighter noble-gas impurities, respectively.

In practice the value is inferred from vacuum ultraviolet or soft X-ray spectroscopy of krypton line emission, or from impurity transport modeling constrained by measured radial profiles. Combining this quantity with [electron_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:electron_density_at_internal_transport_barrier) enables estimates of the local krypton impurity fraction and its contribution to the effective charge $Z_{\mathrm{eff}}$ at the barrier. The krypton density at other radial locations is given by [krypton_density_at_pedestal](name:krypton_density_at_pedestal), [krypton_density_at_limiter](name:krypton_density_at_limiter), and [krypton_density_at_divertor_target](name:krypton_density_at_divertor_target).

NAMES.name: krypton_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: krypton
NAMES.short: Number density of krypton ions evaluated at the magnetic axis, the innermost point of the confined plasma where the gradient of poloidal magnetic flux vanishes.
NAMES.long:
Krypton ($Z = 36$) is a noble-gas impurity that can be seeded into confined plasmas for radiative power exhaust management or employed as a spectroscopic tracer. The krypton number density at the magnetic axis gives the on-axis value of the impurity concentration profile at the innermost nested flux surface, located at coordinates $(R_\mathrm{axis}, Z_\mathrm{axis})$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame where $\nabla\psi = 0$, with $\psi$ the poloidal magnetic flux. It is the krypton-species instance of the [density_at_magnetic_axis](name:density_at_magnetic_axis) family.

The on-axis krypton density is inferred from spectrally resolved line-emission diagnostics — such as charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy or vacuum-ultraviolet spectroscopy — combined with atomic data for the krypton charge-state distribution, and serves as the inner boundary value of the impurity concentration profile in radial transport analyzes.

Comparing this on-axis value with [krypton_density_at_pedestal](name:krypton_density_at_pedestal) and [krypton_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:krypton_density_at_internal_transport_barrier) characterizes the radial accumulation pattern: central peaking indicates the neoclassical inward pinch dominates over turbulent outward diffusion, while a hollow profile signals the reverse. The analogous on-axis density for boron is given by [boron_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:boron_density_at_magnetic_axis).

NAMES.name: lithium_density_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: lithium
NAMES.short: Lithium ion number density evaluated at the representative radial location of an internal transport barrier.
NAMES.long:
Lithium ion number density at the internal transport barrier is the local number of lithium ions per unit volume at the representative radial location of an ITB. The ITB is a localized region of reduced radial transport within the confined plasma, so impurity densities can vary strongly across the barrier.

Using the flux coordinate $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$ (normalized toroidal flux radius), the point value is

$$
n_{\mathrm{Li,ITB}} = n_{\mathrm{Li}}\!\left(\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm,ITB}}\right)
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{Li,ITB}}$ and $n_{\mathrm{Li}}$ are lithium ion number densities in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, and $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm,ITB}}$ is the dimensionless value of the normalized toroidal flux radius selected to represent the ITB. If the barrier has finite radial width, the representative point is commonly chosen as the barrier center, the location of strongest local gradient, or the same ITB location used for related quantities such as [total_ion_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:total_ion_density_at_internal_transport_barrier).

The value is obtained by identifying the ITB location from the radial variation of transport-sensitive plasma quantities and evaluating a lithium-specific density estimate at that location. Lithium density is typically inferred from species-sensitive impurity measurements combined with atomic-physics or transport analysis, and it should be interpreted together with neighboring-location quantities such as [lithium_density_at_pedestal](name:lithium_density_at_pedestal) and [lithium_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:lithium_density_at_magnetic_axis).

Typical trace-to-minor lithium impurity densities in confined tokamak plasmas are about $10^{15}$-$10^{18}\ \mathrm{m}^{-3}$, usually well below the local total ion density. Values outside this order-of-magnitude range can occur depending on lithium source strength, confinement, and diagnostic sensitivity.

NAMES.name: lithium_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: lithium
NAMES.short: Local number density of lithium ions evaluated at the magnetic axis, the innermost point of the confined plasma where the gradient of the poloidal magnetic flux vanishes.
NAMES.long:
The lithium ion number density at the magnetic axis gives the on-axis value of the lithium impurity concentration, summing contributions from all ionization charge states ($\mathrm{Li}^{1+}$, $\mathrm{Li}^{2+}$, and $\mathrm{Li}^{3+}$). As a specialization of the [density_at_magnetic_axis](name:density_at_magnetic_axis) parent, it is evaluated at the coordinates $(R_\mathrm{axis}, Z_\mathrm{axis})$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame — with $R$ the major radius and $Z$ the vertical height — at the unique interior point where $\nabla\psi = 0$.

The on-axis lithium density is defined as:

$$
n_\mathrm{Li,axis} = n_\mathrm{Li}(R_\mathrm{axis},\, Z_\mathrm{axis})
$$

where $n_\mathrm{Li}$ is the total lithium ion number density summed over charge states and $(R_\mathrm{axis}, Z_\mathrm{axis})$ is the location satisfying $\nabla\psi = 0$ inside the confined plasma.

Elevated on-axis lithium density signals impurity accumulation in the plasma core, which dilutes the fuel species and reduces fusion reactivity; this contrasts with the pedestal and edge environments characterized by [lithium_density_at_pedestal](name:lithium_density_at_pedestal) and [lithium_density_at_limiter](name:lithium_density_at_limiter). The quantity is inferred from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy or passive impurity spectroscopy combined with radial profile reconstruction that extrapolates to the axis. The [line_averaged_lithium_density](name:line_averaged_lithium_density) provides a complementary chord-integrated measure, while [lithium_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:lithium_density_at_internal_transport_barrier) characterizes barrier-region impurity content.
NAMES.sign: Positive when lithium ions are present at the magnetic axis; this scalar number density is invariant under reversal of the toroidal magnetic field or plasma current direction.

NAMES.name: loop_voltage_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Toroidal electromotive force integrated around the last closed flux surface, measuring the net inductive and resistive voltage driving ohmic plasma current.
NAMES.long:
The loop voltage at the plasma boundary is the line integral of the total electric field around a toroidal contour lying on the last closed flux surface (LCFS), equal to the time rate of change of the total poloidal magnetic flux threading that boundary.

The defining relation is:

$$
V_{loop} = -\frac{d\Psi_b}{dt}
$$

where $\Psi_b$ is the total poloidal magnetic flux enclosed by the LCFS. In a resistive plasma at quasi-steady state this balances as $V_{loop} \approx R_p I_p$, where $R_p$ is the total parallel plasma resistance and $I_p$ is the plasma current; during ramp phases the inductive term $L_p dI_p/dt$ adds significantly. This quantity therefore characterizes both ohmic flux consumption and the resistive state of the plasma column.

It is inferred from voltage loops or flux loops positioned outside the plasma, after subtracting time derivatives of external coil fluxes. The externally driven component alone is captured by [external_loop_voltage](name:current_weighted_average_external_loop_voltage), and the [toroidal_electric_field](name:toroidal_electric_field) profile provides the radially resolved field from which boundary values are extracted.

Typical magnitudes are 0.1–5 V during the current flat-top in medium-to-large tokamaks, rising to 10–20 V during rapid current ramp-up.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the electromotive force drives plasma current in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$).

NAMES.name: magnetic_shear_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.short: Normalized logarithmic derivative of the safety factor with respect to normalized toroidal flux radius, evaluated at the internal transport barrier location.
NAMES.long:
The magnetic shear at the internal transport barrier is the normalized logarithmic derivative of the safety factor $q$ with respect to the normalized toroidal flux radius $\rho_{tor}$, evaluated at the radial position of the internal transport barrier. The sign and magnitude of this quantity govern the stability of microinstabilities at the barrier, with reversed (negative) shear strongly associated with ITB formation in advanced tokamak scenarios.

The defining relation is:

$$
s = \frac{\rho_{tor}}{q} \frac{dq}{d\rho_{tor}}
$$

where $q$ is the safety factor — the number of toroidal field-line transits per single poloidal circuit — and $\rho_{tor}$ is the normalized toroidal flux radius, equal to zero at the magnetic axis and unity at the last closed flux surface.

The safety-factor profile needed to evaluate this quantity is obtained from equilibrium reconstruction, often constrained by motional Stark effect polarimetry or Faraday rotation measurements resolving the internal $q$-profile. The full radial context is provided by the [magnetic shear](name:magnetic_shear_at_pedestal) profile; analogous point evaluations are defined at [the magnetic axis](name:magnetic_shear_at_magnetic_axis) and [the pedestal top](name:magnetic_shear_at_pedestal).

In reversed-shear configurations the value is negative near the $q$-minimum, commonly ranging from $-2$ to $0$; in conventional positive-shear ITB scenarios values are small and positive, in the range $0$ to $1$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the safety factor $q$ increases with the normalized toroidal flux radius $\rho_{tor}$, i.e., when $dq/d\rho_{tor} > 0$.

NAMES.name: neon_density_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: neon
NAMES.short: Local number density of neon ions at the internal transport barrier reference radius, where reduced cross-field turbulent transport can produce steep impurity-density gradients.
NAMES.long:
Neon density at the internal transport barrier is the local number density of ionized neon nuclei on the flux surface used to mark the internal transport barrier. It represents the neon impurity concentration at the radius where cross-field turbulent transport is reduced and temperature, density, or impurity gradients can become steep.

For a fully resolved charge-state description, the total ionized neon density at the barrier is

$$
n_{\mathrm{Ne}}(\rho_{\mathrm{ITB}}) = \sum_{q=1}^{10} n_{\mathrm{Ne}^{q+}}(\rho_{\mathrm{ITB}})
$$

where $\rho_{\mathrm{ITB}}$ is the chosen flux-surface label for the internal transport barrier, such as the normalized toroidal flux radius $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$, and $n_{\mathrm{Ne}^{q+}}$ is the local density of neon ions with charge state $q$.

In practice this quantity is inferred from impurity spectroscopy, soft-x-ray or extreme-ultraviolet line emission, charge-exchange measurements where available, and collisional-radiative modeling constrained by the local electron temperature and density. Transport analysis evaluates the result on the barrier flux surface identified from steep gradients or reduced inferred diffusivity.

Typical values range from $10^{15}$-$10^{18}$ m^-3 for trace or weakly seeded neon and can approach $10^{19}$ m^-3 during strong neon seeding or impurity accumulation near the barrier. The value is normally much smaller than the electron density but can strongly affect radiation, dilution, and effective charge.

NAMES.name: neon_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: neon
NAMES.short: Number density of neon ions at the magnetic axis, the innermost point of the confined plasma where the gradient of the poloidal magnetic flux vanishes.
NAMES.long:
Neon is a noble-gas impurity commonly introduced into tokamak plasmas for radiative cooling, divertor protection, and impurity transport studies. The on-axis value $n_\mathrm{Ne}$ gives the innermost point of the radial neon density profile, evaluated at the location where $\nabla\psi = 0$, with $\psi$ the poloidal magnetic flux. At this point $(R_\mathrm{axis}, Z_\mathrm{axis})$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, the interplay of the neoclassical inward pinch and anomalous transport governs whether neon accumulates centrally or develops a hollow profile, making $n_\mathrm{Ne,axis}$ a key indicator of impurity accumulation behavior.

This quantity is the neon-specific realization of [density_at_magnetic_axis](name:density_at_magnetic_axis), and it can be compared against the same-species profile at other flux surfaces via [neon_density_at_pedestal](name:neon_density_at_pedestal) and [neon_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:neon_density_at_plasma_boundary). On-axis densities of other noble-gas impurities are cataloged as [argon_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:argon_density_at_magnetic_axis) and [xenon_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:xenon_density_at_magnetic_axis), enabling multi-species accumulation comparisons.

Neon ion densities at the magnetic axis are inferred from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, vacuum-ultraviolet spectroscopy of neon line emission, or from impurity transport modeling constrained by radiated power profiles.
NAMES.sign: Positive when neon ions are present at the magnetic axis location $(R_\mathrm{axis}, Z_\mathrm{axis})$, as particle number density is a non-negative quantity.

NAMES.name: neutral_source_rate
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Net volumetric production rate of neutral particles, equal to creation minus loss processes per unit volume. It enters the neutral particle density balance as a source term, with positive values representing a net gain of neutral particles.
NAMES.long:
Neutral source rate is the local net rate at which neutral particles of a given species are produced or removed by atomic, molecular, and plasma interaction processes. It represents creation minus loss per unit physical volume and directly changes the neutral number density.

A common local neutral continuity equation is

$$
\frac{\partial n_n}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \left(n_n \mathbf{u}_n\right) = S_n
$$

where $n_n$ is the neutral number density in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, $\mathbf{u}_n$ is the neutral flow velocity in $\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, and $S_n$ is the neutral source rate in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$. The equation is coordinate independent; when expressed in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $S_n$ is the net rate per physical volume at position $(R, \phi, Z)$.

In practice, $S_n$ is computed from neutral transport and collisional-radiative models using rates for ionization, recombination, charge exchange, molecular dissociation, recycling, gas fueling, pellet ablation, and neutral beam deposition when relevant. It can also be constrained indirectly by particle balance, spectroscopy, pressure gages, and neutral particle diagnostics, with volume or flux-surface averaging applied only after the local volumetric rate has been defined.

Typical magnitudes vary strongly with plasma region and fueling conditions: core values with weak neutral penetration may be $10^{16}$-$10^{20}\ \mathrm{m}^{-3}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, edge and scrape-off-layer recycling regions are commonly $10^{20}$-$10^{23}\ \mathrm{m}^{-3}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, and highly localized pellet, gas-puff, or beam-related sources can locally exceed $10^{24}\ \mathrm{m}^{-3}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the net processes add neutral particles to the neutral population, increasing the neutral number density.

NAMES.name: neutral_species_atomic_mass
NAMES.subject: neutral_species
NAMES.short: Atomic mass of a neutral species expressed in unified atomic mass units. It identifies the isotope or elemental composition and sets the particle inertia used in mass density, momentum, energy, and transport calculations.
NAMES.long:
Neutral species atomic mass is the rest mass assigned to one neutral atom or isotope, expressed in unified atomic mass units. It is independent of the local plasma state and characterizes the inertia of the neutral constituent used in fluid and kinetic transport quantities.

The particle mass is related to its numerical atomic mass by:

$$
m_s = A_s u
$$

where $m_s$ is the mass of one neutral particle of species $s$, $A_s$ is the numerical atomic mass, and $u$ is the unified atomic mass unit, equal to one twelfth of the mass of a neutral carbon-12 atom in its ground state. In practical calculations $1\,u = 1.66053906660 \times 10^{-27}\,\mathrm{kg}$ may be used for conversion to SI mass.

Atomic masses are normally taken from isotope or elemental reference tables rather than measured as a plasma diagnostic quantity. For isotope-resolved species the tabulated isotope mass is used; for an element without isotope resolution, an abundance-weighted elemental atomic mass may be appropriate. The value enters conversions such as number density to mass density and influences neutral thermal speeds, momentum exchange, source deposition, and transport time scales.

Typical values are about 1.008 u for protium, 2.014 u for deuterium, 3.016 u for tritium, 4.003 u for helium-4, 12 u for carbon-12, 20.18 u for neon, 39.95 u for argon, and 183.84 u for tungsten. Fusion fuel and helium ash are usually in the 1-4 u range, while impurity neutrals can range from about 12-184 u depending on the species.

NAMES.name: ion_atomic_mass
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Atomic mass of an ion species expressed in unified atomic mass units. It identifies the isotope and sets the ion mass scale used in collisionality, inertia, gyroradius, and transport calculations.
NAMES.long:
Ion atomic mass is the isotope-specific mass assigned to an ion species, expressed relative to the unified atomic mass unit. It is primarily a species property: different isotopes of the same element have different atomic masses, while different ionization states of the same isotope have nearly the same mass for most plasma-transport purposes.

The ion mass used in transport calculations is commonly obtained from the atomic-mass parameter as:

$$
m_i = A_i m_u
$$

where $m_i$ is the ion mass, $A_i$ is the ion atomic mass expressed in unified atomic mass units, and $m_u$ is the unified atomic mass constant. Small corrections from removed bound electrons and ionization energies are usually negligible compared with the nuclear mass for fusion-plasma transport modeling.

The value is determined from the isotope composition of the ion species, using tabulated atomic masses or known fuel and impurity inventories. It enters calculations of thermal speed, gyrofrequency, gyroradius, collisional slowing down, diffusion, and neoclassical and turbulent transport coefficients.

Typical values are about 1.008 u for protium, 2.014 u for deuterium, 3.016 u for tritium, 4.003 u for helium-4, exactly 12 u for carbon-12 by definition of the atomic mass scale, and about 182-186 u for common tungsten isotopes. Fusion-plasma ion species typically span roughly 1-250 u.

NAMES.name: neutral_state_convection_velocity
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: State-resolved convection velocity for neutral particle transport across magnetic flux surfaces. It is the advective drift coefficient multiplying the density of a specified neutral state in a flux-surface-averaged radial particle flux law.
NAMES.long:
Neutral-state convection velocity is the effective radial advective velocity for particles belonging to a specified neutral state. It represents the part of the cross-flux-surface particle flux proportional to the neutral-state density, distinct from diffusive transport driven by a density gradient.

For the radial flux coordinate $r_\mathrm{eff}$ (effective minor radius, in meters) increasing from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary, a local flux-surface-averaged closure can be written as:

$$
\Gamma_{n,k,r} = -D_{n,k}\frac{\partial n_{n,k}}{\partial r_\mathrm{eff}} + v_{n,k} n_{n,k}
$$

where $k$ labels the neutral state, $\Gamma_{n,k,r}$ is the particle flux per unit area across a surface of constant $r_\mathrm{eff}$ in $\mathrm{m}^{-2}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, $D_{n,k}$ is the particle diffusivity in $\mathrm{m}^2\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, $n_{n,k}$ is the neutral-state density in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, and $v_{n,k}$ is the convection velocity in $\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$. If a normalized radial flux coordinate $\rho$ is used instead, the gradient term requires the appropriate length or metric factor, such as replacing $\partial/\partial r_\mathrm{eff}$ by $(1/L_\rho)\partial/\partial\rho$, to preserve these units.

The coefficient is usually inferred rather than measured directly, using particle-balance analysis, neutral-transport modeling, or fitted transport closures that separate gradient-driven and advective contributions to the state-resolved neutral flux. The aggregate neutral_convection_velocity describes an effective coefficient for the summed neutral population; it is not generally the arithmetic mean of the state-resolved velocities and becomes a simple density-weighted combination only under additional assumptions about diffusivities and density gradients.

Representative effective values range from -1000-1000 m.s^-1. Core values are often near zero to tens of m.s^-1, while edge or source-dominated neutral transport closures can require hundreds to thousands of m.s^-1 depending on ionization, charge exchange, recycling, and the chosen radial coordinate.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the convective contribution $v_{n,k} n_{n,k}$ carries neutral particles toward increasing radial flux coordinate $r_\mathrm{eff}$, outward from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: neutral_state_energy_convection_velocity
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: Effective convection velocity for the energy density of a neutral species in a specific charge state, used in flux-surface-averaged neutral energy transport equations.
NAMES.long:
The neutral state energy convection velocity is the effective velocity coefficient $v_E$ multiplying the energy density of a specified neutral charge state in the advective term of the neutral energy transport equation. It encapsulates the bulk motion of neutral particles carrying thermal energy, arising from pressure gradients, atomic physics exchanges (ionization, recombination), and neutral-ion momentum transfer. As an undirected quantity in flux-surface-averaged formulations, it complements the directional component [parallel_neutral_state_energy_convection_velocity](name:parallel_neutral_state_energy_convection_velocity), which resolves this velocity along the magnetic field direction.

The convective energy flux for the neutral charge state is:

$$
\Gamma_E = v_E \, \varepsilon_n
$$

where $\varepsilon_n$ is the energy density of the neutral state in J m$^{-3}$.

This quantity is the charge-state-resolved counterpart of neutral_energy_convection_velocity, which aggregates all neutral states; the state-resolved form is required when distinct neutral levels (ground state vs. excited, atomic vs. molecular) exhibit different transport behavior. An analogous quantity for ion charge states is parallel_ion_state_energy_convection_velocity. This velocity is computed as a derived transport coefficient from neutral fluid or kinetic models and serves as input to energy-balance equations in edge and scrape-off-layer plasma transport calculations.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the neutral energy flux is directed outward, toward increasing minor radius.

NAMES.name: neutral_state_energy_flux
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: Signed energy flux density carried by neutrals in a specified quantum state, including directed transport of particle, thermal, kinetic, and internal-state energy.
NAMES.long:
Neutral state energy flux is the signed energy flux density carried by neutral particles belonging to a specified quantum state. It represents the normal component of the total neutral-state energy-flow vector through an oriented surface, including energy transported by particle motion and by non-convective heat flow.

A kinetic definition for the flux through a surface with unit normal $\hat{n}$ is:

$$
\Phi_{E,n,s} = \hat{n} \cdot \int E_s(\mathbf{v})\,\mathbf{v}\,f_{n,s}(\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $\Phi_{E,n,s}$ is the neutral energy flux density for state $s$, $f_{n,s}$ is the neutral velocity distribution function, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity, and $E_s(\mathbf{v})$ is the energy carried by one neutral in that state, including translational kinetic energy and any internal excitation energy relevant to the state definition. In fluid descriptions this same quantity is commonly represented as the sum of a convective energy flux and a conductive or diffusive heat-flux contribution.

In practice it is obtained from neutral transport modeling, kinetic Monte Carlo calculations, moment equations, or diagnostic inference combined with an energy balance. The value depends strongly on neutral density, temperature or energy distribution, drift or streaming velocity, ionization and charge-exchange rates, and wall or recycling sources.

Typical magnitudes in edge and divertor plasmas range from 10^2-10^6 W m^-2, with localized high-recycling or beam-like neutral populations reaching about 10^7 W m^-2.
NAMES.sign: Positive when energy carried by the neutral state crosses the oriented surface in the direction of the positive surface normal.

NAMES.name: neutral_state_momentum
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: Area-normalized vector source of linear momentum for a specified neutral species charge state, representing net momentum transfer from charge exchange, ionization, recombination, elastic scattering, and related collisions.
NAMES.long:
Neutral state momentum is the vector source of linear momentum transferred to a specified neutral species charge state, normalized by the area through which the transfer is represented. It has pressure-like dimensions while retaining the direction of the net impulse acting on the neutral population, and it contributes to the neutral momentum balance together with advection, pressure, and momentum-flux terms.

When the area-normalized source is obtained by integrating a local collisional force density over a representative length, a generic balance for state $s$ can be written as:

$$
\mathbf{M}_s = \int_{\Delta \ell} \left[ m_s n_s \sum_j \nu^{\mathrm{cx}}_{sj}(\mathbf{u}_j-\mathbf{u}_s) + \sum_{\alpha \in \mathcal{B}_s} R_\alpha \Delta\mathbf{p}_{\alpha\to s} - \sum_{\beta \in \mathcal{L}_s} R_\beta \Delta\mathbf{p}_{s\to\beta} + \mathbf{f}^{\mathrm{el}}_s \right] d\ell
$$

where $\mathbf{M}_s$ is the area-normalized momentum source vector, $d\ell$ is a length element in m, and the bracketed term is a local force density. The mass $m_s$ is in kg, $n_s$ is the neutral-state density in m^-3, $\nu^{\mathrm{cx}}_{sj}$ is an effective charge-exchange frequency with collision partner $j$ in s^-1, and $\mathbf{u}_s$ and $\mathbf{u}_j$ are species mean velocities in m s^-1. The sets $\mathcal{B}_s$ and $\mathcal{L}_s$ contain reactions that create and remove state $s$, $R_\alpha$ and $R_\beta$ are volumetric reaction rates in m^-3 s^-1, $\Delta\mathbf{p}$ is the event-averaged momentum increment or removal in kg m s^-1, and $\mathbf{f}^{\mathrm{el}}_s$ is the elastic-scattering force density in kg m^-2 s^-2.

In practice, this quantity is evaluated from plasma and neutral densities, temperatures, species flow velocities, distribution functions, and atomic or molecular rate coefficients. Charge exchange transfers directed momentum between ion and neutral populations while conserving the momentum of the interacting pair, ionization removes the momentum carried by neutrals leaving the state, recombination and molecular channels add product momentum, and elastic scattering redistributes momentum among existing particles. Direct measurement is uncommon; spectroscopy, neutral pressure gages, particle balance, and plasma momentum balance provide indirect constraints.

Projected components may be taken along radial, toroidal, poloidal, or magnetic-field-parallel directions. Related projected quantities include [poloidal_neutral_state_momentum](name:poloidal_neutral_state_momentum), [toroidal_neutral_state_momentum](name:toroidal_neutral_state_momentum), and [parallel_neutral_momentum](name:parallel_neutral_momentum), while momentum-flux analogs such as [parallel_neutral_state_momentum_flux](name:parallel_neutral_state_momentum_flux) and [toroidal_neutral_state_momentum_flux](name:toroidal_neutral_state_momentum_flux) describe transport of neutral-state momentum rather than a local source.

Representative modeled magnitudes are highly regime dependent: 10^-6-10^-2 kg.m^-1.s^-2 in weakly recycling or low-neutral-density edge regions, 10^-2-10^2 kg.m^-1.s^-2 in scrape-off-layer and divertor conditions, and up to about 10^3 kg.m^-1.s^-2 in localized high-recycling, detachment-front, or gas-injection regions. Values may be near zero where the neutral density is small or interacting flows are nearly equilibrated.
NAMES.sign: Positive when a resolved component of the net momentum transfer to the neutral state acts along the positive direction of its basis vector; in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, this is $+\hat{R}$, increasing toroidal angle $\phi$, or $+\hat{Z}$, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height.

NAMES.name: neutral_state_particle_flux
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: Signed number flux of neutral particles in a specified internal state through an oriented surface, per unit area and per unit time. It is the surface-normal component of state-resolved neutral particle transport.
NAMES.long:
Neutral-state particle flux is the signed surface-normal number flux of neutral atoms or molecules belonging to a specified internal state. For a closed control surface, choosing the normal outward from the control volume makes positive values represent neutral particles leaving that volume; choosing the opposite normal reverses the sign.

For an oriented surface with unit normal $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$, the scalar flux is the projection of the vector particle flux:

$$
\Gamma_s = \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_s \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}
$$

where $\Gamma_s$ is the scalar neutral-state particle flux in $m^{-2}\,s^{-1}$, $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_s$ is the vector number flux of neutrals in internal state $s$ in $m^{-2}\,s^{-1}$, and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is the unit normal to the surface. In a local particle balance it enters through $\partial n_s/\partial t + \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_s = S_s$, where $n_s$ is the state-resolved neutral density in $m^{-3}$ and $S_s$ is the net volumetric source in $m^{-3}\,s^{-1}$.

In practice this quantity is computed from neutral kinetic or fluid transport models as a velocity moment of the state-resolved distribution, or from a particle crossing rate divided by the corresponding surface area. Experimental constraints are usually indirect, using spectroscopy, pressure measurements, gas balance, and recycling observations to infer the state-resolved neutral population and its transport.

Typical magnitudes span about $10^{17}$-$10^{22}$ $m^{-2}\,s^{-1}$ in low-density or weakly recycling regions and can reach $10^{22}$-$10^{24}$ $m^{-2}\,s^{-1}$ near strong gas, recycling, or divertor sources. Fluxes for excited internal states are often smaller than ground-state neutral fluxes because excited-state populations are shorter lived.
NAMES.sign: Positive when neutral particles in the specified internal state cross the oriented surface in the direction of the chosen unit normal.

NAMES.name: neutral_state_source_rate
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: Net volumetric particle source rate for neutrals in a specified internal quantum state. It is the local creation rate minus loss rate per unit volume from atomic and molecular processes such as ionization, recombination, charge exchange, excitation, and de-excitation.
NAMES.long:
Neutral state source rate is the net local rate at which neutral particles in a specified internal quantum state are created or removed per unit volume. The state label refers to an internal quantum state of a neutral species, not to an ion charge state. It is the source term associated with the corresponding neutral-state density, including quantities such as [total_neutral_state_density](name:total_neutral_state_density) and [fast_neutral_state_density](name:fast_neutral_state_density).

For a neutral density $n_\alpha$ in internal state $\alpha$, the source rate $S_\alpha$ enters the particle continuity equation as:

$$
\frac{\partial n_\alpha}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \Gamma_\alpha = S_\alpha
$$

where $\Gamma_\alpha$ is the particle flux density of that neutral state and $S_\alpha$ is the net volumetric production rate. Positive contributions include recombination into the state, charge exchange that creates a neutral in the state, de-excitation or excitation from other neutral states into the state, and external neutral injection when represented locally; negative contributions include ionization, charge exchange out of the state, and transitions to other internal states.

In practice, this quantity is usually computed from neutral transport and collisional-radiative models by summing local reaction rates over all processes that populate or depopulate the specified state. The rates may be constrained by diagnostics such as line emission, neutral pressure measurements, charge-exchange spectroscopy, and particle-balance analysis, but the source rate itself is a model-derived local balance term rather than a directly measured primitive.

Typical magnitudes in magnetically confined fusion plasmas span about $10^{18}$-$10^{24}$ m^-3.s^-1 in edge, scrape-off-layer, and divertor regions, with localized recycling, gas fueling, or strong ionization and recombination zones sometimes reaching $10^{25}$ m^-3.s^-1. In hot core regions, thermal neutral source-rate magnitudes are often much smaller because neutral densities are low.
NAMES.sign: Positive when local physical processes produce neutrals in the specified internal quantum state faster than they remove them.

NAMES.name: neutral_state_temperature
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: Kinetic temperature of neutral atoms or molecules occupying a specified internal quantum state.
NAMES.long:
Neutral-state temperature is the translational kinetic temperature of neutral atoms or molecules conditional on occupancy of a specified internal state $s$, such as an electronic, vibrational, or rotational excitation. It characterizes the random kinetic energy of that state-resolved neutral population and is distinct from the internal excitation energy of the state. When state populations are equilibrated it approaches the state-averaged [neutral_temperature](name:neutral_state_temperature), but in weakly collisional or radiating plasmas different states can have different temperatures.

The scalar temperature is defined by the second central moment of the state-resolved velocity distribution:

$$
T_{n,s} = \frac{m_n}{3 e}\left\langle \left|\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{u}_{n,s}\right|^2 \right\rangle_s
$$

where $m_n$ is the neutral particle mass, $e$ is the elementary charge used to express the result in eV, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity, $\mathbf{u}_{n,s}$ is the bulk velocity of neutrals in state $s$, and $\langle\cdot\rangle_s$ denotes an average over that state's velocity distribution. For an isotropic scalar closure, the related [thermal_neutral_state_pressure](name:thermal_neutral_state_pressure) satisfies $p_{n,s}=n_{n,s} e T_{n,s}$ when $T_{n,s}$ is in eV.

Neutral-state temperature is inferred from diagnostics that are sensitive to the velocity distribution of a selected state, especially Doppler broadening of atomic emission lines or molecular bands, and from neutral particle energy spectra when state selectivity is available. It is also computed in state-resolved neutral transport or collisional-radiative models from the velocity-space moment of each state population, including effects of wall recycling, charge exchange, dissociation, excitation, ionization, and recombination.

Typical values for cold wall-recycled ground-state atoms or molecules are 0.01-1 eV. Excited atomic or molecular populations in edge and divertor plasmas are commonly 1-20 eV, while charge-exchange neutrals connected to hotter plasma regions can reach 10-1000 eV depending on the parent ion temperature and collisional history.

NAMES.name: nitrogen_density_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: nitrogen
NAMES.short: Number density of nitrogen ions evaluated at the radial location of the internal transport barrier. It represents the local nitrogen impurity concentration at the barrier position, independent of the diagnostic or reconstruction method used to obtain it.
NAMES.long:
Nitrogen density at the internal transport barrier is the local number density of nitrogen impurity ions evaluated at the barrier position. Unless a charge state is specified separately, the quantity represents the sum over ionized nitrogen charge states present in the plasma, not a single ionization stage.

A useful definition is the charge-state sum evaluated at the barrier location:

$$
n_{\mathrm{N}}(r_{\mathrm{ITB}}) = \sum_Z n_{\mathrm{N}^{Z+}}(r_{\mathrm{ITB}})
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{N}^{Z+}}$ is the number density of nitrogen ions with charge state $Z+$ and $r_{\mathrm{ITB}}$ denotes the radial location assigned to the internal transport barrier.

In practice, this density is inferred from impurity spectroscopy, charge-exchange measurements where available, ionization-balance analysis, or transport modeling constrained by line emission and equilibrium information. The reported value is the local nitrogen density at the identified barrier position rather than a volume average.

Typical values in magnetically confined plasmas are about $10^{16}-10^{19}$ m^-3. Trace nitrogen concentrations are often near the lower end of this range, while deliberate nitrogen seeding or strongly impurity-enriched conditions can give values approaching the upper end.

Conceptually related quantities include total ion density at the internal transport barrier and analogous impurity densities such as oxygen and tungsten density at the internal transport barrier.

NAMES.name: nitrogen_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: nitrogen
NAMES.short: Number density of nitrogen ions at the magnetic axis, the innermost point of the confined plasma where the gradient of the poloidal magnetic flux vanishes.
NAMES.long:
The nitrogen ion number density at the magnetic axis is the total concentration of nitrogen impurity ions evaluated at the point $(R_\mathrm{axis}, Z_\mathrm{axis})$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame where $\nabla\psi = 0$, marking the geometric center of the nested flux-surface family. This on-axis value typically represents the peak of the nitrogen density radial profile in regimes without impurity-transport-driven hollowing.

The total on-axis nitrogen density sums contributions across all ionization states:

$$
n_\mathrm{N}(R_\mathrm{axis}, Z_\mathrm{axis}) = \sum_{k=1}^{7} n_{\mathrm{N}^{k+}}(R_\mathrm{axis}, Z_\mathrm{axis})
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{N}^{k+}}$ is the density of nitrogen ions in charge state $k$ and the sum runs over all seven possible ionization states of nitrogen (atomic number 7). In typical tokamak core conditions the fully stripped $\mathrm{N}^{7+}$ state dominates, and this on-axis value directly influences the effective charge $Z_\mathrm{eff} = \sum_s n_s Z_s^2 / n_e$, governing bremsstrahlung losses and resistivity at the plasma center.

The on-axis value is inferred from impurity transport modeling constrained by charge exchange recombination spectroscopy or passive ultraviolet emission diagnostics, whose line-integrated signals are inverted to yield local density profiles. Comparing this quantity with [nitrogen density at the pedestal](name:nitrogen_density_at_pedestal) yields the impurity peaking factor, while [nitrogen density at the plasma boundary](name:nitrogen_density_at_plasma_boundary) characterizes penetration depth from the edge. The analogous neon quantity is [neon_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:neon_density_at_magnetic_axis), and the species-general parent is [density_at_magnetic_axis](name:density_at_magnetic_axis).
NAMES.sign: Positive when nitrogen impurity ions are present in the confined plasma at the magnetic axis location.

NAMES.name: normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate
NAMES.short: Dimensionless radial coordinate derived from the square root of the normalized poloidal magnetic flux, mapping the magnetic axis to 0 and the last closed flux surface to 1.
NAMES.long:
The normalized poloidal flux coordinate $\rho_{\mathrm{pol,norm}}$ is a dimensionless radial label for nested flux surfaces derived from the poloidal magnetic flux $\psi$, providing a monotonic coordinate that equals zero at the magnetic axis and one at the last closed flux surface.

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{pol,norm}} = \sqrt{\frac{\psi - \psi_{\mathrm{axis}}}{\psi_{\mathrm{LCFS}} - \psi_{\mathrm{axis}}}}
$$

where $\psi$ is the poloidal magnetic flux on the flux surface of interest, $\psi_{\mathrm{axis}}$ is its value at the magnetic axis, and $\psi_{\mathrm{LCFS}}$ is its value at the last closed flux surface.

The coordinate is obtained from equilibrium reconstruction, which solves for the poloidal flux distribution $\psi(R, Z)$ over the poloidal cross-section in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame using magnetic diagnostic measurements. For point measurements, $\rho_{\mathrm{pol,norm}}$ is assigned the local value at the measurement position; for line-integrated diagnostics, it is taken as the minimum value reached along the line of sight within the closed flux surface region.

Typical pedestal locations in H-mode plasmas fall near $\rho_{\mathrm{pol,norm}} = 0.90$–$0.98$. In nearly circular, low-$\beta$ plasmas, $\rho_{\mathrm{pol,norm}}$ closely approximates the normalized minor radius $r/a$ (where $r$ is the local minor radius and $a$ is the separatrix minor radius); in strongly shaped or high-$\beta$ configurations, significant deviations arise. The closely related [normalized toroidal flux coordinate] uses the enclosed toroidal flux and is often preferred for transport calculations requiring a well-behaved Jacobian.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the evaluation point lies on a flux surface between the magnetic axis and the last closed flux surface; the coordinate is non-negative by construction and equals zero only at the magnetic axis.

NAMES.name: oxygen_density_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: oxygen
NAMES.short: Number density of oxygen ions at the radial reference position of the internal transport barrier, where reduced cross-field turbulent transport allows steep impurity density gradients to form.
NAMES.long:
Oxygen ion number density at the internal transport barrier (ITB) reference radius is the total count of oxygen ions per unit volume evaluated at the single flux-surface position assigned to the barrier. The ITB is a localized radial region where cross-field turbulent transport is suppressed — associated with reversed or strongly sheared safety factor profiles — allowing impurity density peaking driven by inward neoclassical pinch.

The local density $n_O$ sums contributions from all ionization states:

$$
n_O(\rho_\mathrm{ITB}) = \sum_{k=1}^{8} n_{O^{k+}}(\rho_\mathrm{ITB})
$$

where $n_{O^{k+}}$ is the density of oxygen in charge state $k+$ at the ITB radial coordinate $\rho_\mathrm{ITB}$, and the sum extends to fully stripped $O^{8+}$. Oxygen (atomic number $Z = 8$) contributes $\sum_k k\, n_{O^{k+}}$ electrons to the quasineutrality balance, so elevated $n_O$ at the ITB directly signals impurity accumulation in the barrier region.

This quantity is inferred from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, which resolves individual ionization states, or estimated from soft X-ray emissivity combined with impurity transport modeling. Typical oxygen densities in tokamak core plasmas range from $10^{16}$ to $10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$, corresponding to concentrations of $10^{-4}$–$10^{-2}$ relative to the local electron density.

This is the oxygen-species instance of [density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:density_at_internal_transport_barrier); analogous point densities at the ITB are defined for [carbon_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:carbon_density_at_internal_transport_barrier), [neon_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:neon_density_at_internal_transport_barrier), [argon_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:argon_density_at_internal_transport_barrier), and [iron_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:iron_density_at_internal_transport_barrier).
NAMES.sign: Positive when oxygen ions are present at the internal transport barrier location.

NAMES.name: oxygen_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: oxygen
NAMES.short: Number density of oxygen ions at the magnetic axis, the innermost flux-surface singular point where the gradient of the poloidal magnetic flux vanishes.
NAMES.long:
The oxygen ion number density at the magnetic axis gives the on-axis value of the oxygen impurity concentration radial profile, evaluated at the point $(R_\mathrm{axis}, Z_\mathrm{axis})$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame where $\nabla\psi = 0$.

On-axis oxygen density enters the plasma quasineutrality constraint:

$$
n_e = \sum_i Z_i \, n_i
$$

where $n_e$ is the electron number density, $Z_i$ is the mean charge number of the $i$-th ion species, and the sum runs over all confined ion populations including oxygen. Through this relation, a higher on-axis oxygen concentration dilutes the hydrogenic fuel-ion population and increases core radiative power losses via line emission.

The on-axis value is inferred from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy targeting oxygen emission lines, vacuum-ultraviolet spectroscopy, or impurity transport modeling constrained by line-integrated brightness measurements. It is evaluated alongside analogous impurity species such as [carbon_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:carbon_density_at_magnetic_axis), [neon_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:neon_density_at_magnetic_axis), and [nitrogen_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:nitrogen_density_at_magnetic_axis), all members of the [density_at_magnetic_axis](name:density_at_magnetic_axis) family.
NAMES.sign: Positive when oxygen ions are present in the confined plasma.

NAMES.name: parallel_anomalous_current_density
NAMES.short: Field-aligned component of the turbulence-driven anomalous current density, projected onto the unit vector along the local magnetic field.
NAMES.long:
The parallel anomalous current density $j_{\parallel,\mathrm{anom}}$ is the component of the full [anomalous current density](name:anomalous_current_density) vector $\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{anom}}$ resolved along the local magnetic field direction $\hat{b} = \mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$. It quantifies the net turbulence-driven charge flux flowing along field lines, arising from correlations between fluctuating plasma velocity and charge density that are not captured by classical or neoclassical transport models.

The defining projection is:

$$
j_{\parallel,\mathrm{anom}} = \mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{anom}} \cdot \hat{b}
$$

where $\hat{b}$ is the unit vector parallel to the magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$.

This component enters the parallel current balance and can influence resistive diffusion of the poloidal magnetic flux in turbulent plasma regimes. It is evaluated from gyrokinetic or reduced-fluid turbulence simulations that resolve fluctuation-driven transport. The cross-field counterparts [radial_anomalous_current_density](name:radial_anomalous_current_density) and [vertical_anomalous_current_density](name:vertical_anomalous_current_density) capture the perpendicular turbulent charge transport driven by the same anomalous process, while the diamagnetic_anomalous_current_density isolates the diamagnetic projection.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the current flows in the direction of the magnetic field vector $\mathbf{B}$.

NAMES.name: parallel_center_of_mass_velocity
NAMES.short: Parallel component of the plasma center-of-mass (bulk fluid) velocity, projected along the local magnetic field.
NAMES.long:
Parallel center-of-mass velocity is the component of the plasma barycentric flow along the local magnetic field. The center-of-mass velocity is the mass-density-weighted mean velocity of the included plasma species, so it is usually dominated by ion motion rather than electron motion.

The parallel component is defined by projecting the barycentric velocity onto the unit vector along the magnetic field:

$$
v_{\parallel,\mathrm{cm}} = \left(\frac{\sum_s m_s n_s \mathbf{v}_s}{\sum_s m_s n_s}\right) \cdot \frac{\mathbf{B}}{|\mathbf{B}|}
$$

where $s$ labels plasma species, $m_s$ is species mass in kg, $n_s$ is number density in m$^{-3}$, $\mathbf{v}_s$ is species flow velocity in m.s$^{-1}$, and $\mathbf{B}$ is magnetic field in T. The resulting $v_{\parallel,\mathrm{cm}}$ is in m.s$^{-1}$.

In experiment, this quantity is inferred from species flow measurements such as Doppler spectroscopy, charge-exchange spectroscopy, probe measurements in the edge, or collective scattering, combined with density and composition information. In transport modeling, it is computed from species momentum densities or velocities and then projected onto the reconstructed or prescribed magnetic-field direction.

Typical magnitudes are 10$^3$-10$^5$ m.s$^{-1}$ in confined and edge tokamak plasmas, depending on heating, momentum input, collisionality, and magnetic geometry. Values can be smaller near stagnation points and larger in strongly driven edge flows or transient events.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the plasma center-of-mass velocity has a component in the local magnetic-field direction $\mathbf{B}$.

NAMES.name: parallel_counter_passing_fast_particle_pressure
NAMES.subject: particle
