It is the dominant current channel in ohmically heated plasmas and its fractional contribution decreases as auxiliary non-inductive drives increase.

The quantity is defined by the flux-surface average:

$$
j_{\mathrm{ohm},\|} = \frac{\langle \mathbf{J}_\mathrm{ohm} \cdot \mathbf{B} \rangle}{B_0}
$$

where $\mathbf{J}_\mathrm{ohm}$ is the local ohmic current density vector, $\mathbf{B}$ is the total magnetic field, $B_0$ is the reference on-axis magnetic field, and $\langle \cdot \rangle$ denotes the flux-surface average. The local Ohm's law $j_{\mathrm{ohm},\|} = \sigma_\| E_\|$ couples this quantity to the [parallel conductivity] $\sigma_\|$ and the inductive parallel electric field $E_\|$.

This profile is obtained in transport analyzes by subtracting the [parallel non-inductive current density] from the total parallel current density, or computed directly from the resistivity profile and the inductive electric field. It enters the magnetic flux diffusion equation and governs current-profile evolution on the resistive timescale. The [parallel wave-driven current density] and bootstrap contributions together constitute the non-inductive complement.

Typical core values range from $10^5$ to $10^6$ A m$^{-2}$ in auxiliary-heated tokamak discharges, decreasing toward the plasma edge and in scenarios with strong non-inductive current drive.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the ohmic current flows in the same direction as the total magnetic field, giving $\langle \mathbf{J}_\mathrm{ohm} \cdot \mathbf{B} \rangle > 0$.

NAMES.name: parallel_pfirsch_schlueter_current_density
NAMES.subject: pfirsch_schlueter
NAMES.short: Field-aligned projection of the Pfirsch-Schlüter neoclassical current density onto the local magnetic field unit vector, capturing the dominant component that flows along field lines to compensate the divergence of the pressure-gradient-driven diamagnetic current.
NAMES.long:
The parallel Pfirsch-Schlüter current density is the scalar projection $j_{\parallel,PS} = \mathbf{j}_{PS} \cdot \hat{b}$, where $\hat{b} = \mathbf{B}/B$ is the local magnetic field unit vector and $\mathbf{j}_{PS}$ is the full [Pfirsch-Schlüter current density](name:pfirsch_schlueter_current_density) vector. This field-aligned component is the physically primary channel of the Pfirsch-Schlüter mechanism: in toroidal confinement devices, the pressure-gradient-driven diamagnetic current $\mathbf{j}_{\text{dia}} = \mathbf{B} \times \nabla p / B^2$ acquires a non-zero divergence due to toroidal geometry, which is balanced by return currents flowing predominantly along field lines to satisfy $\nabla \cdot \mathbf{j} = 0$.

The defining projection is:

$$
j_{\parallel,PS} = \frac{\mathbf{j}_{PS} \cdot \mathbf{B}}{B}
$$

where $B = |\mathbf{B}|$ is the magnetic field magnitude. In simplified circular geometry, this parallel component exhibits a characteristic $\cos\theta$ poloidal variation (where $\theta$ is the poloidal angle measured from the outboard midplane), reversing sign between the inboard and outboard sides of each flux surface.

This quantity is computed from neoclassical transport calculations at each local spatial point and complements the cylindrical decompositions available via [radial_pfirsch_schlueter_current_density](name:radial_pfirsch_schlueter_current_density), [poloidal_pfirsch_schlueter_current_density](name:poloidal_pfirsch_schlueter_current_density), [toroidal_pfirsch_schlueter_current_density](name:toroidal_pfirsch_schlueter_current_density), and [vertical_pfirsch_schlueter_current_density](name:vertical_pfirsch_schlueter_current_density) in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. Unlike those geometric projections, the parallel component is intrinsically field-aligned and is directly suited for field-line-following transport formulations.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the Pfirsch-Schlüter current flows in the direction of the magnetic field vector $\mathbf{B}$.

NAMES.name: parallel_total_current_density
NAMES.short: Flux-surface-averaged parallel total current density, defined by the total current density projected on the magnetic field and normalized by the signed reference toroidal magnetic field. It is the net field-aligned current density used in transport current-balance physics.
NAMES.long:
Parallel total current density is a signed scalar measure of the net total current flowing along the magnetic field, expressed with the flux-surface-averaged, reference-field-normalized convention used in transport physics. It combines all physical mechanisms contributing to the total current before evaluating the field-aligned component.

The defining convention is the flux-surface average of the magnetic-field projection of the total current density divided by the signed reference toroidal magnetic field:

$$
j_{\parallel,\mathrm{tot}} = \frac{\left\langle \mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{tot}}\cdot\mathbf{B}\right\rangle}{B_0}
$$

where $\mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{tot}}$ is the total current density in A m$^{-2}$, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field in T, $B_0$ is the signed reference toroidal magnetic field in T, and $\langle\cdot\rangle$ denotes an average over a magnetic flux surface.

In practice, the quantity is computed by forming the total current density, taking its scalar product with the magnetic field, applying the flux-surface average, and dividing by $B_0$. Magnetic-equilibrium constraints determine the current distribution, while kinetic and current-drive physics may determine how individual contributions add to the total; this quantity is the summed total after applying the same convention.

Representative magnitudes in tokamak transport analyzes are commonly $10^4$-$10^7$ A m$^{-2}$, depending on plasma current, cross-sectional area, magnetic geometry, and non-inductive current drive.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $\left\langle \mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{tot}}\cdot\mathbf{B}\right\rangle$ has the same sign as the signed reference toroidal magnetic field $B_0$; $B_0$ is positive when the reference toroidal field points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ system.

NAMES.name: particle_source_rate
NAMES.subject: particle
NAMES.short: Net volumetric rate of particle production or loss from a distribution function source, serving as the source term in the particle-density transport equation.
NAMES.long:
The particle source rate $S_n$ is the net rate per unit volume at which particles are created or destroyed by processes described through a distribution function, such as neutral beam injection ionization, thermonuclear fusion birth, or pellet ablation.

It enters the particle continuity equation as:

$$
\frac{\partial n}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\Gamma} = S_n
$$

where $n$ is the number density and $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$ is the directed particle flux. Positive values indicate net particle production; negative values indicate a net particle sink from the distribution source.

This quantity is computed from Fokker-Planck or kinetic solvers that track the birth and thermalization of fast particles on a flux-surface-averaged radial grid, and it is used as direct input to particle transport equations in integrated modeling workflows. The [thermal_particle_source_rate](name:thermal_particle_source_rate) isolates the thermal-population contribution, while ion_source_rate and [electron_source_rate](name:electron_source_rate) provide species-resolved counterparts. For neutral particles, the analogous quantity is [neutral_source_rate](name:neutral_source_rate).

Typical values in NBI-heated tokamak core plasmas span $10^{18}$–$10^{21}$ m$^{-3}$ s$^{-1}$, depending on injected power, beam energy, and local plasma density.

NAMES.name: perpendicular_co_passing_fast_particle_pressure
NAMES.subject: particle
NAMES.short: Perpendicular component of the species-summed fast-particle pressure tensor for co-passing orbits, produced by velocity components transverse to the local magnetic field. Co-passing denotes passing guiding-center motion with the same toroidal sense as the plasma current.
NAMES.long:
Perpendicular co-passing fast-particle pressure is the perpendicular component of the fast-particle pressure tensor after restricting the distribution to co-passing passing orbits and summing over the included fast species. It represents kinetic stress from velocity components orthogonal to the local magnetic field. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ system, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, co-passing denotes passing guiding-center orbits whose toroidal motion is in the same sense as the plasma current.

The species-summed kinetic moment is

$$
P_{\perp,\mathrm{co}}(\mathbf{x},t) = \sum_s \int_{\Omega_{\mathrm{co},s}} \frac{1}{2} m_s v_\perp^2 f_s(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v},t)\,d^3v
$$

where $s$ labels the included fast-particle species, $m_s$ is the species mass in kg, $\mathbf{x}$ is position in m, $t$ is time in s, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity in m s$^{-1}$, $v_\perp$ is the speed perpendicular to the local magnetic field in m s$^{-1}$, $f_s$ is the fast-particle distribution function in s$^3$ m$^{-6}$, and $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element in m$^3$ s$^{-3}$. The domain $\Omega_{\mathrm{co},s}$ is the passing part of velocity space whose guiding-center orbit has bounce-averaged toroidal velocity $R\dot{\phi}$, in the same $(R,\phi,Z)$ system, in the same sense as the plasma current; trapped and counter-passing orbits are excluded. For common heating and fusion-product applications the fast species are usually energetic ions, but the definition applies to any suprathermal species included in the sum.

This quantity is computed as a second velocity moment of an orbit-class-resolved fast-particle distribution, typically after classifying particles by pitch, constants of motion, or guiding-center trajectories. It is not usually measured directly as a local tensor component; instead it is inferred through kinetic modeling constrained by diagnostics sensitive to suprathermal particles. Together with [parallel_co_passing_fast_particle_pressure](name:parallel_co_passing_fast_particle_pressure), it describes pressure anisotropy of the co-passing fast population, while [perpendicular_fast_particle_pressure](name:perpendicular_fast_particle_pressure) includes the corresponding perpendicular contributions from all fast-particle orbit classes.

Typical values are strongly scenario dependent. As an order-of-magnitude guide, auxiliary-heated tokamak cores can have perpendicular co-passing fast-particle pressures of about $10^2$-$5\times10^4$ Pa, with much smaller values in weakly heated regions or where the co-passing fast-particle population is depleted.

NAMES.name: perpendicular_fast_ion_pressure
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Perpendicular component of the fast ion pressure for the ion species considered, summed over ionization states. It represents the kinetic pressure associated with suprathermal ion velocity components transverse to the local magnetic field.
NAMES.long:
Perpendicular fast ion pressure is the component of the suprathermal ion pressure tensor associated with motion across the local magnetic field. For a given ion species it is summed over ionization states and complements the parallel component [parallel_fast_ion_pressure](name:parallel_fast_ion_pressure); equality of the perpendicular and parallel components corresponds to an isotropic fast-ion pressure contribution.

A kinetic definition is the second velocity moment of the fast-ion distribution perpendicular to the magnetic field:

$$
p_{\mathrm{fast},\perp} = \sum_q \int \frac{1}{2} m_i v_\perp^2 f_{\mathrm{fast},q}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $m_i$ is the ion mass, $q$ labels ionization state, $f_{\mathrm{fast},q}$ is the fast-ion distribution function normalized so that its velocity integral gives density, and $v_\perp$ is the magnitude of the particle velocity component perpendicular to the local magnetic-field direction. The factor $1/2$ accounts for the two perpendicular degrees of freedom in the pressure tensor moment.

In practice this quantity is computed from modeled or reconstructed fast-ion distribution functions, including source, slowing-down, orbit, and wave-particle effects. It may be constrained by diagnostics sensitive to suprathermal ions, such as neutron emission, neutral-particle analysis, fast-ion D-alpha emission, collective Thomson scattering, or gamma-ray measurements, depending on ion species and energy range.

Typical values range from near zero in weakly heated or edge regions to about 10-10^4 Pa in many auxiliary-heated plasmas, and can reach 10^4-10^5 Pa where energetic neutral-beam ions, radio-frequency-accelerated ions, or fusion-born alpha particles contribute strongly.

NAMES.name: perpendicular_fast_ion_state_pressure
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Perpendicular pressure contributed by non-thermal ions in a specified charge state, equal to the transverse diagonal pressure-tensor component relative to the local magnetic field. It is the charge-state-resolved fast-ion contribution to pressure anisotropy.
NAMES.long:
Perpendicular fast-ion-state pressure is the transverse diagonal component of the kinetic pressure tensor for non-thermal ions in a single charge state. It measures the kinetic stress associated with fast-ion motion perpendicular to the local magnetic field and can differ from the corresponding parallel component for beam ions, fusion products, and radio-frequency-accelerated ion tails.

For an ion charge state $q$, the perpendicular component is defined from the fast-ion velocity distribution as:

$$
P_{\perp,\mathrm{fast}}^{(q)} = \frac{m_i}{2} \int \left|\mathbf{v} - v_\parallel \hat{\mathbf{b}}\right|^2 f_{\mathrm{fast}}^{(q)}(\mathbf{v})\, d^3v
$$

where $m_i$ is the ion mass, $f_{\mathrm{fast}}^{(q)}$ is the non-thermal distribution function for charge state $q$, $\hat{\mathbf{b}}=\mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$ is the unit vector along the magnetic field, and $v_\parallel=\mathbf{v}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{b}}$. The factor $1/2$ converts the total squared speed in the two perpendicular velocity directions into one transverse diagonal pressure component; equivalently, for a gyrotropic distribution it is the pressure associated with either perpendicular velocity component.

This quantity is usually computed by integrating a charge-state-resolved fast-ion distribution from kinetic, Fokker-Planck, orbit-following, bounce-averaged, or Monte Carlo transport modeling. It may be constrained indirectly by fast-ion diagnostics such as neutron emission, neutral-particle analysis, gamma-ray emission, collective scattering, or fast-ion charge-exchange measurements, but the pressure itself is a velocity-space moment rather than a directly measured signal.

Typical core values in neutral-beam-heated or radio-frequency-heated tokamak plasmas are about $10^2$-$10^4$ Pa per important charge state, with lower values near the edge and possible values approaching $10^5$ Pa in high-power scenarios with strong fast-ion confinement. The value should be compared with [parallel_fast_ion_state_pressure](name:parallel_fast_ion_state_pressure) to quantify charge-state-resolved anisotropy, with [perpendicular_fast_ion_pressure](name:perpendicular_fast_ion_pressure) for the sum over charge states, and with [perpendicular_plasma_pressure](name:perpendicular_plasma_pressure) for the corresponding total plasma pressure component.

NAMES.name: perpendicular_fast_neutral_state_pressure
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: Perpendicular kinetic pressure of suprathermal neutral particles in a specified internal quantum or excitation state, arising from velocity components perpendicular to the local magnetic field.
NAMES.long:
The perpendicular fast neutral state pressure is the component of the kinetic pressure tensor of suprathermal (non-thermal) neutral particles associated with motions perpendicular to the local magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$, resolved by the particle's internal quantum or excitation state $s$. It is the state-resolved analog of [perpendicular_fast_neutral_pressure](name:perpendicular_fast_neutral_pressure) and represents a perpendicular projection of [fast_neutral_state_pressure](name:fast_neutral_state_pressure), capturing how individual internal states contribute to the total perpendicular fast-neutral pressure.

The defining relation is the second velocity moment of the state-specific fast neutral distribution restricted to the perpendicular velocity plane:

$$
P_{\perp,\mathrm{fast},s} = \frac{m_n}{2} \int f_{\mathrm{fast},s}(\mathbf{v})\, v_\perp^2 \, d^3v
$$

where $m_n$ is the neutral particle mass, $f_{\mathrm{fast},s}(\mathbf{v})$ is the velocity distribution function of fast neutrals in internal state $s$, and $v_\perp$ is the speed component perpendicular to $\mathbf{B}$.

This quantity is relevant wherever fast neutrals generated by charge-exchange reactions or dissociation events carry significant perpendicular energy, particularly in edge and scrape-off layer plasmas. Values are computed by kinetic neutral transport codes that resolve internal-state populations across the fast neutral velocity distribution, or estimated from state-specific spectroscopic measurements combined with velocity distribution models. The [neutral_state_particle_flux](name:neutral_state_particle_flux) provides complementary state-resolved information on the associated particle transport.
NAMES.sign: Positive when fast neutral particles in state $s$ carry net kinetic energy in the plane perpendicular to the local magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$.

NAMES.name: perpendicular_runaway_electron_diffusivity
NAMES.subject: runaway_electron
NAMES.short: Cross-field diffusion coefficient governing the perpendicular spread of runaway electrons across magnetic flux surfaces.
NAMES.long:
The perpendicular diffusivity $D_\perp$ of runaway electrons quantifies how rapidly the runaway electron population spreads across magnetic flux surfaces due to stochastic magnetic field perturbations, collisional pitch-angle scattering, and turbulent transport processes. It is the perpendicular projection of the full [runaway_electron_diffusivity](name:runaway_electron_diffusivity) tensor, characterizing the diffusive part of cross-field transport for this suprathermal population.

The diffusive contribution to the perpendicular particle flux is defined as:

$$
\Gamma_{\perp}^{\text{diff}} = -D_\perp \nabla_\perp n_r
$$

where $n_r$ is the [runaway electron number density](name:runaway_electron_density). Combined with the convective contribution from [perpendicular_runaway_electron_convection_velocity](name:perpendicular_runaway_electron_convection_velocity), this constitutes the net [perpendicular_runaway_electron_particle_flux](name:perpendicular_runaway_electron_particle_flux).

The value of $D_\perp$ is inferred from runaway electron density evolution measurements or prescribed in disruption transport models based on the estimated level of magnetic field stochasticity. During disruptions with significant stochastic magnetic field perturbations, $D_\perp$ can reach $10^{-2}$–$1\;\text{m}^2\,\text{s}^{-1}$; under quiescent magnetohydrodynamic conditions cross-field stochasticity is substantially weaker. Larger values of $D_\perp$ enhance runaway electron losses to the first wall and suppress the growth of the post-disruption runaway current.

NAMES.name: perpendicular_runaway_electron_particle_flux
NAMES.subject: runaway_electron
NAMES.short: Scalar component of runaway-electron particle flux across magnetic flux surfaces, projected onto the outward flux-surface normal.
NAMES.long:
Perpendicular runaway-electron particle flux is the scalar flux of runaway electrons crossing magnetic flux surfaces. It is the normal component of the runaway-electron particle-flux vector and describes cross-field transport, distinct from particle motion along the local magnetic-field direction as represented by parallel particle-flux components such as [parallel_electron_particle_flux](name:parallel_electron_particle_flux) and [parallel_ion_particle_flux](name:parallel_ion_particle_flux).

The projection defining the scalar perpendicular flux is

$$
\Gamma_{\perp,\mathrm{RE}} = \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{\mathrm{RE}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}_{\mathrm{out}}
$$

where $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{\mathrm{RE}}$ is the runaway-electron particle-flux vector in m^-2.s^-1 and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{\mathrm{out}}$ is the dimensionless unit normal to the magnetic flux surface, oriented from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary. The scalar $\Gamma_{\perp,\mathrm{RE}}$ has units m^-2.s^-1.

In transport modeling this quantity may be computed from the continuity balance for [runaway_electron_density](name:runaway_electron_density) or represented with an effective convection-diffusion closure along a local flux-surface-normal coordinate $r_\perp$ in meters. A common form is $\Gamma_{\perp,\mathrm{RE}} = -D_\perp\,\partial n_{\mathrm{RE}}/\partial r_\perp + V_\perp n_{\mathrm{RE}}$, where $D_\perp$ is [perpendicular_runaway_electron_diffusivity](name:perpendicular_runaway_electron_diffusivity) in m^2.s^-1, $V_\perp$ is [perpendicular_runaway_electron_convection_velocity](name:perpendicular_runaway_electron_convection_velocity) in m.s^-1, $n_{\mathrm{RE}}$ is runaway-electron density in m^-3, and $\partial n_{\mathrm{RE}}/\partial r_\perp$ has units m^-4. This closure is a modeling representation; the physical quantity itself is the normal projection of the particle flux.

The flux is generally inferred rather than measured directly, using reconstructed or modeled runaway-electron density evolution together with transport assumptions. No device-independent numerical range is implied by the standard name; representative magnitudes should be assessed from the scale $|\Gamma_{\perp,\mathrm{RE}}| \sim D_\perp n_{\mathrm{RE}}/L_\perp + |V_\perp| n_{\mathrm{RE}}$, where $L_\perp$ is the characteristic density-gradient length in meters.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the net flux is directed along the outward flux-surface normal from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: poloidal_anomalous_current_density
NAMES.short: Poloidal anomalous current density is the component of fluctuation-driven anomalous current density along increasing poloidal angle theta in a flux-coordinate (rho, theta, phi) system. It is distinct from a vertical component in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal anomalous current density is the poloidal component of the anomalous current-density vector associated with turbulence-driven charge transport. The component is taken along the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in a flux-coordinate $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$ system, not along the vertical $Z$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

The component is defined by projecting the anomalous current-density vector onto the local unit direction of increasing $\theta$:

$$
j_{\mathrm{anom},\theta} = \mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{anom}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}_\theta
$$

where $j_{\mathrm{anom},\theta}$ is the poloidal anomalous current density in A m$^{-2}$, $\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{anom}}$ is the full anomalous current-density vector in A m$^{-2}$, and $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_\theta$ is the unit vector tangent to increasing $\theta$ at fixed radial coordinate and toroidal angle.

In practice this quantity is obtained from turbulence, gyrokinetic, or transport calculations that evaluate fluctuation-driven charge fluxes and separate them from classical, neoclassical, diamagnetic, and collisional friction contributions. It is the poloidal counterpart of [radial_anomalous_current_density](name:radial_anomalous_current_density) and [toroidal_anomalous_current_density](name:toroidal_anomalous_current_density); [vertical_anomalous_current_density](name:vertical_anomalous_current_density) instead refers to projection along $Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. Poloidal current density from other mechanisms is described by quantities such as [poloidal_diamagnetic_current_density](name:poloidal_diamagnetic_current_density) and [poloidal_current_density_due_to_ion_neutral_friction](name:poloidal_current_density_due_to_ion_neutral_friction).

Typical magnitudes are strongly case-dependent, can change sign locally, and are often reported as signed local values in A m$^{-2}$ or normalized to a turbulent charge flux rather than by a universal device-independent range. Values are expected to vanish in models without anomalous electromagnetic charge transport.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the projected anomalous current density is directed along increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in the flux-coordinate $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$ system.

NAMES.name: poloidal_center_of_mass_velocity
NAMES.short: Poloidal component of the plasma center-of-mass velocity, computed as the mass-weighted mean of all contributing species fluid velocities projected onto the poloidal direction.
NAMES.long:
The center-of-mass velocity describes the bulk fluid motion of the plasma as a whole, accounting for all ionic, electronic, and neutral particle species weighted by their mass density. The poloidal component $v_{\theta,\mathrm{cm}}$ characterizes the net poloidal circulation of this composite fluid, which governs neoclassical poloidal rotation and enters the radial force balance that determines the radial electric field.

The defining relation is:

$$
v_{\theta,\mathrm{cm}} = \frac{\sum_s m_s n_s v_{\theta,s}}{\sum_s m_s n_s}
$$

where $m_s$ is the particle mass of species $s$, $n_s$ its number density, and $v_{\theta,s}$ its individual poloidal fluid velocity, with the sum running over all plasma species.

The poloidal component complements [toroidal_center_of_mass_velocity](name:toroidal_center_of_mass_velocity) to describe the bulk plasma flow in the poloidal plane; [poloidal_ion_velocity](name:poloidal_ion_velocity) and [poloidal_neutral_velocity](name:poloidal_neutral_velocity) give the individual species contributions. This quantity is inferred from multi-species charge exchange recombination spectroscopy combined with momentum-balance constraints in fluid transport modeling.

Poloidal rotation speeds in tokamak plasmas are typically small relative to toroidal rotation, with values in the range 0.1-5 km/s in the plasma core and potentially higher magnitudes near internal transport barriers and the separatrix.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the bulk plasma flow is directed in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_conductivity
NAMES.short: Poloidal projection of the electrical conductivity tensor in a flux coordinate system (rho, theta, phi). It is the local diagonal coefficient relating poloidal current density to poloidal electric field.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal conductivity is the poloidal projection of the electrical conductivity tensor in a flux coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, where $\rho$ labels magnetic surfaces, $\theta$ is the poloidal angle, and $\phi$ is the toroidal angle. It represents the local diagonal response of the poloidal current-density projection to the poloidal electric-field projection.

For the diagonal projection used by this quantity, the local Ohm-law relation is

$$
J_\theta = \sigma_\theta E_\theta
$$

where $J_\theta = \mathbf{J}\cdot\hat{e}_\theta$ is the current-density projection along the unit direction $\hat{e}_\theta$ tangent to increasing $\theta$, in A m$^{-2}$; $E_\theta = \mathbf{E}\cdot\hat{e}_\theta$ is the electric-field projection in V m$^{-1}$; and $\sigma_\theta$ is the poloidal conductivity in ohm$^{-1}$ m$^{-1}$. This scalar is the $\theta\theta$ diagonal/projection coefficient; off-diagonal tensor terms, Hall response, and couplings to radial or toroidal electric fields are not included in it.

In practice, poloidal conductivity is specified by a transport model, obtained by projecting a full conductivity tensor onto $\hat{e}_\theta$, or inferred from reconstructed current densities and electric fields when a local diagonal relation is adequate. It may represent classical collisional, neoclassical, or effective anomalous transport, so it depends on plasma temperature, density, collisionality, magnetic geometry, and turbulence assumptions.

Typical effective values are highly model-dependent and can span about $10^{-2}$-$10^{8}$ ohm$^{-1}$ m$^{-1}$. Hot, weakly collisional core plasmas usually have larger projected conductivities, while cold edge regions or cross-field-dominated effective models can be much smaller.

NAMES.name: poloidal_diamagnetic_current_density
NAMES.short: Projection of the diamagnetic current density onto the poloidal direction in a flux-coordinate system (rho, theta, phi). It arises from the cross product of the magnetic field with the plasma pressure gradient in a magnetized plasma.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal diamagnetic current density is the projection of the full [diamagnetic_current_density](name:diamagnetic_current_density) onto the poloidal basis direction $\hat{\theta}$ of a flux-coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$ on magnetic surfaces. It represents the part of the guiding-center diamagnetic-drift current that circulates poloidally, complementing the toroidal_diamagnetic_current_density and [parallel_diamagnetic_current_density](name:parallel_diamagnetic_current_density) projections.

For an isotropic scalar pressure, the defining relation is

$$
j_{\mathrm{dia},\theta} = \mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{dia}}\cdot\hat{\theta} = \left(\frac{\mathbf{B}\times\nabla p}{B^2}\right)\cdot\hat{\theta}
$$

where $j_{\mathrm{dia},\theta}$ is the poloidal component, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field with magnitude $B$ in T, $p$ is the plasma pressure in Pa, and $\nabla p$ is in Pa m$^{-1}$. The flux-coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$ uses the toroidal angle $\phi$ of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height; the result is in A m$^{-2}$.

In practice this quantity is inferred from magnetic-equilibrium reconstruction and kinetic-pressure information by evaluating the pressure gradient, forming $\mathbf{B}\times\nabla p/B^2$, and projecting the result onto $\hat{\theta}$. Direct measurement of this component in isolation is uncommon; uncertainties are usually dominated by pressure-gradient resolution, magnetic-field geometry, and the definition of the poloidal basis near separatrices or strongly shaped flux surfaces.

Typical magnitudes are about $10^3-10^5$ A m$^{-2}$ in moderate-gradient core plasmas and can reach $10^5-10^6$ A m$^{-2}$ in steep edge or pedestal regions. The signed component may pass through zero where the pressure gradient, magnetic geometry, or projection onto the poloidal direction changes.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the projection of $\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{dia}}$ is in the $+\hat{\theta}$ direction of the flux-coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, with $\phi$ increasing counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: poloidal_electron_convection_velocity
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Poloidal component of the effective electron particle convection velocity, the advective coefficient multiplying electron density in a particle-transport flux law.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal electron convection velocity is the effective advective velocity component for electron particle transport in the poloidal direction of a flux coordinate system $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$. It is a transport coefficient rather than necessarily the microscopic electron fluid velocity, representing directed electron particle transport tangent to magnetic flux surfaces after diffusive density-gradient transport is separated.

The poloidal electron particle flux is commonly decomposed into diffusive and convective contributions:

$$
\Gamma_{e,\theta} = -D_{e,\theta}\frac{1}{h_\theta}\frac{\partial n_e}{\partial \theta} + n_e v_{e,\theta}^{\mathrm{conv}}
$$

where $\Gamma_{e,\theta}$ is the [poloidal electron particle flux](name:poloidal_electron_particle_flux), $D_{e,\theta}$ is the poloidal electron particle diffusivity, $n_e$ is the electron number density, $v_{e,\theta}^{\mathrm{conv}}$ is the poloidal electron convection velocity, $\theta$ is poloidal angle, and $h_\theta$ converts angular variation into distance along the poloidal coordinate line.

This quantity is usually inferred as an effective coefficient in transport analysis or computed in fluid, drift-fluid, gyrofluid, or reduced transport models. It can include the modeled effects of drifts, parallel flows projected onto poloidal transport, turbulent pinch terms, sources and sinks, and closure assumptions, so it should not be interpreted automatically as a directly measured electron flow speed.

Typical modeled values are approximately -1000 to 1000 m.s^-1 in edge and scrape-off-layer transport studies, while core effective poloidal convection coefficients are often closer to -100 to 100 m.s^-1 depending on magnetic geometry, collisionality, turbulence, and source localization.
NAMES.sign: Positive when electron particle convection is directed toward increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in the flux coordinate system $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_electron_velocity
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Poloidal component of the electron bulk flow velocity.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal electron velocity $v_{\theta,e}$ is the component of the electron fluid bulk velocity tangent to magnetic flux surfaces in the poloidal direction. In flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, it measures electron flow along increasing or decreasing poloidal angle $\theta$, distinct from the radial component across flux surfaces and the toroidal component around the symmetry axis. It is the electron analog of [poloidal_ion_velocity](name:poloidal_ion_velocity) and complements [radial_electron_velocity](name:radial_electron_velocity), [toroidal_electron_velocity](name:toroidal_electron_velocity), and [parallel_electron_velocity](name:parallel_electron_velocity).

The poloidal component is the projection of the electron fluid mean velocity onto the poloidal unit vector:

$$
v_{\theta,e} = \hat{\mathbf{e}}_\theta \cdot \mathbf{u}_e, \qquad \mathbf{u}_e = \frac{1}{n_e}\int \mathbf{v}\, f_e(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v},t)\, d^3v
$$

where $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_\theta$ is the dimensionless unit vector in the direction of increasing $\theta$, $\mathbf{u}_e$ and $v_{\theta,e}$ are in m.s^-1, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity in m.s^-1, $f_e$ is the electron velocity-space distribution such that $\int f_e\,d^3v=n_e$, and $n_e$ is the electron density in m^-3.

In practice, $v_{\theta,e}$ is computed from kinetic or fluid models by projecting the electron mean flow onto the poloidal basis, or inferred from force-balance and transport constraints using measured density, temperature, electric-field, and current information. In the edge and scrape-off layer it may also be constrained by probe-based flow measurements and by decomposing parallel flow into poloidal and toroidal projections.

Typical magnitudes are commonly in the range 10^3-10^5 m.s^-1, depending on collisionality, pressure gradients, electric fields, magnetic geometry, and proximity to the separatrix.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the electron fluid poloidal flow is directed toward increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in the flux coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_ion_convection_velocity
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Poloidal component, in the flux-coordinate system (rho, theta, phi), of the effective advective (convection) velocity that transports the total ion particle density of an ion species, summed over its charge states. It is a physical linear speed tangent to the poloidal direction, not a contravariant coordinate rate.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal ion convection velocity is the projection onto the poloidal tangent direction of the effective non-diffusive (advective) velocity that carries the total ion particle density of an ion species in the flux-coordinate system $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$, where $\rho$ labels flux surfaces, $\theta$ is the poloidal angle, and $\phi$ is the toroidal angle. It is a true physical velocity component expressed in $\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ along the poloidal tangent, not a contravariant angular coordinate rate. When several charge states of the same element are present, this is the species-level aggregate that sums over all charge states, in contrast to the charge-state-resolved analog [poloidal_ion_state_convection_velocity](name:poloidal_ion_state_convection_velocity).

The species-level convection velocity is fixed by requiring the species convective flux to equal the sum of the charge-state convective fluxes:

$$
v_{\theta,i}^{\mathrm{conv}} = \frac{\sum_{\zeta} n_{i,\zeta}\, v_{\theta,i,\zeta}^{\mathrm{conv}}}{\sum_{\zeta} n_{i,\zeta}}
$$

where $v_{\theta,i}^{\mathrm{conv}}$ is the species-level poloidal convection velocity, $n_{i,\zeta}$ is the density of charge state $\zeta$, $v_{\theta,i,\zeta}^{\mathrm{conv}}$ is the corresponding charge-state-resolved convection velocity, and the total ion density is $n_i = \sum_{\zeta} n_{i,\zeta}$. The ratio is physically meaningful where $n_i$ is nonzero.

This quantity is a derived transport coefficient rather than a directly measured flow: it is the advective (pinch-like) part of the poloidal ion particle flux $\Gamma_{\theta,i}^{\mathrm{conv}} = n_i\, v_{\theta,i}^{\mathrm{conv}}$, distinct from the bulk poloidal ion fluid flow [poloidal_ion_velocity](name:poloidal_ion_velocity). It is estimated by particle-balance inversions, reduced transport closures, or edge fluid and kinetic simulations that separate the non-diffusive part of the poloidal particle flux and divide by the appropriate ion density. Spectroscopic or probe-measured poloidal flows can constrain the calculation but need not equal this effective transport coefficient.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the effective ion particle convection is directed toward increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in the flux-coordinate system $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_ion_momentum_damping_rate
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Rate coefficient for relaxation of the bulk ion fluid momentum component along the poloidal-angle direction θ on magnetic flux surfaces in flux coordinates (ρ, θ, φ).
NAMES.long:
The poloidal ion momentum damping rate is the coefficient for collisional or neoclassical relaxation of the bulk ion fluid momentum component tangent to a magnetic surface in the poloidal-angle direction. The direction is the increasing $\theta$ direction in a flux-coordinate system $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$, with $\phi$ the toroidal angle of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height. This bulk-ion quantity describes the ion population as a whole, rather than one charge state.

A linear damping contribution to the poloidal momentum density may be written as

$$
\left.\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\left(n_i m_i u_{\theta,i}\right)\right|_{\mathrm{damp}} = -\nu_{\theta,i}\, n_i m_i u_{\theta,i}
$$

where $n_i$ is the ion number density, $m_i$ is the ion mass, $u_{\theta,i}$ is the bulk ion velocity component along increasing $\theta$, and $\nu_{\theta,i}$ is the poloidal ion momentum damping rate. The displayed term represents only the local linear relaxation part of a full momentum balance; sources, stresses, inertia, and radial transport can also contribute.

The rate is usually obtained from neoclassical transport theory, reduced momentum-balance modeling, or fits constrained by measured ion rotation and plasma profiles. It depends on collisionality, magnetic geometry, trapped-particle fraction, species composition, temperature, density, and the reference flow about which the momentum perturbation is damped. The charge-state-resolved counterpart is [poloidal_ion_state_momentum_damping_rate](name:poloidal_ion_state_momentum_damping_rate); related component rates are [toroidal_ion_momentum_damping_rate](name:toroidal_ion_momentum_damping_rate) and [radial_ion_momentum_damping_rate](name:radial_ion_momentum_damping_rate).

Representative values in core tokamak transport applications are about 10^2-10^6 s^-1, with lower values typical of hotter, weakly collisional regions and higher values possible in colder or more collisional regions. The range is order-of-magnitude only and should be interpreted relative to local collision, transit, and transport timescales.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the linear term acts to relax, rather than amplify, a perturbation of the poloidal bulk ion momentum.

NAMES.name: poloidal_ion_particle_flux
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Poloidal component of the net ion particle-flux density, giving the number of ions crossing unit area per unit time in the poloidal direction. It is summed over all ion charge states for the ion population considered.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal ion particle flux is the signed component of the net ion particle-flux density along the unit vector tangent to increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$. It represents particle transport around a magnetic flux surface, through a surface whose normal is poloidal, after summing over all charge states of the ion population considered.

For charge-state-resolved ion fluxes, the poloidal component is the projection of the summed particle-flux density onto the poloidal direction:

$$
\Gamma_{i,\mathrm{pol}} = \sum_z \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{i,z}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{e}}_\theta = \sum_z n_{i,z}\,\mathbf{v}_{i,z}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{e}}_\theta = n_i\,\bar{\mathbf{v}}_i\cdot\hat{\mathbf{e}}_\theta
$$

where $z$ labels ion charge state, $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_\theta$ is the unit vector toward increasing $\theta$, $\Gamma_{i,\mathrm{pol}}$ and $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{i,z}$ are in m^-2 s^-1, $n_{i,z}$ and $n_i$ are in m^-3, $\mathbf{v}_{i,z}$ and $\bar{\mathbf{v}}_i$ are in m s^-1, $n_i=\sum_z n_{i,z}$, and $\bar{\mathbf{v}}_i$ is the density-weighted mean ion velocity over charge states.

In practice this quantity is inferred from ion density and flow measurements together with transport analysis, or computed in fluid, kinetic, or hybrid plasma models from the ion continuity and momentum balance. Charge-state-resolved contributions may be obtained from collisional-radiative or impurity-transport modeling and then summed to form the net ion particle flux.

Typical absolute magnitudes are about 10^19-10^21 m^-2 s^-1 in weakly flowing core regions, 10^21-10^23 m^-2 s^-1 near the pedestal or scrape-off layer, and can approach 10^24 m^-2 s^-1 in strong divertor or transient flows.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the net charge-state-summed ion particle flux is directed toward increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_ion_state_diffusion_coefficient
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Poloidal particle diffusivity, also called a diffusion coefficient, for a specified ion charge state in edge plasma. It relates the diffusive particle flux along poloidal arclength to the charge-state density gradient.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal ion-state diffusion coefficient is the scalar transport coefficient for density-gradient-driven particle diffusion of a specified ion species in a specified charge state along the poloidal direction. It represents the diffusive part of particle mixing around magnetic flux surfaces and is distinct from convective, source, sink, or radial transport terms.

The Fickian contribution to the poloidal particle flux is commonly written:

$$
\Gamma_{\theta,i,q}^{\mathrm{diff}} = -D_{\theta,i,q}\,\frac{\partial n_{i,q}}{\partial l_\theta}
$$

where $\Gamma_{\theta,i,q}^{\mathrm{diff}}$ is the poloidal diffusive particle flux of ion species $i$ in charge state $q$ in $m^{-2}\,s^{-1}$, $D_{\theta,i,q}$ is the poloidal diffusion coefficient in $m^2\,s^{-1}$, $n_{i,q}$ is the charge-state density in $m^{-3}$, and $l_\theta$ is poloidal arclength in meters. The leading minus sign means that a positive diffusivity drives particles from higher density toward lower density along the poloidal path.

In practice this coefficient is inferred or prescribed in edge transport modeling from particle balance, impurity or main-ion density evolution, comparison with spectroscopic and probe measurements, or reduced descriptions of turbulent and collisional cross-field mixing. It is often an effective coefficient that may combine unresolved turbulent transport with collisional contributions for the selected charge state.

Typical effective edge and scrape-off-layer values are about 0.1-10 m^2.s^-1, with smaller values possible for nearly neoclassical transport and larger values in strongly turbulent or transient boundary-plasma conditions. As a scalar diffusivity it is normally non-negative; fitted negative values usually indicate limitations of a reduced transport model or missing off-diagonal transport terms rather than physical diffusion.

NAMES.name: poloidal_ion_state_momentum_damping_rate
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Reciprocal of the relaxation time for collisional or neoclassical damping of the poloidal momentum of a specified ion species and charge state. The poloidal component is tangent to a magnetic flux surface in the meridional plane of the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) system and points along increasing theta in explicit flux coordinates such as (rho, theta, phi).
NAMES.long:
Poloidal ion-state momentum damping rate is the reciprocal of the relaxation time over which the poloidal momentum of a specified ion species and charge state is dissipated. The poloidal component is tangent to a magnetic flux surface in the meridional $(R, Z)$ plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ system, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height; equivalently it is the component along increasing $\theta$ in an explicitly specified flux coordinate system such as $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$ at fixed $\rho$ and $\phi$.

In a local momentum-density balance, the damping contribution is represented as a linear relaxation term:

$$
\left(\frac{\partial p_{\theta,a}}{\partial t}\right)_\mathrm{damp} = -\nu_{\theta,a}\, p_{\theta,a}
$$

where $a$ labels the ion charge state, $\nu_{\theta,a}$ is the damping rate, and $p_{\theta,a} = m_a n_a V_{\theta,a}$ is the poloidal momentum density with $m_a$ in kg, $n_a$ in m$^{-3}$, and $V_{\theta,a}$ in m s$^{-1}$. The minus sign makes the term dissipative: a non-negative $\nu_{\theta,a}$ relaxes the existing poloidal momentum toward zero regardless of its sign.

This rate is typically obtained from collisional and neoclassical momentum-balance models, or inferred by fitting observed poloidal-flow relaxation to such a balance. It depends on charge state, ion mass and charge, density, temperature, magnetic geometry, collisionality, and coupling to other species through Coulomb friction and poloidal viscous stresses. Charge-state resolution matters for impurity species occupying several ionization stages simultaneously, each carrying a distinct damping coefficient; the species-summed counterpart is the poloidal ion momentum damping rate.

As an order-of-magnitude guide, hot, weakly collisional core conditions tend to give values near $10^2$-$10^5$ s$^{-1}$, while cooler, denser, more collisional edge conditions and high-charge states can reach $10^5$-$10^7$ s$^{-1}$; these ranges are contextual rather than canonical.

NAMES.name: poloidal_ion_state_velocity
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Poloidal component of the bulk fluid velocity for ions in a specified ionization charge state, projecting the charge-state-resolved mean flow onto the poloidal direction.
NAMES.long:
The poloidal component $v_{\theta,z}$ of the mean fluid velocity for ions in a resolved ionization charge state $z$, obtained by projecting the full [ion_state_velocity](name:ion_state_velocity) vector onto the poloidal direction. In a multi-fluid plasma model, each charge state of an ion species carries its own independent velocity field; the poloidal component can differ substantially between charge states owing to neoclassical friction, charge-dependent transport forces, and orbit effects at the plasma edge.

The poloidal velocity of charge state $z$ enters the radial force balance:

$$
E_r = \frac{1}{Z_z e n_z} \frac{\partial p_z}{\partial r} - v_{\theta,z} B_\phi + v_{\phi,z} B_\theta
$$

where $E_r$ is the radial electric field, $Z_z$ is the ion charge number, $e$ is the elementary charge, $n_z$ is the number density of charge state $z$, $p_z$ is its pressure, $B_\phi$ is the toroidal magnetic field, $B_\theta$ is the poloidal magnetic field, and $v_{\phi,z}$ is the [toroidal_ion_state_velocity](name:toroidal_ion_state_velocity). This coupling links poloidal rotation to measurable pressure gradients and toroidal flow for each charge state.

Poloidal ion velocities are measured by charge exchange recombination spectroscopy (CXRS), resolving Doppler shifts of charge-exchange emission lines in the poloidal viewing direction. The charge-state-averaged counterpart is [poloidal_ion_velocity](name:poloidal_ion_velocity). Typical magnitudes range from tens of meters per second to tens of kilometers per second, depending on ion species, charge state, and radial location.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the ion flow is directed in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_ion_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Poloidal component of the diamagnetic drift velocity for a specific ion charge state, arising from the cross-product of that state's partial pressure gradient with the magnetic field.
NAMES.long:
The diamagnetic drift velocity arises when a pressure gradient perpendicular to the magnetic field drives a fluid-like flow across field lines in a magnetized plasma. This quantity gives the scalar projection of that drift onto the poloidal direction $\hat{\theta}$ for a resolved ion charge state, contributing to net poloidal fluid rotation and cross-field transport in the edge and core plasma.

For an ion charge state with partial pressure $p_s = n_s k_B T_s$, the diamagnetic drift velocity vector is defined as:

$$
\mathbf{v}_{dia} = -\frac{\nabla p_s \times \mathbf{B}}{Z_s e n_s B^2}
$$

where $Z_s$ is the charge number of the state, $e$ is the elementary charge, $n_s$ is the ion charge state number density, $T_s$ is the temperature, and $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field vector with magnitude $B$. The poloidal component is the scalar $v_{dia,\theta} = \mathbf{v}_{dia} \cdot \hat{\theta}$.

This quantity is computed in multi-fluid transport models rather than measured directly; charge-state resolution is important for accurately representing impurity contributions in edge plasmas. The full drift vector is described by [ion_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:ion_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift), and the complementary projections are [toroidal_ion_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:toroidal_ion_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift) and [radial_ion_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:radial_ion_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift). The analogous quantity for neutral species charge states is [poloidal_neutral_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:poloidal_neutral_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the drift velocity points in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_momentum_effective_convection_velocity
NAMES.short: Effective radial convection velocity for transport of aggregate ion poloidal momentum across magnetic flux surfaces. It is the velocity-like coefficient of the convective, or pinch, term rather than the poloidal flow speed itself.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal momentum effective convection velocity is the velocity-like coefficient that represents radial advection of aggregate ion poloidal momentum across magnetic flux surfaces. It is a transport coefficient in the momentum balance, not the poloidal flow speed itself, and no additional moment-arm or angular-momentum normalization is implied.

The coefficient is defined by the convective term in a diffusion-convection decomposition of the radial flux of poloidal ion momentum:

$$
\Pi_{\theta,r} = -D_\theta \frac{\partial (m_i n_i v_\theta)}{\partial r} + V_\theta^{\mathrm{eff}} m_i n_i v_\theta
$$

where $V_\theta^{\mathrm{eff}}$ is this quantity in $m.s^{-1}$, $\Pi_{\theta,r}$ is the radial flux of poloidal momentum in $kg.m^{-1}.s^{-2}$, $D_\theta$ is the poloidal momentum diffusivity in $m^2.s^{-1}$, $m_i$ is ion mass in $kg$, $n_i$ is ion number density in $m^{-3}$, $v_\theta$ is poloidal flow speed in $m.s^{-1}$, and $r$ is a minor-radius-like radial label in meters increasing outward across the flux surfaces. The component $\theta$ is the poloidal direction in flux coordinates $(r,\theta,\phi)$, where $\theta$ is poloidal angle and $\phi$ is toroidal angle. For multiple ion species or charge states, $m_i n_i v_\theta$ denotes the aggregate ion poloidal momentum density used in the balance.

In practice, this coefficient is specified by a transport closure or inferred by fitting an evaluated radial poloidal-momentum flux to a chosen diffusive-convective form. The split between diffusion and convection is meaningful only after the transported momentum density, radial label, and diffusivity convention have been fixed. This aggregate-ion quantity has the same physical role as poloidal_ion_momentum_convection_velocity, while [poloidal_ion_state_momentum_convection_velocity](name:poloidal_ion_state_momentum_convection_velocity) denotes the corresponding charge-state-resolved coefficient; related component analogs include toroidal_ion_momentum_convection_velocity and [parallel_momentum_effective_convection_velocity](name:parallel_momentum_effective_convection_velocity).

Representative magnitudes are strongly model- and regime-dependent. In core momentum-transport studies the magnitude is often of order 0-10 m.s^-1, while fitted edge, pedestal, or transient coefficients can reach several tens of m.s^-1; either sign is possible depending on whether the effective convective transport is outward or inward.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the effective convective transport of poloidal momentum is radially outward, from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: poloidal_neutral_energy_diffusion_coefficient
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Poloidal-direction diffusion coefficient governing the diffusive transport of neutral particle thermal energy in the edge plasma.
NAMES.long:
The poloidal neutral energy diffusion coefficient $D_\mathrm{pol}$ quantifies how neutral particle thermal energy spreads in the poloidal direction through diffusive processes in the edge plasma and scrape-off layer. It is the poloidal projection of the full [neutral_energy_diffusion_coefficient](name:neutral_energy_diffusion_coefficient), isolating the poloidal directional contribution from the general tensor in the anisotropic geometry of the divertor region.

The neutral energy transport equation relates the poloidal diffusive energy flux $q^\mathrm{E}_\mathrm{pol}$ to the local gradient of thermal energy density through:

$$
q^\mathrm{E}_\mathrm{pol} = -D_\mathrm{pol} \, \nabla_\mathrm{pol} w_n
$$

where $w_n = \tfrac{3}{2} n_n T_n$ is the neutral thermal energy density, $n_n$ is the neutral particle number density, and $T_n$ is the neutral temperature.

This coefficient is computed within neutral transport models that resolve atomic and molecular processes in the divertor and scrape-off layer, ranging from fluid moment closures to kinetic Monte Carlo treatments of neutral atoms and molecules.

The particle-transport (not energy) counterpart is [poloidal_neutral_diffusion_coefficient](name:poloidal_neutral_diffusion_coefficient). The charge-state-resolved energy analog is [poloidal_neutral_state_energy_diffusion_coefficient](name:poloidal_neutral_state_energy_diffusion_coefficient), and the equivalent quantity for ion species is [poloidal_ion_energy_diffusion_coefficient](name:poloidal_ion_energy_diffusion_coefficient).

NAMES.name: poloidal_neutral_particle_flux
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Poloidal component of the total neutral particle flux density, summed over all neutral species and internal states, giving the net number of neutrals crossing a unit surface area per unit time in the poloidal direction in the edge plasma.
NAMES.long:
The poloidal neutral particle flux density is the poloidal projection of the total [neutral_particle_flux](name:neutral_particle_flux) vector, integrated over all neutral species and internal atomic or molecular states. It quantifies the net flow of neutral atoms and molecules per unit area per unit time along the poloidal direction, and is the species-integrated counterpart to [poloidal_neutral_state_particle_flux](name:poloidal_neutral_state_particle_flux), which resolves the same quantity for a single specified neutral internal state.

The quantity appears in the neutral particle continuity equation:

$$
\frac{\partial n_n}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_n = S_n
$$

where $n_n$ is the neutral number density, $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_n$ is the neutral particle flux vector, and $S_n$ is the net source density from ionization, recombination, and charge exchange. The poloidal component $\Gamma_{n,\theta} = \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_n \cdot \hat{e}_\theta$ drives neutral transport along the poloidal angle $\theta$.

In the edge plasma, strong poloidal neutral flows arise from recycling at plasma-facing components, charge-exchange momentum transfer with ions, and ionization sinks near the target plates. This flux component is computed within neutral fluid or kinetic transport models covering the scrape-off layer and divertor. The companion quantity [poloidal_neutral_momentum_flux](name:poloidal_neutral_momentum_flux) captures poloidal transport of momentum carried by the same neutral population.
NAMES.sign: Positive when neutrals flow in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_neutral_state_convection_velocity
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: Poloidal component of the effective convection velocity for particle transport of a specified neutral atomic or molecular state. It is the signed advective speed along the poloidal angle in the flux-coordinate system (rho, theta, phi), distinct from species-summed neutral convection and from radial transport.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal neutral state convection velocity is the state-resolved advective speed that multiplies the density of one neutral atomic or molecular state in the poloidal particle flux. It describes directed transport along the poloidal coordinate $\theta$ in flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, separate from radial transport and from the species-summed [poloidal neutral species convection velocity](name:poloidal_neutral_species_convection_velocity). The corresponding energy-transport quantity is [poloidal neutral state energy convection velocity](name:poloidal_neutral_state_energy_convection_velocity).

The convective contribution to the poloidal particle flux density is defined by:

$$
\Gamma_{\theta,a}^{\mathrm{conv}} = n_a\,v_{\theta,a}^{\mathrm{conv}}
$$

where $a$ labels the specified neutral state, $\Gamma_{\theta,a}^{\mathrm{conv}}$ is the convective poloidal particle flux density in $\mathrm{m}^{-2}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, $n_a$ is the neutral-state number density in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, and $v_{\theta,a}^{\mathrm{conv}}$ is the poloidal convection velocity in $\mathrm{m.s}^{-1}$.

In transport modeling, this velocity is usually an effective coefficient inferred from the ratio of poloidal advective particle flux to state density after separating diffusive, source, and sink contributions. It may be constrained by neutral density, emission, and particle-balance measurements, or computed from kinetic or fluid neutral-transport closures; it should not be interpreted automatically as the ballistic speed of individual neutral particles.

Representative modeled magnitudes are strongly regime- and closure-dependent. Values may be close to 0 m.s^-1 where poloidal neutral advection is weak, while effective coefficients of order 1-100 m.s^-1 are common scales used to characterize modest poloidal redistribution; larger local values should be checked against the defining flux-to-density ratio rather than treated as universal typical behavior.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $v_{\theta,a}^{\mathrm{conv}}$ points in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ at fixed $\rho$ and $\phi$ in the flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_neutral_state_energy_convection_velocity
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: Physical poloidal component, along increasing theta in the flux-coordinate system (rho, theta, phi), of the effective energy convection velocity for a specific neutral species state.
NAMES.long:
The poloidal neutral state energy convection velocity is the physical velocity component that advects thermal energy of a specific neutral species state in the poloidal direction. It is the metric velocity along increasing $\theta$ in the flux-coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, not the angular coordinate rate $d\theta/dt$.

In a state-resolved neutral energy balance, the convective contribution to the poloidal energy flux density is represented by

$$
Q_\theta^{\mathrm{conv}} = v_{E,\theta}\,\mathcal{E}
$$

where $Q_\theta^{\mathrm{conv}}$ is the physical poloidal convective energy flux density in W m$^{-2}$, $v_{E,\theta}$ is this energy convection velocity in m s$^{-1}$, and $\mathcal{E}$ is the thermal-energy density of the neutral state in J m$^{-3}$.

The quantity is usually obtained from neutral transport modeling or from balance analysis that separates particle, momentum, and energy transport channels. It is distinct from the particle-transport velocity [poloidal_neutral_state_convection_velocity](name:poloidal_neutral_state_convection_velocity), because energy convection weights the motion by the transported thermal energy rather than by particle number alone.

Representative effective magnitudes in edge and divertor neutral-transport applications are often about $10^2$-$10^4$ m s$^{-1}$, but the value is strongly model dependent and may differ from the microscopic thermal speed when sources, sinks, charge exchange, ionization, recombination, and state-to-state energy redistribution are included.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the physical velocity component points in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in the flux-coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_neutral_state_energy_diffusion_coefficient
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: Effective poloidal diffusivity for energy transport of neutral particles in a specified state.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal neutral-state energy diffusion coefficient is the effective diffusivity multiplying the poloidal gradient of neutral energy density for particles in a specified neutral state. In this context, diffusion coefficient and diffusivity denote the same physical transport coefficient, with dimensions of area per time.

For a Fickian closure in a flux-coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, the poloidal neutral-energy flux density may be written as

$$
q_{E,\theta}^{(n,s)} = -D_{E,\theta}^{(n,s)}\,\frac{1}{h_\theta}\frac{\partial U_E^{(n,s)}}{\partial \theta}
$$

where $q_{E,\theta}^{(n,s)}$ is the poloidal neutral-energy flux density in W m$^{-2}$, $D_{E,\theta}^{(n,s)}$ is this diffusion coefficient in m$^2$ s$^{-1}$, $U_E^{(n,s)}$ is the neutral energy density in J m$^{-3}$, $h_\theta$ is the poloidal metric scale factor in meters, and $(n,s)$ identifies the neutral species and state. The flux component $q_{E,\theta}^{(n,s)}$ is positive in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$; the minus sign means that, for positive $D_{E,\theta}^{(n,s)}$, energy diffuses down the poloidal energy-density gradient.

This coefficient is usually not measured directly. It is inferred or prescribed in neutral transport modeling from collisional mean-free-path estimates, kinetic or fluid neutral calculations, and calibration against measurements sensitive to neutral energy transport, such as neutral pressure, emission, and edge power-balance constraints.

Typical effective values are broad because neutral mean free paths vary strongly with ionization, charge exchange, and wall recycling conditions. Dense, cold divertor or limiter regions may use about $10^{-3}$-$1$ m$^2$ s$^{-1}$, while more weakly collisional edge or scrape-off-layer conditions may require about $1$-$10^{2}$ m$^2$ s$^{-1}$. Negative values are not expected for a physically diffusive diagonal coefficient; they would represent an anti-diffusive model closure rather than ordinary diffusion.

NAMES.name: poloidal_neutral_state_energy_flux
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: Poloidal component of the energy flux density carried by neutral particles in a specified internal state, along increasing theta in flux coordinates (rho, theta, phi).
NAMES.long:
The poloidal neutral state energy flux is the signed component of the energy-flux density of neutral particles in a specified internal quantum state along the poloidal direction in flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, where $\rho$ labels flux surfaces, $\theta$ is poloidal angle, and $\phi$ is toroidal angle. It is the state-resolved contribution to [poloidal_neutral_energy_flux](name:poloidal_neutral_energy_flux) and includes advected thermal enthalpy, directed bulk kinetic energy, internal-state energy, and non-advective heat flow.

A common fluid decomposition for state $s$ writes the poloidal component $Q_{\theta,s}$ as:

$$
Q_{\theta,s} = h_s\Gamma_{\theta,s} + \frac{1}{2}m_s|\mathbf{v}_s|^2\Gamma_{\theta,s} + \epsilon_s\Gamma_{\theta,s} + q_{\theta,s}
$$

where $\Gamma_{\theta,s}=n_s v_{\theta,s}$ is the [poloidal_neutral_state_particle_flux](name:poloidal_neutral_state_particle_flux) in $\mathrm{m^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$, $n_s$ is number density in $\mathrm{m^{-3}}$, $v_{\theta,s}$ is the poloidal bulk velocity component in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $\mathbf{v}_s$ is the bulk velocity vector in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $m_s$ is particle mass in kg, $h_s$ is thermal enthalpy per neutral particle in joules, $\epsilon_s$ is the internal energy assigned to state $s$ in joules, and $q_{\theta,s}$ is the non-advective heat-flux component along $\theta$ in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$. The kinetic-energy factor uses the total bulk speed; the poloidal projection enters through $\Gamma_{\theta,s}$. Each term on the right-hand side has units of $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$.

This quantity is usually inferred from transport analysis rather than measured directly. Neutral fluid, kinetic, or Monte Carlo descriptions compute it from state-resolved density, temperature or enthalpy, velocity, internal-state population energy, and a heat-flow closure; spectroscopy, neutral pressure measurements, calorimetry, and recycling or charge-exchange constraints can provide input information. It is used with [poloidal_neutral_state_energy_convection_velocity](name:poloidal_neutral_state_energy_convection_velocity) to distinguish advective energy transport from the total flux including heat flow.

Typical absolute values in tokamak edge and divertor neutral populations are about $10^0-10^7\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$. Cold, diffuse neutral gas often lies near the lower end, while recycling, charge-exchange, or fast molecular and atomic populations in high-power edge regions can approach the upper end.
NAMES.sign: Positive when neutral-state energy is transported in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_neutral_state_momentum_diffusion_coefficient
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: State-resolved kinematic coefficient for poloidal diffusion of neutral-particle flow momentum, in the direction of increasing poloidal angle theta in flux coordinates (rho, theta, phi). It relates the diffusive poloidal momentum flux of neutrals occupying a specified internal state to the local gradient of their poloidal flow velocity.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal neutral-state momentum diffusion coefficient is the state-resolved kinematic transport coefficient for redistribution of poloidal bulk-flow momentum carried by neutral particles. It applies to neutrals in a specified internal electronic, vibrational, or metastable state and represents the effective spreading of their poloidal flow by collisions, charge exchange, and closure approximations. The positive poloidal direction is the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, with $\phi$ the toroidal angle of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

A local Fickian closure for the diffusive flux of poloidal momentum can be written as:

$$
\Pi_{\theta,\alpha}^{\mathrm{diff}} = - m_\alpha n_\alpha D_{\theta,\alpha}^{\mathrm{mom}} \nabla_\theta u_{\theta,\alpha}
$$

where $\alpha$ labels the neutral internal state, $D_{\theta,\alpha}^{\mathrm{mom}}$ is this coefficient in m^2.s^-1, $m_\alpha$ is the particle mass in kg, $n_\alpha$ is the state density in m^-3, $u_{\theta,\alpha}$ is the poloidal flow velocity in m.s^-1, $\nabla_\theta$ is the derivative per meter along increasing $\theta$, and $\Pi_{\theta,\alpha}^{\mathrm{diff}}$ is the corresponding momentum flux. For slowly varying density, a positive coefficient smooths the poloidal momentum density $m_\alpha n_\alpha u_{\theta,\alpha}$ by driving flux from larger toward smaller poloidal flow velocity. It is the poloidal counterpart of the [toroidal_neutral_state_momentum_diffusion_coefficient](name:toroidal_neutral_state_momentum_diffusion_coefficient) and the state-resolved analog of the species-summed [poloidal_neutral_momentum_diffusion_coefficient](name:poloidal_neutral_momentum_diffusivity).

This coefficient is usually obtained from neutral transport modeling rather than measured directly. It may be estimated from kinetic or fluid neutral calculations using elastic scattering, charge-exchange, ionization, and state-changing collision rates, or adjusted as an effective closure parameter to reproduce observed neutral flows and momentum exchange.

Typical effective values are 0.01-10 m^2.s^-1 for cold, highly collisional edge or divertor neutrals, 10-1000 m^2.s^-1 for warmer charge-exchange-coupled neutrals in the scrape-off layer, and can exceed 1000 m^2.s^-1 when long-mean-free-path neutral motion is represented by a diffusive closure. Values may be near zero where the population of the specified neutral state is negligible.
NAMES.sign: Positive when a positive gradient of the neutral-state poloidal flow velocity along increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ produces a diffusive poloidal momentum flux in the negative poloidal direction.

NAMES.name: poloidal_neutral_state_velocity
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: Poloidal component of the bulk fluid velocity for neutral particles in a specified internal quantum or energy state.
NAMES.long:
The poloidal neutral state velocity is the projection of the [neutral_state_velocity](name:neutral_state_velocity) onto the poloidal direction, giving the mean poloidal convective motion of neutral particles occupying a specific internal quantum, excitation, or energy state. As a fluid moment of the state-resolved neutral distribution function, it captures directed poloidal transport for that neutral population rather than random thermal speeds.

The quantity is defined by projecting the state-resolved neutral bulk flow vector $\mathbf{v}_s$ onto the poloidal unit vector $\hat{\theta}$:

$$
v_{\theta,s} = \mathbf{v}_s \cdot \hat{\theta}
$$

where $s$ labels the internal quantum or energy state and $\hat{\theta}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in the flux coordinate system $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$.

State-resolved poloidal velocities are particularly relevant in edge and divertor plasma modeling, where neutrals in distinct quantum or energy states participate in charge-exchange, ionization, and momentum-exchange processes at state-specific rates, producing different effective flow velocities for each state. The species-summed analog [poloidal_neutral_velocity](name:poloidal_neutral_velocity) integrates over all neutral states, while [poloidal_ion_state_velocity](name:poloidal_ion_state_velocity) provides the equivalent charge-state-resolved quantity for ions. The related [poloidal_neutral_state_momentum_convection_velocity](name:poloidal_neutral_state_momentum_convection_velocity) captures the effective advective velocity governing momentum transport for the same state.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $v_{\theta,s}$ is directed in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in the flux coordinate system $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_neutral_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: Poloidal component of the effective E cross B drift velocity assigned to a neutral species in a specified quantum state, projected along increasing poloidal angle theta in flux coordinates (rho, theta, phi).
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the component along the local poloidal direction of the effective E×B advection velocity associated with a neutral species in a specified quantum state. The poloidal direction is the local tangent to increasing $\theta$ in a specified flux-coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, with $\phi$ the toroidal angle of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height. Because a neutral particle is not directly accelerated by the Lorentz force, this is an effective convective contribution assigned to the neutral-state population rather than a single-particle electromagnetic drift; it is the poloidal component of [neutral_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift](name:neutral_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift).

The component is obtained by projecting the electric-field drift velocity onto the poloidal unit vector:

$$
v_{E,\theta} = \hat{\mathbf{e}}_\theta \cdot \frac{\mathbf{E} \times \mathbf{B}}{B^2}
$$

where $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_\theta$ is the unit vector tangent to increasing $\theta$ at fixed radial flux coordinate and fixed $\phi$, $\mathbf{E}$ is the electric field, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field, and $B=|\mathbf{B}|$.

In practice, the value is computed from an electric field or electrostatic-potential gradient together with a magnetic equilibrium, then projected onto the local poloidal unit vector of the chosen flux-coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$. State-resolved neutral transport models may use it to represent advection of neutrals by plasma E×B motion or by collisional coupling to drifting charged species; direct neutral measurements usually constrain the total neutral velocity rather than this separated contribution. The toroidal counterpart is [toroidal_neutral_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift](name:toroidal_neutral_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift), the analogous ion-state component is [poloidal_ion_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift](name:poloidal_ion_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift), and [poloidal_neutral_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:poloidal_neutral_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift) denotes a different poloidal drift contribution for neutral states.

Typical absolute values are model- and region-dependent. For perpendicular electric fields of 0.1-10 kV.m^-1 and magnetic fields of 1-5 T, characteristic electric-drift speeds span about 20-10^4 m.s^-1; the projected neutral-state effective component can be smaller when the neutral population is weakly coupled to plasma motion.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the projected effective $E\times B$ velocity points in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in the flux-coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, whose toroidal coordinate $\phi$ is the toroidal angle of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: poloidal_neutral_velocity
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Poloidal component of the bulk neutral particle fluid velocity. It is the projection of the neutral mean flow onto the poloidal direction on a magnetic surface.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal neutral velocity is the component of the bulk mean velocity of neutral particles along the poloidal direction, i.e. tangent to a magnetic surface in a meridional plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It is one component of the full [neutral velocity](name:neutral_velocity), complementary to the [radial neutral velocity](name:radial_neutral_velocity) and toroidal neutral velocity.

The component is defined by projecting the neutral mean-flow vector onto the local poloidal unit direction:

$$
v_{\theta,n} = \mathbf{v}_n \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}_\theta
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_n$ is the neutral bulk velocity, $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_\theta$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ on the magnetic surface, and $v_{\theta,n}$ is the signed poloidal neutral velocity.

In kinetic terms, the neutral bulk velocity is the first velocity moment of the neutral distribution function divided by the neutral density; in fluid or transport modeling it is obtained from the neutral momentum balance. Experimentally it is inferred indirectly from neutral-particle diagnostics, spectroscopy, or constrained plasma-edge modeling, because neutrals are not tied to magnetic field lines and can have strongly nonlocal sources from recycling, charge exchange, and ionization.

Typical magnitudes are about $10^2-10^4$ m.s$^{-1}$ in edge and divertor regions, with larger values possible where charge-exchange sources, strong pressure gradients, or rapid recycling flows dominate. In the confined core, neutral densities are usually low and the corresponding mean velocity may be poorly constrained.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the neutral mean flow is in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ on the magnetic surface in the right-handed flux-coordinate system $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$, with $\phi$ increasing in the same sense as the toroidal angle of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: poloidal_pfirsch_schlueter_current_density
NAMES.subject: pfirsch_schlueter
NAMES.short: Poloidal projection of the Pfirsch-Schlüter neoclassical current density, arising in toroidal magnetic confinement devices to enforce current continuity by compensating the divergence of the pressure-gradient-driven diamagnetic current.
NAMES.long:
The Pfirsch-Schlüter current is an intrinsic neoclassical current that satisfies $\nabla \cdot \mathbf{j} = 0$ by returning the divergence of the diamagnetic current $\mathbf{j}_{dia} = \mathbf{B} \times \nabla p / B^2$, where $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field and $p$ is the total plasma pressure. This quantity is the projection of that current density vector onto the poloidal direction $\hat{\theta}$, which encircles the magnetic axis in the $(R, Z)$ plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

In large-aspect-ratio circular geometry, the parallel Pfirsch-Schlüter current density is:

$$
j_{PS,\parallel} \approx -\frac{2q}{B_0} \frac{dp}{dr} \cos\theta
$$

where $q$ is the local safety factor, $B_0$ is the on-axis magnetic field magnitude, $r$ is the local minor radius, $p$ is the total pressure, and $\theta$ is the poloidal angle. The poloidal component is obtained by projecting $j_{PS,\parallel}$ onto $\hat{\theta}$ using the local field-line pitch angle.
