This component is computed from neoclassical transport frameworks or MHD equilibrium reconstructions that resolve flux-surface current distributions. Together with the [parallel](name:parallel_pfirsch_schlueter_current_density), [radial](name:radial_pfirsch_schlueter_current_density), [toroidal](name:toroidal_pfirsch_schlueter_current_density), and [vertical](name:vertical_pfirsch_schlueter_current_density) components, it provides a complete decomposition of the Pfirsch-Schlüter current density vector. The associated [diamagnetic component] captures the pressure-driven source that the return current must balance.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the current flows in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ (from the outboard midplane toward the top of the plasma in the poloidal cross-section).

NAMES.name: power_due_to_neutral_beam_shinethrough
NAMES.short: Power carried by neutral beam particles that traverse the plasma without being ionized or otherwise stopped and leave the far plasma boundary. It represents the unabsorbed fraction of launched neutral beam power that is deposited on plasma-facing surfaces rather than in the plasma.
NAMES.long:
Neutral beam shinethrough power is the portion of injected neutral beam power that remains in fast neutral particles after crossing the confined plasma and exits the far side without being absorbed. It is distinct from prompt fast-ion orbit loss after ionization and from power lost before the beam enters the plasma; the absorbed plasma-heating counterpart is power_due_to_neutral_beam_injection.

For beamlets or beam energy components treated independently, a survival-probability model is:

$$
P_{\mathrm{sh}} = \sum_b P_{b,0}\exp\!\left[-\int_{\ell_b} n_e(\ell)\,\sigma_{\mathrm{eff},b}(\ell)\,d\ell\right]
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{sh}}$ is the shinethrough power, $b$ indexes beamlets or beam energy components, $P_{b,0}$ is the launched neutral-beam power contribution for $b$ whose sum is related to [total_power_of_neutral_beam_injector](name:total_power_of_neutral_beam_injector), $\ell$ is distance along the neutral trajectory in m, $n_e(\ell)$ is electron density in m^-3, and $\sigma_{\mathrm{eff},b}(\ell)$ is the effective stopping cross-section in m^2 including ionization and charge-exchange removal of beam neutrals. The exponential factor is the neutral survival probability, so shinethrough decreases rapidly as the line-integrated density or stopping cross-section increases.

In practice, this quantity is computed by tracing neutral beamlets through reconstructed plasma density, temperature, and impurity distributions and integrating the corresponding attenuation along each path. Experimental constraints can come from calorimetry or thermography of shine-through armor, together with accounting of launched and plasma-deposited neutral beam power.

Typical values in high-density heating plasmas are $10^4-10^6$ W for multi-megawatt injectors, often less than 1-5% of launched power. Low-density startup, current ramp-up, very high beam energy, or long tangency paths can raise values to $10^6-10^7$ W, about 10-50% of launched power in unfavorable cases.

NAMES.name: radial_anomalous_current_density
NAMES.short: Radial component of anomalous current density, the cross-field current associated with turbulence-driven charge transport beyond classical and neoclassical collisional contributions. It is signed with respect to the outward radial direction across magnetic flux surfaces.
NAMES.long:
Radial anomalous current density is the component of the turbulence-driven current-density vector normal to magnetic flux surfaces. It represents nonclassical cross-field charge transport, usually interpreted as the part not accounted for by classical collisional and neoclassical mechanisms.

In a flux-coordinate system $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$ with $\rho$ increasing outward from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary, the radial component is defined by projection onto the outward radial unit vector:

$$
j_{\mathrm{anom},\rho} = \mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{anom}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}_\rho
$$

where $j_{\mathrm{anom},\rho}$ is the radial anomalous current density in A m^-2, $\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{anom}}$ is the anomalous current-density vector in A m^-2, and $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_\rho$ is the dimensionless unit vector in the direction of increasing $\rho$.

In practice this quantity is usually obtained from turbulence or transport modeling, from charge-balance constraints, or as a residual after subtracting classical and neoclassical radial current contributions from the total inferred cross-field current. It may also be related to species anomalous particle fluxes through charge-weighted sums, so departures from ambipolar turbulent transport directly affect its value.

Because quasineutral plasmas are nearly ambipolar, flux-surface-averaged core values are often close to zero, with typical modeled magnitudes below 0.01-1 A m^-2. Localized edge, pedestal, scrape-off-layer, or transient turbulent structures can reach about 1-100 A m^-2, with larger short-lived values possible during strong relaxation events.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the anomalous current density points in the direction of increasing $\rho$ in the flux-coordinate system $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$.

NAMES.name: radial_center_of_mass_velocity
NAMES.short: Radial component of the plasma center-of-mass (barycentric) flow velocity, projected along the major-radius direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.
NAMES.long:
The radial center-of-mass velocity is the projection of the barycentric bulk-flow velocity of the multispecies plasma onto the major-radius direction $\hat{R}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the distance from the toroidal symmetry axis. It is the radial component of [center_of_mass_velocity](name:center_of_mass_velocity), which equals total plasma momentum density divided by total mass density.

The quantity is defined as:

$$
v_{R,\text{cm}} = \hat{R} \cdot \frac{\sum_s m_s n_s \mathbf{v}_s}{\sum_s m_s n_s}
$$

where $m_s$ is the particle mass of species $s$, $n_s$ is its number density, and $\mathbf{v}_s$ is its bulk fluid velocity.

Radial flows transport particles and energy across magnetic flux surfaces and are central to cross-field transport in the plasma edge and divertor. In multi-fluid transport models this component is computed directly from the species momentum equations; spectroscopic Doppler measurements of [radial_ion_velocity](name:radial_ion_velocity) and [radial_neutral_velocity](name:radial_neutral_velocity) for individual species, weighted by their respective mass densities, can provide an observational approximation. The analogous projection along the local magnetic field direction is [parallel_center_of_mass_velocity](name:parallel_center_of_mass_velocity).

Typical magnitudes in the plasma edge range from 10 to 1000 m/s, with larger transient values near the separatrix during particle-loss events.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the flow is directed in the $+\hat{R}$ direction, outward toward increasing major radius.

NAMES.name: radial_conductivity
NAMES.short: Radial conductivity is the diagonal radial component of the electrical conductivity tensor. In the cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, it gives the scalar coefficient multiplying the radial electric-field component to form the radial Ohmic current-density contribution, excluding off-diagonal tensor couplings.
NAMES.long:
Radial conductivity is the radial diagonal component $\sigma_R \equiv \sigma_{RR}$ of the electrical conductivity tensor in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ system, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It represents the local radial Ohmic response to the radial electric-field component, not the full tensor response of the plasma.

For the diagonal scalar component, the local constitutive relation is

$$
J_R = \sigma_R E_R
$$

where $J_R$ is the radial current density in $\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}$, $E_R$ is the radial electric field in $\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$, and $\sigma_R$ is the radial conductivity in $\Omega^{-1}\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}$. Off-diagonal tensor contributions such as $\sigma_{R\phi}E_\phi$ or $\sigma_{RZ}E_Z$ are separate conductivity components and are not included in this scalar coefficient.

In practice, radial conductivity is usually a modeled or inferred transport coefficient rather than a directly measured material property. It may be obtained from collisional, neoclassical, turbulent, or edge-closure transport models, or inferred from radial current balance when the radial electric field and non-Ohmic current contributions are independently constrained.

Typical effective values are highly model dependent because cross-field electrical conduction in a magnetized plasma is strongly suppressed compared with parallel conduction. Representative core-to-edge modeling values can span about $10^{-8}$-$10^{2}\ \Omega^{-1}\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}$, with edge, scrape-off-layer, or numerical closure values sometimes lying outside this range.
NAMES.sign: Positive when a positive radial electric-field component $E_R$ in the $+R$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ system produces a radial current-density component $J_R$ in the $+R$ direction.

NAMES.name: radial_current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift
NAMES.short: Radial current density due to diamagnetic drift is the major-radius component of the pressure-gradient-driven diamagnetic current in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It represents current associated with species diamagnetic drifts, not radial bulk particle flow.
NAMES.long:
Radial current density due to diamagnetic drift is the $\hat{R}$ projection of the macroscopic diamagnetic current density caused by cross-field gradients of total scalar plasma pressure. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $R$ is major radius measured from the toroidal symmetry axis, $\phi$ increases counterclockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height. This quantity describes an electrical current associated with opposing ion and electron diamagnetic drifts, not a center-of-mass radial plasma velocity.

The defining relation for a scalar-pressure plasma description is:

$$
j_{\mathrm{dia},R} = \hat{R} \cdot \frac{\mathbf{B} \times \nabla p}{|\mathbf{B}|^2}
$$

where $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field in T, $|\mathbf{B}|$ is its magnitude, $p = \sum_s p_s$ is the total scalar plasma pressure summed over species in Pa, $\nabla p$ is the pressure gradient in Pa m$^{-1}$, and $j_{\mathrm{dia},R}$ is the radial diamagnetic current density in A m$^{-2}$. If a pressure tensor rather than scalar pressure is retained, this scalar expression represents the isotropic-pressure limit.

In practice, this component is evaluated from reconstructed or modeled magnetic fields and pressure gradients, followed by projection onto $\hat{R}$. It is closely related to [radial_diamagnetic_current_density](name:radial_diamagnetic_current_density); [vertical_current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:vertical_current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift) is the corresponding projection along $+\hat{Z}$.

Representative magnitudes are strongly device- and regime-dependent because $|\mathbf{j}_\mathrm{dia}|$ scales approximately as $|\nabla p|/|\mathbf{B}|$. Order-of-magnitude radial components can be below 1 A m$^{-2}$ in weak-gradient regions and can reach 10$^2$-10$^5$ A m$^{-2}$ where pressure gradients are steep; the radial projection may be much smaller than the full diamagnetic current density if the current is nearly tangential to flux surfaces.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the diamagnetic drift current density has a component in the direction of increasing major radius $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: radial_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity
NAMES.short: Radial component of the heat-viscosity-driven current density, projected onto the major-radius direction in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It is the contribution to the plasma current density arising from heat-viscosity terms in fluid transport theory.
NAMES.long:
Radial current density due to heat viscosity is the major-radius component of the current-density contribution generated by heat-viscosity terms in plasma fluid transport theory. The heat-viscosity contribution is the current density associated with the heat-viscosity part of the stress closure in the fluid-moment equations; this quantity is its projection onto the radial direction.

The radial component is obtained by projecting the heat-viscosity current-density contribution onto the major-radius unit vector:

$$
j_{R,\mathrm{hv}} = \mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{hv}} \cdot \hat{R}
$$

where $j_{R,\mathrm{hv}}$ is the radial current density due to heat viscosity, $\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{hv}}$ is the [heat-viscosity current-density contribution](name:current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity), and $\hat{R}$ is the unit vector toward increasing major radius in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

This quantity is evaluated in transport or fluid-moment modeling from the chosen heat-viscosity closure and the local plasma state, then projected along $\hat{R}$. It is not measured directly; estimates are inferred by combining equilibrium geometry with density, temperature, flow, and current-balance information. It is the radial counterpart of the [parallel](name:parallel_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity), [toroidal](name:toroidal_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity), and [vertical](name:vertical_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity) components of the same heat-viscosity current density.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the heat-viscosity current-density contribution points in the direction of increasing major radius $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: radial_current_density_due_to_ion_neutral_friction
NAMES.short: Radial component, along increasing major radius in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, of the electric current density associated with ion-neutral friction.
NAMES.long:
Radial current density due to ion-neutral friction is the major-radius component of the electric current density contribution associated with collisional momentum exchange between plasma ions and neutral atoms or molecules. It describes charge transport produced by ion-neutral drag and the resulting ion momentum balance, not the ion-neutral friction force density itself.

The component is defined by projecting the ion-neutral-friction current-density vector onto the radial unit vector in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height:

$$
j_{R,\mathrm{in}} = \mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{in}} \cdot \hat{R}
$$

where $j_{R,\mathrm{in}}$ is the radial current density in A.m^-2, $\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{in}}$ is the electric current density contribution due to ion-neutral friction in A.m^-2, and $\hat{R}$ is the dimensionless unit vector in the direction of increasing $R$.

In practice this quantity is computed from fluid or kinetic transport models that include ion momentum balance, charge conservation, ion-neutral collision rates, neutral densities, and ion-neutral relative flows. Experimental constraints commonly come from combinations of plasma density and temperature measurements, spectroscopy of neutral and ion populations, and magnetic or electrostatic constraints on current closure.

Typical magnitudes are often about 0.01-100 A.m^-2 in weakly neutral, magnetized edge plasma regions, and can reach 100-10000 A.m^-2 locally in cold, dense, partially ionized boundary or divertor conditions. The value is sensitive to neutral density, ion-neutral collision frequency, plasma magnetization, and the current-closure path.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the current density contribution due to ion-neutral friction points in the direction of increasing major radius $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: radial_current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity
NAMES.short: Radial component of the current density due to perpendicular viscous stress, projected along the major-radius direction in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The radial current density due to perpendicular viscosity is the $\hat{R}$ projection of the plasma current-density contribution associated with the divergence of the perpendicular viscous stress tensor. It represents the part of that viscosity-driven current flowing along increasing or decreasing major radius in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is measured outward from the toroidal symmetry axis.

A component-level definition is

$$
j_R^{(\Pi_\perp)} = \hat{R}\cdot\mathbf{j}^{(\Pi_\perp)}, \qquad (\mathbf{j}^{(\Pi_\perp)}\times\mathbf{B})_\perp \simeq -\left(\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol{\Pi}_\perp\right)_\perp
$$

where $j_R^{(\Pi_\perp)}$ is this radial component in $\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}$, $\mathbf{j}^{(\Pi_\perp)}$ is the current-density contribution attributed to perpendicular viscosity, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field, and $\boldsymbol{\Pi}_\perp$ is the perpendicular viscous stress tensor whose divergence is a force density in $\mathrm{N\,m^{-3}}$. The force-balance relation identifies the part of the current constrained by the perpendicular Lorentz balance; any field-aligned contribution associated with the same stress source is treated separately, for example by [parallel_current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity](name:parallel_current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity).

This quantity is usually computed from a transport or edge-plasma model using a closure for perpendicular viscosity, the magnetic equilibrium, and spatial gradients of flow and pressure. It is not normally measured directly; it is inferred as one term in current balance and can be compared with [radial_current_density_due_to_viscosity](name:radial_current_density_due_to_viscosity), [radial_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity](name:radial_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity), and other contributions to [radial_current_density](name:radial_total_current_density). The related [poloidal_current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity](name:poloidal_current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity) describes the projection of the same viscosity-driven current onto a poloidal direction.

Representative magnitudes are highly regime- and closure-dependent, so there is no universal device-independent range in $\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}$. The value is expected to be near zero where perpendicular viscous stress gradients are weak and can become localized in edge, scrape-off-layer, or strongly sheared-flow regions; interpretation is usually made relative to the total radial current density and to the other modeled current-density channels in the same calculation.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the current flows in the direction of increasing major radius $R$, outward from the toroidal symmetry axis.

NAMES.name: radial_derivative_of_electron_pressure
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: First derivative of electron pressure with respect to normalized toroidal flux radius. It gives the signed outward variation of electron pressure across nested magnetic flux surfaces.
NAMES.long:
The radial derivative of electron pressure is the rate of change of the electron pressure $p_e$ with the normalized toroidal flux radius $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$. It describes how the flux-surface-labeled electron pressure varies from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary and provides the scalar flux-coordinate gradient used in transport balance terms.

The derivative is defined by

$$
\frac{d p_e}{d\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}}
$$

where $p_e$ is the electron pressure in pascals and $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ is dimensionless, with $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}=0$ at the magnetic axis and $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}=1$ at the boundary reference surface. Because the radial coordinate is dimensionless, the derivative has the same unit as pressure, Pa.

In practice this quantity is computed by forming a smooth electron-pressure function on nested flux surfaces and differentiating it with respect to $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$. If pressure is formed from electron density and temperature, use $p_e=n_e T_e$ when $T_e$ is in joules, or equivalently $p_e=e n_e T_e$ when $T_e$ is reported in electronvolts, where $e$ converts electronvolts to joules. The corresponding physical vector gradient is $\nabla p_e = (d p_e/d\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}})\nabla\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$, so conversion to a spatial gradient depends on the flux-coordinate metric.

Typical absolute magnitudes are about $10^3$-$10^5$ Pa in the core of medium-sized tokamaks and can reach $10^5$-$10^6$ Pa in steep pedestals or internal transport barriers. Values depend strongly on density, temperature, confinement regime, and the radial width over which the pressure changes.
NAMES.sign: Positive when electron pressure increases with increasing $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$, i.e., outward from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: radial_derivative_of_fast_ion_density
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: First derivative of the fast (non-thermal) ion number density with respect to the normalized toroidal flux coordinate, summed over all ionic charge states.
NAMES.long:
The radial derivative of fast ion density quantifies how rapidly the non-thermal ion population varies across nested flux surfaces, expressed as the first derivative of [fast_ion_density](name:fast_ion_density) with respect to the normalized toroidal flux coordinate $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$, which runs from 0 at the magnetic axis to 1 at the last closed flux surface. The density is summed over all charge states of the fast ion population, consistent with its parent quantity.

The defining relation is:

$$
\frac{d n_\mathrm{fast}}{d\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}}
$$

where $n_\mathrm{fast}$ is the total fast ion number density aggregated over charge states and $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$ is dimensionless, so the derivative carries the same unit as the density itself.

This gradient appears directly in transport flux expressions and is required by numerical transport solvers to evaluate radial diffusion and convection terms without recomputing the derivative from raw profiles. For core-peaked fast ion distributions, as typically arise from neutral beam injection or fusion-born alpha deposition, the gradient is negative through most of the plasma interior and steepens near the deposition region. The [second_radial_derivative_of_fast_ion_density](name:second_radial_derivative_of_fast_ion_density) captures the curvature of the same profile, while [radial_derivative_of_fast_ion_state_density](name:radial_derivative_of_fast_ion_state_density) provides the equivalent gradient resolved per charge state.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the fast ion density increases in the direction of increasing $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$, i.e., outward from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: radial_derivative_of_fast_ion_state_density
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: First derivative of the fast (non-thermal) ion number density for a specified charge state with respect to normalized toroidal flux radius rho_tor,norm.
NAMES.long:
The radial derivative of fast-ion state density is the change of the number density of non-thermal ions in a specified charge state with respect to the normalized toroidal flux radius $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$. It is the radial-gradient counterpart of [fast_ion_state_density](name:fast_ion_state_density) and is distinct from the charge-state-summed [radial_derivative_of_fast_ion_density](name:radial_derivative_of_fast_ion_density).

It is defined by differentiating the charge-state-resolved fast-ion density with respect to $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$:

$$
g_s(\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}) = \frac{\partial n_{\mathrm{fast},s}}{\partial \rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}}
$$

where $g_s$ is the radial derivative, $n_{\mathrm{fast},s}$ is the fast-ion state density for charge state $s$ in m$^{-3}$, and $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ is the dimensionless normalized toroidal flux radius, with $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}=0$ at the magnetic axis and $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}=1$ at the plasma boundary.

In practice this derivative is computed numerically from charge-state-resolved fast-ion density estimates obtained from fast-ion modeling, transport analysis, or diagnostic-constrained reconstruction. Finite-difference, spline, or other differentiation methods may be used, so the value is sensitive to radial grid resolution, smoothing, and boundary treatment, especially near localized sources, loss regions, or steep transport barriers. It enters gradient-driven transport terms, for example diffusive particle flux contributions proportional to $-D_s\,\partial n_{\mathrm{fast},s}/\partial \rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$, where $D_s$ is an effective diffusivity for charge state $s$.

Typical absolute magnitudes are often $10^{16}$-$10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$ in neutral-beam- or radio-frequency-heated tokamak plasmas, with values approaching $10^{21}$ m$^{-3}$ in sharply localized deposition, ionization, or loss regions. Weakly heated or nearly flat fast-ion populations can have gradients close to zero.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the fast-ion density of the specified charge state increases with increasing normalized toroidal flux radius $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$, outward from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: radial_derivative_of_ion_pressure
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: First radial derivative of total ion pressure with respect to normalized toroidal flux coordinate, summed over all ion charge states.
NAMES.long:
The radial derivative of total [ion_pressure](name:ion_pressure) quantifies how the aggregate ion pressure $P_i$, summed over all charge states, varies across nested flux surfaces. This pressure gradient drives neoclassical and anomalous transport fluxes, contributes to the radial force balance, and appears as a source term in the ion energy transport equation.

The quantity is defined as:

$$
\frac{dP_i}{d\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}}
$$

where $P_i$ is the total ion pressure in Pa and $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$ is the normalized toroidal flux radius, equal to 0 at the magnetic axis and 1 at the separatrix.

In transport solvers, this derivative is evaluated numerically from the ion pressure profile and used in the discretization of the radial transport equations. The [second_radial_derivative_of_ion_pressure](name:second_radial_derivative_of_ion_pressure) complements this quantity for higher-order finite-difference stencils. For charge-state-resolved calculations, the analogous quantity is [radial_derivative_of_ion_state_pressure](name:radial_derivative_of_ion_state_pressure); the electron counterpart is [radial_derivative_of_electron_pressure](name:radial_derivative_of_electron_pressure).

In typical H-mode plasmas the ion pressure peaks at the core and decreases toward the edge, so this derivative takes negative values throughout most of the profile, with the largest magnitudes occurring in the steep pedestal region.
NAMES.sign: Positive when ion pressure increases with increasing normalized toroidal flux coordinate $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$, that is, in the outward direction from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: radial_derivative_of_ion_state_pressure
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: First radial derivative of the thermal pressure of a specified ion charge state with respect to the normalized toroidal flux coordinate, providing the charge-state-resolved pressure gradient for transport equations.
NAMES.long:
The radial pressure gradient of a single ion charge state, quantifying how the charge-state-resolved thermal pressure changes across nested flux surfaces parametrized by the normalized toroidal flux coordinate $\rho_{\rm tor,norm}$, which runs from 0 at the magnetic axis to 1 at the plasma boundary.

The quantity is defined as:

$$
\frac{\partial p_{i,s}}{\partial \rho_{\rm tor,norm}}
$$

where $p_{i,s}$ is the [ion_state_pressure](name:ion_state_pressure) (thermal pressure of ion charge state $s$) and $\rho_{\rm tor,norm}$ is dimensionless, so the derivative retains the unit of pressure.

This gradient is evaluated numerically by transport solvers discretizing the radial transport equations for each ion charge state. The charge-state-summed counterpart, integrating over all ionization levels of the ion species, is [radial_derivative_of_ion_pressure](name:radial_derivative_of_ion_pressure), and the second-order radial derivative at the charge-state level is [second_radial_derivative_of_ion_state_pressure](name:second_radial_derivative_of_ion_state_pressure). The analogous electron quantity is [radial_derivative_of_electron_pressure](name:radial_derivative_of_electron_pressure). In typical confined plasmas, pressure decreases from core to edge, so this derivative is negative over most of the profile, with steeper magnitudes in pedestal and internal transport barrier regions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the ion charge state pressure increases with increasing normalized toroidal flux coordinate $\rho_{\rm tor,norm}$.

NAMES.name: radial_derivative_of_ion_state_temperature
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: First radial derivative of the temperature of a specified ion charge state with respect to the normalized toroidal flux coordinate, giving the local temperature gradient driving ion energy transport.
NAMES.long:
The radial derivative of [ion_charge_state_temperature](name:ion_charge_state_temperature) with respect to the normalized toroidal flux coordinate $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$ quantifies how steeply the temperature of a specified ion charge state varies across nested flux surfaces. This gradient enters directly into the thermodynamic force terms of the ion energy transport equation, driving both neoclassical and turbulent heat fluxes in the ion channel and controlling the local power balance for that charge state.

The quantity is defined as:

$$
\frac{dT_{i,z}}{d\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}}
$$

where $T_{i,z}$ is the temperature of ions in charge state $z$ and $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm} \in [0, 1]$ is the normalized toroidal flux radius, equal to zero at the magnetic axis and unity at the last closed flux surface.

This derivative is computed from the charge-state-resolved ion temperature profile within transport solver numerics. The companion quantity [second_radial_derivative_of_ion_state_temperature](name:second_radial_derivative_of_ion_state_temperature) provides the profile curvature; [radial_derivative_of_ion_temperature](name:radial_derivative_of_ion_temperature) gives the charge-state-averaged analog. Steep gradients are characteristic of internal transport barriers and the pedestal region.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $T_{i,z}$ increases in the direction of increasing $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$, i.e., outward from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: radial_derivative_of_poloidal_ion_velocity
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: First radial derivative of the poloidal ion bulk-flow velocity with respect to the normalized toroidal flux coordinate, averaged over ion charge states.
NAMES.long:
The radial derivative of the poloidal ion velocity quantifies how sharply the poloidal component of the ion bulk flow changes along the minor-radial direction at a given flux surface. It is the charge-state-averaged quantity; the charge-state-resolved counterpart is [radial_derivative_of_poloidal_ion_state_velocity](name:radial_derivative_of_poloidal_ion_state_velocity). This gradient enters the ion momentum transport equation through viscous stress and flow-shear terms, and transport solvers require it to close the discretized radial momentum balance.

The quantity is defined as

$$
\frac{d v_{\mathrm{pol,ion}}}{d\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}}
$$

where $v_{\mathrm{pol,ion}}$ is the poloidal component of the charge-state-averaged ion bulk velocity (the parent quantity [poloidal_ion_velocity](name:poloidal_ion_velocity)) and $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}} \in [0,1]$ is the normalized toroidal flux radius, equal to 0 at the magnetic axis and 1 at the last closed flux surface. Because $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ is dimensionless, the derivative carries the same unit as the velocity itself.

This quantity is computed numerically within transport solver frameworks from the radial profile of the poloidal ion velocity. It is used together with [second_radial_derivative_of_poloidal_ion_velocity](name:second_radial_derivative_of_poloidal_ion_velocity) to build finite-difference or spectral representations of the momentum equation. The analogous electron-fluid quantity is [radial_derivative_of_poloidal_electron_velocity](name:radial_derivative_of_poloidal_electron_velocity).
NAMES.sign: Positive when $v_{\mathrm{pol,ion}}$ increases with increasing $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$, i.e., when the poloidal ion bulk flow has a positive outward radial gradient.

NAMES.name: radial_derivative_of_total_electron_density
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: First radial derivative of the total (thermal plus non-thermal) electron number density with respect to the normalized toroidal flux coordinate, used to evaluate electron density gradient terms in particle transport equations.
NAMES.long:
The radial derivative of [total_electron_density](name:total_electron_density) quantifies how rapidly the combined thermal and non-thermal electron density changes along the normalized toroidal flux radius $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$, where $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm} = 0$ at the magnetic axis and $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm} = 1$ at the last closed flux surface.

The quantity is defined as:

$$
\frac{dn_e^\mathrm{tot}}{d\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}}
$$

where $n_e^\mathrm{tot}$ is the total electron number density (thermal plus non-thermal contributions, in m$^{-3}$) and $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$ is the dimensionless normalized toroidal flux coordinate.

This gradient term enters directly into the discretized radial particle transport equation for electrons and is evaluated numerically from the density profile during transport solver iterations. The [second_radial_derivative_of_total_electron_density](name:second_radial_derivative_of_total_electron_density) provides the curvature term needed for higher-order discretization schemes. The corresponding quantity for the non-thermal electron sub-population is [radial_derivative_of_fast_electron_density](name:radial_derivative_of_fast_electron_density), while the ion-species analog is [radial_derivative_of_total_ion_density](name:radial_derivative_of_total_ion_density).
NAMES.sign: Positive when total electron density increases in the direction of increasing $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$, i.e., outward from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: radial_diamagnetic_current_density
NAMES.short: Radial component of the diamagnetic current density, driven by the cross product of the magnetic field and the plasma pressure gradient projected onto the major-radius direction.
NAMES.long:
The diamagnetic current density arises in magnetized plasmas wherever a pressure gradient exists perpendicular to the magnetic field, producing a drift current perpendicular to both $\mathbf{B}$ and $\nabla p$. The radial component $j_{\mathrm{dia},R} = \mathbf{j}_\mathrm{dia} \cdot \hat{R}$ is the projection of the full [diamagnetic current density](name:diamagnetic_current_density) vector onto the major-radius direction $\hat{R}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

The defining expression for the diamagnetic current density vector is:

$$
\mathbf{j}_\mathrm{dia} = \frac{\mathbf{B} \times \nabla p}{B^2}
$$

where $\mathbf{B}$ is the local magnetic field vector and $p$ is the total plasma pressure. The radial projection isolates the component crossing magnetic surfaces in the $\hat{R}$ direction, which enters the radial current balance and — through ambipolarity constraints — can influence the radial electric field and plasma rotation.

This component is computed from pressure gradient and magnetic field geometry profiles. In edge and scrape-off-layer regions with steep pressure gradients and complex magnetic geometry, it can be comparable to or larger than the radial ohmic or [radial_current_density](name:radial_total_current_density). The complementary decomposition of the same vector yields toroidal_diamagnetic_current_density and [parallel_diamagnetic_current_density](name:parallel_diamagnetic_current_density).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the diamagnetic current flows in the direction of increasing major radius $R$.

NAMES.name: radial_electron_diffusion_coefficient
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Radial component of the electron particle diffusion coefficient, relating the cross-field electron density flux to the local radial density gradient normal to magnetic flux surfaces.
NAMES.long:
The radial electron diffusion coefficient $D_{e,r}$ characterizes Fickian diffusive transport of electron particle density in the direction perpendicular to magnetic flux surfaces. It is the cross-field particle diffusivity for the electron species, distinct from the thermal energy diffusivity captured by [radial_electron_energy_diffusion_coefficient](name:radial_electron_energy_diffusion_coefficient).

The coefficient enters the electron continuity equation through Fick's first law:

$$
\Gamma_{e,r} = -D_{e,r} \frac{\partial n_e}{\partial r}
$$

where $\Gamma_{e,r}$ is the outward radial electron particle flux, $n_e$ is the electron number density, and $r$ is the coordinate normal to the local flux surface.

In edge-plasma transport simulations, $D_{e,r}$ encodes the net cross-field diffusion from both neoclassical and anomalous (turbulence-driven) mechanisms; in practice the anomalous contribution from drift-wave and interchange turbulence dominates by one or more orders of magnitude over the classical collisional value. The coefficient is an input or output of fluid transport solvers employing unstructured grid descriptions of the edge and scrape-off-layer regions. The ion-species analog is [radial_ion_diffusion_coefficient](name:radial_ion_diffusion_coefficient), and the neutral-particle counterpart is [radial_neutral_diffusion_coefficient](name:radial_neutral_diffusion_coefficient).

Typical values in the edge plasma and scrape-off layer range from 0.01 to 1 m²·s⁻¹, with anomalously enhanced values of 0.1–1 m²·s⁻¹ common across L-mode and H-mode regimes.

NAMES.name: radial_electron_energy_diffusion_coefficient
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Cross-field diffusivity for electron thermal energy transport in the radial, flux-surface-normal direction, appearing as the Fickian coefficient in the electron energy flux.
NAMES.long:
Radial electron energy diffusion coefficient is the effective cross-field diffusivity for electron thermal energy transported normal to magnetic flux surfaces. It parameterizes the part of electron energy transport driven by gradients of electron thermal energy density, distinct from convective transport, sources, sinks, and exchange terms.

In an energy-density formulation, the radial diffusive electron energy flux is commonly written as:

$$
q_{r,e}^{\mathrm{diff}} = -D_{r,e}^{E}\,\frac{\partial w_e}{\partial r}
$$

where $q_{r,e}^{\mathrm{diff}}$ is the outward radial diffusive electron energy flux in W m$^{-2}$, $D_{r,e}^{E}$ is the radial electron energy diffusion coefficient, $w_e$ is the electron thermal energy density in J m$^{-3}$, and $r$ is an outward-increasing radial distance variable normal to magnetic flux surfaces. The minus sign expresses down-gradient diffusion. For a nonrelativistic Maxwellian electron population, $w_e=3p_e/2$; if temperature is used instead, it must be converted consistently to energy density, for example through $p_e=n_e k_B T_e$ when $T_e$ is in kelvin.

This coefficient is inferred from power-balance analysis, perturbative heat-pulse experiments, or transport modeling by separating diffusive transport from convection, local heating, radiation, and electron-ion energy exchange. It is an effective transport coefficient, so turbulent, neoclassical, and unresolved cross-field processes may all contribute.

Typical core values in magnetically confined plasmas range from 0.1-1 m$^2$.s$^{-1}$ in weakly turbulent or near-neoclassical regimes to 1-50 m$^2$.s$^{-1}$ in strongly turbulent or edge transport regions; larger effective values can occur during transients or in poorly confined plasmas.

NAMES.name: radial_electron_energy_flux
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Radial component of the net electron energy flux density crossing magnetic flux surfaces, representing electron energy transported per unit area per unit time.
NAMES.long:
Radial electron energy flux is the outward-normal component of the electron energy-flux density across magnetic flux surfaces. It represents net cross-field transport of electron energy, independent of the particular closure used to separate diffusive, convective, or other contributions.

For a radial flux coordinate $\rho$ in a flux-coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, with $\rho$ increasing from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary, the radial component is

$$
q_{e,r} = \mathbf{q}_e \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}_\rho
$$

where $\mathbf{q}_e$ is the electron energy-flux density in W m$^{-2}$ and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}_\rho = \nabla\rho / |\nabla\rho|$ is the unit normal to surfaces of constant $\rho$ in the direction of increasing $\rho$.

In transport analysis this quantity is inferred from the electron energy balance, using sources and sinks such as auxiliary heating, collisional exchange with ions, radiation, particle sources, and the time variation of electron thermal energy. Modeling may parameterize it with effective diffusion and effective energy-convection coefficients, but those coefficients describe a chosen transport closure rather than the definition of the flux itself.

Typical magnitudes range from about $10^3$-$10^6$ W m$^{-2}$ in magnetically confined plasmas, depending on heating power, confinement regime, radius, and edge gradients. Larger transient values can occur during rapid profile changes or near strong localized power deposition.
NAMES.sign: Positive when electron energy is transported toward increasing radial flux coordinate $\rho$, from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: radial_electron_particle_flux
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Net number of electrons crossing a unit area oriented perpendicular to the radial direction per unit time, combining diffusive and convective cross-field transport contributions in the electron density continuity equation.
NAMES.long:
The radial electron particle flux $\Gamma_{e,r}$ is the projection of the electron particle-flux density vector onto the radial direction, quantifying the net cross-field electron transport per unit area per unit time. It combines contributions from collisional diffusion, bulk convective flow, and turbulent fluctuations, and enters directly into the electron continuity equation governing the evolution of the electron density profile.

In 1D transport modeling, the flux is commonly decomposed into diffusive and convective components:

$$
\Gamma_{e,r} = -D_e \frac{\partial n_e}{\partial r} + V_e n_e
$$

where $D_e$ is the radial electron particle diffusion coefficient, $V_e$ is the effective convection velocity (see [radial_electron_convection_velocity](name:radial_electron_convection_velocity)), and $n_e$ is the local electron number density.

This quantity is computed by transport models incorporating measured electron density profiles together with reconstructed or modeled diffusion and convection coefficients. The radial integral of $\Gamma_{e,r}$ must close the global particle balance, including ionization sources and wall recycling. The analogous quantity for individual ion charge states is given by [radial_ion_state_particle_flux](name:radial_ion_state_particle_flux).
NAMES.sign: Positive when electrons flow radially outward, away from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: radial_electron_velocity
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Projection of the electron fluid bulk flow velocity onto the major-radius direction, giving the net electron flow toward or away from the machine symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The radial electron velocity $v_{e,R}$ is the component of the electron bulk fluid velocity resolved along the major-radius direction $\hat{R}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is measured from the machine symmetry axis. It governs cross-field electron mass transport in the poloidal plane and enters the electron continuity equation through the divergence of the radial particle flux $n_e v_{e,R}$. It is one component of the parent vector [electron_velocity](name:electron_velocity).

The quantity is defined as the first velocity-space moment of the electron distribution function $f_e$ projected onto $\hat{R}$:

$$
v_{e,R} = \frac{1}{n_e} \int v_R \, f_e(\mathbf{v}) \, d^3v
$$

where $n_e$ is the local electron number density and $v_R$ is the $\hat{R}$-component of a particle velocity $\mathbf{v}$.

Radial electron flow is generally much smaller in magnitude than [parallel_electron_velocity](name:parallel_electron_velocity) but is significant for cross-field particle transport, particularly in the edge and scrape-off layer. It is most often inferred from transport analysis using measured density profiles and particle source rates, or derived from fluid simulations. The sibling components [poloidal_electron_velocity](name:poloidal_electron_velocity) and [toroidal_electron_velocity](name:toroidal_electron_velocity) complete the cylindrical decomposition; the ion analog is [radial_ion_velocity](name:radial_ion_velocity).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the electron fluid flows in the direction of increasing major radius $R$, i.e., radially outward from the machine symmetry axis.

NAMES.name: radial_ion_diffusion_coefficient
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Effective cross-field diffusivity relating the total ion particle flux to the outward radial gradient of total ion density across magnetic flux surfaces. It applies to the sum over ion charge states and is local to the radial position or flux surface used in the transport model.
NAMES.long:
Radial ion diffusion coefficient is the effective particle diffusivity for total ions moving across nested magnetic flux surfaces. It parameterizes collisional, stochastic, and turbulent cross-field mixing of ion density and is summed over all ion charge states rather than resolving a specific ionization state. The quantity is local to the radial position or magnetic flux surface where the transport balance is evaluated; when densities and fluxes are flux-surface averaged, it represents the corresponding flux-surface-averaged effective coefficient.

In a flux-coordinate description $(r, \theta, \phi)$, where $r$ is a physical radial distance increasing outward from the magnetic axis toward the separatrix and wall, $\theta$ is poloidal angle, and $\phi$ is toroidal angle, the diffusive part of the ion particle flux is commonly written as:

$$
\Gamma_{i,r}^{\mathrm{diff}} = -D_{i,r}\,\frac{\partial n_i}{\partial r}
$$

where $\Gamma_{i,r}^{\mathrm{diff}}$ is the radial diffusive ion particle flux, $D_{i,r}$ is the radial ion diffusion coefficient, and $n_i$ is the total ion density summed over charge states. The minus sign expresses down-gradient diffusion: for a density that decreases outward, a positive diffusivity gives an outward diffusive flux. If a dimensionless flux coordinate such as $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ is used in $(\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}, \theta, \phi)$, metric factors convert derivatives with respect to $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ into a physical radial gradient so that $D_{i,r}$ retains units of m^2.s^-1.

The coefficient is obtained from interpretive particle-balance analysis, inferred effective transport modeling, or predictive neoclassical and turbulence calculations. It describes the diffusive component of radial ion particle transport and is distinct from convective pinch terms; for charge-state-resolved transport use [radial_ion_state_diffusion_coefficient](name:radial_ion_state_diffusion_coefficient), and for electron particle transport use [radial_electron_diffusion_coefficient](name:radial_electron_diffusion_coefficient).

Typical effective values are about 0.01-1 m^2.s^-1 in well-confined core plasmas, 0.1-10 m^2.s^-1 in edge and scrape-off-layer conditions, and may be smaller for nearly neoclassical transport or larger during strong turbulence and transient events.

NAMES.name: radial_ion_energy_diffusion_coefficient
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Radial component of the diffusion coefficient governing cross-field transport of total ion thermal energy across magnetic flux surfaces, aggregating all ion species and charge states.
NAMES.long:
The radial ion energy diffusion coefficient quantifies the diffusive transport of total ion thermal energy in the direction perpendicular to magnetic flux surfaces, combining contributions from all ion species and charge states into a single aggregate transport parameter.

In the radial ion energy transport equation, the diffusive energy flux $q_{E}^{\rm rad}$ is proportional to the radial gradient of the ion energy density:

$$
q_{E}^{\rm rad} = -D_{E,\rm ion}^{\rm rad} \, \nabla_r \!\left(\tfrac{3}{2} n_i T_i\right)
$$

where $n_i$ is the total ion number density, $T_i$ is the ion temperature, and $\nabla_r$ denotes the gradient in the radial direction perpendicular to flux surfaces.

This coefficient encapsulates both neoclassical contributions from collisional ion dynamics and anomalous contributions arising from plasma turbulence; in edge plasma regions the anomalous component typically dominates by one to two orders of magnitude. It is inferred from transport power balance analysis or prescribed in edge transport models. Typical magnitudes lie between $10^{-2}$ and $10$ m$^2$ s$^{-1}$ in the edge plasma.

For charge-state-resolved ion energy transport, the analogous quantity is [radial_ion_state_energy_diffusion_coefficient](name:radial_ion_state_energy_diffusion_coefficient). The radial ion particle transport analog is [radial_ion_diffusion_coefficient](name:radial_ion_diffusion_coefficient), and the radial momentum transport analog is [radial_ion_momentum_diffusion_coefficient](name:radial_ion_momentum_diffusion_coefficient).

NAMES.name: radial_ion_state_diffusion_coefficient
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Radial particle diffusion coefficient for a specific ion charge state, relating the outward radial particle flux of that charge state to its number density gradient across magnetic flux surfaces.
NAMES.long:
The radial ion-state diffusion coefficient $D_r^z$ quantifies the Fickian diffusive transport of ions in a given charge state $z$ across magnetic flux surfaces in the radial direction. It is the particle-channel transport coefficient in charge-state-resolved ion fluid models, complementing [radial_ion_state_energy_diffusion_coefficient](name:radial_ion_state_energy_diffusion_coefficient) for thermal energy transport and [radial_ion_state_momentum_diffusion_coefficient](name:radial_ion_state_momentum_diffusion_coefficient) for momentum transport.

The radial particle flux $\Gamma_r^z$ of the charge state is modeled according to Fick's law:

$$
\Gamma_r^z = -D_r^z \frac{\partial n_z}{\partial r}
$$

where $n_z$ is the number density of ions in charge state $z$ in m$^{-3}$ and $r$ is the coordinate normal to flux surfaces in m.

This coefficient is charge-state-resolved, distinguishing it from [radial_ion_diffusion_coefficient](name:radial_ion_diffusion_coefficient), which aggregates over all charge states of an ion species. The analogous quantity for neutral species resolved by excitation state is [radial_neutral_state_diffusion_coefficient](name:radial_neutral_state_diffusion_coefficient). The present quantity is the radial projection of the parent [ion_state_diffusion_coefficient](name:ion_state_diffusion_coefficient). It is typically prescribed by turbulence simulations, mixing-length estimates, or neoclassical calculations for each ionization stage, and is used in multi-fluid edge transport solvers tracking individual charge states.

Typical values in edge and scrape-off-layer plasma models range from $10^{-2}$ to $10$ m$^2$·s$^{-1}$, with anomalous turbulence-driven diffusion dominating over neoclassical contributions in the edge.

NAMES.name: radial_ion_state_energy_flux
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Radial energy-flux density for a resolved ion charge state, representing net power per unit area transported across nested magnetic-flux surfaces. Positive values denote outward transport from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary.
NAMES.long:
Radial ion state energy flux is the component of energy-flux density carried by one resolved ion charge state across nested magnetic-flux surfaces. It represents thermal energy transported per unit area by conductive, convective, turbulent, neoclassical, and collisional processes. Here “radial” refers to the outward normal to flux surfaces, or equivalently to increasing normalized toroidal flux radius in a flux-coordinate system $(\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}, \theta, \phi)$.

A common transport decomposition writes the radial energy flux density as the sum of conductive and convective enthalpy contributions:

$$
Q_{E,z}^{r} = - n_z \chi_{E,z} \nabla_r T_z + \frac{5}{2} T_z \Gamma_z^{r}
$$

where $Q_{E,z}^{r}$ is the radial energy flux density for charge state $z$ in W m^-2, $n_z$ is the charge-state density in m^-3, $\chi_{E,z}$ is an effective energy diffusivity in m^2 s^-1, $\nabla_r$ is the derivative along the outward flux-surface normal, $T_z$ is an energy-like temperature in joules, and $\Gamma_z^{r}$ is the radial particle-flux density in m^-2 s^-1. If the temperature is expressed in eV, $e T_z$ and $e \nabla_r T_z$ must be used in this equation, where $e$ is the elementary charge, so that both terms have units W m^-2.

In practice this quantity is inferred from transport analysis, power balance, fluid or kinetic modeling, and diagnostics constraining ion charge-state densities, temperatures, gradients, and particle fluxes. Summing over charge states gives an ion-species radial energy flux, while summing over ion species gives an aggregate ion or total ion energy flux.

Typical magnitudes span a wide range because they depend on charge-state abundance, heating power, collisional coupling, and radial location. Trace impurity charge states can have fluxes of 0.01-1000 W m^-2, dominant ion charge states commonly reach 10^3-10^6 W m^-2 in heated plasmas, and transient edge transport can exceed 10^6 W m^-2.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the energy flux is directed toward increasing $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$, from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: radial_ion_state_momentum_diffusion_coefficient
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Radial ion-state momentum diffusion coefficient is the scalar diffusivity for radial transport of the momentum density of a specified ion charge state. In the diffusive closure it multiplies the outward radial gradient of that momentum density, with positive values representing down-gradient momentum diffusion.
NAMES.long:
Radial ion-state momentum diffusion coefficient is an effective transport coefficient for the radial diffusion of linear momentum carried by ions in a specified charge state. It is the charge-state-resolved ion form of [radial_ion_charge_state_momentum_diffusivity](name:radial_ion_charge_state_momentum_diffusivity) and specializes [radial_momentum_diffusivity](name:radial_momentum_diffusivity) to a selected ion state. The quantity describes diffusion of momentum density, not diffusion driven directly by a velocity gradient; a viscosity closure would additionally include mass-density factors.

The diffusive closure for the radial flux density of ion-state momentum can be written as:

$$
\boldsymbol{\Pi}_{r,i,q}^{\mathrm{diff}} = -D_{r,i,q}^{(p)} \frac{\partial \mathbf{p}_{i,q}}{\partial r}
$$

where $D_{r,i,q}^{(p)}$ is this coefficient in $m^2\,s^{-1}$, $\boldsymbol{\Pi}_{r,i,q}^{\mathrm{diff}}$ is the radial diffusive flux density of linear momentum in $kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-2}$, $i$ labels the ion species, $q$ labels the charge state, $\mathbf{p}_{i,q}=m_i n_{i,q}\mathbf{u}_{i,q}$ is the ion-state momentum density in $kg\,m^{-2}\,s^{-1}$, $m_i$ is the ion mass in $kg$, $n_{i,q}$ is number density in $m^{-3}$, $\mathbf{u}_{i,q}$ is flow velocity in $m\,s^{-1}$, and $r$ is an outward radial coordinate in meters. The minus sign gives down-gradient diffusion for positive coefficient values.

In practice this coefficient is inferred from a radial momentum balance or supplied by a transport model. Determinations use measured or reconstructed ion flows and densities together with estimates of convective momentum transport, external torque, electromagnetic forces, collisional exchange between species and charge states, and other nondiffusive terms.

Typical effective core values in magnetically confined plasmas are about 0.1-10 m^2 s^-1. Transport-barrier regions can have values below 0.1 m^2 s^-1, while edge or strongly turbulent conditions can require 10-100 m^2 s^-1. Negative fitted values may occur when the remaining transport after modeled sources, sinks, and convection is up-gradient, and should be interpreted as effective model coefficients.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the radial diffusive momentum flux density is opposite to the outward radial gradient of the ion-state momentum density for a radial coordinate $r$ that increases from the magnetic axis toward the plasma edge.

NAMES.name: radial_ion_state_velocity
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Radial component of the mean bulk flow velocity of ions in a specified ionization charge state, projected along the major-radius direction.
NAMES.long:
The radial ion-state velocity is the projection of the mean bulk fluid velocity of ions in a single resolved ionization charge state onto the major-radius direction $\hat{R}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius measured from the machine symmetry axis. This charge-state-resolved quantity characterizes cross-field radial transport for a specific ion population and is the radial component of the parent vector [ion_state_velocity](name:ion_state_velocity).

In a multi-fluid treatment, each ionization charge state $z$ of a given ion species carries its own velocity field. The radial component is defined as the first velocity moment of the charge-state distribution function $f_z$ normalized by the local charge-state number density $n_z$:

$$
v_{R,z} = \frac{1}{n_z} \int v_R \, f_z(\mathbf{v}) \, d^3v
$$

where $v_R$ is the velocity component along $\hat{R}$.

The charge-state-averaged analog is [radial_ion_velocity](name:radial_ion_velocity), which integrates over all charge states; the field-aligned projection is [parallel_ion_state_velocity](name:parallel_ion_state_velocity). The analogous quantities for neutral states and electrons are [radial_neutral_state_velocity](name:radial_neutral_state_velocity) and [radial_electron_velocity](name:radial_electron_velocity). Radial ion velocities are typically small in the core compared to parallel flow but become significant in the edge and scrape-off layer where cross-field transport drives net particle fluxes across flux surfaces; they are constrained by charge exchange recombination spectroscopy and multi-fluid transport modeling.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the ion flow is directed in the direction of increasing major radius $R$, i.e., radially outward from the magnetic axis.

NAMES.name: radial_ion_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Major-radius component of the diamagnetic drift velocity of a charged ion state in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It is driven by the magnetic field crossed with that ion state's partial pressure gradient.
NAMES.long:
Radial ion-state diamagnetic drift velocity is the major-radius component of the pressure-gradient-driven fluid drift of a single charged ion state. In a magnetized plasma a pressure gradient perpendicular to the magnetic field produces a net fluid motion perpendicular to both, without requiring individual particles to cross field lines. This component is the projection of that drift onto $\hat{R}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

For an ion charge state $s$ with charge $q_s = Z_s e > 0$, the major-radius component is obtained by projecting the diamagnetic drift velocity onto $\hat{R}$:

$$
v_{\ast s,R} = \hat{R} \cdot \frac{\mathbf{B} \times \nabla p_s}{Z_s\, e\, n_s\, |\mathbf{B}|^2}
$$

where $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field in T, $p_s$ is the ion-state partial pressure in Pa, $\nabla p_s$ is its gradient in Pa m$^{-1}$, $n_s$ is the ion-state number density in m$^{-3}$, $Z_s$ is the dimensionless ion charge number, $e$ is the elementary charge in C, and $|\mathbf{B}|$ is the magnetic-field magnitude in T. The ordering $\mathbf{B} \times \nabla p_s$ gives the diamagnetic drift direction for a positive ion species. This is the radial counterpart of the toroidal and vertical components that together decompose the full drift vector.

In practice the quantity is computed from the ion-state density and temperature or pressure, the local magnetic-field vector, and the spatial gradient of the ion-state partial pressure. If the temperature is tabulated in eV it must be converted so that $p_s$ is in Pa before applying the formula. The radial projection can change sign across a poloidal cross-section because it depends on the local orientation of both $\mathbf{B}$ and $\nabla p_s$.

Typical radial components are about 1-1000 m s$^{-1}$ in core transport conditions and can reach 1000-10000 m s$^{-1}$ in steep-gradient edge or pedestal regions. The magnitude scales approximately with $T_s/(Z_s e B L_p)$ before projection, so it grows for hotter ions, weaker magnetic field, smaller charge number, or shorter pressure-gradient scale length $L_p$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $\mathbf{B} \times \nabla p_s$ has a positive projection along $+\hat{R}$, toward increasing major radius $R$, in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: radial_ion_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Major-radius component of the E×B guiding-center drift velocity for a specified ion charge state, arising from the cross-product of the local electric and confining magnetic fields in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.
NAMES.long:
The radial E×B drift velocity gives the projection of the guiding-center drift onto the major-radius direction $R$ for a specified ion charge state. This drift arises from crossed electric and magnetic fields and is species-independent: it is identical for all ion masses and charge state values at a given plasma location, depending only on the local field ratio.

The full E×B drift velocity is defined as:

$$
\mathbf{v}_{E \times B} = \frac{\mathbf{E} \times \mathbf{B}}{|\mathbf{B}|^2}
$$

where $\mathbf{E}$ is the local electric field and $\mathbf{B}$ is the confining magnetic field. The radial component is then $v_R = \mathbf{v}_{E \times B} \cdot \hat{R}$, where $\hat{R}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing major radius $R$.

In edge and scrape-off-layer plasmas, the radial E×B drift drives significant cross-field particle and momentum transport and contributes to flow shear that can suppress turbulence. It is computed from local electric and magnetic field profiles, typically derived from equilibrium reconstruction combined with electrostatic potential measurements or kinetic simulations. The toroidal and field-parallel counterparts are [toroidal_ion_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift](name:toroidal_ion_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift) and [parallel_ion_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift](name:parallel_ion_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift); the full parent vector is [ion_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift](name:ion_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift). The analogous quantity for neutral species is [radial_neutral_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift](name:radial_neutral_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift), while the total radial ion flow including all drift contributions is [radial_ion_state_velocity](name:radial_ion_state_velocity).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the E×B drift is directed in the direction of increasing major radius $R$, i.e., radially outward from the magnetic axis.

NAMES.name: radial_ion_velocity
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Radial (major-radius) component of the charge-state-averaged ion bulk flow velocity in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Radial ion velocity is the $R$ component of the charge-state-averaged ion bulk flow in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius measured from the toroidal symmetry axis, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It describes ion convection across surfaces of constant major radius and is the charge-state-averaged analog of [radial_ion_state_velocity](name:radial_ion_state_velocity).

The component is defined by projecting the charge-state-averaged ion velocity vector onto the radial unit vector:

$$
v_{i,R} = \mathbf{v}_i \cdot \hat{R}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_i$ is the charge-state-averaged ion bulk velocity and $\hat{R}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing major radius. When resolved charge-state velocities are available, $\mathbf{v}_i$ is commonly formed as a density-weighted charge-state average before taking the projection.

Direct determination of this component is often difficult because radial ion flows are usually smaller than toroidal or poloidal flows. It may be inferred from particle continuity, momentum balance, radial particle flux divided by ion density, or by projecting a reconstructed ion velocity vector; charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy and Doppler spectroscopy can provide constraints on related flow components used in such inferences.

Typical flux-surface-averaged core transport velocities are about 0.01-10 m.s^-1, while local edge, scrape-off-layer, or transient radial flows can reach 10-1000 m.s^-1 depending on turbulence, electric fields, and plasma conditions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the ion bulk flow is directed toward increasing major radius $R$, outward from the toroidal symmetry axis.

NAMES.name: radial_momentum_diffusivity
NAMES.short: Diffusion coefficient relating the diffusive radial plasma momentum flux across magnetic flux surfaces to the local momentum-density gradient.
NAMES.long:
Radial momentum diffusivity is the scalar coefficient for diffusive redistribution of plasma momentum between neighboring magnetic flux surfaces. It is the cross-surface projection of the more general [momentum diffusivity](name:momentum_diffusivity); radial means along the outward normal from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary.

The diffusive part of the radial momentum flux is commonly written as Fickian transport of the relevant momentum-density component, with the flux taken positive outward along the flux-surface normal:

$$
\Gamma_{p,r}^{\mathrm{diff}} = -D_{p,r}\,\frac{\partial p_{\mathrm{mom}}}{\partial \ell_r}
$$

where $\Gamma_{p,r}^{\mathrm{diff}}$ is the diffusive radial momentum flux, $D_{p,r}$ is the radial momentum diffusivity, $p_{\mathrm{mom}}$ is the relevant plasma momentum density (for a single species, $m n u$ with particle mass $m$, number density $n$, and bulk flow velocity $u$), and $\ell_r$ is physical distance measured outward normal to the flux surfaces. The minus sign means that for $D_{p,r} > 0$, an outward-increasing momentum density produces an inward diffusive flux, while an outward-decreasing momentum density produces an outward diffusive flux.

In transport analysis, $D_{p,r}$ is inferred or prescribed from momentum balance using measured or reconstructed flow fields, momentum sources and sinks, collisional exchange, and estimates of radial fluxes. It can represent neoclassical viscosity, turbulence-driven anomalous transport, or an effective coefficient combining several cross-field momentum-transport mechanisms; species-specific variants include [ion momentum diffusivity](name:ion_momentum_diffusivity) and [radial ion charge-state momentum diffusivity](name:radial_ion_charge_state_momentum_diffusivity). Directional and formulation analogs include [poloidal momentum diffusivity](name:poloidal_neutral_momentum_diffusivity), [parallel momentum diffusivity](name:parallel_edge_plasma_momentum_diffusivity), [radial plasma momentum diffusion coefficient](name:radial_plasma_momentum_diffusion_coefficient), and [radial momentum diffusion coefficient](name:radial_neutral_momentum_diffusion_coefficient).

Typical effective core values in magnetically confined plasmas are about 0.1-10 m$^2$ s$^{-1}$, with neoclassical contributions often near the lower end and turbulence-dominated or edge-localized transport reaching 10-100 m$^2$ s$^{-1}$ in strong-gradient regions.

NAMES.name: radial_neutral_energy_diffusion_coefficient
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Radial component of the Fickian diffusion coefficient governing cross-field thermal energy transport for the aggregated neutral particle population across magnetic flux surfaces.
NAMES.long:
The radial neutral energy diffusion coefficient $D_r^{E,\mathrm{n}}$ quantifies the proportionality between the cross-flux-surface thermal energy flux carried by neutrals and the radial gradient of the neutral thermal energy density, entering the radial term of the neutral energy transport equation.

In a Fickian closure the cross-flux-surface thermal energy flux is:

$$
q_r^{\mathrm{n}} = -D_r^{E,\mathrm{n}} \, \nabla_r \!\left(\tfrac{3}{2} n_\mathrm{n} T_\mathrm{n}\right)
$$

where $n_\mathrm{n}$ is the neutral number density, $T_\mathrm{n}$ is the neutral temperature, and $\nabla_r$ denotes the gradient in the cross-flux-surface (radial) direction.

This coefficient aggregates contributions from all neutral charge and excitation states; the state-resolved counterpart is [radial_neutral_state_energy_diffusion_coefficient](name:radial_neutral_state_energy_diffusion_coefficient). The particle- and momentum-transport diffusivities for the same neutral population are [radial_neutral_diffusion_coefficient](name:radial_neutral_diffusion_coefficient) and [radial_neutral_momentum_diffusion_coefficient](name:radial_neutral_momentum_diffusion_coefficient), while the corresponding ion-channel energy analog is [radial_ion_energy_diffusion_coefficient](name:radial_ion_energy_diffusion_coefficient). In edge-plasma transport models this coefficient is evaluated on generalized-geometry (GGD) unstructured grid subsets and provided as an input to or output from neutral fluid transport solvers; its magnitude depends on neutral mean free path and collision frequencies with the background plasma.

NAMES.name: radial_neutral_energy_flux
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Radial component of total neutral energy flux across magnetic flux surfaces, summed over all neutral species and states and oriented along an outward-increasing flux-surface label.
NAMES.long:
Radial neutral energy flux is the signed rate per unit area at which energy carried by neutral atoms or molecules crosses magnetic flux surfaces. It is the radial projection of the total neutral energy-flux vector, summed over all neutral species, isotopes, molecular populations, and internal states included in the physical description.

For a fluid moment description in a flux coordinate set $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, with radial label $\rho$ increasing outward, the decomposition into convective enthalpy transport and conductive or kinetic heat transport is commonly written as:

$$
q_r^{\mathrm{neu}} = \sum_s \left( h_s \Gamma_{r,s}^{\mathrm{neu}} + q_{r,s}^{\mathrm{cond}} \right)
$$

where $q_r^{\mathrm{neu}}$ is the total radial neutral energy flux, $s$ labels neutral species or states, $\Gamma_{r,s}^{\mathrm{neu}} = n_s v_{r,s}$ is the radial neutral particle flux, $h_s$ is the enthalpy per neutral particle, and $q_{r,s}^{\mathrm{cond}}$ is the non-convective thermal energy flux. For a monatomic ideal neutral gas with temperature expressed as energy, $h_s \simeq 5T_s/2$.

The quantity is usually obtained from neutral transport calculations or coupled plasma-neutral reconstructions by taking radial moments of a kinetic neutral distribution or by combining fluid neutral density, temperature, velocity, and heat-flux moments. Experimental constraints come indirectly from neutral pressure, recycling, Balmer-line emission, charge-exchange, and ionization-source measurements rather than from a direct energy-flux diagnostic.

Typical magnitudes are highly edge-localized: in well-ionized core regions they are often near zero to 10^3 W m^-2, while edge, scrape-off-layer, and divertor recycling regions commonly span 10^3-10^6 W m^-2 and can approach 10^7 W m^-2 during strong fueling or detachment transients. The sign may change where inward cold-neutral penetration competes with outward energy convection.
NAMES.sign: Positive when neutral energy is transported in the direction of increasing radial flux-surface label $\rho$ in the flux coordinate set $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, from the magnetic axis toward the last-closed flux surface or material boundary.

NAMES.name: radial_neutral_particle_flux
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Radial component of the neutral particle flux density: the net number of neutral particles crossing a flux surface per unit area per unit time. It quantifies outward or inward neutral transport across magnetic surfaces.
NAMES.long:
Radial neutral particle flux is the flux-surface-normal component of the neutral particle flux density. In flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, with $\rho$ increasing from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary, it represents the signed rate at which neutral particles cross a surface of constant $\rho$ per unit area.

The local constitutive definition is

$$
\Gamma_{n,r} = n_n \langle v_r \rangle
$$

where $\Gamma_{n,r}$ is the radial neutral particle flux density in m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$, $n_n$ is the neutral particle density in m$^{-3}$, and $\langle v_r \rangle$ is the mean neutral velocity component in m s$^{-1}$ along the outward radial direction. Equivalently, $\Gamma_{n,r}$ is the radial first velocity moment of the neutral distribution function.

In transport analysis this quantity is obtained from neutral kinetic or fluid models, particle balance inversions, or coupled plasma-neutral simulations. It enters the neutral density continuity equation as the radial transport term and is affected by ionization, recombination, charge exchange, recycling, and wall or divertor sources.

Typical magnitudes in the edge and scrape-off-layer range from $10^{18}$-$10^{22}$ m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$, with the largest values usually occurring near recycling regions, gas sources, and steep neutral density gradients. Core values are often much smaller because neutral penetration is limited by ionization and charge exchange.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the neutral particle flow is in the direction of increasing radial coordinate $\rho$ in flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, outward from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: radial_neutral_state_convection_velocity
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: Radial projection of the effective advective drift velocity for a specified neutral charge state, used as the convection coefficient in the flux-surface-averaged radial particle transport equation for that state.
NAMES.long:
The radial neutral-state convection velocity is the cross-flux-surface component of the advective drift for a specified neutral charge state. It enters the flux-surface-averaged particle continuity equation as the coefficient multiplying the local neutral-state number density, representing the pinch-like, non-diffusive contribution to radial particle transport.

The radial particle flux $\Gamma_r$ for the neutral state is decomposed as:

$$
\Gamma_r = v_{\mathrm{conv},r}\, n - D_r\, \frac{\partial n}{\partial r}
$$

where $v_{\mathrm{conv},r}$ is this radial convection velocity, $n$ is the neutral-state number density in m$^{-3}$, and $D_r$ is the radial diffusion coefficient. This quantity captures the advective term only; the diffusive contribution is governed by a separate transport coefficient.

This quantity is state-resolved, making it more specific than [radial_neutral_convection_velocity](name:radial_neutral_momentum_convection_velocity), which applies to the neutral species as a whole without charge-state resolution. The corresponding advective velocities for energy and momentum transport of the same neutral state are provided by [radial_neutral_state_effective_energy_convection_velocity](name:radial_neutral_state_energy_convection_velocity) and [radial_neutral_state_effective_momentum_convection_velocity](name:radial_neutral_state_momentum_convection_velocity). This coefficient is computed from fluid or kinetic-neutral transport calculations in edge plasma models, typically defined on unstructured grid geometries spanning the scrape-off layer and divertor regions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the advective neutral-state particle flux is directed radially outward, in the direction of increasing major radius $R$.

NAMES.name: radial_neutral_state_diffusion_coefficient
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: Effective radial particle diffusivity of a specified neutral state across nested magnetic flux surfaces. It is the radial component of the neutral-state diffusion tensor in flux-surface coordinates (r, theta, phi), where r increases outward, and relates outward particle flux to the radial gradient of neutral density.
NAMES.long:
Radial neutral-state diffusion coefficient is the effective particle diffusivity for a particular neutral state across nested magnetic flux surfaces. It is the radial component of the [neutral_state_diffusion_coefficient](name:neutral_state_diffusion_coefficient) tensor when neutral-state particle transport is written in flux-surface coordinates $(r,\theta,\phi)$, where $r$ is an outward-increasing radial label, $\theta$ is poloidal angle, and $\phi$ is toroidal angle. It is state-resolved, unlike the state-summed [radial_neutral_diffusion_coefficient](name:radial_neutral_diffusion_coefficient).

For a local diffusive closure, the radial particle flux of neutral state $s$ is modeled by Fick's law:

$$
\Gamma_{\mathrm{n},s,r} = -D_{\mathrm{n},s,r}\,\frac{\partial n_{\mathrm{n},s}}{\partial r}
$$

where $D_{\mathrm{n},s,r}$ is the radial neutral-state diffusion coefficient, $n_{\mathrm{n},s}$ is the neutral density, and $\Gamma_{\mathrm{n},s,r}$ is the radial particle flux. The flux $\Gamma_{\mathrm{n},s,r}$ is positive toward increasing $r$, so the minus sign gives an outward diffusive flux when the neutral density decreases outward.

In practice this coefficient is prescribed or inferred in reduced neutral-transport and plasma-transport models from particle balance, edge diagnostics, or comparison with kinetic neutral calculations.
