It represents the random-walk part of radial neutral spreading after separating convective transport and source or loss terms; ionization, recombination, and charge exchange affect neutral continuity and the inferred effective value, but they are not themselves the diffusion coefficient. Because neutrals are not tied to magnetic field lines, the diffusion approximation is an effective closure and may be less accurate when the neutral mean free path is comparable to the plasma size.

Typical effective values in magnetically confined plasmas are about 0.1-100 m^2 s^-1 in dense edge and scrape-off-layer conditions. Weakly collisional regions or volume-averaged reduced models may use values up to 1000 m^2 s^-1, while near-zero values represent negligible radial diffusive spreading for that neutral state.

NAMES.name: parallel_neutral_state_diffusivity
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: Particle diffusion coefficient for a specified neutral species state along the magnetic field direction, relating the parallel neutral-particle flux to the gradient of neutral state number density.
NAMES.long:
The parallel neutral state diffusivity $D_{\parallel,s}$ characterizes diffusive transport of particles belonging to a specific neutral atomic or molecular state along the magnetic field direction in edge and scrape-off-layer plasmas. State resolution enables multi-state fluid-neutral models to track individual electronic or vibrational levels separately, rather than treating all neutrals as a single population.

The parallel particle flux for neutral state $s$ follows the Fickian relation:

$$\Gamma_{\parallel,s} = -D_{\parallel,s} \, \nabla_\parallel n_s$$

where $\nabla_\parallel = \hat{b} \cdot \nabla$ is the gradient along the local magnetic field unit vector $\hat{b}$ and $n_s$ is the number density of state $s$ in m$^{-3}$.

This is the parallel component of the full neutral-state diffusion tensor, complementing the radial (cross-flux-surface) component described by [radial_neutral_state_diffusion_coefficient](name:radial_neutral_state_diffusion_coefficient) and the state-summed parallel version [parallel_diffusivity](name:parallel_neutral_species_particle_diffusivity). The corresponding momentum transport coefficient is [parallel_neutral_state_momentum_diffusivity](name:parallel_neutral_state_momentum_diffusivity), while the non-directional particle analog is [neutral_state_diffusivity](name:radial_neutral_state_diffusion_coefficient). For charged species the equivalent quantity is [parallel_ion_charge_state_diffusivity](name:parallel_ion_charge_state_diffusivity).

Determined from fluid-neutral or kinetic transport models on unstructured edge-plasma grids. Typical values for hydrogen isotope neutrals in tokamak edge conditions range from order 1 m$^2$ s$^{-1}$ in highly collisional divertor regions to $10^3$ m$^2$ s$^{-1}$ or more in low-density regions where the neutral mean free path greatly exceeds the density-gradient scale length.

NAMES.name: radial_neutral_state_energy_convection_velocity
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: Radial convection velocity for the energy density of a neutral charge state, taken along the major-radius direction R in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It multiplies neutral energy density in the convective part of the radial energy flux.
NAMES.long:
Radial neutral-state energy convection velocity is the signed component of the velocity that advects the energy density of a specified neutral charge state through surfaces of constant major radius $R$. The radial direction is the $\hat{R}$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical basis $(\hat{R},\hat{\phi},\hat{Z})$, with $R$ major radius, $\phi$ toroidal angle, and $Z$ vertical height.

The coefficient is defined by the convective part of the radial energy flux density:

$$
Q_{E,a}^{R,\mathrm{conv}} = \mathcal{E}_a\, v_{E,a}^{R}
$$

where $a$ labels the neutral charge state, the subscript $E$ denotes energy transport, $\mathrm{conv}$ denotes the convective contribution, $Q_{E,a}^{R,\mathrm{conv}}$ is the radial convective energy flux density in W m$^{-2}$, $\mathcal{E}_a$ is the neutral-state energy density in J m$^{-3}$, and $v_{E,a}^{R}$ is this radial energy convection velocity in m s$^{-1}$. The superscript $R$ denotes projection onto $\hat{R}$.

It is usually obtained from a neutral energy balance or transport model rather than from a direct velocity measurement. Values are inferred by matching radial energy fluxes to neutral density, neutral temperature or energy-density estimates, atomic and molecular source terms, wall recycling, and spectroscopic or charge-exchange constraints when available.

Typical absolute magnitudes are highly scenario dependent: fitted transport velocities may be 1-100 m s$^{-1}$ when neutral energy evolves slowly, 100-10000 m s$^{-1}$ in recycling-dominated conditions near material boundaries, and order 10000-100000 m s$^{-1}$ for fast atomic or molecular streaming associated with energetic neutrals. The signed value may be inward or outward depending on the balance of sources, losses, and neutral motion.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the energy convection is directed toward increasing major radius $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: radial_neutral_state_energy_flux
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: Radial energy flux density carried by neutrals in a specified internal state. It is the signed rate of neutral energy transport per unit area across magnetic flux surfaces.
NAMES.long:
Radial neutral-state energy flux is the flux-surface-normal component of the energy-flux vector for neutral particles in a specified internal state. It represents the net energy carried across a magnetic flux surface per unit area and per unit time, retaining the sign of inward or outward transport.

The radial scalar is defined by projecting the neutral-state energy-flux vector onto the normal of the chosen radial flux coordinate $\rho$ in the flux-coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$:

$$
q^\rho_{n,a} = \mathbf{q}_{n,a}\cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}_\rho
$$

where $q^\rho_{n,a}$ is the radial neutral-state energy flux density in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$, $\mathbf{q}_{n,a}$ is the corresponding neutral-state energy-flux vector in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$, $a$ labels the internal neutral state, and $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_\rho = \nabla\rho/|\nabla\rho|$ points toward increasing $\rho$.

In transport analysis this quantity is computed from the neutral-state energy balance or from moments of a kinetic neutral distribution, with convective, diffusive, conductive, charge-exchange, ionization, recombination, and source contributions included according to the model. It is usually inferred from coupled plasma-neutral modeling constrained by diagnostics such as spectroscopy, bolometry, and neutral-pressure measurements rather than measured directly. Summing over internal states gives [radial_neutral_energy_flux](name:radial_neutral_energy_flux); the state label follows the neutral internal-state convention used by [parallel_neutral_state_particle_flux](name:parallel_neutral_state_particle_flux), and is distinct from ion charge-state quantities such as [radial_ion_charge_state_energy_flux](name:radial_ion_state_energy_flux).

Typical magnitudes are highly problem dependent and are interpreted in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$. They are generally small where neutral densities are negligible and larger in edge, divertor, and recycling regions where neutral populations and charge-exchange rates are high; no universal numerical range is implied by the standard name.
NAMES.sign: Positive when energy flows toward increasing radial flux coordinate $\rho$.

NAMES.name: radial_neutral_state_momentum_diffusion_coefficient
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: Radial component of the momentum diffusion coefficient for neutral particles in a resolved neutral-state channel. It gives the Fickian diffusivity multiplying the outward gradient of neutral momentum per unit volume.
NAMES.long:
The radial neutral-state momentum diffusion coefficient is the scalar diffusivity used for diffusive radial transport of momentum carried by neutral particles in a specified neutral-state channel. The state qualifier denotes one resolved neutral population selected by a state identifier, such as an atomic, molecular, or internal-state population when those channels are modeled separately, rather than a sum over all neutral states.

For a Fickian closure applied component-wise to the neutral momentum density, the diffusive radial momentum flux is

$$
\Pi^{\mathrm{diff}}_{n,s,r} = -D^{\mathrm{mom}}_{n,s,r}\,\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left(\rho_{n,s} u_{n,s}\right)
$$

where $\Pi^{\mathrm{diff}}_{n,s,r}$ is the radial diffusive flux of the selected neutral momentum component in momentum per unit area per unit time, $D^{\mathrm{mom}}_{n,s,r}$ is the momentum diffusion coefficient, $r$ is the outward radial transport coordinate, $\rho_{n,s}=m_{n,s} n_{n,s}$ is the mass density of neutral state $s$, $m_{n,s}$ is the particle mass, $n_{n,s}$ is the number density, and $u_{n,s}$ is the mean velocity component whose momentum is being transported. The minus sign means that a positive diffusivity drives momentum from larger toward smaller momentum per unit volume.

In practice this coefficient is obtained from kinetic neutral calculations, Monte Carlo or random-walk estimates, analytic collisional mean-free-path models, or inference as a closure parameter in transport modeling. It complements the particle-channel coefficient [radial_neutral_state_diffusion_coefficient](name:radial_neutral_state_diffusion_coefficient) and should be interpreted together with the convective contribution represented by [radial_neutral_state_momentum_convection_velocity](name:radial_neutral_state_momentum_convection_velocity). The state-averaged counterpart is [radial_neutral_momentum_diffusion_coefficient](name:radial_neutral_momentum_diffusion_coefficient), and the analogous energy-channel diffusivity is [radial_neutral_energy_diffusion_coefficient](name:radial_neutral_energy_diffusion_coefficient).

Typical effective values in edge-plasma and neutral-transport applications are about 0.1-100 m^2.s^-1. Dense divertor or short mean-free-path thermal-neutral conditions may use 0.01-1 m^2.s^-1, while fast or weakly collisional neutrals represented by an effective diffusive closure can require 10-1000 m^2.s^-1.

NAMES.name: radial_neutral_state_velocity
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: Radial (major-radius) component of the bulk convection velocity of neutral particles in a specified internal quantum or energy state.
NAMES.long:
The radial neutral state velocity is the projection of the bulk fluid velocity of a state-resolved neutral population onto the major-radius direction $\hat{R}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height. It is a fluid moment of the state-resolved neutral distribution function, restricted to neutrals occupying a specified excitation, ionization, or molecular energy state, and quantifies their net radial convective transport — not random thermal motion.

The defining relation is:

$$
v_{r,s} = \frac{\int v_R \, f_s(\mathbf{v}) \, d^3v}{\int f_s(\mathbf{v}) \, d^3v}
$$

where $f_s(\mathbf{v})$ is the distribution function of neutrals in internal state $s$, $v_R$ is the particle velocity component along $\hat{R}$, and integration is over all of velocity space.

In edge plasma modeling this quantity enters the radial momentum and continuity equations for each neutral internal state, governing recycling fluxes and fueling efficiency in the scrape-off layer and divertor. It is computed by kinetic or fluid neutral transport codes rather than measured directly. The state-averaged counterpart is [radial_neutral_velocity](name:radial_neutral_velocity), and the parallel_neutral_state_velocity provides the analogous field-aligned component for state-resolved neutrals. The full velocity vector from which this component is extracted is described under [neutral_state_velocity](name:neutral_state_velocity).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the neutral state velocity is directed in the direction of increasing major radius $R$.

NAMES.name: radial_pfirsch_schlueter_current_density
NAMES.subject: pfirsch_schlueter
NAMES.short: Major-radius component of the Pfirsch-Schlüter neoclassical current density in a right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It is the return-current contribution produced by toroidal geometry to maintain current continuity in the presence of pressure-gradient-driven diamagnetic current.
NAMES.long:
Radial Pfirsch-Schlüter current density is the major-radius component of the local Pfirsch-Schlüter neoclassical current density in a toroidal plasma. The Pfirsch-Schlüter current is the return-current contribution associated with toroidal magnetic geometry and pressure-gradient-driven diamagnetic current, arranged so that the total current remains continuous.

The component is defined by projecting the Pfirsch-Schlüter current density vector onto the radial basis vector of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height:

$$
J_{R,\mathrm{PS}} = \mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{PS}} \cdot \hat{R}
$$

where $J_{R,\mathrm{PS}}$ is in A.m^-2, $\mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{PS}}$ is the Pfirsch-Schlüter current density vector, and $\hat{R}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing major radius. This is a local vector component, not a flux-surface average.

In neoclassical transport modeling, $\mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{PS}}$ is obtained from the requirement of current continuity together with magnetic geometry, pressure-gradient information, and collisional transport closures. The radial projection can be nonzero because field-line pitch and flux-surface geometry are not generally aligned with the cylindrical $R$ direction. This quantity is closely related to pfirsch_schlueter_diamagnetic_current_density; together with components such as [toroidal_pfirsch_schlueter_current_density](name:toroidal_pfirsch_schlueter_current_density), it helps specify the full Pfirsch-Schlüter current density vector.

Direct diagnostics usually constrain magnetic geometry, pressure profiles, and total current distributions rather than isolating this component. It is therefore normally inferred from equilibrium or transport calculations and should be interpreted as a signed local contribution to the current density.

No device-independent range exists. As order-of-magnitude guidance, modeled local magnitudes are often near zero in weak-gradient regions and can span 10^1-10^5 A.m^-2 where pressure gradients and geometric projection are strong; the signed value may change across a flux surface.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the Pfirsch-Schlüter current density has a component in the direction of increasing major radius $R$, away from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: radial_total_thermal_electron_energy_flux
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Radial flux of total thermal energy carried by electrons.
NAMES.long:
Radial total thermal electron energy flux is the flux-surface-normal component of thermal energy flux density carried by electrons across nested magnetic flux surfaces. It represents net thermal electron power crossing unit area per unit time, including conductive and convective contributions and any turbulent or neoclassical pieces included in the total electron thermal energy balance.

With a flux coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$ where $\rho$ labels magnetic flux surfaces and increases outward from the magnetic axis to the plasma boundary, the radial flux density is defined as the surface-normal projection of the total thermal electron energy flux density vector:

$$
q_{e,\rho}^{\mathrm{th,tot}}(\rho)=\left\langle \mathbf{q}_e^{\mathrm{th,tot}}\cdot\frac{\nabla \rho}{|\nabla \rho|}\right\rangle_\rho
$$

where $\mathbf{q}_e^{\mathrm{th,tot}}$ is the total thermal electron energy flux density vector and $\langle\cdot\rangle_\rho$ denotes an average over the surface $\rho=\mathrm{constant}$. The corresponding electron thermal power is obtained by integrating this normal flux over the surface; this quantity is a flux density, not the surface-integrated power.

In practice it is inferred from radial electron energy balance using electron density and temperature evolution, heating deposition, radiation losses, interspecies energy exchange, and reconstructed flux-surface geometry, or computed directly by transport models as the sum of modeled electron thermal transport channels. It is the total-thermal counterpart of [radial_electron_energy_flux](name:radial_electron_energy_flux) and is commonly compared with ion and neutral energy-flux contributions.

Typical core magnitudes in tokamak transport studies are 10^3-10^6 W m^-2, rising to 10^6-10^7 W m^-2 in strongly heated edge or pedestal regions. Smaller values or sign reversals can occur during transients, in regions with hollow temperature structure, or where inward convective transport offsets conductive losses.
NAMES.sign: Positive when thermal electron energy is transported toward increasing flux-surface radial coordinate $\rho$, outward from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: ratio_of_deuterium_tritium_density_to_electron_density
NAMES.short: Ratio of the fictitious combined deuterium-tritium fuel-ion density to the electron density, measuring the DT fuel purity fraction of the plasma composition.
NAMES.long:
The combined deuterium-tritium fuel-ion density fraction characterizes what proportion of the electron charge is balanced by DT fuel ions, where the DT pseudo-species treats deuterium and tritium as a single effective ion; see [deuterium_tritium_density](name:deuterium_tritium_density) for the definition of the underlying density. This ratio parametrizes fuel purity and dilution relative to helium ash and impurity ion loading.

$$
f_{DT} = \frac{n_{DT}}{n_e}
$$

where $n_{DT}$ is the combined DT fuel-ion number density and $n_e$ is the electron number density, both in m$^{-3}$.

In a pure DT plasma, quasi-neutrality ($n_e \approx n_{DT}$ for singly charged fuel ions) gives $f_{DT} \approx 1$. Helium ash accumulation and impurity seeding reduce this ratio below unity, and sustaining $f_{DT}$ close to 1 is important for maintaining fusion reactivity in burning-plasma scenarios. The ratio relates to the individual isotope analogs [ratio_of_tritium_density_to_electron_density](name:ratio_of_tritium_density_to_electron_density) and [volume_averaged_deuterium_fraction](name:volume_averaged_deuterium_fraction), which resolve the D and T components separately.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the deuterium-tritium fuel species is present in the plasma.

NAMES.name: runaway_electron_density
NAMES.subject: runaway_electron
NAMES.short: Local number density of runaway electrons, the suprathermal electron population that remains in the accelerating tail of the electron distribution rather than thermalizing with the bulk plasma.
NAMES.long:
Runaway electron density $n_\mathrm{RE}$ is the number of runaway electrons per unit physical volume at a point in the plasma. It is a non-negative scalar field describing the local population of electrons whose high momentum makes collisional slowing-down ineffective compared with continued acceleration by the electromagnetic fields.

A local particle balance for the runaway population is commonly written as

$$
\frac{\partial n_\mathrm{RE}}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_\mathrm{RE} = S_\mathrm{RE} - L_\mathrm{RE}
$$

where $n_\mathrm{RE}$ is the runaway electron density in m$^{-3}$, $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_\mathrm{RE}$ is the runaway electron particle flux in m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$, and $S_\mathrm{RE}$ and $L_\mathrm{RE}$ are local volumetric source and loss rates in m$^{-3}$ s$^{-1}$. Source terms may represent mechanisms such as Dreicer generation, avalanche multiplication, or hot-tail formation; loss terms represent removal from the runaway population or transport out of the local volume, depending on the model.

The quantity is usually inferred rather than measured directly, using hard x-ray, gamma-ray, synchrotron, bremsstrahlung, or current measurements interpreted with kinetic or fluid runaway-electron models. A volume average of this local field gives the corresponding volume-averaged runaway electron density.

Typical modeled values span about $10^{12}$-$10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$. Disruption-generated runaway beams often have local densities around $10^{15}$-$10^{17}$ m$^{-3}$, generally well below the bulk thermal electron density even when they carry a large fraction of the plasma current.

NAMES.name: runaway_electron_energy_density
NAMES.subject: runaway_electron
NAMES.short: Kinetic energy per unit volume of the runaway electron population, incorporating their characteristically relativistic energies reached through electric-field acceleration beyond the Dreicer threshold.
NAMES.long:
The runaway electron energy density is the local kinetic energy stored per unit volume by the runaway electron (RE) population on a given flux surface. Unlike thermal electrons, runaway electrons are accelerated to suprathermal and relativistic energies by a parallel electric field exceeding the critical (Dreicer) threshold, so their energy density must account for relativistic kinematics. It is the electron-population analog of [ion_species_kinetic_energy_density](name:ion_species_kinetic_energy_density) but for the non-thermal, suprathermal runaway component.

The defining expression integrates the relativistic kinetic energy over the RE momentum-space distribution:

$$
\mathcal{E}_{RE} = \int (\gamma - 1) \, m_e c^2 \, f_{RE}(\mathbf{p}) \, d^3p
$$

where $\gamma = (1 + p^2/m_e^2 c^2)^{1/2}$ is the Lorentz factor, $m_e$ is the electron rest mass, $c$ is the speed of light, and $f_{RE}(\mathbf{p})$ is the runaway electron distribution function in momentum space $\mathbf{p}$.

This quantity is computed from kinetic Fokker–Planck solvers or fluid-moment RE models that evolve the runaway population. Volumetrically integrating $\mathcal{E}_{RE}$ over the confined plasma yields the total [runaway electron kinetic energy](name:runaway_electron_kinetic_energy), while averaging over the plasma volume gives the [volume-averaged energy density](name:volume_averaged_runaway_electron_kinetic_energy_density). The current density carried by the same population is characterized by [parallel runaway electron current density](name:parallel_runaway_electron_current_density).

Post-disruption runaway beams in tokamaks can accumulate MeV-range electrons at number densities of $10^{16}$–$10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$, producing local energy densities of order $10^3$–$10^6$ J m$^{-3}$.

NAMES.name: runaway_electron_kinetic_energy
NAMES.subject: runaway_electron
NAMES.short: Total relativistic kinetic energy integrated over the entire runaway electron population, providing a global measure of runaway beam energy content relevant to disruption mitigation.
NAMES.long:
The runaway electron kinetic energy is the total relativistic kinetic energy carried by all electrons in the runaway population, integrated over both velocity space and the plasma volume. It quantifies the collective destructive energy of a runaway beam and is a primary figure of merit for assessing damage potential to plasma-facing components during disruptions.

The quantity is obtained by integrating the single-particle relativistic kinetic energy over the runaway electron distribution function $f_{RE}(\mathbf{p})$:

$$
W_{RE} = \int (\gamma - 1)\, m_e c^2 \, f_{RE}(\mathbf{p}) \, d^3\mathbf{p} \, dV
$$

where $\gamma = \sqrt{1 + p^2/(m_e^2 c^2)}$ is the Lorentz factor, $m_e$ is the electron rest mass, $c$ is the speed of light, $\mathbf{p}$ is the relativistic momentum, and $V$ is the plasma volume.

This global integral complements the local [runaway_electron_energy_density](name:runaway_electron_energy_density), which expresses the same energy per unit volume. Combined with runaway_electron_count, it yields the mean kinetic energy per runaway electron, characterizing the typical particle energy in the beam.

In large-tokamak disruption scenarios, runaway beam energies range from tens of kJ in minor events to tens of MJ in full-current disruptions, with individual electron energies of 1–100 MeV. The total energy is inferred from hard X-ray bremsstrahlung spectroscopy, synchrotron radiation imaging, or computed from kinetic simulations of runaway generation and transport.

NAMES.name: runaway_electron_source_rate_due_to_compton_scattering
NAMES.subject: runaway_electron
NAMES.short: Local volumetric production rate of runaway electrons generated by Compton scattering of high-energy gamma-ray photons off plasma electrons. It counts scattering events in which the recoiling electron gains enough momentum to exceed the critical runaway momentum and join the runaway population.
NAMES.long:
Runaway-electron source rate due to Compton scattering is the local rate of increase of runaway-electron number density caused by Compton scattering of high-energy gamma-ray photons off plasma electrons. In a scattering event a photon transfers part of its energy and momentum to an electron; if the recoiling electron's momentum exceeds the critical runaway momentum, the electron joins the runaway population. The relevant threshold is the critical momentum shared by avalanche, Compton, and tritium-decay generation channels, described by [volume_averaged_critical_momentum](name:volume_averaged_runaway_electron_critical_momentum_due_to_avalanche) and [critical_momentum_due_to_avalanche](name:critical_momentum_due_to_avalanche).

This source rate is obtained schematically by folding the local photon flux against the Compton scattering kinematics and retaining only events that push the electron above the runaway threshold:

$$
S_\mathrm{Compton} = n_e \int \Phi_\gamma(E_\gamma) \left[ \int_{p > p_\mathrm{crit}} \frac{d\sigma}{dp}\, dp \right] dE_\gamma
$$

where $S_\mathrm{Compton}$ is this source rate in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, $n_e$ is the target-electron number density in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, $\Phi_\gamma(E_\gamma)$ is the differential gamma-ray photon flux as a function of photon energy $E_\gamma$, $d\sigma/dp$ is the Compton differential cross section for producing a recoil electron of momentum $p$, and $p_\mathrm{crit}$ is the critical runaway momentum. This term enters the local runaway-electron density balance additively alongside other source and loss terms such as Dreicer generation, hot-tail seeding, avalanche multiplication, tritium-decay seeding, and transport losses.

In practice this rate is computed rather than measured directly: it relies on a model of the local gamma-ray photon spectrum (typically from activated structural materials), the local electron density, the Compton differential cross section, and the runaway-threshold momentum. It is constrained indirectly through photon-source modeling, gamma-ray measurements, and comparison with the resulting runaway-electron density or current evolution.

Typical values are strongly scenario dependent because the rate scales with the local gamma-ray flux, the photon energy spectrum, the target-electron density, and the critical momentum. In configurations without a penetrating high-energy gamma source the appropriate value is $0\ \mathrm{m}^{-3}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$. As a local volumetric rate it should be compared with sibling local source terms such as [runaway_electron_source_rate_due_to_hot_tail](name:runaway_electron_source_rate_due_to_hot_tail); its spatial mean over the plasma volume, with the same unit, is [volume_averaged_runaway_electron_source_rate](name:volume_averaged_runaway_electron_source_rate), which is a volume average rather than the volume-integrated total production rate. The corresponding source rate for the broader suprathermal population produced by the same mechanism is [fast_electron_source_rate_due_to_compton_scattering](name:fast_electron_source_rate_due_to_compton_scattering).
NAMES.sign: Positive when Compton scattering increases the local runaway-electron number density.

NAMES.name: runaway_electron_source_rate_due_to_hot_tail
NAMES.subject: runaway_electron
NAMES.short: Local volumetric rate at which a rapid thermal quench converts surviving suprathermal electrons of the pre-quench distribution into runaway electrons by the hot-tail mechanism. It counts only electrons driven above the runaway threshold, and is a non-negative production term.
NAMES.long:
Runaway electron source rate due to hot-tail generation is the local rate of increase of runaway electron density produced when suprathermal electrons fail to thermalize during a rapid electron-temperature collapse and are left above the runaway threshold. It is a scalar volumetric source density in real space; its value at a point is independent of the coordinate labeling, including the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The source rate is defined as the hot-tail contribution to the time derivative of the runaway electron density:

$$
S_\mathrm{ht} = \left.\frac{\partial n_\mathrm{RE}}{\partial t}\right|_\mathrm{hot\text{-}tail}
$$

where $n_\mathrm{RE}$ is the runaway electron density in m$^{-3}$. The magnitude depends on the competition between collisional slowing-down and the thermal-quench time scale, and on the evolving critical runaway momentum threshold, quantified by critical_momentum_due_to_hot_tail (expressed as a physical momentum in kg m$^{-1}$ s$^{-1}$); electrons retaining momentum above this threshold after cooling are counted as runaways.

This quantity is computed from kinetic or reduced runaway-electron models by integrating the part of the pre-quench electron distribution that survives above the critical momentum after rapid cooling. By construction it is a one-sided production term: it represents only the addition of runaway electrons and is therefore non-negative, with losses handled by separate sink terms. It is often compared with the [Dreicer source](name:runaway_electron_source_rate_due_to_dreicer) and can dominate seed formation when the temperature drop is fast compared with suprathermal-electron collisional relaxation. The analogous rate for the broader fast-electron population produced by the same mechanism is [fast_electron_source_rate_due_to_hot_tail](name:fast_electron_source_rate_due_to_hot_tail), part of the aggregate [fast_electron_source_rate](name:fast_electron_source_rate); the volume-averaged counterpart of all runaway generation channels is [volume_averaged_runaway_electron_source_rate](name:volume_averaged_runaway_electron_source_rate).

The rate is essentially zero outside a rapid thermal quench and rises sharply during disruptions, with the peak local value set by the pre-quench temperature and density, the cooling time, the effective charge, and the post-quench electric field.

NAMES.name: safety_factor
NAMES.short: Dimensionless ratio of toroidal to poloidal magnetic flux increments per field-line circuit, equal to the number of times a field line winds toroidally per complete poloidal transit of a flux surface.
NAMES.long:
The safety factor $q(\psi)$ measures the helical winding of magnetic field lines on a given flux surface: it equals the number of complete toroidal transits a field line completes for each poloidal circuit around the inner plasma region.

The formal definition relates $q$ to the ratio of magnetic flux increments:

$$
q = \frac{d\Phi_{\rm tor}}{d\Phi_{\rm pol} / (2\pi)}
$$

where $\Phi_{\rm tor}$ is the toroidal magnetic flux (Wb) enclosed within the flux surface and $\Phi_{\rm pol}$ is the poloidal magnetic flux (Wb) encircled by the flux-surface boundary. Surfaces where $q = m/n$ (integers $m$, $n$) are resonant with magnetohydrodynamic perturbations of poloidal mode number $m$ and toroidal mode number $n$, enabling tearing modes and neoclassical tearing modes; the $q = 1$ resonant surface underpins sawtooth instabilities, and the $q = 2$ surface is associated with the onset of neoclassical tearing modes in high-performance discharges.

In conventional H-mode operation, the [safety factor at the magnetic axis](name:safety_factor_at_magnetic_axis) is typically near 1, while the [safety factor at the 95% normalized poloidal flux surface](name:safety_factor_at_normalized_poloidal_magnetic_flux_equal_to_0_95) lies in the range 3–5. Reversed-shear configurations have an interior $q$ minimum, and elevated $q$ at the [pedestal](name:safety_factor_at_pedestal) constrains edge stability. The $q$ profile is inferred from equilibrium reconstruction augmented by internal measurements such as motional Stark effect polarimetry or Faraday rotation; it is also evaluated locally on individual flux surfaces in gyrokinetic turbulence simulations.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the toroidal magnetic field $B_\phi$ and the plasma current $I_p$ are both directed in the sense of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: second_radial_derivative_of_electron_pressure
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Second derivative of electron pressure with respect to the normalized toroidal flux radius. It represents the local radial curvature of electron pressure across nested magnetic-flux surfaces.
NAMES.long:
The second radial derivative of [electron pressure](name:electron_pressure) is the curvature of $p_e$ as a function of the normalized toroidal flux radius $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$. The coordinate $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$ is a dimensionless flux coordinate defined from toroidal magnetic flux, with value 0 at the magnetic axis and 1 at the plasma boundary.

The derivative is defined by differentiating electron pressure twice with respect to $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$:

$$
\frac{d^2 p_e}{d\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}^2}
$$

where $p_e$ is electron pressure in pascals and $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$ is dimensionless. Because the differentiating coordinate is dimensionless, this quantity has the same unit as electron pressure.

In practice it is obtained from measured, fitted, or reconstructed electron-pressure radial variation by applying numerical differentiation or by differentiating a smooth analytic representation. Second derivatives are sensitive to noise and radial resolution, so smoothing, regularization, or differentiable basis functions are commonly used before evaluating the curvature.

Typical magnitudes span a wide range, roughly $10^3$-$10^8$ Pa in core and edge transport analyzes, with larger absolute values possible where the electron pressure changes over a narrow interval in $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the slope $d p_e/d\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$ increases as $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$ increases outward.

NAMES.name: second_radial_derivative_of_fast_electron_pressure
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Second derivative of the suprathermal electron perpendicular pressure with respect to normalized toroidal flux coordinate; equal to the local radial curvature of the fast electron pressure profile.
NAMES.long:
The second radial derivative of [fast_electron_pressure](name:fast_electron_pressure) measures the curvature of the perpendicular pressure profile of suprathermal (fast) electrons with respect to the normalized toroidal flux coordinate $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$. Fast electrons — those with kinetic energies substantially above the local bulk electron thermal energy — are produced during electron cyclotron heating, lower hybrid current drive, and runaway electron generation, and their pressure supplements the thermal electron contribution in the total plasma pressure balance.

The quantity is defined as:

$$
\frac{d^2 p_{e,\mathrm{fast},\perp}}{d\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}^2}
$$

where $p_{e,\mathrm{fast},\perp}$ is the fast electron perpendicular pressure and $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$ ranges from 0 at the magnetic axis to 1 at the last-closed flux surface.

This derivative is computed numerically within integrated transport solvers as part of the complete set of first- and second-order radial profile derivatives required for accurate higher-order spatial discretization of the transport equations. It is the second-order counterpart to [radial_derivative_of_fast_electron_pressure](name:radial_derivative_of_fast_electron_pressure), the fast-particle analog of [second_radial_derivative_of_electron_pressure](name:second_radial_derivative_of_electron_pressure) for the thermal bulk electron population, and mirrors the fast ion quantity [second_radial_derivative_of_fast_ion_pressure](name:second_radial_derivative_of_fast_ion_pressure).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the radial gradient of fast electron perpendicular pressure increases in the direction of increasing $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$, corresponding to a locally concave-upward pressure profile.

NAMES.name: second_radial_derivative_of_fast_ion_density
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Second derivative of fast (non-thermal) ion number density with respect to the normalized toroidal flux coordinate, capturing the radial curvature of the non-thermal ion density profile.
NAMES.long:
The second radial derivative of fast-ion density measures the local curvature of the non-thermal ion population density profile along the normalized toroidal flux coordinate $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm} \in [0, 1]$. It quantifies how rapidly the radial slope of [fast_ion_density](name:fast_ion_density) changes across nested flux surfaces, which is central to higher-order spatial discretization of fast-ion transport equations.

The quantity is formally defined as:

$$
\frac{d^2 n_\mathrm{fast}}{d\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}^2}
$$

where $n_\mathrm{fast}$ is the fast-ion number density summed over all charge states, and $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$ is the normalized toroidal flux radius equal to 0 at the magnetic axis and 1 at the separatrix. Because $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$ is dimensionless, differentiation preserves the dimensions of $n_\mathrm{fast}$.

This derivative is computed numerically within transport solver frameworks as part of the internal spatial discretization of fast-ion transport equations. The first radial derivative [radial_derivative_of_fast_ion_density](name:radial_derivative_of_fast_ion_density) provides the corresponding radial slope, while [second_radial_derivative_of_fast_ion_state_density](name:second_radial_derivative_of_fast_ion_state_density) gives the charge-state-resolved version. The species-summed counterpart [second_radial_derivative_of_total_ion_density](name:second_radial_derivative_of_total_ion_density) includes both thermal and non-thermal ion contributions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the fast-ion density profile is concave upward with respect to increasing $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$, i.e., when the radial gradient of $n_\mathrm{fast}$ increases with increasing $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$.

NAMES.name: second_radial_derivative_of_fast_ion_pressure
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Second derivative of the charge-state-averaged fast ion pressure with respect to normalized toroidal flux coordinate, quantifying the radial curvature of the non-thermal ion pressure profile for transport solver numerics.
NAMES.long:
The second radial derivative of fast ion pressure measures the spatial curvature of the charge-state-averaged non-thermal ion pressure profile along the normalized toroidal flux coordinate. Fast ions — including fusion-born alpha particles, neutral-beam-injected ions, and ions accelerated by radio-frequency waves — carry a suprathermal pressure contribution that departs substantially from a local Maxwellian; summing over charge states yields the total [fast_ion_pressure](name:fast_ion_pressure) $p_{fast,i}$ from which this derivative is computed.

The quantity is defined as:

$$
\frac{d^2 p_{fast,i}}{d\rho_{tor,norm}^2}
$$

where $p_{fast,i}$ is the fast ion pressure summed over charge states and $\rho_{tor,norm} \in [0, 1]$ is the normalized toroidal flux radius, equal to 0 at the magnetic axis and 1 at the last closed flux surface.

This second derivative is evaluated internally by transport solvers from kinetic fast-ion pressure profiles, typically provided by Fokker-Planck or Monte Carlo fast-ion models. It is the charge-state-averaged analog of [second_radial_derivative_of_fast_ion_state_pressure](name:second_radial_derivative_of_fast_ion_state_pressure), which resolves individual charge states; the corresponding electron quantity is [second_radial_derivative_of_fast_electron_pressure](name:second_radial_derivative_of_fast_electron_pressure). The first-order spatial derivative of the same pressure profile is [radial_derivative_of_fast_ion_pressure](name:radial_derivative_of_fast_ion_pressure).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the fast ion pressure profile curves upward with increasing $\rho_{tor,norm}$, i.e., when the radial slope of $p_{fast,i}$ increases with increasing normalized toroidal flux.

NAMES.name: second_radial_derivative_of_ion_pressure
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Second derivative of total ion pressure (thermal and non-thermal contributions, summed over all charge states) with respect to the normalized toroidal flux coordinate.
NAMES.long:
The second radial derivative of total ion pressure quantifies the local curvature of the ion pressure profile along the normalized toroidal flux coordinate $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$. The pressure $P_i$ includes both thermal and non-thermal contributions, summed over all ion species and charge states, making this the aggregate counterpart to [second_radial_derivative_of_ion_state_pressure](name:second_radial_derivative_of_ion_state_pressure), which resolves individual charge states.

The quantity is defined as:

$$
\frac{d^2 P_i}{d\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}^2}
$$

where $P_i$ is the total ion pressure and $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ is the normalized toroidal flux coordinate ranging from 0 at the magnetic axis to 1 at the last closed flux surface. Because $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ is dimensionless, this second derivative is dimensionally equivalent to [ion_pressure](name:ion_pressure) itself.

This curvature quantity is computed numerically from the radial ion pressure profile and is used by transport solvers for higher-order spatial discretization of the pressure transport equation. It complements the first-order slope captured by [radial_derivative_of_ion_pressure](name:radial_derivative_of_ion_pressure) and the electron-channel analog [second_radial_derivative_of_electron_pressure](name:second_radial_derivative_of_electron_pressure). In H-mode plasmas, the magnitude can be large near the pedestal region, where the pressure gradient slope changes rapidly.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the radial gradient of ion pressure is increasing with increasing $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$, corresponding to positive curvature of the ion pressure profile.

NAMES.name: second_radial_derivative_of_ion_state_pressure
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Second derivative of the thermal pressure of a specified ion charge state with respect to the normalized toroidal flux coordinate, giving the local radial curvature of that charge-state pressure profile.
NAMES.long:
The second radial derivative of [ion_state_pressure](name:ion_state_pressure) quantifies the local curvature of the partial-pressure profile for a single ionic charge state along the normalized toroidal flux coordinate $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$. It is the charge-state-resolved counterpart of [second_radial_derivative_of_ion_pressure](name:second_radial_derivative_of_ion_pressure), which aggregates over all charge states, and the second-order extension of [radial_derivative_of_ion_state_pressure](name:radial_derivative_of_ion_state_pressure).

The quantity is defined as:

$$
\frac{d^2 p_z}{d\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}^2}
$$

where $p_z$ is the thermal pressure of the ion species in charge state $z$ and $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$ is the normalized toroidal flux radius, ranging from 0 at the magnetic axis to 1 at the last closed flux surface. Because $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$ is dimensionless, the second derivative retains the same units as the pressure itself.

Transport solvers require higher-order radial derivatives of species profiles for accurate discretization of the transport equations and for Jacobian evaluation in implicit time-advance schemes. This quantity is computed alongside the analogous [second_radial_derivative_of_ion_state_temperature](name:second_radial_derivative_of_ion_state_temperature). In a typical peaked-pressure core, the second derivative is positive near the magnetic axis where the pressure gradient is shallow, and can become strongly negative across a steep pedestal region.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the ion charge-state pressure profile is concave upward as a function of increasing $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$, i.e., when $d^2 p_z / d\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}^2 > 0$.

NAMES.name: second_radial_derivative_of_poloidal_ion_velocity
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Second derivative of the charge-state-averaged poloidal ion bulk flow velocity with respect to rho_tor_norm, the normalized toroidal flux radius. Because the differentiation coordinate is dimensionless, the quantity retains velocity units and characterizes the radial curvature of the signed poloidal ion flow profile.
NAMES.long:
The second radial derivative of poloidal ion velocity is the second derivative, taken with respect to the normalized toroidal flux radius $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$, of the charge-state-averaged poloidal component of the ion bulk flow velocity. It quantifies the radial curvature of the signed poloidal ion flow as it varies across nested magnetic flux surfaces.

$$
\frac{\partial^2 v_{\mathrm{pol,i}}}{\partial \rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}^2}
$$

where $v_{\mathrm{pol,i}}$ is the charge-state-averaged poloidal ion bulk velocity in m s$^{-1}$ and $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ is the dimensionless normalized toroidal flux radius, equal to 0 at the magnetic axis and 1 at the last closed flux surface. The result carries units of m s$^{-1}$ because the differentiation coordinate is dimensionless.

In practice the quantity is evaluated numerically from a smooth radial representation of the poloidal ion velocity, which itself derives from charge-exchange spectroscopy, spectroscopic flow inference, neoclassical estimates, or transport modeling. Charge-state averaging combines the individual ion charge states into a single bulk ion velocity before differentiation; the resulting curvature is sensitive to the radial resolution and smoothing applied to the underlying velocity profile.

Magnitudes are typically modest across the broad plasma core and become substantially larger within narrow pedestal or transport-barrier regions, where the poloidal flow changes rapidly over a short radial extent. The sign follows the local concavity of the velocity profile as a function of $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the radial gradient of the poloidal ion velocity increases with increasing $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ (the velocity profile is concave upward), with positive poloidal ion velocity defined in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in the flux coordinates $(\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}, \theta, \phi)$.

NAMES.name: second_radial_derivative_of_total_electron_density
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Second derivative of total electron number density with respect to the normalized toroidal flux coordinate, quantifying the radial curvature of the electron density profile.
NAMES.long:
The second radial derivative of total electron density characterizes the curvature of the electron density profile along the normalized toroidal flux coordinate $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$. The total electron density $n_e$ encompasses both thermal and non-thermal (fast) electron sub-populations, making this derivative applicable across all plasma regimes where both contribute — consistent with [total_electron_density](name:total_electron_density).

The quantity is formally defined as:

$$
\frac{\partial^2 n_e}{\partial \rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}^2}
$$

where $n_e$ is the total electron number density and $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm} \in [0, 1]$ is the normalized toroidal flux coordinate, with $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm} = 0$ at the magnetic axis and $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm} = 1$ at the last-closed flux surface. Because $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$ is dimensionless, this second derivative carries the same units as the density itself.

This derivative is computed numerically within transport solver discretizations, where second-order spatial operators appear in the diffusion terms of the radial transport equations. It complements the first-order [radial_derivative_of_total_electron_density](name:radial_derivative_of_total_electron_density), together providing both the gradient and curvature information needed for higher-order numerical schemes. The corresponding quantity for the fast electron sub-population is [second_radial_derivative_of_fast_electron_density](name:second_radial_derivative_of_fast_electron_density), and the analogous ion-state quantity is [second_radial_derivative_of_total_ion_state_density](name:second_radial_derivative_of_total_ion_state_density).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the total electron density profile is concave upward with respect to increasing $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$, i.e., when the outward radial gradient of $n_e$ increases with increasing normalized toroidal flux.

NAMES.name: thermal_electron_power_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Volumetric Coulomb-collisional energy transfer rate into the bulk thermal electron population from a fast or otherwise non-Maxwellian particle population. It is integrated over trapped and passing guiding-center orbit classes and is positive for thermal-electron heating.
NAMES.long:
Thermal electron power density due to collisions is the local rate per unit volume at which Coulomb collisions transfer kinetic energy from a fast or otherwise non-Maxwellian particle population to the bulk thermal electron population. It is the orbit-class-integrated electron-channel collisional heating term, including trapped and passing guiding-center contributions when those classes are distinguished.

The quantity can be written as the negative kinetic-energy moment of the fast-particle collision operator associated with collisions against thermal electrons:

$$
p_{e,\mathrm{th}}^{\mathrm{coll}}(\mathbf{x}) = -\int \frac{1}{2} m_f v^2\, C_{fe}[f_f](\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\, d^3v
$$

where $p_{e,\mathrm{th}}^{\mathrm{coll}}$ is this power density, $m_f$ is the fast-particle mass, $v=|\mathbf{v}|$ is particle speed, $f_f$ is the fast-particle distribution function with units m^-6 s^3, $C_{fe}[f_f]$ is the rate of change of $f_f$ caused by Coulomb collisions with thermal electrons with units m^-6 s^2, and $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element with units m^3 s^-3. The minus sign converts fast-particle kinetic-energy loss into thermal-electron energy gain, giving units W m^-3.

This quantity is not measured directly. It is inferred from kinetic or transport calculations that evaluate Coulomb drag and diffusion of the non-Maxwellian population using the local thermal electron density and temperature; experimental constraints may include fast-particle, neutron, charge-exchange, radiation, and thermal-electron diagnostics depending on the source species and plasma regime.

Typical values in auxiliary-heated magnetic-fusion plasmas are 10^3-10^6 W m^-3, with strongly localized deposition reaching about 10^7 W m^-3. Values can be near zero in weak fast-particle regions and can be negative if collisions transfer energy from the thermal electrons to the non-Maxwellian population.
NAMES.sign: Positive when Coulomb collisions transfer energy to the bulk thermal electron population.

NAMES.name: co_passing_thermal_electron_power_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Collisional power density deposited in thermal electrons by Coulomb interactions with co-passing fast particles. It is the co-passing orbit-class contribution to thermal-electron collisional heating and is positive for net heating of the thermal electron population.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the volumetric rate of collisional energy transfer into the thermal electron population from fast particles whose guiding-center orbits are co-passing. Co-passing denotes the passing-orbit class with toroidal circulation in the same sense as the net plasma current, complementing the counter-passing class in an orbit-resolved decomposition of collisional heating.

The quantity is defined as the co-passing contribution to the time rate of change of thermal-electron internal energy density caused by Coulomb collisions with the fast-particle distribution:

$$
P_{\mathrm{co}\to e,\mathrm{th}}^{\mathrm{coll}} = \left(\frac{\partial U_{e,\mathrm{th}}}{\partial t}\right)_{\mathrm{coll},\,\mathrm{co}\to e}
$$

where $U_{e,\mathrm{th}}$ is the thermal-electron internal energy density in J m^-3, $t$ is time in s, and the subscript $\mathrm{co}\to e$ denotes energy transfer from the co-passing fast-particle orbit class to thermal electrons. The resulting unit is W m^-3.

In kinetic calculations it is obtained from a Coulomb or Fokker-Planck collision operator, or from an equivalent Monte Carlo slowing-down treatment, by assigning fast-particle phase-space elements to the co-passing orbit class and accumulating the energy gained by the bulk electron population. Together with the [counter-passing thermal-electron contribution](name:counter_passing_thermal_electron_power_density_due_to_collisions) and any trapped-orbit contribution, it forms the orbit-class decomposition of [thermal_electron_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:thermal_electron_power_density_due_to_collisions); the corresponding co-passing thermal-ion heating channel is [co_passing_thermal_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:co_passing_thermal_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions).

Typical magnitudes in auxiliary-heated tokamak plasmas are 10^2-10^6 W m^-3 over much of the confined plasma, with localized fast-particle slowing-down regions reaching 10^6-10^7 W m^-3. Values approach zero where the co-passing fast-particle density is small, and may be negative if collisions transfer net energy from thermal electrons to this orbit class.
NAMES.sign: Positive when Coulomb collisions increase the thermal electron internal energy density through energy transfer from co-passing fast particles.

NAMES.name: counter_passing_thermal_electron_power_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Power density deposited in the bulk thermal electron population by Coulomb collisions with fast particles on counter-passing guiding-center orbits.
NAMES.long:
Counter-passing thermal electron power density due to collisions is the rate per unit plasma volume at which Coulomb collisions transfer kinetic energy from the counter-passing part of a fast-particle population to the bulk thermal electrons. Its unit is W m$^{-3}$. Counter-passing denotes passing guiding-center orbits whose orbit-averaged toroidal motion is opposite to the net plasma-current direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

Using a collision operator acting on the fast-particle distribution, the deposited power density may be written as

$$
P_{e,\mathrm{th}}^{\mathrm{cp,coll}} = -\int_{\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{cp}}} \mathcal{E}_f\, C_{fe}^{(f)}[f_f] \, d^3v
$$

where $\mathcal{E}_f$ is the fast-particle kinetic energy in J, $f_f$ is the fast-particle distribution with units s$^3$ m$^{-6}$ for velocity-space coordinates, $C_{fe}^{(f)}[f_f]$ is the Coulomb collision operator for fast-particle changes caused by thermal electrons and has units of $f_f$ per second, and $d^3v$ has units m$^3$ s$^{-3}$. The minus sign makes the expression positive when the selected fast particles lose energy to the thermal electrons; equivalently, an electron-gain collision operator would enter with the opposite sign. The integration domain $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{cp}}$ contains the passing guiding-center states satisfying $\langle \dot{\phi} \rangle I_p < 0$, with $\langle \dot{\phi} \rangle$ the orbit-averaged toroidal angular velocity and $I_p$ positive for plasma current in the direction of increasing $\phi$.

This quantity is generally inferred from kinetic modeling of the fast-particle distribution and Coulomb slowing-down physics, often constrained by fast-particle, neutron, radiation, and thermal-electron measurements. It can be evaluated locally or as an average over magnetic surfaces, but in all cases it represents an energy-transfer rate density rather than the total deposited power.

Typical magnitudes in heated tokamak plasmas are about $10^3$-$10^6$ W m$^{-3}$ across much of the plasma volume, with localized core values reaching $10^7$ W m$^{-3}$ for strong neutral-beam, radio-frequency-generated, or fusion-alpha fast-particle populations. Values near zero occur where the counter-passing population is weak, and negative values indicate net collisional energy transfer from thermal electrons to that selected fast-particle population.
NAMES.sign: Positive when collisions transfer energy from the counter-passing fast-particle population to the bulk thermal electron population.

NAMES.name: thermal_electron_power_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Volume-integrated Coulomb collisional power transferred from a fast non-Maxwellian particle population, including trapped and passing orbit classes, to bulk thermal electrons. Positive values denote heating of the thermal electrons.
NAMES.long:
Thermal electron power due to collisions is the total rate at which Coulomb collisions transfer energy from a specified fast, non-Maxwellian particle population to the bulk Maxwellian electron population over the plasma volume. It includes trapped and passing orbit classes of the fast population when both are present, and excludes collisional transfer to thermal ions and non-Coulomb sinks or sources.

The global power is the volume integral of the local thermal-electron collisional power density:

$$
P_{e,\mathrm{coll}} = \int_V p_{e,\mathrm{coll}}(\mathbf{x})\,dV
$$

where $P_{e,\mathrm{coll}}$ is the total collisional power in W, $p_{e,\mathrm{coll}}$ is the local power density delivered to thermal electrons in W m$^{-3}$, $dV$ is the physical volume element in m$^3$, and $V$ is the plasma volume over which the fast-particle distribution and thermal background are defined.

In kinetic calculations, $p_{e,\mathrm{coll}}$ is obtained as an energy-transfer moment of the Coulomb interaction between the fast-particle distribution and the thermal electron Maxwellian. If the distribution function is normalized so that integration over velocity gives number density in m$^{-3}$, then the distribution has units s$^3$ m$^{-6}$ and the velocity-space measure $d^3v$ has units m$^3$ s$^{-3}$; the resulting energy-transfer moment has units W m$^{-3}$ before volume integration. Orbit-following, Fokker-Planck, and Monte Carlo calculations usually sum contributions over all resolved fast-particle orbit classes, including trapped and passing particles.

Typical magnitudes are 10$^4$-10$^7$ W for energetic-particle electron heating in present medium-size and high-power tokamaks, and 10$^7$-10$^8$ W in burning-plasma scenarios where fusion alpha particles provide substantial electron heating. Values near zero or negative can occur when the modeled fast population receives net collisional energy from hotter thermal electrons.
NAMES.sign: Positive when Coulomb collisions transfer net energy to the bulk thermal electron population.

NAMES.name: thermal_electron_pressure_at_post_sawtooth_crash
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Thermal electron pressure of the bulk Maxwellian electron population evaluated at the first resolved state after a sawtooth crash, excluding suprathermal and fast-electron pressure.
NAMES.long:
Thermal electron pressure at post-sawtooth crash is the isotropic kinetic pressure associated with random thermal motion of the bulk Maxwellian electron population after the rapid sawtooth collapse. The post-crash qualifier denotes evaluation at the first resolved plasma state after the collapse has ended and before substantial reheating in the next sawtooth ramp. It is the thermal component of [electron_pressure_at_post_sawtooth_crash](name:electron_pressure_at_post_sawtooth_crash) and excludes nonthermal contributions that can make [total_electron_pressure](name:total_electron_pressure) larger.

For a Maxwellian thermal electron population, the pressure is given by the equation of state:

$$
p_{e,\mathrm{th}} = n_{e,\mathrm{th}}\,T_{e,\mathrm{th}}
$$

where $p_{e,\mathrm{th}}$ is the thermal electron pressure, $n_{e,\mathrm{th}}$ is the [thermal_electron_density](name:thermal_electron_density) in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, and $T_{e,\mathrm{th}}$ is the thermal electron temperature expressed as an energy in joules. If temperature is quoted in electronvolts, the joule-valued temperature is $e\,T_{e,\mathrm{th}}[\mathrm{eV}]$, where $e$ is the elementary charge.

A sawtooth crash rapidly redistributes thermal energy from the central plasma, typically flattening or reducing the core electron pressure inside the inversion region. In practice, the post-crash value is inferred by combining electron density and temperature measurements synchronized to an identified crash time, for example from Thomson scattering, interferometry, electron cyclotron emission, or soft-X-ray signals. The distinction from [electron_pressure_over_scrape_off_layer](name:electron_pressure_over_scrape_off_layer) is the plasma region and event context: this quantity characterizes the confined plasma after a sawtooth event, not the scrape-off-layer electron pressure.

Typical post-crash core values are order-of-magnitude 1e3-1e5 Pa in many tokamak plasmas, with high-density or high-temperature cases reaching 1e5-1e6 Pa. These values follow directly from representative thermal densities of 1e19-1e20 m^-3 and post-crash thermal electron temperatures of 0.1-10 keV.

NAMES.name: thermal_ion_density
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Number density of thermalized (Maxwellian) ions of a given atomic species at a local plasma point, summed over all ionization states and excluding suprathermal fast ions.
NAMES.long:
The thermal ion density $n_{i,\mathrm{th}}$ counts thermalized ions of a given atomic species per unit volume at a local plasma point, summing over all ionization charge states of that species while excluding suprathermal particles produced by auxiliary heating, neutral beam injection, or fusion reactions. As a fundamental moment of the thermal ion velocity distribution, it governs ion particle transport and enters the local quasi-neutrality constraint alongside the electron density.

The thermal component relates to the total [ion_density](name:ion_density) by subtracting the non-thermal contribution:

$$
n_{i,\mathrm{th}} = n_i - n_{i,\mathrm{fast}}
$$

where $n_i$ is the total ion number density (thermal plus non-thermal) and $n_{i,\mathrm{fast}}$ is the [fast_ion_density](name:fast_ion_density). The charge-state-resolved counterpart, which retains the individual ionization-state label $z$, is [thermal_ion_state_density](name:thermal_ion_state_density), with $n_{i,\mathrm{th}} = \sum_z n_{i,z,\mathrm{th}}$ where $n_{i,z,\mathrm{th}}$ is the density for charge state $z$.

This quantity is inferred from particle balance calculations, charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, or kinetic and fluid transport codes that explicitly separate thermal from non-thermal ion populations. Typical deuterium core values in H-mode tokamaks range from $0.5$–$5 \times 10^{19}$ m$^{-3}$, comparable to the electron density under quasi-neutrality in low-impurity plasmas; in the scrape-off layer, values drop by one to two orders of magnitude. The [total_ion_density](name:total_ion_density) combines both thermal and fast-ion contributions across all charge states for the same species.

NAMES.name: thermal_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Net collisional power density delivered by fast or non-thermal particles to the total thermal ion population, summed over ion species and charge states and over all guiding-center orbit classes.
NAMES.long:
Thermal ion power density due to collisions is the local volumetric rate of kinetic-energy transfer by Coulomb collisions from fast or non-thermal particle distributions to the bulk thermal ion population. The recipient thermal-ion population is the aggregate over all thermal ion species and their charge states, and the fast-particle contribution is aggregated over all guiding-center orbit classes.

The aggregate source density can be written as a sum of species- and charge-state-resolved collisional energy-transfer densities:

$$
p_{\mathrm{th\,i}}^{\mathrm{coll}} = \sum_{\alpha \in \mathcal{F}} \sum_{s \in \mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{th}}} \sum_{q \in \mathcal{Q}_s} Q_{s q \leftarrow \alpha}^{\mathrm{coll}}
$$

where $\mathcal{F}$ denotes the fast or non-thermal particle populations, including orbit-class subdivisions when they are treated separately; $\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{th}}$ denotes thermal ion species; $\mathcal{Q}_s$ denotes the charge states of species $s$; and $Q_{s q \leftarrow \alpha}^{\mathrm{coll}}$ is the Coulomb-collisional kinetic-energy transfer rate per unit volume into thermal ion species $s$ in charge state $q$ from population $\alpha$.

This quantity is usually obtained from kinetic or transport calculations rather than measured directly. The calculation evaluates the collisional slowing-down, drag, and diffusion of the fast distribution against each thermal ion background component, takes the appropriate velocity-space energy moments, and sums the orbit-resolved and species-resolved contributions. Its volume integral gives [thermal_ion_power_due_to_collisions](name:thermal_ion_power_due_to_collisions), while [fast_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:fast_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions) is the corresponding fast-population energy-balance term.

Typical magnitudes are highly scenario dependent. Values are near zero where fast particles have little overlap with the thermal ions; in auxiliary-heated tokamak plasmas, local source densities are often of order 10^3-10^6 W m^-3, with larger values possible in compact high-power deposition regions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when Coulomb collisions transfer kinetic energy from fast or non-thermal particle populations into the total thermal ion population.

NAMES.name: co_passing_thermal_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Local volumetric rate at which Coulomb collisions transfer energy from co-passing fast particles to the bulk thermal ion population. Co-passing fast particles are circulating particles whose guiding centers transit poloidally with parallel velocity in the plasma-current direction; the qualifier does not describe the receiving thermal ions.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is a local source term in the thermal-ion energy balance caused by Coulomb collisions with the co-passing part of a non-thermal particle distribution. The co-passing qualifier identifies the fast-particle orbit class: circulating guiding-center orbits with parallel velocity in the plasma-current direction, so the particles transit poloidally in the co-current passing sense. It does not imply that the bulk thermal ions themselves are passing particles.

The local power density can be written as the energy moment of the fast-particle collision operator restricted to the co-passing orbit domain:

$$
P_{\mathrm{co}\to\mathrm{th},i}(\mathbf{x}) = -\int_{\Omega_{\mathrm{co}}(\mathbf{x})} \frac{1}{2} m_f v^2\, C_{fi}[f_f,f_{\mathrm{th},i}](\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\, d^3v
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{co}\to\mathrm{th},i}$ is the volumetric power density in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-3}}$, $m_f$ is the fast-particle mass in kg, $v$ is particle speed in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $C_{fi}$ is the Coulomb collision operator giving the rate of change of the fast-particle distribution due to collisions with thermal ions of species $i$, $f_f$ is the fast-particle distribution, $f_{\mathrm{th},i}$ is the receiving thermal-ion distribution, and $\Omega_{\mathrm{co}}$ is the co-passing fast-particle orbit domain. The minus sign converts fast-particle kinetic-energy loss into thermal-ion energy gain.

This quantity is usually inferred from kinetic or transport modeling rather than measured directly. The computation classifies fast-particle guiding-center orbits, evaluates the collisional energy exchange with the thermal-ion background, and sums over the relevant thermal-ion states when an unresolved ion-population quantity is required. The state-resolved counterpart is [co_passing_thermal_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:co_passing_thermal_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions); the corresponding electron heating channel is [co_passing_thermal_electron_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:co_passing_thermal_electron_power_density_due_to_collisions).

Representative values are highly scenario dependent: regions with little co-passing fast-particle density are near 0 W m^-3, while auxiliary-heated core plasmas commonly give order-of-magnitude local values around 10^3-10^6 W m^-3. The co-passing contribution is one orbit-class component of the total thermal-ion collisional heating, together with trapped and counter-passing contributions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when net collisional energy transfer from the co-passing fast-particle population increases the thermal-ion energy.

NAMES.name: counter_passing_thermal_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Collisional power density transferred from counter-passing fast particles to thermal ions through Coulomb collisions. It is a local volumetric energy source for thermal ions, with sign determined by the direction of energy transfer.
NAMES.long:
Counter-passing thermal-ion power density due to collisions is the local rate per unit volume at which Coulomb collisions transfer kinetic energy from the counter-passing part of a fast-particle population to thermal ions. Counter-passing denotes passing orbits whose guiding-center motion is opposite to the co-passing, plasma-current-aligned branch. This quantity is an ion heating term when fast particles slow down on thermal ions and an ion cooling term if the net energy transfer is reversed.

For a fast-particle species $\alpha$, the power density received by thermal ions from the counter-passing velocity-space domain can be written as the negative of the fast-particle energy moment of the ion-collision operator:

$$
P_{\alpha \rightarrow i}^{\mathrm{cp}}(\mathbf{x}) = -\int_{\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{cp}}} \frac{1}{2} m_\alpha v^2\, C_{\alpha i}[f_\alpha,f_i](\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\, d^3v
$$

where $\mathbf{x}$ is position in m, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity in m s$^{-1}$, $v=|\mathbf{v}|$, $m_\alpha$ is fast-particle mass in kg, $f_\alpha$ and $f_i$ are velocity distribution functions with units s$^3$ m$^{-6}$, $C_{\alpha i}$ is the rate of change of $f_\alpha$ due to Coulomb collisions with thermal ions with units s$^2$ m$^{-6}$, $d^3v$ has units m$^3$ s$^{-3}$, and $\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{cp}}$ is the counter-passing region of velocity space. The result $P_{\alpha \rightarrow i}^{\mathrm{cp}}$ has units W m$^{-3}$. The minus sign converts the fast-particle energy-change moment into the power received by the thermal ions.

This quantity is normally computed from a kinetic fast-particle distribution and a Coulomb collision operator, for example in Fokker-Planck, guiding-center, or transport calculations. It is not the total thermal-ion collisional heating unless summed consistently over the relevant fast-particle species and over the co-passing, counter-passing, and trapped parts of phase space.

Typical magnitudes are about $10^2$-$10^5$ W m$^{-3}$ in auxiliary-heated tokamak plasmas and can reach $10^6$ W m$^{-3}$ in strongly heated or burning-plasma core regions. Values approach zero where the counter-passing fast-particle density is small, and negative values may occur when thermal ions transfer net energy to the counter-passing fast-particle population.
NAMES.sign: Positive when Coulomb collisions transfer energy from the counter-passing fast-particle population to the thermal ions.

NAMES.name: thermal_ion_pressure
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Isotropic kinetic pressure from random thermal motion of all thermal ion species and ionization states. It is the aggregate of charge-state-resolved thermal ion pressures and excludes fast or suprathermal ion contributions.
NAMES.long:
Thermal ion pressure is the scalar kinetic pressure carried by the bulk thermal ion population. It is summed over all thermal ion species and ionization states, so it is the aggregate counterpart of [thermal_ion_state_pressure](name:thermal_ion_state_pressure), and it excludes pressure from fast or suprathermal ions.

For a plasma with multiple thermal ion species or charge states, the defining relation is:

$$
p_{i,\mathrm{th}} = \sum_s p_{i,s,\mathrm{th}} = \sum_s n_s k_B T_s
$$

where $p_{i,\mathrm{th}}$ is the thermal ion pressure, $p_{i,s,\mathrm{th}}$ is the thermal pressure of ion state $s$, $n_s$ is its number density in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, $T_s$ is its thermodynamic temperature in kelvin, and $k_B$ is the Boltzmann constant. If ion temperature is expressed in electronvolts, the factor $k_B T_s$ is replaced by $e T_s$, where $e$ is the elementary charge. When all thermal ions share a common temperature, this reduces to the total thermal ion density multiplied by the common thermal energy per ion.

In practice, thermal ion pressure is computed from ion density and ion temperature estimates for each relevant species or charge state, using kinetic diagnostics and consistency constraints such as quasineutrality. It is combined with [thermal_electron_pressure](name:thermal_electron_pressure_at_post_sawtooth_crash) to form the dominant bulk thermal pressure contribution, and is conceptually related to [total_ion_pressure](name:total_ion_pressure) when total ion pressure is decomposed into thermal and nonthermal parts.

Representative values vary widely with confinement regime and radius: cool edge or scrape-off-layer plasma can be below 1 Pa to about 10^3 Pa, while confined hot plasma is commonly in the 10^3-10^5 Pa range and can reach a few 10^5 Pa in high-performance conditions.

NAMES.name: radial_derivative_of_thermal_ion_pressure
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Derivative of total thermal ion pressure with respect to normalized toroidal flux radius. Because that radial flux coordinate is dimensionless, the derivative retains units of pressure.
NAMES.long:
The radial derivative of [thermal_ion_pressure](name:thermal_ion_pressure) is the rate of change of total thermal ion pressure with respect to the flux coordinate $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$, the normalized toroidal flux radius. It quantifies the outward pressure gradient across nested magnetic flux surfaces and provides a pressure-gradient drive term for ion energy transport.

The defining derivative is

$$
G_{p_i}(\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}) = \frac{\partial p_{i,\mathrm{th}}}{\partial \rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}}
$$

where $G_{p_i}$ is the radial derivative, $p_{i,\mathrm{th}}$ is the total thermal ion pressure summed over the thermal ion species being modeled, and $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$ ranges from 0 at the magnetic axis to 1 at the last closed flux surface. Since $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$ is dimensionless, the derivative has the same unit as pressure, Pa.

In practice, this quantity is computed by differentiating the radial dependence of thermal ion pressure inferred from ion density and temperature measurements, or from a transport calculation. Smoothing, fitted basis functions, or conservative finite differences are commonly used to reduce noise before differentiation. The related [radial_derivative_of_ion_pressure](name:radial_derivative_of_ion_pressure) is the analogous derivative for the corresponding ion pressure quantity, [second_radial_derivative_of_thermal_ion_pressure](name:second_radial_derivative_of_thermal_ion_pressure) gives the associated curvature, and [radial_derivative_of_ion_temperature](name:radial_derivative_of_ion_temperature) is often used with density gradients to decompose the pressure gradient.

Typical magnitudes are about $10^3$-$10^5$ Pa in broad core regions and can reach $10^5$-$10^6$ Pa in steep pedestal or edge-gradient regions, depending on density, ion temperature, plasma size, and confinement regime. In many confined plasmas the value is negative over much of the radius because thermal ion pressure is largest near the magnetic axis.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the total thermal ion pressure increases with increasing normalized toroidal flux radius $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$, outward from the magnetic axis toward the last closed flux surface.

NAMES.name: second_radial_derivative_of_thermal_ion_pressure
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Second derivative of total thermal ion pressure with respect to normalized toroidal flux radius, quantifying the local radial curvature of the thermal ion pressure profile.
NAMES.long:
The second radial derivative of thermal ion pressure quantifies the curvature of the [thermal_ion_pressure](name:thermal_ion_pressure) profile along the normalized toroidal flux radius. Negative values indicate a concave-down pressure profile, characteristic of the plasma core where pressure is peaked, while positive values indicate concave-up curvature, which can arise near internal transport barriers or in pedestal-like structures.

The quantity is defined as:

$$
\frac{\partial^2 p_i^{th}}{\partial \rho_{tor,norm}^2}
$$

where $p_i^{th}$ is the total thermal ion pressure and $\rho_{tor,norm} \in [0, 1]$ is the normalized toroidal flux radius running from 0 at the magnetic axis to 1 at the last closed flux surface. Because $\rho_{tor,norm}$ is dimensionless, the resulting derivative carries the same unit as the pressure.

This quantity is evaluated numerically by transport solvers, where it enters the spatial discretization of diffusive terms in the radial ion heat and momentum transport equations. It is the second-order companion to the first-order [radial_derivative_of_thermal_ion_pressure](name:radial_derivative_of_thermal_ion_pressure), and it is structurally analogous to the [second_radial_derivative_of_fast_ion_pressure](name:second_radial_derivative_of_fast_ion_pressure) for the fast ion population and to [second_radial_derivative_of_ion_pressure](name:second_radial_derivative_of_ion_pressure) for the total (thermal plus fast) ion pressure.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the thermal ion pressure profile is concave upward with respect to increasing $\rho_{tor,norm}$.

NAMES.name: thermal_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Volumetric Coulomb-collisional power density transferred from a fast or non-Maxwellian particle distribution to bulk thermal ions in one specified ionic charge state. Positive values represent heating of that charge-state population.
NAMES.long:
Thermal ion state power density due to collisions is the local rate at which Coulomb collisions transfer kinetic energy between a fast or non-Maxwellian particle distribution and the bulk thermal ions in one specified ionic charge-state population.
