NAMES.short: Local source rate of toroidal angular momentum per unit volume acting on counter-passing particles, whose guiding-center parallel velocity is opposite to the plasma current. It includes the major-radius lever arm and is summed over particle species and momentum-exchange mechanisms.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal counter-passing torque density is the source rate of toroidal angular momentum per unit volume applied to the counter-passing orbit-class population. Counter-passing particles are passing guiding centers whose parallel velocity is opposite to the plasma-current direction; trapped particles are excluded. The aggregate includes the major-radius lever arm and sums over particle species and momentum-exchange mechanisms.

At a point with major radius \(R\) in the right-handed cylindrical \((R,\phi,Z)\) frame, where \(R\) is major radius, \(\phi\) is toroidal angle, and \(Z\) is vertical height, the defining velocity-space moment is

$$
\tau_{\phi,\mathrm{cp}} = \sum_a \sum_k R \int_{\Omega_{\mathrm{cp},a}} m_a\, v_\phi\, S_{a,k}[f_a] \, d^3v
$$

where \(\tau_{\phi,\mathrm{cp}}\) is the torque density in N m^-2, \(a\) indexes particle species, \(k\) indexes momentum-exchange mechanisms, \(R\) is in m, \(m_a\) is the particle mass in kg, \(v_\phi\) is the toroidal component of guiding-center velocity along \(\hat{\phi}\) in m s^-1, \(S_{a,k}[f_a]\) is the rate of change of the distribution function due to mechanism \(k\) in s^2 m^-6 when \(f_a\) has units s^3 m^-6, and \(d^3v\) is the velocity-space volume element in m^3 s^-3. The domain \(\Omega_{\mathrm{cp},a}\) is the counter-passing part of velocity space outside the trapped region, and the factor \(R\) converts a toroidal force-density moment into an angular-momentum source rate per unit volume.

In practice this quantity is computed by orbit-classifying kinetic distribution functions and taking the same moment of collisional, wave-particle, electromagnetic, and external-source operators over the counter-passing domain. It can also be inferred indirectly from toroidal momentum balance when the other transport and source terms are constrained. Together with [toroidal_co_passing_torque_density](name:toroidal_co_passing_torque_density) and [toroidal_trapped_torque_density](name:toroidal_trapped_torque_density), it partitions the total orbit-class torque density; [toroidal_counter_passing_torque_density_due_to_j_cross_b_force](name:toroidal_counter_passing_torque_density_due_to_j_cross_b_force) is a mechanism-specific contribution.

Typical orbit-class-resolved values in tokamak transport analyzes are about 10^-3-10 N m^-2, while localized strong external momentum input can produce values of 10-100 N m^-2. The value is zero when there is no net angular-momentum exchange with the counter-passing population or when positive and negative mechanism contributions cancel.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the summed source increases toroidal angular momentum corresponding to motion in the direction of increasing toroidal angle \(\phi\) in the right-handed cylindrical \((R,\phi,Z)\) frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_counter_passing_torque_density_due_to_j_cross_b_force
NAMES.short: Flux-surface-averaged toroidal torque density exerted on counter-passing particles by the J cross B force arising from the current component normal to the flux surface. Counter-passing particles are those whose guiding-center parallel velocity is directed opposite to the plasma current.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal counter-passing torque density due to the $J\times B$ force is the rate of change of toroidal angular momentum per unit volume assigned to the orbit class whose guiding-center parallel velocity is directed opposite to the plasma current. The toroidal direction is the $\phi$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, and this quantity retains only the Lorentz-force contribution produced by the current component normal to the flux surface. It is interpreted as the flux-surface-averaged toroidal angular-momentum source for the counter-passing population.

The flux-surface-averaged source may be written as

$$
T_{\phi,\mathrm{cp}}^{J\times B}=\left\langle R\,\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}\cdot\left(J_{\perp,\mathrm{cp}}\,\hat{\mathbf{n}}\times\mathbf{B}\right)\right\rangle
$$

where $\langle\cdot\rangle$ denotes the flux-surface average, $R$ is major radius in m, $\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing $\phi$, $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is the outward unit normal to the flux surface, $J_{\perp,\mathrm{cp}}$ is the counter-passing current density along that normal in $\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}$, and $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field in T. The relevant current component is the one normal to the flux surface; this coincides with the cylindrical radial direction $\hat{R}$ only in the special case of circular, concentric surfaces, and in general differs from it once the equilibrium is shaped, so the two should not be treated as identical.

The quantity is obtained from kinetic or Fokker-Planck transport models that partition the particle distribution by orbit class, retaining only the counter-passing segment when forming the current and the associated $J\times B$ force. Together with the [co-passing](name:toroidal_co_passing_torque_density_due_to_j_cross_b_force) and [trapped](name:toroidal_trapped_torque_density_due_to_j_cross_b_force) orbit-class contributions, it decomposes the [total toroidal J cross B torque density](name:toroidal_torque_density_due_to_j_cross_b_force); summing the orbit classes recovers that aggregate. It is the mechanism-specific counterpart of the broader [counter-passing toroidal torque density](name:toroidal_counter_passing_torque_density).

Magnitudes scale with the local fast-particle current and the magnetic field, and are largest where radial current or fast-particle gradients are strong; the sign and amplitude depend on scenario, beam geometry, and orbit-class cancelation.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the $J\times B$ force from the flux-surface-normal current component drives counter-passing toroidal angular momentum in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift
NAMES.short: Toroidal projection of the plasma current density carried by the diamagnetic drift, arising from cross-field pressure gradients acting on magnetized plasma species.
NAMES.long:
The diamagnetic drift gives rise to a plasma current density flowing perpendicular to both the magnetic field and the plasma pressure gradient; this quantity is the scalar projection of that current density vector along the toroidal direction $\hat{\phi}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

The toroidal diamagnetic current density is given by:

$$
j_{\phi,\mathrm{dia}} = \left(\frac{\mathbf{B} \times \nabla p}{B^2}\right) \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $p$ is the total plasma pressure, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field vector, and $B = |\mathbf{B}|$.

This is the toroidal projection of the parent [current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift) vector; the analogous poloidal component is described by [poloidal_current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:poloidal_current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift). It is computed from kinetic pressure profiles combined with magnetic equilibrium geometry, and enters the current budget in MHD force-balance and edge-transport models, with greatest importance in steep-gradient regions such as the H-mode pedestal and internal transport barriers.

Typical magnitudes span $10^4$–$10^7$ A m$^{-2}$ in fusion-relevant pedestal and transport-barrier regions where pressure gradients are steepest.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the toroidal diamagnetic current density is directed in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity
NAMES.short: Toroidal projection of the heat-viscosity-driven current density, taken along increasing toroidal angle phi in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It represents the electric current-density contribution associated with heat-flow-related viscous stress in a plasma.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal current density due to heat viscosity is the component of electric current density associated with the heat-flow-dependent part of viscous stress in a magnetized plasma. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, it is the projection along $\hat{\phi}$, the direction of increasing toroidal angle. It is one contribution to [toroidal_current_density_due_to_viscosity](name:toroidal_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity) and is distinct from current-density terms due to parallel or perpendicular viscosity.

The toroidal component is defined by projecting the heat-viscosity current-density vector onto the toroidal basis direction:

$$
j_{{\rm hv},\phi} = \mathbf{j}_{\rm hv} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $j_{{\rm hv},\phi}$ is the toroidal current density due to heat viscosity in $\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}$, $\mathbf{j}_{\rm hv}$ is the heat-viscosity contribution to current density in $\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}$, and $\hat{\phi}$ is the dimensionless unit vector toward increasing toroidal angle $\phi$. The vector $\mathbf{j}_{\rm hv}$ represents the current response associated with heat-flow-related viscous stress; the detailed constitutive closure is model-dependent.

In transport analysis this quantity is usually computed from the heat-viscosity term in a momentum-balance or generalized-Ohm-law closure and then projected onto $\hat{\phi}$. It is normally inferred from plasma state variables and transport-model terms rather than measured as an independent diagnostic signal. Related resolved quantities include [poloidal_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity](name:poloidal_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity), [parallel_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity](name:parallel_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity), and the heat-current counterpart [parallel_heat_current_density_due_to_viscosity](name:parallel_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity).

Representative magnitudes are strongly closure- and scenario-dependent. Values may be near 0 A.m^-2 when heat-viscosity stress is weak or omitted, while local corrections of order 10^2-10^5 A.m^-2 can occur in steep-gradient transport calculations; these are scale estimates rather than hard bounds and should be interpreted relative to the local total toroidal current-density budget.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the heat-viscosity-driven current density has a toroidal component in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the current density driven by perpendicular viscous stress in the plasma fluid, projected along increasing toroidal angle phi in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal current density due to perpendicular viscosity is the toroidal component of the current density associated with perpendicular viscous stress in a magnetized plasma. The toroidal direction is the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height. This quantity is the toroidal projection of [current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity](name:current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity) and complements the radial, poloidal, and field-aligned projections of the same physical contribution.

The component is defined by projecting the perpendicular-viscosity-driven current-density vector onto the toroidal unit vector:

$$
j_{\perp\mathrm{visc},\phi} = \mathbf{j}_{\perp\mathrm{visc}} \cdot \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}
$$

where $\mathbf{j}_{\perp\mathrm{visc}}$ is the current density due to perpendicular viscous stress, measured in A m$^{-2}$, $\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing $\phi$, and $j_{\perp\mathrm{visc},\phi}$ is the toroidal component, also measured in A m$^{-2}$.

This contribution is usually computed rather than measured directly. It is obtained from the perpendicular viscous stress tensor used in a fluid, drift-kinetic, or transport model, inserted into the momentum and charge-balance relations that define viscosity-driven current, and then projected onto $\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}$. It contributes alongside other viscous-current terms, such as [toroidal_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity](name:toroidal_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity) and [toroidal_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity](name:toroidal_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity), to [toroidal_current_density_due_to_viscosity](name:toroidal_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity).

Typical magnitudes are strongly regime dependent. Core values may be below 1 A m$^{-2}$ when perpendicular viscous forces are weak or symmetry cancels the toroidal projection, while edge, pedestal, and scrape-off-layer calculations commonly span 1-10^4 A m$^{-2}$, with larger localized values possible in steep-gradient or strongly sheared flows.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the perpendicular-viscosity-driven current density has a component in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_deuterium_tritium_velocity_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: deuterium_tritium
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the bulk flow velocity of the fictitious deuterium-tritium single-species (atomic mass 2.5 amu) evaluated at the magnetic axis, the innermost point of the confined plasma where the poloidal flux gradient vanishes.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal deuterium-tritium velocity at the magnetic axis is the $\hat{\phi}$-component of the bulk flow velocity of a fictitious single-ion species representing the DT fuel mixture, evaluated at the location where $\nabla\psi = 0$. The effective DT species carries an atomic mass of 2.5 amu — the arithmetic mean of deuterium (2 amu) and tritium (3 amu) — allowing transport simulations to model the combined fuel population as a single fluid without separately resolving each isotope.

The toroidal projection is defined as:

$$
v_\phi = \mathbf{v}_\mathrm{DT} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_\mathrm{DT}$ is the bulk flow velocity of the fictitious DT species and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

In experiment, ion toroidal rotation near the magnetic axis is inferred from charge exchange recombination spectroscopy via the Doppler shift of fuel-ion or impurity emission lines; the fictitious DT value at the axis is then extracted through transport modeling or extrapolation. The on-axis velocity sets the innermost boundary condition for the toroidal momentum transport equation. Analogous quantities at other radial positions are captured by [toroidal_deuterium_tritium_velocity_at_pedestal](name:toroidal_deuterium_tritium_velocity_at_pedestal) and [toroidal_deuterium_tritium_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:toroidal_deuterium_tritium_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier); the single-isotope deuterium counterpart at the same location is [toroidal_deuterium_velocity_at_magnetic_axis](name:toroidal_deuterium_velocity_at_magnetic_axis).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the toroidal flow is directed in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise when viewed from above in the $+\hat{Z}$ direction).

NAMES.name: toroidal_deuterium_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: deuterium
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the deuterium ion flow velocity evaluated at the radial location of the internal transport barrier.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal deuterium velocity at the internal transport barrier (ITB) is the $\hat{\phi}$-component of the bulk deuterium ion flow vector sampled at the ITB — a region of reduced turbulent transport in the plasma interior, characterized by steep gradients in temperature, density, and rotation velocity, often associated with reversed or weak magnetic shear.

The quantity is defined by the projection:

$$
v_\phi^D = \mathbf{v}_D \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $R$ is the major radius and $Z$ is the vertical coordinate.

Toroidal ion flow at the ITB is measured primarily by charge exchange recombination spectroscopy (CXRS), where the Doppler shift of emission lines from reactions between injected neutral beam atoms and plasma deuterium ions yields the local bulk velocity. Rotation velocities in ITB plasmas range from a few km/s to several tens of km/s depending on plasma current, heating power, and barrier strength. Velocity shear at the ITB location is closely linked to radial electric field structure and plays a central role in turbulence suppression. For toroidal velocities of other species at the same location, see [toroidal_tritium_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:toroidal_tritium_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier) and [toroidal_hydrogen_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:toroidal_hydrogen_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the deuterium ion flow is directed in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise when viewed from above along $+\hat{Z}$).

NAMES.name: toroidal_deuterium_velocity_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: deuterium
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the bulk deuterium ion flow velocity at the magnetic axis, taken along the phi direction in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal deuterium velocity at the magnetic axis is the central value of the deuterium ion bulk flow projected onto the toroidal direction. It characterizes rotation of the deuterium population at the radial center of the nested magnetic flux surfaces, not a full radial variation of the flow.

The quantity is defined by projecting the deuterium bulk velocity onto the toroidal unit vector at the magnetic-axis location:

$$
v_{\phi,D,\mathrm{axis}} = \mathbf{v}_D(\mathbf{x}_\mathrm{axis}) \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $v_{\phi,D,\mathrm{axis}}$ is in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $\mathbf{v}_D$ is the deuterium ion bulk velocity in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $\mathbf{x}_\mathrm{axis}$ is a point on the magnetic-axis curve, and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

In practice, this value is obtained from central ion-flow measurements when available, or inferred from nearby core measurements together with equilibrium geometry and transport or momentum-balance constraints. Such estimates should be interpreted as contextual determinations of the magnetic-axis value rather than as part of the definition.

Representative magnitudes are device- and scenario-dependent, commonly about $10^3$-$10^5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ in low-torque plasmas and up to a few $10^5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ when strong external momentum input is present.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the deuterium bulk flow is in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_electric_field
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the electric field in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It is the signed projection of the electric field along increasing toroidal angle phi.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal electric field is the component of the electric-field vector along the toroidal basis direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. In tokamak plasmas it is the component most directly associated with inductive electron acceleration, plasma initiation, toroidal current drive, and ohmic dissipation.

The component is defined by projection onto the toroidal unit vector:

$$
E_\phi = \mathbf{E} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $E_\phi$ is the toroidal electric field in $\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$, $\mathbf{E}$ is the electric-field vector in $\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$, and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle.

In practice, $E_\phi$ is inferred from loop-voltage measurements, magnetic-flux evolution, transport analysis, or local electric-field estimates. For an axisymmetric field that is approximately uniform along a circular contour of major radius $R$ in the cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, the local relation is commonly interpreted as $E_\phi \approx V_\mathrm{loop}/(2\pi R)$, where $V_\mathrm{loop}$ is the voltage around that contour in volts and $R$ is in meters; this approximation should not be treated as a general pointwise equality when the field varies poloidally or toroidally. During plasma initiation, $E_\phi$ is considered together with [prefill pressure] and [perpendicular magnetic field] because these affect ionization avalanche and electron confinement. During ohmic operation, the product of toroidal electric field and toroidal current density contributes to Joule heating and is related to [plasma resistance].

Representative magnitudes are typically about $0.01-0.2\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$ during established ohmic current sustainment, and about $0.1-10\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$ during startup, breakdown, or rapid current ramp phases. The value depends on device size, applied loop voltage, plasma resistivity, gas conditions, and magnetic-field error levels.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the electric-field component points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_electron_velocity
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the electron bulk fluid velocity in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal electron velocity is the projection of the electron bulk fluid velocity onto the toroidal basis direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It represents the mean electron flow around the torus and is a signed component of the electron momentum balance.

For an electron distribution function, the toroidal bulk velocity is the first velocity moment projected onto $\hat{\phi}$:

$$
v_{e,\phi} = \mathbf{v}_e \cdot \hat{\phi} = \frac{1}{n_e}\int v_\phi f_e(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v},t)\,d^3v
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_e$ is the electron bulk velocity, $\hat{\phi}$ is the toroidal unit vector, $v_\phi$ is the particle velocity component along $\hat{\phi}$, $f_e$ is the electron distribution function, and $n_e$ is the electron density.

In practice, toroidal electron velocity may be inferred from momentum-balance modeling, kinetic measurements, charge and current balance, or transport calculations. Because electrons carry much of the toroidal current response, this velocity is closely related to the electron contribution to toroidal current density, while remaining distinct from the ion counterpart [toroidal_ion_velocity](name:toroidal_ion_velocity) and from radial, poloidal, or field-parallel electron flow components.

Typical values are strongly scenario dependent: magnitudes of 1e3-1e5 m.s^-1 are common in magnetically confined plasmas, while low-density edge regions, strong current drive, or transient conditions can produce values of several 1e5 m.s^-1 or more.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the electron bulk flow is in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: radial_derivative_of_toroidal_electron_velocity
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Radial derivative of the signed toroidal electron fluid velocity, the phi component in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, with respect to the normalized toroidal flux radius rho_tor,norm.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the flux-coordinate derivative of the signed toroidal component of the electron fluid velocity in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It describes how the toroidal electron flow changes between neighboring magnetic surfaces as the normalized toroidal flux radius $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ increases from the magnetic axis toward the last closed flux surface.

The derivative is defined by differentiating the toroidal electron velocity with respect to $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$:

$$
\frac{\partial v_{\phi,e}}{\partial \rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}}
$$

where $v_{\phi,e}$ is the [toroidal electron velocity](name:toroidal_electron_velocity) in m.s^-1 and $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ is a dimensionless flux coordinate equal to 0 at the magnetic axis and 1 at the last closed flux surface. Because the differentiation coordinate is dimensionless, the derivative has the same unit as the velocity.

In practice the quantity is obtained from the radial dependence of $v_{\phi,e}$ on magnetic surfaces, using a smooth fitted representation or local numerical differentiation with respect to $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$. It is the first-derivative counterpart of [second_radial_derivative_of_toroidal_electron_velocity](name:second_radial_derivative_of_toroidal_electron_velocity), and uses the same flux-coordinate differentiation concept as [radial_derivative_of_electron_pressure](name:radial_derivative_of_electron_pressure).

Representative magnitudes in tokamak transport analysis are often of order 10^3-10^5 m.s^-1 per unit $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$, with values near zero where the toroidal electron velocity is radially flat. Larger local magnitudes can occur where the signed electron flow changes rapidly over a narrow interval in $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the signed toroidal electron velocity component $v_{\phi,e}$, taken positive in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, increases as $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ increases from the magnetic axis toward the last closed flux surface.

NAMES.name: second_radial_derivative_of_toroidal_electron_velocity
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Second derivative of the toroidal electron fluid velocity with respect to the normalized toroidal flux radius, quantifying the radial curvature of the electron toroidal rotation profile.
NAMES.long:
The second radial derivative of the toroidal electron velocity quantifies the curvature of the $v_{e,\phi}$ profile along the normalized toroidal flux coordinate, where $v_{e,\phi}$ is the $\hat{\phi}$-component of the electron bulk fluid velocity as defined in [toroidal_electron_velocity](name:toroidal_electron_velocity). A nonzero curvature indicates that the first-order radial shear [radial_derivative_of_toroidal_electron_velocity](name:radial_derivative_of_toroidal_electron_velocity) is itself varying radially, which is physically significant near transport barriers and velocity inflection layers.

The quantity is defined as:

$$
\frac{d^2 v_{e,\phi}}{d\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}^2}
$$

where $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$ is the normalized toroidal flux radius, dimensionless and ranging from 0 at the magnetic axis to 1 at the separatrix. Because $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$ is dimensionless, the second derivative retains the same unit as the velocity itself.

This higher-order derivative is used in numerical transport solvers for spatial discretization of the electron momentum equation. The analogous ion quantity is [second_radial_derivative_of_toroidal_ion_velocity](name:second_radial_derivative_of_toroidal_ion_velocity), and the poloidal counterpart is [second_radial_derivative_of_poloidal_electron_velocity](name:second_radial_derivative_of_poloidal_electron_velocity).
NAMES.sign: Positive when $d^2 v_{e,\phi}/d\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}^2 > 0$, inheriting the convention that $v_{e,\phi}$ is positive when the electron fluid flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_fast_electron_torque_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Toroidal fast-electron torque density due to Coulomb collisions is the rate of toroidal angular-momentum transfer per unit volume to fast electrons from thermal electrons. It equals major radius times the phi-directed collisional force density in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal fast-electron torque density due to collisions is the local rate at which Coulomb collisions with thermal electrons transfer toroidal angular momentum to the fast-electron population per unit volume. The toroidal direction is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height. This is an angular torque density, so it includes the major-radius lever arm multiplying the toroidal force density.

For a kinetic fast-electron distribution, the quantity is the toroidal velocity moment of the collision operator multiplied by $R$:

$$
\tau^{\mathrm{coll}}_{\phi,\mathrm{fe}}(R,Z) = R \int m_e v_\phi\, C^{\mathrm{coll}}_{\mathrm{fe}\leftarrow e}[f_\mathrm{fe},f_e] \, d^3v
$$

where $\tau^{\mathrm{coll}}_{\phi,\mathrm{fe}}$ is in $\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$, $R$ is in m, $m_e$ is the electron mass in kg, $v_\phi$ is the particle velocity component along $+\hat{\phi}$ in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, and $C^{\mathrm{coll}}_{\mathrm{fe}\leftarrow e}$ is the Coulomb collision operator giving the rate of change of the fast-electron distribution $f_\mathrm{fe}$ due to thermal electrons with distribution $f_e$. The velocity integral gives the collisional toroidal force density on fast electrons in $\mathrm{N\,m^{-3}}$; multiplication by $R$ gives angular torque density.

This quantity is usually computed from a kinetic or reduced fast-electron transport model by taking the toroidal moment of the electron-electron collision term, and may then be volume-integrated to obtain [toroidal_fast_electron_torque_due_to_collisions](name:toroidal_fast_electron_torque_due_to_collisions). Orbit-resolved contributions such as [toroidal_trapped_fast_electron_torque_density_due_to_collisions](name:toroidal_trapped_fast_electron_torque_density_due_to_collisions) and [toroidal_co_passing_fast_electron_torque_density_due_to_collisions](name:toroidal_co_passing_fast_electron_torque_density_due_to_collisions) separate the same collisional momentum exchange by fast-electron orbit class. It is distinct from a total fast-particle collisional torque density because only the fast-electron population and its collisions with thermal electrons are included.

Typical signed magnitudes are strongly scenario dependent: values of $10^{-4}$-$10^{1}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$ are common in modeled fast-electron current-drive or weak runaway-electron conditions, while localized relaxation of dense fast-electron populations can reach $10^{2}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$ or more.
NAMES.sign: Positive when Coulomb collisions exert a toroidal force on the fast electrons in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_fast_electron_torque_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Volume-integrated toroidal torque transferred to the fast (non-thermal) electron population through Coulomb collisions with the thermal background plasma.
NAMES.long:
This quantity represents the total toroidal angular momentum per unit time exchanged between the fast (non-thermal) electron population and the thermal plasma constituents via Coulomb collisions, integrated over the entire plasma volume. It measures the net collisional momentum transfer that modifies the toroidal rotation of the fast-electron distribution function.

The volume-integrated toroidal torque is obtained from the angular-momentum moment of the Coulomb collision operator acting on the fast electron distribution:

$$
T_\phi = \int m_e R \, v_\phi \, C[f_{\rm fast}] \, d^3v \, dV
$$

where $m_e$ is the electron mass, $R$ is the major radius in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $v_\phi$ is the toroidal velocity component, $C$ is the Coulomb collision operator acting on the fast electron distribution function $f_{\rm fast}$, and the integral is taken over both velocity space $d^3v$ and the plasma volume $dV$.

This quantity is evaluated from kinetic modeling of the fast electron distribution function using Fokker-Planck or bounce-averaged solvers. The complementary torque on the thermal electron sub-population is given by [toroidal_thermal_electron_torque_due_to_collisions](name:toroidal_thermal_electron_torque_due_to_collisions), while [toroidal_fast_torque_due_to_collisions](name:toroidal_fast_torque_due_to_collisions) aggregates collisional torque over all fast particle species. The orbit-resolved local torque density for co-passing fast electrons is available as [toroidal_co_passing_fast_electron_torque_density_due_to_collisions](name:toroidal_co_passing_fast_electron_torque_density_due_to_collisions).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the net toroidal torque on fast electrons is in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_fast_ion_state_torque_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Collisional toroidal torque density transferred to fast ions in a specified charge state by Coulomb collisions with background particles. It is the toroidal angular-momentum source per unit volume, summed over all fast-ion orbit topologies.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal fast-ion state torque density due to collisions is the Coulomb-collisional source of mechanical toroidal angular momentum for fast ions in a specified charge state, expressed per unit plasma volume. It is summed over all fast-ion orbit topologies and is associated with the $\phi$ direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The local kinetic form is the toroidal angular-momentum moment of the collisional operator:

$$
\mathcal{T}_{\phi,\mathrm{coll}}^{(q)} = R\,m_q \int v_\phi \left[\sum_b C_{qb}(f_q, f_b)\right] \, d^3v
$$

where $\mathcal{T}_{\phi,\mathrm{coll}}^{(q)}$ is this torque density for charge state $q$ in N m$^{-2}$, $R$ is major radius in m, $m_q$ is the fast-ion mass in kg, $v_\phi$ is the particle velocity component in the $+\hat{\phi}$ direction in m s$^{-1}$, $f_q$ and $f_b$ are fast-ion and background distribution functions normalized to number density with units s$^3$ m$^{-6}$, $C_{qb}$ is the Coulomb collision operator for interactions with background population $b$ with units of $f_q$ per second, and $d^3v$ has units m$^3$ s$^{-3}$. The integral without $R$ is a toroidal force density in N m$^{-3}$; multiplying by $R$ gives torque per unit volume in N m$^{-2}$.

In practice the quantity is computed by applying Fokker-Planck, Monte Carlo, orbit-following, or transport collision operators to the fast-ion distribution and then taking the toroidal velocity moment for the selected charge state. Experimental analyzes infer it indirectly from fast-ion distribution modeling and toroidal momentum balance, constrained by diagnostics such as neutron emission, neutral-particle analysis, gamma-ray emission, charge exchange, or collective scattering. Conceptually, it is the toroidal component of [fast_ion_state_torque_density_due_to_collisions](name:fast_ion_state_torque_density_due_to_collisions); summing over charge states gives [toroidal_fast_ion_torque_density_due_to_collisions](name:toroidal_fast_ion_torque_density_due_to_collisions), volume integration gives [toroidal_fast_ion_state_torque_due_to_collisions](name:toroidal_fast_ion_state_torque_due_to_collisions), and the trapped-orbit contribution is [toroidal_trapped_fast_ion_state_torque_density_due_to_collisions](name:toroidal_fast_ion_state_torque_density_due_to_collisions).

Typical core magnitudes in beam-heated tokamak plasmas are $10^{-2}$-$10$ N m$^{-2}$. Strongly localized slowing-down or pitch-angle-scattering regions can approach $10$-$100$ N m$^{-2}$, while weak fast-ion populations or outer-plasma regions may be below $10^{-3}$ N m$^{-2}$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the collisional torque accelerates the fast-ion charge-state population in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_fast_ion_torque_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Rate per unit plasma volume at which Coulomb collisions with background ion species transfer toroidal angular momentum to the fast-ion population, taken about the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It aggregates contributions over fast-ion orbit classes and over the background ion species included in the collision model.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal fast-ion torque density due to collisions is the local rate per unit plasma volume at which Coulomb collisions with background ion species change the toroidal angular momentum of the fast-ion population. The toroidal direction is $\hat{\phi}$ of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. Unless a more resolved quantity is specified, it represents the aggregate over fast-ion orbit classes and over the background ion species retained in the collision operator; collisional momentum exchange with electrons is excluded.

The quantity is the toroidal moment of the collisional force density acting on the fast ions:

$$
\tau_{\phi,\mathrm{coll}}^{\mathrm{fast\ ion}}(\mathbf{x}) = R \sum_{a \in \mathrm{fast\ ions}} \sum_{b \in \mathrm{ions}} \hat{\phi} \cdot \int m_a\,\mathbf{v}\, C_{ab}[f_a,f_b](\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\, d^3v
$$

where $\tau_{\phi,\mathrm{coll}}^{\mathrm{fast\ ion}}$ is the torque density in $\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $R$ is the toroidal moment arm in meters, $a$ indexes fast-ion populations, $b$ indexes background ion species or charge states, $m_a$ is the fast-ion mass in kg, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $f_a$ and $f_b$ are distribution functions, and $C_{ab}$ is the Coulomb collision operator acting on $f_a$ due to species $b$. The velocity-space integral is a toroidal force density in $\mathrm{N\,m^{-3}}$; multiplication by $R$ converts it to a torque per unit volume.

This quantity is normally computed from kinetic fast-ion distributions using Fokker-Planck, orbit-following, or slowing-down collision models constrained by energetic-particle diagnostics and equilibrium information. Charge-state-resolved ion contributions are the local constituents of [toroidal_fast_ion_state_torque_due_to_collisions](name:toroidal_fast_ion_state_torque_due_to_collisions). It is distinct from the all-background-species aggregate [toroidal_fast_torque_due_to_collisions](name:toroidal_fast_torque_due_to_collisions), which sums collisional torque from both thermal ions and electrons; the present quantity retains only the ion-collision contribution.

Magnitudes vary widely with heating power, fast-ion content, and background rotation, and can be positive, negative, or near zero across the radius depending on the fast-ion distribution, collisional slowing-down, and pitch-angle scattering. The largest local values arise in strongly neutral-beam- or energetic-ion-heated regimes.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the collisional force on the fast ions has a $+\hat{\phi}$ component, increasing their toroidal angular momentum in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_helium_3_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: helium_3
NAMES.short: Toroidal velocity of helium-3 ions at the radial location of the internal transport barrier.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal helium-3 velocity at an internal transport barrier is the component of the helium-3 ion mean fluid velocity along the toroidal direction, evaluated at the radial location of the barrier. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, this is the velocity component parallel to $\hat{\phi}$, describing motion around the machine symmetry axis.

The quantity is the local helium-3 toroidal velocity sampled at the barrier location:

$$
v_{\phi,\mathrm{ITB}}^{(^3\mathrm{He})} = v_{\phi}^{(^3\mathrm{He})}(r_{\mathrm{ITB}})
$$

where $v_{\phi}^{(^3\mathrm{He})}$ is the helium-3 toroidal velocity in m/s and $r_{\mathrm{ITB}}$ is the radial coordinate of the internal transport barrier, for example a minor-radius coordinate or an explicitly named flux coordinate such as normalized toroidal flux radius $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$.

In practice, this velocity may be inferred from Doppler shifts of helium-3 spectral lines, charge-exchange spectroscopy when suitable transitions are available, or transport analysis constrained by momentum balance. The internal transport barrier location is usually identified from steep gradients or reduced transport in temperature, density, rotation, or related transport coefficients, and the local velocity is obtained by interpolation or fitting at that radial position.

Typical absolute values of toroidal ion rotation at internal transport barriers are about $10^3-10^5$ m/s, depending on momentum input, collisionality, magnetic configuration, and radial electric-field shear.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the helium-3 toroidal velocity is in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_helium_4_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: helium_4
NAMES.short: Toroidal velocity of helium-4 ions at the internal transport barrier, taken along increasing toroidal angle in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It is the species-specific helium-4 form of the bulk toroidal rotation evaluated on the flux surface representing the barrier location.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal helium-4 velocity at the internal transport barrier is the component of the bulk $^{4}\mathrm{He}$ ion flow along the toroidal direction, evaluated on the flux surface chosen to represent the barrier location. The internal transport barrier is a region of locally suppressed turbulent transport identified by steepened pressure or temperature gradients. This species-resolved rotation can differ from main-ion, electron, or other impurity rotation because sources, collisional coupling, and radial electric-field effects are species dependent.

The quantity is the projection of the helium-4 bulk velocity onto the toroidal unit vector at the barrier flux surface:

$$
v_{\phi}^{(^{4}\mathrm{He})} = \mathbf{v}^{(^{4}\mathrm{He})} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}^{(^{4}\mathrm{He})}$ is the helium-4 bulk ion velocity and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, with $R$ the major radius and $Z$ the vertical height.

The value is commonly inferred from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy through the Doppler shift of helium charge-exchange emission lines, with the line-of-sight velocity converted to the toroidal component using viewing geometry and magnetic-equilibrium information. The barrier radius is identified from the steepening of electron or ion temperature gradient profiles in the equilibrium reconstruction.

Typical magnitudes range from near zero in weakly rotating plasmas up to about $2 \times 10^{5}$ m.s^-1 in strongly heated, neutral-beam-driven discharges, with either sign possible depending on momentum input, intrinsic rotation, and local transport.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the helium-4 bulk flow points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$).

NAMES.name: toroidal_hydrogen_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: hydrogen
NAMES.short: Toroidal hydrogen ion flow velocity evaluated at the radial location of the internal transport barrier in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal hydrogen ion velocity at an internal transport barrier is the component of the hydrogen ion bulk flow parallel to the toroidal basis direction, evaluated at the radial position where the barrier is identified. It describes the local hydrogen rotation associated with the barrier and is a signed velocity component, not a speed magnitude.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, the component is defined by projecting the hydrogen ion flow velocity onto the toroidal unit vector at the internal-transport-barrier location:

$$
v_{\phi,\mathrm{H},\mathrm{ITB}} = \mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{H}}(r_{\mathrm{ITB}}) \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{H}}$ is the hydrogen ion bulk flow velocity, $r_{\mathrm{ITB}}$ is a radial label for the barrier location, and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

This quantity is commonly obtained from Doppler spectroscopy of hydrogen-related emission, often with charge-exchange or beam-assisted interpretation, and may also be constrained through transport analysis using species force balance. In such analyzes it is coupled to poloidal flow, pressure gradients, and magnetic-field components in determining the radial electric field and flow shear near the barrier.

Typical magnitudes in core tokamak plasmas are often $10^3$-$10^5$ m.s^-1, depending on external momentum input, collisional coupling to other ion species, neutral-beam geometry, and the strength of the internal transport barrier. Values near zero or sign reversals can occur in weakly rotating or counter-rotating conditions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the hydrogen ion flow is directed in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_hydrogen_velocity_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: hydrogen
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the hydrogen ion fluid velocity evaluated at the magnetic axis, the innermost point of the confined plasma where the gradient of the poloidal magnetic flux vanishes.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal hydrogen velocity at the magnetic axis quantifies the bulk fluid flow of hydrogen ions along the $\hat{\phi}$ direction at the plasma center, where the gradient of the poloidal magnetic flux $\psi$ vanishes. On-axis toroidal rotation reflects the integrated effect of plasma momentum transport driven by neutral beam injection, intrinsic torques, and wave-driven momentum deposition.

The toroidal velocity component is defined as the projection onto the toroidal unit vector:

$$
v_{\phi,\mathrm{H}} = \mathbf{v}_\mathrm{H} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_\mathrm{H}$ is the hydrogen ion fluid velocity and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

This quantity is measured by charge exchange recombination spectroscopy (CXRS), which derives the ion flow velocity from the Doppler shift of hydrogen emission lines when a neutral beam intersects the plasma; the on-axis value corresponds to the innermost resolvable CXRS channel. Typical on-axis values range from a few km/s in Ohmic discharges to 100–300 km/s in strongly beam-heated plasmas. Analogous on-axis velocities for other ion species — including [toroidal helium-4 velocity at the magnetic axis](name:toroidal_helium_4_velocity_at_magnetic_axis), [toroidal helium-3 velocity at the magnetic axis](name:toroidal_helium_3_velocity_at_magnetic_axis), and [toroidal tungsten velocity at the magnetic axis](name:toroidal_tungsten_velocity_at_magnetic_axis) — follow the same definition and enable cross-species rotation comparisons that constrain radial electric field profiles and neoclassical transport models.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $v_{\phi,\mathrm{H}}$ points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_inertial_current_density
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the inertial current density, defined as the projection of the inertial-current-density vector onto the positive phi direction in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It represents the current-density contribution associated with plasma-fluid inertia terms in momentum or generalized-Ohm-law balances.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal inertial current density is the physical component of the inertial-current-density vector along $\hat{\phi}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It describes the part of a current-density balance attributed to finite plasma mass density and acceleration of charged species, rather than to resistive, pressure-gradient, viscous, or externally driven terms.

The component definition is the projection of the inertial-current-density vector onto the toroidal unit vector:

$$
j_{\mathrm{inertial},\phi} = \mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{inertial}} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $j_{\mathrm{inertial},\phi}$ is the toroidal inertial current density in A m$^{-2}$, $\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{inertial}}$ is the inertial-current-density vector in A m$^{-2}$, and $\hat{\phi}$ is a dimensionless unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle. This equation defines only the component convention; the construction of $\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{inertial}}$ depends on the fluid, kinetic, or transport momentum model being evaluated.

This quantity is generally computed rather than measured directly. It is inferred from momentum-balance or generalized-Ohm-law calculations using species densities, charges, velocities, time derivatives, velocity gradients, and any model terms used to isolate the inertial contribution from the total current-density balance.

Typical magnitudes are highly scenario and model dependent. In slowly evolving core transport analyzes the value may be close to zero or much smaller than the total toroidal current density, while rapidly evolving edge or transient conditions can produce local magnitudes of about 10$^{2}$-10$^{6}$ A m$^{-2}$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the inertial current density vector points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_ion_momentum_damping_rate
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Inverse relaxation time for damping the bulk ion momentum component along the toroidal phi direction in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, where R is major radius and Z is vertical height. It quantifies how rapidly toroidal ion rotation is relaxed by collisional, neoclassical, neutral, or modeled transport processes.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal ion momentum damping rate is an inverse timescale for relaxation of the bulk ion momentum density associated with velocity along $\hat{\phi}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height. It is a rate coefficient: larger values imply faster loss of organized toroidal ion rotation to collisional, neoclassical, neutral, or other modeled momentum sinks.

A common local relaxation representation defines the damping contribution to the toroidal momentum source density as

$$
S_{\phi,\mathrm{damp}} = -m_i n_i \nu_{\phi,i}\left(u_{\phi,i}-u_{\phi,i}^{\mathrm{ref}}\right)
$$

where $S_{\phi,\mathrm{damp}}$ is the damping part of the toroidal ion momentum source density in kg m^-2 s^-2, $m_i$ is the ion mass in kg, $n_i$ is the ion density in m^-3, $\nu_{\phi,i}$ is the toroidal ion momentum damping rate in s^-1, and $u_{\phi,i}$ and $u_{\phi,i}^{\mathrm{ref}}$ are toroidal ion velocities in m s^-1 along $\hat{\phi}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. If the full momentum balance uses $S_\phi$ for a total toroidal momentum source density, $S_\phi$ has the same units. For a damping term $\nu_{\phi,i}$ is non-negative and reduces the velocity relative to the reference rotation; a negative fitted coefficient represents anti-damping or drive rather than damping.

The rate is usually inferred rather than measured directly. It can be estimated from ion momentum-balance analysis using toroidal rotation measurements, ion density and temperature, neutral interaction estimates, and equilibrium geometry, or computed from neoclassical and kinetic transport models that represent collisional viscosity, trapped-particle effects, charge-exchange with neutrals, applied three-dimensional magnetic perturbations, and other effective momentum sinks. Transient spin-up or spin-down observations constrain it through the observed exponential relaxation time of toroidal ion rotation.

Typical effective values in confined tokamak core conditions are about 0.1-100 s^-1, corresponding to relaxation times of 10 ms-10 s. Neutral-rich edge plasmas, high-collisionality regimes, or strong applied non-axisymmetric magnetic perturbations can give modeled local values of 10^2-10^4 s^-1, while weakly damped core conditions may be below 0.1 s^-1.

NAMES.name: toroidal_ion_momentum_flux
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Radial flux density across magnetic flux surfaces of the toroidal component of ion linear momentum in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It includes convective and ion pressure-stress contributions and has the dimensions of a stress.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal ion momentum flux is the scalar flux-surface-normal transport rate of the toroidal component of ion linear momentum per unit area. The toroidal component is defined along the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. This quantity is a momentum-flux density, not a full vector; its dimensions are those of stress.

For a magnetic flux surface labeled by a radial flux coordinate $\rho$ increasing outward from the magnetic axis, a local scalar definition is

$$
\Pi_{i,\phi}^{\rho} = \hat{\mathbf{n}}_{\rho} \cdot \left(n_i m_i \mathbf{v}_i \mathbf{v}_i + \mathbf{P}_i\right) \cdot \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}
$$

where $\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{\rho}$ is the outward unit normal to the flux surface, $\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $n_i$ is ion number density, $m_i$ is ion mass, $\mathbf{v}_i$ is the ion bulk velocity, and $\mathbf{P}_i$ is the ion pressure-stress tensor including thermal, viscous, and turbulent stress contributions as appropriate. The dyadic term $n_i m_i \mathbf{v}_i \mathbf{v}_i$ gives the convective transport of toroidal momentum.

In practice this flux is inferred from ion momentum balance, from transport models using measured or calculated rotation, density, temperature, torque, and stress terms, or from kinetic and fluid calculations of turbulent and neoclassical momentum transport. Related component and species resolutions include [radial_ion_momentum_flux](name:radial_ion_momentum_flux_over_edge_region), [toroidal_ion_charge_state_momentum_flux](name:toroidal_ion_charge_state_momentum_flux), and [toroidal_total_momentum_flux](name:toroidal_total_momentum_flux).

Typical magnitudes are often $10^{-3}-10$ kg.m^-1.s^-2 in confined tokamak plasmas, with values approaching $10-100$ kg.m^-1.s^-2 in regions with strong rotation shear, strong external torque, or large edge stresses.
NAMES.sign: Positive when ion linear momentum in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame is transported outward, from lower to higher radial flux coordinate $\rho$, across a magnetic flux surface.

NAMES.name: toroidal_ion_momentum_implicit_source_rate
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Rate coefficient for the implicit source proportional to ion momentum in the toroidal phi direction of the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. Its magnitude is an inverse time scale; its sign distinguishes proportional drive from damping.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal ion momentum implicit source rate is the scalar coefficient multiplying the existing ion toroidal momentum density in a linearized momentum-balance source term. The toroidal direction is the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height.

The linearized implicit contribution to the toroidal ion momentum source density is represented as:

$$
S_{\phi,\mathrm{impl}} = \gamma_{\phi,\mathrm{impl}}\,p_\phi
$$

where $\gamma_{\phi,\mathrm{impl}}$ is this rate coefficient with unit $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, $p_\phi$ is the toroidal ion angular-momentum density with unit $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-1}}$, and $S_{\phi,\mathrm{impl}}$ is the corresponding toroidal ion angular-momentum source density with unit $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$.

This coefficient is normally obtained by linearizing momentum-source and momentum-sink models about the current plasma state rather than by direct measurement as an independent diagnostic observable. It is used to treat source terms proportional to the existing toroidal flow, such as viscous relaxation, collisional or neutral drag, and wave-particle momentum exchange; non-proportional applied torque is represented separately by [toroidal_ion_torque](name:toroidal_ion_torque). Closely related rate or coefficient names are [toroidal_ion_momentum_coefficient](name:toroidal_ion_momentum_implicit_source_rate), [toroidal_ion_implicit_source_rate](name:toroidal_ion_momentum_implicit_source_rate), and the more general [ion_momentum_implicit_source_rate](name:ion_momentum_implicit_source_rate).

There is no device-independent typical range because the value depends on the chosen linearization, species, collisionality, and local plasma conditions. Its magnitude is best interpreted as an inverse relaxation time: $|\gamma_{\phi,\mathrm{impl}}|=1\ \mathrm{s}^{-1}$ corresponds to a 1 s proportional time scale, while $|\gamma_{\phi,\mathrm{impl}}|=10^3\ \mathrm{s}^{-1}$ corresponds to a 1 ms stiff time scale; zero means no implicit proportional contribution is included.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $S_{\phi,\mathrm{impl}}$ has the same sign as $p_\phi$, so the implicit contribution amplifies the existing toroidal ion momentum.

NAMES.name: toroidal_ion_rotation_frequency
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Toroidal angular rotation frequency of an ion species, averaged over charge states, defined as the toroidal velocity divided by the local major radius.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal rotation frequency $\Omega_\mathrm{tor}$ characterizes the bulk angular rotation of an ion species about the machine symmetry axis in the toroidal direction, with contributions from all charge states combined into a single effective frequency. It is the primary scalar measure of ion toroidal rotation used in momentum transport analysis and serves as a profile quantity spanning core to edge plasma regions.

The defining relation connects $\Omega_\mathrm{tor}$ to the toroidal fluid velocity $v_\mathrm{tor}$ and the local major radius $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame:

$$
\Omega_\mathrm{tor} = \frac{v_\mathrm{tor}}{R}
$$

where $v_\mathrm{tor}$ is the toroidal component of the ion mass-flow velocity, and $R$ is the major radius at the evaluation point. When multiple charge states are present, this frequency is the charge-state-averaged value, weighted by respective particle densities. The charge-state-resolved counterpart is [toroidal ion state rotation frequency](name:toroidal_ion_state_rotation_frequency), which distinguishes contributions from individual ionization levels.

Toroidal rotation is routinely inferred from charge exchange recombination spectroscopy, which measures the Doppler shift of impurity emission lines to obtain $v_\mathrm{tor}$; $\Omega_\mathrm{tor}$ then follows by dividing by the local $R$. The closely related quantity [toroidal ion velocity](name:toroidal_ion_velocity) gives the same physical flow in velocity units. In NBI-heated core plasmas, $\Omega_\mathrm{tor}$ typically spans $10^3$–$10^5$ rad/s, with co-current rotation being predominant during tangential beam injection.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the ions rotate in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$).

NAMES.name: toroidal_ion_state_momentum_convection_velocity
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Effective across-flux-surface convection velocity for radial transport of toroidal momentum carried by a specified ion charge state. The toroidal label identifies the transported momentum component, not the direction of this velocity.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal ion-state momentum convection velocity is the effective radial velocity coefficient for the non-diffusive transport of toroidal momentum carried by ions of a specified species and charge state. The toroidal momentum component is defined along $\hat{\phi}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height; the coefficient itself describes transport across magnetic flux surfaces labeled by a radial flux coordinate such as $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$.

In a local flux-surface-averaged momentum balance, the convective contribution to the radial flux of toroidal ion-state momentum can be written as

$$
\Gamma^{\mathrm{conv}}_{\phi,i,z} = V_{\phi,i,z} p_{\phi,i,z}
$$

where $\Gamma^{\mathrm{conv}}_{\phi,i,z}$ is the convective radial flux density of toroidal momentum for ion species $i$ in charge state $z$ in kg m$^{-1}$ s$^{-2}$, $V_{\phi,i,z}$ is this convection velocity in m s$^{-1}$, and $p_{\phi,i,z}$ is the toroidal momentum density in kg m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$. The density is often represented as $p_{\phi,i,z}=m_i n_{i,z} u_{\phi,i,z}$, with $m_i$ the ion mass in kg, $n_{i,z}$ the charge-state density in m$^{-3}$, and $u_{\phi,i,z}$ the ion flow component along $\hat{\phi}$ in m s$^{-1}$. The total radial momentum flux may also contain a diffusive term proportional to the radial gradient of toroidal momentum; this quantity represents the pinch-like or outward non-diffusive part.

It is not usually measured directly. It is inferred from momentum-balance analysis using rotation measurements, ion densities, momentum sources and sinks, collisional exchange, and neoclassical or turbulent transport modeling; charge-state-resolved values are most relevant when impurity transport, partial ionization, or state-dependent momentum exchange is important.

Typical inferred core values are about -20-20 m s$^{-1}$ in tokamak transport analyzes, with strong momentum-pinch, edge, or barrier conditions occasionally giving magnitudes of 50-100 m s$^{-1}$. Values near zero indicate that non-diffusive convection is small compared with diffusive transport and applied momentum sources.
NAMES.sign: Positive when a positive toroidal momentum density, with ion flow in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, produces a convective flux directed toward increasing radial flux coordinate $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$, from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: toroidal_ion_state_momentum_damping_rate
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Rate coefficient for collisional or neoclassical damping of the toroidal phi component of fluid momentum for a specified ion charge state in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) system.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal ion state momentum damping rate is a charge-state-resolved effective relaxation coefficient for the toroidal component of ion fluid momentum. The toroidal direction is the direction of increasing angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ system, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height. In radial transport balances it is normally an effective flux-surface-averaged coefficient for the selected ion charge state, not a microscopic point-particle collision frequency.

A common defining use is as the coefficient multiplying the toroidal momentum density in a radial flux-surface momentum balance written with a minor-radius-like flux-surface label $r$ measured in meters:

$$
\frac{\partial P_{\phi,q}}{\partial t}
+ \frac{1}{V'}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left(V'\Gamma_{\phi,q}^{r}\right)
= S_{\phi,q} - \nu_{\phi,q} P_{\phi,q}
$$

where $\nu_{\phi,q}$ is the toroidal ion state momentum damping rate, $q$ labels the ion charge state, $P_{\phi,q}=m_i n_{i,q} v_{\phi,i,q}$ is the toroidal linear momentum density in $\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-2}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, $m_i$ is ion mass in $\mathrm{kg}$, $n_{i,q}$ is charge-state density in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, and $v_{\phi,i,q}$ is toroidal fluid velocity in $\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$. Also, $V'=dV/dr$ is differential plasma volume per unit $r$ in $\mathrm{m}^{2}$, $\Gamma_{\phi,q}^{r}$ is the radial flux of toroidal momentum in $\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-1}\,\mathrm{s}^{-2}$, and $S_{\phi,q}$ represents non-damping sources of toroidal momentum density in $\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-2}\,\mathrm{s}^{-2}$. A dissipative damping model has $\nu_{\phi,q}\ge 0$; a negative value would represent an effective toroidal momentum drive rather than damping.

The rate is usually inferred or prescribed in transport modeling rather than measured directly. It may be computed from Coulomb collision operators, neoclassical viscosity closures, charge-state-resolved impurity momentum exchange, or reduced relaxation models. It is the toroidal component of [ion_state_momentum_damping_rate](name:ion_state_momentum_damping_rate), the charge-state-resolved counterpart of [toroidal_ion_momentum_damping_rate](name:toroidal_ion_momentum_damping_rate), and is analogous to [poloidal_ion_state_momentum_damping_rate](name:poloidal_ion_state_momentum_damping_rate), [radial_ion_state_momentum_damping_rate](name:radial_ion_state_momentum_damping_rate), and [parallel_ion_state_momentum_damping_rate](name:parallel_ion_state_momentum_damping_rate). The corresponding electron momentum concept is represented by toroidal_electron_momentum_damping_rate.

Typical effective values are highly model and regime dependent. In core tokamak transport studies they may range from near 0 to about $10^5$ s^-1; edge, impurity-rich, or strongly collisional cases, and models with different closure assumptions, can lie outside this broad range.

NAMES.name: toroidal_ion_state_momentum_flux
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Flux density of the toroidal component of linear momentum for ions in a specified ion state, with the toroidal direction given by increasing phi in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It includes convective cross-surface transport and non-convective stress contributions.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal ion-state momentum flux is the cross-surface flux density of the toroidal component of linear momentum carried by ions in a specified state. The toroidal component is defined along the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height. The quantity includes both convective transport by flow normal to the transport surface and non-convective transport by stresses.

For a transport surface with outward unit normal $\hat{n}$, the flux can be decomposed into convective and non-convective parts:

$$
F_{\phi,s} = m_s n_s u_{\phi,s} u_{n,s} + \Pi^{\mathrm{nc}}_{n\phi,s}
$$

where $F_{\phi,s}$ is the toroidal momentum flux for ion state $s$, $m_s$ is the ion mass, $n_s$ is the state density, $u_{\phi,s}=\mathbf{u}_s\cdot\hat{\phi}$ is the toroidal flow velocity, $u_{n,s}=\mathbf{u}_s\cdot\hat{n}$ is the outward-normal flow velocity, and $\Pi^{\mathrm{nc}}_{n\phi,s}$ is the non-convective normal flux of toroidal momentum. The non-convective term represents viscous, turbulent, collisional, or kinetic stress transport as a flux contribution; it is not a separate scalar pressure term.

In practice this quantity is obtained from state-resolved momentum balance in fluid, gyrofluid, or kinetic transport calculations. The convective part uses density and flow estimates for the selected ion state, while the non-convective part is inferred from stress closures, fluctuation correlations, collisional transport models, or constraints from spectroscopic measurements of ion flows and temperatures. Related quantities include the total-ion [toroidal_ion_momentum_flux](name:toroidal_ion_momentum_flux), the charge-state variant [toroidal_ion_charge_state_momentum_flux](name:toroidal_ion_charge_state_momentum_flux), and directional ion-state components such as [radial_ion_state_momentum_flux](name:radial_ion_state_momentum_flux), [poloidal_ion_state_momentum_flux](name:poloidal_ion_state_momentum_flux), parallel_ion_state_momentum_flux, and [vertical_ion_state_momentum_flux](name:vertical_ion_state_momentum_flux).

Order-of-magnitude estimates follow from the convective scale $m_s n_s |u_{\phi,s}u_{n,s}|$ together with the modeled stress contribution. For edge and scrape-off-layer conditions with $n_s=10^{18}-10^{20}$ m^-3, $|u_{\phi,s}|=10^3-10^5$ m s^-1, and $|u_{n,s}|=0.1-10^2$ m s^-1, representative convective magnitudes are about 10^-7-1 kg m^-1 s^-2; strong rotation, steep shear, or intermittent turbulence can give larger local stress-like fluxes.
NAMES.sign: Positive when toroidal momentum in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame is transported along the outward normal of the transport surface.

NAMES.name: toroidal_ion_state_rotation_frequency
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Toroidal angular rotation frequency of a specific ion charge state, equal to the toroidal bulk velocity divided by the local major radius.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal rotation frequency of an ion charge state quantifies the angular velocity at which ions belonging to a given ionization level revolve around the machine symmetry axis. It characterizes the toroidal spin of a charge-state-resolved ion population, providing finer kinetic detail than species-averaged quantities.

The defining relation is:

$$
\Omega_\mathrm{tor} = \frac{v_\mathrm{tor}}{R}
$$

where $v_\mathrm{tor}$ is the bulk toroidal velocity of the charge-state population and $R$ is the local major radius measured from the symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

This charge-state-resolved quantity distinguishes specific ionization levels of an ion species, in contrast to [toroidal_ion_rotation_frequency](name:toroidal_ion_rotation_frequency), which averages over all charge states. Different ionization states can rotate at distinct rates owing to their differing charge-to-mass ratios, neoclassical poloidal asymmetries, and differential collisional coupling to the bulk plasma. The corresponding linear velocity is [toroidal_ion_state_velocity](name:toroidal_ion_state_velocity), related by $v_\mathrm{tor} = \Omega_\mathrm{tor} R$.

Toroidal rotation is measured by charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, which resolves Doppler-shifted emission from specific charge states and, combined with the local major-radius profile, yields $\Omega_\mathrm{tor}$ directly. In tokamak H-mode core plasmas, values typically range from $10^3$ to a few times $10^5$ rad/s, with impurity charge states occasionally showing rotation rates distinct from the hydrogenic bulk.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the ion charge state rotates in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$).

NAMES.name: toroidal_ion_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the diamagnetic drift velocity of a specified ion charge state in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, driven by the magnetic-field cross ion-state pressure-gradient direction.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal ion-state diamagnetic drift velocity is the projection of the fluid diamagnetic drift of a specified ion charge state onto $\hat{\phi}$, the direction of increasing toroidal angle in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It is associated with the pressure gradient of that charge state and is distinct from the center-of-mass toroidal flow of the ions.

For charge state $z$, the toroidal component is defined by projecting the magnetic-field-cross-pressure-gradient drift onto $\hat{\phi}$:

$$
v_{\phi,*,z} = \left(\frac{\mathbf{B} \times \nabla p_z}{q_z n_z B^2}\right) \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $p_z$ is the partial pressure in $\mathrm{Pa}$, $\nabla p_z$ has units $\mathrm{Pa\,m^{-1}}$, $n_z$ is the number density in $\mathrm{m^{-3}}$, $q_z$ is the charge in $\mathrm{C}$, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field in $\mathrm{T}$, and $B=|\mathbf{B}|$ is its magnitude in $\mathrm{T}$. The resulting $v_{\phi,*,z}$ has units $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

In practice it is computed from charge-state-resolved density and temperature, or directly from the partial pressure, together with the local magnetic-field direction and magnitude. The toroidal projection is the component of $\mathbf{B} \times \nabla p_z$ along $\hat{\phi}$ and is related to the radial counterpart [radial_ion_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:radial_ion_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift) and the full drift vector [ion_state_diamagnetic_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:ion_state_diamagnetic_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift).

The magnitude scales approximately as $p_z/(|q_z| n_z B L_p)$, where $L_p=p_z/|\nabla_\perp p_z|$ is the perpendicular pressure-gradient scale length. Typical toroidal components are $10-10^4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; main-ion core values are often $10^2-10^3\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, while steep edge gradients or lower magnetic field can produce larger values.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the diamagnetic drift velocity of the ion charge state points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_ion_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the E×B drift velocity for an ion charge state, arising from the cross-product of the local electric and magnetic fields perpendicular to both.
NAMES.long:
The E×B drift is a charge-independent bulk plasma drift that transports all species at the same velocity perpendicular to both the electric field $\mathbf{E}$ and magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$. The full drift velocity is given by

$$
\mathbf{v}_{E\times B} = \frac{\mathbf{E} \times \mathbf{B}}{B^2}
$$

where $\mathbf{E}$ is the local electric field and $B = |\mathbf{B}|$ is the magnetic field magnitude. The toroidal component reported here is the projection of $\mathbf{v}_{E\times B}$ onto the $\hat{\phi}$ direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. In the edge and scrape-off layer regions of tokamaks, radial electric fields of order 1–100 kV/m combined with poloidal magnetic fields of 0.1–1 T yield toroidal E×B velocities of order $10^3$–$10^5$ m/s. This quantity is relevant to particle and momentum transport modeling, where toroidal E×B flow contributes to the total toroidal rotation of a given ion charge state alongside diamagnetic and neoclassical drifts. The complementary spatial projections [radial_ion_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift](name:radial_ion_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift) and [poloidal_ion_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift](name:poloidal_ion_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift) complete the vector decomposition, while [toroidal_neutral_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift](name:toroidal_neutral_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift) provides the analogous quantity for neutral charge states.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the toroidal E×B drift velocity component points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_ion_velocity
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the charge-state-averaged ion fluid velocity, quantifying the bulk ion flow along the toroidal direction in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal ion velocity is the $\phi$-component of the mean ion fluid velocity vector, obtained by projecting [ion_velocity](name:ion_velocity) onto the toroidal unit vector $\hat{\phi}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. When multiple charge states are present, it represents the charge-state-averaged bulk flow and is the dominant rotation component governing toroidal angular momentum transport and confinement.

The toroidal component is defined as:

$$
v_\phi^{(i)} = \mathbf{v}_i \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_i$ is the charge-state-averaged ion fluid velocity vector and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

The toroidal ion velocity is measured experimentally through charge exchange recombination spectroscopy (CXRS), where Doppler shifts of emission lines from impurity ions yield the local ion flow velocity along the line of sight. Neoclassical transport models and multi-fluid solvers additionally compute this quantity from the radial force balance on the ion fluid, connecting it to the radial electric field and pressure gradient.

Typical magnitudes range from a few km/s in ohmic discharges to 100–300 km/s in neutral-beam-heated H-mode plasmas. Its radial gradient drives the [radial_edge_ion_momentum_flux](name:radial_ion_momentum_flux_over_edge_region) and the effective convection characterized by [radial_ion_effective_momentum_convection_velocity](name:radial_plasma_effective_momentum_convection_velocity). The related [toroidal_plasma_velocity](name:toroidal_impurity_ion_velocity_at_measurement_position) captures whole-plasma toroidal rotation inferred from X-ray spectroscopy, while [toroidal_ion_state_momentum](name:toroidal_ion_state_momentum) provides the charge-state-resolved toroidal momentum source in edge transport equations.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the ion flow is directed in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise when viewed from above in the $+\hat{Z}$ direction).

NAMES.name: second_radial_derivative_of_toroidal_ion_velocity
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Second derivative, with respect to the normalized toroidal flux radius rho_tor_norm, of the charge-state-averaged ion velocity component along the phi direction in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The second radial derivative of toroidal ion velocity is the curvature of the charge-state-averaged ion toroidal velocity with respect to the flux coordinate $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ (normalized toroidal flux radius). The velocity component is along the $\phi$ direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height; $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ increases from 0 at the magnetic axis to 1 at the last closed flux surface.

It is defined by differentiating the signed toroidal ion velocity twice with respect to the dimensionless radial flux coordinate:

$$
D_{\rho\rho} v_{i,\phi} = \frac{\partial^2 v_{i,\phi}}{\partial \rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}^2}
$$

where $D_{\rho\rho} v_{i,\phi}$ is this second derivative, $v_{i,\phi}$ is the charge-state-averaged toroidal ion velocity in m s$^{-1}$, and $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ is dimensionless. The derivative has units of m s$^{-1}$ because the differentiating coordinate is dimensionless.
