The total fast-ion pressure represents the full gyrotropic kinetic stress of the suprathermal ion population, summed over all charge states, as a contribution to the plasma pressure balance. Fast ions — including fusion-born alpha particles, neutral-beam-injected ions, and radio-frequency-accelerated ions — retain pressure anisotropy with $P_\parallel \neq P_\perp$ relative to the local magnetic field because their pitch-angle scattering rate is slow compared with their energy transfer rate to the bulk plasma. The anisotropic structure is fully captured by the two independent scalar components [parallel total fast-ion pressure](name:parallel_total_fast_ion_pressure) and [perpendicular total fast-ion pressure](name:perpendicular_total_fast_ion_pressure).

For a gyrotropic fast-ion distribution, the pressure tensor is:

$$
\overleftrightarrow{P}_\text{fast} = P_{\perp}\,\overleftrightarrow{I} + (P_{\parallel} - P_{\perp})\,\hat{b}\hat{b}
$$

where $P_{\parallel}$ and $P_{\perp}$ are the parallel and perpendicular scalar pressure components, $\hat{b} = \mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$ is the unit vector along the local magnetic field, and $\overleftrightarrow{I}$ is the identity tensor.

Fast-ion pressure profiles are obtained from kinetic particle-following or Fokker-Planck solvers that evolve the suprathermal distribution function under collisional slowing-down and pitch-angle scattering. The anisotropic fast-ion stress enters the MHD force balance and can drive pressure-anisotropy-driven instabilities when $P_{\parallel}/P_{\perp}$ departs significantly from unity. The parent quantity [fast_ion_pressure](name:fast_ion_pressure) provides per-charge-state resolution.

In high-performance discharges with strong neutral beam or ion cyclotron resonance heating, fast-ion pressure can reach 10–50% of the total plasma pressure in the core, with anisotropy ratios $P_{\parallel}/P_{\perp}$ ranging from near unity for isotropized distributions to several for strongly beam-like distributions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the fast-ion population exerts compressive kinetic pressure, consistent with the second velocity moment of a non-negative distribution function being positive.

NAMES.name: parallel_total_fast_ion_pressure
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Total fast-ion parallel pressure is the fast (suprathermal) ion pressure in the direction parallel to the local magnetic field, summed over all fast-ion species and charge states. It is the parallel component of the gyrotropic fast-ion pressure tensor and differs from the perpendicular component when the fast-ion distribution is anisotropic.
NAMES.long:
Parallel total fast-ion pressure is the field-aligned component of the gyrotropic pressure tensor for non-thermal ions, summed over all fast-ion species and charge states. It is the total counterpart of [parallel_fast_ion_pressure](name:parallel_fast_ion_pressure) and [parallel_fast_ion_state_pressure](name:parallel_fast_ion_state_pressure), and it complements [perpendicular_fast_ion_pressure](name:perpendicular_fast_ion_pressure) and [perpendicular_total_fast_ion_pressure](name:perpendicular_total_fast_ion_pressure) in describing fast-ion pressure anisotropy.

The kinetic definition is the parallel second central velocity moment of the fast-ion distribution functions:

$$
P_{\parallel,\mathrm{fast,total}} = \sum_s m_s \int \left(v_\parallel - u_{\parallel,s}\right)^2 f_{\mathrm{fast},s}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $s$ indexes fast-ion species, $m_s$ is the ion mass, $f_{\mathrm{fast},s}$ is the fast-ion distribution function, $v_\parallel = \mathbf{v}\cdot\hat{b}$ is the velocity component along the local magnetic-field unit vector $\hat{b}$, and $u_{\parallel,s}$ is the species mean parallel flow velocity. For a gyrotropic pressure tensor, this quantity and the perpendicular pressure determine the trace-equivalent scalar fast-ion pressure through the inline relation $p_\mathrm{fast} = (P_{\parallel,\mathrm{fast,total}} + 2P_{\perp,\mathrm{fast,total}})/3$.

In practice it is computed from fast-ion distribution functions inferred from diagnostics such as neutron emission, gamma-ray emission, neutral-particle analysis, fast-ion D-alpha spectroscopy, or collective Thomson scattering, often combined with orbit-following, Fokker-Planck, or Monte Carlo transport calculations. Strong neutral-beam injection, ion-cyclotron heating, or fusion-born alpha populations can make the parallel and perpendicular components substantially different before pitch-angle scattering and slowing down reduce the anisotropy.

Typical values in magnetically confined fusion plasmas are about 10^2-10^6 Pa. Values near the upper end occur in high-power beam-heated or alpha-heated core regions, while weakly heated regions or locations with little confined fast-ion population can be much lower.

NAMES.name: perpendicular_total_fast_ion_pressure
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Total fast-ion perpendicular pressure, summed over all species, is the component of the suprathermal ion gyrotropic pressure tensor associated with ion motion perpendicular to the local magnetic field.
NAMES.long:
The perpendicular total fast-ion pressure $P_{\perp,\text{fast}}$ is the principal perpendicular component of the gyrotropic pressure tensor of suprathermal ions, summed over all ion species and charge states. It quantifies the kinetic energy of fast ions stored in the two velocity degrees of freedom transverse to the local magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$. Together with [parallel_total_fast_ion_pressure](name:parallel_total_fast_ion_pressure), it fully characterizes the pressure anisotropy of the fast-ion population described by the parent [total_fast_ion_pressure](name:total_fast_ion_pressure) tensor.

The perpendicular pressure is the second velocity moment of the fast-ion distribution function in the plane perpendicular to $\mathbf{B}$:

$$
P_{\perp,\text{fast}} = \sum_s \frac{m_s}{2} \int v_\perp^2 \, f_{\text{fast},s}(\mathbf{v}) \, d^3v
$$

where $m_s$ is the ion mass for species $s$, $v_\perp$ is the particle speed in the plane perpendicular to $\mathbf{B}$, and $f_{\text{fast},s}$ is the fast-ion velocity distribution function for species $s$, with the sum running over all fast-ion species.

This quantity is computed from guiding-center kinetic models or Fokker-Planck solvers that evolve the fast-ion distribution function. Preferential perpendicular energization by ion cyclotron resonance heating drives $P_{\perp,\text{fast}} \gg P_{\parallel,\text{fast}}$, while neutral beam injection at oblique angles produces more moderate anisotropy. The charge-state-resolved analog is [perpendicular_fast_ion_state_pressure](name:perpendicular_fast_ion_state_pressure), and the thermal-ion counterpart is [total_thermal_ion_pressure](name:total_thermal_ion_pressure).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the fast-ion population carries nonzero kinetic energy in degrees of freedom perpendicular to the local magnetic field; this quantity is non-negative for all physically realizable fast-ion distributions.

NAMES.name: total_ion_density
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Total ion number density at a local plasma point, summed over all ion species and charge states and including both thermal and non-thermal ion populations. It represents the aggregate ion population, not the density of one selected species or ionization state.
NAMES.long:
Total ion density is the aggregate number density of ions at a plasma point, obtained by summing the densities of all ion species, all resolved charge states, and both thermal and non-thermal ion populations. It is distinct from a species-resolved ion density or a single charge-state density.

The total may be expressed as a sum over species, charge states, and population components:

$$
n_{i,\mathrm{total}} = \sum_s \sum_q \left(n^{\mathrm{th}}_{s,q} + n^{\mathrm{nth}}_{s,q}\right)
$$

where $s$ labels ion species, $q$ labels charge state, $n^{\mathrm{th}}_{s,q}$ is the thermal density of that species and charge state, and $n^{\mathrm{nth}}_{s,q}$ is the corresponding non-thermal density. Equivalently, it is the sum of [total ion state density](name:total_ion_state_density) over all resolved species and charge states; [total thermal ion density](name:total_thermal_ion_density) is the thermal part of this aggregate.

In experiments and simulations, total ion density is usually inferred by combining composition measurements, charge-state balance, impurity diagnostics, neutral-beam or fast-ion modeling, and quasineutrality constraints. In a nearly pure deuterium-tritium plasma with singly charged main ions, it is close to the electron density, while in plasmas with significant impurities or multiple ionization states it differs because each ion contributes one particle to $n_{i,\mathrm{total}}$ regardless of charge.

Typical values range from about $10^{18}$-$10^{20}$ m^-3 in the edge and scrape-off-layer plasma and about $0.1$-$2 \times 10^{20}$ m^-3 in the confined core of medium to large tokamaks. Non-thermal ion populations are often a small correction to the total density but can be important in plasmas with strong auxiliary heating or energetic fusion products.

NAMES.name: radial_derivative_of_total_ion_density
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: First-order radial derivative of total ion number density (thermal plus non-thermal, summed over all charge states) with respect to the normalized toroidal flux coordinate.
NAMES.long:
The first radial derivative of [total_ion_density](name:total_ion_density) with respect to the normalized toroidal flux coordinate $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$ characterizes the spatial variation of the total ion particle inventory across nested flux surfaces. The total ion population encompasses both thermal and non-thermal (fast) ions, aggregated over all charge states.

The defining expression is:

$$
\frac{d n_i^\mathrm{tot}}{d\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}}
$$

where $n_i^\mathrm{tot}$ is the total ion number density (in m$^{-3}$, thermal plus non-thermal, summed over charge states) and $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$ is the normalized toroidal flux radius, with $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm} = 0$ at the magnetic axis and $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm} = 1$ at the last closed flux surface. Because $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$ is dimensionless, this derivative carries the same unit as the density itself.

This quantity is evaluated numerically within transport solver frameworks as part of diffusion-advection flux computation for the ion particle transport equation. It enters the diffusive ion particle flux as $\Gamma_i \sim -D_i \, dn_i^\mathrm{tot}/d\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$, where $D_i$ is the ion diffusion coefficient. The [second_radial_derivative_of_total_ion_density](name:second_radial_derivative_of_total_ion_density) is its higher-order companion used in more accurate discretization schemes. For charge-state-resolved calculations, [radial_derivative_of_total_ion_state_density](name:radial_derivative_of_total_ion_state_density) provides per-state gradients, while [radial_derivative_of_fast_ion_density](name:radial_derivative_of_fast_ion_density) isolates the non-thermal contribution alone.
NAMES.sign: Positive when total ion density increases with increasing $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$, directed toward the plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: second_radial_derivative_of_total_ion_density
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Second derivative of total ion number density (thermal plus non-thermal, summed over all charge states) with respect to the normalized toroidal flux coordinate, quantifying the radial curvature of the ion density profile.
NAMES.long:
The second radial derivative of total ion density describes the curvature of the ion density profile along the normalized toroidal flux coordinate $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$. The total ion density $n_i$ encompasses both thermal and non-thermal (fast) ion contributions, summed over all charge states, providing a complete representation of the ion population's radial structure as required by 1D transport equations.

The quantity is defined as:

$$
\frac{d^2 n_i}{d\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}^2}
$$

where $n_i$ is the total ion density and $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm} \in [0, 1]$ is the normalized toroidal flux coordinate, with $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm} = 0$ at the magnetic axis and $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm} = 1$ at the last closed flux surface. Because $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$ is dimensionless, this second derivative carries the same unit as the density itself.

This curvature term arises in second-order spatial discretization of radial ion transport equations, where both first- and second-order derivatives are needed to evaluate diffusive flux terms accurately. It is computed numerically from the total ion density profile during transport solver iterations, complementing the [first radial derivative of total ion density](name:radial_derivative_of_total_ion_density). Analogous second-derivative quantities are defined for the fast-ion sub-population in [second_radial_derivative_of_fast_ion_density](name:second_radial_derivative_of_fast_ion_density) and for individual charge states in [second_radial_derivative_of_total_ion_state_density](name:second_radial_derivative_of_total_ion_state_density).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the total ion density profile is concave upward as a function of increasing $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$, i.e., when the local profile curvature $d^2 n_i / d\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}^2 > 0$.

NAMES.name: total_ion_density_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Total ion density at an internal transport barrier is the local unweighted number-density sum over all ion populations present there, including fuel, minority, impurity, and non-thermal ions when they are part of the ion inventory. It excludes neutral particles and is not charge weighted.
NAMES.long:
Total ion density at an internal transport barrier (ITB) is the local ion number density obtained by adding the number densities of all ion populations at the barrier. The sum includes thermal and, when represented, non-thermal ion populations for fuel, minority, and impurity ions; neutral particles are excluded. It is an unweighted particle count, not a charge density, mass density, or pressure.

The local total is defined by the population sum evaluated at the ITB location:

$$
n_{i,\mathrm{total}}(\mathbf{x}_\mathrm{ITB}) = \sum_{\alpha \in \mathrm{ions}} n_\alpha(\mathbf{x}_\mathrm{ITB})
$$

where $\mathbf{x}_\mathrm{ITB}$ is the position of the internal transport barrier and $\alpha$ labels an ion population, which may distinguish chemical species, charge state, and thermal or non-thermal component. Both $n_\alpha$ and $n_{i,\mathrm{total}}$ are number densities in m^-3. If charge states are resolved, each charge-state population contributes its own number density term; the charge $Z_\alpha$ is not used as a weight in this sum.

In practice this quantity is obtained by combining local density and composition information at the identified ITB location. Electron-density measurements constrain the charge-weighted ion inventory through quasineutrality, while spectroscopy, charge-exchange recombination measurements, neutron or neutral-particle information, and transport analysis may constrain selected ion species or energetic-ion components. The total ion number density is then computed from the inferred population densities and composition model by applying the unweighted sum above.

Typical local values in tokamak plasmas with internal transport barriers are of order 1 x 10^19-1 x 10^20 m^-3. This range is an order-of-magnitude guide rather than a device-independent bound, because the value depends on the local electron density, impurity content, fuel mix, and any non-thermal ion population included in the ion inventory.

NAMES.name: total_ion_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Total number density summed over all ion species, evaluated at the magnetic axis where the gradient of the poloidal magnetic flux vanishes.
NAMES.long:
The total ion density at the magnetic axis $n_{i,\mathrm{total}}$ is the sum of local number densities of all ion species — fuel ions, impurity ions, and minority ion species — at the innermost point of the confined plasma, the magnetic axis defined by $\nabla\psi = 0$. Neutral particles are excluded from this sum by convention.

The defining relation is:

$$
n_{i,\mathrm{total}} = \sum_s n_s
$$

where $n_s$ is the number density of ion species $s$ in m$^{-3}$, with the sum running over all ion species present in the plasma.

This on-axis value is obtained from Thomson scattering, charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, or multi-chord interferometry, with the magnetic-axis location determined from equilibrium reconstruction. Combined with [electron_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:electron_density_at_magnetic_axis), it constrains the quasi-neutrality condition $n_e = \sum_s Z_s n_s$, where $Z_s$ is the charge number of species $s$. Analogous values at the boundary and pedestal are provided by [total_ion_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:total_ion_density_at_plasma_boundary) and [total_ion_density_at_pedestal](name:total_ion_density_at_pedestal). Typical on-axis values in tokamak discharges span $10^{19}$–$10^{21}$ m$^{-3}$, increasing toward the upper bound in high-density pellet-fueled scenarios.
NAMES.sign: Positive when ion particles are present at the magnetic axis.

NAMES.name: total_ion_energy_flux
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Net local ion energy flux density vector carried by all ion species and charge states. It sums conductive heat flow and convective enthalpy transport by bulk ion motion, giving the rate and direction of ion thermal-energy transport per unit area.
NAMES.long:
Total ion energy flux is the local vector flux density of thermal energy carried by the combined ion population, including main fuel ions and impurities in all charge states. It represents transport per unit area by both random thermal conduction and directed ion-fluid motion; it is not a flux-surface-averaged or area-integrated power. The vector is expressed in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height.

For a multi-species plasma it is the sum of conductive heat flux and convective enthalpy flux over all ion species:

$$
\mathbf{Q}_i^{\mathrm{tot}} = \sum_{s \in \mathrm{ions}} \left( \mathbf{q}_s + \frac{5}{2} p_s \mathbf{v}_s \right)
$$

where $\mathbf{Q}_i^{\mathrm{tot}}$ is the total ion energy flux density in W m$^{-2}$, $\mathbf{q}_s$ is the conductive heat-flux contribution of ion species $s$ in W m$^{-2}$, $p_s$ is the scalar ion pressure of species $s$ in Pa, and $\mathbf{v}_s$ is the mean ion flow velocity of species $s$ in m s$^{-1}$. The factor $5/2$ gives the ideal monatomic-plasma enthalpy flux; if temperatures are represented in electron-volts, the pressure uses the corresponding energy conversion.

In transport modeling and interpretive power balance this quantity is computed from ion density, temperature, and velocity profiles together with heat-transport closure models, or inferred indirectly from diagnostic constraints on profiles and power flows. The [radial_total_ion_energy_flux](name:radial_total_ion_energy_flux), poloidal_total_ion_energy_flux, and [parallel_total_ion_energy_flux](name:parallel_total_ion_energy_flux) are projections of this local vector onto chosen geometry axes, and ion_energy_convection_velocity parameterizes its convective contribution. The closely related [total_thermal_ion_heat_flux](name:total_thermal_ion_heat_flux) describes the same ion thermal-energy channel, while [total_energy_flux](name:total_thermal_ion_heat_flux) aggregates the full energy balance across plasma species.

Typical magnitudes in scrape-off-layer and edge-plasma conditions are $10^4$-$10^7$ W m$^{-2}$, depending on heating power, density, temperature gradients, connection length, and divertor geometry; core conductive fluxes are generally lower. Cross-field components tend toward the lower end of this range, while field-aligned components carrying energy toward material surfaces can be substantially larger.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the normal component carries ion energy through an oriented surface in the direction of that surface's positive normal.

NAMES.name: parallel_total_ion_energy_flux
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Component of the total ion energy flux along the local magnetic field direction, equal to the net thermal power per unit area transported field-aligned by all ion species combined.
NAMES.long:
The parallel total ion energy flux is the projection of the [total_ion_energy_flux](name:total_ion_energy_flux) vector onto the local magnetic field unit vector $\hat{b} = \mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$. It captures both conductive heat transport and convective enthalpy flux, summed over all ion species in the plasma.

The defining relation is:

$$
q_{\parallel,\mathrm{ion}}^{\mathrm{total}} = \mathbf{Q}_{\mathrm{ion}}^{\mathrm{total}} \cdot \hat{b}
$$

where $\mathbf{Q}_{\mathrm{ion}}^{\mathrm{total}}$ is the total ion energy flux vector and $\hat{b} = \mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$ is the unit vector aligned with the local magnetic field. Summing over all ion species distinguishes this quantity from [parallel_ion_state_energy_flux](name:parallel_ion_state_energy_flux), which resolves the flux per individual charge state. In the scrape-off layer and divertor, parallel transport far exceeds cross-field transport, making this flux the primary determinant of plasma-facing component heat loads. Typical magnitudes along SOL field lines range from $10^7$–$10^9$ W m$^{-2}$ depending on plasma power exhaust conditions and field-line connection length. The corresponding electron contribution is described by [parallel_electron_energy_flux](name:parallel_electron_energy_flux).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the energy flux is directed along the magnetic field unit vector $\hat{b} = \mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$.

NAMES.name: radial_total_ion_energy_flux
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Radial component of the total ion thermal energy flux density, combining conductive heat transport and convective enthalpy flux summed over all ion species and charge states.
NAMES.long:
The radial total ion energy flux is the projection of the [total_ion_energy_flux](name:total_ion_energy_flux) vector onto the radial coordinate direction, quantifying the net rate of thermal energy transport per unit area by the combined ion population. It encompasses both conductive heat transport and convective enthalpy carried by radial ion fluid motion, and is summed over all ion species and charge states present in the plasma.

For a multi-species ion plasma, the defining expression is:

$$
Q_{r,\text{ion}}^{\text{tot}} = \sum_s \left( q_{r,s} + \frac{5}{2}\, n_s T_s u_{r,s} \right)
$$

where $s$ indexes ion species, $q_{r,s}$ is the radial conductive heat flux of species $s$, $n_s$ is the number density, $T_s$ is the ion temperature, and $u_{r,s}$ is the radial fluid velocity of species $s$.

This quantity appears in the radial ion energy conservation equation and is evaluated by edge and core transport solvers. The [radial_total_ion_effective_energy_convection_velocity](name:radial_ion_energy_convection_velocity) represents the effective convection velocity derived from this flux normalized by the local ion pressure, while [radial_ion_energy_convection_velocity](name:radial_ion_energy_convection_velocity) captures the convective component for individual ion species. Typical values in the edge plasma and scrape-off layer range from $10^5$ to $10^7$ W m$^{-2}$, increasing near the separatrix in high-power scenarios.
NAMES.sign: Positive when ion energy is transported in the outward radial direction, away from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: total_ion_power
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Net rate of energy transfer from a specified source to the ion population, summed over all ion species and integrated over the plasma volume.
NAMES.long:
Total ion power is the volume-integrated contribution of a specified source to the ion energy balance. It includes the net energy coupled to all ion species and excludes power coupled directly to electrons, which is represented separately by quantities such as [total_electron_power](name:total_electron_power).

For ion species indexed by $a$, the total ion power is the volume integral of the local ion power density summed over species:

$$
P_{\mathrm{ion}}^{\mathrm{tot}} = \sum_a \int_V p_a(\mathbf{x})\, dV
$$

where $p_a$ is the net power density coupled to ion species $a$ in W m$^{-3}$, $dV$ is the plasma volume element, and $V$ is the plasma volume over which the source contribution is evaluated.

In practice this quantity is computed from source modeling or diagnostic inference by integrating the spatial distribution of ion heating or cooling and summing over thermal and fast ion species as appropriate. It is the ion-channel contribution to the source power balance; adding the corresponding electron-channel contribution gives the total plasma power from the same source when no other channels are included.

Typical values range from 0 W for an absent or inactive source to $10^3$-$10^6$ W for weak source terms, and up to $10^6$-$5 \times 10^7$ W for strong auxiliary ion heating in medium to large tokamak plasmas.
NAMES.sign: Positive when energy is transferred from the source to the ion population.

NAMES.name: total_ion_power_density
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Net volumetric power density deposited into the ion channel, aggregated over all ion species and charge states, representing the total energy source term in the ion energy transport equation.
NAMES.long:
The total ion power density is the net volumetric rate of energy deposition into the combined ion population, summed across all ion species and charge states. It serves as the source term on the right-hand side of the ion energy transport equation, balancing all energy gains and losses to the ion channel from simultaneously active processes in the plasma.

The governing ion energy balance takes the form:

$$
\frac{\partial W_i^{\rm tot}}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \mathbf{q}_i = P_{\rm ion}^{\rm tot}
$$

where $W_i^{\rm tot}$ is the total ion thermal energy density in J m$^{-3}$, $\mathbf{q}_i$ is the total ion heat flux in W m$^{-2}$, and $P_{\rm ion}^{\rm tot}$ is the volumetric source density accumulated from neutral beam injection, ion-cyclotron heating, fusion product thermalization, charge exchange, and collisional energy transfer from electrons.

This quantity is obtained by summing energy source contributions across all ion species and ionization states, making it the aggregate counterpart to the per-charge-state [ion_state_power_density](name:ion_state_power_density) and the complementary electron-channel quantity [electron_power_density](name:electron_power_density). The related [ion_power_density](name:total_ion_power_density) similarly represents a species-summed ion power density; the `total_` qualifier here explicitly emphasizes aggregation over all charge states as well as species. The corresponding particle source is described by [total_ion_source_rate](name:total_ion_source_rate).
NAMES.sign: Positive when net energy flows into the ion channel, representing a volumetric energy gain by the total ion population.

NAMES.name: total_ion_pressure
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Total isotropic scalar pressure of the ion fluid at a plasma location, summing thermal and fast (non-thermal) contributions over all charge states of a given ion species.
NAMES.long:
The total ion pressure is the isotropic scalar pressure of the entire ion fluid at a given point in the plasma, combining the Maxwellian thermal bulk and suprathermal fast-ion contributions summed over all charge states of the species. It represents the physically complete ion kinetic pressure entering force-balance and energy-transport equations in multi-fluid and magnetohydrodynamic models.

The total ion pressure decomposes additively as:

$$
P_i = P_{i,\mathrm{th}} + P_{i,\mathrm{fast}}
$$

where $P_{i,\mathrm{th}}$ is the [thermal ion pressure](name:thermal_ion_pressure) from the Maxwellian bulk, satisfying $P_{i,\mathrm{th}} = n_i k_B T_i$ with $n_i$ the ion number density and $T_i$ the ion temperature, and $P_{i,\mathrm{fast}}$ is the suprathermal fast-ion contribution. The [total thermal ion pressure](name:total_thermal_ion_pressure) isolates the bulk-only term; the [total ion state pressure](name:total_ion_state_pressure) provides per-charge-state resolution.

Together with [total electron pressure](name:total_electron_pressure), the total ion pressure contributes to the full plasma pressure $P = P_e + P_i$ appearing in the MHD force-balance $\nabla P = \mathbf{j} \times \mathbf{B}$. Fast-ion contributions can become comparable to or exceed the thermal term during neutral beam injection or ion cyclotron resonance heating. The quantity is inferred by combining ion temperature and density profile diagnostics with energetic-particle measurements and fast-ion transport modeling.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the ion population has nonzero kinetic energy, which holds for all physical ion populations; scalar ion pressure is an intrinsically non-negative quantity.

NAMES.name: total_ion_source_rate
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Net volumetric source term for total ion particle density, summed over all ion species and charge states. It includes ionization, recombination, charge exchange, fueling, and external particle injection or removal processes.
NAMES.long:
Total ion source rate is the net local rate at which processes create or remove ion particles per unit volume, after summing over all ion species and charge states. It is the species-summed particle source term corresponding to ion_source_rate, and is distinct from energy deposition quantities such as [total_ion_power_density](name:total_ion_power_density).

In a local particle balance, the total ion source rate $S_{i,\mathrm{tot}}$ enters the continuity equation:

$$
\frac{\partial n_{i,\mathrm{tot}}}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{i,\mathrm{tot}} = S_{i,\mathrm{tot}}
$$

where $n_{i,\mathrm{tot}}$ is the total ion particle density in m$^{-3}$, $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{i,\mathrm{tot}}$ is the total ion particle flux density in m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$, and $S_{i,\mathrm{tot}}$ is in m$^{-3}$ s$^{-1}$. The divergence is evaluated in physical space; for example, in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. In flux-surface-averaged transport, the same balance is interpreted after averaging on surfaces labeled by an explicitly named flux coordinate, for example $(\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}, \theta, \phi)$.

In practice, this quantity is computed from particle balance using models or measurements of ionization, recombination, charge exchange with neutrals, neutral beam fueling, gas puffing, pellet ablation, and other particle exchange processes. It may also be inferred from density evolution and particle flux estimates when the transport divergence term is known.

Typical core and edge magnitudes are about $10^{18}$-$10^{21}$ m$^{-3}$ s$^{-1}$ in magnetically confined plasmas, with larger local values possible near strong fueling, pellet deposition, or intense recycling regions. Negative values occur where recombination, charge exchange, or outward particle exchange removes ions faster than they are created.
NAMES.sign: Positive when local processes produce a net increase in the total ion particle density.

NAMES.name: total_ion_state_density
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Total particle number density of a specific ion charge state, summing both thermal and non-thermal (fast) ion contributions at a given plasma location.
NAMES.long:
The total ion charge-state density $n_{i,z}^{\rm tot}$ quantifies the number of particles per unit volume for ion species $i$ in charge state $z$, aggregating both the Maxwellian thermal bulk and any non-thermal (fast) population occupying that charge state. This distinguishes it from the thermal-only [ion_state_density](name:ion_state_density), which excludes suprathermal contributions, making this quantity the appropriate building block for transport models that account for neutral beam injection or fast-particle thermalization.

The total density decomposes as:

$$
n_{i,z}^{\rm tot} = n_{i,z}^{\rm thermal} + n_{i,z}^{\rm fast}
$$

where $n_{i,z}^{\rm thermal}$ is the thermal (Maxwellian) component and $n_{i,z}^{\rm fast}$ is the non-thermal component for species $i$ in charge state $z$.

This quantity is computed from multispecies fluid or kinetic transport codes resolving individual charge states, and is inferred observationally by combining charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy with fast-ion population modeling. Its radial gradient drives diffusive particle fluxes encoded in [radial_ion_state_particle_flux](name:radial_ion_state_particle_flux), and its radial e-folding decay in the scrape-off layer is characterized by [total_ion_decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer](name:total_ion_decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer).

Typical values range from $10^{18}$ to $10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$ for main-ion charge states in the edge plasma, with trace impurity charge states several orders of magnitude lower depending on species and plasma conditions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when ion particles of the specified charge state contribute to the local particle count per unit volume.

NAMES.name: second_radial_derivative_of_total_ion_state_density
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Second-order radial derivative of total ion charge-state density (thermal plus non-thermal) with respect to the normalized toroidal flux coordinate, resolved per ion charge state.
NAMES.long:
The second radial derivative of total ion charge-state density quantifies the curvature of the density profile for a specific ion charge state with respect to the normalized toroidal flux coordinate $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$, spanning 0 at the magnetic axis to 1 at the last closed flux surface. The total density encompasses both thermal and non-thermal particle contributions for the identified charge state, distinguishing this quantity from charge-state-summed counterparts.

The quantity is defined as:

$$
\frac{d^2 n_{i,s}}{d\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}^2}
$$

where $n_{i,s}$ is the total number density of ion charge state $s$ and $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$ is the dimensionless normalized toroidal flux coordinate on $[0, 1]$.

Transport solvers use this second derivative to discretize diffusion terms in the ion particle continuity equation; it encodes the radial variation in the density gradient required for evaluating radial particle fluxes. The quantity is computed numerically from the radial density profile during each solver time step.

Unlike [second_radial_derivative_of_total_ion_density](name:second_radial_derivative_of_total_ion_density), which sums contributions across all charge states, this quantity is resolved per individual charge state, paralleling the first-derivative sibling [radial_derivative_of_total_ion_state_density](name:radial_derivative_of_total_ion_state_density). The electron analog is [second_radial_derivative_of_total_electron_density](name:second_radial_derivative_of_total_electron_density). Because $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$ is dimensionless, the second derivative retains the same units as the density itself.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the ion charge-state density profile is concave upward with respect to $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$, i.e., when the radial density gradient $dn_{i,s}/d\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$ is increasing with increasing $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$.

NAMES.name: time_derivative_of_total_ion_state_density
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Density-equivalent temporal evolution contribution for the total ion density of a single ion charge state, including both thermal and non-thermal particles in the plasma edge and scrape-off layer. It represents the finite-time change associated with the local time derivative, expressed as a density rather than as an instantaneous rate.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the density-equivalent change $\Delta n_k^{(t)}$ in the total ion state density $n_k$ for charge state $k$ of a given ion species. The underlying density includes thermal and non-thermal populations, $n_k = n_{k,\mathrm{thermal}} + n_{k,\mathrm{fast}}$, and is used to describe charge-state evolution in edge and scrape-off-layer plasmas. It should be distinguished from the instantaneous physical rate $\partial n_k / \partial t$, which has units $\mathrm{m}^{-3}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$; this interval-integrated contribution has units $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$.

The density-equivalent change over an evolution interval is related to the charge-state continuity balance by:

$$
\Delta n_k^{(t)} = \int_{t_0}^{t_1} \frac{\partial n_k}{\partial t}\,dt = \int_{t_0}^{t_1} \left[-\nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_k + P_k - L_k\right] \, dt
$$

where $t_0$ and $t_1$ are the start and end times, $\Delta t = t_1 - t_0$ is in seconds, $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_k$ is the particle flux density for charge state $k$ in $\mathrm{m}^{-2}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, and $P_k$ and $L_k$ are the summed production and loss rates in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$. The production and loss terms include charge-state coupling processes such as ionization, recombination, charge exchange, external particle sources, and losses to neighboring charge states or neutrals. For a short interval, the associated instantaneous rate is approximately $\Delta n_k^{(t)} / \Delta t$.

This quantity is not measured directly as a standalone observable. It is inferred from time-resolved estimates of charge-state-resolved ion densities, from particle-balance analysis, or from transport calculations that combine thermal and non-thermal populations and evaluate the net effect of transport and atomic processes.

Typical values are highly problem dependent because the quantity scales with both the parent density and the chosen evolution interval. As an order-of-magnitude guide, edge and scrape-off-layer ion state densities can range from trace impurity values below $10^{14}\ \mathrm{m}^{-3}$ to main-ion values near $10^{20}\ \mathrm{m}^{-3}$; fractional changes of $10^{-6}-10^{-1}$ over an evolution interval correspond to density-equivalent changes of roughly $10^{8}-10^{19}\ \mathrm{m}^{-3}$. During rapid fueling, impurity injection, or edge transients, the magnitude can approach the local total ion state density.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the total ion state density for the charge state increases over the evolution interval.

NAMES.name: total_ion_state_pressure
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Total pressure of one ion charge state, equal to the sum of its thermal Maxwellian pressure and its non-thermal fast-particle scalar pressure.
NAMES.long:
Total ion-state pressure is the kinetic scalar pressure carried by ions of one element in a specified ionization charge state. It combines the Maxwellian pressure of the thermal part of that charge-state population with the scalar pressure moment of any non-thermal particles in the same charge state.

For a charge state labeled $s$, the total pressure can be written as:

$$
p_s^{\mathrm{tot}} = n_s^{\mathrm{th}} T_s^{\mathrm{th}} + p_s^{\mathrm{fast}}, \qquad
p_s^{\mathrm{fast}} = \frac{1}{3}\operatorname{Tr}\mathbf{P}_s^{\mathrm{fast}} = \frac{1}{3}\int m_s |\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{u}_s|^2 f_s^{\mathrm{fast}}(\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $p_s^{\mathrm{tot}}$ and $p_s^{\mathrm{fast}}$ are in Pa, $n_s^{\mathrm{th}}$ is the thermal number density of that charge state in m$^{-3}$, and $T_s^{\mathrm{th}}$ is the thermal ion temperature expressed as an energy in J. If temperature is expressed in eV, the thermal term is $n_s^{\mathrm{th}} e T_s^{\mathrm{th}}$. The density $n_s^{\mathrm{th}}$ excludes fast ions so that non-thermal particles are not double counted. $\mathbf{P}_s^{\mathrm{fast}}$ is the fast-particle pressure tensor, $m_s$ is the ion mass in kg, $\mathbf{v}$ and $\mathbf{u}_s$ are velocities in m s$^{-1}$, and $f_s^{\mathrm{fast}}$ is normalized by $\int f_s^{\mathrm{fast}} d^3v = n_s^{\mathrm{fast}}$ with units s$^3$ m$^{-6}$. The factor $\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{Tr}$ gives the scalar, isotropic-equivalent pressure; for an anisotropic fast population it is not a directional pressure component.

In practice the thermal contribution is obtained from the thermal charge-state density and temperature, often constrained by spectroscopy, ionization balance, and transport analysis. The non-thermal contribution is computed as a kinetic pressure moment of the fast-particle distribution, which may be constrained by fast-ion diagnostics, collisional slowing-down models, or kinetic simulations.

Typical magnitudes vary strongly with species, charge-state abundance, temperature, and heating scenario. Trace or weakly populated charge states can have pressures below 1 Pa, edge and scrape-off-layer ion charge states are often about 0.1-10^3 Pa, and abundant fuel-ion charge states in hot confined plasmas can reach 10^2-10^5 Pa. Strong auxiliary heating can make the fast-particle scalar pressure comparable to or larger than the thermal term for selected charge states.

NAMES.name: total_neutral_state_density
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: Total number density of neutral particles occupying a specified internal quantum state, combining contributions from both thermal (Maxwellian) and suprathermal populations within that state.
NAMES.long:
The total neutral state density is the number of neutral particles per unit volume residing in a specific internal quantum state — electronic, vibrational, or rotational — of the neutral species, accumulated over all velocity-distribution populations. It is the natural sum of the population-resolved contributions and represents the complete state occupation without separating velocity-distribution classes.

The governing decomposition is:

$$
n_{\text{neutral,state}}^{\text{total}} = n_{\text{neutral,state}}^{\text{thermal}} + n_{\text{neutral,state}}^{\text{fast}}
$$

where $n_{\text{neutral,state}}^{\text{thermal}}$ is the [thermal neutral state density](name:thermal_neutral_state_density) (Maxwellian population) and $n_{\text{neutral,state}}^{\text{fast}}$ is the [fast neutral state density](name:fast_neutral_state_density) (suprathermal population). Integrating over all internal quantum states yields the [total neutral density](name:total_neutral_density), providing a consistency check between state-resolved and state-summed descriptions.

State-resolved neutral densities are essential inputs to collisional-radiative models of the plasma edge and divertor, where quantum-state populations determine line radiation intensities, ionization rate coefficients, and charge-exchange rates. The quantity is inferred from absolute spectroscopic line emission combined with collisional-radiative modeling, or computed directly in neutral-transport simulations across core and edge plasma regions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when neutral particles occupy the specified quantum state.

NAMES.name: total_neutron_power
NAMES.subject: neutron
NAMES.short: Total neutron power is the rate at which kinetic energy is carried away from the plasma by fusion-born neutrons, summed over all neutron-producing fusion reaction branches. Because neutrons are uncharged, they escape magnetic confinement rather than depositing their energy locally, so this energy flow is complementary to the charged-product power that is deposited in the plasma.
NAMES.long:
Total neutron power is the total kinetic-energy flow carried by fusion-born neutrons leaving the reacting plasma. It includes neutrons from all neutron-producing fusion branches, including thermal deuterium-deuterium (DD), deuterium-tritium (DT), and tritium-tritium (TT) reactions, as well as nonthermal or secondary neutron-producing channels when present. It is closely related to the total neutron emission rate, but it weights each emitted neutron by its kinetic energy rather than counting neutrons alone.

The total neutron power can be written as an energy moment of the volume-integrated neutron source spectrum over all neutron-producing channels:

$$
P_n = \sum_k \int_0^\infty E_n\,S_k(E_n)\,dE_n
$$

where $P_n$ is the total neutron power, $E_n$ is the neutron kinetic energy, and $S_k(E_n)$ is the volume-integrated differential neutron emission rate for channel $k$, with units of s^-1 J^-1 when $E_n$ is expressed in joules. For a nearly monoenergetic channel such as primary DT (about 14.1 MeV) or the DD neutron branch (about 2.45 MeV), $S_k$ is concentrated near the characteristic neutron energy; for multi-neutron or continuum channels such as TT, $S_k$ includes the full emitted-neutron multiplicity and energy distribution.

This quantity is complementary to, and must not be confused with, the charged-product power deposited in the plasma. Because the neutrons are charge-neutral, they are not confined by the magnetic field and stream out of the plasma without slowing down on the background ions and electrons, whereas alpha particles and other charged fusion products deposit their energy locally. The neutron-carried power $P_n$ and the deposited charged-product power tracked by [fusion_power](name:fusion_power) together account for the total thermonuclear energy release; [fusion_power](name:fusion_power) explicitly excludes the neutron-carried energy.

In practice, this quantity is computed by integrating fusion reaction rates over the plasma volume and folding them with the neutron energy spectrum for each reaction branch. It may also be inferred from calibrated neutron diagnostics, such as fission chambers, activation foils, or scintillator-based detectors, by converting measured neutron emission rates or spectra into an energy-weighted power. The [total neutron flux] gives the corresponding total neutron production rate, while the [thermal neutron flux](name:total_neutron_source_rate_due_to_thermal_fusion) identifies the contribution from thermal ion fusion reactions.

Typical values range from less than 1 W in low-yield plasmas to 10^3-10^6 W in high-performance deuterium plasmas, 10^6-10^7 W in large DT experiments, and 10^8-10^9 W in reactor-scale DT plasmas.

NAMES.name: total_particle_count
NAMES.subject: particle
NAMES.short: Total number of particles in the kinetic distribution, obtained by integrating the distribution function over velocity space and the entire plasma volume.
NAMES.long:
The total particle count is the global normalization integral of the particle distribution function $f(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{v})$: it quantifies the total number of particles of the described species present in the plasma at a given instant, summed over all spatial positions within the plasma volume and all velocities in phase space. Being a pure count, it is dimensionless.

The quantity is defined by the phase-space integral

$$
N = \int_V \int f(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{v}) \, d^3v \, d^3x
$$

where $V$ is the plasma volume, $\mathbf{x}$ is the position vector, and $\mathbf{v}$ is the particle velocity. In marker-based kinetic simulations, $N$ reduces to the weighted sum over all simulation markers.

Monitoring $N$ over time provides a particle-conservation diagnostic in kinetic modeling: systematic drift from the initial value indicates numerical particle sources or losses. This quantity is closely related to [total_count](name:total_particle_count), which carries the same physical meaning with a less species-explicit name, and contrasts with [fast_count](name:fast_count), which integrates only over the non-thermal sub-population of the distribution. The local spatial counterpart is total_particle_density, whose volume integral recovers $N$.

NAMES.name: total_plasma_energy
NAMES.short: Total internal kinetic energy of the confined plasma, equal to 3/2 times the volume integral of the total kinetic pressure summed over all electron and ion populations, excluding electromagnetic-field and bulk-flow energy.
NAMES.long:
Total plasma energy $W_\mathrm{total}$ is the aggregate internal kinetic energy carried by all confined plasma particles — thermal electrons, thermal ions, and nonthermal fast-particle populations — integrated over the plasma volume. It excludes magnetic-field energy, electrostatic-field energy, rest-mass energy, and macroscopic bulk-flow kinetic energy, making it the fundamental global stored-energy figure of merit for confinement assessment.

The defining relation is:

$$
W_\mathrm{total} = \frac{3}{2} \int p_\mathrm{tot} \, dV
$$

where $p_\mathrm{tot} = p_e + \sum_i p_i$ is the total kinetic pressure summing the electron partial pressure $p_e$ and the ion partial pressures $p_i$ over each species (including fast ions), and the integral extends over the confined plasma volume $V$ enclosed within the last closed flux surface.

It is inferred from diamagnetic loop measurements, which directly probe the total perpendicular stored energy, or from equilibrium reconstruction constrained by external magnetic diagnostics combined with kinetic profile measurements. The global energy confinement time $\tau_E$ is defined by $W_\mathrm{total} = \tau_E P_\mathrm{heat}$, linking this scalar directly to the net [total_plasma_heating_power](name:total_plasma_heating_power) absorbed by the plasma.

Stored plasma energies span from a few kilojoules in small research devices to tens of megajoules in large tokamaks during high-performance H-mode discharges. The integration domain is the [plasma_volume](name:volume_of_flux_surface) bounded by the last closed flux surface. This quantity is distinct from [total_energy](name:total_energy), which quantifies energy deposited in or extracted from a plasma-facing component rather than energy stored in the plasma itself. The parent quantity [plasma_energy](name:plasma_energy) captures the same aggregate concept without an explicit aggregation qualifier.

NAMES.name: total_thermal_ion_density
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Number density of thermal (Maxwellian) ions summed over all ion species and charge states, excluding fast (non-thermal) ion contributions.
NAMES.long:
The total thermal ion number density sums the thermal (Maxwellian) ion particle density over all ion species and charge states present in the plasma, giving the total local thermal ion particle inventory per unit volume. Suprathermal ions — those generated by external heating systems or fusion reactions — are excluded, separating the thermal bulk from the non-Maxwellian fast-particle population. This is the fully species-summed form of [thermal_ion_density](name:thermal_ion_density), which resolves contributions from individual ion species.

The defining relation is:

$$
n_{i,\text{th,total}} = \sum_{\sigma} \sum_{z} n_{i,\sigma,z}^{\text{th}}
$$

where $\sigma$ indexes ion species, $z$ denotes the ionization state, and $n_{i,\sigma,z}^{\text{th}}$ is the local thermal number density of species $\sigma$ in charge state $z$.

In the edge plasma and scrape-off layer, the radial gradient of $n_{i,\text{th,total}}$ drives cross-field particle transport, and its e-folding scale is characterized by the [total_ion_decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer](name:total_ion_decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer). Experimental determination combines charge-exchange spectroscopy for impurity charge-state populations, Thomson scattering electron density profiles with quasi-neutrality constraints, and Langmuir probe ion saturation current measurements in the SOL.

Typical values span $10^{19}$–$10^{21}$ m$^{-3}$ in the confined core and decrease to $10^{17}$–$10^{19}$ m$^{-3}$ in the scrape-off layer.
NAMES.sign: Positive when thermal ions are present; a number density is intrinsically non-negative.

NAMES.name: total_thermal_ion_energy
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Volume-integrated thermal energy of the total ion population, defined as 3/2 times the volume integral of thermal ion pressure summed over all ion species and charge states.
NAMES.long:
Total thermal ion energy content $W_{i,th}$ is a global scalar representing the volume-integrated kinetic energy of the Maxwellian ion component, summed over all ion species and charge states. It quantifies the isotropic thermal kinetic energy of the confined ion population, explicitly excluding contributions from fast or suprathermal ions.

The defining relation is:

$$
W_{i,th} = \frac{3}{2} \int p_{i,th} \, dV
$$

where $p_{i,th}$ is the total thermal ion pressure (see [total_thermal_ion_pressure](name:total_thermal_ion_pressure)), the integral spans the entire confined plasma volume, and the factor $3/2$ arises from equipartition for an isotropic Maxwellian velocity distribution in three dimensions.

$W_{i,th}$ is inferred by integrating measured ion temperature and density profiles, obtained from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy or neutron emission diagnostics, over the equilibrium-reconstructed plasma volume.

Together with the electron thermal energy, $W_{i,th}$ enters the total stored energy used to compute the global energy confinement time $\tau_E = W_{tot}/P_{loss}$. Typical values range from tens of kilojoules in small devices to several megajoules in large H-mode discharges. The companion quantity [total_thermal_ion_density](name:total_thermal_ion_density) provides the corresponding number density context, and [total_energy_flux](name:total_thermal_ion_heat_flux) characterizes the associated radial energy transport across flux surfaces.

NAMES.name: total_thermal_ion_heat_flux
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Net flux density of ion thermal energy through a transport surface, summed over all ion species and charge states. It includes conductive heat transport and convective enthalpy carried by ion particle fluxes.
NAMES.long:
Total thermal ion heat flux is the surface-normal flux density of thermal energy carried by ions, summed over all ion species and charge states. It represents the ion contribution to heat transport by random thermal motion and by enthalpy carried with particle motion, excluding electron heat flux, electromagnetic energy flow, and directed bulk kinetic-energy flux.

A common decomposition is

$$
q_{i,\mathrm{th}}^{\mathrm{tot}} = \sum_{s \in \mathrm{ions}} \left( q_{s,\mathrm{cond}} + h_{s,\mathrm{th}}\,\Gamma_s \right)
$$

where $q_{s,\mathrm{cond}}$ is the conductive thermal heat-flux density of ion species or charge state $s$, $\Gamma_s$ is its particle-flux density normal to the transport surface, and $h_{s,\mathrm{th}}$ is its thermal enthalpy per particle. For an ideal Maxwellian ion population with no additional internal-state energy, $h_{s,\mathrm{th}}$ is approximately $5T_s/2$ when $T_s$ is expressed as energy per particle.

In practice this quantity is inferred from ion energy balance across transport surfaces. It is constrained by measurements or modeling of ion temperature, density, particle fluxes, external ion heating, collisional electron-ion energy exchange, atomic and charge-exchange losses, and the time rate of change of ion stored thermal energy. Transport analyzes may further separate the total into neoclassical, turbulent, and source-driven components, but the summed quantity is the net ion thermal heat flux.

Typical magnitudes are about $10^3$-$10^6$ W m^-2 in core transport analyzes of magnetically confined plasmas, and can reach $10^5$-$10^7$ W m^-2 near steep-gradient edge regions. The value can be small or change sign locally when convective enthalpy flow, temperature-gradient-driven conduction, and local sources nearly balance.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the net ion thermal energy flow is directed outward through the transport surface, from the enclosed plasma volume toward the surrounding plasma edge.

NAMES.name: total_thermal_ion_pressure
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Total isotropic pressure of the thermal ion population, summed over all ion species and charge states, excluding fast (suprathermal) ion contributions.
NAMES.long:
The total thermal ion pressure is the aggregate isotropic pressure arising from the random thermal motion of all ion species in the plasma, summed over all species and their respective charge states. It captures the purely thermal (Maxwellian-distributed) ion pressure contribution and explicitly excludes fast and suprathermal ion pressure, which may be anisotropic and is accounted for separately.

The defining relation is:

$$
p_{i,\mathrm{th}} = \sum_{s} \sum_{z} n_{s,z} \, T_{s,z}
$$

where $n_{s,z}$ is the number density of ion species $s$ in charge state $z$ (in m$^{-3}$) and $T_{s,z}$ is the corresponding thermal temperature in energy units. This is the species- and charge-state-aggregated form of [thermal_ion_pressure](name:thermal_ion_pressure) and constitutes the ion contribution to the total thermal plasma pressure when combined with the electron thermal pressure.

This quantity is distinct from [total_ion_pressure](name:total_ion_pressure), which additionally includes fast (non-thermal) ion pressure contributions, and from thermal_pressure, which sums thermal pressure over both ion and electron species. The companion density quantity is [total_thermal_ion_density](name:total_thermal_ion_density).

The total thermal ion pressure is derived from transport simulations or equilibrium reconstructions by summing density-weighted temperature profiles across all ion species. It enters the ion energy balance equation, MHD pressure equilibrium, and parallel momentum transport in both core and edge plasma regions.

Typical magnitudes in the plasma core of tokamak H-mode plasmas are in the range 10-100 kPa, falling by several orders of magnitude in the scrape-off layer where lower densities and temperatures prevail.
NAMES.sign: Positive for all physically realizable thermal ion populations, as thermal pressure is a non-negative thermodynamic quantity.

NAMES.name: trapped_fast_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Local volumetric rate of Coulomb-collisional energy transfer to the fast-ion population, restricted to fast ions on trapped guiding-center orbits that mirror-reflect before completing a full poloidal transit.
NAMES.long:
The trapped-orbit fast-ion collisional power density is the orbit-class component of [fast_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:fast_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions) arising specifically from fast ions on trapped banana orbits, obtained by restricting the velocity-space integration to the trapped portion of the fast-ion distribution function. Trapped fast ions mirror-reflect between the low- and high-field sides of the torus, and their orbit-averaged Coulomb energy exchange with background plasma species differs from that of co-passing and counter-passing ions due to the distinct bounce-orbit geometry.

In Fokker-Planck kinetics, the quantity is defined as:

$$
P_\mathrm{trap}^\mathrm{fast} = \int_\mathrm{trapped} C[f_\mathrm{fast}]\, \mathcal{E} \, d^3v
$$

where $C[f_\mathrm{fast}]$ is the Coulomb collision operator acting on the fast-ion distribution function $f_\mathrm{fast}$, $\mathcal{E}$ is the particle kinetic energy, and the integral is restricted to the trapped velocity domain defined by the mirror condition on the local flux surface. A positive value indicates net energy gain by the trapped fast-ion population from collisions with background ions.

This quantity is computed from Fokker-Planck or Monte Carlo slowing-down models that resolve the orbit-class structure of the fast-ion phase space, relevant for heating scenarios involving neutral beam injection or fusion-born alpha particles. The complete orbit-class decomposition of the fast-ion collisional power is recovered by summing this trapped contribution with the [counter_passing_fast_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:counter_passing_fast_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions) and [co_passing_fast_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:co_passing_fast_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions) components. The charge-state-resolved counterpart for trapped fast ions is [trapped_fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:trapped_fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions).

NAMES.name: trapped_fast_particle_density
NAMES.subject: particle
NAMES.short: Number density of suprathermal particles on trapped orbits, obtained by integrating the fast-particle distribution function over the velocity-space region whose guiding-center orbits mirror between bounce points.
NAMES.long:
Trapped fast particle density is the local number density contributed by suprathermal particles whose guiding-center orbits are trapped by magnetic mirroring. These particles bounce between mirror points because their parallel velocity changes sign along the magnetic field, so they do not make passing transits around the torus. The quantity is the trapped-orbit contribution to [fast_particle_density](name:fast_particle_density), complementary to passing fast-particle contributions such as [co_passing_fast_particle_density](name:co_passing_fast_particle_density).

The density is the velocity-space integral of the fast-particle distribution function restricted to trapped orbits:

$$
n_{\mathrm{fast,tr}}(\mathbf{x},t) = \int_{\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{tr}}(\mathbf{x})} f_{\mathrm{fast}}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v},t)\, d^3v
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{fast,tr}}$ is in $m^{-3}$, $\mathbf{x}$ is position in m, $t$ is time in s, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity in $m\,s^{-1}$, $d^3v$ has units $m^3\,s^{-3}$, and $f_{\mathrm{fast}}$ has units $s^3\,m^{-6}$. The domain $\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{tr}}(\mathbf{x})$ contains velocities whose guiding-center invariants give mirror reflection before a complete passing transit.

In computations, the orbit class is determined from the magnetic equilibrium and constants of motion such as energy and magnetic moment $\mu = m_s v_\perp^2/(2B)$, where $\mu$ is in $J\,T^{-1}$, $m_s$ is particle mass in kg, $v_\perp$ is perpendicular speed in $m\,s^{-1}$, and $B$ is magnetic-field magnitude in T. The local ratio $v_\perp^2/v^2$ is useful as a pitch descriptor but is not, by itself, a pitch invariant in a spatially varying magnetic field. Experimentally this density is inferred indirectly by combining fast-particle-sensitive diagnostics, magnetic-equilibrium information, and kinetic forward modeling.

Typical values span a wide range: $10^{14}-10^{17}$ m^-3 for weak trapped energetic tails, $10^{16}-10^{19}$ m^-3 in the core of strongly heated plasmas, and occasionally a few percent of the bulk ion density when neutral-beam ions or fusion alpha particles are well confined. The trapped fraction depends on aspect ratio, magnetic-field variation along the orbit, particle energy, pitch distribution, and radial position.

NAMES.name: trapped_fast_particle_power_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: particle
NAMES.short: Coulomb-collisional power density deposited in or removed from the fast-particle population by the trapped-orbit part of the fast-particle distribution.
NAMES.long:
Trapped fast-particle collisional power density is the local rate per unit volume at which Coulomb collisions exchange kinetic energy with the fast-particle population, restricted to particles on trapped orbits. It is the trapped-orbit contribution to [fast_particle_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:fast_particle_power_density_due_to_collisions), complementary to co-passing and counter-passing orbit-class contributions.

For a species $s$, a kinetic definition is the energy moment of the collision operator over the trapped region of velocity space:

$$
P_{\mathrm{trap}} = \int_{\Omega_{\mathrm{trap}}} \frac{1}{2} m_s v^2\, C_{\mathrm{fast}}[f_{\mathrm{trap}}](\mathbf{v})\, d^3v
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{trap}}$ is in W m^-3, $m_s$ is the particle mass in kg, $\mathbf{v}$ is the velocity vector, $v = |\mathbf{v}|$ is in m s^-1, $f_{\mathrm{trap}}$ is the trapped-orbit part of the fast-particle distribution with units m^-3 (m s^-1)^-3, $C_{\mathrm{fast}}[f_{\mathrm{trap}}]$ is the Coulomb-collisional rate of change of that distribution contributing to the fast population with units m^-3 s^-1 (m s^-1)^-3, and $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element with units m^3 s^-3. The domain $\Omega_{\mathrm{trap}}$ contains velocity-space points whose guiding-center orbits are trapped; in large-aspect-ratio notation this is often approximated by $v_\parallel^2/v^2 < \epsilon$, where $v_\parallel$ is the velocity parallel to the magnetic field and $\epsilon \simeq r/R$ is the local inverse aspect ratio.

This quantity is computed from kinetic transport, Fokker-Planck, Monte Carlo, or reduced fast-particle models by applying Coulomb collision operators to the trapped part of the distribution and taking the kinetic-energy moment. Experimentally constrained estimates use reconstructed fast-particle distributions, magnetic-equilibrium information for orbit classification, and background density and temperature profiles that determine the collisional coefficients.

Typical absolute magnitudes are about 10^3-10^7 W m^-3 in neutral-beam, radio-frequency, or fusion-alpha fast-particle populations, with values below 10^3 W m^-3 in weak tails or near depleted regions and localized peaks approaching 10^8 W m^-3 in compact high-power scenarios. The sign can be either positive or negative depending on whether collisions heat or slow the trapped fast-particle population.
NAMES.sign: Positive when Coulomb collisions transfer kinetic energy to the fast-particle population associated with trapped orbits.

NAMES.name: trapped_fast_particle_pressure
NAMES.subject: particle
NAMES.short: Flux-surface-averaged isotropic pressure carried by energetic non-thermal particles on trapped guiding-center orbits. It is the scalar pressure moment of the trapped part of the fast-particle distribution function.
NAMES.long:
Trapped fast-particle pressure is the scalar kinetic pressure contributed by energetic non-thermal particles whose guiding-center orbits bounce between magnetic mirror points rather than circulating freely around the torus. It is the trapped-orbit component of the total fast-particle pressure and contributes to equilibrium pressure balance and energetic-particle drive while giving little direct contribution to net toroidal current in an axisymmetric plasma.

For a set of fast-particle species, the trapped scalar pressure is the second velocity moment of the distribution over the trapped part of velocity space:

$$
p_{\mathrm{fast,tr}} = \left\langle \sum_s \frac{m_s}{3} \int_{\Omega_{\mathrm{tr},s}} v^2 f_{\mathrm{fast},s}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\, d^3v \right\rangle_{\mathrm{FS}}
$$

where $s$ labels fast species, $m_s$ is particle mass in kg, $v$ is speed in m/s, $f_{\mathrm{fast},s}$ is the fast-particle phase-space density with units $s^3\,m^{-6}$ when integrated over velocity space to give number density, $d^3v$ has units $m^3\,s^{-3}$, $\Omega_{\mathrm{tr},s}$ is the trapped-orbit region of velocity space, and $\langle\cdot\rangle_{\mathrm{FS}}$ denotes a flux-surface average. The factor $1/3$ converts the scalar second moment into isotropic pressure. A common trapped-passing boundary uses pitch-angle cosine $\xi = v_\parallel/v$ with $|\xi| < \xi_T$ and $\xi_T = \sqrt{1 - B_{\min}/B_{\max}}$, where $B_{\min}$ and $B_{\max}$ are the minimum and maximum magnetic-field magnitudes sampled along the orbit.

In an orbit-class decomposition, the total fast-particle pressure is the sum of trapped, co-passing, and counter-passing scalar contributions when those classes partition the same distribution. The quantity is computed from kinetic distribution functions produced by Fokker-Planck, Monte Carlo, guiding-center, or full-orbit models, or inferred by combining energetic-particle diagnostics with an equilibrium and a reconstructed distribution. Anisotropic descriptions instead use separate parallel and perpendicular pressure moments; those are distinct from this isotropic scalar pressure.

Typical flux-surface-averaged trapped fast-particle pressures are about 10^2-10^4 Pa in weakly heated plasmas, 10^4-10^5 Pa in strongly beam- or radio-frequency-heated tokamaks, and can approach 10^5-10^6 Pa locally in high-performance deuterium-tritium plasmas with significant alpha-particle pressure.

NAMES.name: parallel_trapped_fast_particle_pressure
NAMES.subject: particle
NAMES.short: Flux-surface-averaged field-aligned component of the pressure tensor for trapped fast particles. It is evaluated from the trapped-orbit part of the non-thermal distribution function and represents the parallel kinetic stress of that population.
NAMES.long:
Parallel trapped fast particle pressure is the component of the fast-particle pressure tensor along the magnetic field, restricted to particles whose guiding-center orbits are trapped between mirror points. It is a flux-surface-averaged second velocity moment of the trapped-orbit part of the non-thermal distribution and quantifies the field-aligned kinetic stress carried by that population.

The flux-surface-averaged parallel pressure is defined by the trapped fast-particle velocity moment:

$$
p_{\parallel,\mathrm{fast,tr}}(\psi) = \left\langle \sum_s m_s \int \left(v_\parallel - U_{\parallel s}\right)^2 f_{\mathrm{fast,tr},s}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v \right\rangle_\psi
$$

where $\langle\cdot\rangle_\psi$ denotes an average over a closed magnetic flux surface labeled by $\psi$, $s$ indexes fast-particle species, $m_s$ is the species mass in kg, $v_\parallel$ and $U_{\parallel s}$ are velocities along the magnetic field in m s$^{-1}$, and $f_{\mathrm{fast,tr},s}$ is normalized so that $\int f_{\mathrm{fast,tr},s}\,d^3v = n_{\mathrm{fast,tr},s}$ with density in m$^{-3}$. If the retained fast-particle distribution has negligible mean parallel flow, $U_{\parallel s}$ is set to zero; for multiple fast species, the result is the mass-weighted sum of their separate moment contributions.

This quantity is usually computed from a kinetic fast-particle distribution after classifying phase-space elements by trapped-orbit topology in the reconstructed magnetic equilibrium. It is not a direct diagnostic observable, but it can be constrained by energetic-particle measurements and by consistency with equilibrium and transport analysis. Because trapped particles reverse $v_\parallel$ along their bounce motion, the first parallel moment may be small while this second moment remains finite.

Typical flux-surface-averaged values range from 10$^2$-10$^5$ Pa in heated tokamak core plasmas, with lower values toward the edge or in weak fast-particle populations. High-fast-pressure regimes can approach 10$^6$ Pa locally or on central flux surfaces, while the trapped parallel component may be much smaller than the total fast-particle pressure when the distribution is strongly perpendicular-anisotropic.

NAMES.name: perpendicular_trapped_fast_particle_pressure
NAMES.subject: particle
NAMES.short: Perpendicular trapped fast-particle pressure is the species-summed component of the kinetic pressure tensor perpendicular to the local magnetic field for suprathermal particles on trapped guiding-center orbits. It is obtained from the second perpendicular velocity moment of the trapped fast-particle distribution function.
NAMES.long:
Perpendicular trapped fast-particle pressure is the species-summed gyrotropic pressure component perpendicular to the local magnetic field contributed by suprathermal particles whose guiding-center orbits are magnetically trapped. It represents the perpendicular part of the fast-particle kinetic stress associated with bounce motion between mirror points, excluding passing-orbit contributions.

The defining velocity-space moment is

$$
P_{\perp,\mathrm{tr,fast}}(\mathbf{x},t) = \sum_s \int_{\Omega_{\mathrm{tr}}} \frac{1}{2} m_s v_\perp^2 f_{s,\mathrm{fast}}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v},t)\, d^3v
$$

where the sum is over all species contributing to the fast-particle population, $m_s$ is the species mass in kg, $v_\perp$ is the speed perpendicular to the local magnetic field in m s$^{-1}$, $f_{s,\mathrm{fast}}$ is the fast-particle distribution function in m$^{-3}$(m s$^{-1}$)$^{-3}$, and $d^3v$ has units (m s$^{-1}$)$^3$. The factor $1/2$ accounts for the two velocity components perpendicular to the magnetic field, and $\Omega_{\mathrm{tr}}$ is the trapped part of velocity space. For a particle at magnetic-field strength $B$ on an orbit with maximum accessible field strength $B_{\max}$, conservation of energy and magnetic moment gives the trapped-orbit condition $v_\perp^2/v^2 > B/B_{\max}$, with equality at the trapped-passing boundary.

In practice this quantity is computed from reconstructed or simulated fast-particle distribution functions, using orbit classification to retain only trapped guiding-center trajectories before taking the perpendicular second moment. The distribution may be constrained by diagnostics sensitive to suprathermal particles, such as neutron emission, gamma-ray emission, neutral-particle analysis, fast-ion loss measurements, or spectroscopic measurements of energetic ions, combined with kinetic modeling.

Typical magnitudes range from 10$^2$-10$^5$ Pa in auxiliary-heated tokamak cores, depending on fast-particle density, energy, pitch-angle distribution, and magnetic geometry. Values can be below 1 Pa where the trapped fast-particle population is weak, and can approach 10$^6$ Pa in high-performance burning-plasma or strong heating scenarios.

NAMES.name: trapped_power_density
NAMES.short: Volumetric energy source rate for the trapped orbit-class particle population, giving the local power density deposited into or extracted from magnetically bouncing particles through heating and collisional processes.
NAMES.long:
Trapped particles are those whose parallel velocity is insufficient to overcome the magnetic mirror force and complete a full poloidal orbit; they execute closed banana orbits between two turning points on a given flux surface. The trapped power density is the net volumetric rate at which energy enters or leaves this orbit-class subpopulation through all active heating and collisional mechanisms.

In a Fokker-Planck kinetic description, the trapped power density is the energy moment of the total distribution-function source operator $S(\mathbf{v})$ restricted to the trapped velocity-space domain:

$$
P_\mathrm{trap} = \int_\mathrm{trap} \frac{m v^2}{2} \, S(\mathbf{v}) \, d^3v
$$

where $m$ is the particle mass, $v$ is the particle speed, and the integral covers pitch angles satisfying $|v_\parallel/v| < \sqrt{1 - B_\mathrm{min}/B_\mathrm{max}}$, with $B_\mathrm{min}$ and $B_\mathrm{max}$ the minimum and maximum field strength on the flux surface.

This quantity is computed in kinetic transport models that partition velocity space into orbit classes, appearing alongside [co-passing power density](name:co_passing_power_density) and [counter-passing power density](name:counter_passing_power_density) as components of the orbit-resolved local energy budget. Sources include neutral beam injection, ion cyclotron resonance heating, and Coulomb collisions that preferentially populate or drain trapped orbits. The corresponding particle source for the same subpopulation is [trapped_thermal_particle_source_rate](name:trapped_thermal_particle_source_rate), and the total trapped particle number density is [trapped_density](name:total_trapped_particle_density).

NAMES.name: trapped_thermal_electron_power_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Volumetric rate at which Coulomb collisions transfer energy from the trapped guiding-center source-orbit class of a fast, non-Maxwellian particle population to bulk thermal electrons. Positive values denote local thermal-electron heating.
NAMES.long:
Trapped thermal-electron collisional power density is the local energy-transfer rate per unit volume from trapped fast particles to the bulk thermal-electron population. The trapped source-orbit class consists of guiding centers that bounce between magnetic mirror points rather than circulating poloidally, so its collisional coupling can differ from passing-orbit contributions.

A common kinetic definition is the trapped-orbit energy moment of the electron-collision part of the fast-particle Fokker-Planck operator:

$$
P_{e,\mathrm{coll}}^{\mathrm{trap}} = -\int_{\Lambda \in \mathrm{trap}} \frac{1}{2} m_s v^2\, C_e[f_s](\mathbf{v})\, d^3v
$$

where $P_{e,\mathrm{coll}}^{\mathrm{trap}}$ is in W m$^{-3}$, $m_s$ is the source-particle mass in kg, $v$ is speed in m s$^{-1}$, $f_s$ is the fast-particle distribution in s$^3$ m$^{-6}$, $C_e[f_s]$ is the part of the collision operator due to interactions with thermal electrons in s$^2$ m$^{-6}$, $d^3v$ has units m$^3$ s$^{-3}$, and $\Lambda \in \mathrm{trap}$ denotes the trapped region of guiding-center phase space. The minus sign converts loss of kinetic energy by the trapped fast-particle population into gain of thermal-electron energy.

This quantity is usually computed rather than directly measured, using kinetic or Fokker-Planck modeling of the non-Maxwellian source distribution together with Coulomb collision coefficients and an orbit-class decomposition. It enters the electron energy-balance equation as a local collisional heating source; summing over source-orbit classes gives the corresponding total [thermal_electron_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:thermal_electron_power_density_due_to_collisions).

Typical magnitudes are strongly scenario-dependent and are best interpreted relative to the total collisional electron heating and the total deposited fast-particle power. The value is zero when no trapped fast-particle source population is present, may vary by orders of magnitude across a plasma, and can be negative if the trapped fast-particle component is being heated by thermal electrons rather than slowing down on them.
NAMES.sign: Positive when bulk thermal electrons gain kinetic energy from the trapped fast-particle population through Coulomb collisions.

NAMES.name: trapped_thermal_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Collisional volumetric power density delivered to the bulk thermal ion population by fast particles in the trapped guiding-center source-orbit class. It is positive for thermal-ion heating and represents the trapped-orbit contribution to collisional ion energy exchange.
NAMES.long:
Trapped thermal-ion collisional power density is the local rate per unit volume at which Coulomb collisions transfer kinetic energy to the bulk thermal ion population from fast particles in the trapped guiding-center source-orbit class. It is the trapped contribution to [thermal_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:thermal_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions); the complete orbit-class decomposition also includes co-passing and counter-passing contributions.

A receiving-population energy-moment definition is

$$
P_{\mathrm{th}i,\mathrm{coll}}^{\mathrm{tr}} = \sum_{\alpha,s} \int \frac{1}{2} m_\alpha v^2\, C_{\alpha s}\left[f_\alpha, f_s^{\mathrm{tr}}\right] \, d^3v
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{th}i,\mathrm{coll}}^{\mathrm{tr}}$ is in W m^-3, $\alpha$ labels receiving thermal-ion species, $s$ labels fast-particle species, $m_\alpha$ is in kg, $v$ is the thermal-ion speed in m s^-1, $f_\alpha$ is the thermal-ion velocity distribution, $f_s^{\mathrm{tr}}$ is the trapped source-orbit component of the fast-particle distribution, $C_{\alpha s}$ is the Coulomb collision operator acting on $f_\alpha$ due to $f_s^{\mathrm{tr}}$ with units of distribution function per second, and $d^3v$ has units m^3 s^-3. With the common normalization in which velocity-space integration of $f$ gives number density, the integral has units of W m^-3.
