NAMES.long:
This quantity is a normalized moment of the perturbed gyrocenter distribution function formed with charge, parallel velocity, and a first-order Bessel weight. The $J_1$ factor isolates the finite-Larmor-radius contribution to the parallel current response, distinct from the $J_0$ gyroaveraged parallel current moment.

A representative definition is

$$
\hat{j}_{\parallel,J_1} = \frac{1}{j_\mathrm{ref}} \sum_s q_s \int v_\parallel J_1(\lambda_s)\,\delta f_s\,d^3v
$$

where the sum is over species $s$, $q_s$ is the signed species charge, $v_\parallel$ is velocity along the equilibrium magnetic field, $\delta f_s$ is the perturbed gyrocenter distribution function, $J_1$ is the first-order Bessel function, $\lambda_s = k_\perp v_\perp/|\Omega_s|$ is the gyroaveraging argument, and $j_\mathrm{ref}$ is the reference current density used for normalization. The numerator has the dimensions of current density, and division by $j_\mathrm{ref}$ makes the reported quantity dimensionless with unit 1.

In practice this moment is computed from the eigenmode perturbation in velocity space. Because $J_1(x) \simeq x/2$ for small $x$, the moment is small at long perpendicular wavelength and becomes more important when $k_\perp \rho_s$ is appreciable, where finite-Larmor-radius electromagnetic effects contribute to the parallel current response.

Because a linear eigenmode has arbitrary overall amplitude, typical magnitudes depend on the chosen eigenvector normalization. For perturbations normalized so that the dominant fluctuating field or distribution component is order unity, values below $10^{-3}$ indicate a negligible $J_1$-weighted current response, while $10^{-2}-1$ is typical when finite-Larmor-radius electromagnetic coupling is significant.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the $J_1$-weighted perturbed current density is directed along the positive parallel direction, defined by the equilibrium magnetic-field direction used for positive $v_\parallel$.

NAMES.name: parallel_normalized_perturbed_magnetic_field
NAMES.short: Signed dimensionless projection of a magnetic-field perturbation onto the local equilibrium magnetic-field direction, divided by the equilibrium reference magnetic-field magnitude. It captures the compressional electromagnetic fluctuation channel, in which the perturbation changes the field strength rather than only bending the field line.
NAMES.long:
Parallel normalized perturbed magnetic field is the dimensionless signed component of a magnetic-field perturbation along the local equilibrium magnetic-field direction. Physically it represents the compressional part of an electromagnetic fluctuation: to first order it alters the local field strength rather than only tilting the field line, and it is distinct from the shear (field-bending) channel carried by the perturbed vector potential.

The quantity is obtained by projecting the real magnetic perturbation onto the equilibrium-field unit vector and dividing by a positive reference field strength:

$$
\delta B_{\parallel,\mathrm{norm}} = \frac{\delta\mathbf{B}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{b}}_0}{B_\mathrm{ref}}
$$

where $\delta\mathbf{B}$ is the perturbed magnetic field in tesla, $\mathbf{B}_0$ is the equilibrium magnetic field in tesla, $\hat{\mathbf{b}}_0 = \mathbf{B}_0/|\mathbf{B}_0|$ is the dimensionless equilibrium field-line-following unit vector, and $B_\mathrm{ref}$ is the positive reference magnetic-field strength in tesla, conventionally taken as the equilibrium field magnitude $|\mathbf{B}_0|$ evaluated at the reference position of the flux surface. The parallel direction $\hat{\mathbf{b}}_0$ follows the total equilibrium field, which in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame combines the toroidal and poloidal components.

In turbulence analysis this signed variable is formed from the fluctuating field after subtracting the equilibrium field and is normalized by the same $B_\mathrm{ref}$ used for the rest of the electromagnetic fluctuation set. Statistics such as fluctuation intensities or spectra derived from it describe the amplitude of this signed quantity; they should not be confused with a complex eigenmode coefficient or its modulus, the latter represented by [parallel_normalized_perturbed_magnetic_field_amplitude](name:parallel_normalized_perturbed_magnetic_field_amplitude).

Typical magnitudes in magnetized-plasma turbulence span roughly $10^{-6}$ to $10^{-2}$, with the larger values reached at high plasma pressure where electromagnetic effects are strong. The signed instantaneous value fluctuates about zero and may be positive or negative.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the parallel component of the magnetic perturbation is aligned with the local equilibrium magnetic-field direction $\hat{\mathbf{b}}_0$.

NAMES.name: parallel_normalized_perturbed_magnetic_field_amplitude
NAMES.short: Modulus of the complex normalized perturbed magnetic field parallel to the equilibrium magnetic field for a gyrokinetic eigenmode. It measures compressional magnetic fluctuation strength independent of eigenmode phase.
NAMES.long:
Parallel normalized perturbed magnetic field amplitude is the non-negative modulus of the complex eigenmode for the magnetic-field perturbation along the equilibrium magnetic-field direction. It quantifies the strength of compressional magnetic fluctuations after normalization to a positive reference magnetic-field magnitude, with the arbitrary complex phase of the eigenmode removed.

The amplitude is defined by projecting the complex perturbed magnetic field onto the equilibrium field direction and normalizing by the reference field magnitude:

$$
A_{\delta B_\parallel} = \frac{\left|\hat{\mathbf{b}}\cdot\widetilde{\delta\mathbf{B}}\right|}{B_\mathrm{ref}}
$$

where $A_{\delta B_\parallel}$ is the normalized amplitude, $\widetilde{\delta\mathbf{B}}$ is the complex perturbed magnetic-field eigenfunction, $\hat{\mathbf{b}}=\mathbf{B}_0/|\mathbf{B}_0|$ is the unit vector along the equilibrium magnetic field, $B_\mathrm{ref}$ is a positive reference magnetic-field magnitude in tesla, and the vertical bars denote complex modulus. The resulting amplitude has unit 1.

In linear electromagnetic gyrokinetic theory, the quantity is computed from the eigenmode fields after a common eigenfunction normalization has been chosen, either from a solved $\delta B_\parallel$ field or from $\delta\mathbf{B}=\nabla\times\delta\mathbf{A}$ when the vector-potential representation is used. It is commonly analyzed along a selected magnetic field line in flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, where $\rho$ labels the magnetic flux surface, $\theta$ is a poloidal angle, and $\phi$ is the toroidal angle; the variable used along the field line may be parameterized by $\theta$ but represents position along the selected field line rather than an independent geometric poloidal coordinate.

Typical values depend strongly on the eigenmode normalization. For physical fluctuation estimates, $|\delta B_\parallel|/B_\mathrm{ref}$ is often $10^{-5}$-$10^{-3}$ in weakly electromagnetic drift-wave cases and $10^{-3}$-$10^{-1}$ in electromagnetic or high-beta branches; a normalized eigenfunction can have an order-unity maximum when it has been rescaled for numerical convenience.

NAMES.name: parallel_normalized_perturbed_vector_potential_amplitude
NAMES.short: Modulus of the complex normalized perturbed parallel vector potential eigenfunction for a gyrokinetic mode. It quantifies the dimensionless electromagnetic fluctuation amplitude associated with field-aligned current and magnetic flutter.
NAMES.long:
Parallel normalized perturbed vector potential amplitude is the non-negative modulus of the complex dimensionless perturbation $\delta \tilde{A}_\parallel$, where the parallel component is taken along the local equilibrium magnetic field. It characterizes the electromagnetic part of a gyrokinetic fluctuation and vanishes for a purely electrostatic perturbation.

For a complex normalized eigenfunction $\delta \tilde{A}_\parallel = \delta A_\parallel/A_\mathrm{ref}$, the amplitude is defined by:

$$
|\delta \tilde{A}_\parallel| = \left|\frac{\delta A_\parallel}{A_\mathrm{ref}}\right| = \sqrt{\left(\Re\,\delta \tilde{A}_\parallel\right)^2 + \left(\Im\,\delta \tilde{A}_\parallel\right)^2}
$$

where $\delta A_\parallel$ is the physical perturbed parallel vector potential with units of T m, $A_\mathrm{ref}$ is the reference vector-potential scale with the same units, and $\delta \tilde{A}_\parallel$ is dimensionless. The exact reference scale is set by the gyrokinetic normalization; common choices include a magnetic scale such as $\rho_\mathrm{ref} B_\mathrm{ref}$, with $\rho_\mathrm{ref}$ in meters and $B_\mathrm{ref}$ in tesla, or an equivalent potential-based scale specified by the chosen nondimensionalization.

In gyrokinetic modeling, $\delta A_\parallel$ is computed from the electromagnetic field solve and is constrained by parallel Ampere's law. In Fourier representation, this relates $k_\perp^2 \delta A_\parallel$ to the perturbed parallel-current moment, for example $\mu_0 \sum_s q_s \int v_\parallel g_s\,d^3v$, where $k_\perp$ is the perpendicular wavenumber in m^-1, $q_s$ is species charge, $v_\parallel$ is parallel velocity, and $g_s$ is the non-adiabatic distribution perturbation. For linear eigenmodes the overall complex scale may be arbitrary, so this amplitude is most meaningful together with the stated eigenmode normalization, relative variation, or ratios to other fluctuating fields.

Typical dimensionless amplitudes are strongly normalization dependent. With equilibrium-scale normalizations, electrostatic drift-wave cases are often near 0, weakly electromagnetic microturbulence commonly gives about 1e-6-1e-3, and kinetic-ballooning or shear-Alfvenic cases can reach 1e-3-1; eigenfunctions rescaled to unit maximum can have peak amplitude of order 1 by construction.

NAMES.name: perpendicular_normalized_gyrocenter_gyroaveraged_perturbed_energy
NAMES.subject: gyrocenter
NAMES.short: Dimensionless gyrocenter moment of the perturbed distribution weighted by perpendicular kinetic energy times total speed squared and by the zeroth-order gyroaverage factor J0. It describes the perpendicular-energy-weighted response of a linear gyrokinetic eigenmode.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is a normalized velocity-space moment of the gyrocenter perturbed distribution for a linear gyrokinetic eigenmode. The weighting emphasizes particles with large perpendicular kinetic energy and large total speed, while the zeroth-order Bessel factor represents the finite-Larmor-radius gyroaverage of the perturbation at fixed gyrocenter.

For one species and a specified normalization, the moment is commonly written as

$$
M_{\perp E,J_0} = \frac{1}{\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{ref}}} \int J_0(k_\perp \rho)\,\frac{1}{2} m v_\perp^2 v^2\,\delta f(\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $m$ is the species mass, $v_\perp$ is velocity perpendicular to the equilibrium magnetic field, $v^2 = v_\parallel^2 + v_\perp^2$, $k_\perp$ is the perpendicular wavenumber, $\rho$ is the particle Larmor radius, and $J_0$ is the Bessel function of the first kind of order zero. The perturbation $\delta f$ has units of number density per velocity-space volume, $\mathrm{m}^{-3}(\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1})^{-3}$, and $d^3v$ has units $(\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1})^3$. The reference factor $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{ref}}$ has the same units as the unnormalized integral; a common gyrokinetic choice is $n_{\mathrm{ref}} T_{\mathrm{ref}} v_{\mathrm{ref}}^2$, with $n_{\mathrm{ref}}$ in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, $T_{\mathrm{ref}}$ expressed as energy per particle in joules, and $v_{\mathrm{ref}}$ in $\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$.

In practice this moment is computed by velocity-space quadrature of the eigenmode distribution function, using the local value of $k_\perp \rho$ for the species and wavevector of interest. For linear eigenmodes, $\delta f$ and therefore $M_{\perp E,J_0}$ are generally complex amplitudes; the kernel is real, but the eigenfunction phase is arbitrary, so magnitudes, phases relative to other moments, and ratios are usually more meaningful than an absolute sign.

Typical dimensionless magnitudes depend strongly on the eigenmode normalization. With a Maxwellian-sized perturbation and normalization by $n_{\mathrm{ref}} T_{\mathrm{ref}} v_{\mathrm{ref}}^2$, values are commonly of order 0.1-10; finite-Larmor-radius averaging can reduce the magnitude through cancelation when $k_\perp \rho$ is not small. If the eigenfunction is normalized so that $|\delta f|/f_0$ is 10^-4-10^-2, the moment scales linearly and typically lies in the same 10^-4-10^-2 fraction of its calibration value.

NAMES.name: perpendicular_normalized_gyrocenter_gyroaveraged_pressure
NAMES.subject: gyrocenter
NAMES.short: Dimensionless perpendicular pressure moment of the perturbed gyrocenter distribution, weighted by the zeroth-order Bessel gyroaverage and normalized to a positive reference thermal pressure. It represents the gyrotropic perpendicular thermal response of a linear gyrokinetic eigenmode.
NAMES.long:
Perpendicular normalized gyrocenter gyroaveraged pressure is the perpendicular kinetic-energy moment of the perturbed gyrocenter distribution after zeroth-order finite-Larmor-radius gyroaveraging. It measures the gyrotropic perpendicular thermal part of a linear gyrokinetic perturbation, normalized to a positive reference thermal pressure. It excludes nongyrotropic stress, off-diagonal viscous response, and heat-flux moments.

A common defining velocity-space moment is

$$
\tilde{p}_{\perp,\mathrm{gc}}^{J_0} = \frac{1}{p_\mathrm{ref}} \int \frac{m v_\perp^2}{2}\, J_0(k_\perp \rho_L)\, \delta f_\mathrm{g}(\mathbf{v})\, d^3v
$$

where $m$ is the species mass in kg, $v_\perp$ is the speed perpendicular to the background magnetic field in m s$^{-1}$, $J_0$ is the zeroth-order Bessel function, $k_\perp$ is the perpendicular wavenumber in m$^{-1}$, $\rho_L = v_\perp/|\Omega_c|$ is the Larmor radius in meters, $\delta f_\mathrm{g}$ is the perturbed gyrocenter distribution function with units such that $\delta f_\mathrm{g} d^3v$ gives a perturbed number density, and $p_\mathrm{ref} > 0$ is the reference species thermal pressure in Pa. The numerator has pressure units, so the normalized moment is dimensionless.

In practice this quantity is computed from the linear gyrokinetic eigenfunction by integrating the perturbed gyrocenter distribution over velocity space at the specified perpendicular scale. For $k_\perp \rho_L \ll 1$, $J_0 \approx 1$ and the moment approaches the ungyroaveraged perpendicular pressure perturbation; at finite $k_\perp \rho_L$, the Bessel weighting represents finite-Larmor-radius cancelation from gyromotion. Together with the parallel gyroaveraged pressure companion it describes the gyrotropic diagonal pressure response, but not the full pressure tensor.

Because the absolute amplitude and phase of a linear eigenmode are set by the chosen eigenfunction normalization, this dimensionless moment has no universal range. With common thermal-pressure normalization and order-unity eigenfunction amplitudes, absolute values are often about $10^{-3}$-$1$, can be much smaller for weakly participating species, and may reach order $1$-$10$ for strongly compressive or resonant kinetic responses. Ratios and relative phases with density, temperature, and parallel-pressure moments in the same eigenmode are usually the physically meaningful comparisons.

NAMES.name: perpendicular_normalized_gyrocenter_perturbed_pressure
NAMES.subject: gyrocenter
NAMES.short: Dimensionless perpendicular gyrotropic pressure moment of the perturbed gyrocenter distribution function for a linear gyrokinetic eigenmode, normalized to a reference thermal pressure.
NAMES.long:
The perpendicular normalized gyrocenter perturbed pressure is the second velocity-space moment of the perturbed gyrocenter distribution function $\delta f_s$, integrated with the perpendicular kinetic-energy weight and normalized by a reference thermal pressure $p_{\mathrm{ref}} = n_{\mathrm{ref}} T_{\mathrm{ref}}$. It characterizes the perturbation to the gyrotropic pressure component in the plane orthogonal to the background magnetic field $\mathbf{B}_0$ for a given linear gyrokinetic eigenmode.

The defining velocity-space integral is:

$$
\delta \tilde{p}_{\perp} = \frac{1}{p_{\mathrm{ref}}} \int \frac{m_s v_{\perp}^2}{2} \, \delta f_s \, d^3v
$$

where $m_s$ is the particle mass, $v_{\perp}$ is the gyrocenter speed perpendicular to $\mathbf{B}_0$, and $\delta f_s$ is the perturbed gyrocenter distribution function. The absence of the $J_0(k_{\perp} \rho_s)$ gyroaveraging factor distinguishes this moment from [normalized_perpendicular_gyroaveraged_gyrocenter_perturbed_pressure](name:normalized_perpendicular_gyroaveraged_gyrocenter_perturbed_pressure), where $k_{\perp}$ is the perpendicular wavenumber and $\rho_s$ is the species Larmor radius.

This moment is computed in local delta-f flux-tube gyrokinetic simulations as part of the linear eigenmode structure. It is the second (perpendicular) entry of the ordered component pair in [normalized_gyrocenter_perturbed_pressure](name:normalized_gyrocenter_perturbed_pressure), complementing [parallel_normalized_gyrocenter_perturbed_pressure](name:parallel_normalized_gyrocenter_perturbed_pressure) which carries the parallel component. Together these two moments fully characterize the gyrotropic pressure response of each kinetic species to the eigenmode perturbation.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the perturbed gyrocenter distribution contributes a net increase in perpendicular thermal pressure relative to the local equilibrium value.

NAMES.name: perpendicular_normalized_particle_perturbed_energy
NAMES.subject: particle
NAMES.short: Dimensionless velocity-space moment of the perturbed particle distribution weighted by 0.5 times the species mass, the squared perpendicular speed, and the total speed squared. It measures the perpendicular-speed-weighted kinetic response of a linear gyrokinetic eigenmode relative to the chosen normalization.
NAMES.long:
Perpendicular normalized particle perturbed energy is a dimensionless moment of the perturbed particle distribution for a species in a linear gyrokinetic eigenmode. Its weighting is the total kinetic-energy factor multiplied by squared speed perpendicular to the local magnetic field; it is not the product of perpendicular kinetic energy and total kinetic energy.

The normalized moment may be written as

$$
M_{\perp E,s} = \frac{1}{N_{\perp E,s}} \int \frac{1}{2} m_s v_\perp^2 v^2 \, \delta f_s(\mathbf{v}) \, d^3v
$$

where $m_s$ is the species mass, $v_\perp$ is the particle speed perpendicular to the local magnetic field, $v^2 = v_\parallel^2 + v_\perp^2$ is the total speed squared, $\delta f_s$ is the perturbed particle distribution with units $s^3 m^{-6}$, and $d^3v$ has units $m^3 s^{-3}$. The normalization factor $N_{\perp E,s}$ has units $kg\,m\,s^{-4}$, matching the unnormalized integral, so that $M_{\perp E,s}$ has unit 1.

This quantity is computed from the velocity-space representation of the linear eigenfunction by numerical quadrature over $\delta f_s$. It is mainly used to compare how strongly different species or modes populate high-perpendicular-speed parts of velocity space, relative to the selected eigenmode normalization.

No device-independent numerical range is physically meaningful for this normalized moment. A linear eigenmode can be multiplied by an arbitrary real or complex amplitude, and this moment scales by the same factor; therefore only comparisons made with the same normalization and eigenfunction phase convention are physically meaningful.

NAMES.name: perpendicular_normalized_particle_perturbed_pressure
NAMES.subject: particle
NAMES.short: Dimensionless perpendicular-pressure moment of the perturbed particle distribution of a linear gyrokinetic eigenmode, normalized by a reference thermal pressure. It is the second velocity-space moment in perpendicular kinetic energy of the perturbed distribution rather than an independent thermodynamic pressure.
NAMES.long:
Perpendicular normalized particle perturbed pressure is the dimensionless perpendicular-pressure moment of the perturbed particle distribution function for a linear gyrokinetic eigenmode. It measures the fluctuating perpendicular thermal energy density carried by the perturbed distribution, expressed in particle (laboratory) velocity variables and scaled by a reference thermal pressure. It is a velocity-space moment of the perturbation, not an independent thermodynamic state variable.

For species $s$, the normalized perpendicular pressure moment is

$$
\delta \hat{p}^{\mathrm{particle}}_{\perp s} = \frac{1}{n_{\mathrm{ref}} T_{\mathrm{ref}}} \int \frac{m_s v_\perp^2}{2}\, \delta f^{\mathrm{particle}}_s(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v},t)\, d^3v
$$

where $m_s$ is the particle mass in kg, $v_\perp$ is the speed perpendicular to the equilibrium magnetic field in m s$^{-1}$, $\delta f^{\mathrm{particle}}_s$ is the perturbed particle distribution in units m$^{-3}$ (m s$^{-1}$)$^{-3}$, and the velocity-space element $d^3v$ has units (m s$^{-1}$)$^3$. The reference density $n_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is in m$^{-3}$ and the reference temperature $T_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is an energy per particle in J; a temperature given in eV must be multiplied by the elementary charge before forming the reference pressure $n_{\mathrm{ref}} T_{\mathrm{ref}}$.

The perpendicular and parallel particle pressure moments combine into the total particle pressure moment of the eigenmode. With the perpendicular component counting the two degrees of freedom orthogonal to $\mathbf{B}$ and the parallel component the single field-aligned degree of freedom, the trace-weighted combination $\delta \hat{p}^{\mathrm{particle}}_s = (2\,\delta \hat{p}^{\mathrm{particle}}_{\perp s} + \delta \hat{p}^{\mathrm{particle}}_{\parallel s})/3$ recovers [normalized_total_perturbed_particle_pressure_of_gyrokinetic_eigenmode](name:normalized_total_perturbed_particle_pressure_of_gyrokinetic_eigenmode), where $\delta \hat{p}^{\mathrm{particle}}_{\parallel s}$ is [parallel_normalized_particle_perturbed_pressure](name:parallel_normalized_particle_perturbed_pressure). The difference between this particle-frame moment and its gyrocenter counterpart [perpendicular_normalized_gyrocenter_perturbed_pressure](name:perpendicular_normalized_gyrocenter_perturbed_pressure) reflects the coordinate transformation between particle and gyrocenter velocity variables.

The moment is obtained by integrating the eigenmode perturbed distribution over velocity space in particle variables; the reference density and temperature defining the normalization are part of the prescribed normalization convention of the calculation. Because a linear eigenmode has an arbitrary overall amplitude, no absolute magnitude range is meaningful: the quantity scales with the chosen eigenfunction normalization and is generally complex.

The complex value carries both magnitude and phase relative to the arbitrary global phase of the eigenmode, which is itself set by the eigenfunction normalization convention. Only relative magnitudes and phase differences between moments of the same eigenmode are physically meaningful; the sign of the real part by itself is not an invariant quantity.

NAMES.name: perpendicular_normalized_perturbed_pressure_bessel_1
NAMES.short: Dimensionless perpendicular pressure moment of the perturbed gyrocenter distribution for a linear gyrokinetic eigenmode, weighted by the first-order Bessel function J1 of the gyroaveraging argument. It is the Bessel-1 counterpart of the normalized perpendicular gyrocenter pressure perturbation.
NAMES.long:
The perpendicular normalized perturbed pressure Bessel-1 moment is the perpendicular kinetic-energy moment of the perturbed gyrocenter distribution weighted by $J_1$. It represents the finite-Larmor-radius part of the perpendicular pressure response of a linear gyrokinetic eigenmode and is generally a complex eigenfunction amplitude.

The normalized moment is defined by

$$
\hat{\delta p}_{\perp,J_1} = \frac{1}{n_\mathrm{ref} T_\mathrm{ref}} \int_{\mathbb{R}^3} \frac{m v_\perp^2}{2}\, J_1\!\left(k_\perp \rho(v_\perp)\right)\, \delta f_\mathrm{gc}(\mathbf{v})\, d^3v
$$

where $\hat{\delta p}_{\perp,J_1}$ is dimensionless, $n_\mathrm{ref}$ is the reference density in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, and $T_\mathrm{ref}$ is the reference particle energy so that $n_\mathrm{ref}T_\mathrm{ref}$ is a reference pressure. Here $m$ is the species mass in kg, $v_\perp$ is the speed perpendicular to the background magnetic field in $\mathrm{m\,s}^{-1}$, $J_1$ is the dimensionless first-order Bessel function, $k_\perp$ is the perpendicular wave-number magnitude in $\mathrm{m}^{-1}$, and $\rho(v_\perp)=v_\perp/|\Omega|$ is the velocity-dependent gyroradius in meters for cyclotron angular frequency $\Omega$ in $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$. The perturbed gyrocenter distribution $\delta f_\mathrm{gc}$ has units $\mathrm{s}^3\,\mathrm{m}^{-6}$, and the velocity-space measure $d^3v$ has units $\mathrm{m}^3\,\mathrm{s}^{-3}$; using velocity variables $(v_\parallel,v_\perp,\alpha)$, $d^3v = v_\perp\,dv_\perp\,d\alpha\,dv_\parallel$, with $v_\parallel$ the velocity along the background magnetic field and $\alpha$ the gyroangle.

This quantity is computed from the eigenmode distribution function by carrying out the velocity-space moment for each species and wave vector. It is not a directly measured thermodynamic pressure; experimental fluctuation measurements may constrain related density, temperature, or field perturbations, while this gyrocenter moment is obtained through gyrokinetic interpretation or simulation.

The $J_1$ weighting separates a finite-Larmor-radius contribution from the unweighted or $J_0$-gyroaveraged perpendicular pressure moments, linking it to related quantities such as [perpendicular_normalized_gyrocenter_perturbed_pressure](name:perpendicular_normalized_gyrocenter_perturbed_pressure) and [perpendicular_normalized_gyrocenter_gyroaveraged_pressure](name:perpendicular_normalized_gyrocenter_gyroaveraged_pressure). The complementary parallel contribution is [parallel_normalized_perturbed_pressure_bessel_1](name:parallel_normalized_perturbed_pressure_bessel_1), and their combination gives the corresponding total Bessel-1 pressure moment.

There is no normalization-independent typical magnitude for a linear eigenmode, because multiplying the eigenfunction by any nonzero complex constant rescales this moment. Values are therefore interpreted as relative complex amplitudes only after the eigenmode amplitude and phase have been fixed by the chosen normalization.
NAMES.sign: Positive when, after the eigenmode phase has been fixed by the selected reference perturbation, the Bessel-weighted excess of perpendicular gyrocenter kinetic energy in the defining velocity-space integral is positive.

NAMES.name: radial_derivative_of_elongation_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short: Radial rate of change of the flux surface elongation kappa with respect to normalized minor radius, measuring how rapidly the poloidal cross-section aspect ratio varies across nested flux surfaces.
NAMES.long:
The radial derivative of flux surface elongation quantifies how the vertical-to-horizontal shape of nested toroidal magnetic surfaces changes as a function of radial position. The flux surface elongation $\kappa$ equals the ratio of the vertical to horizontal semi-axis of the poloidal cross-section, so its radial derivative captures the rate at which flux surfaces become more (or less) vertically elongated moving outward from the magnetic axis.

The quantity is defined as:

$$
\frac{d\kappa}{d\hat{r}}
$$

where $\kappa$ is the [elongation of the flux surface](name:elongation_of_flux_surface) and $\hat{r}$ is the normalized minor radius running from 0 at the magnetic axis to 1 at the plasma boundary. Both $\kappa$ and $\hat{r}$ are dimensionless, so the derivative is also dimensionless.

This derivative is a required geometric input to local gyrokinetic flux-tube simulations, entering the metric coefficients that govern field-line curvature and grad-$B$ drift terms within the flux-tube domain. It belongs to the broader family of radial flux surface shape coefficient derivatives that also includes the [radial derivative of flux surface shape coefficient](name:radial_derivative_of_elongation_of_flux_surface). In plasmas with significant edge shaping, this quantity grows in magnitude toward the separatrix, while remaining near zero for nearly circular flux surfaces where $\kappa \approx 1$ throughout the minor radius.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the elongation $\kappa$ increases with increasing normalized minor radius $\hat{r}$, corresponding to flux surfaces that become more vertically elongated toward the plasma boundary.
